Company promotion must stay within the package insert
Rofecoxib was approved for acute pain for up to 5 days but was widely prescribed off-label for chronic pain
The high dose (50 mg/day) was linked to a 5-fold increase in myocardial infarction risk

front: What do randomisation and blinding each control, and how are the common trial designs compared?
back: Randomisation (including stratified randomisation by age, sex or severity) balances known and unknown confounders and prevents selection bias. Blinding hides allocation: single-blind keeps the subject unaware, double-blind keeps subject and investigator unaware, with the code held by a third party. Designs: parallel group (test and control run together) versus crossover (each subject is own control, smaller sample, but carry-over effect and only suited to stable chronic disease); sequential and multicentric designs speed results; non-inferiority trials show the new drug is not worse.

front: How are type I error, type II error, power and sample size related in a trial?
back: Type I error is finding a difference that does not exist (its probability is the significance level, e.g. 0.05). Type II error is missing a real difference; power is its complement, so power 0.9 means a 10% chance of missing it. Sample size is calculated from significance level, power, the clinically significant difference and the variability of the end point; a smaller expected difference or greater variation needs more subjects.

front: Essay: Clinical trial design and control of bias

points: Answer precisely framed questions by comparing equivalent groups treated by two or more modalities
Healthy volunteers for PK and tolerability; patients for most efficacy questions
Approval by an independent ethics committee; Good Clinical Practice (ICH) guidelines
National ethical guidelines (ICMR in India); Declaration of Helsinki
Written informed consent
Principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice
Control group: placebo (if ethical) or standard treatment (active control)
Parallel group vs cross-over (subjects as own controls; carry-over effects; only for stable chronic diseases)
Inclusion/exclusion criteria, dose regimen and sample size fixed in advance
Superiority or non-inferiority aims
Randomisation (simple or stratified by age, sex, severity)
Blinding: single or double; allocation code held by a third party
Pre-specified end points and statistical plan
Type I (alpha) error: false difference; type II (beta) error: missed real difference
Results apply only to the population and dose regimen studied; dose-ranging needs separate trials

front: A new drug passes phase III but a rare serious adverse effect appears after marketing. Why was it missed and how is it found?
back: Phase III enrols only 500-3000 selected patients for limited periods, so very rare reactions, delayed effects and effects in children, elderly or pregnant patients stay invisible. Phase IV postmarketing surveillance in large unselected populations detects them. A cohort study (users versus non-users) can reveal unsuspected adverse events; a case-control study tests a suspected link by comparing affected patients with matched controls for past exposure.

front: How should the dose of a renally excreted drug be altered in renal impairment?
back: Loading dose is generally kept unchanged (unless oedema is present). The maintenance dose is reduced in proportion to creatinine clearance, or the dosing interval is lengthened. Examples: aminoglycosides, digoxin, phenobarbitone. Drugs partly excreted unchanged need smaller reductions.

front: Why must a dose always be stated with the response it is meant to produce?
back: A drug has different effective doses for different effects, and prophylactic, therapeutic and toxic doses of the same drug differ. Example: aspirin 0.3-0.6 g for headache, 60-150 mg/day for antiplatelet action, 3-5 g/day for rheumatoid arthritis. Recommended doses come from population data for an average patient, so individual patients need adjustment.

front: What is cumulation and which drugs are particularly prone to it?
back: Any drug accumulates when the rate of administration exceeds the rate of elimination; slowly eliminated drugs are most liable and cause cumulative toxicity (chloroquine retinal damage on prolonged use). Practical rules: do not give a full digoxin loading dose if one was taken in the past week, and do not repeat an emetine course within 6 weeks.

front: What is rational prescribing and what are its criteria?
back: WHO: patients get medicines suited to their clinical need, in individual doses, for adequate time, at lowest cost to them and the community. Criteria: appropriate indication, appropriate drug (efficacy, safety, suitability, cost), appropriate dose, route and duration, an appropriate patient, correct dispensing with information, and monitoring of adherence, benefit and adverse effects. Knowing the drug alone does not make prescribing rational.

front: What are the strategies for individualising drug dose, and which fits which drug?
back: Four strategies. 1) Standard dose: one dose suits nearly everyone because variation is small or the safety margin is wide (penicillin, oral contraceptives, chloroquine). 2) Regulated dose: the drug modifies an easily measured body function, so dose is adjusted to that reading (antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics, anticoagulants, diuretics); plasma levels are not needed. 3) Target-level dose: response is hard to measure but tied to a plasma range, so an empirical dose is later adjusted by drug-level monitoring (digoxin, antiepileptics, antidepressants, theophylline). 4) Titrated dose: the full effect cannot be given because of adverse effects, so dose is titrated to a tolerable level of toxicity (anticancer drugs, corticosteroids, levodopa).

Synergy: sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim, levodopa with carbidopa, isoniazid with rifampin
Components with different mechanisms (amlodipine with atenolol) add effect without adding the same side effects
Avoids giving one drug alone in TB, HIV and falciparum malaria
Patient may not need every component; dose of each cannot be adjusted separately
Components may have different time courses and be differently affected by kidney or liver disease
Hard to tell which drug caused an adverse effect; allergy to one component bars the whole product
Fosters false confidence, especially with antimicrobial combinations; corticosteroids should never be combined with other internal-use drugs
Only a handful of FDCs are rational
Each ingredient must be needed; never justified to give an unneeded drug to supply another
Many irrational FDCs have been banned in India
Drug response depends on the time of administration, which is linked to the body's circadian rhythm
Circadian control extends to hormone release (GH, prolactin, ACTH)

A single morning corticosteroid dose causes less pituitary-adrenal suppression
Hypnotics work more easily when taken at night
Quick-release bromocriptine, taken early in the morning, is used in type 2 diabetes
Pineal hormone secreted at night that synchronises the sleep-wake cycle
Used mainly for jet lag and shift work; not a dependable hypnotic

front: How do you choose between titrated and target-level dosing for a drug?
back: Ask what can be measured. If response is hard to measure but a plasma range is known to work (digoxin, antiepileptics, theophylline), aim at the target level and adjust by monitoring. If the maximal effect cannot be given because of toxicity (anticancer drugs, corticosteroids, levodopa), titrate to a tolerable level of adverse effect: low start and upward titration in non-critical illness, high start and downward titration in critical illness.

Monitor adherence, goal attainment and adverse events; modify therapy

Wrong drug, wrong route (injection when oral works), wrong dose or duration

points: First-pass bioavailability rises; albumin falls so more free acidic drug
Metabolism of morphine, lidocaine, propranolol falls: reduce dose
Prefer oxazepam, lorazepam, atenolol; prodrugs needing activation work poorly
Reduce maintenance dose or lengthen interval with creatinine clearance; loading dose usually unchanged
Examples: aminoglycosides, digoxin, phenobarbitone
Avoid pethidine, nephrotoxic drugs; thiazides fail, use furosemide
Absorption falls, elimination slows; lower loading doses of lidocaine, procainamide; digitalis sensitivity rises
Hypothyroid: more sensitive to digoxin and morphine; hyperthyroid: resistant to digoxin inotropy

front: Essay: Factors that modify drug response and how to individualise therapy

points: Variation between patients and within the same patient
Changes can be quantitative (concentration/effect) or qualitative (allergy, idiosyncrasy)
Body size, age, sex and pregnancy
Genetics (pharmacogenetics)
Disease states: renal, hepatic, cardiac, thyroid
Tolerance, cumulation and drug interactions
Route of administration and formulation
Timing relative to meals and circadian factors
Placebo and nocebo responses
Enzyme inducers from diet or smoking
Choose drug and dose according to the factors above
Start with a standard or target-level dose, then adjust by response or drug levels
Monitor and document response in the individual

front: Why is body weight or body surface area used for dosing in children and very obese or lean adults?
back: Adult doses assume a medium build. Paediatric and atypical-build doses are scaled to body weight (weight / 70 x adult dose). BSA is physiologically closer to water and metabolic mass but has limited dosing data, so weight is the usual index (BSA is used mainly for anticancer drugs). Dubois: BSA = 0.007184 x W^0.425 x H^0.725.

front: Why do newborns clear renally excreted drugs slowly?
back: Newborn GFR is low and tubular transport immature, so half-life of drugs excreted by filtration (gentamicin) or secretion (penicillin) is prolonged 3-5 times. GFR reaches adult rates by about 5 months and tubular secretion matures by about 7 months. Hepatic metabolism is also inadequate, and the blood-brain barrier is more permeable (kernicterus). Infant doses must be learned, not derived by formula.

front: Why must doses of renally cleared drugs be cut in the elderly?
back: Nephron loss lowers GFR to about 75% of the young-adult value at 50 years and about 50% at 75 years, so such drugs accumulate. Example: streptomycin 0.75 g daily after 50 years and 0.5 g after 70, against 1 g in young adults. Reduced liver metabolism and blood flow add to cumulative toxicity on prolonged use.

front: Which adverse effects are special to children?
back: Growing tissue is vulnerable: corticosteroids suppress growth; androgens cause early epiphyseal fusion and stunting; tetracyclines deposit in growing teeth, discolouring and deforming them; phenothiazines cause dystonic reactions more often. Solid dosage forms and metered inhalers are hard for young children, while rectal diazepam solution (fast, predictable absorption) controls febrile seizures under 5 years.

front: Why is chloramphenicol dangerous in neonates (grey baby syndrome)?
back: Neonatal hepatic conjugation (glucuronidation) is immature, so the drug accumulates. Result: abdominal distension, vasomotor collapse, cyanosis and grey skin. Also, the newborn has low GFR and immature tubular function, which prolongs half-life of renally cleared drugs.

front: Short note: Dose adjustment in children and the elderly

points: Dose by body weight; infant absorption and skin permeability differ
Immature renal function prolongs elimination of renally cleared drugs
Grey baby syndrome with chloramphenicol
Faster metabolism after infancy: shorter half-life, higher mg/kg dose
Falling GFR with age; reduce renally cleared drugs
Reduced hepatic metabolism and liver blood flow; risk of cumulative toxicity
Lower albumin: changed protein binding
Higher sensitivity to CNS and anticholinergic effects; more drug interactions (polypharmacy)

front: How does pregnancy change drug disposition?
back: Reduced GI motility delays absorption; plasma and extracellular fluid expand, raising volume of distribution; albumin falls while alpha-1 acid glycoprotein rises, so unbound acidic drugs rise and basic ones fall; renal blood flow rises, speeding polar drug removal; hepatic enzyme induction speeds metabolism. The net effect is complex and hard to predict.

front: Why are adverse reactions commoner in the elderly, and how do you prescribe safely for them?
back: Cause chain: lower GFR and hepatic clearance cause accumulation; lower albumin raises free drug; volume of distribution shifts (up for lipophilic, down for hydrophilic drugs); receptor responsiveness changes (digitalis poorly tolerated, adrenergic responses reduced); prostatism makes even mild anticholinergic action cause retention; polypharmacy multiplies interactions and brings postural instability, giddiness and confusion. Safe practice: reduce renally cleared doses, review the drug list and monitor.

front: What is the pharmacogenetic risk with TPMT deficiency?
back: Low thiopurine methyltransferase activity raises the risk of severe bone marrow toxicity with 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine. Poor-metaboliser status for NUDT15 has the same effect; TPMT poor metabolisers are rare in East Asians, who instead more often carry NUDT15 variants.

front: Pharmacogenetic examples (drug, gene or enzyme, consequence)
text: G6PD deficiency: {{primaquine}} haemolysis; TPMT deficiency: {{azathioprine}} marrow toxicity; CYP2D6 poor metaboliser: {{codeine}} fails to give analgesia; CYP2C9 variant: {{warfarin}} bleeding; NAT2 slow acetylator: {{isoniazid}} neuropathy.

back: Pharmacogenetics: study of the genetic basis of variable drug response and handling. Pharmacogenomics: use of genetic information to choose drug and dose for an individual (personalised medicine). SNP: single base-pair substitution found in more than 1% of a population. Most drugs show bell-shaped (Gaussian) variation, with specific genetic defects adding discontinuous variation.

front: What is the clinical effect of slow acetylator status (NAT2)?
back: NAT2 polymorphism creates rapid and slow acetylators. Slow acetylators accumulate drugs cleared by acetylation, so isoniazid neuropathy and procainamide- or hydralazine-induced lupus occur mainly in them.

front: Which drugs are classically linked to haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, and how is the trait inherited?
back: X-linked monogenic trait, commoner in Mediterranean, African and Southeast Asian people. Oxidising drugs trigger haemolysis, e.g. primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides/cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, chloramphenicol, quinine, methylene blue. Haemolysis is largely dose-related, and its severity varies with the gene variant (worst in homozygous deficient individuals).

front: Why does codeine fail to relieve pain in some patients? (CYP2D6)
back: Codeine is a prodrug: CYP2D6 converts it to morphine, which gives the analgesia. Poor CYP2D6 metabolisers form little morphine, so analgesia is absent. Ultrarapid metabolisers form excess morphine and may develop features of opioid excess, including respiratory depression.

front: Short note: Pharmacogenetics in drug therapy

points: Pharmacogenetics: genetic basis of variable drug response
Pharmacogenomics: use of genetic information to guide choice of drug and dose
Polymorphisms of drug-metabolising enzymes (CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, NAT2, TPMT, pseudocholinesterase)
Variants of drug targets (VKORC1 for warfarin) and transporters (P-gp)
HLA alleles causing immune hypersensitivity; enzyme deficiencies such as G6PD
Succinylcholine apnoea: atypical pseudocholinesterase
Warfarin bleeding and lower dose need: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 variants
Clopidogrel (prodrug) ineffective in CYP2C19 poor metabolisers: use an alternative antiplatelet
Isoniazid neuropathy; hydralazine and procainamide lupus: slow acetylators
Carbamazepine and phenytoin with HLA-B*15:02 (East and South Asians); abacavir with HLA-B*57:01; allopurinol with HLA-B*58:01
Malignant hyperthermia after halothane: ryanodine receptor defect
Monogenic traits predict response well; polygenic traits poorly

front: Which genetic variants predict chemotherapy toxicity or resistance?
back: UGT1A1*28 allele (low glucuronyl transferase) raises irinotecan neutropenia and diarrhoea; DPD (dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase) deficiency causes severe 5-fluorouracil toxicity; TPMT deficiency causes marrow toxicity with 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine; P-glycoprotein overexpression pumps drugs out of tumour cells and causes resistance.

front: Genetic defects that make a drug dangerous
text: Atypical pseudocholinesterase: prolonged {{succinylcholine}} apnoea; abnormal ryanodine receptor: {{halothane}} malignant hyperthermia; acute intermittent porphyria: precipitated by {{barbiturates}}; abnormal VKOR enzyme: resistance to {{coumarin}} anticoagulants; inability to hydroxylate: {{phenytoin}} toxicity at usual doses.

front: Why is routine genotyping to guide drug therapy still limited, and where does it work best?
back: Dose may vary 4-6 fold between people and all determinants of response (transporters, enzymes, channels, receptors) are genetically controlled, yet practice is limited because each drug needs its own genotype screen and much variability is unexplained. Genotype predicts phenotype best for monogenic traits (G6PD, CYP2D6, TPMT), poorly for polygenic ones. Genotyping is needed only once in life; simple spot tests (G6PD) are already used.

front: One patient gets no pain relief from codeine and another develops marrow failure on azathioprine. Explain each.
back: Codeine is a prodrug converted to morphine by CYP2D6; a poor metaboliser forms little morphine, so no analgesia. Azathioprine is cleared by TPMT; deficiency (and NUDT15 variants, which also alter thiopurine metabolite levels) leaves toxic thiopurine levels and marrow toxicity. In both the gene alters drug handling, not receptor action, so genotype-guided drug choice or dose reduction is the remedy.

front: Define placebo and nocebo, and name one placebo use in a trial.
back: Placebo: an inert substance given as if it were active; its effect comes from the therapeutic setting and expectation (psychodynamic). Nocebo: a negative response driven by pessimism or loss of faith in the drug or doctor. A placebo serves as the dummy control in a clinical trial.

front: What is tachyphylaxis and which drugs show it most?
back: Rapid loss of response when doses are repeated closely. It is seen most with indirect sympathomimetics (ephedrine, tyramine, nicotine), which work by releasing catecholamines; the stores are depleted faster than they are refilled.

front: What is tolerance and what are its types?
back: Need for a higher dose to get the same response. Natural: species or individual inherently less sensitive (rabbits to atropine). Acquired: develops with repeated use in an initially responsive person, most evident with CNS depressants. Refractoriness is loss of efficacy after prolonged use (sulfonylureas in type 2 diabetes, agonists in asthma). Little or none develops to atropine, digoxin, cocaine or nitroprusside.

front: What is cross tolerance? Give examples.
back: Tolerance to pharmacologically related drugs; the closer two drugs are, the more complete. Alcoholics tolerate barbiturates and general anaesthetics. Morphine and barbiturates show partial cross tolerance, but morphine and pethidine show complete cross tolerance.

front: What is the difference between pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic tolerance?
back: Pharmacokinetic tolerance: less drug reaches the site, usually because elimination is enhanced, e.g. enzyme induction by barbiturates and carbamazepine. Pharmacodynamic (cellular) tolerance: target cells become less responsive, e.g. morphine, barbiturates, nitrates; due to receptor desensitisation or down-regulation, or weaker response effectuation.

points: Tolerance: a larger dose is needed to produce the same effect
Refractoriness: loss of efficacy after prolonged or intensive use (sulfonylureas in type 2 diabetes; beta-2 agonists in asthma)
Natural: inherent low sensitivity (rabbits to atropine; some people to alcohol)
Acquired: repeated use; obvious with CNS depressants; little or none with atropine, digoxin, cocaine, nitroprusside
Cross tolerance between related drugs (alcoholics to barbiturates and general anaesthetics)
Tachyphylaxis: rapid tolerance on closely repeated doses (ephedrine, tyramine, nicotine)
Pharmacokinetic: enzyme induction, faster elimination
Pharmacodynamic: receptor desensitisation or down-regulation, weaker response effectuation, homeostatic adaptation
Chlorpromazine: to sedation but not antipsychotic action
Phenobarbitone: to sedation more than antiepileptic action
Morphine: to analgesia and euphoria more than to constipation and miosis

front: How does a placebo work, where is it used, and what limits it?
back: It acts through psychodynamic, not pharmacodynamic, means: the whole therapeutic setting and physician-patient relation matter. It can release endorphins (placebo analgesia is blocked by naloxone). Uses: dummy control in trials, and rarely for a patient who needs no active drug. Common placebos are lactose tablets and distilled water injection. Responses vary even in one person (sleep on night one, not later), so practical value is limited; nocebo is the negative counterpart.

front: Tolerance does not develop equally to all effects of a drug. What follows for therapy?
back: The therapeutic index may rise or fall with prolonged use. Chlorpromazine: tolerance to sedation but not antipsychotic action (index improves). Phenobarbitone: tolerance to sedation, less to antiepileptic action. Morphine: tolerance to analgesia and euphoria, little to constipation and miosis (index worsens). So dose escalation can raise toxicity without matching benefit.

front: Compare tolerance, tachyphylaxis, refractoriness and drug resistance.
back: Tolerance: gradual need for higher dose, by pharmacokinetic (induced elimination, e.g. carbamazepine) or pharmacodynamic (receptor desensitisation or down-regulation) mechanisms. Tachyphylaxis: rapid tolerance on closely repeated doses, typical of indirect sympathomimetics (ephedrine, tyramine, nicotine) whose catecholamine stores deplete. Refractoriness: loss of efficacy after prolonged intensive use. Drug resistance: tolerance of microorganisms to antimicrobials (staphylococci to penicillin).

front: Essay: Comprehensive plan for drug development to meet an unmet need: diabetes mellitus

points: Type 2 diabetes is over 90% of cases; insulin resistance plus beta-cell failure
Existing agents: insulin needs multiple daily injections, hypoglycaemia and weight gain
Many patients cannot reach normoglycaemia; concern about hyperinsulinaemia and premature atherosclerosis
Rational approach: choose a target (insulin resistance, insulin secretion, incretin or glucose handling) and find a lead that binds it
Lead sources: natural products, lead optimisation of congeners, combinatorial chemistry with high-throughput screening (high failure rate), biotechnology (recombinant insulin, monoclonal antibodies)
Screening and pharmacodynamic tests; hypoglycaemic activity in animal models
Pharmacokinetics and acute, subacute and chronic toxicity in a rodent and a non-rodent
Reproductive toxicity, mutagenicity and carcinogenicity studies before human use
IND licence, then Phase I (safety, PK), Phase II (dose range, efficacy), Phase III (randomised, double-blind, comparative, larger population)
Surrogate endpoints such as HbA1c shorten trials; FDA expects cardiovascular safety data (rosiglitazone precedent)
Marketing permission follows Phase III, with indications finalised; drugs may be restricted to hospitals or specialists
Phase IV surveillance for rare and long-term adverse effects and interactions
Trials in special groups (children, elderly, renal impairment) and new formulations or combinations

front: What are the main limitations of current drugs in type 2 diabetes?
back: Insulin needs multiple daily injections and can cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain. Sulfonylureas, biguanides, thiazolidinediones and the others, apart from DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists, share these problems and often fail to achieve normoglycaemia alone. Insulin excess is also linked to premature atherosclerosis. These gaps define the unmet need.

front: What is a surrogate endpoint and why is it used in premarketing trials?
back: A biomarker or other measure believed to mediate or predict the true clinical endpoint (survival, disease prevention, symptoms, function). It shortens or shrinks trials. Examples: blood pressure, lipid levels, HbA1c and CD4 count. Some are excellent predictors (HIV RNA load), others have misled.

front: Why did the FDA require larger cardiovascular safety data for new antidiabetic drugs?
back: Rosiglitazone was approved in 1999 on short-term glycaemic trials. A 2007 meta-analysis of randomised trials then linked it to more myocardial infarctions. The FDA responded by asking that new antidiabetic trials exclude a cardiovascular risk increase of 30% or more; a two-stage route allowed premarketing trials to exclude 80% with postmarketing studies completing the 30% margin.

front: Short note: Integrated approach in pharmacotherapy

points: Rational prescribing is a whole therapeutic set-up, not only choosing the right drug
Knowledge alone does not guarantee rational use: role models, patient load and drug promotion also shape prescribing
Diagnose (at least provisionally), define the problem and goal
Choose the class, then the drug on efficacy, safety, suitability and cost
Decide route, dose and duration; instruct the patient
Monitor adherence, goal attainment and adverse effects; modify therapy
Body size, age (neonatal and elderly clearance), sex, race, genetics
Pathological states: renal, hepatic, cardiac and thyroid disease alter disposition or sensitivity
Other drugs, cumulation and tolerance
Drug when none is needed; wrong drug, route, dose or duration
Needless combinations and polypharmacy without regard to interactions

front: Which patient-related factors change the response to the same drug dose?
back: Body size (weight or body surface area), age, sex, species and race, genetic make-up, route, environment and timing relative to meals, psychological expectation, disease states, other drugs, cumulation and tolerance. These act quantitatively (plasma level or effect changes, adjusted by dose) or qualitatively (allergy or idiosyncrasy).

front: Short note: Biomarkers in clinical evaluation of drugs

points: A measurable indicator that anticipates a therapeutic or adverse response to a drug
Surrogates are biomarkers used as stand-ins for the real clinical outcome
Genetic markers: G-6PD deficiency (spot test), CYP2D6, TPMT and NAT2 polymorphisms
Disease or response markers: HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids, CD4 count, HIV RNA load
Monitoring markers that show progress or failure of treatment
Reduce the size and duration of premarketing trials
Expedited programmes such as Accelerated Approval can rest on surrogate endpoints
Some surrogates predict outcome well, others mislead
A drug can alter the marker without changing survival or symptoms
Genotype testing is limited by the need for drug-specific screening

front: Define a biomarker and say how it differs from a surrogate endpoint.
back: A biomarker is any measurable marker (genetic, biochemical or imaging) that predicts or tracks drug response, therapeutic or adverse. A surrogate endpoint is a biomarker chosen to replace the clinical endpoint in a trial, so it must reliably predict that endpoint.

front: Why is G-6PD status a useful pre-treatment biomarker?
back: G-6PD deficiency is an X-linked monogenic trait. Oxidant drugs such as primaquine, dapsone and sulfonamides cause haemolysis in deficient people, and the risk depends on the variant. A simple spot test identifies deficiency before the drug is given, which makes it a practical clinical biomarker.

front: Short note: Features of an ideal randomised clinical trial

points: Precise, pre-specified objective with primary and secondary end points fixed in advance
Population set by inclusion and exclusion criteria; results apply only to that population
Control arm is the comparator against which the test drug is judged
Randomised allocation; stratify by age, sex or disease severity where needed
Single blind (subject unaware) or double blind (subject and investigator unaware)
Look-alike preparations; allocation code held by a third data-management party and opened after analysis
Fixed beforehand from significance level, power, the clinically meaningful difference and variability of the end point
Minimum number that still gives a decisive answer, for cost and ethical reasons
Independent committee can stop early on a decisive result or if one arm is clearly inferior

sections.h: Why it is the strongest design
points: Randomised double-blind controlled trial is the most credible source of evidence on efficacy, safety and comparative value

front: Essay: Design and conduct of a 6-month repeated-dose toxicity study for a new drug

points: Characterise the toxicity profile on repeated dosing, identify target organs and the dose-response relation
Find the maximum recommended starting dose for the first human use
Clinical use beyond 3 months needs repeated-dose studies of 6 months in a rodent and in a non-rodent
Regulators may ask for 12 months or accept 6 months case by case
At least one rodent and one non-rodent, chosen on pharmacokinetic similarity to humans
Same route as the intended clinical use; run under Good Laboratory Practice
Highest dose: produces observable toxicity
Intermediate dose: some symptoms but no gross toxicity or death, placed logarithmically between the other two
Lowest dose: no observable toxicity
Cage-side observations, body weight, food and water intake
Blood biochemistry and haematology; renal parameters (urea, creatinine, urine specific gravity)
Non-rodents: electrocardiogram and fundus examination
Gross and microscopic examination of all viscera and tissues; injection sites if given parenterally
Reproduction and teratogenicity; mutagenicity battery (Ames test, in vitro chromosome or mouse lymphoma assay, mouse micronucleus)
Carcinogenicity studies are needed when expected clinical use is about 6 months or longer
Local tolerance at sites of contact

front: Short note: Evaluating the hypersensitivity potential of a new drug

points: Allergic reactions are immune-mediated and not predicted by the drug's pharmacology
Single-dose tests miss them: prior sensitisation is needed and a latent period of 1-2 weeks follows the first exposure
Checks tolerance at every body site the drug touches
Separates mechanical or physicochemical irritation from true toxicological or pharmacodynamic effects
Local lymph node assay: compares lymphocyte proliferation in treated and control groups
Stimulation index of at least 3 is needed before a substance is judged a potential skin sensitiser
Patch tests confirm non-irritancy in people, and are used only after the chemical passes the in vitro non-corrosion and mutagenicity screens
Hypersensitivity findings feed the safety profile and the monitoring plan for trials and marketing

front: What is the local lymph node assay and what result flags a skin sensitiser?
back: An animal test for skin sensitisation that compares lymphocyte proliferation in treated and control groups after topical exposure. A stimulation index of at least 3 means the substance needs further evaluation as a potential skin sensitiser.

A trial that tries to show the new drug is not clinically worse than an existing treatment. Superior efficacy is not required; the new drug may still be useful if it offers better tolerability, safety, convenience, cost or use in a special subgroup.
A measurable characteristic that indicates a normal biological process, a disease process, or the response to an exposure or treatment. It can be molecular, histologic, radiographic or physiologic.

front: What was materia medica, and why could it not become a true science of drug action?
back: Materia medica was the older study of preparing drugs and their medical uses, the forerunner of pharmacology. Real understanding of mechanism was blocked because there were no methods to purify active agents from crude materials and no experimental way to test ideas about how drugs act; therapeutics was governed by authority and dogma rather than experiment.

front: Who first purified morphine from opium, when, and why was this important?
back: Friedrich Serturner, a young German apothecary, in 1805. It showed that a defined chemical, not a vital force, produced the effect of a plant extract, and it opened the era of purifying active plant principles (quinine, digitalis, atropine, ephedrine, strychnine and others).

front: Give four examples of drugs whose use began from human experience with plants.
back: Caffeine (coffee berries, noticed from the behaviour of goats); atropine (Atropa belladonna extract used to dilate the pupils); ephedrine (Chinese herb ma huang, used as a stimulant); curare (used by South American hunters to paralyse prey); morphine (poppy juice, for pain and diarrhoea). Such drugs were chosen for their effect, with no idea of a target.

front: What do Indian Ayurveda and Chinese plant-based systems contribute to new medicines, and what does 'ayurveda' mean?
back: They have a strong philosophical and experiential base, and ayurveda also has an experimental basis. 'Ayurveda' means 'science of life' in Sanskrit. The Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas describe the pharmacological and therapeutic properties of more than 700 plants.

front: Which early synthetic substances became drugs before the era of synthetic chemistry, and which is called the first 'rational' therapeutic drug?
back: Diethyl ether and nitrous oxide (Humphry Davy, 1799) were used socially before becoming anaesthetics in the mid-19th century. Amyl nitrite (made 1859) is called the first rational drug, because its benefit in angina was predicted from its physiological actions. Aspirin was first made in 1853 and commercialised by Bayer in 1899.

front: Contrast how plant drugs like atropine or ephedrine came into use with how amyl nitrite did.
back: Plant drugs were adopted from experience of their effects, with no knowledge of any target; use came first and explanation (if any) later. Amyl nitrite was the reverse: Brunton (1857) gave it by inhalation for angina once its vasodepressor action was known.

front: Trace how the way new drugs are found has changed from antiquity to today.
back: Antiquity: remedies from plants chosen by experience, governed by dogma (materia medica). 19th century: purification of active principles (morphine, 1805) showed that chemicals cause drug effects, and synthetic compounds followed (aspirin, amyl nitrite). 20th century: receptor ideas (Langley, Ehrlich) and target-directed drugs (Black's beta-blocker and H2 antagonist). Since the 1980s: biotechnology products and structure-based design.

front: Who is regarded as the 'father of pharmacology', and which pupils carried his work forward?
back: Oswald Schmiedeberg (late 19th century). With disciples such as J Langley, T Frazer, P Ehrlich, AJ Clark and JJ Abel he laid down several fundamental concepts of pharmacology.

front: Who founded the first institute of pharmacology, and in which year?
back: Rudolf Buchheim, in 1847, which marked the start of pharmacology as an experimental science. KDT places it in Germany; Rang & Dale say it was set up in his own house in Estonia.

front: Which two physiologists pioneered animal experiments and applied them to the study of drugs?
back: Francois Magendie and his student Claude Bernard (late 18th to 19th century). They developed the methods of experimental physiology and adapted them to study the effects of drugs.

front: Who is called the 'father of Indian pharmacology', and where was India's first pharmacology research centre set up?
back: Sir Ram Nath Chopra. He established the first centre for study and research in pharmacology in India, at the Calcutta School of Tropical Medicine. He held the chair titled Professor of Pharmacology including Indigenous Drugs.

front: Name three pharmacologists from industry who made landmark discoveries, with their contributions.
back: Henry Dale: foundations of chemical transmission and the autonomic nervous system. George Hitchings and Gertrude Elion: the antimetabolite principle and the first effective anticancer drugs. James Black: the first beta-adrenoceptor and histamine H2-receptor antagonists.

front: What is reverse pharmacology, and what did Gananath Sen and Kartik Bose show in 1931?
back: Reverse pharmacology starts from the clinically documented effects of a traditional remedy and then moves to laboratory study, the reverse of the usual laboratory-to-clinic route. Chopra and Sen introduced the concept for Ayurvedic drugs in India. In 1931 Sen and Bose showed that Rauwolfia serpentina had antihypertensive and tranquillising effects.

points: Plant remedies from antiquity: opium, belladonna, ma huang, curare
Materia medica guided by dogma; no purification or experimental testing
Magendie and Claude Bernard: animal experiments applied to drugs
Serturner purifies morphine (1805)
Buchheim founds first pharmacology institute (1847)
Schmiedeberg, 'father of pharmacology', and pupils (Langley, Ehrlich, Clark, Abel)
Amyl nitrite (1859) and aspirin (Bayer, 1899)
Ehrlich's receptor idea and arsphenamine for syphilis
Domagk's prontosil (1935); penicillin by Chain and Florey
Langley's receptor concept (1905), developed by Clark, Gaddum, Schild
Discovery of hormones, transmitters, mediators; rise of biochemistry
Sulfanilamide deaths: 1938 safety law
Thalidomide: efficacy and teratogenicity testing (1962)
Receptor purification and cloning from the 1970s; orphan receptors
Biopharmaceuticals since the 1980s; gene and cell therapy
Computer-aided design: drugs now invented rather than discovered

front: Who discovered the first clinically useful sulfonamide, and what did it start?
back: Gerhard Domagk (1935) showed that the dye prontosil was dramatically effective against streptococcal infection. This launched the era of antibacterial chemotherapy, later expanded by penicillin (Fleming's work developed by Chain and Florey during the Second World War).

front: Who first proposed the receptor concept, and who developed it further?
back: Langley proposed receptors for chemical mediators in 1905. The idea was taken up by Clark, Gaddum, Schild and others and remains central to drug discovery and therapeutics.

front: What are biopharmaceuticals, and since when have they become a major source of drugs?
back: Since the 1980s, biotechnology has supplied antibodies, enzymes and regulatory proteins (hormones, growth factors, cytokines), mostly made by genetic engineering. The pharmacological principles are the same as for small molecules, but absorption, distribution, elimination, specificity, toxicity and cost differ greatly. Gene- and cell-based therapies are the next step.

front: How did Paul Ehrlich's work on dyes lead to chemotherapy?
back: Selective staining of tissues by dyes led Ehrlich to propose chemical receptors that 'fixed' the dye, and that microbes might carry unique receptors so a chemical could kill them while sparing host tissue. This produced arsphenamine (salvarsan), an organic arsenical for syphilis (GG14 dates the invention to 1907), used until penicillin arrived.

front: How did receptors change from theoretical entities to molecules that could be studied?
back: In the 1970s receptor-labelling methods allowed receptors to be extracted and purified. Partial amino-acid sequences then allowed cloning; later, expression cloning and genome-based homology cloning identified several hundred receptors. Cloning revealed many subtypes and 'orphan receptors' whose natural ligand is unknown.

front: Why does GG14 argue that modern drugs are 'invented' rather than 'discovered'?
back: Only a fraction of new drugs now come from nature. Most are new compounds optimised against many criteria through repeated cycles of design and experiment (medicinal chemistry, high-throughput screening, structure-based and computer-aided design), so they are created rather than found.

text: The Pure Food and Drug Act ({{1906}}) banned mislabelling and adulteration; the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act ({{1938}}) required proof of {{safety}}; the {{Kefauver-Harris}} Amendments (1962) added proof of {{efficacy}}; the {{Orphan Drug}} Amendment (1983) gave incentives for drugs for rare diseases; the 1984 Drug Price Competition Act created abbreviated applications for {{generic}} drugs based on bioequivalence.

front: Which Indian Act regulates the import, manufacture and distribution of drugs, and what does Section 17B empower?
back: The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Section 17B empowers government agencies to inspect, seize and confiscate drugs found to be adulterated or spurious.

front: Who must authorise a new drug before it is imported or manufactured in India, including an orphan drug?
back: The CDSCO (Central Drugs Standard Control Organization). Any entity seeking to market a new drug, orphan drugs included, must obtain its authorisation to import or manufacture it.

front: When did India join the WHO drug monitoring programme, and where is its national centre?
back: India joined the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring in 1997. The programme is managed by the Uppsala Monitoring Centre, Sweden. India's national centre is in the Department of Pharmacology, AIIMS, New Delhi.

front: Describe the thalidomide disaster and its regulatory consequence.
back: Thalidomide, launched in Europe in 1957 as a 'non-toxic' sedative and promoted for use in pregnancy, caused phocomelia (seal-like limbs) when taken in the first trimester; about 10,000 children were affected and it was withdrawn worldwide. It led to mandatory teratogenicity testing and, in the USA, the Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 1962. Thalidomide is now used in restricted settings (immunomodulator, leprosy reactions, cancer).

front: Which tragedy prompted the US Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act of 1938, and what did the Act require?
back: Deaths from a sulfanilamide preparation marketed before it and its vehicle had been adequately tested. The Act required new drugs to be shown safe as well as pure (proof of efficacy came only in 1962).

front: Link each drug disaster to the law it produced and what that law added.
back: Elixir sulfanilamide deaths led to the 1938 US Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act: new drugs must be proved safe. Thalidomide (phocomelia) led to the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments: proof of efficacy as well as safety. In India the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (1940) governs manufacture, sale and distribution. Pattern: regulation tightens after harm exposes a gap.

front: List the four main protein targets of drugs and give non-protein or unusual targets.
back: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters (carriers). Exceptions: colchicine binds the structural protein tubulin; ciclosporin binds cytosolic immunophilins; some therapeutic antibodies act by sequestering cytokines; antimicrobial and anticancer drugs may target DNA or cell-wall constituents.

front: Give one drug that inhibits an enzyme competitively, one irreversibly, and one acting as a false substrate.
back: Captopril: substrate-analogue competitive inhibitor of angiotensin-converting enzyme. Aspirin: irreversible inhibitor of cyclo-oxygenase (acetylates a serine). Fluorouracil: converted to fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate, which inhibits thymidylate synthase and so blocks DNA synthesis. Enzymes are one of the four main protein targets.

front: Why are transporters drug targets, and what are ABC transporters?
back: Ions and polar molecules cross membranes through channels or carriers, so blocking a carrier changes how cells handle them (cocaine blocks monoamine uptake into nerve terminals). ABC transporters have an ATP-binding site and use ATP hydrolysis to pump solutes out of the cell against a gradient, e.g. P-glycoprotein (MDR1), which ejects cytotoxic drugs and causes resistance. Other carriers couple organic molecules to Na+ by symport or antiport.

front: In what ways can drugs alter ion channel function? Give examples.
back: By binding the agonist (orthosteric) site of a ligand-gated channel; by binding an allosteric site that changes gating (benzodiazepines enhance GABA opening of the GABA-A chloride channel; dihydropyridines inhibit L-type calcium channel opening); or by physically plugging the pore (local anaesthetics in the voltage-gated sodium channel).

front: Why does no drug act with complete specificity, and what are on-target versus off-target side effects?
back: Targets bind classes of drug selectively but not exclusively, so higher doses (or low-potency drugs) reach other targets. On-target effects act through the same receptor as the wanted effect (opioid constipation and respiratory depression); off-target effects arise by a different mechanism (dry mouth from tricyclics, which block other receptors besides monoamine transporters).

front: Compare the four protein target classes: for each give a drug example and say where poor specificity could cause unwanted effects.
back: Receptor: albuterol on beta-2 receptors (the agonist/antagonist distinction applies only here). Enzyme: statins on HMG-CoA reductase, aspirin on COX. Transporter: cocaine or tricyclics on monoamine carriers. Ion channel: local anaesthetics on Na+ channels, benzodiazepines on GABA-A. Specificity is reciprocal but never absolute: tricyclics also hit other receptors, and rising dose widens the targets reached. Exceptions to protein targets include DNA (antimicrobial and antitumour drugs), tubulin (colchicine) and immunophilins (ciclosporin).

text: Type 1 {{ligand-gated ion channels}} (ionotropic; e.g. nicotinic, GABA-A; act in {{milliseconds}}); Type 2 {{G protein-coupled receptors}} (metabotropic, 7-transmembrane; e.g. muscarinic, adrenoceptors; seconds); Type 3 {{kinase-linked and related receptors}} (single transmembrane helix; e.g. insulin, growth factor, cytokine receptors); Type 4 {{nuclear receptors}} (regulate {{gene transcription}}; e.g. steroid receptors; hours to days).

front: What are kinase-linked and related receptors, and which non-enzymic receptors belong to this group?
back: Membrane receptors with an extracellular ligand-binding domain joined by one transmembrane helix to an intracellular domain that is often an enzyme (protein kinase or guanylyl cyclase). They respond mainly to protein mediators (insulin, growth factors). Some lack enzyme activity and signal through adaptor proteins, such as cytokine (e.g. TNF) receptors and pattern-recognition receptors of innate immunity.

front: List the four main G protein classes with their effector and a toxin that affects them.
back: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase (cAMP up); cholera toxin keeps it active by blocking its GTPase. Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase (cAMP down); pertussis toxin blocks it. Go acts mainly through beta-gamma subunits and is pertussis-sensitive. Gq activates phospholipase C, giving IP3 and DAG (Ca2+ release, protein kinase C). G12/13 activates Rho and Rho kinase. Different receptors couple to different G proteins, e.g. cardiac M2 and beta-1 receptors give opposite effects.

front: What makes a ligand-gated channel the typical fast receptor, and what is the nicotinic receptor's structure?
back: What makes a ligand-gated channel the typical fast receptor, and what is the nicotinic receptor's structure? Type 1 receptors are ionotropic: agonist binding directly opens the pore, giving effects in milliseconds (fast synaptic transmission). The nicotinic ACh receptor is a pentamer of different subunits around a central pore lined by the M2 helices; ACh binding twists the subunits and swivels the kinked M2 segments open.

front: Describe the G protein activation cycle and why the signal is self-limiting.
back: Agonist-bound receptor makes the alpha subunit swap GDP for GTP; alpha-GTP leaves the receptor and the beta-gamma complex and acts on an effector. The alpha subunit's own GTPase hydrolyses GTP to GDP, ending the signal; alpha-GDP rejoins beta-gamma. Binding of the effector speeds the GTPase, so effector activation limits itself. Cholera toxin blocks the GTPase, so Gs stays active.
