back: Different agonists acting at the same site on one receptor favour different downstream pathways, because they stabilise different active (R*) states. Examples include ligands at angiotensin receptors and inverse agonists at beta-adrenoceptors. It adds a dimension to efficacy beyond affinity and intrinsic activity.

front: What are receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMPs)? Give the classic example.
back: Membrane proteins that associate with some GPCRs (mostly class B peptide receptors) and change their pharmacology. Calcitonin receptor-like receptor is inactive alone; with RAMP1 it becomes the CGRP receptor, and with RAMP2 it becomes an adrenomedullin receptor.

front: How are G protein-coupled receptors desensitised?
back: Two main processes: phosphorylation of serine and threonine residues (mainly in the C-terminal tail) by GPCR kinases (GRKs) or by PKA and PKC, and internalisation (endocytosis) of the receptor. Homologous desensitisation affects only the receptor activated by the agonist; heterologous desensitisation also affects other GPCRs.

front: What is constitutive receptor activity, and how does an inverse agonist differ from a neutral antagonist?
back: Some receptors (e.g. benzodiazepine, cannabinoid and serotonin receptors; histamine H3 even in vivo) show activation with no ligand bound, also caused by some disease mutations. An inverse agonist lowers this basal activity (negative efficacy); a neutral antagonist only blocks agonists. Most clinical antagonists behave as inverse agonists in constitutively active systems.

front: Explain the two-state model of receptor activation.
back: The receptor switches between a resting state (R) and an active state (R*), which may exist even without ligand. A ligand with higher affinity for R* shifts the balance towards activation (agonist; full or partial depending on the size of the preference); one with equal affinity is a neutral antagonist; one preferring R is an inverse agonist. Its weakness is that receptors actually adopt many conformations.

front: Short note: Newer concepts in GPCR biology

points: One gene, one receptor protein, one G protein, one response
GABA-B functions only as a heterodimer of two subunits
Most GPCRs can form homo- or hetero-oligomers, e.g. opioid receptor heterodimers, dopamine D2 with somatostatin receptors
Dopamine D5 can directly inhibit the GABA-A channel
RAMPs change agonist specificity (CRLR with RAMP1 = CGRP receptor)
Constitutive activity: inverse agonists differ from neutral antagonists
Biased agonism: different agonists select different pathways
Arrestins bound to the receptor can activate the MAP kinase cascade
Cross-talk with tyrosine-kinase adaptor proteins

front: How are ion channels characterised, and what are the main gating types?
back: By ion selectivity (set by pore size and lining; cation or anion selective) and by gating. Gating types: voltage-gated (open on depolarisation, then inactivate; Na+, K+, Ca2+ channels), ligand-gated by extracellular transmitters (glutamate, ACh, GABA, 5-HT, ATP), channels gated by intracellular signals (Ca2+-activated K+ and Cl- channels, ATP-sensitive K+ channels), calcium-release channels (IP3 and ryanodine receptors) and store-operated channels.

front: Give an example of a ligand-gated channel that responds to the local environment rather than a transmitter.
back: TRPV1 on sensory nerves: activated by capsaicin, by protons when tissue pH falls in inflammation, and by heat.

front: Name the three ways drugs can change ion channel function, with an example of each.
back: 1) Direct binding to the channel: orthosteric site, allosteric site (benzodiazepines, dihydropyridines) or pore plug (local anaesthetics). 2) Indirect, through a G protein subunit or other intermediary. 3) Altering channel expression at the cell surface (gabapentin reduces insertion of neuronal calcium channels).

front: Where are IP3 receptors and ryanodine receptors, and why are they called ligand-gated channels?
back: They sit on the endoplasmic or sarcoplasmic reticulum, not the plasma membrane. They are a special class of ligand-gated calcium channel, opened by intracellular signals, that release Ca2+ from intracellular stores into the cytosol. Store-operated channels in the plasma membrane open when those stores are depleted.

front: Name the sites where drugs act on the voltage-gated sodium channel, with examples.
back: Channel block: tetrodotoxin and saxitoxin, plus local anaesthetics, antiepileptics (phenytoin) and antidysrhythmics. Block of inactivation (channel stays open): veratridine, batrachotoxin, scorpion toxins, DDT and pyrethroids. Gating is also altered by phosphorylation by PKA or PKC after GPCR activation. Multiple binding sites are typical of many ion channels.

front: Distinguish a pore blocker, an allosteric modulator and an expression modulator of ion channels.
back: Pore blocker (local anaesthetics on the Na+ channel) physically plugs the channel. Allosteric modulator binds a separate site and changes gating: benzodiazepines facilitate GABA-triggered opening of the GABA-A Cl- channel (so they work with GABA), dihydropyridines inhibit opening of L-type Ca2+ channels. Expression modulator (gabapentin) reduces the number of channels inserted in the membrane.

front: Tabulate ion channels as drug targets with examples.
back: Ligand-gated (extracellular ligand): nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, glutamate, 5-HT3, P2X; benzodiazepines act on GABA-A. Voltage-gated: Na+ (local anaesthetics, phenytoin), Ca2+ (dihydropyridines; gabapentin reduces insertion), K+ (many subtypes). Gated by intracellular signals: Ca2+-activated K+ and Cl- channels; ATP-sensitive K+ channel (partner of the sulfonylurea receptor, closed by ATP). Intracellular Ca2+ release channels: IP3 and ryanodine receptors. Store-operated Ca2+ channels. Environment-sensitive: TRPV1 (capsaicin, protons, heat). Drug mechanisms: pore block, allosteric gating change, indirect modulation, altered expression.

front: Distinguish affinity from efficacy, and say what each tells you about an agonist, a partial agonist and a simple antagonist.
back: Affinity is the tendency to bind the receptor (occupation); efficacy is the ability, once bound, to activate it. An agonist has both. A partial agonist binds but activates less, so it cannot give the full response. A simple antagonist has affinity but zero efficacy, so it only blocks agonists. This split is why binding alone never predicts a drug's effect.

points: Glutamate and aspartate are the main excitatory amino acid transmitters in the brain
Glutamate is the most abundant and the principal fast excitatory transmitter
NMDA, AMPA and kainate receptors are ligand-gated ion channels
NMDA receptors need glutamate plus a co-agonist (glycine) to open
NMDA receptors are Ca2+ permeable
Metabotropic glutamate receptors are GPCRs (mGluRs)
Fast synaptic excitation
Long-term potentiation and long-term depression, the proposed basis of learning and memory
Neuronal and glial transporters remove glutamate from the synapse
Glial EAAT1 and EAAT2 carry most of the uptake and limit excitotoxicity
GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter, acting through Cl- channels (GABAA) or GPCRs (GABAB)
Excess glutamate causes excitotoxicity in stroke, ischaemia and neurodegeneration
Memantine blocks NMDA receptors in a use-dependent way

front: What is the NMDA receptor, and what two agonists does it need?
back: An ionotropic glutamate receptor (ligand-gated Ca2+-permeable cation channel). It needs glutamate plus glycine to open.

front: What are EAAT1 and EAAT2, and why do they matter?
back: Glial glutamate transporters that take up most of the synaptic glutamate; they limit excitotoxic damage.

points: Early drugs were found by serendipity; modern discovery starts from a chosen target
Drug discovery in the past often came from observing effects of plant extracts or chemicals
Plants: morphine, ephedrine, quinine, curare, atropine, artemisinin
Animal products: adrenaline, thyroxine, insulin, liver extract
Microbes: penicillin (1941) opened the antibiotic source
Natural products mostly serve as lead compounds
Random synthesis has low chance of a useful hit; now rarely used (barbiturates and chlorpromazine were serendipitous)
Chemical congeners of natural products are made to improve properties
Validated target leads to a clinical candidate, refined by structure-activity relationships
High-throughput screening of chemical libraries on cells, enzymes or receptors (phenotypic or target-based)
Combinatorial chemistry generates many compounds for robotic screening
Three-dimensional protein structures allow molecular modelling and docking
Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib, etoricoxib) show selectivity for one isoform can be built in
Recombinant proteins (insulin, growth hormone, interferon), monoclonal antibodies
Pharmacogenomics aims at individualised drugs

back: A compound (often natural) with a useful activity that is chemically modified to give a better drug.
Combining chemical groups in many ways to make large numbers of compounds, which are then screened in automated assays.

front: Essay: Tools and techniques to study ion channels

points: Ion channels are membrane proteins that form ion-selective pores; many drugs act on them
Study methods range from current recording to structure and molecular genetics
Voltage clamp: holds membrane potential and records macroscopic currents; used since the 1950s (squid axon work)
Pharmacological separation of Na+ and K+ currents with blockers such as TTX
Devised by Neher and Sakmann; measures current through a single channel
Showed a physical pore (about 10^7 ions/s) and that conductance is the same for all agonists while open time varies
Gives gating kinetics and permeability of ligand-gated and voltage-gated channels
Radioligand binding measures receptor occupancy and density (Bmax)
Torpedo nicotinic receptor purified and characterised as a pentamer (four subunit types)
X-ray crystallography and NMR give three-dimensional structures; docking models ligand binding
Cloning and expression cloning; recombinant expression systems
Site-directed mutagenesis maps residues that form binding sites or gates
Combine recording, binding, structure and mutagenesis to link a drug's site to its effect on channel gating

front: What does the patch clamp technique measure?
back: The very small current passing through a single ion channel, so single-channel gating and conductance can be studied directly. Devised by Neher and Sakmann.

front: What does voltage clamp measure, and what did it first reveal?
back: Membrane current recorded at a fixed voltage, so that separate ionic currents can be isolated. Hodgkin and Huxley used it on the squid giant axon to show sodium and potassium currents.

front: Essay: Endoplasmic reticulum and calcium dynamics in neurodegenerative disease

points: Cytosolic Ca2+ is a second messenger, kept low by pumps in the plasma membrane and endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
Gq activates phospholipase C; IP3 is made and mobilises Ca2+ from ER stores
IP3 receptors and ryanodine receptors are intracellular ligand-gated Ca2+ release channels
SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum; phospholamban inhibits it when not phosphorylated
RyR1 in skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum
Abnormal ryanodine receptor underlies malignant hyperthermia triggered by halothane
Excess glutamate overactivates NMDA receptors, causing Ca2+ overload and neuronal death
Free radicals and toxins such as MPTP add to damage in Parkinson's disease
Loss of 70-80% of dopamine neurons at symptomatic stage; Lewy bodies made of aggregated alpha-synuclein
Memantine reduces excitotoxicity by use-dependent NMDA blockade
Neuroprotection targets excitotoxicity; the books reviewed do not show a drug acting on ER calcium stores in these diseases

back: Neuronal injury caused by excess glutamate, mainly through NMDA-receptor Ca2+ overload; it drives neuronal death in stroke and neurodegeneration.
An intracellular Ca2+ release channel on the sarcoplasmic reticulum; abnormal in malignant hyperthermia.
Sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase; pumps cytosolic Ca2+ back into the store, keeping cytosolic Ca2+ low. Phospholamban inhibits it.

front: What is a drug-drug interaction, and when is it most likely?
back: Modification of one drug's response by another given together or in quick succession. The change is usually quantitative (more or less effect) and sometimes qualitative (a different or abnormal response). Risk rises with the number of drugs, so it is highest in polypharmacy.

Physical or chemical incompatibility between drugs mixed before administration, for example in one syringe or infusion bottle, leading to inactivation or precipitation. Examples: penicillin or ampicillin with an aminoglycoside, thiopentone with succinylcholine or morphine, heparin with penicillin, noradrenaline in bicarbonate solution. Avoid mixing parenteral drugs.

front: Name the three categories of drug interaction.
back: Pharmacokinetic: the concentration of the object drug at its site changes. Pharmacodynamic: the response changes although concentration is unchanged. Pharmaceutical: the drugs inactivate each other when mixed in vitro before administration.

front: At which sites can a pharmacokinetic interaction occur?
back: Absorption, protein binding, metabolism and excretion. Each alters how much active drug reaches the site of action, so effect rises or falls without any change in receptor behaviour.

front: Short note: Classification of drug interactions

points: Modification of one drug's effect by another
Quantitative (more or less effect) or qualitative (abnormal response)
Changes the concentration of the object drug at its site of action
Sites: absorption, protein binding, metabolism, excretion
Changes the response at the target site, concentration unchanged
Synergism, antagonism or an abnormal response
Incompatibility before administration (same syringe or bottle)
Narrow safety margin drugs: aminoglycosides, digoxin, lithium
Saturation-kinetic drugs: phenytoin, theophylline

front: Classify: tetracycline plus iron, probenecid plus penicillin, penicillin plus tetracycline, and penicillin with an aminoglycoside in one syringe.
back: Tetracycline-iron: pharmacokinetic (absorption, insoluble complex in gut). Probenecid-penicillin: pharmacokinetic (excretion). Penicillin-tetracycline: pharmacodynamic (bactericidal antagonized by bacteriostatic). Penicillin-aminoglycoside in one syringe: pharmaceutical (inactivation).

front: Why does interaction risk rise sharply in patients on many drugs, and which drug types are most vulnerable?
back: Each added drug adds possible pairs, so polypharmacy multiplies risk. Most vulnerable are drugs with a narrow safety margin (aminoglycosides, digoxin, lithium), drugs controlling closely regulated functions (antihypertensives, antidiabetics, anticoagulants) and highly protein-bound or saturation-kinetics drugs.

front: A patient on several drugs has lost the effect of one drug and gained toxicity from another. Reason out which interaction categories could explain each and how you would tell them apart.
back: Loss of effect: reduced absorption or enterohepatic recycling, enzyme induction, increased excretion, or pharmacodynamic antagonism. Toxicity: enzyme inhibition, reduced excretion, displacement from binding, or additive pharmacodynamic effect. If drug levels move, the cause is pharmacokinetic; if levels are unchanged but response differs, it is pharmacodynamic. Pharmaceutical incompatibility applies only to drugs mixed before injection.

text: Highly {{protein-bound}} drugs with a small {{volume of distribution}} are most at risk, e.g. {{coumarin anticoagulants}}, {{sulfonylureas}}, certain {{NSAIDs}} and {{antiepileptics}}.

front: What is enterohepatic recycling and why does it matter for interactions?
back: A drug conjugated in the liver is excreted in bile, then deconjugated by gut bacteria and reabsorbed. Antibiotics such as ampicillin, tetracyclines or cotrimoxazole reduce gut flora, cut recycling and lower levels of drugs like oral contraceptive steroids.

front: Why are tetracyclines poorly absorbed when taken with iron, calcium or antacids?
back: They form insoluble chelate complexes in the gut lumen, so less drug is absorbed and treatment can fail. Separate the doses by 2 to 3 hours so they do not meet in the gut.

front: How can broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives?
back: Normal gut flora deconjugate steroid glucuronides excreted in bile, which allows enterohepatic recycling. Ampicillin, tetracyclines and cotrimoxazole reduce this flora, so less steroid is recycled and contraceptive levels fall. Advise alternative contraception.

front: When does protein-binding displacement become clinically important?
back: Only when the displaced drug is highly bound with a small volume of distribution, and the displacer binds the same site with higher affinity. The rise in free drug is usually brief because free drug is quickly cleared. It matters most when tissue binding is also displaced or when metabolism or excretion is inhibited, as with quinidine raising digoxin levels.

points: Displacer competes for the same plasma protein site with higher affinity
Free fraction of the object drug rises transiently
Highly bound, small volume of distribution
Coumarin anticoagulants, sulfonylureas, some NSAIDs, antiepileptics
Free drug is distributed, metabolised and excreted
Steady-state levels rise only marginally
Tissue binding is also displaced
Metabolism or excretion is also inhibited
Sulfonamides with phenytoin, warfarin and sulfonylureas
Quinidine with digoxin

front: Compare how iron and an antibiotic course can each make a drug fail, and say how management differs.
back: Iron or antacids chelate tetracycline in the gut, a local absorption block fixed by separating doses by 2 to 3 hours. A broad-spectrum antibiotic depletes gut flora and breaks enterohepatic recycling of oral contraceptive steroids, a systemic effect that spacing cannot fix, so alternative contraception is advised.

text: Enzyme inducers include {{rifampicin}}, {{carbamazepine}}, {{phenytoin}} and {{phenobarbitone}}, plus chronic {{alcohol}} and {{cigarette smoking}}. Enzyme inhibitors include {{erythromycin}}, {{ketoconazole}}, {{cimetidine}} and {{ciprofloxacin}}.

front: What is P-glycoprotein, and how do its inhibitors cause interactions?
back: P-glycoprotein is an ATP-dependent efflux transporter that pumps drugs out of cells. Inhibitors such as quinidine reduce renal and biliary clearance of substrates like digoxin and also reduce tissue binding, so digoxin blood levels can nearly double with toxicity.

front: Which drugs are metabolised by saturation kinetics and why does that make inhibition dangerous?
back: Phenytoin and theophylline. Their metabolic enzymes are near saturation at usual doses, so a small drop in enzyme activity from an inhibitor produces a disproportionate rise in plasma level and toxicity.

front: How do enzyme inhibition and enzyme induction differ in onset and offset?
back: Inhibition develops quickly and wears off soon after the inhibitor is stopped. Induction takes about 1 to 2 weeks to reach full effect and regresses over 1 to 3 weeks after withdrawal. Inhibition matters most for drugs cleared by saturation kinetics.

front: Why does grapefruit juice interact with some oral drugs?
back: Grapefruit juice constituents (e.g. naringin, furanocoumarins) inhibit CYP3A4, especially in the intestinal wall. Less first-pass metabolism raises the bioavailability of oral CYP3A4 substrates, so some drug labels advise avoiding grapefruit juice. Terfenadine was withdrawn partly because erythromycin or grapefruit juice blocked its CYP3A4 metabolism and the accumulated parent drug caused arrhythmias.

front: Give two excretion interactions and their clinical use.
back: Probenecid blocks tubular secretion of penicillins and cephalosporins and prolongs their half-life; this is used deliberately for single-dose treatment of gonorrhoea. Diuretics (and to a lesser extent tetracyclines, ACE inhibitors and some NSAIDs) raise steady-state lithium levels by increasing its tubular reabsorption; monitor lithium levels and reduce the dose.

points: Mostly drugs actively secreted by renal tubular transport
Urine pH changes ionisation and excretion of weak acids and bases
Blocks secretion of penicillins and cephalosporins
Used deliberately in single-dose gonorrhoea therapy
Blocks the uricosuric action of probenecid
Reduces tubular secretion of methotrexate
Reduces secretion of canrenone, blunting spironolactone's K+-sparing action
Diuretics (including furosemide), tetracyclines, ACE inhibitors, some NSAIDs and metronidazole raise levels
Monitor level and reduce dose
Altering urine pH has been used to hasten excretion in poisoning

front: A patient stable on warfarin is started on rifampicin. What happens and why?
back: Rifampicin induces hepatic microsomal enzymes, so warfarin is metabolised faster and its effect is lost. Induction builds over 1 to 2 weeks and regresses over 1 to 3 weeks after stopping rifampicin, so monitor INR and adjust the dose both ways.

front: Essay: Enzyme induction versus enzyme inhibition

points: Hepatic microsomal (CYP450) metabolism is the main route of many interactions
Two opposite effects: loss of effect (induction) and toxicity (inhibition)
Inhibition: competition for the same isoenzyme or cofactor, rapid onset
Induction: gene-mediated increase in enzyme synthesis, slow onset
Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone, smoking, chronic alcohol
Lower levels of oral contraceptives, warfarin, corticosteroids, sulfonylureas
Macrolides, azole antifungals, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, HIV protease inhibitors
Raise levels of phenytoin, carbamazepine, warfarin, theophylline, cyclosporine
Greatest for saturation-kinetic drugs such as phenytoin and theophylline
Narrow-margin drugs need level or response monitoring
Check inducer or inhibitor status before adding or stopping a drug
Adjust dose and monitor; induction fades slowly after withdrawal

text: Benzodiazepines with opioids cause additive {{CNS depression}} and {{respiratory depression}}; {{ACE inhibitors}} with potassium-sparing diuretics cause {{hyperkalaemia}}; propranolol with insulin can cause {{hypoglycaemia}} that is silent.

front: What is the difference between synergism and antagonism in a drug interaction?
back: Synergism: the combined effect is greater than from either drug alone. Antagonism: one drug blunts the effect of the other. Both occur without change in drug concentration when pharmacodynamic.

front: Which drug combinations cause additive CNS depression?
back: Benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, neuroleptics, opioids and alcohol in any combination. The result is excessive sedation, respiratory depression and motor incoordination.

front: Why should a bactericidal beta-lactam not be combined with a bacteriostatic antibiotic?
back: Bacteriostatic drugs halt bacterial growth, and the bactericidal action of penicillins and cephalosporins can be antagonized by them. Tetracycline with penicillin is the classic pair to avoid; the chapter advises against concurrent use.

front: Short note: Pharmacodynamic interactions in practice

points: Change in response at the target site without a change in concentration
Synergism (enhanced), antagonism (blunted) or an abnormal response
Benzodiazepine, sedating antihistamine, neuroleptic, opioid or alcohol
Sedation, respiratory depression, motor incoordination
Alpha blockers, vasodilators, ACE inhibitors, high-ceiling diuretics, cardiac depressants
Postural hypotension and fainting
Propranolol blocks recovery from hypoglycaemia and some warning symptoms
Hypoglycaemia can be silent with insulin or sulfonylureas
Levodopa blocked by neuroleptics and metoclopramide (dopamine blockade)
Macrolides, clindamycin and chloramphenicol block each other at the 50S ribosome
ACE inhibitors with potassium-sparing diuretics
Monitor potassium

front: Why is sildenafil (or tadalafil) contraindicated with organic nitrates?
back: Nitrates increase generation of cGMP, while sildenafil inhibits PDE5, which breaks cGMP down. Together they cause marked potentiation: a precipitous fall in BP and myocardial ischaemia. Concurrent use is contraindicated.

front: Why can propranolol mask hypoglycaemia in a diabetic on insulin, and why do ACE inhibitors plus K+-sparing diuretics cause hyperkalaemia?
back: Beta blockade blunts the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycaemia and impairs recovery, so low sugar goes unnoticed. ACE inhibitors plus K+-sparing diuretics together cause severe hyperkalaemia.

front: A hypertensive patient takes an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic and is given an NSAID for arthritis. Reason out the outcome.
back: NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, which blunts the antihypertensive effect of ACE inhibitors and diuretics, so BP rises. Avoid concurrent use.

front: Interacting pairs with theophylline and statins
text: Theophylline is metabolised by {{saturation}} kinetics and has a narrow margin, so enzyme inhibitors such as {{ciprofloxacin}}, erythromycin or allopurinol can cause toxicity. Statin myopathy risk rises with fibrates such as {{gemfibrozil}}, {{niacin}}, {{erythromycin}}, {{azole antifungals}} and {{HIV protease inhibitors}}.

front: Why is warfarin so prone to interactions?
back: It is highly protein-bound and its effect is closely regulated (INR monitored), so displacers, metabolic inhibitors, enzyme inducers, drugs that cut gut vitamin K production, and antiplatelet drugs all shift bleeding risk.

front: Which drugs raise digoxin toxicity risk when combined?
back: Quinidine (reduces tissue binding and P-gp clearance, nearly doubling levels), diuretics causing hypokalaemia (give a K+-sparing diuretic or K+ supplements), and propranolol (marked bradycardia in digitalized patients).

front: List the main ways other drugs raise the bleeding risk with warfarin.
back: Displacement plus inhibited metabolism plus less gut vitamin K (sulfonamides, cotrimoxazole); inhibited metabolism (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, macrolides, azole antifungals, chloramphenicol, allopurinol); less vitamin K from gut flora (ampicillin, amoxicillin, sulfonamides); additive hypoprothrombinaemia (ceftriaxone, cefoperazone); added antiplatelet effect (aspirin, clopidogrel, carbenicillin). Inducers (rifampin, barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine) do the opposite and reduce warfarin effect. Monitor INR and adjust the dose.

front: Which important interactions occur with aspirin and other NSAIDs?
back: They reduce the effect of ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and diuretics (thiazides, furosemide) by inhibiting renal prostaglandin synthesis. They displace and/or reduce elimination of sulfonylureas, phenytoin, valproate and methotrexate (toxicity; paracetamol is the safer substitute). With warfarin or heparin they add bleeding risk (antiplatelet action plus gastric damage). With fluoroquinolones they increase CNS toxicity and seizures. With alcohol or corticosteroids they raise gastric mucosal damage and bleeding. Aspirin also blunts spironolactone by reducing tubular secretion of canrenone.

front: Why do ciprofloxacin, erythromycin and allopurinol raise theophylline toxicity?
back: They inhibit theophylline metabolism, and because theophylline is cleared by saturable kinetics with a narrow margin, plasma levels rise disproportionately, causing toxicity.

front: Why are MAO inhibitors dangerous when combined with other drugs?
back: Non-selective MAO inhibitors stop breakdown of monoamines. Tyramine-rich foods (cheese, beer, wine, yeast extract) or ephedrine-containing cold remedies release large amounts of noradrenaline: hypertensive crisis ('cheese reaction'). Interactions also occur with TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs and levodopa; SSRIs combined with serotonergic drugs (MAOIs, tramadol, pethidine) can cause serotonin syndrome. Pethidine with an MAOI causes excitation, fever, convulsions and respiratory depression (excess norpethidine). CNS depressants are potentiated. Moclobemide (reversible MAO-A inhibitor) carries little tyramine risk.

front: Short note: Digoxin and QT-prolonging combinations

points: Quinidine reduces tissue binding and P-gp-mediated renal and biliary clearance of digoxin, nearly doubling levels
Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia increases toxicity: give a K+-sparing diuretic or K+ supplement
Propranolol in digitalised patients: marked bradycardia
Serum digoxin and potassium levels
Heart rate and rhythm

sections.h: QT-prolonging drugs (risk of torsades de pointes)
points: Antiarrhythmics: quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide, propafenone, amiodarone
Antimalarials: quinine, mefloquine, artemisinin, halofantrine
Antibacterials: sparfloxacin, moxifloxacin; antihistamines: terfenadine, astemizole, ebastine
Tricyclic antidepressants; antipsychotics (thioridazine, pimozide, aripiprazole, ziprasidone); cisapride
Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia predispose to torsades
Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia raises the torsades risk with quinidine
CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, ketoconazole) raised terfenadine, astemizole and cisapride levels, causing arrhythmias

front: What are the practical steps to prevent or manage a drug interaction?
back: Take a detailed history of every drug the patient is already taking, especially regular medication (antidiabetics, antihypertensives, anticoagulants, antiepileptics, oral contraceptives). Consider interactions whenever a drug is added. Stagger doses of complex-forming drugs by 2 to 3 hours. Adjust the dose and monitor levels or effects (INR, lithium, digoxin), or avoid the combination if the interaction is serious. A possible interaction does not always forbid concurrent use.

text: ACE inhibitors with diuretics treat {{hypertension}}; {{sulfamethoxazole}} with {{trimethoprim}} is a synergistic antibacterial pair; {{furosemide}} with {{amiloride}} prevents {{hypokalaemia}}; adrenaline is added to {{lidocaine}} for local anaesthesia.

front: Give deliberate drug combinations that exploit an interaction and explain why each works.
back: Sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim: synergistic antibacterial pair. Adrenaline added to lidocaine: complementary action in local anaesthesia. Furosemide with amiloride: K+-sparing action offsets potassium loss.

front: Probenecid is added to penicillin deliberately, but a diuretic is added to a patient on lithium. How is each handled?
back: Probenecid blocks tubular secretion of penicillin and prolongs its action; used on purpose in single-dose gonorrhoea treatment. Diuretics raise lithium by promoting tubular reabsorption; tetracyclines, ACE inhibitors and certain NSAIDs do similarly, and metronidazole or tinidazole reduce its excretion. Reduce the lithium dose and monitor its level, or avoid the combination.

front: Essay: Preventing and managing drug interactions in a patient on several drugs

points: Risk rises with the number of drugs, especially regular medication for chronic disease
Some combinations are deliberate and useful
Narrow safety margin: aminoglycosides, digoxin, lithium
Closely regulated functions: antihypertensives, antidiabetics, anticoagulants
Highly protein-bound: NSAIDs, oral anticoagulants, sulfonylureas
Saturation kinetics: phenytoin, theophylline
Detailed drug history of all current medication
Consider interactions whenever a drug is added or stopped
Avoid mixing parenteral drugs in one syringe or bottle
Laboratory: INR, lithium, digoxin, potassium
Clinical: bleeding, bradycardia, sedation, hypotension, hypoglycaemia
Dose adjustment
Staggered administration (2-3 h gap)
Substitution, e.g. paracetamol instead of an NSAID
A possible interaction is not always a contraindication
Knowing the mechanism allows safe concurrent use with appropriate adjustments

front: Why is paracetamol more dangerous in a chronic alcoholic or a patient on enzyme inducers?
back: One metabolite of paracetamol causes the overdose hepatotoxicity, and induced enzymes form more of it, so the toxic dose is lower. In chronic alcoholism doses below 3 g/day are considered safe.

front: Why must neuroleptics and metoclopramide be avoided in a patient on levodopa-carbidopa?
back: Both block dopamine receptors, so they antagonise the antiparkinsonian effect of levodopa; concurrent use is contraindicated. Separately, levodopa with antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors, vasodilators, prazosin) causes excessive postural hypotension, so reduce the antihypertensive dose.

front: Which drugs reduce absorption of ketoconazole and of phenytoin, and by what mechanism?
back: Ketoconazole needs gastric acid to dissolve, so H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors lower its absorption. Sucralfate binds phenytoin in the gut lumen, so less is absorbed.

front: What reaction can occur when a patient on metronidazole (or tinidazole, cefoperazone) drinks alcohol, and what is the advice?
back: Disulfiram-like or bizarre distressing symptoms in some individuals; the chapter suggests acetaldehyde accumulation, though the mechanism is not known. Warn the patient not to drink alcohol.

front: What interactions does allopurinol have with ampicillin, 6-mercaptopurine/azathioprine and warfarin or theophylline?
back: With ampicillin: more skin rashes (mechanism unexplained), so avoid. It inhibits metabolism of 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine, so reduce their dose to one-third. It inhibits metabolism of warfarin and theophylline: monitor and reduce the dose of the object drug.

front: Name pharmacodynamic interactions of TCAs with adrenaline in local anaesthetic, and of furosemide with aminoglycosides.
back: TCAs block neuronal uptake of adrenaline, potentiating it and raising BP, so use plain local anaesthetic solution. Furosemide with aminoglycosides gives additive ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, so avoid the pair.

front: Why does propranolol prolong lidocaine action?
back: Lidocaine metabolism depends on hepatic blood flow; propranolol reduces liver blood flow, so lidocaine half-life lengthens. Hence the ceiling amount of lidocaine used in local anaesthesia is reduced.

front: Name the regular-medication drug classes the chapter flags as likely to be involved in interactions.
back: Antidiabetics, antihypertensives, antianginals, antiarthritic drugs, antiepileptics, antiparkinsonian drugs, oral contraceptives, anticoagulants, antiasthmatics, psychopharmacological agents, antiulcer/reflux drugs, corticosteroids, antitubercular and anti-HIV drugs. Patients on these are on long-term therapy, so any newly added drug meets them.

front: Why must carbenicillin or ticarcillin be avoided in a patient on aspirin or another antiplatelet drug?
back: They perturb platelet surface receptors, adding to the platelet inhibition of aspirin, so bleeding risk rises. This is a pharmacodynamic additive effect, not a change in drug level; avoid the combination.

front: Why should erythromycin and clindamycin (or chloramphenicol) not be combined?
back: They bind to nearby sites on the bacterial 50S ribosome and interfere with each other, giving mutual antagonism of antibacterial action. Avoid concurrent use.

front: How do cimetidine or isoniazid change the effect of diazepam, and what is advised?
back: They inhibit diazepam metabolism, so levels rise and CNS depression is exaggerated. Avoid the pair or reduce the benzodiazepine dose.

front: DIPS: what does the Drug Interaction Probability Scale estimate?
back: How likely it is that an observed event in a given patient was caused by a drug-drug interaction (not by either drug alone). Scored question by question.

front: Short note: Drug Interaction Probability Scale (DIPS)

points: Causality tool for suspected drug-drug interactions (Horn, Hansten and Chan, 2007)
Adapts the Naranjo ADR probability scale from single drugs to a pair of drugs
10 questions, each with three response options and a score
Affirmative answers raise the probability of an interaction cause; negative answers lower it
Needs knowledge of the pharmacology of both the precipitant and the object drug
Below 2: doubtful
2 to 4: possible
5 to 8: probable
Above 8: highly probable
Does not guide management of the interaction itself
Needs data that are often unavailable (dose, timing, levels)

front: Pharmacokinetics vs pharmacodynamics: what is the basic difference?
back: PK is what the body does to the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion). PD is what the drug does to the body (mechanism and effects).

front: How does the WHO (1966) define a drug?
back: Any substance used, or intended to be used, to alter or explore physiological systems or pathological states for the benefit of the recipient.

text: Drug sources include {{plants}}, {{animals}}, {{microbes}}, {{minerals}}, {{synthetic chemistry}} and {{biotechnology}}.

front: Why does KDT prefer the word 'medicine' to 'drug' in some places, and how is a drug defined?
back: 'Drug' is sometimes used for addictive or illicit substances, a degraded sense, so 'medicine' names a substance with a health-promoting, therapeutic or diagnostic use. KDT's own definition: the single active chemical entity in a medicine used for diagnosis, prevention or treatment of disease. It leaves out contraceptives and health improvement, which is why WHO's wider definition is used.

front: Why do most drugs weigh 100 to 1000 D, and what follows for very large drugs?
back: Below 100 D a molecule lacks the shape, charge and chirality features needed to bind one target selectively. Above 1000 D it crosses body membranes poorly and cannot reach target tissues. Bulky drugs (heparin, gonadotropins, enzymes, antibodies) therefore have to be given parenterally.

front: Compare pharmacodynamic agents with chemotherapeutic agents, and define chemotherapy.
back: Pharmacodynamic agents are designed to produce effects in the recipient. Chemotherapeutic agents are designed to inhibit or kill invading parasites or malignant cells with little or no pharmacodynamic effect on the host. Chemotherapy is treatment of systemic infection or malignancy with drugs that have selective toxicity for the invader.

front: Essay: Sources of drugs and their nomenclature

points: Drugs obtained from plants, animals, microbes, minerals, synthetic chemistry and biotechnology
Alkaloids (morphine, atropine, quinine) are the most important plant principles
Glycosides (digoxin; senna anthraquinones), oils, tannins, gums, resins
Animal: insulin, thyroxine, antisera
Microbes: most antibiotics; vaccines
Minerals: iron and calcium salts, lithium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide
Synthetic chemistry: now the largest source; pure and uniform products; entirely synthetic families such as benzodiazepines and fluoroquinolones
Recombinant DNA: human insulin, growth hormone, alteplase, interferon; monoclonal antibodies, erythropoietin
Chemical, non-proprietary (rINN/USAN/BAN) and proprietary (brand) names
Brand names vary between makers and countries
Essential medicines list
Prescription (Schedule H), OTC and orphan drug categories

front: Name the three categories of drug names.
back: Chemical name (describes the structure), non-proprietary name (INN/USAN/BAN, the approved generic name), and proprietary (brand) name given by the manufacturer.

front: In India, which drugs are placed under Schedule H?
back: Prescription drugs: most drugs, including all antibiotics, placed in Schedule H of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules (1945, as amended). They may be sold at retail only against a prescription from a registered medical practitioner. Relatively harmless drugs (simple analgesics, antacids, some laxatives, vitamins, iron salts) are non-prescription (OTC) drugs.

front: Which name should you write on a prescription and why: chemical, non-proprietary or brand?
back: The non-proprietary (generic) name. The chemical name is cumbersome, and brand names differ between makers. rINN keeps non-proprietary names of newer drugs uniform in WHO member countries, though some older drugs still have two (pethidine/meperidine, lignocaine/lidocaine).

Drugs for diagnosing, preventing or treating a rare disease, or a commoner disease confined to resource-poor regions, where sales are not expected to recover the cost of development and marketing. Governments in developed countries offer tax benefits and other incentives to encourage them. USA (Orphan Drug Act 1983): a rare disease affects fewer than 0.2 million people. Examples: sodium stibogluconate, rifaximin, iloprost, rituximab.

front: What criteria define a WHO essential medicine?
back: WHO: medicines that satisfy the priority health-care needs of the population. Selected on public-health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness; they should be available at all times, in adequate amounts and suitable dosage forms, with assured quality and at an affordable price. Mostly single compounds; fixed-dose combinations only with proven advantage; the list is revised continuously. WHO Model List began in 1977 (20th list, 2017: 433 medicines); India's National List of Essential Medicines 2015 has 376 medicines graded for primary, secondary and tertiary care (figures as printed in KDT8).

points: Describes the structure; cumbersome, unfit for prescribing
Manufacturer may give a code name first (RO 15-1788, later flumazenil)
Accepted by a scientific authority: USAN, BAN; rINN used across WHO members
Called 'generic name' in common use; some older drugs have two names
Brand name chosen by the maker; catchy, short, often suggestive
Many brands for one drug (amlodipine) cause confusion
Non-proprietary: uniformity, convenience, economy, better comprehension
Brand name only when product consistency matters and quality control is weak
Medicines meeting the priority health-care needs of the population
Proven efficacy and safety
Assured quality, bioavailability and stability
Cost-effective; mostly single compounds, fixed-ratio combinations only with proven advantage

India: National Essential Drugs List 1996, revised 2011; NLEM 2015 has 376 medicines, graded by care level
Focuses limited resources on needed drugs; adoption improved availability, saved cost and made use more rational

text: Local routes include {{topical}} application, {{deeper tissue}} injection, and {{arterial}} delivery of selected agents.

front: What is the principle of a local route, and give one drug used both locally and systemically?
back: Local routes put a high concentration at the site of need with little systemic toxicity. GTN is the example: applied as ointment or patch it acts systemically for angina, while inhaled salbutamol acts locally on bronchi.

front: List the systemic routes of drug administration.
back: Oral, sublingual or buccal, rectal, cutaneous or transdermal, inhalation, nasal and parenteral. Knowing the list lets you ask, for each route, whether first pass is avoided and how fast absorption is.

front: Short note: Classification of routes of drug administration

points: Effect confined to an accessible site; systemic absorption minimal
Topical, deeper-tissue (e.g. intra-articular, perineural) and selected arterial delivery
Fewer systemic adverse effects
Oral, sublingual/buccal, rectal
Oral is the commonest; sublingual avoids first pass
Rectal is useful when vomiting or unconscious
Cutaneous and transdermal
Inhalational (gases, volatile liquids, aerosols)
Nasal
Subcutaneous, intramuscular, intravenous, intradermal
Faster and more predictable than oral; needs sterility and skill

front: What factors decide the route chosen for a patient?
back: Drug properties, site of action, absorption rate wanted, first-pass effect, urgency, accuracy of dose and the patient's condition. For example an unconscious or vomiting patient cannot take oral drugs, and an emergency needs a fast route such as IV.

points: Route determines onset, intensity, duration and predictability of the response
Two broad groups: local and systemic routes
Physical and chemical properties of the drug (solid, liquid or gas; solubility, stability, pH, irritancy)
Site of desired action; speed of onset and accuracy of dose needed
Effect of digestive juices and first-pass metabolism
Patient condition (unconscious, vomiting)
Topical (skin, mucosa, eye, ear; non-absorbed oral drugs such as sucralfate; inhaled salbutamol)
Deeper tissues: intra-articular, perineural, intrathecal, retrobulbar
Close intra-arterial: angiography contrast, regional cancer chemotherapy
High local level, minimal systemic toxicity
Oral: safe, cheap, convenient; but slow, variable, first pass
Sublingual/buccal: rapid, bypasses liver (GTN, buprenorphine)
Rectal: vomiting or unconscious patient; about half bypasses liver (diazepam, paracetamol)
Cutaneous and transdermal patches for lipid-soluble drugs (GTN, fentanyl, nicotine, estradiol)
Inhalation: gaseous anaesthetics, rapid and controllable
Nasal: desmopressin, calcitonin, GnRH agonists
Subcutaneous (including dermojet, pellet implantation, implants), intramuscular, intravenous, intradermal

front: Name drugs destroyed by digestive juices and drugs destroyed in the liver when given orally.
back: Digestive juices: penicillin G, insulin. Liver (first pass): glyceryl trinitrate, testosterone, lidocaine.

front: Sublingual route: why is it used, and which drugs are given this way?
back: Lipid-soluble, non-irritant drugs are absorbed from the oral mucosa within minutes straight into the systemic veins, bypassing the liver. Useful for drugs with high hepatic first-pass loss. The tablet can be spat out once effect is achieved. Examples: glyceryl trinitrate, buprenorphine, desamino-oxytocin.

front: What is first-pass metabolism and why does it matter for oral drugs?
back: Drug is degraded in the gut wall and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation, so less active drug is available. Oral dosing is affected most (GTN, testosterone, lidocaine are largely destroyed), while sublingual, transdermal, nasal and parenteral routes largely avoid it.

front: Which routes largely bypass hepatic first-pass metabolism?
back: Sublingual/buccal, transdermal, nasal, and the external haemorrhoidal part of rectal absorption. Inhalation avoids first pass in the gut and liver, although the lungs contribute a minor first-pass effect.

front: Short note: Oral route of drug administration

points: Most common and convenient
Non-invasive, cheap, no need for sterility
Self-administration possible
Slow onset; unsuitable in emergencies
Vomiting, unpalatable drugs, unconscious patient
Erratic absorption; some drugs poorly absorbed (streptomycin)
Degraded by gastric acid or enzymes (penicillin G, insulin); hepatic first pass
Enteric coating, sustained or controlled release
Capsules can hold unpalatable drugs; oral drops are preferred for infants and young children
Sublingual route as an alternative to avoid first pass

front: A patient with an acute angina attack needs GTN. Why give it sublingually rather than swallowed, and what does this show about route choice?
back: Swallowed GTN is largely destroyed in the liver (first pass). Under the tongue it is absorbed within minutes into sublingual veins draining to the SVC and heart, bypassing the liver, and the tablet can be spat out once relief occurs. Route choice here is driven by first-pass loss plus urgency. The same drug as patch or ointment gives a slower, sustained systemic effect.

front: Why are only aqueous solutions given intravenously?
back: Suspensions and oily preparations can cause embolism when injected intravenously.

front: Which parenteral routes allow depot preparations, and why?
back: Subcutaneous and intramuscular routes. Oily solutions or aqueous suspensions release the drug slowly from the injection site over a prolonged period.

front: What is the bioavailability of an IV dose and what does that imply?
back: 100%, since the drug enters blood directly with no absorption step. The smallest dose is needed and onset is immediate; there is also no depot.

front: Why is the intravenous route considered the riskiest parenteral route?
back: There is no depot effect, and vital organs such as the heart and brain are exposed to a high drug concentration almost at once. Dose titration is possible only for short-acting drugs with a measurable response.

front: Short note: Subcutaneous, intramuscular and intravenous injection

points: Loose tissue, rich in nerves, less vascular
Small volumes only; irritants not suitable
Slow absorption; delayed in shock (vasoconstriction)
Depot forms possible as aqueous suspensions
Large muscle; more vascular, so faster absorption
Mild irritants tolerated; depot preparations possible
Avoid in anticoagulated patients (haematoma risk)
Immediate effect; bioavailability 100%
Only true solutions; titration possible for short-acting drugs
Risks: embolism, thrombophlebitis, extravasation necrosis, high concentration at heart/brain

front: Compare subcutaneous, intramuscular and intravenous injection for speed, irritants and depot use.
back: IV: fastest, 100% bioavailable, even irritants can be given because the vein intima is insensitive and blood dilutes the drug, but only aqueous solutions, no depot, riskiest. IM: faster than SC because muscle is more vascular, tolerates mild irritants, allows depot preparations, avoid in anticoagulated patients (haematoma). SC: slow, small volumes, irritants unsuitable, depots possible. Choose by urgency, drug nature and need for prolonged action.

front: What is a transdermal therapeutic system and which drugs are delivered this way?
back: A patch holding a drug reservoir behind a rate-controlling membrane that delivers drug through the skin into the circulation at a steady rate for typically 1 to 3 days. Examples: glyceryl trinitrate, fentanyl, nicotine, estradiol. It avoids first pass.

front: Which kinds of drug are given by inhalation, and for what effect?
back: Gases and volatile liquids (e.g. general anaesthetics) act systemically. Aerosolised drugs such as salbutamol act locally on the bronchi. Absorption is very rapid and stops when inhalation stops, because the drug diffuses back and is exhaled.

front: Why does particle size matter for inhaled aerosols?
back: Particles of about 1 to 5 micrometres reach the bronchioles and alveoli. Larger ones are deposited in the oropharynx, and very fine ones are breathed out again, so the dose delivered falls either way.

front: Why do transdermal therapeutic systems give a steady plasma level?
back: A rate-controlling micropore membrane keeps drug delivery slower than the skin's absorption capacity. Site-to-site variation in skin absorption therefore matters less and the output stays constant.

points: Gases and volatile liquids (general anaesthetics) for systemic action
Non-volatile drugs as aerosols for local action in airways
Pressurised metered-dose inhaler (propellant, e.g. HFA)
Jet nebuliser (compressed air or oxygen)
Dry-powder devices such as rotahaler and spinhaler
About 1 to 5 micrometres reach bronchioles and alveoli
Larger particles deposit in oropharynx; very fine ones are exhaled
Very rapid absorption; controllable by stopping
Irritant vapours (ether) cause airway inflammation and secretion
Drug reservoir (solution or polymer-bound) between backing film and rate-controlling micropore membrane
Adhesive layer with priming dose; release liner peeled off before use
Drug diffuses through skin into systemic circulation at a constant rate
Membrane limits delivery below the skin's absorption ceiling
Steady plasma levels, no first-pass loss
Less inter-individual variation; better compliance
Duration typically 1 to 3 days
Costlier than tablets
Local irritation or erythema; rotate application site
Highly lipid-soluble drugs are the ones suited to skin absorption
Glyceryl trinitrate, fentanyl, nicotine, estradiol

text: Solid forms include {{tablets}}, {{capsules}}, {{lozenges}} and {{pills}}, while {{suppositories}} and pessaries are inserted into body orifices.
Ointments have an {{oily}} base and are {{occlusive}}; pastes contain {{hydrophilic}} powders; gels are viscous {{colloidal}} preparations that wash off with water.
{{Elixirs}} are hydro-alcoholic solutions; {{suspensions}} need a suspending agent; {{emulsions}} hold two immiscible liquids together with an {{emulsifying agent}}.

front: Match skin preparations to lesions: ointment, paste, gel, lotion.
back: Ointment: oily base, occlusive. Paste: thick, non-greasy, hydrophilic powders, for inflamed or oozing skin. Gel: viscous colloid, washable, used for oral ulcers. Lotion: better than creams or ointments on hairy skin. Pick the base that suits the lesion's wetness and site.

front: What factors guide the choice of dosage form?
back: Palatability: unpalatable drugs (e.g. chloramphenicol) can be filled in capsules. Swallowing: oral drops are the preferred form for infants and young children. Stability: drugs that deteriorate in aqueous medium can be dispensed as dry syrups. Duration: sustained or controlled-release tablets prolong action.

points: Drug plus excipients packed into a specific form
Gives shape, defines single doses, protects drug, suits route
Powders, tablets (plain, coated, chewable, dispersible, sublingual, enteric, sustained-release), capsules
Pills, lozenges, suppositories and pessaries
Aqueous solutions, suspensions, emulsions
Elixirs, syrups, linctus, drops, lotions and liniments
Injections: ampoules, vials, prefilled syringes, infusions
Ointments (oily base, occlusive), creams, pastes (hydrophilic powders), gels
Metered-dose inhalers, nebulisers, dry-powder devices
Stability, solubility, patient age and ability to swallow
Speed of onset required and need for controlled release

front: Compare a pharmacopoeia with a formulary: contents and who uses each.
back: Pharmacopoeia: official standards for approved drugs (structure, physical and chemical properties, identification and assay, purity standards, storage, dosage forms); used by manufacturers and regulators, rarely by doctors (IP, BP, USP, Eur P). Formulary: pocket booklet for prescribers listing indications, doses, contraindications, adverse effects and storage of selected drugs by therapeutic class (BNF, National Formulary of India). Formularies are the practical tool for prescribers. Both are government-issued official compendia with legal status.

front: When is the rectal route chosen, and why is only part of a rectal dose protected from first pass?
back: Used for irritant or unpleasant drugs and when the patient is vomiting or unconscious (diazepam solution, paracetamol suppository work well in children). Drug absorbed into external haemorrhoidal veins (about 50%) bypasses the liver; drug entering internal haemorrhoidal veins does not. Absorption is otherwise slower and unpredictable.

front: Name the special subcutaneous forms and what each is suited for.
back: Dermojet: needle-free high-velocity jet, painless, suits mass inoculation. Pellet implant: solid pellet placed with trochar for release over weeks to months (testosterone, DOCA). Non-biodegradable or biodegradable implants (Norplant): slow constant leaching over months; the non-biodegradable type must be removed later.

front: What is the intradermal route and what is it used for?
back: Drug is injected into the skin to raise a small bleb, or put on the epidermis and scratched or punctured through. Used only for specific purposes such as BCG vaccine and sensitivity testing.

front: Which drugs are given by the nasal route and why is the route useful?
back: The nasal mucosa absorbs many drugs and bypasses digestive juices and the liver. Used as spray or nebulised solution for GnRH agonists, calcitonin and desmopressin; being tried for peptides like insulin and to bypass the blood-brain barrier.

front: Distinguish drug action from drug effect.
back: Drug action is the first event: the drug binds its receptor, causing a conformational change (agonist) or blocking one (antagonist). Drug effect is the final change in biological function, produced through intermediate transducer steps.

front: Name the four major classes of protein targets for drug action, with one example each.
back: Enzymes (acetylcholinesterase, inhibited by neostigmine); ion channels (L-type Ca2+ channel, blocked by nifedipine); transporters (serotonin transporter, blocked by fluoxetine); receptors (beta-adrenergic receptor, activated by salbutamol).

front: Define drug selectivity and give the classic example.
back: Selectivity is the separation between dose-response curves for different effects of the same drug. Salbutamol separates bronchodilatation from cardiac stimulation far better than isoprenaline, so it is the more selective bronchodilator.

text: Quinidine blocks myocardial {{Na+}} channels; nifedipine blocks {{L-type Ca2+}} channels; furosemide inhibits the {{Na+-K+-2Cl-}} cotransporter; probenecid blocks the {{OAT}} transporter in renal tubules.

Competitive inhibitors raise the apparent {{Km}} but leave {{Vmax}} unchanged; noncompetitive inhibitors lower {{Vmax}} with {{Km}} unchanged; organophosphates bind covalently, giving {{nonequilibrium (irreversible)}} inhibition.

front: Short note: Cell membrane as a system for drug action

points: Bilayer of phospholipid and cholesterol with a nonpolar core
Proteins and glycoproteins sit on or pass through the bilayer
Membrane is dynamic: lipids and proteins move laterally
Gives high electrical resistance and low permeability
Drugs cross by passive diffusion, aqueous pores, carriers or vesicles
Four major drug target classes: enzymes, ion channels, transporters and receptors
Ion channels, transporters and receptors are typically membrane-bound
Ligand-gated ion channels respond fastest, within milliseconds
G protein-coupled receptors often act through cAMP
Receptor tyrosine kinases control cell functions by phosphorylation
Lipid solubility decides how quickly a drug reaches its target
pH differences across the membrane can trap weak electrolytes
Chiral drugs exist as enantiomers: R and S forms (or d and l isomers)
Activity depends on the 3D fit with the target, so enantiomers can differ in action and in metabolic breakdown
Often only one enantiomer is active
The second enantiomer may be a silent passenger, add side effects or toxicity, load metabolism, or antagonise the active form
A single-enantiomer product can be superior to the racemate
Levo-isomer of atropine is much more active than the dextro-isomer
S(-) bupivacaine (levobupivacaine) is equally potent but less cardiotoxic and less prone to seizures
Labetalol has four diastereomers with different alpha and beta profiles
Regulators such as the US-FDA require separate study of the enantiomers of a new chiral drug
Approval is withheld unless the pure enantiomers are shown to be no better than the racemate

front: Omeprazole, chlorpromazine and dexamethasone: why do their effects differ in breadth?
back: Breadth depends on how many targets a drug hits and how widely each target is expressed. Omeprazole acts on one very restricted target (the gastric proton pump of parietal cells), so it is highly specific. Chlorpromazine blocks several receptors (D2, alpha-1 and others), so it is multi-target and has varied effects. Dexamethasone acts only on the glucocorticoid receptor, yet nearly every cell expresses it, so its effects are widespread despite a single target.

front: Define affinity and intrinsic activity (efficacy) of a drug.
back: Affinity is the ability to bind the receptor, which sets the concentration needed for binding. Intrinsic activity is the ability to change the receptor after binding, scored from 0 (none) to 1 (maximal). The two properties are independent.

front: What is a partial agonist? Give an example and its clinical consequence.
back: A ligand with affinity and submaximal intrinsic activity, giving a lower ceiling than a full agonist; it can also antagonise a full agonist. Buprenorphine (mu opioid receptor) is a partial agonist and can precipitate withdrawal in a morphine-dependent patient.

front: What is an inverse agonist, and in which receptors does it act?
back: A ligand with affinity but negative intrinsic activity (between 0 and -1): it stabilises the receptor in its inactive state and so produces an effect opposite to the agonist. It shows only where the receptor has constitutive (basal) activity in the absence of agonist. Classic example: beta-carbolines such as DMCM at the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors. Many drugs earlier labelled competitive antagonists turn out to be inverse agonists.

front: What are allosteric modulators? Give examples.
back: Drugs that bind a site on the receptor separate from the agonist (orthosteric) site and alter the receptor's response to its agonist. Positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) enhance it: benzodiazepines and barbiturates on GABA-A receptors; cinacalcet on the calcium-sensing receptor. Negative allosteric modulators (NAMs) reduce it: maraviroc on CCR5 (blocks HIV entry).

front: Short note: Receptor concept of drug action

points: Regulatory macromolecules that combine with signal molecules, including drugs, and mediate their action
Agonist: activates a receptor to produce an effect like the physiological agent
Antagonist: blocks the receptor; competitive antagonism is seen between specific agonists and antagonists

front: Short note: Pharmacophore and structure-activity relationships

points: Pharmacophore: the chemical features a drug needs for optimal action at its receptor
Features include size, shape, position and orientation of charged groups, and hydrogen-bond donors
Worked out from the structures and activities of a group of related compounds, using computer analysis
Structure-activity relationships (SAR) guide the synthesis of many analogues
Chemical structure determines both affinity and intrinsic activity
Small structural changes can alter receptor binding and the pharmacological profile
Early lead compounds are optimised towards a clinical candidate
Therapeutic antagonists can be made by chemically modifying the physiological agonist

front: Essay: Receptor occupancy theory and the two-state model

points: Receptor: a macromolecule that recognises a signal molecule and transduces it into a response
Clark applied the law of mass action to drug-receptor binding
Effect proportional to the fraction of receptors occupied
Occupancy alone is not enough: the drug must also activate the receptor (intrinsic activity)
Independent properties of a drug
Full agonist IA = 1; partial agonist 0 to 1; antagonist 0; inverse agonist 0 to -1
Receptor exists in active (Ra) and inactive (Ri) states in equilibrium
Agonist binds Ra preferentially and shifts the equilibrium toward it
Competitive antagonist binds both states equally and does not shift it
Inverse agonist favours Ri; partial agonist has only slightly greater affinity for Ra
Constitutively active receptors signal without any agonist
Many full agonists give maximal response while occupying under 1 percent of receptors (spare receptors)
Where receptor numbers are limited, they cap the maximal response
Basis for designing selective agonists, partial agonists and inverse agonists

back: A ligand at one receptor preferentially activates one downstream pathway over another (e.g. G-protein signalling rather than beta-arrestin), so different agonists at the same receptor can produce different effect profiles. Oliceridine, a recently approved mu-opioid agonist, was designed as a G-protein-biased agonist to separate analgesia from adverse effects; whether it truly does so has been questioned.

front: Differentiate potency from efficacy, with an example.
back: Potency is the dose needed for a given effect (its position on the dose axis). Efficacy is the maximum attainable response. Morphine is more efficacious than aspirin for pain; pethidine is less potent than morphine but equally efficacious.

front: Define the therapeutic index and state why the clinical therapeutic window is used instead.
back: In animals, therapeutic index = median lethal dose / median effective dose (LD50 / ED50). This is irrelevant clinically: the therapeutic range ('therapeutic window') is bounded by the dose giving minimal therapeutic effect and the dose giving maximal acceptable adverse effect. Individual variability means a dose effective in one patient may be toxic in another. Low-safety-margin drugs (digoxin, lithium, aminoglycosides, theophylline, anticonvulsants) need monitoring.

front: Graded versus quantal dose-response curve: what does each measure?
back: A graded curve records the size of response in one individual as dose rises. A quantal curve records an all-or-none response across a population, plotted as the percentage responding at each dose. The quantal curve is what yields median effective and median toxic doses, which feed the therapeutic index.

points: Bounded by the dose giving minimal therapeutic effect and the dose giving maximal acceptable adverse effect
Individual variation shifts the window for each patient
Some drugs act only in a narrow concentration band, e.g. antidepressants (imipramine, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, about 50-200 ng/ml)

front: Furosemide versus metolazone, and hydralazine versus hydrochlorothiazide: what do the curves tell you about drug choice?
back: Furosemide is less potent but more efficacious than metolazone, so it is chosen when a large diuresis is needed; potency only changes the milligram dose, while efficacy sets the ceiling of effect. A steep curve (hydralazine) means a small dose change causes a big response, so the dose must be individualised; a flat curve (hydrochlorothiazide) means standard doses suit most patients.

points: Systemic dose-response has two parts: dose to plasma level (pharmacokinetics) and level to response (pharmacodynamics)
Rectangular hyperbola on a linear scale, following the law of mass action
Sigmoid on a log-dose scale, with a linear mid-range (30 to 70 percent)
Potency = position on the dose axis; compare by EC50
Efficacy = maximum response
The two vary independently and efficacy usually matters more clinically
Steep curve (hydralazine) needs individualised dosing
Flat curve (hydrochlorothiazide) allows standard doses
Separation of curves for different effects defines selectivity
The gap between therapeutic and adverse effect curves is the safety margin
Graded (degree of relief) vs quantal (percentage achieving an end point)
Risk-benefit judgement relies on population data and clinical experience
Sigmoid on a log-dose axis; the other curves in this subtopic assume it
Seen for hormones, endocrine disrupters, essential metals and vitamins
Low dose harms by deficiency, a middle zone is safe (homeostasis), high dose harms again
Response falls at higher concentrations
Can follow receptor down-regulation or desensitisation on exposure to the ligand, or a distinct negative effect at higher concentration

front: How do competitive and noncompetitive antagonists change the agonist dose-response curve?
back: Competitive (equilibrium) antagonist: parallel rightward shift, same maximum; surmountable by more agonist (atropine vs acetylcholine). Nonequilibrium (irreversible) antagonist, e.g. phenoxybenzamine: rightward shift and then a fall in maximum once spare receptors are used up. Noncompetitive antagonist acting at another site: flattened curve with depressed maximum that more agonist cannot overcome.

text: Activated charcoal adsorbing alkaloids is {{physical}} antagonism; BAL with arsenic is {{chemical}} antagonism; histamine versus adrenaline on bronchial muscle is {{physiological}} antagonism; atropine blocking acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors is {{receptor}} antagonism.

front: Define drug antagonism and name its four kinds.
back: Antagonism is one drug decreasing or abolishing the action of another. The kinds are physical (charcoal adsorbing alkaloids), chemical (chelators with metals), physiological or functional (two drugs on different receptors with opposing effects, e.g. histamine versus adrenaline on bronchi) and receptor antagonism (blocking the same receptor, e.g. atropine versus acetylcholine).

front: Short note: Types of drug antagonism

points: Based on a physical property: charcoal adsorbs alkaloids and prevents their absorption
Drugs react to form an inactive product: KMnO4 oxidises alkaloids; tannins precipitate them
Chelation: BAL or calcium disodium edetate with arsenic or lead
Nitrite-induced methaemoglobin binds cyanide
Incompatibility in the same syringe or infusion (thiopentone or penicillin G with succinylcholine; heparin with some antibiotics or hydrocortisone)
Different receptors or mechanisms, opposite effects on one function
Histamine vs adrenaline on bronchi and BP; glucagon vs insulin on blood sugar; hydrochlorothiazide vs amiloride on urinary K+
Competitive (equilibrium): parallel shift, surmountable (atropine vs acetylcholine)
Nonequilibrium: irreversible binding, maximum depressed (phenoxybenzamine on alpha receptors)
Noncompetitive: acts at a different site, flattened curve

front: Short note: Drug synergism and potentiation

points: Synergism: the action of one drug is facilitated or increased by another
Additive: combined effect equals the sum of individual effects
Supra-additive (potentiation): combined effect exceeds the sum; always so when one drug has no effect alone
Aspirin + paracetamol (analgesic)
Nitrous oxide + halothane (anaesthetic)
Amlodipine + atenolol (antihypertensive)
Glibenclamide + metformin (hypoglycaemic)
Ephedrine + theophylline (bronchodilator)
Acetylcholine + physostigmine: inhibited breakdown
Levodopa + carbidopa/benserazide: inhibited peripheral metabolism
Adrenaline + cocaine/desipramine: neuronal uptake blocked
Sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim: sequential blockade
Enalapril + hydrochlorothiazide: two contributory factors tackled
Tyramine + MAO inhibitors: larger releasable catecholamine store
Lower doses of each component, so the combination is better tolerated, as side effects of each often differ
Competitive antagonism is seen between specific agonists and antagonists acting at the same receptor (Langley, 1878, quoted in KDT8)

front: Essay point: therapeutic applications of drug antagonism, with an example of each type.
back: Receptor: naloxone reverses morphine; atropine opposes acetylcholine. Chemical: BAL and calcium disodium edetate chelate arsenic and lead; protamine neutralises heparin; nitrite forms methaemoglobin that binds cyanide. Physiological: adrenaline opposes histamine in bronchi and BP; glucagon opposes insulin. Rescue: folinic acid for methotrexate toxicity. Physical: charcoal adsorbs alkaloids in poisoning. The type chosen depends on whether the poison is in the gut, in blood, or acting at a receptor.

front: Name the five families of receptors with one example each.
back: G-protein coupled receptors (adrenergic); ligand-gated ion channels (nicotinic, GABA-A); enzyme-linked receptors (insulin receptor tyrosine kinase); cytokine JAK-STAT receptors (growth hormone, interferons); intracellular nuclear receptors (steroid hormones, thyroxine).

text: GPCRs have {{seven}} transmembrane helices and signal through {{G proteins}}; nicotinic and GABA-A are {{ligand-gated ion channels}}; the insulin receptor is a {{receptor tyrosine kinase}}; cytokine receptors use the {{JAK-STAT}} pathway; steroid receptors are {{intracellular nuclear receptors}}.

front: Which receptor family acts fastest, and which slowest?
back: Ligand-gated ion channels act within milliseconds (the channel opens directly), G-protein coupled receptors within seconds (second messengers), enzyme-linked receptors over minutes to hours, and intracellular nuclear receptors slowest, over hours, because gene transcription and protein synthesis are needed. Nuclear effects also outlast the hormone since the proteins made turn over slowly.

front: What are autoreceptors and heteroreceptors? Why do they matter clinically?
back: Both are presynaptic receptors that modulate transmitter release from the terminal. An autoreceptor responds to the neuron's own transmitter (e.g. M2/M4 on cholinergic terminals, alpha-2 on noradrenergic terminals), giving negative feedback. A heteroreceptor responds to a transmitter from another neuron or cell (e.g. NE on alpha-2 receptors reducing ACh release). Clinically, blocking presynaptic muscarinic receptors can raise ACh release and partly offset a postsynaptic antagonist, and 5-HT1 autoreceptors help explain the delay in antidepressant action.

front: Which G-protein subtypes act on which effectors?
back: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase (cAMP rises) and opens Ca2+ channels. Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase and opens K+ channels. Go inhibits neuronal Ca2+ channels. Gq activates phospholipase C, producing IP3 (Ca2+ release) and DAG (protein kinase C). G12/13 activates the small GTPase RhoA.

text: Gs activates {{adenylyl cyclase}}; Gi {{inhibits}} it and opens {{K+}} channels; Gq activates {{phospholipase C}}, producing {{IP3}} and DAG.

front: What is a second messenger? Name the main ones in this chapter.
back: A second messenger is an intracellular molecule made or released after a receptor is activated; it carries and amplifies the signal inside the cell, so one receptor can drive many effects. Main ones: cAMP (via PKA), cGMP (via PKG), IP3 (releases Ca2+ from the ER), DAG (activates protein kinase C) and Ca2+ itself (acting through calmodulin).

front: Distinguish homologous from heterologous desensitisation, and both from down-regulation.
back: Homologous: loss of response limited to the receptor being activated, via GRK phosphorylation and beta-arrestin binding (fast). Heterologous: loss across agonists acting on different receptors, via PKA and PKC phosphorylation. Down-regulation: fewer receptors from reduced synthesis or increased degradation, developing over weeks to months and receding slowly.

points: Agonist binds a GPCR, which activates Gs (GTP replaces GDP on the alpha subunit)

cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates functional proteins
