Phosphorylation of troponin increases force of contraction
Phosphorylation of phospholamban speeds relaxation
Phosphodiesterases hydrolyse cAMP to 5'-AMP; PDE3 and PDE4 are cAMP-selective
Intrinsic GTPase of Gs-alpha returns it to the GDP-bound state
Cyclic nucleotide-gated channels
Gene transcription through CREB
EPAC proteins
Beta agonists act through this pathway; Gi-coupled receptors oppose it
PDE5 is cGMP-selective (target of sildenafil)

front: Short note: Receptor desensitisation and tachyphylaxis

points: Desensitisation (refractoriness): continued or intense stimulation makes the receptor less efficient at transducing response
Tachyphylaxis: rapid tolerance when doses are repeated in quick succession
Masking or internalisation of receptors (homologous: GRK phosphorylation, beta-arrestin)
Heterologous: PKA/PKC phosphorylation affecting several receptors
Down-regulation by reduced synthesis or increased degradation (slow)
Depletion of releasable catecholamine stores (indirect sympathomimetics)
Asthmatics on continuous adrenergic agonists; parkinsonian patients on high-dose levodopa
Tachyphylaxis to ephedrine, tyramine, nicotine
Prolonged deprivation of agonist (denervation, continued antagonist) causes up-regulation
Relevant to clonidine, CNS depressant and opioid withdrawal, and sudden stopping of propranolol in angina

front: Define tolerance, tachyphylaxis and cross-tolerance, with an example of each.
back: Tolerance: a given dose produces less effect because target cells become less responsive (morphine, barbiturates, nitrates), possibly by receptor desensitisation or down-regulation. Tachyphylaxis: tolerance developing rapidly when doses are repeated in quick succession, typically with indirectly acting drugs (tyramine, ephedrine). Cross-tolerance: tolerance to pharmacologically related drugs, e.g. alcoholics tolerate barbiturates and general anaesthetics. Tolerance can be selective: it develops to morphine analgesia and euphoria more than to constipation and miosis.

points: Gs raises, Gi lowers adenylyl cyclase; acts via PKA; broken down by phosphodiesterases (PDE3, PDE4)
Cardiac beta-1: troponin phosphorylation raises force, phospholamban speeds relaxation
Made by soluble guanylyl cyclase, activated by nitric oxide; acts via PKG
Vascular relaxation: nitrates and nitroprusside; PDE5 breaks it down (sildenafil target)
Gq activates phospholipase C, splitting PIP2 into IP3 (Ca2+ release) and DAG (protein kinase C)
Ca2+-calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase and contraction
GTPase of G-alpha, RGS proteins, phosphodiesterases, GRK and arrestin desensitisation
Beta agonists, nitrates and sildenafil act through these pathways
Prolonged drive leads to desensitisation; deprivation leads to supersensitivity

front: Why can abrupt withdrawal of propranolol or clonidine cause a rebound, and how does this contrast with tachyphylaxis?
back: Prolonged blockade or reduced input leaves receptors and effector systems supersensitive, through unmasking or proliferation (up-regulation) of receptors or greater signal amplification; when the drug stops, the unopposed agonist gives an exaggerated response (angina worsening, withdrawal syndrome). Desensitisation is the opposite adaptation: continued intense stimulation makes receptors less efficient, as in asthmatics on continuous beta agonists.

front: How do drug tolerance, drug dependence and drug addiction differ?
back: Tolerance: the same dose gives less effect because target cells become less responsive. Dependence: an altered physiological state from repeated dosing that needs the drug to stay present; stopping it causes a characteristic withdrawal syndrome. Addiction: compulsive drug use with overwhelming involvement, prone to relapse. Dependence is not essential for addiction: amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis and LSD cause addiction with little or no dependence.

Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors are nuclear receptors that act as ligand-activated regulators of gene transcription. Three forms exist: alpha, beta/delta and gamma. Fatty acids and eicosanoids are among their natural ligands. They switch on genes for lipid and glucose handling, so drugs that activate them lower lipids or insulin resistance.

front: Which PPAR do fibrates and thiazolidinediones each act on, and what does each do?
back: Fibrates activate PPAR-alpha: fatty acid oxidation and lipoprotein lipase synthesis rise, and hepatic triglyceride synthesis falls, so triglycerides drop. Thiazolidinediones activate PPAR-gamma, easing insulin resistance so circulating insulin falls.

front: Essay: PPARs and their role in drug development

points: PPARs are nuclear receptors, so they act through gene expression rather than fast ion-channel or enzyme effects
Three isoforms: alpha, beta/delta and gamma
Ligand-activated; partners with retinoid X receptor (RXR) and binds response elements in gene enhancers
Natural ligands include fatty acids and eicosanoids
Main effect is lower triglycerides, by about 20 to 50% depending on baseline level
Raise fatty acid oxidation and lipoprotein lipase
Pioglitazone improves insulin sensitivity and lowers circulating insulin
Adverse effects include plasma volume expansion and oedema
Rosiglitazone is banned in India and was withdrawn in Europe over cardiovascular risk
Gemfibrozil, a PPAR-alpha activator, raises the risk of myopathy with several statins
PPARs are a receptor family where ligands have been developed for dyslipidaemia (fibrates) and diabetes (thiazolidinediones)

front: Which cannabinoid receptors exist, and where are they?
back: CB1 is found at high density throughout the brain, so it mediates most central effects; CB2 is mainly on immune cells, so it drives immune-related effects. Both are G-protein coupled receptors coupling to Gi/Go.

Synthetic delta-9-THC in sesame oil, given as a capsule or oral solution. It is a low-efficacy agonist at CB1 and CB2, with oral bioavailability of only about 10 to 20%. Used for chemotherapy-induced vomiting and appetite loss in HIV.

Nabiximols (THC plus CBD oromucosal spray): spasticity in multiple sclerosis
Non-intoxicating; approved for seizures in Lennox-Gastaut, Dravet and tuberous sclerosis complex
Muscle spasm and pain in MS and dystonia; neuroprotection after head injury or cerebral ischaemia
Anxiety, migraine, glaucoma (lowers intraocular pressure)
Hallucinogenic and psychomotor effects restrict use
Delta-9-THC is the psychoactive principle of cannabis, acting on CB1 (CNS) and CB2 (immune) receptors

Muscle spasm and pain in MS and dystonia; neuroprotection after head injury or cerebral ischaemia
Anxiety, migraine and glaucoma (lowers intraocular pressure)

Peripherally restricted CB1 antagonists are in development

back: Lipid messengers such as anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG). They are synthesised on demand rather than stored in vesicles; anandamide is the principal one in the brain.

front: How do endocannabinoids reduce transmitter release?
back: They are made by the postsynaptic neuron and cross the synapse backwards to presynaptic CB1 receptors, which suppress transmitter release. The suppression can be transient or long-lasting, depending on the pattern of activity.

front: Short note: Targeting the endocannabinoid system

points: Receptors (CB1, CB2), endogenous ligands (anandamide, 2-AG), and the enzymes that make and break them down
Rimonabant: synthetic CB1 antagonist with inverse agonist action; developed for smoking cessation
Peripherally restricted CB1 antagonists are in development
FAAH inhibitors raise anandamide; PF-04457845 is covalent and irreversible, with up to tenfold rises in circulating anandamide; tested in a phase 2a trial for cannabis withdrawal in men
MAGL inhibitors raise 2-AG; they have been tested less than FAAH inhibitors

front: Essay: Endocannabinoid system as a therapeutic target

points: Three parts: CB1 and CB2 GPCRs, endogenous lipid ligands, and the enzymes that synthesise and degrade them
Gi/Go coupling: inhibits adenylyl cyclase, modulates Ca2+ and K+ channels
Made on demand and act as retrograde messengers across synapses
Pain perception, memory and cognition, feeding and energy metabolism
CB1 blockade with rimonabant; peripherally restricted CB1 antagonists are in development
FAAH inhibition raises anandamide; MAGL inhibition raises 2-AG
The FAAH inhibitor PF-04457845 was tested in a phase 2a trial for cannabis withdrawal in men; MAGL inhibitors have been less extensively tested
THC is a partial agonist; synthetic cannabinoids ('spice') are high-efficacy CB1 agonists with uncharacterised off-target activity

back: A model that bridges pharmacokinetics (drug level over time) and pharmacodynamics (response), so the response to a dose can be forecast over time.

front: Why does plasma concentration not always match drug effect?
back: Only drugs with an almost instantaneous link between free plasma level and effect (for example antiarrhythmics) show a direct match. For other drugs the effect lags behind or differs from the plasma level, so the time course is modelled separately.

front: Short note: Labetalol as a PK-PD example

points: A racemic mixture whose isomers have different kinetics and effects
Bioavailability only about 20 to 40%, variable, and raised by food
Extensive hepatic first-pass clearance; metabolism sensitive to hepatic blood flow
Elimination half-life about 8 h; the R,R isomer (dilevalol) about 15 h

front: Essay: PK-PD modelling and clinical relevance

points: PK links dose to concentration; PD links concentration to effect; the PK-PD model links both over time
Forecast response to a dose; select dose and dosing interval; estimate duration of response; estimate the therapeutic window
Effect often lags plasma level, so the model describes the concentration-time course in the effect compartment
Only near-instantaneous drugs (e.g. antiarrhythmics) track free plasma level directly
Age, sex, body weight and disease status change the dose-response-time relation
Individuals differ in both PK and PD handling
Labetalol: isomers with different half-lives (8 h versus 15 h for dilevalol)
Antimicrobials: efficacy is linked to MIC and exposure indices; dosing aims for a high chance of exceeding the target index
Early human trials gather PK and PD data to set dose and to define efficacy and safety

front: Quantitative versus qualitative modification of drug action
back: Quantitative: the plasma level or action rises or falls; most factors do this and are handled by changing the dose. Qualitative: the type of response changes, as in drug allergy or idiosyncrasy, which often rules out that drug.

front: Why are child and elderly doses worked out differently from adult doses?
back: Children are dosed on body weight; newborns have immature glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, which prolongs half-life of renally cleared drugs. In the elderly, GFR falls to about half by 75 years and hepatic metabolism and liver blood flow drop, so doses are reduced and cumulative toxicity is watched for.

front: Short note: Sex and pregnancy as modifiers of drug action

points: Women are smaller and usually need doses at the lower end of the range
Some side effects are sex-specific, e.g. gynaecomastia in men with ketoconazole or digitalis
Reduced gut motility delays oral absorption
Plasma volume rises, so volume of distribution may increase
Albumin falls and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein rises, changing free fractions of acidic and basic drugs
Renal blood flow rises, so polar drugs clear faster; hepatic enzymes are induced

front: Short note: Genetic and racial factors in drug response

points: Dose needed for the same effect can vary 4 to 6 fold between people
Transporters, enzymes, ion channels, receptors and couplers are genetically controlled
Pharmacogenetics studies the genetic basis of response; pharmacogenomics uses it to choose drug and dose
Some groups differ, e.g. beta-blockers are less effective as antihypertensives in Afro-Caribbeans
Species differ: rabbits are resistant to atropine; rats and mice are resistant to digitalis

front: Why does atropine's effect on heart rate depend on the patient's vagal tone?
back: Atropine raises heart rate only when vagal tone is present to be blocked. Propranolol lowers heart rate only in proportion to sympathetic tone, and captopril lowers blood pressure more when body sodium is low. The response depends on the physiological state, not only on receptor occupancy.

front: Essay: Factors influencing drug action and their clinical relevance

Changes are quantitative (dose adjustment) or qualitative (allergy, idiosyncrasy)
Plasma or target concentration varies more for drugs cleared by metabolism (propranolol) than for drugs excreted unchanged (atenolol)
Number and state of receptors and coupling proteins can vary
Tone decides the response: atropine tachycardia depends on vagal tone; propranolol bradycardia on sympathetic tone
Child and obese or lean doses are based on body weight; newborns and elderly differ in renal function and metabolism
Women are smaller; pregnancy changes drug disposition
Dose for the same effect can vary 4 to 6 fold; pharmacogenomics guides choice
Species and racial differences change responsiveness, so animal data need care
Choose the drug and starting dose using these factors, then adjust by observing the patient's response

front: Short note: Neurokinin receptor system and its therapeutic role

front: What is a bioassay, and when is it used?
back: Measuring the amount or potency of a substance from the biological response it produces in a living animal or isolated tissue. It is used when the chemical composition is unknown, or when chemical assay is too complex or insensitive, e.g. adrenaline and histamine in microgram amounts.

front: How is adrenaline bioassayed on an isolated tissue?
back: The response of a sensitive isolated tissue is compared with a standard to find the unknown concentration. Rat colon is one such preparation; it responds more strongly to noradrenaline than to adrenaline, so the result must be read with that selectivity in mind.

front: What protection does a patent give a new drug?
back: In the US system, a patent gives the holder exclusive rights to market and sell the drug for 20 years from filing.

front: Short note: Membrane transporters and adverse drug reactions

points: Transporters control how much drug reaches each cell, so they set exposure and toxicity
Decreased uptake or excretion at clearance organs raises systemic levels
Increased uptake or decreased efflux at target organs raises local drug levels
Drugs alter transport of endogenous compounds at target organs
Gemfibrozil glucuronide reduces hepatic uptake of cerivastatin, raising its systemic levels

front: Short note: Drugs affecting dopamine signalling

points: Five dopamine receptor subtypes, grouped as D1-like and D2-like
Used in Parkinson disease, restless legs syndrome and hyperprolactinaemia
Dopamine does not cross the BBB; levodopa does and is converted to dopamine in the brain
Given with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor to limit peripheral conversion
Long-term use loses effect and causes levodopa-induced dyskinesias

front: What is a designer drug, and how does a therapeutic designer drug differ?
back: A designer drug is a chemically altered form of an existing drug. Ecstasy, the MDMA-derived class, is the prototypic designer drug. Vigabatrin, the first designer drug in epilepsy, is a vinyl-substituted GABA analogue designed as an irreversible GABA-transaminase inhibitor.

front: Why is oral bioavailability usually less than 100%?
back: Incomplete absorption from the gut, plus loss from first-pass metabolism in the gut wall or liver, or excretion in bile. IV dosing gives 100% by definition.

Pharmaceutical equivalents contain the same active ingredient in the same strength, dosage form and route. Two such products are bioequivalent when the rate and extent of bioavailability of the active drug do not differ significantly under suitable, identical test conditions. Equal drug content alone does not guarantee this (formulation affects dissolution), which matters for narrow-margin drugs such as digoxin.

front: At what pH is a weak acid 50% ionised, and what does a 1-unit change in pH do?
back: At pH equal to pKa. Each 1-unit change in pH alters the ionised to unionised ratio tenfold.

A weak electrolyte crossing a membrane becomes ionised on the far side, cannot diffuse back, and so accumulates there. Example: unionised aspirin enters gastric mucosal cells (pH about 7) and is trapped.

front: Why are acidic drugs excreted faster in alkaline urine?
back: They stay ionised in alkaline urine and cannot back-diffuse across the renal tubular epithelium. Acidifying urine speeds the excretion of basic drugs by the same logic.

front: How do facilitated diffusion and primary active transport differ?
back: Facilitated diffusion is passive, follows the concentration gradient and needs no energy. Primary active transport uses ATP hydrolysis (ABC transporters) to move the solute against its gradient, usually out of the cell.

front: Which efflux transporter is encoded by MDR1, and where does it limit drug entry?
back: P-glycoprotein (ABCB1). It limits absorption from the gut and entry into the brain, testes and foetus, and promotes biliary and renal elimination.

front: Why can quinidine or verapamil raise digoxin levels?
back: Both inhibit the efflux pump P-glycoprotein. Less P-gp efflux in the gut epithelium raises digoxin's oral bioavailability. Quinidine also cuts digoxin's renal and biliary clearance (again via P-gp) and displaces it from tissue binding sites, nearly doubling its plasma level.

front: Define apparent volume of distribution and give its formula.
back: The hypothetical volume into which the total amount of drug in the body would have to be dispersed to give the measured plasma concentration. Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma concentration.

front: Why does a large volume of distribution make haemodialysis ineffective?
back: Most of the drug sits in tissues, so very little is in plasma at any time to be cleared by dialysis. Highly protein-bound drugs are also poorly removed.

front: What is redistribution, and why does a single dose of thiopentone act only briefly?
back: Highly lipid-soluble drugs first enter well-perfused organs such as brain, then move to muscle and fat as plasma levels fall. Brain levels drop, so the action ends within minutes.

front: What makes the blood-brain barrier, and where is it deficient?
back: Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells plus a glial investment, with lipoidal limits on entry and efflux pumps. It is deficient at the chemoreceptor trigger zone and some periventricular sites, which is why emetics can act there.

front: Why can a salicylate be absorbed from the stomach, while a basic drug such as morphine is absorbed only after reaching the duodenum?
back: Acidic drugs (salicylates, barbiturates) are mostly unionised in acid gastric juice, so they cross the lipoidal mucosa. Basic drugs (morphine, quinine) are largely ionised there and are absorbed only in the duodenum. Even acidic drugs absorb faster from the intestine, because its villi give a far larger surface than the thick, mucus-covered stomach.

front: Why is the placenta only an incomplete barrier to drugs?
back: Lipid-soluble drugs cross freely, and nonlipid-soluble drugs get through when they are present at high concentration or for long periods. Some influx transporters also operate there, so almost any maternal drug can affect the foetus or newborn.

front: How do heat, exercise and a local vasoconstrictor change absorption from an injection site?
back: Heat and muscular exercise speed absorption by raising blood flow. A co-injected vasoconstrictor such as adrenaline slows it, which is why it is added to local anaesthetics.

front: Why does drug diffusion across capillaries depend on blood flow rather than lipid solubility?
back: Capillaries with large paracellular spaces do not obstruct even large lipid-insoluble molecules or ions, so only blood flow limits transfer. Brain capillaries have tight junctions and lack these spaces, so there lipid solubility matters.

front: Short note: Plasma protein binding and its effect on duration and renal excretion

points: Bound fraction is not available for metabolism or excretion, so highly bound drugs act longer
Glomerular filtration does not lower free-drug concentration in the efferent vessel, because water is also filtered
Tubular secretion removes drug without solvent, so free drug falls and bound drug dissociates
Renal clearance can exceed total renal blood flow

front: Why does repeated dosing make a redistribution-limited drug act longer?
back: Low-perfusion, high-capacity tissues (muscle, fat) gradually fill up. Redistribution away from the target organ then stops, so the drug's action lasts longer.

front: What kind of transporter is P-gp, and why does that matter for drugs?
back: P-gp is a primary active (ABC family) transporter that uses ATP to pump drugs out of cells. ABC transporters only mediate efflux, so P-gp acts as a protective pump that keeps xenobiotics out of tissues.

front: Which two drugs have low oral bioavailability partly because of gut P-gp?
back: Digoxin and cyclosporine. Part of the absorbed dose is pumped back into the gut lumen by P-gp in the epithelium, so less reaches blood.

front: Name P-gp inhibitors and inducers, and the effect of each on oral bioavailability of P-gp substrates.
back: Inhibitors (quinidine, verapamil, erythromycin) raise bioavailability; inducers (rifampin, phenobarbitone) lower it. Less pumping means more drug absorbed, more pumping means less.

front: A patient is stable on digoxin and then rifampin is added. Predict the effect and explain why P-gp and CYP3A4 are often considered together.
back: Rifampin induces gut P-gp, so more digoxin is pumped back into the lumen and oral bioavailability and plasma level fall, risking loss of effect. Many xenobiotics that induce or inhibit P-gp do the same to CYP3A4, so the two act together as a detoxifying system and an interacting drug can change absorption and metabolism at once.

front: Name drugs that are poorly effective orally because of ionisation or gut degradation.
back: Highly ionised drugs such as gentamicin and neostigmine are poorly absorbed. Penicillin G is destroyed by acid and insulin by peptidases. Hence these are given parenterally, or protected e.g. with enteric coating.

front: Why is a weak acid like aspirin absorbed well from acidic gastric fluid but a strongly ionised drug is not?
back: In acid, a weak acid stays mostly unionised and lipid soluble, so it crosses membranes. Highly ionised drugs such as gentamicin cannot diffuse across lipoidal membranes and are poorly absorbed orally.

front: Synthesis: how do pH differences between compartments (stomach, plasma, urine) decide where a weak acid or base accumulates, and how can this be used clinically?
back: Unionised drug diffuses freely, but whichever side has the pH that ionises it holds it. A weak acid ionises more in alkaline fluid and is trapped there; a weak base ionises more in acid fluid. Ionised drug cannot diffuse back, so urine pH alters excretion: acidic drugs are excreted faster in alkaline urine, basic drugs in acidified urine.

front: Compare primary and secondary active transport, with examples.
back: Primary uses ATP directly (ABC transporters, e.g. P-gp, efflux only). Secondary (SLC transporters) uses the downhill movement of another solute, mostly Na+, as energy: symport (same direction, e.g. SGLT1 glucose uptake in the intestine) or antiport (opposite direction, e.g. Na+/Ca2+ exchanger). SLC carriers can move drugs in and out.

front: Why are enteric-coated and sustained-release tablets used, and which problems do they solve?
back: An acid-resistant coat protects acid-labile drugs from gastric juice and spares the stomach from irritant drugs. Sustained-release particles are coated with slowly dissolving material, which lengthens the action of drugs with a brief duration. Drugs destroyed in the gut (penicillin G by acid, insulin by peptidases) still fail orally and need another route.

front: Why does levodopa act in the brain when dopamine itself does not?
back: The blood-brain barrier is lipoidal and has tight junctions, so nonlipid-soluble dopamine cannot enter. Levodopa, its precursor, gets in using the aromatic amino acid carrier (the same carrier that absorbs it from the gut), and is then converted to dopamine in the brain.

front: How can a co-administered drug or food reduce oral absorption, and how is it minimised?
back: In the gut lumen they can form poorly absorbed complexes, e.g. tetracyclines or iron with calcium salts, antacids or milk, and phenytoin with sucralfate. Food also dilutes drug and delays gastric emptying. Spacing the two drugs by 2-3 hours minimises the complexing.

Asymmetric movement of a drug across a polarised epithelial or endothelial layer: it is taken up at one membrane and pumped out at the opposite membrane. Why it matters: this is how drugs pass from the gut lumen into blood and how the liver and kidney excrete them.

front: In the liver, why does transcellular transport need an uptake and an efflux transporter together?
back: Sinusoidal uptake transporters (OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OATP2B1) take the compound into the hepatocyte, and canalicular efflux transporters (MDR1, MRP2, BCRP) pump it into bile. The combination moves a wide range of compounds across the cell.

front: How much of body weight is fat in obese and in lean adults?
back: Up to about 50% in obese individuals and about 10% in lean individuals. Fat is therefore a reservoir for lipid-soluble drugs.

front: Why does obesity raise the volume of distribution of a lipophilic drug?
back: A lipophilic drug dissolves in the larger fat mass, so more drug sits outside plasma and apparent V rises. A hydrophilic drug stays out of fat, so extra fat adds little to its distribution.

front: On what basis is the dose often calculated in exceptionally obese patients?
back: On body weight: individual dose = body weight (kg) / 70 x average adult dose. Body surface area has been argued to be a more accurate basis.

front: Why is adipose tissue a stable reservoir for lipid-soluble drugs?
back: It has low blood flow, so the stored drug leaves slowly and its levels stay steady for longer.

front: What is the lipid:water partition coefficient of a drug, and why does it matter?
back: The ratio of the drug's solubility in lipid to its solubility in water. A higher ratio means more of the drug dissolves in the membrane, so it diffuses faster across it.

front: Why is biotransformation needed for drug elimination?
back: Most drugs are lipid soluble and would be reabsorbed in renal tubules and persist for a long time. Metabolism converts them into polar, ionised products that kidney and bile can clear.

front: Where does drug metabolism mainly occur, and which other organs contribute?
back: Liver is the main site. Kidney, intestinal wall, lungs and plasma also metabolise drugs.

front: Phase I and phase II biotransformation reactions
text: Phase I reactions include {{oxidation}}, {{reduction}} and {{hydrolysis}}; phase II (synthetic) reactions include {{glucuronidation}}, {{acetylation}}, {{methylation}} and {{sulfation}}.

front: Compare phase I and phase II drug metabolism.
back: Phase I (functionalisation: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) adds or exposes a polar group; the product may be active or inactive. Phase II (conjugation) attaches an endogenous polar molecule, usually giving an inactive, excretable product. Morphine-6-glucuronide is a notable active conjugate.

front: Microsomal vs non-microsomal drug-metabolising enzymes: how do they differ?
back: Microsomal enzymes sit on the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, mainly of liver (also kidney, gut mucosa, lungs): CYP450 monooxygenases, UGTs, epoxide hydrolases. They carry out most oxidations, reductions, hydrolyses and glucuronidation, and are inducible. Non-microsomal enzymes lie in cytoplasm, mitochondria and plasma (esterases, amidases, some flavoprotein oxidases, most conjugases); they carry out all conjugations except glucuronidation, are not inducible, but many show genetic polymorphism (acetyltransferase, pseudocholinesterase). Hofmann elimination (atracurium) is spontaneous, non-enzymatic breakdown in body fluids.

front: Which CYP450 isoform metabolises the largest share of drugs, and name two inhibitors of it.
back: CYP3A4/5, which handles roughly half of all drugs. Inhibitors include erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice.

front: Which CYP families handle most drugs, and where do these enzymes sit in the cell?
back: CYP1, CYP2 and CYP3 families mediate about 70-80% of drug metabolism; 57 human CYPs exist. They sit in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (microsomes), mainly in liver, and CYP3A4 is also in the gut wall.

text: {{Erythromycin}}, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice inhibit CYP3A4/5; {{quinidine}}, fluoxetine and paroxetine inhibit CYP2D6; fluconazole and gemfibrozil inhibit CYP2C8/9; {{disulfiram}} and fomepizole inhibit CYP2E1.

front: Which CYP isoform forms the toxic metabolite of paracetamol, and what induces it?
back: CYP2E1 converts paracetamol to the reactive metabolite NAPQI. Chronic alcohol use and isoniazid induce CYP2E1. Glutathione conjugation normally detoxifies NAPQI; depletion leads to hepatotoxicity.

front: Why does codeine fail in CYP2D6 poor metabolisers but cause toxicity in ultrarapid metabolisers?
back: CYP2D6 O-demethylates codeine to morphine, which provides the analgesia. Poor metabolisers form little morphine and get weak pain relief; ultrarapid metabolisers form too much and can be toxic at usual doses.

front: A patient on simvastatin is started on clarithromycin. Explain the interaction and how it differs when the new drug is an inducer.
back: Simvastatin is a CYP3A4/5 substrate and clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4/5, so simvastatin clearance falls and its level rises. Inhibition acts within hours. An inducer such as rifampin instead lowers levels, but only after days because new enzyme must be synthesised. Drugs with saturable metabolism through a shared isoform are most prone to significant inhibition.

front: Describe the time course of microsomal enzyme induction.
back: Metabolic rate rises about 2 to 4 fold as enzyme synthesis increases. The peak develops over about 4 to 14 days while the inducer is given, and activity returns to baseline over roughly 1 to 3 weeks after withdrawal.

text: Phenobarbitone, phenytoin and carbamazepine induce {{CYP3A}}; rifampin induces {{CYP3A}} and {{CYP2C}}; chronic alcohol and {{isoniazid}} induce {{CYP2E1}}; cigarette smoke induces {{CYP1A}}.

front: What is the mechanism of enzyme induction, and how does its speed compare with inhibition?
back: Inducers increase synthesis of microsomal enzyme protein, mainly CYP450 and UGTs, through nuclear receptors such as PXR and CAR. Because new protein must be made, induction takes days, whereas inhibition acts within hours.

front: Why can rifampin cause contraceptive failure, and what other consequences does induction have?
back: Rifampin induces CYP3A and other enzymes, so oestrogen of oral contraceptives is inactivated faster and protection is lost. Induction also lowers nevirapine action, lets paracetamol toxicity occur at lower doses (more NAPQI forms), can precipitate acute intermittent porphyria (ALA synthetase derepressed), and speeds clearance of steroids and bilirubin.

front: Contrast the harmful and useful consequences of enzyme induction, with an example of each.
back: Harm: therapeutic failure of drugs cleared by the induced pathway (contraceptive failure, loss of nevirapine action), more toxic metabolite from paracetamol, porphyria, and unpredictable levels when an inducer is used intermittently with anticoagulants, hypoglycaemics, antiepileptics or antihypertensives. Use: phenobarbitone hastens bilirubin clearance in congenital non-haemolytic jaundice, phenytoin in Cushing syndrome, and faster clearance of accumulated poison in chronic poisoning. Autoinduction (carbamazepine, rifampin, nevirapine) means doses may need adjusting with time.

front: What is the most important conjugation pathway in drug metabolism?
back: Glucuronidation by UDP-glucuronosyl transferases (UGTs), acting on -OH and -COOH groups. Glucuronides excreted in bile can be cleaved by gut bacteria and reabsorbed, causing enterohepatic cycling.

text: N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) polymorphism gives {{slow}} and {{fast}} acetylator phenotypes. Acetylated drugs include {{isoniazid}}, {{hydralazine}}, procainamide, dapsone and sulfonamides; isoniazid neuropathy and hydralazine or procainamide {{lupus}} occur mainly in slow acetylators.

front: List the phase II conjugation reactions with their co-substrates and one drug for each.
back: Glucuronidation (UDP-glucuronic acid; morphine, paracetamol); acetylation (acetyl-CoA; isoniazid, sulfonamides); methylation (methionine; adrenaline, methyldopa); sulfation (sulfotransferases; chloramphenicol, steroids); glutathione conjugation (glutathione-S-transferase; NAPQI); glycine conjugation (salicylates, minor pathway). Conjugates are usually inactive and more polar.

front: What is the enzyme defect in Gilbert syndrome and why does it matter for drugs?
back: UGT1A1 activity is reduced (mainly the UGT1A1*28 promoter variant, with seven TA repeats). UGT1A1 glucuronidation is the rate-limiting step of bilirubin clearance, so drugs that compete for or inhibit it raise bilirubin. Irinotecan's active metabolite SN-38 is inactivated by UGT1A1, so Gilbert patients get higher SN-38 levels and more haematological and GI toxicity.

front: Why are newborns more vulnerable to chloramphenicol and opioids?
back: Neonatal drug-metabolising enzymes are immature: phase I activity reaches adult levels only over the first few months, and glucuronidation and other conjugations are slower. Drugs cleared by these routes accumulate. Species differences show the same principle (cats lack glucuronidation, dogs lack acetylation).

front: Define first-pass metabolism and give the formula for oral bioavailability.
back: First-pass (presystemic) metabolism is metabolism of an orally given drug in the gut wall (CYP3A4 is expressed in intestine) and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation. Oral F = fraction absorbed x (1 - hepatic extraction ratio). Sublingual, transdermal and parenteral routes avoid it; rectal avoids it only partly.

front: Define clearance and give its formula.
back: Clearance is the theoretical volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time. CL = rate of elimination / plasma concentration.

front: Give the formula for elimination half-life and state how many half-lives are needed for near-complete elimination.
back: t1/2 = 0.693 x V / CL. It is a derived value and is constant only for first-order elimination. About 4 to 5 half-lives are needed for nearly complete elimination (about 94 percent after four).

front: A drug has a high hepatic extraction ratio. Predict its oral dose, bioavailability and levels in severe liver disease or with a competing drug.
back: High extraction means a large oral fraction is lost on first pass, so the oral dose is much higher than the parenteral one and varies widely between individuals. In severe liver disease or when a competing drug occupies the enzyme, extraction falls, oral bioavailability rises and levels can become toxic at the usual dose. Clearance of such drugs follows hepatic blood flow, so a drug that lowers hepatic blood flow slows it (propranolol reduces lidocaine metabolism this way). Routes bypassing first pass (sublingual, transdermal, parenteral) are used instead, e.g. glyceryl trinitrate.

The proximal tubule secretes organic {{acids}} through the OAT system and organic {{bases}} through the OCT system; efflux pumps {{P-gp}} and {{MRP2}} sit on the luminal membrane.

front: What are the three processes of renal drug excretion and which matters most?
back: Net excretion = (glomerular filtration + tubular secretion) minus tubular reabsorption. Only unbound drug is filtered (GFR about 120 mL/min). Reabsorption is passive and depends on lipid solubility and ionisation. Tubular secretion is active transport: OAT for acids and OCT for bases.

front: Which drugs are excreted in bile, and why can this prolong their action?
back: Biliary excretion suits conjugates and compounds of molecular weight above about 300, handled by OATP, MRP2, OCT and P-gp. High biliary levels occur with erythromycin, ampicillin, rifampin, tetracycline, oral contraceptives and vecuronium. Gut bacteria can free the drug from its glucuronide so it is reabsorbed (enterohepatic cycling), prolonging action.

front: How does urine pH affect renal excretion of weak acids and weak bases?
back: Only un-ionised drug is reabsorbed from the tubule. Weak acids are excreted faster in alkaline urine and weak bases in acidic urine. Urine is alkalinised in barbiturate and salicylate poisoning. Acidifying urine could speed excretion of bases (morphine, amphetamine) but is not practised, because acidosis can cause rhabdomyolysis and cardiotoxicity.

front: Explain the effect of probenecid on penicillin and uric acid.
back: Probenecid competes for the OAT organic-acid secretory transporter, so penicillin and ampicillin secretion falls and their action is prolonged. It also blocks urate reabsorption, so uric acid excretion rises (uricosuric); aspirin blocks this uricosuric effect.

front: Write the formula for a loading dose and say what it depends on.
back: Loading dose = target plasma concentration x V / F. It depends on volume of distribution and bioavailability, not on clearance or half-life.

front: Short note: Zero-order kinetics of elimination

points: Elimination rate is constant whatever the plasma concentration
A constant amount is eliminated per unit time
Clearance falls as concentration rises
Ethyl alcohol (example in KDT8)
Some drugs move from first-order to zero-order at high doses, so plasma concentration rises disproportionately with dose

front: Define first-order and zero-order elimination with an example of each.
back: First order: rate of elimination is proportional to concentration, so clearance and half-life are constant (most drugs, as enzymes are in excess). Zero order (capacity-limited, Michaelis-Menten): a constant amount is eliminated per unit time, clearance falls as concentration rises and half-life lengthens with dose (ethanol; phenytoin and tolbutamide at higher doses).

front: How is steady-state concentration determined, and what is the plateau principle?
back: Css = dose rate / CL, so for a target Css, dose rate = Css x CL (divide by F for oral). With repeated dosing, drug accumulates until intake equals elimination, and this takes about 4 to 5 half-lives regardless of dose.

front: Short note: Prolongation of drug action

points: Less frequent dosing and better adherence
Smoother plasma levels with fewer peak-related side effects
Round-the-clock control (e.g. overnight)
Slow absorption: sustained or controlled-release oral forms, depot i.m. or s.c. injections, implants, transdermal patches
Highly protein-bound congeners released slowly (e.g. sulfadoxine)
Slower metabolism: chemical change (ethinyl estradiol vs estradiol) or enzyme inhibition (allopurinol with 6-mercaptopurine; ritonavir boosting)
Reduced tubular secretion: probenecid with penicillin
Controlled-release forms suit drugs with half-life under 4 h
Not needed for drugs with half-life over 12 h (doxycycline, amlodipine) or for brief-effect drugs (hypnotics)

front: Maintenance dose and steady state: what is the formula, and how long does steady state take?
back: Maintenance dose rate = target Css x CL / F; it depends on clearance (or half-life). With repeated dosing at a fixed rate, drug accumulates until intake equals elimination (plateau principle); steady state is reached in about 4 to 5 half-lives. A loading dose is used when waiting this long is unacceptable (digoxin, chloroquine, amiodarone).

points: Narrow-margin drugs: digoxin, lithium, aminoglycosides, anticonvulsants, theophylline
Large individual variation: antidepressants, lithium
Toxic drugs in renal failure
Suspected poisoning
Unexplained treatment failure or adherence check
Long-acting drugs: trough steady-state level, just before the next dose
Short-acting drugs: post-absorptive peak, about 1 to 2 h after oral or IM dose
Poisoning: early sample, then repeated to track clearance
Drugs with easily measured effect: antihypertensives, oral anticoagulants, diuretics
Prodrugs such as levodopa
Hit-and-run drugs: reserpine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole
Irreversible drugs such as organophosphates
Revised dose rate = previous dose rate x target Css / measured Css
Elimination = metabolism + excretion
Clearance: volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time
Constant fraction eliminated per unit time; rate proportional to concentration
Clearance and half-life constant; plasma level falls exponentially
Applies to most drugs in the therapeutic range; dose rate and steady-state level linearly related
Constant amount eliminated per unit time once enzymes are saturated (ethyl alcohol)
Rate = Vmax x C / (Km + C)
Clearance falls and half-life lengthens as dose rises
Phenytoin, tolbutamide, theophylline and warfarin shift from first to zero order at higher doses
Plasma concentration rises disproportionately with dose (nonlinear elimination)
Small dose increments can cause toxicity; increase in small steps
Monitor plasma levels (TDM)
Know whether a drug's elimination is saturable before adjusting its dose

front: Short note: Pharmacometrics in individual dosing

points: Dosing tools use pharmacokinetic models built from representative patient populations
Such tools predict an individual's dose from that patient's measured response
Compare predicted pharmacokinetic parameters with the measured concentration
Example: expected clearance 5.5 L/h; a higher measured level gives a revised clearance of 3.5 L/h, so the daily dose is halved
The implicit method is misleading before steady state
At least a week of regular dosing (four half-lives) must pass first

front: Digoxin has a long half-life. Explain how you would start therapy and adjust it after a measured level.
back: Waiting 4 to 5 half-lives to reach steady state is too slow, so a loading dose (target Cp x V / F, depending on V not on CL) is given, then maintenance doses (target Css x CL / F). If a measured level differs from prediction by more than 20%, revise V or CL for that patient (Katzung). Individual Css can be 1/3 to 3 times the population estimate. Digoxin has a low therapeutic index, so therapeutic drug monitoring is useful.

front: What is Hofmann elimination, and why does it make a drug independent of liver and kidney function?
back: Hofmann elimination is inactivation in body fluids by spontaneous molecular rearrangement, with no enzyme involved (e.g. atracurium). Since no organ enzyme or excretory route is needed, its disposal does not depend on hepatic metabolism, unlike enzyme-mediated biotransformation.

front: How can you tell from renal clearance that a drug is actively secreted by the tubules?
back: Glomerular filtration rate is about 120 mL/min, which is the most that filtration alone can clear. If a drug renal clearance is above that, extra removal by tubular secretion (OAT or OCT transporters) must be happening.

front: What is the "boosted" protease inhibitor strategy and which enzyme does it exploit?
back: Low-dose ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4, so the levels of co-given protease inhibitors (atazanavir, lopinavir, saquinavir) rise and their doses can be lowered. Inhibition is dose related and can precipitate toxicity of the affected drug.

front: What happens to a high first-pass drug that inhibits its own metabolism, for example verapamil?
back: Oral bioavailability rises and systemic clearance falls, so half-life is prolonged. With chronic dosing verapamil bioavailability nearly doubles for this reason.

front: Name the routes by which drugs and metabolites leave the body.
back: Urine (the main route), bile into faeces, exhaled air, saliva and sweat (minor), and breast milk.
A drug or its glucuronide is secreted in bile, split by gut bacteria, and the freed drug is reabsorbed back to the liver. This keeps the drug in the body longer.

front: Why are general anaesthetic gases and alcohol removed by the lungs whatever their lipid solubility?
back: Alveolar transfer depends on the partial pressure of the gas or vapour in blood, not on its lipid solubility.

front: Why does drug excretion into breast milk matter mainly for the infant?
back: Most drugs cross by passive diffusion, so lipid-soluble, weakly protein-bound drugs pass best. The infant receives a small dose, but a lactating mother should take any drug only when essential.

front: Name the drugs or substances excreted in significant amounts in saliva or sweat.
back: Lithium, potassium iodide, rifampin and heavy metals. Saliva and sweat are of minor importance for drug excretion.

front: Why does renal excretion of aminoglycosides parallel GFR?
back: They are highly ionised and poorly lipid-soluble, so tubules do not reabsorb them. Their excretion therefore follows GFR.

front: Essay: Routes of drug excretion, with examples

points: Drugs and metabolites leave the body by urine, bile and faeces, exhaled air, saliva and sweat, and milk
Urine is the most important route for most drugs
Net excretion = (filtration + secretion) minus reabsorption
Only free drug is filtered; GFR about 120 mL/min
Active secretion by OAT (penicillin, probenecid) and OCT (procainamide, cimetidine)
Urine pH traps weak acids and bases; aminoglycosides follow GFR
Active secretion into bile by OATP, MRP2, OCT and P-gp
Molecules above MW 300 favour bile
Enterohepatic cycling prolongs action; e.g. erythromycin, rifampin
Anthracene purgatives and heavy metals go directly into the colon
Volatile anaesthetics and alcohol leave by the lungs
Depends on blood partial pressure, not lipid solubility
Saliva and sweat are minor routes: lithium, potassium iodide, rifampin, heavy metals
Milk: passive diffusion of lipid-soluble drugs; infant exposure is small but drugs should be used in lactation only when essential
Route depends on lipid solubility, ionisation, MW and protein binding
Renal route falls with age and renal failure, so doses are adjusted

front: Short note: Pharmacokinetic parameters governing drug disposition

points: Bioavailability (F), volume of distribution (V) and clearance (CL)
Elimination rate constant k and half-life are derived from V and CL
CL = rate of elimination / plasma concentration
First-order: CL constant; zero-order: CL falls as concentration rises
Apparent volume the drug would occupy at plasma concentration
Example: 1000 mg giving 50 mg/L means V = 20 L
Large V (digoxin 6 L/kg) means drug is in tissues, so haemodialysis removes little
k = CL / V
Nearly complete elimination in 4 to 5 half-lives
Css = dose rate / CL
Oral dose rate for target Css = target Css x CL / F
Loading dose = target Cp x V / F (depends only on V); maintenance depends on CL
Penicillin G t1/2 30 min; aspirin 4 h; digoxin 40 h; phenobarbitone 90 h; digitoxin 7 days

front: Which three fundamental parameters govern drug disposition, and what are their symbols?
back: Bioavailability (F), volume of distribution (V) and clearance (CL). F sets how much of the dose arrives, V sets the loading dose, and CL sets the maintenance dose. Half-life and k derive from V and CL.

front: Define apparent volume of distribution and give a worked example.
back: The volume the drug would occupy if spread uniformly at the plasma concentration. 1000 mg giving 50 mg/L means V = 20 L.

front: Why is half-life not an exact index of drug elimination?
back: t1/2 = 0.693 x V / CL depends on two variables that can change independently, so it is a useful guide rather than an exact measure.

front: Why are drugs with a large volume of distribution not easily removed by haemodialysis?
back: Most of the drug is held in tissues, so plasma concentration is low. Examples: digoxin 6 L/kg, propranolol 4 L/kg, morphine 3.5 L/kg.

front: Which parameter governs the maintenance dose rate, and which governs the loading dose?
back: The maintenance dose rate depends on clearance (Css = dose rate / CL), since it must replace what is cleared. The loading dose depends only on volume of distribution (with F), since it fills the distribution volume.

front: Why do drugs with long half-lives need a loading dose?
back: Steady state takes about 4 half-lives, which can be clinically too slow. A loading dose gives a rapid effect and the maintenance dose then sustains it.

The kinetic side of chronopharmacology: how the body absorbs, distributes, metabolises and excretes a drug depends on the time of day it is given. Why it matters: the same dose can give different levels, and so different effect and toxicity, at different hours.

front: How does dose timing change toxicity for aminoglycosides and ceftriaxone?
back: Aminoglycosides (amikacin, gentamicin): a single daily dose given in the active day period lowers renal toxicity. Ceftriaxone: night-time dosing lowers toxicity because its total clearance is highest at night.

points: Study of how the time of administration alters absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion
One branch of chronopharmacology, alongside chronotherapeutics, chronesthesy, chronergy and chronotoxicology
Master clock sits in the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus; light entrains it
Rhythms in gastric acid and pH, motility and emptying, GI blood flow, protein binding, hepatic enzyme activity and blood flow, renal filtration, tubular reabsorption and urinary pH
Antibiotics: efficacy tracks the time concentration stays above MIC; ciprofloxacin is eliminated faster at 10 am than at 10 pm
Antihypertensives: lipophilic drugs give higher Cmax and shorter tmax in the morning; non-dipper patients are dosed once daily in the evening (ACE inhibitors, sartans, calcium antagonists)
Antiepileptic: valproic acid Cmax and absorption rate are higher in the morning
Anticancer: cisplatin renal toxicity is lower with evening dosing
Statins: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors work better in the evening, except atorvastatin
Not every drug shows it, and the timing effects here are reported drug by drug, not for a whole class
Circadian results for an individual drug are not transferable to other drugs of the same class without data
Time doses to gain efficacy or cut toxicity, a principle called chronotherapy
In cancer, time of day can change outcome (chronomodulation), since leukaemic and normal cells keep different rhythms

front: Short note: Pharmacokinetic changes in pregnancy

points: Reduced gastrointestinal motility delays absorption of oral drugs
Plasma and extracellular fluid volume expand: volume of distribution may rise
Albumin falls but alpha-1 acid glycoprotein rises: free fraction of acidic drugs increases, of basic drugs decreases
Marked rise in renal blood flow: polar drugs cleared faster
Hepatic microsomal enzymes induced: many drugs metabolised faster
Changes are greatest in the third trimester
Overall effect is complex and hard to predict

front: Which drug properties govern transfer across the placenta?
back: Lipid solubility (thiopental crosses almost at once and can sedate the newborn), degree of ionisation (succinylcholine and tubocurarine cross slowly), molecular weight (250-500 cross readily, 500-1000 with difficulty, above 1000 very poorly), placental transporters such as P-glycoprotein, and protein binding. Basic drugs with pKa above 7.4 are ion-trapped in the slightly more acidic fetal blood (pH 7.3).

front: What is ion trapping across the placenta, and which drugs does it affect?
back: Fetal blood is slightly more acidic than maternal blood (about pH 7.3 versus 7.4). Basic drugs with a pKa above 7.4 therefore tend to accumulate in the fetus, so fetal exposure can exceed what maternal levels suggest.

front: Salicylate is almost fully ionised, so why does it still cross the placenta readily?
back: The small unionised fraction is highly lipid-soluble and crosses freely. Ionisation alone does not stop transfer. Contrast succinylcholine and tubocurarine, which are highly ionised and cross slowly.

front: Why is heparin preferred to warfarin for anticoagulation in pregnancy?
back: Heparin (including low-molecular-weight heparins) is a large polar molecule that does not cross the placenta, whereas warfarin crosses and is teratogenic; warfarin should be avoided in the first trimester and beyond, because the fetal brain keeps developing.

front: How do placental transporters limit fetal drug exposure? Give examples.
back: P-glycoprotein (MDR1) pumps drugs such as vinblastine, doxorubicin and HIV protease inhibitors back into the maternal blood (for protease inhibitors this may raise the risk of vertical HIV transmission). Glyburide is effluxed by BCRP and MRP3 and is also more than 98.8% protein bound, so fetal levels stay lower than maternal.

front: Why can prednisolone be used in a pregnant woman with little fetal corticosteroid exposure?
back: The placenta converts prednisolone to the inactive prednisone, so the fetus is largely spared active steroid. The placenta also oxidises some drugs (e.g. pentobarbital), but may create toxic metabolites (e.g. from ethanol, benzpyrenes).

front: Do large protein drugs such as monoclonal antibodies reach the fetus?
back: Yes. From the second trimester the placenta develops transporters that carry immunoglobulins to the fetus. Biological drugs such as anti-TNF agents have been found in cord blood, with reports of neonatal neutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia and disseminated BCG infection.

front: Essay: Drug transfer across the placenta and fetal exposure

points: Placenta is not an absolute barrier: most drugs cross, and polar compounds cross in measurable amounts when the maternal-fetal gradient is high
Maternal physiology also shifts kinetics (larger fluid volume, lower albumin, faster renal and hepatic clearance)
Lipid solubility: thiopental crosses almost at once
Ionisation: succinylcholine and tubocurarine cross slowly; salicylate still crosses via its unionised fraction
Molecular weight: 250-500 cross readily, 500-1000 with difficulty, above 1000 very poorly (heparin)
Very lipid-soluble drugs: transfer limited by placental blood flow
Maternal binding higher than fetal for sulfonamides, barbiturates, phenytoin, local anaesthetics
Fetal pH 7.3 vs maternal 7.4: basic drugs trapped in the fetus
P-glycoprotein pumps vinblastine, doxorubicin and HIV protease inhibitors back to the mother
Glyburide effluxed by BCRP and MRP3, plus very high protein binding
Placenta converts prednisolone to inactive prednisone; may make toxic metabolites from ethanol
Immunoglobulin transporters from the second trimester carry antibodies and anti-TNF drugs
Heparin chosen over warfarin
Prednisolone spares the fetus
Antiretrovirals and maternal drugs for fetal arrhythmia can be given to treat the fetus

front: What are the three stages at which drugs can affect the foetus?
back: Fertilisation and implantation (conception to day 17): pregnancy fails, often unnoticed. Organogenesis (days 18-55): most vulnerable, structural deformities. Growth and development (day 56 onwards): functional and developmental defects, e.g. organ hypoplasia with ACE inhibitors, ductus closure with NSAIDs, masculinisation by androgens and progestins, foetal goitre with antithyroid drugs and lithium.

front: Match: human teratogens and their defects
text: Thalidomide: {{phocomelia}}; warfarin: {{depressed nose}}, eye and hand defects; phenytoin: hypoplastic phalanges, {{cleft lip/palate}}; valproate and carbamazepine: {{neural tube defects}}; stilboestrol: {{vaginal carcinoma}} in teenage daughters; tetracyclines: {{discoloured teeth}}; ACE inhibitors: {{organ hypoplasia}}; lithium: {{heart}} and other defects; isotretinoin: craniofacial, heart and CNS defects; alcohol: {{foetal alcohol syndrome}}; indomethacin/aspirin: premature closure of {{ductus arteriosus}}.

front: What three criteria define a drug as a teratogen?
back: It produces a characteristic set of malformations (selectivity for target organs); it acts at a particular stage of development, such as the organogenesis window of those organs; and its incidence is dose-dependent. Teratogenic effects also include growth restriction, miscarriage, stillbirth and neurocognitive delay.

front: Which supplement reduces neural tube defects, and by how much?
back: Folic acid taken before and during early pregnancy; Katzung cites a reduction in neural tube defects of up to 75%.

front: How has the US FDA changed pregnancy labelling, and why?
back: The old A, B, C, D, X letter categories were removed under rules effective 30 June 2015. Labels now carry narrative sections (Risk Summary, Clinical Considerations, Data) including pregnancy-registry data, and cover lactation and people of reproductive potential. The letters were dropped because about three-quarters of drugs fell into category C, and the grading had become outdated.

front: What points should be covered when counselling a pregnant woman about drug exposure?
back: Fewer than 30 drugs are proven human teratogens and hundreds are known to be safe. The baseline risk of a neonatal abnormality without any exposure is about 3%. The risk of leaving the maternal condition untreated must be weighed (stopping SSRIs for depression has caused serious maternal morbidity). Good counselling has been shown to prevent unnecessary abortions.

front: Why does the stage of exposure change the kind of fetal harm? Give drug examples.
back: Before day 17 the outcome is all-or-none (failure of pregnancy). In organogenesis (days 18-55) structural defects arise, e.g. thalidomide limb defects (phocomelia). From day 56 the effects are functional or growth-related: ACE inhibitors cause hypoplasia of lungs and kidneys, NSAIDs in late pregnancy close the ductus arteriosus, androgens and progestins masculinise a female fetus, and antithyroid drugs or lithium cause fetal goitre.

points: Type of malformation depends on the drug and on the stage of exposure
Foetal exposure depends on maternal blood level and duration of drug in maternal circulation
Table of human teratogens lists defects such as limb, cardiac and neural tube defects, growth retardation, and foetal alcohol syndrome
Teratogenic potential must be judged against the background risk of congenital abnormality

front: Why is it wise to avoid all drugs in pregnancy even when a drug has a reassuring FDA category, and what can lower neural tube defects?
back: The FDA graded birth-defect risk in five categories (A safe to X contraindicated), but the grading is outdated for many drugs as evidence accumulates. Only a few exposed mothers deliver a deformed baby, so the exact risk is hard to estimate; hence avoid drugs unless compelling. Folate therapy in pregnancy can reduce neural tube defects, spontaneous or drug-induced.

front: How do mutagenicity and carcinogenicity of a drug arise, and which drugs are implicated?
back: Oxidation of the drug forms reactive intermediates that bind DNA covalently and cause mutations, which can be heritable. If the altered DNA affects proto-oncogenes or their inhibitors, a tumour can follow, usually after 10-40 years. Implicated: anticancer drugs, radioisotopes, estrogens, tobacco. Such drugs are generally not approved, or are withdrawn, unless needed in life-threatening disease.

front: When is infant exposure through breast milk considered negligible, and why avoid stopping breastfeeding needlessly?
back: When the infant receives under 10% of the weight-corrected maternal dose, toxicity is unlikely. Most drugs reach milk only in small amounts, while formula feeding carries higher infant illness and death, so stopping is not free of harm.

front: How can a mother time a relatively safe drug to minimise infant exposure?
back: Take it 30-60 minutes after nursing and 3-4 hours before the next feed, so milk levels are lowest when the baby feeds. A drug such as chloral hydrate can sedate the infant if feeding falls at the peak milk concentration.

front: Which drugs reach clinically meaningful levels in breast milk?
back: Lithium, amiodarone and atenolol. Lithium reaches a milk concentration equal to the mother's serum level, so infant exposure can be large.

front: Why is codeine risky for breastfeeding mothers?
back: Mothers who are CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers make much more morphine, which passes into milk; a neonatal death from opioid toxicity was traced to this. Neonates are also extra sensitive because their blood-brain barrier has little P-glycoprotein, so more morphine enters the brain. The FDA issued a warning on codeine-containing painkillers in lactation.

front: Why are tetracycline, isoniazid, chloramphenicol and radioiodine a concern during breastfeeding?
back: Tetracycline stains the infant's developing teeth permanently. Isoniazid can cause infant pyridoxine deficiency, so the mother should take pyridoxine. Chloramphenicol risks marrow suppression, so it is advised against. Radioiodine suppresses the infant's thyroid and may raise later thyroid cancer risk up to 10-fold; breastfeeding is stopped after large doses and withheld after small ones.

front: How should sedatives and opioids be handled in a breastfeeding mother?
back: Hypnotic barbiturates cause infant lethargy and poor suck; diazepam sedates and accumulates because of its long half-life. Chronic maternal opioid use can prolong neonatal dependence. Methadone may be continued under supervision without abrupt stopping, with the infant watched for withdrawal; codeine is risky if the mother is a CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser.

front: Short note: Drug use during lactation

points: Most drugs appear in milk, usually in low amounts
Infant dose below 10% of the maternal weight-corrected dose: toxicity unlikely
Formula feeding carries higher infant morbidity, so avoid needless stopping of breastfeeding
Take a relatively safe drug 30-60 min after a feed and 3-4 h before the next
Lithium: milk level equals maternal serum
Amiodarone, atenolol: clinically meaningful exposure
Tetracycline: milk about 70% of serum, tooth staining
Isoniazid: pyridoxine deficiency unless mother supplemented
Barbiturates, chloral hydrate, diazepam: sedation; diazepam accumulates
Methadone: breastfeeding possible with care; taper slowly
Codeine in CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser mothers: neonatal opioid death; FDA warning

front: Short note: Pharmacokinetics in the neonate

points: Low gastric acid (slower rise in preterm) and gastric emptying up to 6-8 h
Irregular peristalsis; low bile acids and lipase
Thin skin: faster transdermal absorption; rectal absorption fast and reliable
Erratic i.m. absorption in sick preterm infants with poor perfusion
Body water 70-75% (preterm 85%) vs adult 50-60%; extracellular water 40% vs 20%
Larger volume for water-soluble drugs (aminoglycosides)
Lower protein binding: more free drug
Leaky blood-brain barrier
CYP and conjugation activity 50-70% of adult
Glucuronidation matures by 3-4 years
Chloramphenicol gray baby syndrome
GFR 30-40% of adult at birth; reaches adult values by 6-12 months (Katzung)
Half-life of gentamicin and penicillin prolonged 3-5 times (KDT)

front: How should a child's dose be calculated, and why not with old age-based formulae?
back: Preferably by body weight (mg/kg), as most manufacturers recommend. Age-based formulae are no longer used. Infant doses must be learnt as such, because infants differ physiologically from adults and cannot be dosed from a formula.

front: Name four adverse effects that occur particularly in growing children.
back: Growth suppression with corticosteroids; early epiphyseal fusion and stunting with androgens; tetracycline deposition in growing teeth causing discolouration and deformity; dystonic reactions to phenothiazines are more frequent.

front: Why can metered-dose inhalers and solid dosage forms be a problem in young children?
back: Young children find solid dosage forms and metered-dose inhalers difficult to administer.

front: How can drugs cause kernicterus in a neonate, and which drug is avoided for this reason?
back: Some drugs displace bilirubin from albumin; because the neonatal blood-brain barrier is permeable, free bilirubin enters the brain. This happened when sulfonamides were given to preterm neonates. Ceftriaxone is avoided completely in infants under 2 months. Conversely, rising bilirubin can displace drugs such as phenytoin and raise their free level.

front: Why do toddlers and young children often need a higher mg/kg dose than adults?
back: After the first year, drug metabolism and renal elimination often exceed adult rates. The half-lives of theophylline, phenytoin and carbamazepine are shorter than in adults, and the daily per-kg digoxin dose is higher in children (KDT: about 8-12 microgram/kg vs 3-5 microgram/kg in adults).

front: What practical problems with dosage forms and adherence occur in paediatric practice?
back: Suspensions (e.g. phenytoin) must be shaken each time or early doses are weak and late doses toxic; elixirs need no shaking. Household teaspoons vary from 2.5 to 7.8 mL, so a calibrated spoon or syringe should be used. Parents often stop antibiotics once the child feels well. Weight-based calculations risk tenfold decimal errors (e.g. digoxin): use a leading zero, avoid trailing zeros and double-check high-risk drugs.

front: Why is the digoxin dose per kg higher in children, yet it accumulates in neonates?
back: Toddlers clear digoxin faster than adults, so the dose per kg is much higher. Neonates eliminate it slowly (digoxin half-life 60-70 h in neonates vs 30-60 h in adults) because renal clearance is immature, so it accumulates.

front: Short note: Drug therapy in neonates

points: Infants are not small adults
Renal clearance is low and tubular transport immature at birth
Conjugation is inefficient, so drugs such as chloramphenicol accumulate
Grey baby syndrome occurs after high doses, especially in premature neonates
Feeding stops, vomiting and hypotonia follow
Benzyl alcohol preservative has been linked to a fatal toxic syndrome in neonates
Unpreserved epoetin is therefore used for anaemia of prematurity

front: Short note: Principles of drug administration in children

points: Children's dose can be calculated on body weight: child weight (kg) / 70 x average adult dose
Body surface area is argued to be a more accurate basis for dose calculation
Oral drops are the preferred dosage form for infants and young children

Rectal route (suppository or retention enema) can be used with recurrent vomiting or unconsciousness; in general absorption is slower and less predictable, though diazepam solution and paracetamol suppository are dependably absorbed. In infants and young children rectal absorption is fast and predictable, which is why diazepam solution is given rectally for febrile seizures under 5 years
Children can react more strongly: a single triflupromazine dose causes muscular dystonias in some, especially children

front: Short note: Pharmacokinetic changes in the elderly

points: Little real change; slower gastric emptying and reduced gut motility and blood flow may slow it
Less lean mass and body water, more fat
Volume of distribution rises for lipophilic and falls for hydrophilic drugs
Albumin falls; alpha-1 acid glycoprotein may rise
Hepatic blood flow falls to about 55-60% of young adult
Phase I (CYP) affected more than phase II conjugation
Lower clearance of e.g. diazepam, imipramine, propranolol, theophylline; not of lorazepam, oxazepam, warfarin
GFR about 75% at 50 years and 50% at 75 years (KDT)
Serum creatinine misleads because muscle mass falls; estimate creatinine clearance from age, weight and serum creatinine

front: Write the formula used to estimate creatinine clearance in an elderly patient.
back: CLcr (mL/min) = (140 - age) x weight (kg) / (72 x serum creatinine in mg/dL); multiply by 0.85 for women. It is only a population estimate; up to a third of elderly people have normal renal function, and a timed 12- or 24-h clearance is needed for precision.
A list of potentially inappropriate medications for older persons. It is organised by body system and therapeutic category, and gives the rationale and quality of evidence for each entry.

front: What do the START and STOPP tools do in prescribing for older patients?
back: START lists evidence-based prescribing indicators by body system, to alert the prescriber to the right treatment. STOPP identifies potentially inappropriate medicines in older persons' prescriptions and is used for medication review.

front: What does the Medication Appropriateness Index check for each prescribed drug?
back: Whether the drug is indicated, whether it is effective, whether the dose is appropriate, whether it is cost-effective, and whether it duplicates another therapy.

front: Give examples of altered drug sensitivity in the elderly.
back: More sensitive to sedative-hypnotics and to respiratory depression by opioids; relatively intolerant to digitalis; reduced responsiveness to beta-adrenoceptor agonists and antagonists; even mild anticholinergic action worsens voiding in men with prostatism; phenothiazines cause more orthostatic hypotension. Benzodiazepine and barbiturate half-lives rise by 50-150% between 30 and 70 years.

front: Why are adverse drug reactions so common in the elderly, and what is a 'brown bag' review?
back: ADR incidence is at least twice that of younger people, rising from about 10% with one drug to nearly 100% with ten. Causes: altered kinetics, several prescribers, OTC and herbal products, interactions (e.g. cimetidine inhibiting metabolism of phenytoin, warfarin, beta blockers) and nonadherence. In a brown bag review the patient brings every medicine and supplement; duplicates and unnecessary drugs are removed, often cutting the total by 30-50%.

front: State the principles of prescribing for geriatric patients.
back: Take a careful drug history; prescribe only for a specific rational indication; define the goal, start low and titrate, waiting at least three (age-adjusted) half-lives before increasing; check blood levels if the usual dose fails; keep a high suspicion for reactions and interactions, including OTC and herbal products; simplify the regimen and reduce the number of drugs.

front: How should digoxin loading and maintenance doses be adjusted in an elderly patient?
back: Reduce the loading dose because the apparent volume of distribution is smaller (less lean mass and water), and reduce the maintenance dose because renal clearance is lower.

points: Kinetic changes: larger Vd, altered binding, faster renal and hepatic clearance
Placental transfer: lipid solubility, ionisation, size, transporters
Teratogenic stages; known teratogens; FDA narrative labelling since 2015
Avoid drugs unless compelling; folate supplementation
Most drugs low in milk; under 10% infant dose is safe
Concern: lithium, amiodarone, atenolol, tetracycline, sedatives, codeine
Immature metabolism and GFR; more body water; leaky BBB
Gray baby, kernicterus
Faster clearance in toddlers; weight-based dosing; dosage-form errors
Reduced renal clearance; estimated creatinine clearance
Altered Vd and phase I metabolism; more sensitivity to CNS drugs
Polypharmacy, ADRs, brown bag review; start low, go slow
Higher bioavailability, low albumin, reduced clearance
Prefer oxazepam/lorazepam; avoid hepatotoxins
Reduce maintenance dose by CLcr; loading dose unchanged
Avoid nephrotoxins, pethidine, K-sparing diuretics, thiazides

front: What parameters make up the Child-Pugh score, and what are the classes?
back: The score uses bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy. Class A (mild) is 5-6 points, class B (moderate) 7-9 points and class C (severe) 10-15 points. Class B and C patients have decompensated cirrhosis.

front: Why is ponesimod not recommended in some patients with liver disease?
back: It is not recommended for patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment, that is Child-Pugh class B or C.

front: Which fluoroquinolone is avoided in liver disease, and which was withdrawn for hepatotoxicity?
back: Pefloxacin is listed among antimicrobials to avoid in liver disease, and it is mainly eliminated by the liver. Trovafloxacin was hepatotoxic and was withdrawn from the US market.
