front: One cited study: one-year mortality by Child-Pugh class?
back: Class A 0%, class B 20%, class C 55%.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Use of the Child Pugh Score in Liver Disease (2023) https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542308/

front: How does cirrhosis change drug handling, per the expert panel's introduction?
back: Reduced metabolic capacity, decreased protein synthesis and portosystemic shunting.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

front: Which Child-Pugh stages did the cirrhosis dosing panel cover?
back: Stages A, B and C.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

front: What three recommendation options did the panel use for each drug?
back: No dose adjustment, dose adjustment, or avoidance of administration.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

front: How is the starting dose of obeticholic acid set according to liver disease stage?
back: Used when there is no adequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid after at least 1 year, or when it is not tolerated. Non-cirrhotic or Child-Pugh A: start 5 mg once daily for 3 months, then 10 mg once daily at most. Child-Pugh B or C, or a prior decompensation event: start 5 mg once weekly for 3 months, then 5 mg twice weekly, at most 10 mg twice weekly (doses at least 3 days apart).

front: Why is succinylcholine unsafe in hepatic failure?
back: Succinylcholine is broken down by plasma pseudocholinesterase. An acquired deficiency of this enzyme, as in liver disease, predisposes to prolonged apnoea, so the drug is unsafe there.

front: Which antitubercular drugs are safe in liver disease, and which is most hepatotoxic?
back: Streptomycin and ethambutol are non-hepatotoxic and are used when the liver is damaged, with a fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin. Pyrazinamide is the most hepatotoxic, followed by rifampicin; isoniazid is also hepatotoxic. On rechallenge after hepatitis, drugs are restarted one at a time in the order rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide.
refs: Case-Based Learning in Pharmacology PDF p225

front: Does a Child-Pugh class alone decide the dose of a drug?
back: No. Dosing decisions rely on the drug's prescribing information, not the score alone. Reassess the score when the patient's condition changes.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Use of the Child Pugh Score in Liver Disease (2023) https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542308/

front: How did expert agreement change with Child-Pugh severity?
back: It fell: about 83% agreement in stage A, 47% in B and 41% in C.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

front: What did the panel's consensus recommendations mostly say?
back: No dose adjustment or avoidance.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

front: Why is cirrhosis dosing hard to apply, per the panel?
back: Stage-specific dosing guidance is inconsistent and prescribing information is often unclear.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

front: Did pharmacists and hepatologists favour the same advice?
back: No. Pharmacists and clinical pharmacologists more often advised dose adjustment; hepatologists more often chose standard dosing or avoidance.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Recommendations on Drug Selection and Dose Adjustment for Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: Results from a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel Clin Drug Investig 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12999791

front: Why do high-extraction drugs given orally need a large dose cut in cirrhosis?
back: Their clearance depends on liver blood flow and first-pass extraction. In cirrhosis, portosystemic shunting and loss of hepatocytes let much more of an oral dose escape first-pass metabolism, so bioavailability and blood levels rise sharply (e.g. morphine, propranolol).

front: In hepatic impairment, how are loading and maintenance doses handled?
back: Loading dose depends on volume of distribution and is usually unchanged (it may even need to be larger if ascites expands the volume of a water-soluble drug). Maintenance dose depends on clearance, so it is reduced or the interval lengthened as Child-Pugh class worsens.

front: What drug problems arise in liver disease apart from reduced clearance?
back: Cirrhosis markedly increases CNS sensitivity to morphine and barbiturates (coma at normal doses). Brisk diuresis in impending encephalopathy causes hypokalaemic alkalosis, converting NH4+ to NH3 that enters the brain. Oral anticoagulants prolong prothrombin time sharply because clotting factors are already low. Prodrugs needing hepatic activation work less well.

front: Short note: Drug therapy in liver disease

points: Bioavailability of high first-pass drugs rises (loss of hepatocytes, portocaval shunting)
Low albumin: more free acidic drugs (diclofenac, warfarin)
Reduced clearance of morphine, lidocaine, propranolol: lower doses
Prodrugs needing hepatic activation (bacampicillin) less effective
Oxazepam or lorazepam instead of diazepam
Atenolol as the beta blocker
Morphine and barbiturates may cause coma in cirrhotics
Brisk diuresis: hypokalaemic alkalosis, more NH3, hepatic encephalopathy
Oral anticoagulants markedly prolong prothrombin time
NSAID fluid retention and metformin lactic acidosis worsen
No simple test (unlike creatinine clearance) predicts the change
Avoid hepatotoxic drugs

front: Short note: Dose adjustment in hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh approach)

points: A: mild, compensated; most drugs at usual dose, care with narrow-margin drugs
B: moderate; reduce dose or lengthen interval of hepatically cleared drugs and monitor
C: severe; avoid drugs cleared mainly by the liver and hepatotoxic drugs unless the label allows a reduced dose
Oral bioavailability rises with shunting and lost hepatocytes (morphine, propranolol, lidocaine)
Reduce the oral dose markedly
Clearance falls with enzyme capacity; free fraction rises when albumin is low
Reduce the maintenance dose or lengthen the interval; loading dose usually unchanged
Prefer drugs cleared by the kidney or by glucuronidation (lorazepam, oxazepam)
Avoid sedatives, NSAIDs and drugs that precipitate encephalopathy or bleeding
Start low, titrate slowly, monitor effect and levels
No test of liver function predicts drug clearance the way creatinine clearance does for the kidney

front: Classify: antimicrobials needing dose reduction in renal failure
text: Even in mild failure: {{aminoglycosides}}, {{cephalexin}}, {{ethambutol}}, {{vancomycin}}, {{amphotericin B}}, {{acyclovir}}. Only in severe failure: {{cotrimoxazole}}, {{carbenicillin}}, {{cefotaxime}}, {{norfloxacin}}, {{ciprofloxacin}}, {{metronidazole}}.

front: In renal impairment, how should the dose change relate to clearance?
back: Reduce the dose in proportion to the calculated fall in drug clearance.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Renal Failure Drug Dose Adjustments https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560512/

front: Which CKD stage requires renal replacement therapy, and what GFR defines it?
back: Stage 5, with a GFR of 14 to 0 mL/min.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Renal Failure Drug Dose Adjustments https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560512/

front: Which creatinine equation has largely replaced older methods for estimating kidney function?
back: The CKD-EPI creatinine equation, recommended by the NKF and ASN task force; older methods were Cockcroft-Gault and MDRD.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Renal Failure Drug Dose Adjustments https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560512/

front: Why does protein binding limit how much drug dialysis removes?
back: Only unbound drug crosses the dialysis membrane, so the bound fraction is not available for removal.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

front: Which drugs are mainly removed by diffusion during dialysis?
back: Small molecules; drugs under about 1000 daltons are mainly removed this way.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

front: How are doses of renally excreted drugs adjusted in kidney disease?
back: Clearance of drugs excreted unchanged (aminoglycosides, digoxin, phenobarbitone) falls in parallel with creatinine clearance. Loading dose is unchanged (unless oedema), but maintenance dose is cut or interval lengthened. KDT guide: CLcr 50-70 mL/min, 70% of the dose rate; 30-50, 50%; 10-30, 30%; 5-10, 20%. Steady state is reached later if half-life is prolonged.

front: Which drugs should be avoided or used with care in renal failure, and why?
back: Nephrotoxic drugs: aminoglycosides, tetracyclines (except doxycycline; also anti-anabolic, worsen uraemia), sulfonamides (crystalluria), vancomycin, nitrofurantoin, cyclosporine, amphotericin B. Thiazides are ineffective and reduce GFR (use furosemide). Potassium-sparing diuretics cause hyperkalaemia. Pethidine: norpethidine accumulates and causes seizures. Urinary antiseptics fail to reach urinary levels and cause systemic toxicity. NSAIDs increase fluid retention.

front: How does renal failure alter drug distribution and sensitivity?
back: Albumin is low or altered, so binding of acidic drugs falls (basic drugs little changed). The blood-brain barrier becomes more permeable, so opiates, barbiturates, phenothiazines and benzodiazepines cause more CNS depression. Antihypertensives cause more postural hypotension.

front: How does haemodialysis change the vancomycin dosing schedule?
back: With non-high-flux dialysis membranes, about 1 g (around 15 mg/kg) every 5 to 7 days typically gives adequate levels. With intermittent high-efficiency or high-flux dialysis, maintenance doses are needed after each dialysis session.

front: Why are renal dose changes usually coarse, and when is more care needed?
back: Changes are often halving or doubling, since a 20% change is usually impractical. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index need more careful adjustment.
refs: WEB NCBI StatPearls Renal Failure Drug Dose Adjustments https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560512/

front: Why must dialysis dosing be reviewed as residual kidney function changes?
back: Residual renal function clears renally excreted drugs, and it can change daily, so dosing should be reassessed as it improves or declines.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

front: For intermittent drugs in dialysis, what timing point matters?
back: Exposure depends on the dose timing relative to the start and length of the session, so these doses are planned around dialysis.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

front: Why are pethidine, thiazides and potassium-sparing diuretics problematic in renal failure?
back: Pethidine: norpethidine accumulates on repeated dosing and causes seizures and twitching. Thiazides are ineffective and can worsen uraemia, so furosemide is used. Potassium-sparing diuretics are contraindicated because of hyperkalaemia and cardiac depression.

front: In extended dialysis (SLED), what do studies suggest to replace drug removed during a session?
back: Giving a dose after the session, or both before and after it.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

front: Can intermittent haemodialysis dosing advice be applied straight to SLED?
back: Not safely: it may underdose and risk treatment failure, and the evidence base for SLED is small.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Principles of Drug Dosing in SLED and Review of Antimicrobial Dosing (Brown and Battistella, Pharmacy 2020) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7151685/

front: Essay: Prescribing drugs in renal impairment

points: Estimate function with creatinine clearance; the fall in clearance with age is not mirrored by serum creatinine because muscle mass and creatinine production also fall
Clearance of unchanged drugs falls in parallel with creatinine clearance
Albumin low or altered: acidic drug binding falls
Blood-brain barrier more permeable: more CNS depression with opiates, barbiturates, phenothiazines, benzodiazepines
Loading dose unchanged (unless oedema); cut maintenance dose or lengthen interval
Dose rate as % of normal by creatinine clearance: 50-70 mL/min 70%, 30-50 50%, 10-30 30%, 5-10 20%
Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B, acyclovir need reduction even in mild failure
Tetracyclines (except doxycycline), sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, cyclosporine are nephrotoxic or worsen uraemia
Thiazides ineffective; potassium-sparing diuretics contraindicated; pethidine accumulates norpethidine

front: Give examples of gastrointestinal disease altering drug absorption.
back: In coeliac disease amoxicillin absorption falls but cephalexin and cotrimoxazole absorption rises, so malabsorption does not reduce all drugs. Gastric stasis in a migraine attack delays absorption. Achlorhydria reduces aspirin absorption by increasing its ionisation.

front: How is the dose calculated for an exceptionally obese or lean adult?
back: On a body weight basis: individual dose = (body weight in kg / 70) x average adult dose. The average adult dose refers to a person of medium build. Body surface area has been argued to be a more accurate basis.

front: Why do myasthenia gravis patients need special care with neuromuscular blockers?
back: Myasthenic patients are very sensitive to curare-type drugs, and quinine aggravates their weakness.

front: How do achlorhydria and peptic ulcer disease alter drug handling?
back: Achlorhydria reduces aspirin absorption by favouring its ionisation. In peptic ulcer disease, NSAIDs can aggravate the ulcer, so avoid them.

front: How does congestive heart failure alter drug kinetics?
back: Absorption falls from mucosal oedema and splanchnic vasoconstriction (procainamide, hydrochlorothiazide); volume of distribution may change, so loading doses of lidocaine and procainamide should be lowered; elimination slows from hepatic congestion and low GFR, so dosing rates of lidocaine, procainamide and theophylline may need cutting; the failing heart is more sensitive to digitalis.

front: How does thyroid status alter drug response?
back: Hypothyroid patients are more sensitive to digoxin, morphine and CNS depressants. Hyperthyroid patients resist the inotropic action of digoxin but are more prone to its arrhythmias. Digoxin clearance roughly follows thyroid function.

front: Compare how heart failure, hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism change the response to digitalis.
back: Failing heart: more sensitive to digitalis. Hypothyroid: more sensitive to digoxin (with morphine and CNS depressants). Hyperthyroid: resists its inotropic action yet is more prone to its arrhythmias. Digoxin clearance roughly follows thyroid function, which explains only part of the change.

front: Short note: Effect of disease states on drug response

points: Absorption falls (mucosal oedema, splanchnic vasoconstriction)
Lower loading doses of lidocaine and procainamide
Slower elimination of lidocaine, procainamide, theophylline; more sensitive to digitalis
Hypothyroid: more sensitive to digoxin, morphine, CNS depressants
Hyperthyroid: resists digoxin inotropy, more arrhythmias
Coeliac: amoxicillin absorption falls, cephalexin and cotrimoxazole rises
Migraine stasis delays absorption; achlorhydria cuts aspirin absorption
NSAIDs aggravate ulcers
Myasthenia: very sensitive to curare-type drugs
See renal and hepatic cards: dose by clearance, check binding and CNS sensitivity
Obese or lean adult: dose = body weight/70 x average dose; surface area argued better

front: What is orthostatic (postural) hypotension, and why does it matter in older patients?
back: A fall in blood pressure on standing. Homeostatic reflexes are blunted with age, and symptomatic orthostatic hypotension becomes much more common, so older patients cannot compensate. Alpha-1 blocking drugs make it worse. The result is dizziness and falls.

front: Which antihypertensive causes postural hypotension, and what injury can follow in an elderly patient?
back: Prazosin (alpha-1 blocker). Postural hypotension, mainly with the first dose or with dose increments, can cause a fall with fracture of the neck of femur in an elderly patient. Starting with a low dose at bedtime minimises it.

front: Why do antipsychotics and tricyclics add to fall risk in the elderly?
back: Alpha-1 blockade causes orthostatic hypotension; low-potency first-generation antipsychotics carry more of this risk than high-potency ones. Tricyclics also block H1 receptors (sedation) and muscarinic receptors (cognitive dulling and confusion).

front: How does polypharmacy in older patients raise the chance of a fall?
back: Elderly patients take several drugs for hypertension, heart disease, diabetes and arthritis. Each added drug multiplies the chance of an interaction, and the combined effects on blood pressure and the CNS cause postural instability, giddiness and confusion. ADRs are much more common in the elderly.

front: Short note: Drugs that increase fall risk in the elderly, with prescribing concerns

points: GFR about 75% of the young-adult value at 50 years and about 50% at 75
Reduced hepatic microsomal activity and liver blood flow
Lower plasma albumin and slower absorption; cumulative toxicity with prolonged use
Benzodiazepine and barbiturate half-lives rise 50-150% between ages 30 and 70; lorazepam and oxazepam less affected
Relatively intolerant to digitalis
Responsiveness of beta-adrenergic receptors to agonists and antagonists is reduced
Mild anticholinergic activity can worsen voiding in elderly males with prostatism
Multiple drugs for hypertension, heart disease, diabetes and arthritis raise interaction risk
ADR incidence is much higher and rises with the number of drugs
Alpha-1 blockers and other antihypertensives: postural hypotension; prazosin can fracture the neck of femur
Antipsychotics: low-potency FGAs and alpha-1 blocking agents cause orthostasis; sedation and EPS add to risk
Tricyclics: alpha-1 orthostasis, H1 sedation and anticholinergic confusion
Any drug causing dizziness adds to postural instability
Start low and titrate slowly; antipsychotic doses in older patients are often about 50% of the younger dose
Postural hypotension is worst with the first dose and with dose increments: start low (prazosin at bedtime) and titrate slowly
Review and cut drugs without a clear indication

front: Why do women usually need doses at the lower end of the range?
back: Women have a smaller body size, so their doses are kept on the lower side of the usual range.

front: Which sex hormones are unacceptable to the opposite sex?
back: Androgens are unacceptable to women and estrogens to men, so sex hormone prescribing must match the patient's sex.

front: Which drugs affect sexual function or breast tissue only in men?
back: Clonidine, methyldopa, beta-blockers and diuretics can impair sexual function in males but not females. Gynaecomastia from ketoconazole, metoclopramide, chlorpromazine or digitalis occurs only in men.

front: How do pregnancy changes alter drug disposition?
back: Reduced GI motility delays absorption; plasma volume expands; albumin falls while alpha-1 acid glycoprotein rises, so the free fraction of acidic drugs rises and of basic drugs falls. Renal blood flow rises, speeding elimination of polar drugs, and hepatic enzymes are induced. The net effect is complex. Menstruation and lactation also need review.

front: Why does citalopram exposure differ between women and men?
back: The R-enantiomer of citalopram is cleared more slowly in women than in men, so women have higher exposure to it. This is a reported sex-based pharmacokinetic difference.

front: What do the data show about sex differences in opioid analgesia?
back: Females account for most chronic pain syndromes. Acute-pain studies report either no sex difference or greater sensitivity in females. The duration of morphine analgesia increases progressively with age, though the degree of analgesia at a given dose is similar.

front: Short note: Gender-based differences in drug therapy

points: Smaller body size: doses on the lower side of the range
Subjective effects of drugs may differ in females
Citalopram R-enantiomer cleared more slowly in women, so exposure is higher
Androgens unacceptable to women; estrogens unacceptable to men
Sexual dysfunction from clonidine, methyldopa, beta-blockers and diuretics occurs in men, not women
Gynaecomastia (ketoconazole, metoclopramide, chlorpromazine, digitalis) occurs only in men
Consider menstruation, pregnancy and lactation before prescribing
Pregnancy: reduced GI motility, expanded volume, higher renal blood flow, hepatic enzyme induction
Major depression about twice as frequent in women; some evidence for sex-based response to antidepressants
Maintenance digoxin in heart failure reported with higher mortality in women than men (association)
Females have most chronic pain syndromes
Acute-pain studies: no sex difference or greater sensitivity in females

front: How common is major depression in women compared with men?
back: About twice as frequent. There is some evidence for a sex-based difference in response to antidepressant drugs.

front: Why is maintenance digoxin in heart failure a concern for women?
back: Maintenance digoxin in heart failure has been reported to carry higher mortality in women than in men. The book describes this as an association, not a settled cause, so women on digoxin need careful review.

front: Trace catecholamine synthesis from phenylalanine and name the rate-limiting enzyme.
back: Phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine, tyrosine hydroxylase converts it to DOPA (the rate-limiting step), and DOPA decarboxylase gives dopamine. Dopamine enters the storage vesicle, where dopamine beta-hydroxylase converts it to noradrenaline. In adrenal medullary cells, phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), induced by the high local cortisol level, methylates noradrenaline to adrenaline.

front: Which drug blocks catecholamine synthesis, and where is it used?
back: Metyrosine (alpha-methyl-p-tyrosine) inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase and depletes catecholamines. It is used to reduce catecholamine output in pheochromocytoma before surgery and in inoperable cases.

front: How is noradrenaline stored in the nerve terminal, and how does reserpine act?
back: It is held in vesicles, complexed with ATP (about 4:1) and bound to chromogranin. VMAT-2 pumps amines into the vesicle in exchange for H+. Reserpine blocks VMAT-2, so transmitter leaks into the cytoplasm, is destroyed by MAO, and the stores become depleted.

text: Catecholamines are made from {{phenylalanine}} via tyrosine and {{DOPA}} to dopamine; the rate-limiting enzyme is {{tyrosine hydroxylase}}, blocked by {{metyrosine}}.

front: Classify: drugs acting on noradrenergic neurones
text: {{Cocaine}} and {{desipramine}} block NET and potentiate noradrenaline; {{reserpine}} blocks VMAT-2 and depletes stores; {{selegiline}} inhibits MAO-B; {{entacapone}} inhibits COMT.

front: Compare uptake-1 and uptake-2 for catecholamines.
back: Uptake-1 is the Na+-coupled norepinephrine transporter (NET) in the neuronal membrane. It recaptures 75 to 90 percent of released noradrenaline, is blocked by cocaine and desipramine, and is the main way neuronal action ends. Uptake-2 is an extraneuronal transporter in other tissues. It is Na+-independent, prefers adrenaline, is not blocked by cocaine, and is quantitatively minor.

front: Which enzymes metabolise catecholamines, and why does metabolism matter little for neuronally released noradrenaline?
back: MAO acts first on the intraneuronal and leaked pool; COMT acts first on circulating amines in liver and other tissues. Aldehyde reductase, dehydrogenases and ADH take part in the intermediate steps. Urinary products are VMA, MOPEG, metanephrines and DOMA, mostly conjugated. Metabolism is slow compared with reuptake, so it contributes little to ending neuronal action.

front: Essay: Drugs that modify adrenergic neurotransmission

points: Stages: synthesis, storage, release, reuptake, metabolism, receptor action
Metyrosine inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase (used in pheochromocytoma)
Methyldopa forms alpha-methyl-noradrenaline, which displaces noradrenaline and acts as an alpha-2 agonist
Reserpine blocks VMAT-2 and depletes stores
Guanethidine and bretylium block impulse-coupled release
Result: loss of adrenergic transmission
Cocaine and desipramine block NET
Result: potentiation of endogenous and exogenous noradrenaline
Nonselective MAO inhibitors (nialamide, tranylcypromine)
MAO-A: moclobemide; MAO-B: selegiline (raises brain dopamine)
COMT inhibitors: tolcapone, entacapone
Agonists and antagonists act at receptor level (see sympathomimetic and blocker notes)

front: Short note: Pheochromocytoma and catecholamine chemistry

points: Tumour of adrenal medullary cells; excess catecholamines cause intermittent or persistent hypertension
Urinary metabolites (VMA, normetanephrine) are measured for diagnosis
Phenoxybenzamine (alpha blockade) first; then a beta-blocker; labetalol is useful

front: Using the Ahlquist classification, compare the potency order of adrenaline, noradrenaline and isoprenaline at alpha and beta receptors.
back: Alpha: adrenaline greater than or equal to noradrenaline, both much greater than isoprenaline. Beta: isoprenaline greater than adrenaline, which is greater than or equal to noradrenaline. Ahlquist (1948) used these two distinct rank orders of agonist potency to divide adrenoceptors into alpha and beta; the split was later confirmed by selective antagonists.

front: Compare alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors: location, transducer, effector and selective drugs.
back: Alpha-1 is postjunctional on effector organs. It acts through Gq, IP3/DAG and calcium, causing vasoconstriction, mydriasis and contraction of the bladder trigone and prostate. Phenylephrine is the selective agonist and prazosin the selective antagonist. Alpha-2 is mainly prejunctional, where it inhibits transmitter release, and is also found in the brain and platelets. It acts through Gi, lowering cAMP. Clonidine is the selective agonist and yohimbine the antagonist.

front: Where are beta-1, beta-2 and beta-3 receptors found, and which selective drugs act on them?
back: Beta-1: heart and juxtaglomerular cells; dobutamine is the relatively selective agonist, and metoprolol or atenolol the antagonists. Beta-2: bronchi, blood vessels, uterus, liver, skeletal muscle; salbutamol and terbutaline are agonists, ICI 118551 an antagonist. Beta-3: adipose tissue and bladder detrusor; mirabegron is the agonist used in overactive bladder.

front: Classify: adrenergic receptor coupling and location
text: Alpha-1 receptors couple to {{Gq}} and raise {{IP3/DAG}}; alpha-2 receptors couple to {{Gi}} and lower {{cAMP}}; beta-1 receptors are mainly in the {{heart}}; beta-2 receptors are mainly in {{bronchial}} smooth muscle.

front: What is distinctive about the beta-3 adrenoceptor?
back: It is a lower-affinity receptor than beta-1 and beta-2 and is more resistant to desensitisation. Beta-3 agonists such as mirabegron act on it, e.g. to relax the bladder.

front: Short note: Isoprenaline (isoproterenol) and receptor potency order

points: Alpha: adrenaline is at least as potent as noradrenaline; isoprenaline is much weaker
Beta: isoprenaline greater than adrenaline, which is at least as potent as noradrenaline
Isoprenaline acts strongly on beta receptors and is used mainly for heart block (older use)

front: Short note: Heart failure and catecholamines (adrenergic basis)

points: Long-term catecholamine exposure damages the heart and speeds heart failure
Catecholamine overactivity drives progression; blockers are used to counter it

text: Tyramine and amphetamine are {{indirect}} sympathomimetics; {{ephedrine}} and {{mephentermine}} are {{mixed-acting}}; {{phenylephrine}} is a selective {{alpha-1}} agonist.

front: Classify: uses of selective beta-2 agonists
text: Selective beta-2 agonists are used in {{bronchial asthma}} and COPD, to delay {{preterm labour}} (ritodrine), and in {{familial hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis}}.

front: How does clonidine lower blood pressure?
back: Clonidine is a more potent alpha-2 than alpha-1 agonist. Stimulating postjunctional alpha-2 receptors in the brain reduces sympathetic outflow from the CNS, which accounts for much of its antihypertensive effect.

front: Short note: Direct, indirect and mixed-acting sympathomimetics

points: Act on receptors directly: adrenaline, noradrenaline, isoprenaline, phenylephrine, methoxamine, dobutamine, terbutaline
Release noradrenaline from nerve terminals: tyramine, ephedrine and amphetamine
Release is rapid but brief, so the effect is short
Ephedrine acts both directly and by releasing transmitter

front: Which sympathomimetics act selectively on alpha-1 receptors, and which of them are given by mouth?
back: Phenylephrine and methoxamine are direct alpha-1 selective vasoconstrictors; midodrine is an oral prodrug converted to desglymidodrine, a direct alpha-1 agonist. Mephentermine and metaraminol act both directly and by releasing NE. Because heart stimulation is minimal, the pressure rise is accompanied by reflex slowing.

front: Dobutamine: receptor action, clinical dose and why it is useful as an inotrope.
back: It is a dopamine derivative with no dopamine-receptor activity. Its main action is a relatively beta-1 selective agonism. At 2 to 8 mcg/kg/min IV it raises contractility and output with little change in peripheral resistance or BP, and less tachycardia than isoprenaline. It is less arrhythmogenic than adrenaline. Uses: pump failure after MI or cardiac surgery, short-term severe heart failure, and pharmacological stress testing.

front: Describe ephedrine: mechanism, duration and why its use is now restricted.
back: A mixed-acting sympathomimetic: it releases noradrenaline and also acts directly on alpha and beta receptors. It resists MAO, so it is orally active and lasts 4 to 6 hours, but it is about 100 times less potent than adrenaline, and tachyphylaxis develops on repeated doses. Its use is restricted because it lacks selectivity and its efficacy is low. Remaining uses: hypotension during spinal anaesthesia, mild chronic bronchial asthma, and occasionally postural hypotension.

front: Methyldopa: how does it lower BP?
back: It is decarboxylated and hydroxylated to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, which acts as a false transmitter and as an alpha-2 agonist. The result is reduced sympathetic outflow from the CNS, similar to clonidine.

back: Dobutamine preferentially stimulates cardiac beta-1 receptors, giving inotropic support with less peripheral vasoconstriction than mixed-action agents.

front: Tizanidine and lofexidine: what class are they and what are they used for?
back: Both are alpha-2 agonists related to clonidine. Tizanidine relieves spasticity. Lofexidine suppresses opioid withdrawal symptoms, as clonidine does.

front: Fenoldopam: what is it and when is it used?
back: A benzazepine dopamine (D1) agonist and rapidly acting vasodilator, used for no more than 48 h to control severe hypertension, such as malignant hypertension with end-organ damage, in hospitalised patients.

front: What is the drug of choice in anaphylactic shock, what is the dose, and why?
back: Adrenaline, injected intramuscularly without delay: 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 in 1000) in adults, 0.3 mL for children 6 to 12 years and 0.15 mL up to 6 years; repeat every 5 to 10 minutes if there is no or only transient improvement. It raises BP, counters bronchospasm and laryngeal oedema, acts fast, and also suppresses mediator release from mast cells. IV adrenaline is used only for immediately life-threatening shock, diluted and infused slowly with monitoring. H1 antihistamines and IV hydrocortisone are adjuncts only.

front: What is the vasomotor reversal of Dale, and why does noradrenaline not show it?
back: After alpha blockade, adrenaline's pressor effect turns into a fall in BP. Adrenaline at ordinary doses causes alpha-1 vasoconstriction and beta-2 vasodilatation. Blocking alpha leaves only the beta-2 vasodilatation. Noradrenaline has no beta-2 action, so its pressor effect persists after alpha blockade.

front: Why do alpha-1 blockers cause postural hypotension?
back: They block alpha-1 mediated constriction of arterioles and veins, so peripheral resistance and venous tone fall and blood pools in capacitance vessels. Venous return and cardiac output drop, and the postural reflex that normally compensates on standing is impaired, so BP falls on standing and dizziness or syncope can follow.

front: Describe phenoxybenzamine: mechanism, duration and uses.
back: A halogenated alkylamine that forms a reactive intermediate and covalently binds alpha receptors. The blockade is irreversible and non-equilibrium and lasts 3 to 4 days until new receptors are made. Its main effects are postural hypotension, nasal stuffiness, miosis and failure of ejaculation. It is used mainly in pheochromocytoma and occasionally in peripheral vascular disease. Oral dose 20 to 60 mg/day; i.m. and s.c. injection is painful and should be avoided.

front: What is phentolamine used for, and what does its diagnostic test involve?
back: It is a short-acting, nonselective alpha-1 and alpha-2 antagonist; alpha-2 block increases noradrenaline release, so reflex tachycardia is marked. Uses: hypertensive episodes in pheochromocytoma, clonidine withdrawal or cheese reaction, local infiltration for extravasation of noradrenaline or dopamine, and intracavernosal injection with papaverine. Book test: 5 mg IV over 1 minute; a fall above 35 mm Hg systolic or 25 mm Hg diastolic suggests pheochromocytoma, but false results occur. Katzung notes it is now rarely used, and diagnosis rests on raised plasma or urinary catecholamines and metanephrines.

front: Prazosin vs yohimbine: what do they block?
back: Prazosin is a selective alpha-1 antagonist; yohimbine is an alpha-2 antagonist. Prazosin is used for hypertension and BPH; yohimbine is used as a tool to define alpha-2 effects.

front: Prazosin: selectivity, first-dose effect and why it replaced phenoxybenzamine.
back: It is a selective alpha-1 blocker (about 1000 times more selective for alpha-1 than alpha-2) that blocks all alpha-1 subtypes equally. Sparing prejunctional alpha-2 keeps reflex tachycardia mild. The first-dose effect (postural syncope) is reduced by starting with a low dose at bedtime, and tolerance to it develops. Being competitive and short acting (half-life 2 to 3 h, effect 6 to 8 h), it is easier to control than irreversible phenoxybenzamine. Uses: hypertension, BHP and Raynaud's phenomenon.

front: Tamsulosin: receptor profile, advantages and key adverse effects in BHP.
back: It is a uroselective alpha-1A/1D blocker. The 1A subtype dominates in the prostate and bladder base, so it relieves BHP symptoms with little change in BP or heart rate and little postural hypotension. It lacks the apoptosis-promoting effect seen with terazosin and doxazosin. Side effects: retrograde ejaculation and dizziness. Floppy iris syndrome is a concern during cataract surgery. It is given once daily as a modified-release capsule.

front: Why do alpha-1 blockers relieve BHP faster than finasteride, and what do they not do?
back: BHP obstruction has a static part (enlarged gland) and a dynamic part (alpha-1 mediated tone of the bladder neck and prostate). Alpha-1 blockers relax the dynamic part and give relief within about 2 weeks. Finasteride acts on the static part and takes around 6 months. Alpha-1 blockers do not reduce prostate size, and the benefit stops when the drug is stopped.

front: Alfuzosin: duration, indication and key drug interaction.
back: A short-acting prazosin congener (half-life about 3 to 5 hours), nonselective among alpha-1 subtypes. It is indicated only for symptomatic BHP and is not approved as an antihypertensive. It is metabolised by CYP3A4, so strong inhibitors such as erythromycin, ketoconazole and ritonavir should be avoided. Dose: 10 mg OD as extended release.

back: Pindolol, acebutolol and celiprolol. They partly activate beta receptors, so resting bradycardia and cardiac depression are minimal, exercise tachycardia is still blocked, rebound after withdrawal is less likely, and plasma lipids are less affected. Limitations: they are not useful for migraine prophylaxis (they dilate cerebral vessels) and are not suited to secondary prevention after MI.

front: Labetalol: receptor action, clinical niche and main side effect.
back: It blocks alpha-1 and nonselectively blocks beta receptors, with beta blockade about 3 to 5 times stronger than alpha. Its fall in BP comes from alpha-1 block plus beta-2 vasodilatation. Heart rate is usually unchanged and limb blood flow increases. It is used in pheochromocytoma, clonidine withdrawal, pregnancy-induced hypertension and hypertensive emergencies (20 to 40 mg IV repeated). Its main side effect is postural hypotension.

front: Propranolol: why does the antihypertensive effect appear only after some weeks?
back: Acutely, propranolol lowers cardiac output, and total peripheral resistance rises, so BP changes little. With chronic use, resistance vessels adapt to the lower output, peripheral resistance falls and BP drops. Other contributions: less renin release (beta-1 mediated), less noradrenaline release, and central effects of lipophilic agents.

front: Esmolol: why is it so short acting, and where is it used?
back: It is a cardioselective beta-1 blocker without partial agonist or membrane-stabilising action. It is given as a 0.5 mg/kg loading dose, then 0.05 to 0.2 mg/kg/min. Uses: supraventricular tachycardia, intraoperative arrhythmias, control of HR and BP during cardiac surgery and aortic dissection, and early MI.

front: Droxidopa: what is it and why does it raise BP in orthostatic hypotension?
back: A synthetic amino acid (L-DOPS) that dopa-decarboxylase converts into norepinephrine, so it acts as a noradrenaline precursor. Added NE raises peripheral resistance, which helps chronic orthostatic hypotension; midodrine is the older alpha-1 agonist choice.

front: Moxonidine and guanfacine: how are they related to clonidine?
back: Both lower BP by reducing sympathetic outflow from the CNS. Moxonidine is a mixed alpha-2 and imidazoline I1 receptor agonist. Guanfacine is more alpha-2 selective than clonidine and acts on brainstem receptors.

front: Parent structure of sympathomimetic amines, and what makes a catecholamine?
back: Beta-phenylethylamine: a benzene ring with an ethylamine side chain. Catecholamines add hydroxyls at ring positions 3 and 4 (a catechol).

front: How do ring hydroxyls at positions 3 and 4 change activity and oral use?
back: They give maximal alpha and beta potency; removing them lowers it. Catechols are destroyed in the gut and liver, so they work poorly orally. Hydroxyl-free compounds escape COMT and act longer.

front: How does the amino substituent steer alpha versus beta activity?
back: Bigger alkyl groups favour beta activity (isoprenaline has almost no alpha). Small groups favour alpha: adrenaline is the most alpha-active catecholamine, noradrenaline less. N-methylation boosts primary amines, yet phenylephrine stays alpha-selective.

front: Which ring pattern, with a large amino group, gives beta2 selectivity?
back: Hydroxyls at positions 3 and 5. Terbutaline is the example; it relaxes bronchial muscle with less direct cardiac stimulation than non-selective catecholamines.

front: Why do hydroxyl-free phenylethylamines act centrally and mainly by releasing NE?
back: Losing polar hydroxyls makes them more lipophilic, so they cross the blood-brain barrier (ephedrine, amphetamine, methamphetamine). Without both ring and beta-hydroxyls they lose direct agonist action and mainly release noradrenaline.
An indirect amine enters the nerve vesicle and replaces NE. If the replacement is much weaker than NE, transmission falls.

front: Why can an MAO inhibitor plus tyramine-rich food cause a hypertensive crisis?
back: Gut and liver MAO normally destroy dietary tyramine. With MAO blocked, tyramine reaches the circulation, enters nerve terminals and displaces NE. The sudden large NE release can cause severe hypertension.

Neurotransmission by nerves that are neither adrenergic nor cholinergic. Nitric oxide from NANC nerves relaxes smooth muscle, e.g. in the corpus cavernosum. It has been shown in the gut and vas deferens.

front: Why does adrenaline added to a local anaesthetic help?
back: Local vasoconstriction slows absorption of the anaesthetic. The block lasts longer, systemic toxicity falls, and local bleeding is reduced.

front: What is familial hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis, and how do beta2 agonists help?
back: Periodic muscle weakness with high plasma K+. Beta2 agonists increase K+ uptake into muscle, which lowers plasma K+.

front: Why does amphetamine calm a hyperkinetic child with ADHD?
back: ADHD is a reduced span of attention. Amphetamine lengthens the span, so the child settles. The effect looks paradoxical.

front: How do PDE-5 inhibitors act in erectile dysfunction, and what do they depend on?
back: They block PDE-5, the enzyme that breaks down cGMP in cavernosal smooth muscle, so cGMP builds up and potentiates NO action. They need NO release from NANC nerves and endothelium to work.

front: How do competitive and depolarising neuromuscular blockers differ at the end plate?
back: Competitive blockers occupy the nicotinic receptor without activating it, so ACh cannot open the channel. Depolarising blockers (succinylcholine, decamethonium) activate the receptor like ACh, but they resist acetylcholinesterase and keep the end plate depolarised until it becomes inexcitable.

front: Phase I and phase II depolarising block: how do they differ?
back: Phase I (classical) block: rapid onset, fasciculation then flaccid paralysis, no fade on train-of-four. Phase II (desensitisation) block: slow recovery, fade present, partly reversed by anticholinesterases. Phase II appears with high or infused doses, after fluorinated anaesthetics, or in atypical pseudocholinesterase.

front: How is train-of-four monitoring done, and what does the ratio tell you?
back: Four supramaximal stimuli at 2 Hz are applied to the ulnar nerve and adductor pollicis responses recorded. The TOF ratio is the fourth response divided by the first. Competitive block shows fade, with the ratio falling in proportion to the depth of block; depolarising (phase I) block reduces all four twitches equally, without fade. During recovery from competitive block the ratio climbs back towards 1.0: a ratio above 0.7 usually allows spontaneous breathing, but full clinical recovery needs a ratio above 0.9 (Katzung).

front: Neostigmine reversal of competitive neuromuscular block: how it works and its limits
back: Neostigmine inhibits cholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up at the end plate and overcomes the competitive blocker. KDT dose: 0.5 to 2 mg (30 to 50 µg/kg) IV, given almost routinely after long- and intermediate-acting blockers, preceded by atropine or glycopyrrolate (5 to 10 µg/kg) to block muscarinic effects such as bradycardia, hypotension and bronchospasm. Reversing residual block matters because residual weakness causes hypoventilation and hypoxia in recovery. It does not reverse depolarising (phase I) succinylcholine block; it worsens it. Sugammadex is an alternative for rocuronium.

front: Succinylcholine: dose, onset, duration and how it is terminated.
back: IV dose: Katzung gives 0.75 to 1.5 mg/kg (KDT quotes a lower range); fasciculations over the chest and abdomen appear within about 30 s, followed by paralysis lasting about 5 to 10 min. It is hydrolysed rapidly by plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) to succinylmonocholine and then succinic acid and choline, so recovery is spontaneous. Neostigmine does not reverse the block and may worsen it.

front: What happens to succinylcholine in atypical (deficient) pseudocholinesterase?
back: An abnormal genetic variant of plasma cholinesterase hydrolyses succinylcholine poorly. Homozygotes (roughly 1 in 3000) develop prolonged block (phase II) with apnoea lasting hours, which needs continued mechanical ventilation. The dibucaine number identifies the variant: dibucaine inhibits the normal enzyme by about 80% but the abnormal one by only about 20%. Testing is not routine but is indicated with a family history. Mivacurium is also prolonged, but that block can be reversed by neostigmine, unlike succinylcholine paralysis.

front: Sugammadex: what does it bind, how does it reverse block, and what is its advantage?
back: A modified gamma-cyclodextrin that encapsulates (chelates) rocuronium and, less so, vecuronium into an inactive complex excreted unchanged by the kidney, so it should be avoided in severe renal impairment. It does not inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so there are no muscarinic effects. Katzung doses: 2 mg/kg for shallow block (second twitch has returned), 4 mg/kg for deep block, 16 mg/kg for immediate reversal after a single 1.2 mg/kg dose of rocuronium. Adverse effects: altered taste, nausea, hypersensitivity and occasional anaphylaxis (about 0.3% with the 16 mg/kg dose). It can also bind progesterone-based contraceptives, reducing their effect.

front: Classify: neuromuscular blockers by route of elimination
text: Agents broken down mainly in the {{liver or plasma}} (e.g. {{vecuronium}}, {{atracurium}}, {{mivacurium}}) act briefly, whereas agents excreted mainly by the {{kidney}} (e.g. {{pancuronium}}, {{doxacurium}}) act longer.

front: Why can rocuronium replace succinylcholine for rapid tracheal intubation?
back: Rocuronium is a non-depolarising aminosteroid blocker with the fastest onset in its class, so it is the alternative to succinylcholine for tracheal intubation. It avoids the drawbacks of depolarising block (fasciculations, K+ efflux) and has negligible effects on BP and heart rate, and is used for maintenance as well. Even profound block can be reversed by sugammadex (16 mg/kg reverses a 1.2 mg/kg dose within a few minutes). It depends on liver and biliary elimination, so its action is prolonged in liver disease.

front: Atracurium versus cisatracurium: elimination and side effects.
back: Atracurium undergoes spontaneous Hofmann elimination as well as ester hydrolysis, so its action is not prolonged in hepatic or renal failure. It releases histamine in a dose-related way, causing hypotension. Its breakdown product laudanosine has a long half-life, crosses the blood-brain barrier and at high levels can cause seizures, a concern during long ICU infusions. Cisatracurium, its potent stereoisomer, depends less on hepatic inactivation, forms less laudanosine and is much less likely to release histamine; it is preferred in liver or kidney disease and the elderly and has largely replaced atracurium.

front: A patient with kidney and liver disease needs a muscle relaxant for rapid intubation and a smooth reversal. Choose and justify.
back: Rocuronium has a rapid onset among the non-depolarisers and can replace succinylcholine; it avoids the drawbacks of depolarising block and seldom needs reversal, but it is cleared by liver and bile, so its action lasts longer in liver disease. For maintenance, cisatracurium is inactivated mainly by Hofmann elimination (not hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase), so its action is little altered by liver or kidney failure, and it does not release histamine; it is a preferred relaxant in liver or kidney disease. Avoid pancuronium (renal excretion) and avoid succinylcholine where hyperkalaemia is a danger (burns, nerve damage). Reversal after rocuronium or vecuronium can use sugammadex, which encapsulates the blocker, rather than neostigmine; but sugammadex is cleared by the kidney, so in significant renal failure (Katzung: CrCl below 30 mL/min) it is avoided unless essential, and cisatracurium, which seldom needs reversal, becomes the safer maintenance choice.

It blocks RyR1 calcium-release channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle and prevents calcium-induced calcium release. Excitation-contraction coupling fails although the membrane still depolarises, so end-plate transmission is unaffected. Cardiac and smooth muscle channels (RyR2) are only weakly affected. Fast twitch fibres are affected more than slow antigravity fibres.

front: Dantrolene in malignant hyperthermia: why it works, the dose, and what limits its oral use
back: Malignant hyperthermia is persistent calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in genetically susceptible people, triggered by fluorinated anaesthetics and succinylcholine. Dantrolene blocks the RyR1 calcium-release channel, so IV dantrolene is the drug of choice. Dose in the owner's books: 1 mg/kg IV, repeated as needed up to a maximum of 10 mg/kg (KDT, Katzung). Oral use for spasticity is limited because the muscle weakness it causes offsets the benefit, and long-term use causes dose-related hepatotoxicity (a black-box warning).

front: How do local anaesthetics block the axonal Na+ channel?
back: The unionised base crosses the membrane and re-ionises inside the axon. The cation binds a receptor in the inner pore of the Na+ channel (segment S6 of domain IV), stabilises the inactivated state, and so raises the threshold and stops conduction. Blockade is use-dependent: it builds faster at higher firing frequencies, and higher extracellular Ca2+ reduces it.

front: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity: CNS and cardiovascular features and management
back: CNS: early circumoral numbness, tongue tingling, dizziness, tinnitus; then restlessness, twitching, convulsions, coma and respiratory arrest. Cardiovascular: bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmias, asystole and vascular collapse; bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic. Management: stop injection, secure airway, give oxygen and ventilate, treat convulsions with diazepam or midazolam, support circulation, and give IV lipid emulsion, which has been shown to resuscitate bupivacaine cardiotoxicity.

front: Which form of a local anaesthetic crosses the axon, and which form blocks the Na+ channel?
back: The unionised base is lipid-soluble, so it penetrates the axon; potency tracks the lipid solubility of this base. Inside, the cationic form is the main active species: it binds the open or inactivated channel more avidly than the resting one, prolonging the inactivated state and the refractory period. The pKa sets how much base is available at pH 7.4, which later decides onset.

front: Classify: ester-linked and amide-linked local anaesthetics
text: Ester-linked local anaesthetics include {{procaine}}, {{chloroprocaine}}, {{tetracaine}} and {{benzocaine}}; amide-linked ones include {{lidocaine}}, {{bupivacaine}}, {{prilocaine}} and {{ropivacaine}}.

front: Why does the pKa of a local anaesthetic determine its onset?
back: Only the unionised base crosses the nerve membrane. Lidocaine (pKa about 7.6 to 7.8) has 30 to 40% unionised at pH 7.4, so onset is fast. Bupivacaine, tetracaine and procaine (pKa 8.1 to 8.9) have 15% or less unionised, so onset is slow. Chloroprocaine is an exception: rapid onset despite a high pKa.

Ester types (procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine) are hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterase, act for shorter periods and cause more hypersensitivity; allergy cross-reacts among esters. Amide types (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine) are broken down in the liver, act longer and more intensely, rarely cause allergy, and do not cross-react with esters. Methylparaben preservative is a common allergen.

front: Why is adrenaline added to local anaesthetic solutions, and where should it be avoided?
back: Adrenaline (1 in 50,000 to 1 in 200,000) slows absorption from the injection site: the block lasts longer and is more intense, systemic toxicity falls and the field is less bloody. Classical teaching avoids it in ring blocks of fingers, toes, penis and pinna, where collateral flow is poor; Katzung notes some now question this rule. Use with caution in ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension, thyrotoxicosis, and with beta-blockers (unopposed alpha effect) or tricyclic antidepressants.

front: Why are ester local anaesthetics more prone to allergy than amide ones?
back: Hypersensitivity is more common with ester-linked LAs, and cross-reactivity is frequent among esters but not with amides. Methylparaben preservatives are often the real cause.

front: Why does propranolol affect lidocaine levels?
back: Propranolol (and probably other beta-blockers) reduces hepatic blood flow, lowering the metabolism of lidocaine and other amide LAs.

front: What is EMLA and how is it used?
back: A eutectic mixture of local anaesthetics: lidocaine 2.5% and prilocaine 2.5% form a mixture with a lower melting point, made into a 5% cream that can penetrate keratinised skin. Applied under an occlusive dressing for about 1 hour, it numbs intact skin to about 5 mm, lasting 1 to 2 hours after removal. Used before venepuncture or IV cannulation (especially in children), skin graft harvest and superficial procedures. A prilocaine metabolite can cause methaemoglobinaemia.

The most potent and most toxic local anaesthetic is {{dibucaine}}; the eutectic lidocaine and prilocaine cream anaesthetises {{intact skin}}; {{proparacaine}} is the commonly used ophthalmic surface anaesthetic; {{oxethazaine}} can act on gastric mucosa.

front: Recall: maximum doses of local anaesthetics for nerve block (KDT)
text: Maximum doses for nerve block are about {{300 mg}} for lidocaine, {{150 mg}} for bupivacaine and {{200 mg}} for ropivacaine; the highest peak blood levels follow {{intercostal}} block, so limits are respected most carefully there.

front: Which local anaesthetic is used for surface anaesthesia of the anal canal, and why is it not used for long spinal block?
back: Dibucaine (cinchocaine): the most potent, most toxic and longest-acting local anaesthetic. It is used on less delicate mucous membranes such as the anal canal; its use for long-duration spinal anaesthesia has been abandoned.
Intravenous lipid emulsion, which probably extracts the lipophilic bupivacaine from plasma and cardiac tissue.

front: Why is epidural bupivacaine popular for labour analgesia?
back: At low concentration (0.25%), bupivacaine blocks sensory fibres more readily than motor fibres, giving pain relief with little leg weakness. The mother can push during contractions. In postoperative continuous epidural analgesia, the same separation allows early walking and exercise. Ropivacaine gives a similar sensory-motor separation.

front: Lidocaine versus bupivacaine: how do they compare?
back: Lidocaine: relative potency 1, fast onset, duration about 60 to 120 min, relatively low cardiotoxicity; also used as an antiarrhythmic. Bupivacaine: about 4 to 5 times as potent, slower onset, long duration (about 120 to 360 min), markedly more cardiotoxic, and avoided in IV regional block. Its sensory-selective epidural use at low concentration is its main advantage. Levobupivacaine is less cardiotoxic.

front: Why is cocaine no longer used as a local anaesthetic?
back: Its only classical indication was ocular surface anaesthesia, but it constricts conjunctival vessels and can cloud and even slough the cornea, so even this use is not justified. It blocks reuptake of noradrenaline and adrenaline, causing vasoconstriction, hypertension, tachycardia and mydriasis. It is a powerful CNS stimulant with high abuse potential. It must never be injected, because it is a protoplasmic poison that causes tissue necrosis.

back: Epidural 0.75% bupivacaine in labour caused a few deaths from cardiac arrest, so this concentration is contraindicated. Bupivacaine is more prone to QTc prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias.

front: Choose the local anaesthetic and technique for: labour analgesia, an upper-limb Bier's block, and a dental extraction; state the main hazard in each.
back: Labour: continuous epidural low-concentration bupivacaine (0.125%) or ropivacaine; 0.75% bupivacaine is contraindicated since cardiac arrest has occurred, and bupivacaine cardiotoxicity is treated with IV lipid emulsion. Bier's block: 0.5% lidocaine IV into a tourniquet-isolated limb; the hazard is toxic release if the cuff is deflated early. Dental: lidocaine 2% with adrenaline (1:80,000) for longer action and a bloodless field; avoid adrenaline mixtures in ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis or uncontrolled hypertension, and with beta-blockers or tricyclics.

front: Spinal anaesthesia: injection site, site of action and level of block.
back: The drug is injected into the subarachnoid space at L2-3 or L3-4, below the end of the cord, so it acts mainly on cauda equina nerve roots. Spread depends on dose, volume, specific gravity and posture; hyperbaric (glucose) solutions move to the dependent part. Sympathetic block is about 2 segments higher than the sensory level and motor block about 2 segments lower. The level becomes fixed about 10 min after injection.

front: Why does spinal anaesthesia cause hypotension, and how is it treated?
back: Block of sympathetic fibres dilates veins, so blood pools and venous return falls (limb paralysis adds to this). Treat by raising the foot end and giving a pressor such as ephedrine or mephentermine. Knowing the cause explains why the sympathetic block must be anticipated before the incision.

front: What causes post-spinal headache and how is it reduced?
back: CSF leaks out through the dural puncture. A smaller-bore needle lowers the chance of leakage and so of headache.

front: What is the epidural space and what decides how far the block spreads?
back: It is a space filled with semi-liquid fat that the nerve roots cross. The volume injected governs the spread, which is why the thoracic space (narrow) needs small volumes and the lumbar space needs large ones.

front: Bier's block: how is it done and what is the main hazard?
back: Lidocaine 0.5% (20-40 ml) is injected IV into an exsanguinated limb isolated by a tourniquet inflated above arterial BP, and it diffuses back to the nerves. The cuff stays up 15-60 min to avoid ischaemic injury; deflating in under 15 min can let toxic amounts of drug enter the circulation. Safety rests on rapid tissue uptake: only about a quarter of the dose reaches the circulation on release.

front: Compare spinal and epidural anaesthesia: dose, onset, separation of sensory and motor block, and side effects.
back: Spinal: drug goes into the subarachnoid space (L2-3 or L3-4), acts on cauda equina roots, needs a small dose (even less in late pregnancy), and risks hypotension and headache. Epidural: drug acts on roots from the fat-filled space, needs large volumes, bupivacaine is slower and longer than lidocaine, 0.25% bupivacaine or ropivacaine gives sensory block with little motor block, and headache and neurological risk are lower. So epidural suits labour analgesia and continuous postoperative pain relief, while spinal suits quick dense block for lower body surgery.

front: What are the four cardinal features of general anaesthesia?
back: Loss of all sensation, especially pain; unconsciousness with amnesia; immobility with muscle relaxation; and abolition of somatic and autonomic reflexes.

front: What is MAC, and what changes it?
back: MAC is the minimum alveolar concentration that prevents movement in response to a surgical incision in 50% of patients. It is the standard measure of inhalational potency (the lower the MAC, the more potent the agent). It declines progressively beyond about 50 years of age, is lowered by sedative or opioid premedication, and is additive when two agents are combined (for example, 0.5 MAC of nitrous oxide plus 0.5 MAC of isoflurane gives about the effect of 1 MAC isoflurane).

front: Second gas effect and diffusion hypoxia.
back: Second gas effect: a high-concentration gas such as nitrous oxide (70 to 80%) draws in extra gas volume, so a simultaneously given potent agent such as halothane reaches blood faster. Diffusion hypoxia: when nitrous oxide is stopped, its rapid outflow dilutes alveolar oxygen. It is prevented by giving 100% oxygen for a few minutes after stopping nitrous oxide.

front: Describe Guedel's four stages of anaesthesia.
back: Stage I, analgesia: from start of inhalation to loss of consciousness. Stage II, delirium: excitement until regular breathing returns; no stimulus should be given. Stage III, surgical anaesthesia: regular breathing to cessation of spontaneous breathing, with four planes. Stage IV, medullary paralysis: breathing and circulation fail. These stages are blurred in modern practice.

front: Halothane: main adverse effects and why it has declined.
back: It causes dose-related depression of myocardial contractility and a fall in BP, and sensitises the heart to adrenaline, which can cause arrhythmias. It depresses respiration and reduces urine output by lowering GFR. About 20% is metabolised; immune reactions against trifluoroacetylated liver proteins can cause halothane hepatitis (about 1 in 10,000 exposures, about 50% fatal), presenting days after surgery with fever, nausea, rash and eosinophilia. It triggers malignant hyperthermia. Low cost keeps it in use in developing countries, but newer agents have replaced it elsewhere.

text: Nitrous oxide has a MAC of about {{105%}} and so cannot produce surgical anaesthesia alone; {{halothane}} has a MAC of about {{0.75%}}, {{isoflurane}} about {{1.2%}} and {{desflurane}} about {{6%}}.
Stage I is {{analgesia}}, stage II is {{delirium}}, stage III is {{surgical anaesthesia}} with four planes, and stage IV is {{medullary paralysis}}.

front: Inhalational anaesthetic MAC and recovery numbers
text: The MAC of nitrous oxide is {{105%}}; 1.3 MAC immobilises {{95%}} of subjects; patients wake when the concentration falls to {{0.4 MAC}}.

front: Justify the rationale of balanced anaesthesia.
back: No single agent gives all components. Nitrous oxide has a MAC of 105%, so it cannot anaesthetise alone at 1 atmosphere, although it gives analgesia. Halothane gives poor analgesia and relaxation, so it is covered with N2O, opioids or neuromuscular blockers. Combining inhaled and IV drugs, each for one purpose, lets each be used at a lower dose with fewer side effects.

front: A child needs face-mask induction and a day-case adult needs fast recovery. Which inhalational agents and why?
back: Child: sevoflurane, non-pungent and low in blood solubility, so induction by mask is smooth and quick. Day-case adult: desflurane, very low blood and tissue solubility, so recovery is fastest, but its pungency causes cough and laryngospasm on induction.

front: Thiopentone: why is its action short, and what are its main risks?
back: It is highly lipid-soluble, so it reaches the brain within one arm-to-brain circulation time (about 15 to 20 s). Redistribution into muscle and fat ends the effect in 6 to 10 min, while slow hepatic metabolism (half-life 8 to 12 h) leaves residual sedation for over 12 h. Risks: apnoea, hypotension, laryngospasm, poor analgesia; contraindicated in porphyria. Extravasation or inadvertent intra-arterial injection causes intense pain, necrosis and gangrene. It must not be mixed with succinylcholine in the same syringe.

A 1% emulsion; induction 2 mg/kg IV, maintenance 100 to 200 µg/kg/min. Recovery is fast with little nausea (it has antiemetic activity), so it suits day-case surgery; it is also used in asthmatics. Drawbacks: pain on injection (reduced by lidocaine or an opioid), induction apnoea, dose-related hypotension from vasodilatation and dose-dependent respiratory depression. Prolonged high-dose infusion can cause metabolic acidosis, lipaemia and heart failure (propofol infusion syndrome); unexplained tachycardia during propofol anaesthesia should prompt a check for acidosis.

front: Ketamine: dissociative anaesthesia and when to avoid it.
back: It blocks NMDA receptors, giving dissociative anaesthesia: profound analgesia and amnesia while the eyes stay open and airway reflexes persist. It preserves respiration and dilates bronchi, but raises heart rate, BP, cerebral blood flow and oxygen demand. Emergence delirium and hallucinations are common. Avoid in hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and heart failure; it suits hypovolaemic patients and asthmatics. It has traditionally been avoided with raised intracranial pressure, though Katzung notes the cerebral effects may be blunted by keeping CO2 normal. Its S-isomer, esketamine, is given intranasally for depression.

front: Remifentanil: why does its effect end so quickly?
back: It is hydrolysed rapidly by plasma and tissue esterases rather than by the liver or kidney, so its effect fades within about 10 to 15 min even after prolonged infusion. This titratability and quick recovery suit short, intensely painful procedures and infusion techniques. It still causes respiratory depression and can cause chest wall rigidity.

text: {{Thiopentone}} is an ultrashort {{thiobarbiturate}}; {{propofol}} is given as a {{1%}} emulsion; {{etomidate}} is a briefly acting inducing agent with little cardiovascular depression; {{midazolam}} is the water-soluble benzodiazepine.

{{Glycopyrrolate}} is about {{twice}} as potent as atropine with no central effects; {{ondansetron}} is the {{5-HT3}} blocker used as antiemetic of choice; {{ranitidine}} is an H2 blocker that raises gastric pH.

front: Dexmedetomidine: mechanism, advantages and adverse effects
back: The active S-enantiomer of medetomidine, a centrally acting selective alpha-2A agonist (clonidine-like action). Given by IV infusion, it produces sedation and analgesia with little respiratory depression, amnesia or anaesthesia, and blunts the sympathetic response to stress. Uses: sedation of ventilated ICU patients, sedation during endoscopy and regional anaesthesia, and as an adjunct that lowers the dose of inhalational anaesthetic. Rapid hepatic metabolism, half-life 2 to 3 h. Side effects resemble clonidine: hypotension, bradycardia and dry mouth.

front: Which receptors do nitrous oxide and ketamine act on, and how does this differ from volatile agents?
back: Nitrous oxide and ketamine mainly inhibit NMDA glutamate receptors, which gate Ca2+ channels. Volatile agents, barbiturates, propofol and benzodiazepines potentiate GABA-A chloride currents; some volatile agents and barbiturates also inhibit neuronal nicotinic channels. General anaesthetics mainly depress synaptic transmission, unlike local anaesthetics, which block axonal conduction.

back: Four electrical pulses given to a peripheral nerve at 2 Hz. The TOF ratio is the strength of the fourth twitch divided by the first; fade in the later twitches points to nondepolarising blockade.

Three pulses at 50 Hz, a 700 ms rest, then the set repeats. It is an alternative pattern for judging neuromuscular transmission beside the TOF; it lets the clinician detect residual block by hand when TOF is hard to judge.

A period of 50 Hz tetanic stimulation, a short rest, then single slow stimuli; the number of posttetanic twitches still detectable is the count. The tetanus releases a large ACh burst, which temporarily relieves nondepolarising blockade.

front: Which in vitro preparation is used for neuromuscular blockers in the chick?
back: The innervated biventer cervicis muscle, hung in an organ bath and stimulated through its nerve, with the twitch recorded on a writing lever. Used for suxamethonium and tubocurarine, among others, because the muscle responds to these blockers.

front: Which in vitro rat preparation tests neuromuscular blockers?
back: The rat phrenic nerve-diaphragm preparation: the phrenic nerve is stimulated and the diaphragm twitch is recorded. It is used to evaluate neuromuscular blocking agents.

front: What does the guinea pig pinch test measure?
back: Whether a forceps pinch still produces a squeak on the drug-treated flank compared with the saline-treated control flank of the same animal. Loss of the squeak means local anaesthesia.

front: What is the corneal reflex test in local anaesthetic screening?
back: A cotton tip touched to the corneoscleral junction of a rabbit eye normally makes the eye close. A local anaesthetic applied to the cornea abolishes this blink.

front: What does the frog foot-withdrawal test check?
back: Procaine 1% is placed over the exposed sciatic nerve in the abdominal cavity for 5 min. The control leg is dipped in saline and the test leg in 0.1 N HCl; withdrawal from the test leg absent while the control leg still withdraws means local anaesthesia.

front: Which drug and form are used in the guinea pig pinch test?
back: Lignocaine 2% gel applied to the test flank; the control flank gets saline or control jelly. Responses are read at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45 and 60 min.

front: Etomidate: why choose it, and what are its drawbacks?
back: A short-acting IV induction agent (0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg, action 4 to 8 min) with little cardiovascular or respiratory depression, so it suits patients with poor cardiovascular reserve or at risk of hypotension. Drawbacks: motor restlessness and rigidity, pain on injection, nausea and vomiting on recovery, and poor analgesia.

front: What are the three main mechanisms that generate cardiac arrhythmias?
back: Enhanced or ectopic automaticity (a steeper phase-4 slope or abnormal pacemaker sites); triggered activity from early or delayed after-depolarisations; and re-entry, where an impulse recirculates because of conduction block or slowing (circus movement or functional re-entry).

front: What is the Vaughan Williams classification?
back: A four-class scheme based on the main electrophysiological action: class I sodium channel blockers (subclasses IA, IB and IC), class II beta blockers, class III drugs that prolong repolarisation (mainly potassium channel blockers), and class IV calcium channel blockers. Many drugs act in more than one class, so the scheme is only a guide.

front: Class IA antiarrhythmics: name the drugs and their main electrophysiological effects.
back: Quinidine, procainamide and disopyramide block open-state sodium channels and dissociate with intermediate (moderate) kinetics. They prolong the action potential, refractoriness and QT interval, widen the QRS, and depress conduction. Their proarrhythmic risk, including torsades de pointes, is significant.

front: Why is lidocaine a class IB drug, and what is it used for?
back: It preferentially blocks inactivated sodium channels, so it acts mainly on depolarised or ischaemic tissue. It suppresses ectopic automaticity and ventricular arrhythmias, and it has practically no effect on atrial action potentials, so it is ineffective in atrial arrhythmias. It is given only intravenously because of high first-pass metabolism, and it has the lowest proarrhythmic potential of the antiarrhythmics.

front: Class IC drugs: name the two main examples and explain why their use is restricted.
back: Flecainide and propafenone are the most potent sodium channel blockers, with very slow recovery. They markedly slow conduction and widen the QRS, and they can be proarrhythmic. The CAST trials found excess sudden death with class IC drugs after myocardial infarction, so they are avoided in structural heart disease and ischaemia. Propafenone also has beta-blocking activity and is metabolised by CYP2D6.

text: Class IB drugs such as {{lidocaine}} and {{mexiletine}} preferentially block {{inactivated}} sodium channels and are ineffective in {{atrial}} arrhythmias.

front: Drugs for transient or acute atrioventricular block
back: Atropine 0.6-1.2 mg i.m. when block is vagal (e.g. digitalis toxicity, some MIs); sympathomimetics such as isoprenaline in partial or complete block until a pacemaker can be placed. Drugs are only an interim measure until a pacemaker can be implanted.

front: How do beta blockers suppress arrhythmias, and which arrhythmias respond best?
back: They block adrenergically driven automaticity and after-depolarisations, and they prolong AV nodal refractoriness, which slows AV conduction. They work best in sympathetically mediated arrhythmias, inappropriate sinus tachycardia and AV-node-dependent tachycardias, and they control ventricular rate in AF and flutter. Long-term beta blockade reduces sudden cardiac death after myocardial infarction.

front: What is amiodarone's drug class and why is it called a multichannel blocker?
back: It is an iodine-containing, very lipophilic, long-acting class III drug. It blocks delayed-rectifier K+ channels (prolonging repolarisation), also inactivated Na+ channels, partly Ca2+ channels, and gives non-competitive beta blockade, so it acts across several Vaughan Williams classes.

front: Why does amiodarone rarely cause torsades de pointes despite prolonging the QT?
back: Its action-potential prolongation does not depend on heart rate (no reverse use-dependence), so it does not lengthen repolarisation excessively at slow rates, which is the setting that favours early after-depolarisations.

Resistant ventricular tachycardia and recurrent ventricular fibrillation are the key uses. It is also used to maintain sinus rhythm in AF when other drugs fail, and in WPW tachyarrhythmias. Its broad efficacy and relatively low proarrhythmic potential make it widely used despite organ toxicity.

front: Amiodarone: list its main electrophysiological actions and its long-term benefit.
back: It prolongs the action potential and QT interval by blocking delayed rectifier potassium channels. It also blocks inactivated sodium channels, partly blocks L-type calcium channels, and has non-competitive adrenergic blocking activity; its torsades risk is low despite QT prolongation. Its half-life is weeks. KDT notes that, apart from propranolol, it is the only antiarrhythmic shown to reduce long-term sudden cardiac death; however, its modest mortality benefit in heart failure seen in a meta-analysis was not confirmed in the SCD-HeFT trial.

front: Adenosine: dose, route and mechanism in PSVT.
back: Given as a rapid intravenous bolus over 1 to 3 seconds, usually 6 to 12 mg of adenosine (or 10 to 20 mg of ATP). It acts on A1 receptors to hyperpolarise SA and AV nodal fibres and reduce calcium current, which interrupts AV-node re-entry. More than 90% of AV-node-dependent PSVT episodes terminate within about 30 seconds. Its half-life in blood is about 10 seconds.

front: Classify: Adenosine effects on the heart
text: Adenosine acts on {{A1}} receptors to hyperpolarise the {{SA node}} and slow conduction in the {{AV node}}; its half-life in blood is about {{10 seconds}}.

front: Why is adenosine given as a rapid IV bolus and why is its effect so short?
back: It has a plasma half-life of about 10 s because red cells and endothelium take it up quickly, and almost all is cleared in one passage through the coronary circulation. A fast bolus terminates AV-node-dependent PSVT (over 90% within 30 s), but the brief action makes it unsuitable for preventing recurrences.

front: Which drugs modify the response to adenosine, and why does it matter clinically?
back: Theophylline and caffeine block A1 receptors and blunt its effect, so heavy tea or coffee drinkers may need higher doses. Dipyridamole inhibits its cellular uptake and potentiates it. Patients on carbamazepine have a greater risk of heart block.

front: What are the main adverse effects of IV adenosine, and when is verapamil preferred?
back: Transient dyspnoea, chest discomfort, flushing and a fall in BP are common. Brief asystole or ventricular fibrillation can occur and usually resolves quickly. It can precipitate bronchospasm, so verapamil is preferred in asthma. Its action is too brief for prophylaxis. Unlike verapamil, it is safe in wide-QRS tachycardia and in patients with hypotension or heart failure.

front: Verapamil: which cardiac actions make it useful in PSVT, and why is it contraindicated in broad-QRS WPW tachycardia?
back: It blocks L-type calcium channels, slows SA nodal firing and markedly prolongs AV nodal refractoriness, which terminates AV-node re-entry. A dose of 5 mg IV is given over 2 to 3 minutes. It is contraindicated in broad-QRS WPW tachycardia, where it can shorten the accessory pathway refractory period and speed conduction. Avoid it with IV beta blockers, in hypotension or heart failure, and in VT, where it may precipitate VF.
