front: Case: PSVT in a patient with hypotension and heart failure on a beta blocker. Choose between adenosine and verapamil and justify.
back: Choose adenosine. Its A1-mediated AV-nodal block is so brief that it is safe in hypotension, CHF, beta blockade and wide-QRS tachycardia, whereas verapamil depresses contractility and AV conduction and adds to beta-blocker effects. Reverse the preference in asthma, where adenosine can cause bronchospasm and verapamil is preferred. Higher doses may be needed in heavy tea or coffee drinkers (A1 antagonism); dipyridamole potentiates adenosine.

front: Classical (stable) angina and variant (Prinzmetal) angina: how do their causes and drug approaches differ?
back: Classical angina is caused by fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of epicardial arteries. It is provoked by exertion or emotion and relieved by rest, so drugs that reduce cardiac work help. Variant angina is due to recurrent coronary vasospasm, occurs at rest or during sleep, and needs drugs that prevent or relieve spasm, such as nitrates and calcium channel blockers.

front: How do organic nitrates relax vascular smooth muscle?
back: They are denitrated inside the smooth muscle cell to release nitric oxide, which activates soluble guanylyl cyclase. The rise in cGMP activates protein kinase G, which reduces myosin light-chain kinase activity and relaxes the muscle. Veins contain more of the mitochondrial enzyme that generates NO from GTN (aldehyde dehydrogenase), which may explain their venodilator preference.

front: What are the main haemodynamic effects of nitrates in angina?
back: Venodilatation pools blood and lowers preload, end-diastolic volume and wall tension, which reduces myocardial oxygen demand. Mild arteriolar dilatation lowers afterload. Large epicardial coronary arteries dilate, which can redistribute flow to the ischaemic subendocardium. They have no direct effect on heart rate or contractility, but a large fall in BP can cause reflex tachycardia.

front: Sublingual GTN for an acute attack: onset, duration and key dosing points.
back: The tablet acts within 1 to 2 minutes and peaks in 3 to 6 minutes because it is absorbed straight into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver. Plasma half-life is about 2 minutes, and duration depends on how long the tablet stays in the buccal mucosa. A usual dose is 0.5 mg sublingual at the onset of pain or before exertion. Pain not relieved after three tablets 5 minutes apart needs urgent review, since IV GTN may be started in acute coronary syndrome.

text: Sublingual GTN acts within {{1 to 2 minutes}} and has a plasma half-life of about {{2 minutes}}; oral GTN is largely inactivated by {{first-pass metabolism}} in the liver.

front: Classify: Primary action of antianginal drugs
text: Nitrates mainly reduce {{preload}}; calcium channel blockers mainly reduce {{afterload}} and improve {{coronary flow}}; beta blockers reduce cardiac work by lowering {{heart rate}} and contractility.

front: Why is isosorbide mononitrate different from isosorbide dinitrate?
back: Mononitrate is the active metabolite of the dinitrate: little first-pass metabolism, high and consistent bioavailability, half-life 4-6 hours. Its last dose is taken in the afternoon.

front: Nitrate tolerance: when does it occur, and how is it prevented?
back: Continuous exposure, especially with oral, transdermal, infusion or sustained-release therapy, blunts the haemodynamic and anti-ischaemic effects. Tolerance wears off within hours of stopping and is cross-tolerant between nitrates. Oxidative stress from denitration impairs the NO-generating enzyme, and neurohormonal compensation contributes. The main preventive measure is a daily nitrate-free interval. Intermittent sublingual GTN causes no significant tolerance.

front: When must GTN be withheld in suspected myocardial infarction?
back: When systolic BP is below 90 mm Hg, when heart rate is below 50 or above 100 per minute, and when right ventricular infarction is suspected. It must also be withheld if sildenafil was taken in the previous 24 hours. Nitrate-induced hypotension can also prevent the use of beta blockers, which have stronger long-term benefit.

front: Why must nitrates be avoided after sildenafil?
back: Sildenafil and other PDE-5 inhibitors raise cGMP, the same second messenger that nitrates act through. The combination can cause profound hypotension, and MI and death have been reported. Nitrates should not be given within 24 hours of a PDE-5 inhibitor, and a longer gap is needed after tadalafil because of its long half-life. If hypotension occurs, fluids and alpha-agonists are used for support. Other vasodilators add to the hypotension.

front: Beta blockers in stable angina: how do they help, and which should be preferred?
back: They lower heart rate, contractility and BP, cutting myocardial oxygen demand, especially during exercise. A slower heart prolongs diastole, which improves subendocardial perfusion. Total coronary flow falls slightly, but flow to the ischaemic region is not reduced. Cardioselective agents (atenolol, metoprolol) are preferred, since nonselective agents can worsen vasospastic angina. They reduce mortality after a recent MI and in heart failure, and in stable angina trials they gave better outcomes than calcium channel blockers. Abrupt withdrawal should be avoided.

front: Cyanide poisoning: which antidotes are used and why?
back: Sodium nitrite forms methaemoglobin, which binds cyanide as cyanomethaemoglobin; sodium thiosulfate then converts cyanide to thiocyanate for urinary excretion. Hydroxocobalamin (high dose, i.v.) and dicobalt edetate are alternatives; hydroxocobalamin is particularly indicated in smoke inhalation (smoke contains HCN).

front: Classify: Vaughan Williams class IV drugs
text: Class IV agents are calcium channel blockers such as {{verapamil}} and {{diltiazem}}, which slow {{AV nodal}} conduction and prolong {{AV nodal refractoriness}}.

front: Classify: Calcium channel blocker chemical classes
text: The three CCB classes are {{dihydropyridines}} such as nifedipine, {{phenylalkylamines}} such as verapamil, and {{benzothiazepines}} such as diltiazem.

front: Calcium channel blockers in hypertension: which agents are used, and what are their main advantages?
back: Dihydropyridines, mainly amlodipine, are used most; verapamil and diltiazem are equally effective but less used. They lower BP by reducing peripheral resistance without reducing cardiac output or causing fluid retention. Advantages include no CNS effects, no sexual dysfunction, neutral effects on lipids, uric acid and electrolytes, and suitability in asthma, peripheral vascular disease and pregnancy. Short-acting nifedipine is not used for hypertension.

front: Why is nimodipine used after subarachnoid haemorrhage?
back: It is a short-acting dihydropyridine that crosses the blood-brain barrier well and acts on cerebral vessels; used to prevent and treat neurological deficit from cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage or ruptured aneurysm (30-60 mg 4-6 hourly for 3 weeks).

front: Amlodipine: why does it cause few early vasodilator side effects?
back: Slow oral absorption with peak level at 6-9 hours, more consistent bioavailability (less first-pass), and a very long half-life, so the blood level fluctuates little across the day.

front: Felodipine: distinguishing features and approved use
back: Greater vascular selectivity and larger tissue distribution than nifedipine with a longer half-life; approved for symptomatic treatment of Raynaud's disease; ER form once daily.

front: Cilnidipine: what makes it different from other dihydropyridines?
back: It blocks N-type (neuronal) calcium channels as well as L-type, and is claimed not to cause the reflex tachycardia seen with other DHPs.

back: Verapamil (and diltiazem) block L-type Ca2+ channels, slow the SA and AV nodes and depress contractility, so they suit PSVT and angina but are avoided with beta blockers. Nifedipine acts mainly on vessels and does not slow the SA or AV node, so it causes reflex tachycardia.

front: Trimetazidine: how does it work, and why is it not a haemodynamic drug?
back: It inhibits long-chain 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (LC3-KAT), a key enzyme of fatty acid oxidation. Myocardium shifts toward glucose oxidation, which needs less oxygen per unit of ATP. It has no effect on heart rate or BP at rest or on exercise, yet it reduces angina frequency and increases exercise capacity. Side effects include GI upset; it can cause movement disorders such as parkinsonism, especially in the elderly; GG14 lists it as a second-choice add-on for exertional angina. It is not approved in the USA.

front: Nicorandil: mechanism and main adverse effects.
back: It opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in smooth muscle, causing hyperpolarisation, and it also acts as a nitric oxide donor that raises cGMP. It lowers preload and afterload and increases coronary flow, with no significant effect on contractility or conduction. Adverse effects include flushing, headache, palpitation and painful oral aphthous ulcers. Concurrent PDE-5 inhibitors are contraindicated, and it does not cause nitrate-type tolerance.

text: Dipyridamole raises total coronary flow but causes {{coronary steal}} by dilating non-ischaemic resistance vessels, so it is not an effective {{antianginal}} drug; it is used as an adjunct {{antiplatelet}} agent.

front: Classify: Drugs for peripheral vascular disease
text: {{Cilostazol}} is a {{PDE-3}} inhibitor used for intermittent {{claudication}}; {{pentoxifylline}} acts mainly by reducing {{blood viscosity}}.

front: Cilostazol: mechanism, indication and key cautions
back: PDE-3 inhibitor raising cAMP in platelets and vascular smooth muscle; used only for intermittent claudication without rest pain; avoid in heart failure; CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 inhibitors increase toxicity.

front: Pentoxifylline: how does it help intermittent claudication?
back: Acts mainly on rheology: lowers whole-blood viscosity and improves red cell flexibility, improving microcirculatory flow without a major change in heart rate, total peripheral resistance or BP.

front: Ranolazine: mechanism, effect on heart rate and BP, and key safety issues.
back: It inhibits the late sodium current, which indirectly reduces calcium overload during ischaemia and helps preserve myocardial function. It does not change heart rate or BP, and it prolongs exercise duration. It prolongs the QT interval, so it must not be combined with other QT-prolonging drugs, and CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided. It can be used with sildenafil.

front: How do the major guidelines define hypertension and set treatment thresholds (NICE 2011, JNC 8, ACC/AHA 2017, ESC 2018)?
back: NICE 2011 (as in KDT): stage I 140 to 159/90 to 99, stage II 160 to 179/100 to 109, severe 180/110 mm Hg or more. JNC 8 (2014): treat from 140/90, except in people aged 60 or over, where the systolic threshold and goal are 150 mm Hg (diastolic stays 90). ACC/AHA 2017: normal below 120/80, elevated 120 to 129/below 80, stage 1 130 to 139/80 to 89, stage 2 140/90 or more; so hypertension in the USA starts at 130/80 and the target is below 130/80, with drugs in stage 1 only if there is atherosclerotic disease or a 10-year risk of 10% or more. ESC 2018: hypertension remains 140/90 or more, with a systolic target below 140 and close to 130. The lower targets followed SPRINT, where a systolic target of 120 rather than 140 mm Hg cut cardiovascular events and total mortality by about 25%.

front: Thiazide diuretics: the usual antihypertensive dose and why higher doses are avoided.
back: Low-dose hydrochlorothiazide (12.5 to 25 mg/day) or chlorthalidone is preferred. Maximal antihypertensive effect is reached at 25 mg/day, which gives the best benefit-risk ratio; higher doses mainly add adverse effects. Higher doses cause hypokalaemia, glucose intolerance, dyslipidaemia and hyperuricaemia without much further BP fall. Thiazides are ineffective in advanced chronic kidney disease.

front: Clonidine: mechanism of action and the withdrawal syndrome.
back: Clonidine is a central alpha-2A agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow from the medulla, lowering BP and heart rate. Stopping it abruptly, especially after missed doses, can cause severe rebound hypertension with tachycardia, anxiety, sweating and headache, resembling phaeochromocytoma. It is treated with an alpha plus beta blocker, nitroprusside, or clonidine itself. Tricyclic antidepressants antagonise its effect.

front: Methyldopa: active metabolite, site of action, and why it is used in pregnancy.
back: Methyldopa is converted in the body to alpha-methylnoradrenaline, a central alpha-2 agonist that lowers sympathetic tone and reduces total peripheral resistance more than heart rate or output. It is now used mainly in pregnancy because of its long safety record. Sedation and mental slowing are common. A positive Coombs test is common, but haemolytic anaemia is rare.

front: Hydralazine: mechanism, reflex effects, and main limitations.
back: It is a direct arteriolar vasodilator with little venous action, so it lowers diastolic BP more than systolic. Baroreflex activation causes tachycardia, higher cardiac output and renin release, leading to salt and water retention and tolerance unless a diuretic or beta blocker is added. It can provoke angina. Prolonged use above 100 mg/day can cause a lupus-like syndrome, more often in women and slow acetylators.

front: Reserpine: mechanism and why it is no longer used as an antihypertensive.
back: Reserpine irreversibly inhibits the vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2), so noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin are gradually lost and degraded. The effect outlasts the drug for weeks. Central depletion causes sedation, depression and extrapyramidal symptoms. It has been replaced by safer agents and is now used mainly as a pharmacological tool.

Low-dose {{hydrochlorothiazide}} (12.5 to 25 mg/day) is first-line; {{spironolactone}} and {{eplerenone}} are aldosterone antagonists that reduce potassium loss but can cause {{hyperkalaemia}} with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

front: Minoxidil: why is it used topically?
back: Oral minoxidil is no longer used because of vasodilator effects and cardiac risk; 2% topical solution applied twice daily promotes hair growth in male pattern baldness and alopecia areata, with a slow, incomplete response that is lost on stopping.

front: ACE inhibitors in hypertension: where are they preferred, and what is the main limiting adverse effect?
back: They are first-line in most grades of essential and renovascular hypertension, except bilateral renal artery stenosis. They are preferred with diabetes, nephropathy, left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, angina and after MI. Dry, persistent cough, from raised bradykinin, is the most common reason to stop them. They are contraindicated in pregnancy.

front: ARBs compared with ACE inhibitors: practical advantages, and which combination is discouraged?
back: ARBs block the angiotensin receptor without raising kinin levels, so the ACE inhibitor cough is avoided; angioedema and taste disturbance are rare. They share the metabolic and prognostic benefits of ACE inhibitors. JNC 8 and NICE advise against combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB. ARBs are also avoided in pregnancy.

front: Beta blockers in hypertension: why are they no longer first-line?
back: They are mild antihypertensives, and in primary prevention they are less effective than diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs for stroke and MI. Nonselective agents raise triglycerides and worsen quality of life, and rebound hypertension and angina can follow abrupt withdrawal. They remain indicated for compelling reasons such as post-MI, stable heart failure or high coronary risk.

front: Resistant hypertension: common causes and drug approach
back: Many patients need two, three or four drugs at optimal doses. Common reasons for apparent resistance are inadequate doses, poor adherence, combining drugs that act by the same mechanism, high salt intake and salt retention caused by vasodilators (so diuretic therapy is often inadequate), and interfering drugs: NSAIDs, sympathomimetic decongestants, ciclosporin, erythropoietin, ephedra, liquorice, cocaine and amphetamines. Many resistant patients have primary hyperaldosteronism and respond to adding spironolactone 25 to 50 mg daily; alternatives at this step are another diuretic, an alpha-1 blocker or a beta blocker. Renal denervation may help selected patients with well-defined resistant hypertension.

front: How is a hypertensive emergency defined, and name its major indications.
back: BP above about 220 systolic or 120 diastolic with active target-organ damage. Typical settings: stroke or head injury, acute LVF with pulmonary oedema, ACS or MI, aortic dissection, acute renal failure, eclampsia, and pheochromocytoma, cheese reaction or clonidine withdrawal. The organ damage, not the number alone, makes it an emergency needing controlled IV therapy.

front: Sodium nitroprusside: why it suits hypertensive emergencies, and what limits its use.
back: It acts within seconds and wears off within minutes, so BP can be titrated by the infusion rate. It dilates both arterioles and veins, and its NO release does not produce nitrate-type tolerance. Cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity, lactic acidosis, and the need for an infusion pump and arterial monitoring limit its use. It should be avoided in stroke and in eclampsia.

front: What is the angina index and why does it matter?
back: Heart rate multiplied by systolic BP. It tracks myocardial oxygen consumption, and each patient has a threshold at which angina starts.

front: What is the subendocardial crunch in an attack of angina?
back: The ischaemic ventricle's end-diastolic pressure rises (about 5 to 25 mm Hg), so subendocardial blood flow, which occurs only in diastole, falls. Drugs that lower preload relieve it.

front: Thallium-201 and Tc-99m pyrophosphate in myocardial ischaemia: where does each localise?
back: Thallium-201 localises to well-perfused myocardium, so ischaemia shows as a defect. Tc-99m pyrophosphate localises to necrosed myocardium.

front: Computerised exercise stress test for an antianginal: what is the outcome measure?
back: Exercise tolerance before pain and ECG change appear. A drug that delays both shows antianginal activity when the test is repeated after dosing.

front: What does a Langendorff preparation measure in cardiac screening?
back: An isolated perfused heart, perfused retrograde. It records inotropic and chronotropic effects and coronary resistance from the rate of drip collection.

front: Tail-cuff method in rodents: what does it measure and what limits it?
back: Non-invasive systolic BP in conscious or unconscious rats and mice. Restraint stress can produce misleading readings.

front: DOCA-salt model: how is hypertension produced in rats?
back: DOCA 20 mg/kg s.c. with saline as drinking water for about four weeks. Sodium and water retention raise volume and sympathetic and RAAS activity.

front: Which agent, given at high dose, produces experimental acute MI in animals?
back: Isoprenaline (isoproterenol). Its strong beta-1 action causes myocyte necrosis.

front: Why must a controlled trial be used to judge an antianginal drug?
back: Placebo responses are 30 to 80% in chronic stable angina, so an apparent benefit can be a placebo effect.

front: Crossover trial design: which chronic conditions suit it?
back: Chronic stable disease such as hypertension or stable angina, where the baseline is reached at the start of each treatment arm.

front: Why is acetazolamide not used as a diuretic today?
back: Its diuresis is self-limiting. Bicarbonate loss causes acidosis and hypokalaemia, so it is used for glaucoma, urinary alkalinisation, adjunct epilepsy and altitude sickness.

front: Spironolactone: why is it a weak diuretic yet useful in combination?
back: It antagonises aldosterone in the late distal tubule, where most Na+ is already reabsorbed. It conserves K+ and offsets the K+ loss caused by thiazide and loop diuretics.

front: Digoxin: which enzyme does it inhibit, and what is its main clinical role?
back: Inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase, so less Na+ is exported by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and cytosolic Ca2+ rises, increasing contractility. Used for positive inotropy in heart failure and ventricular rate control in atrial fibrillation.

front: Digoxin therapeutic window: what does the DIG trial show?
back: Benefit at about 0.5 to 0.8 ng/mL. Concentrations of 1.2 ng/mL and above tend to link to higher mortality. Digoxin has an extremely narrow therapeutic index, so the margin to toxicity is small.

front: What did the IONA trial show for nicorandil?
back: Fewer acute coronary events in high-risk patients with stable angina. Nicorandil opens KATP channels and donates NO, so it dilates arteries and veins and lowers preload and afterload.

front: Thiazide diuretics: what is the effect on glucose tolerance?
back: They can worsen glucose tolerance and precipitate diabetes. Low-dose thiazides still benefit more than this risk, so they are not contraindicated in diabetics.

front: Working myocardium versus automatic fibres: what separates them?
back: Working (non-automatic) fibres hold a stable resting potential of about -90 mV and cannot fire on their own. Automatic fibres in the SA and AV nodes and His-Purkinje system show slow phase-4 depolarisation and generate their own impulses.

front: Which ion carries phase 0 in fast-channel versus slow-channel action potentials?
back: Fast-channel fibres (atria, ventricles, Purkinje) depolarise through Na+ entry. Slow-channel fibres (SA and AV nodes) depolarise through Ca2+ entry, which is slower and has a less negative threshold.

front: Why is conduction slow in SA and AV nodal tissue?
back: Slow-channel action potentials have a slow 0 phase, low amplitude and small overshoot, so the wave moves decrementally. Conduction velocity is about 0.01 to 0.1 m/s in slow-channel tissue against 0.5 to 5 m/s in fast-channel tissue.

front: How do effective refractory period and action potential duration compare in fast-channel and slow-channel fibres?
back: Fast-channel fibres recover Na+ channels voltage-dependently, so ERP is shorter than APD (ERP/APD below 1). Slow-channel fibres recover Ca2+ channels with time, so ERP is longer than APD (ERP/APD above 1).

front: Which tissue is the normal pacemaker, and what is its key feature?
back: The SA node. It has the steepest phase-4 slope and so reaches threshold first. Other automatic tissue fires more slowly and acts as latent pacemaker if the SA node fails.

front: How does hyperpolarisation change excitability, and what happens below about -55 mV?
back: Hyperpolarisation widens the gap to threshold, so the fibre is less excitable. Below about -55 mV in fast-channel fibres, all Na+ channels are inactivated and the fibre cannot respond.

front: Vagal (ACh) versus sympathetic (adrenaline) effects on the heart: automaticity, refractoriness, conduction and contractility.
back: Vagal stimulation slows SA automaticity, shortens atrial refractoriness, prolongs refractoriness in conducting tissue and depresses conduction. Sympathetic stimulation increases automaticity and contractility, shortens refractoriness and enhances conduction.

front: Which histamine receptor types are clinically relevant, and what is the role of H3 and H4?
back: H1 and H2 are the main clinically targeted types. H3 is mainly a presynaptic autoreceptor in the brain that limits histamine release; KDT lists no H3 drug in use, but GG14 notes pitolisant, an H3 inverse agonist, is approved for narcolepsy. H4, cloned in 2001, is on eosinophils, mast cells and basophils and promotes their chemotaxis.

front: What are the signalling pathways of H1 and H2 receptors?
back: H1 is Gq-coupled: PIP2 hydrolysis gives IP3 and DAG, releasing intracellular Ca2+ and activating protein kinase C. H2 is Gs-coupled: adenylyl cyclase is stimulated and cAMP rises.

front: Describe the triple response produced by intradermal histamine.
back: Red spot from intense capillary dilatation; wheal from fluid leaking out of capillaries and venules; flare, a surrounding redness from arteriolar dilatation that is driven by an axon reflex.

front: Why is histamine inactive when given orally?
back: It is rapidly broken down by oxidation and methylation, and the liver degrades all histamine absorbed from the intestine before it reaches the circulation.

back: They cross the blood-brain barrier and block central H1 receptors that help maintain wakefulness. Diphenhydramine, promethazine, hydroxyzine and dimenhydrinate are the highly sedating members, while chlorpheniramine and clemastine are only mildly sedating.

front: Why were terfenadine and astemizole withdrawn, and how does fexofenadine avoid this problem?
back: Both caused torsades de pointes through blockade of cardiac delayed rectifier K+ channels, especially at higher doses or with CYP3A4 inhibitors. Fexofenadine, the active metabolite of terfenadine, blocks these channels only weakly and is minimally metabolised, so it does not prolong the QTc interval.

front: What additional actions does cyproheptadine have beyond H1 blockade, and what are its uses?
back: It also blocks 5-HT2A receptors and is sedating. Uses include pruritus, appetite stimulation (including off-label use in underweight patients), and control of carcinoid intestinal symptoms and SSRI-induced priapism.

front: Describe the synthesis and degradation of 5-HT.
back: 5-HT is made from L-tryptophan: tryptophan hydroxylase forms 5-hydroxytryptophan, which is decarboxylated to 5-HT. It is degraded mainly by MAO-A to 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid. It is taken up into platelets and nerve endings by the serotonin transporter, which SSRIs and tricyclics inhibit, and its vesicular storage (VMAT-2) is blocked by reserpine.

front: How are the 5-HT receptor families classified by their signalling?
back: 5-HT1 receptors (Gi/Go) reduce cAMP. 5-HT2 receptors (Gq) generate IP3 and DAG. 5-HT4, 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 (Gs) raise cAMP. 5-HT3 is not G-protein coupled but a ligand-gated cation channel that depolarises nerve endings quickly.

front: What is the role of 5-HT1A agonists such as buspirone?
back: Buspirone, gepirone and ipsapirone are azapirones that act as partial agonists at 5-HT1A receptors. They are anxiolytics that do not cause sedation.

front: Which receptor mediates the emetic reflex, and which antagonist is the prototype?
back: 5-HT3 receptors on nerve endings in the gut wall (myenteric plexus), in the area postrema and in the nucleus tractus solitarius. Ondansetron is the prototype selective 5-HT3 antagonist, used against vomiting from highly emetic cytotoxic drugs and radiotherapy.

Acting on 5-HT2A receptors it changes platelet shape and causes weak aggregation, but it does not induce the release reaction. Platelets store and release 5-HT, which amplifies aggregation with collagen and other mediators.

back: It is a potent 5-HT2A/2C antagonist used for migraine prophylaxis, carcinoid and postgastrectomy dumping syndrome. It was withdrawn because it caused fibrosis in the abdomen, lungs and endocardium.

front: What is the first-line treatment for a mild migraine attack, and what adjunct is useful for nausea?

Prophylaxis for 6 months or more
Dispersible or effervescent analgesics because gastric stasis hampers absorption
Diazepam, diphenhydramine or caffeine help some patients

front: Why triptans must be avoided in ischaemic heart disease
back: Triptans are contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, epilepsy, hepatic or renal impairment and pregnancy. Coronary vasospasm and myocardial infarction are rare but serious adverse effects.

front: Why sumatriptan has low oral bioavailability
back: Oral bioavailability averages about 15%. Subcutaneous injection is absorbed rapidly and completely. Nasal spray is absorbed faster, but its bioavailability is about the same. It is the only triptan available for nasal and parenteral use.

front: Why caffeine is combined with ergotamine
back: Caffeine (100 mg) taken with ergotamine enhances its absorption from oral and rectal routes and adds to the cranial vasoconstricting action.

front: Why dispersible analgesics are preferred in migraine
back: Gastric stasis during a migraine attack delays absorption from a regular tablet. Dispersible or effervescent forms of the analgesic are therefore preferred.

front: Propranolol in migraine prophylaxis: dose and mechanism
back: Start 40 mg twice daily and increase as needed (KDT8 appendix). It is the first-choice prophylactic drug. The mechanism is not established, and the role of beta-blockade has been questioned.

front: Why pindolol is not used in migraine prophylaxis
back: Pindolol and other beta-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity are not useful in migraine. KDT8 states the fact without a mechanism, so the card does not give one.

front: Flunarizine in migraine: class, dose and adverse effects
back: Weak calcium channel blocker. Adult dose 10-20 mg once daily; children 5 mg once daily. Adverse effects: sedation, constipation, dry mouth, hypotension, flushing, weight gain and rarely extrapyramidal symptoms.

Gabapentin 300-1200 mg a day
Topiramate: start 25 mg once daily, increase to 50 mg once or twice daily
Two randomised trials: about half the patients had 50% fewer attacks with topiramate
Less effective than beta-blockers

Mediators include 5-HT, substance P, neurokinin, CGRP and nitric oxide

Mild: simple analgesics or NSAIDs with an antiemetic
Moderate: NSAID combinations or a triptan or ergot
Severe: triptan or ergot with antiemetic, sometimes with a longer-acting NSAID

front: Name the precursor and the two main enzymatic pathways for eicosanoid synthesis.
back: The precursor is arachidonic acid (a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid), released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2. The cyclooxygenase pathway makes prostaglandins, thromboxanes and prostacyclin. The lipoxygenase pathway (5-LOX) makes leukotrienes. Eicosanoids are not stored; they are made when needed.

front: How do COX-1 and COX-2 differ in function?
back: COX-1 is expressed constitutively in most cells and makes prostanoids for housekeeping functions: gastric mucosal protection, platelet TXA2 and renal function. COX-2 is induced by cytokines, shear stress and growth factors and is the main source of prostanoids in inflammation (pain, fever) and cancer. The split is not absolute: COX-2 also contributes constitutively in some tissues, such as gastric epithelium. Selective COX-2 inhibitors include celecoxib and etoricoxib.

front: How does aspirin differ from other NSAIDs in inhibiting COX?
back: Aspirin acetylates a serine residue on COX and inhibits it irreversibly. Other NSAIDs are competitive and reversible. Because platelets cannot make new COX-1 and the vessel wall can, low-dose aspirin inhibits platelet thromboxane for days.

text: The contractile group (EP1, {{FP}}, {{TP}}) couples through {{Gq}}; the relaxant group (DP1, EP2, EP4, {{IP}}) couples through {{Gs}}; {{EP3}} is the inhibitory receptor coupling through Gi.
Platelets synthesise {{TXA2}}; endothelium synthesises {{PGI2}}; macrophages make {{LTC4 and LTD4}}; neutrophils make {{LTB4}}.

front: What are the opposing actions of platelet TXA2 and endothelial PGI2?
back: TXA2, made by platelets, promotes aggregation and vasoconstriction. PGI2, made by the endothelium, inhibits aggregation and causes vasodilatation. The two act as a balanced system that keeps blood flowing and allows plugging when a vessel is injured.

front: Why COX-2 inhibitors can delay ulcer healing
back: COX-1 makes the protective gastric prostaglandins normally, but COX-2 is induced during ulcer healing. COX-2 inhibitors are less ulcerogenic, yet by blocking this induced COX-2 they have the potential to delay healing.

front: Which prostanoids constrict bronchi, and which dilate them?
back: PGF2alpha, PGD2 and TXA2 constrict bronchi, more strongly than histamine. PGE2 is a powerful bronchodilator and PGI2 a mild one. Inhaled PGE2 is not clinically useful because it irritates the airway and its action is brief.

front: What are the gastroprotective actions of PGE2?
back: PGE2 reduces basal and stimulated acid and pepsin secretion, suppresses gastrin release, and increases mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow. The ulcer-causing effect of NSAIDs is attributed to losing this protection.

front: Why prostaglandins cause colic and watery diarrhoea
back: PGE2 increases intestinal propulsive activity in man, especially. It also acts on the mucosa to increase water, electrolyte and mucus secretion. Together these produce colic and watery diarrhoea, the important side effects of PGE2.
A synthetic PGI2 analogue used in pulmonary arterial hypertension. It is given by inhalation, and transient coughing is the most common inhalation adverse effect.

front: Selexipag: class and role in pulmonary arterial hypertension
back: Selexipag is an oral IP receptor agonist. It is added to existing pulmonary vasodilator therapy in a majority of patients in the clinical trials.

front: Carboprost: what is it, and how is it used in postpartum haemorrhage?
back: Carboprost is 15-methyl PGF2-alpha; the methyl group prolongs its action. For PPH from uterine atony not responding to oxytocin and ergometrine: 0.25 mg (250 mcg) IM, repeated every 30 to 120 minutes if needed (KDT); Katzung cites about 80% success. It is also used for second-trimester and missed abortion. Adverse effects: vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, flushing and transient bronchoconstriction.

front: Which PGF2alpha analogues are first-line for open-angle glaucoma and how do they work?
back: Latanoprost, travoprost and bimatoprost are FP receptor agonists. They lower intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral and trabecular outflow of aqueous humour, and are non-irritating compared with the parent PGF2alpha.

front: Ophthalmic prostaglandin analogues: why they lower intraocular pressure
back: Latanoprost, travoprost and bimatoprost are FP receptor agonists and first-line in open-angle glaucoma. They increase uveoscleral and trabecular outflow of aqueous humour. Latanoprost, a stable long-acting PGF2-alpha derivative, was the first prostanoid used for glaucoma. Adverse effects include increased iris pigmentation and eyelash changes.

front: Alprostadil in neonates: purpose and risk
back: Alprostadil (PGE1) maintains patency of the ductus arteriosus in neonates with congenital heart defects until corrective surgery. Ampoule 0.5 mg in 1 ml is diluted and infused intravenously. Apnoea occurs in a few cases.

front: Epoprostenol: uses and a key caution
back: Epoprostenol (PGI2) prevents platelet aggregation and damage during haemodialysis or bypass. It is used for pulmonary hypertension. It is contraindicated in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and carries bleeding and pulmonary oedema risks.

front: Medical termination with prostaglandins: precautions and side effects
back: Exclude ectopic pregnancy beforehand and confirm complete expulsion afterwards. Common effects are uterine cramps, vaginal bleeding, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Methotrexate with misoprostol is also effective for abortion in the first few weeks of pregnancy.

front: Which leukotriene receptor antagonists are used in asthma, and what do they block?
back: Montelukast and zafirlukast block the cysLT1 receptor, which is mainly on bronchial and intestinal smooth muscle and binds LTD4 more avidly than LTC4. They are useful antiasthmatic drugs.

front: What is platelet activating factor chemically, and how is it made?
back: It is acetylglyceryl ether phosphorylcholine, with an ether-linked alkyl chain of 16 or 18 carbons. It is made on demand from membrane phospholipids, with the second step rate-limiting. It is active at subnanomolar concentrations.

front: How does prostacyclin (PGI2) relax pulmonary arterial smooth muscle?
back: It binds the IP receptor, which activates Gs and raises cAMP. This causes vasodilatation and reduces smooth muscle proliferation in the pulmonary circulation.

front: What is the NO-cGMP pathway in the pulmonary circulation, and which enzyme breaks cGMP down?
back: NO activates soluble guanylate cyclase to form cGMP, which relaxes pulmonary artery smooth muscle. PDE5 degrades cGMP.

front: Sildenafil in PAH: class, dose and place in therapy
back: A selective PDE5 inhibitor, given orally. The printed dose is 20 mg three times daily. It is a preferred agent for moderate PAH (functional class II to III).

front: Why must PDE5 inhibitors never be combined with nitrates?
back: Both raise cGMP signalling. Sildenafil markedly potentiates the vasodilator action of nitrates, which can cause a precipitous fall in BP and MI.
An sGC stimulator. It sensitises sGC to endogenous NO and also stimulates the enzyme directly. It is approved for PAH and was also effective in CTEPH.
Co-use with nitroglycerin or PDE5 inhibitors can cause severe hypotension and syncope.

front: What does endothelin-1 do in pulmonary hypertension?
back: ET-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor released by endothelial cells. Sustained overproduction of endothelins is implicated in PAH.

front: Oral endothelin receptor antagonists used in PAH
back: Bosentan, ambrisentan and macitentan. Each is first-line for moderate PAH (functional class II to III) and is teratogenic (FDA REMS programme).

front: Bosentan: monitoring and interaction to remember
back: Liver transaminases must be monitored closely, and it should be avoided or dose-reduced in moderate or severe hepatic impairment. It is metabolised mainly by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4.

front: Which calcium channel blockers are used in PAH, and when?
back: Nifedipine (long-acting), amlodipine, diltiazem and verapamil, but only in patients with a positive acute vasodilator test. The test uses inhaled NO (10 ppm for 10 min); a 30% fall in PVR is associated with a good CCB response.

front: What must be monitored when titrating CCBs in PAH?
back: Systemic blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturation. Systemic hypotension is the main concern, and loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction can worsen V/Q mismatch.

front: Inhaled nitric oxide: main clinical uses
back: It is used in term and near-term neonates with persistent PH of the newborn and in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. In adults with PAH it is used off-label for acute vasodilator testing.
Doses of 500 to 1000 ppm can be lethal, and doses below 40 ppm are well tolerated chronically.

front: Treprostinil: class, routes and key use
back: A PGI2 analogue with a longer half-life than epoprostenol. It can be given IV, subcutaneously, by inhalation or orally, and is first-line for PH due to interstitial lung disease.

The tablet shell does not dissolve, so it can be seen in stool and may lodge in intestinal blind-end pouches or diverticula, with a possible link to appendicitis and diverticulitis. It is a CYP2C8 substrate, so gemfibrozil and rifampin interact.

front: Inhaled iloprost: dosing and adverse effects
back: Used four times a day, with the number of breaths slowly titrated up to a maximum of 12 breaths four times a day. Transient coughing is the most common adverse effect of inhalation.

front: Selexipag: pharmacokinetics that set its dosing
back: An oral, selective IP receptor agonist. The parent drug is hydrolysed quickly to an active metabolite with a half-life of 10 to 14 h, which allows twice-daily dosing. It is a substrate of CYP2C8, CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, and is contraindicated with strong CYP2C8 inhibitors.

front: Where is most of the body's iron, and where is the stored fraction kept?
back: An adult carries about 3.5 g of iron. Roughly 62% is in haemoglobin and about 25% is stored as ferritin and haemosiderin, mainly in reticuloendothelial cells in liver, spleen and marrow. The rest is in myoglobin and iron-containing enzymes.

front: Compare the absorption of haeme iron with that of inorganic dietary iron.
back: Haeme iron is absorbed best (up to about 35%) through a haeme carrier protein, without needing to be freed from its complex first. Inorganic iron averages about 5%: it must be reduced to the ferrous form, then enters the enterocyte through DMT1 and leaves the cell through ferroportin.

front: Which substances impair the absorption of non-haeme iron, and which help it?
back: Impairing: antacids and other alkalis (keep iron insoluble and block its reduction), phytates in cereals, phosphates, tetracyclines (chelation), and a heavy mixed meal in the stomach. Helping: gastric acid, reducing agents such as ascorbic acid and sulfhydryl amino acids, and meat, which adds haeme iron and stimulates acid.

front: What is the mucosal block (ferritin curtain) and when is it overcome?
back: Iron entering the enterocyte can be trapped as ferritin, which is lost when the cell is shed after 2 to 4 days. This limits absorption. The block is weakened in iron deficiency or brisk erythropoiesis, when more iron passes into plasma, and is overwhelmed by a gross excess of iron.

front: What oral elemental iron dose gives the maximal haemopoietic response, and what is the prophylactic dose?
back: KDT: about 200 mg of elemental iron a day in three divided doses gives the maximal haemopoietic response; about 30 mg a day is prophylactic. GG14 adds that a single dose of about 65 mg elemental iron (one 325 mg ferrous sulfate tablet) every other day maximises the fraction absorbed. Doses are always counted as elemental iron, not salt weight.

front: When is parenteral iron indicated instead of oral iron?
back: When oral iron is not tolerated, when it is not absorbed (malabsorption, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic inflammation), when the patient does not take it, in severe deficiency with ongoing blood loss, and in chronic kidney disease patients on erythropoietin who need iron faster than oral intake can supply.

text: Dissociable oral salts include {{ferrous sulfate}}, {{ferrous fumarate}} and {{ferrous gluconate}}; {{carbonyl iron}} is a fine metallic powder with about three-quarters the bioavailability of ferrous sulfate.

Iron {{dextran}} can be given both i.m. and i.v.; {{ferrous sucrose}} is given only i.v., with a single dose of up to {{200 mg}}; {{ferric carboxymaltose}} and {{iron isomaltoside 1000}} allow large single infusions.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed only when bound to {{intrinsic factor}} made in the {{stomach}}; folate is absorbed mainly in the {{upper intestine}}; the body's folate stores last only {{3 to 4 months}} without a supply.

front: Cloze: iron in haemoglobin and blood loss
text: Haemoglobin contains about {{0.33%}} iron; loss of 100 ml blood (15 g Hb) removes about {{50 mg}} elemental iron, and raising blood Hb by 1 g/dl needs about {{200 mg}} iron.

front: Iron dextran: what makes it unusual, and what are its main risks?
back: It is the only iron preparation that can be given both i.m. and i.v. About 25% extra is added to the calculated dose because some stays locally bound at the injection site. It has the highest rate of hypersensitivity, including anaphylactoid collapse, because dextran is antigenic. A test dose is no longer recommended, and resuscitation facilities must be ready before any i.v. dose.

front: Which newer intravenous iron products are the most convenient and safest, and why?
back: Ferric carboxymaltose and iron isomaltoside 1000 are considered the two most convenient and safest i.v. options. Ferric carboxymaltose can be given as a single infusion of up to 1000 mg in saline (not glucose) and must not be given i.m. Iron isomaltoside 1000 allows a single 1 to 2 g infusion over 15 to 30 minutes, because its tight matrix releases little labile iron.

front: Which drug is the chelator of choice in acute iron poisoning, and why is dimercaprol (BAL) avoided?
back: Desferrioxamine (deferoxamine). It is given when plasma iron exceeds the total iron-binding capacity, and the IV route is used to chelate iron already absorbed; early chelation has cut the mortality of iron poisoning sharply. BAL (dimercaprol) is avoided because its iron complex is itself toxic.

front: Which clotting tests explore the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, and what does each test?
back: The aPTT explores the intrinsic (contact-activation) pathway and the common pathway. The prothrombin time (PT) explores the extrinsic (tissue factor) pathway and the common pathway. The extrinsic route activates factor X within seconds; the intrinsic route is slow and takes minutes.

front: How does vitamin K take part in blood clotting?
back: Vitamin K is a cofactor for the hepatic enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which adds carboxyl groups to glutamate residues of factors II, VII, IX and X. This lets them bind calcium and phospholipid surfaces. Protein C, protein S and osteocalcin use the same step.

front: How do coumarin anticoagulants block clotting?
back: They inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), so reduced vitamin K cannot be regenerated. The liver then makes under-carboxylated, inactive factors II, VII, IX and X. Coumarins work only in vivo and act with a delay of 1 to 3 days, because already-circulating factors must decay.

front: On warfarin, which clotting factor falls first, and why does the effect take days to appear?
back: Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 h), so it falls first, followed by factor IX (about 24 h), factor X (about 40 h) and prothrombin (about 60 h). Synthesis slows within hours, but the full effect appears over 1 to 3 days as circulating factors decline. A larger loading dose only slightly hastens it.

front: What INR ranges are used for warfarin therapy?
back: INR 2 to 3 for most indications, such as venous thromboembolism and atrial fibrillation. A higher range of 2.5 to 3.5 is used for mechanical heart valves in the mitral position, or mechanical valves in another position with atrial fibrillation or a prior stroke. Intracranial bleeding risk rises steeply above INR 4. The INR corrects the prothrombin time for the sensitivity of the thromboplastin used, so results are comparable between laboratories.

text: The vitamin K-dependent clotting factors are {{II}}, {{VII}}, {{IX}} and {{X}}; the anticoagulant proteins {{protein C}} and {{protein S}} are also vitamin K-dependent.

front: Complete: metabolism of the warfarin enantiomers
text: Warfarin is a racemate; the {{S}} enantiomer is 3 to 5 times more potent and is cleared mainly by {{CYP2C9}}, whose polymorphisms (with {{VKORC1}} variants) alter dose needs. KDT states the less potent R enantiomer is degraded by side-chain reduction through CYP1A and CYP3A4.

front: Classify: vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants
text: {{Warfarin}} has a half-life of {{36 to 48 h}}; {{acenocoumarol}} has an overall effective duration of about {{24 h}} through its active metabolite; {{ethyl biscoumacetate}} acts rapidly and briefly; {{bishydroxycoumarin}} is slowly and unpredictably absorbed.

front: Cloze: clotting factor fall on warfarin
text: Factor {{VII}} falls first, with a half-life of about {{6 h}}; factor IX ({{24 h}}), factor X ({{40 h}}) and prothrombin ({{60 h}}) follow.

front: Which drugs and conditions increase the effect of warfarin, and by what mechanism?
back: Broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce gut vitamin K production; ceftriaxone and cefoperazone add a direct hypoprothrombinaemic effect; aspirin adds platelet inhibition and GI bleeding; sulfonamides, phenytoin and indomethacin displace warfarin from albumin; chloramphenicol, erythromycin, metronidazole, amiodarone, cimetidine and allopurinol inhibit its metabolism. Liver disease, malnutrition and hyperthyroidism also increase the effect.

front: Which drugs reduce the effect of warfarin, and why is stopping them dangerous?
back: Barbiturates (not benzodiazepines), carbamazepine, rifampicin and griseofulvin induce warfarin metabolism; oral contraceptives raise clotting factor levels. If an inducer is withdrawn while warfarin continues, the INR can rise sharply, and fatal bleeding has occurred.

front: How is excess anticoagulation or bleeding on warfarin managed?
back: No bleeding, raised INR: hold warfarin and restart at a lower dose once the INR is in range; if the INR is 10 or more, give oral vitamin K1 2.5 to 5 mg, which lowers the INR within 24 to 48 h without causing warfarin resistance. Serious bleeding: four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate improves haemostasis (GG14); avoid IV vitamin K because it can cause severe anaphylactoid reactions (KDT8). Vitamin K acts slowly because factors must be resynthesised, and high doses make the patient unresponsive to warfarin for several days.

front: Why does warfarin dose requirement vary so much between patients?
back: Genetic variation in two genes. CYP2C9 variants alter metabolism of the more potent S-warfarin (pharmacokinetic effect). VKORC1 variants make the target enzyme more sensitive to inhibition (pharmacodynamic effect). About 10% of patients need less than 1.5 mg a day to reach INR 2 to 3, often because they carry these variants. Genotyping both genes can help choose the starting dose. Diet, interacting drugs and illness add further variation.

front: A patient on stable warfarin starts rifampicin for 2 months, then stops it. What happens to the INR, and how do you plan monitoring?
back: Rifampicin induces liver enzymes, so warfarin is cleared faster and the INR falls (loss of effect, risk of clots). The dose must be raised with repeat INR checks. When rifampicin is stopped, induction fades over time, the same dose becomes too strong and bleeding risk rises, so the dose must be cut back with close INR monitoring. Target is usually INR 2 to 3. Bleeding with a high INR: hold warfarin, give vitamin K; stopping inducers is as dangerous as starting inhibitors.

Heparin binds antithrombin III and greatly speeds its inhibition of factors Xa, IIa (thrombin), IXa, XIa and XIIa, but not VIIa. Its long chain also acts as a scaffold that brings thrombin and antithrombin together. The effect is immediate in vivo and in vitro.

front: Why does low-concentration heparin prolong aPTT more than PT?
back: At low concentration heparin mainly blocks factor Xa-driven thrombin generation, which amplifies the intrinsic pathway, so aPTT rises while PT barely changes. At high concentration it also blocks the common pathway, and PT is prolonged.

front: What is the standard i.v. heparin regimen and the monitoring target?
back: Continuous IV infusion after a bolus: GG14 gives a 5000 U fixed or weight-adjusted bolus, then 800 to 1600 U/h (KDT: 5000 to 10000 U bolus, then 750 to 1000 U/h). Titrate to an aPTT of 1.5 to 2.5 times control (about 50 to 80 s). Intermittent IV bolus dosing is no longer recommended.

front: What is danaparoid, and when is it used?
back: A heparinoid preparation consisting mainly of heparan sulfate from pig gut mucosa. Its anticoagulant action is weaker than heparin's. It is used in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

front: Cloze: heparin dosing and monitoring numbers
text: Infusion is titrated so that aPTT stays at about {{50-80 s}} or {{1.5-2.5}} times control; protamine neutralises heparin at {{1 mg per 100 U}}, and {{1 mg}} of heparin sodium is about {{120-140 U}}.

front: How is heparin reversed with protamine, and what are its limits and dangers?
back: Protamine, a basic protein, neutralises heparin about 1 mg per 100 U. It does not reverse fondaparinux and only partly reverses low molecular weight heparins. Inject it slowly (about 5 mg/min); rapid injection causes flushing and breathlessness. It can itself act as an anticoagulant and can cause hypersensitivity.

front: Fondaparinux: mechanism, kidney caveat and monitoring
back: Synthetic pentasaccharide that binds antithrombin III and selectively inactivates factor Xa, not thrombin. Given s.c. with 100% bioavailability, half-life about 17 hours, largely excreted unchanged by the kidney, so avoid in renal failure. No aPTT monitoring; little thrombocytopenia or osteoporosis; not reversed by protamine.

front: Bivalirudin: why a direct thrombin inhibitor is chosen
back: Synthetic 20-amino-acid analogue of leech hirudin. Binds both catalytic and substrate sites of thrombin directly, so it needs no antithrombin. Short acting (half-life about 25 minutes). Not a heparin, so it suits patients at risk of HIT; used in PCI for STEMI with aspirin and/or clopidogrel or a GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor. Protamine does not reverse it.

front: On day 7 of heparin a patient with renal failure has a falling platelet count and a new leg thrombosis. Name the diagnosis and the anticoagulant plan, with reasons.
back: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: antibodies to heparin-PF4 complexes activate platelets, causing paradoxical thrombosis. Stop all heparin and avoid LMWH (cross-reacts). Give a non-heparin agent such as argatroban, which is cleared by the liver so suits renal failure; bivalirudin is another option. Fondaparinux is renally excreted, so it is poor in renal failure. Do not start warfarin until platelets recover because it can cause venous limb gangrene.

front: How does aspirin inhibit platelets, and why does its effect last for days?
back: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, which stops thromboxane A2 synthesis. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts until new platelets are formed; bleeding time stays prolonged for 5 to 7 days. Low daily doses accumulate. Daily doses of 100 mg or less are used for most indications; higher doses also inhibit vascular prostacyclin and add bleeding without extra benefit.

text: GP IIb/IIIa antagonists include {{abciximab}}, {{eptifibatide}} and {{tirofiban}}; the thienopyridines {{clopidogrel}} and {{prasugrel}} irreversibly block the {{P2Y12}} receptor; {{ticagrelor}} blocks the same receptor reversibly.

front: Which P2Y12 blockers are prodrugs and which are active drugs, and what does this mean for onset and offset?
back: Clopidogrel and prasugrel are thienopyridine prodrugs that need hepatic activation and block P2Y12 irreversibly, so platelets recover only as new ones form (about 5 days for clopidogrel, 7 for prasugrel). Ticagrelor is active as given and reversible, so it acts and wears off faster.

front: Why are glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antagonists the most potent antiplatelet drugs?
back: The GPIIb/IIIa integrin binds fibrinogen and vWF to cross-link platelets, which is the final common step of aggregation. Blocking it stops aggregation whatever the agonist. Agents are abciximab, eptifibatide and tirofiban, given with aspirin and heparin in ACS and PCI. Bleeding and thrombocytopenia are the main hazards.

front: How do rivaroxaban and apixaban work, and what is their route of use?
back: Both are oral direct factor Xa inhibitors, so they block thrombin generation at a key point of the cascade. They work rapidly, are given at fixed doses and need no routine laboratory monitoring. Uses include DVT/PE and stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation; bleeding is the main adverse effect.

front: Give the practical advantages of DOACs over warfarin.
back: Rapid onset and offset, fixed doses, no INR monitoring and fewer drug interactions. They are comparable or better than warfarin for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF. Limits: avoid with mechanical heart valves (dabigatran is contraindicated there); bleeding still occurs, so specific reversal agents exist.

front: Dabigatran: how is it given, and how is it reversed?
back: Dabigatran etexilate is an oral prodrug converted to dabigatran, a reversible direct thrombin inhibitor. About 80% of absorbed drug is excreted unchanged by the kidney, so the dose is reduced in severe renal impairment. It has no CYP3A4 interaction, but it is a P-glycoprotein substrate. Idarucizumab, a humanised antibody fragment, is the specific reversal agent. It must not be used with mechanical heart valves or triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome.

front: Andexanet alfa: what is it and when is it used?
back: A recombinant factor Xa analogue with its active-site serine replaced and its Gla domain removed, so it has no clotting activity. It acts as a decoy that binds circulating rivaroxaban or apixaban and rapidly reverses their anti-Xa effect. Given as an IV bolus then a 2 h infusion, for serious bleeding such as intracranial haemorrhage. It also reverses heparin and LMWH, so it is avoided before procedures that need heparin. It is costly; four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is used if it is unavailable.

front: What roles do chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL and HDL play in lipid transport?
back: Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride from the gut. VLDL carries liver-made triglyceride. Its remnant, IDL, loses more triglyceride and becomes LDL, which carries cholesterol to tissues and liver. HDL removes excess cholesterol from tissues. Raised LDL and VLDL are atherogenic; HDL is protective.

front: How do statins lower LDL cholesterol?
back: They competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Hepatic cholesterol falls, which increases LDL receptor expression on liver cells, so more IDL and LDL are cleared from blood. Over the long term, feedback partly restores synthesis, leaving a dose-dependent lowering of LDL.

front: Why are statins given at bedtime, and which statins are exceptions?
back: Cholesterol synthesis by HMG-CoA reductase peaks around midnight, so statins are given at night for maximal effect. Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin have long half-lives and can be taken at any time of day.

front: Statin myopathy: how common is it, and which drugs raise the risk?
back: Muscle aches are common, but true myopathy is rare (under 1 in 1000) and rhabdomyolysis deaths are on record. Pravastatin, fluvastatin and rosuvastatin are not extensively metabolised by CYP3A4, so they carry less interaction risk. Simvastatin 80 mg is not advised; simvastatin should not exceed 20 mg with amlodipine or amiodarone, or 10 mg with diltiazem or verapamil.

front: How does ezetimibe lower LDL cholesterol, and what is its main role?
back: It blocks NPC1L1, the intestinal transporter for dietary and biliary cholesterol and phytosterols, lowering LDL by about 15 to 20%. It is mainly an add-on to a statin, with a synergistic effect. Its extra outcome benefit is small, about 2% in IMPROVE-IT with simvastatin.

front: Why are bile acid sequestrants seldom used, and what do they do to triglycerides?
back: Cholestyramine, colestipol and colesevelam bind bile acids in the gut, which increases hepatic LDL receptor expression and lowers LDL by about 15 to 25%. Triglycerides are not lowered and may rise. They are seldom used because they are unpalatable, need large doses, cause flatulence and GI upset, bind other drugs, and are poorly accepted.

front: How do fibrates work, and what lipid changes do they produce?
back: They activate PPAR-alpha, which increases lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid oxidation and reduces hepatic triglyceride synthesis. Triglycerides fall by 20 to 50%, LDL falls by 5 to 15%, and HDL rises by 10 to 20%. Their main use is severe hypertriglyceridaemia.

front: Why is nicotinic acid useful, and what limits its use?
back: It is the most effective drug for raising HDL, and it also lowers triglycerides, LDL and lipoprotein(a). It inhibits adipocyte lipolysis and hepatic VLDL production. Flushing (mediated by prostaglandin D2) limits use; aspirin before a dose reduces it. Dyspepsia, hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia and liver damage are other limits, and doses above 2 g a day are poorly tolerated. Added to statins it gave no outcome benefit (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE), and in 2016 the FDA withdrew approval of extended-release niacin as statin add-on therapy.

front: Which step limits acetylcholine synthesis, and which drug blocks it?

front: Botulinum toxin: where and how does it act at cholinergic terminals?

front: What are the contraindications and cautions for anticholinesterase drugs?
back: Contraindicated in sick sinus, AV conduction defects and hypotensive states, because accumulated ACh causes bradycardia and fall in cardiac output. Use cautiously in peptic ulcer, hypertension, asthma, COPD and seizure disorders.

front: Why do anticholinesterases differ in their CNS and neuromuscular actions?

front: How does edrophonium's enzyme binding differ from an organophosphate's?
back: Edrophonium binds only the anionic site through weak hydrogen bonds, with no covalent bond, so the enzyme recovers within minutes and the action is brief. Organophosphates bind the esteratic site covalently, phosphorylating it; recovery is very slow and the enzyme can age and become resistant to reactivation.

front: What is the basic defect in myasthenia gravis and why do anticholinesterases help?
back: Autoantibodies against nicotinic receptors at the muscle endplate leave only about a third or fewer free receptors, causing weakness that worsens with repeated activity and recovers with rest. Anticholinesterases let released ACh persist and act on the remaining receptors repeatedly, restoring strength, but they do not treat the disease itself.

front: What does atropine achieve in anticholinesterase poisoning, and how is it dosed?
back: It counters the muscarinic features, but needs higher doses for central effects and does not reverse nicotinic muscle paralysis. Give 2 mg IV, repeated every 10 minutes until atropinisation (dry mouth); maintenance may be needed for 1 to 2 weeks. It is given in every carbamate or organophosphate case.

front: List the general measures in anticholinesterase poisoning before specific antidotes.
back: Stop exposure (fresh air, wash skin and mucosa with soap and water, lavage as needed), keep the airway open and ventilate if breathing fails, support BP and hydration, and control convulsions carefully with diazepam. Death is usually from respiratory failure, so airway comes first.

front: Why is pralidoxime used in organophosphate poisoning but contraindicated in carbamate poisoning?
back: Pralidoxime's quaternary nitrogen binds the anionic site, which the organophosphate leaves free, and its oxime end attacks the phosphorus on the esteratic site; the oxime-phosphonate diffuses away and the enzyme is reactivated (only before ageing). In carbamate poisoning the anionic site is not free, the carbamylated enzyme is not reactivated, and pralidoxime's own weak anti-ChE activity can add to toxicity, so it is not recommended (KDT: contraindicated).

front: Which mushroom poisonings are reversed by atropine, and which are not?
back: Early muscarine-type poisoning (Inocybe species) gives muscarinic signs within an hour and is promptly reversed by atropine. The hallucinogenic type (Amanita muscaria, due to muscimol) has no specific treatment and atropine is contraindicated. The late phalloidin type (Amanita phalloides) damages the gut, liver and kidney and is managed supportively.

OP-induced delayed polyneuropathy is different: it follows some fluorinated or triaryl compounds after 1 to 2 weeks, is due to inhibition of neuropathy target esterase rather than AChE, and causes sensory disturbance then limb weakness.

front: What is delayed organophosphate neuropathy and why does atropine or an oxime not prevent it?
back: Certain fluorine-containing and triaryl organophosphates cause polyneuritis and demyelination after days to weeks: sensory disturbance, then lower motor neurone weakness, later spastic upper motor neurone paralysis. It is not due to cholinesterase inhibition, so enzyme-directed antidotes do nothing; there is no specific treatment and recovery can take years.

front: What kind of antagonist is atropine, and how does its selectivity change with dose?
back: It is a competitive antagonist at muscarinic receptors and blocks all muscarinic subtypes. It is selective for muscarinic receptors at usual doses, but this selectivity is lost at very high doses.

front: Atropine's central effects at low and high doses.
back: Low doses have little central effect because brain entry is restricted, though atropine suppresses vestibular excitation (motion sickness) and reduces tremor and rigidity in parkinsonism by blocking relative cholinergic overactivity in the basal ganglia. High doses cause cortical excitation, restlessness, hallucinations and delirium, then respiratory depression and coma.

front: What are the ocular effects of topical atropine, and what is the risk?
back: Mydriasis, loss of the light reflex and cycloplegia lasting about 7 to 10 days, causing photophobia and blurred near vision. The ciliary muscle recovers before the sphincter pupillae. It can raise intraocular pressure and is dangerous in narrow-angle glaucoma.

front: Rank the organs in order of sensitivity to atropine.
back: Most sensitive: saliva, sweat and bronchial secretions. Next: eye, bronchial muscle and heart. Less sensitive: intestinal and bladder smooth muscle. Least sensitive: gastric glands and gastric smooth muscle. The pattern reflects how much each function depends on cholinergic tone.

front: Atropine pharmacokinetics: how is it cleared, and what is its half-life?
back: About half is metabolised in the liver and the rest is excreted unchanged in urine. The half-life is about 3 to 4 hours. Passage across the BBB is somewhat restricted.

front: Name the contraindication and the caution for atropinic drugs.
back: Absolute contraindication: narrow iridocorneal angle, because it can precipitate acute congestive glaucoma. Caution: elderly men with prostatic hypertrophy, in whom urinary retention can occur.

front: Classify: mydriatics by onset and duration
text: {{Tropicamide}} acts in {{20 to 40 min}} and lasts {{3 to 6 hours}}; {{cyclopentolate}} acts in {{30 to 60 min}} and lasts about {{one day}}; {{homatropine}} is about {{10 times}} less potent than atropine.

front: What is atropine flush and why does it occur?
back: Dilation of cutaneous vessels in the blush area, seen with toxic and sometimes therapeutic atropine doses. It is thought to be a compensatory heat-loss response to the rise in body temperature caused by suppressed sweating.

front: Why does atropine cause tachycardia, and why does the effect vary between patients?
back: It blocks M2 receptors on the SA node, removing vagal slowing. The rise depends on the existing vagal tone, so it is greatest in young adults and smaller in children and the elderly. Small IM/SC doses can first cause a transient bradycardia, now attributed to block of prejunctional M1 autoreceptors on vagal endings, which increases ACh release.

front: What is the antidote for belladonna poisoning, and why is it a last resort?
back: Physostigmine, 0.5 to 2 mg IV repeated as required. It crosses the BBB and reverses central and peripheral effects, but it can cause hypotension and arrhythmias, so it is used only as a last resort. Neostigmine does not reverse central effects. A useful bedside test: methacholine 5 mg or neostigmine 1 mg s.c. fails to produce muscarinic effects in an atropinised patient.

front: How does hyoscine differ from atropine?
back: Hyoscine (l-hyoscine, scopolamine) is more potent on the eye and secretory glands and has better anti-motion sickness action. It is a central depressant even at low doses, penetrates the BBB better, is more completely metabolised, and acts for a shorter time than atropine.

front: How does inhaled ipratropium differ from atropine in airway use?
back: It acts mainly on the larger central airways and does not dry secretions or impair mucociliary clearance. Its onset is gradual, with peak effect at 40 to 60 minutes and duration of 4 to 6 hours. It suits regular prophylaxis rather than rescue. It works better in COPD than asthma, and is combined with a beta-2 agonist in acute exacerbations.

front: Why is tiotropium suited to once-daily maintenance in COPD?
back: It binds M1 and M3 bronchial receptors very tightly and binds M2 less tightly. This gives long-lasting bronchodilatation for once-daily use, and M2 sparing avoids enhanced acetylcholine release from vagal nerve endings. Regular use reduces COPD exacerbations.

front: Why is hyoscine the preferred drug for motion sickness, and how is it given?
back: It is the most effective antimotion sickness antimuscarinic and works best when given prophylactically: 0.2 mg orally, or a transdermal patch behind the pinna about 4 hours before travel, which protects for up to 3 days. Dry mouth and sedation can occur, so driving is risky.

back: They are quaternary amines that do not cross the blood-brain barrier or readily cross membranes. Inhaled absorption is inefficient, so systemic effects are small.

front: Classify: ganglion blockers and nicotinic agents

front: What does nicotine do at nicotinic receptors, and what is its only clinical use?
back: It is an agonist at both NN and NM receptors; it stimulates sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, and larger doses cause persistent depolarisation and ganglionic blockade. Its only use is short-term replacement therapy in tobacco-abstinent people; stimulating both ganglion divisions together has no therapeutic value.

front: Name the competitive ganglion blockers and their present status.
back: Hexamethonium, trimethaphan and mecamylamine. Once used for hypertension and peptic ulcer, they were replaced because of intolerable side effects and none is marketed now. Trimethaphan was an ultrashort-acting infusion for controlled hypotension (aortic dissection); mecamylamine was tried for smoking cessation.

front: Why do quaternary antimuscarinics carry a higher risk of ganglion and neuromuscular blockade?
back: Quaternary ammonium antagonists generally show more nicotinic-blocking activity than tertiary antagonists, so they are more likely to interfere with ganglionic or neuromuscular transmission.

front: Predict the side effects of ganglionic blockade from the dominant autonomic tone of each organ.
back: Parasympathetic-dominant organs lose tone: tachycardia, mydriasis, cycloplegia, reduced gut motility (constipation), bladder atony. Sympathetic-dominant vessels dilate, giving postural hypotension and syncope; erection and ejaculation are inhibited. This explains why the drugs were abandoned.

front: Compare nicotine patch, varenicline and bupropion for smoking cessation.
back: Patch: replaces nicotine, eases withdrawal but only partly craving because the intermittent peaks of smoking are missing; avoid in arrhythmia or ischaemic heart disease. Varenicline: alpha4beta2 partial agonist, gives some substitution while blocking reward; limited by mood changes and suicidal-thought warning. Bupropion: blocks DA and NA reuptake, equal efficacy with fewer side effects.

front: What is Alzheimer's disease, and what is its cholinergic defect?
back: A progressive neurodegenerative dementia of older people, with amyloid plaques and tau tangles. Brain cholinergic transmission is markedly deficient.

front: Why is donepezil given once daily at bedtime?
back: Its half-life is about 70 hours. Rivastigmine and galantamine have shorter half-lives and need twice-daily dosing.

front: How does memantine act in Alzheimer's disease?
back: It blocks NMDA-type glutamate receptors in a use-dependent way, limiting glutamate excitotoxicity. It is not a cholinesterase inhibitor.

front: Why was tacrine withdrawn from Alzheimer's therapy?
back: It was the first centrally acting anticholinesterase for AD, but caused hepatotoxicity (raised alanine aminotransferase), so its use fell away.

front: Compare donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine in Alzheimer's disease.
back: Donepezil: reversible, cerebroselective AChE inhibitor, once daily. Rivastigmine: lipophilic carbamate inhibiting AChE and BuChE, also available as a patch. Galantamine: natural alkaloid, selective for cerebral AChE, with some direct nicotinic agonism, twice daily. All three give similar modest benefit.

front: What is the cholinergic hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease?
back: Acetylcholine deficiency is critical to the symptoms. Support: the ACh deficit is selective, and central antagonists such as atropine can cause a confusional state resembling AD. AD also involves glutamate, 5HT and neuropeptide systems.

front: What are the main adverse effects of cholinesterase inhibitors in AD?
back: GI upset (diarrhoea, anorexia, nausea), muscle pain, weird dreams, fatigue, insomnia and hallucinations. GI effects are the main dose-limiting side effect; bradycardia and syncope are less common.

front: When is memantine used instead of a cholinesterase inhibitor in AD?
back: Memantine is indicated for moderate-to-severe dementia, as evidence in earlier stages is weak. It may replace or supplement cholinesterase inhibitors, which are used in mild or moderate AD.

back: A drug that relieves spasm of smooth muscle (gut, bladder, biliary tract) or of skeletal muscle in spasticity, easing colic and spasm pain. Gut antispasmodics include antimuscarinics such as atropine, glycopyrrolate and dicyclomine, plus non-anticholinergic drotaverine.

front: Why is glycopyrrolate preferred when central effects must be avoided?
back: It is a potent, rapidly acting antimuscarinic that lacks central effects, unlike atropine (CNS stimulation) and hyoscine (central depression).

front: What is dicyclomine's action on the gut?
back: A weak muscarinic antagonist with a direct, nonspecific spasmolytic effect on GI smooth muscle. Occasionally used for diarrhoea-predominant IBS.
On RyR1 calcium release channels of the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum. It blocks the Ca2+ release that couples excitation to contraction, without affecting neuromuscular transmission.

A selective GABA-B agonist that acts mainly in the spinal cord, decreasing transmitter release and depressing mono- and polysynaptic reflexes. It causes some weakness and is less sedating than diazepam.

front: How does botulinum toxin reduce muscle contraction?
back: It causes long-lasting loss of cholinergic transmission by interfering with exocytotic release of ACh at the nerve ending. Localised injection treats focal spasms.

Antimuscarinics (atropine methonitrate, clidinium, cimetropium, glycopyrrolate) block muscarinic receptors and so cause dry mouth and other antimuscarinic effects. Drotaverine is a non-anticholinergic smooth muscle antispasmodic, so it lacks these effects.

front: Where is atropine least useful as an antispasmodic?
back: In biliary colic and biliary spasm induced by opioids. In renal colic, parenteral opioids and NSAIDs relieve pain better; anticholinergics do not help infective diarrhoea.

front: Which relaxant suits spinal spasticity, and why?
back: Baclofen, for MS, ALS and spinal injury, because it is less sedative than diazepam. Dantrolene's weakness limits it to bedridden patients, and diazepam works through benzodiazepine receptors that enhance GABA transmission.

back: An organophosphate insecticide (thionophosphate) that is a prodrug: it must be converted to malaoxon. Plasma carboxylesterases hydrolyse it quickly, giving a wider safety margin than parathion.

front: How are dietary supplements regulated in the USA under DSHEA (1994)?
back: Herbal (botanical) products, vitamins, minerals, amino acids and similar products are legally dietary supplements, regulated as foods rather than drugs. Manufacturers need not prove efficacy or safety before marketing (only a new dietary ingredient needs some safety data); the FDA must prove harm before removing or restricting a product. Labels carry structure-function claims.

front: What quality problems affect herbal supplements?
back: GMP standards required by DSHEA were finalised only in 2007, so manufacturers long self-regulated: plant misidentification and species substitution (DNA barcoding found substitution in about a third of samples), adulteration with pharmaceuticals, contamination, and variable potency. Since 2006, manufacturers must report serious adverse events to the FDA.

front: Which quality practices does WHO advise for herbal medicines?
back: Good Agricultural and Collection Practice (GACP) at cultivation, Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) from crude powder or extract to purified product, and Good Supply Practice (GSP) during marketing. Traditional medicines generally lack controlled trials and documented safety and efficacy data.

front: What is a phytopharmaceutical drug under India's New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019?
back: A new-drug category: a purified, standardised fraction of a medicinal plant extract with at least four defined bioactive or phytochemical compounds, assessed qualitatively and quantitatively, for internal or external (not parenteral) use. It must show quality, safety and efficacy and is distinct from Ayurvedic, Unani or Siddha medicines.

front: Under which FSSAI regulation are nutraceuticals and health supplements governed?
back: The Food Safety and Standards (Health Supplements, Nutraceuticals, Food for Special Dietary Use, Food for Special Medical Purpose, Functional Food and Novel Food) Regulations, 2016, gazetted on 23 December 2016.

front: What is the legal status of the AYUSH pharmacopoeias?
back: They are the official standards for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules. Drugs must meet the monograph standards; failing ones are not of standard quality.

front: Why is 'natural' not the same as safe? List the hazards of herbal products.
back: Botanicals may be inert or intrinsically toxic; products may be misidentified, adulterated or contaminated; they are rarely tested for dose-response, mutagenicity, carcinogenicity or teratogenicity; adverse effects are under-reported and seldom chemically analysed; and their many constituents make drug-interaction testing difficult. Placebo effects (30-50% of response) also confound efficacy claims.

front: How can traditional remedies cause heavy metal or stimulant toxicity?
back: Some folk medicines, including certain Ayurvedic preparations, and kohl cosmetics contain lead; skin-lightening creams and folk remedies may contain mercury. 'Fat burner' supplements may contain caffeine, and the herb ma-huang contains ephedrine, which can cause stimulant toxicity.
