front: Garlic supplement: active principle, claimed effects and interactions.
back: Alliin is converted by alliinase to allicin (the odour principle); enteric coating protects the enzyme from gastric acid. Claimed effects: modest lipid lowering (allicin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase in vitro), antiplatelet and fibrinolytic action, antimicrobial activity. Adverse: GI upset, breath and body odour, hypotension, rare bleeding. Use cautiously with anticoagulants and antiplatelets (including ibuprofen); may lower saquinavir levels.

front: Ginkgo biloba: claimed uses, evidence and safety concerns.
back: Leaf extract (flavone glycosides, ginkgolides, bilobalide) increases blood flow, antagonises platelet-activating factor and scavenges free radicals. Promoted for dementia and claudication, but trial benefits are inconsistent and unlikely to be clinically relevant. Risks: bleeding with aspirin or warfarin, so avoid with antiplatelets or anticoagulants; seizures from ginkgotoxin in seed contamination, so avoid in epilepsy.

front: Ginseng: active principles, uses and precautions.
back: Panax species contain ginsenosides (Siberian ginseng is a different plant with eleutherosides). Promoted as an adaptogen; best evidence is modest lowering of fasting glucose and possible cold prevention. Adverse: insomnia, nervousness, mania, hypertension, oestrogen-like effects (mastalgia, vaginal bleeding). Interactions: mania with phenelzine, lithium or neuroleptics; antiplatelet effect, so avoid with anticoagulants and around surgery; caution with hypoglycaemic drugs.

Used for colds and respiratory infections as an immune modulator. A Cochrane review found no significant benefit in treating colds overall, at most a small preventive effect. Adverse: unpleasant taste, GI upset, allergic rash (more in children). Avoid in immune deficiency (e.g. AIDS, cancer) and autoimmune disease until its immune effects are clarified.

front: Milk thistle: constituent, use and safety.
back: Silymarin (mainly silybin) from fruit and seeds; poor oral bioavailability. Claimed hepatoprotection via antioxidant, free-radical scavenging, glutathione-raising and anti-inflammatory (NF-kB) actions; clinical evidence in liver disease is insufficient. Adverse effects are rare (laxative at high doses), and it poses no meaningful drug-interaction risk.

Promoted for benign prostatic hyperplasia. In vitro it inhibits 5-alpha-reductase I and II, blocks DHT binding and alpha-1 receptors, but human effects on DHT are inconsistent. Generic extracts showed no benefit, while a hexane extract improved nocturia and flow. It does not lower PSA, so it does not interfere with prostate cancer screening; side effects are mild and fewer sexual effects than tamsulosin or finasteride are claimed.

front: Coenzyme Q10: claimed uses, evidence and interaction.
back: A mitochondrial antioxidant (ubiquinone). Evidence: small BP reductions, modest improvement in heart failure outcomes and ejection fraction, uncertain benefit in ischaemic heart disease; it did not reduce statin-induced myopathy in meta-analysis (statins lower its synthesis). Well tolerated. Because it resembles vitamin K, it may reduce warfarin effect.

front: Glucosamine: use, formulation issue and precautions.
back: Cartilage substrate used for knee osteoarthritis. The sulfate (especially crystalline) form may help pain and joint-space narrowing; the hydrochloride form is ineffective, which explains conflicting trials. It has no direct analgesic effect and functional gains, if any, may take up to 12 months. Mild GI effects; possible shellfish cross-allergy; may raise INR with warfarin.

front: Melatonin supplement: uses, adverse effects and interactions.
back: Pineal hormone regulating the sleep-wake cycle. Used for jet lag (best taken at target bedtime, more effective eastbound and across 5 or more time zones), insomnia and pre-operative anxiety; it inspired the receptor agonist ramelteon. Adverse: next-day drowsiness, headache, BP changes; may lower prolactin, so use cautiously or not at all while nursing. Metabolised by CYP1A2 (fluvoxamine interaction); may reduce warfarin effect; interacts with nifedipine.

front: Why might coenzyme Q10 be tried for statin myopathy, and why does the trial evidence not support it?
back: Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, which is also needed to make CoQ10, so low CoQ10 was thought to cause the muscle pain. A meta-analysis found no benefit on muscle pain or creatine kinase; whether low CoQ10 causes the myopathy is unknown.

front: Compare the warfarin interactions of coenzyme Q10, glucosamine and melatonin. Which direction and why?
back: CoQ10 resembles vitamin K, so it may reduce warfarin effect. Glucosamine can raise INR with bruising/bleeding risk. Melatonin may shorten prothrombin time, theoretically reducing warfarin effect. All three need INR monitoring when given with warfarin.

back: Drug discovery that runs 'clinics to laboratory': documented clinical experience with traditional (e.g. Ayurvedic) remedies is the starting point, followed by experimental validation of activity and targets. It is cheaper and faster with a higher success rate than random screening, and relies on a 'golden triangle' of traditional knowledge, modern medicine and modern science.

front: What role can physicians play in ethnopharmacology?
back: Field work documenting patients who use herbal remedies and the diseases treated; clinical studies of herbs to identify drug candidates; and comparing benefit and harm of herbal, modern and combined therapy in patients who take both.

front: What did an IIT Delhi and AIST Japan study suggest about ashwagandha and Covid-19, and what does it not establish?
back: Withanone from ashwagandha was reported to have the potential to interact with and block the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro), so ashwagandha was proposed as a possible drug candidate. The book gives no clinical outcome data, so this is a lead, not a proven treatment.

front: When is an Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug called misbranded?
back: If damage is concealed or it looks more valuable than it is, if it is not labelled as prescribed, or if its label carries a false or misleading claim (section 33E).
refs: WEB Govt of India Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, Chapter IVA https://ayush.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/ayush/custom/drugs_cosmetics_act.pdf

front: When is an Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug called adulterated?
back: If it contains filthy, putrid or decomposed matter, is prepared or stored in insanitary conditions, or its container has a harmful substance (section 33EE).

front: When is an Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug called spurious?
back: If sold under another drug's name, passed off as an imitation, bearing a fictitious manufacturer, or substituted in whole or part by another substance (section 33EEA).

front: Hepatoprotective herbs in viral hepatitis: name the four options Padmaja lists.
back: Silymarin (milk thistle), Picrorhiza kurroa (Kutaki) extracts, Phyllanthus species extracts and glycyrrhizin. Padmaja lists these four as the herbs promising in viral hepatitis.

front: Carbon tetrachloride model: how is a hepatoprotective herb tested?
back: Rats get CCl4 (metabolised to a free radical that damages liver membranes) with or without the test herb. Lower serum GOT, GPT, ALP, ACP and bilirubin in the herb group than in the toxin-only group suggest protection. Pentothal sleep time in mice is a second read-out: a shorter sleep means the liver metabolised the barbiturate better.
Picrosides are the hepatoprotective constituent. The herb acts as an antioxidant like tocopherol and alters glutathione metabolism in the liver.

front: Phyllanthus species: which constituent group, and which activities does Sarkar list for it?
back: Phyllanthins. Sarkar lists antiviral, immunomodulatory, nephroprotective and anticancer actions; Padmaja names Phyllanthus among herbs promising in viral hepatitis.

front: Name the two cyclooxygenase isoforms and the role of each.
back: COX-1 is constitutive and maintains housekeeping functions such as gastric mucosal protection and platelet TXA2. COX-2 is induced by cytokines at inflamed sites and drives local prostaglandin generation. In the kidney, constitutive COX-2 in juxtaglomerular cells supports renal salt and water handling.

front: Classify: drugs used to close a patent ductus arteriosus
text: Ductus arteriosus is kept open by {{PGE2}} made by {{COX-2}}; after birth it closes naturally, but if it does not, small doses of {{indomethacin}} or {{aspirin}} close it by blocking PG synthesis.

front: Why can indomethacin or aspirin close a patent ductus arteriosus, and why should NSAIDs be avoided near term?
back: Foetal ductus is held open by PGE2 made by COX-2. Blocking PG synthesis lets it close, so indomethacin or aspirin is used when it fails to shut after birth. The same effect late in pregnancy can close the ductus prematurely and raises post-partum bleeding risk.

front: Which NSAID suits each situation: mild pain, post-operative pain, renal colic, RA flare?
back: Mild pain with little inflammation: paracetamol or low-dose ibuprofen. Short post-operative pain: injectable ketorolac or diclofenac, or oral propionic acid derivative or nimesulide. Parenteral NSAID for renal colic or acute gout: ketorolac, diclofenac or parecoxib. RA or gout flare: naproxen, piroxicam, indomethacin or high-dose aspirin. Reason: pain-to-inflammation ratio and patient risk drive the pick.

front: How does aspirin inhibit COX differently from most other NSAIDs?
back: Aspirin acetylates a serine residue of COX irreversibly, so activity returns only when new enzyme is synthesised. Most other NSAIDs are competitive and reversible; their effect ends when the drug dissociates from the enzyme.

text: Aspirin is converted to {{salicylic acid}}; its antiplatelet effect results from {{irreversible}} acetylation of COX-1 and lasts about {{one week}}; low-dose secondary prevention uses {{75 to 150 mg}} daily; analgesic doses are {{0.3 to 0.6 g}} every 6 to 8 hours.

front: What is salicylism and at what aspirin dose does it appear?
back: Syndrome from anti-inflammatory doses (3 to 5 g/day): dizziness, tinnitus, vertigo, reversible hearing and vision impairment, excitement, hyperventilation and electrolyte imbalance.

front: Why does a low daily dose of aspirin protect platelets for about a week, while ibuprofen's antiplatelet effect is short?
back: Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX-1 and hence TXA2 synthesis. Platelets cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts about a week, the platelet lifespan. Ibuprofen binds reversibly and its effect is short lived.

front: What happens when ibuprofen is taken with low-dose aspirin?
back: Ibuprofen occupies the active site of platelet COX-1 reversibly, so aspirin cannot acetylate it. This abolishes aspirin's antiplatelet and cardioprotective effect, so ibuprofen should not be used in patients relying on aspirin for cardioprotection.

front: What paracetamol dose signals serious toxicity, and when is fatality likely?
back: KDT: above about 150 mg/kg (over 10 g in an adult) can cause serious toxicity, and fatality is common above about 250 mg/kg. GG14: hepatotoxicity may follow a single 10 to 15 g (150 to 250 mg/kg) in adults or more than 150 mg/kg in children; 20 to 25 g or more is potentially fatal. Alcoholics and fasting or malnourished patients are at risk at lower doses. Early features are only nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain; centrilobular necrosis develops after 12 to 18 hours, clinical liver damage shows in 2 to 4 days, and transaminases peak at 72 to 96 hours.

front: Which analgesic-antipyretic is safest in pregnancy, and why is aspirin avoided in children with viral infections?
back: Paracetamol is the safest choice in pregnancy, with low-dose aspirin probably second best. Aspirin is avoided in children with varicella or influenza because of its link with Reye's syndrome, a rare hepatic encephalopathy; paediatric aspirin formulations are prohibited in India and the UK.

front: What does paracetamol lack compared with aspirin, and where is it used?
back: It has negligible anti-inflammatory action, does not affect platelets, clotting, gastric mucosa, respiration or acid-base balance, and is not uricosuric. Used for headache, mild migraine, musculoskeletal pain, dysmenorrhoea, first-choice analgesic in osteoarthritis and antipyretic for fever, especially in children (no Reye risk). It is weak where inflammation dominates, e.g. RA.

front: Why is paracetamol a good antipyretic but a poor anti-inflammatory drug?
back: It is a weak inhibitor of peripheral COX. Peroxides generated at inflamed sites block its action there, but no such peroxides are present in the brain, where it inhibits COX well. Action on the brain isoform COX-3 may also contribute.

front: What is the mechanism of paracetamol-induced hepatic injury?
back: A minor oxidative metabolite, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NABQI), is normally detoxified by conjugation with glutathione. After a very large dose, glucuronidation saturates, more NABQI forms and hepatic glutathione is depleted. NABQI then binds liver and renal tubular proteins, causing necrosis.

front: Paracetamol poisoning: antidote, how it works, and the dosing regimen.
back: N-acetylcysteine (NAC). It replenishes hepatic glutathione and can also conjugate NAPQI directly, so the toxic metabolite is detoxified instead of binding liver proteins. Standard regimen (GG12): IV 150 mg/kg over 60 min, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h; or oral 140 mg/kg loading, then 70 mg/kg every 4 h for 17 doses. KDT gives a simpler scheme: 150 mg/kg IV over 15 min, then the same dose over 20 h, or 75 mg/kg orally every 4 to 6 h for 2 to 3 days. Start before blood levels return if overdose is suspected; given within 8 to 16 h, mortality falls below 1%, but it is practically ineffective if started 16 h or later. Side effects: rash, nausea, vomiting, rare anaphylactoid reactions.

front: Aspirin plus paracetamol: is the combination better?
back: Their effects are additive, not supra-additive, and analgesia reaches a ceiling when aspirin plus paracetamol totals about 1000 mg. No convincing evidence shows the combination is more effective or safer than single agents, so limit it to short use.

text: Among the coxibs, {{etoricoxib}} has the highest COX-2 selectivity and is given once daily; {{celecoxib}} is metabolised mainly by {{CYP2C9}}; {{parecoxib}} is an injectable prodrug of {{valdecoxib}}.

front: Compare celecoxib and etoricoxib: COX-2 selectivity and key points.
back: Celecoxib is only modestly COX-2 selective (about 10-fold), as effective as naproxen or diclofenac in RA, spares platelet COX-1 and gastric mucosa; side effects are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, mild diarrhoea, oedema and small BP rise. Etoricoxib has the highest selectivity, half-life about 24 h so once daily, and thrombotic CV event rate similar to diclofenac.

front: What is parecoxib, and what hazard does it share with valdecoxib?
back: Parecoxib is an injectable prodrug of valdecoxib for post-operative or similar short-term pain, with efficacy like ketorolac. It shares valdecoxib's risk of serious skin reactions, so stop it at the first rash.

front: Why were rofecoxib and valdecoxib withdrawn?
back: Both were linked to increased myocardial infarction. Rofecoxib was stopped in the APPROVE trial and withdrawn globally in 2004; valdecoxib was withdrawn in 2005 after cardiac events in patients undergoing bypass surgery, and also because of severe skin reactions.

front: What are the main safety concerns with nimesulide, and where is it still specifically useful?
back: It can cause fulminant hepatic failure and has been withdrawn in several countries; its use in children is banned in India. Its specific value lies in patients with asthma or aspirin intolerance, most of whom do not cross-react with it.

front: Case: RA patient with a past peptic ulcer and hypertension needs an NSAID. Reason out the choice.
back: Gastric risk argues for a COX-2 selective drug (or paracetamol), or a traditional NSAID with a PPI. But hypertension and CV risk argue against coxibs, which lack antiplatelet action and give a small BP rise. So the lowest dose for the shortest time of a propionic acid derivative such as naproxen (lower thrombotic risk than diclofenac or etoricoxib) plus a PPI is the balanced answer; consider a DMARD to cut NSAID need.

front: List the main mechanisms of NSAID-induced gastric mucosal injury.
back: Loss of COX-1-derived protective PGE2 and PGI2 reduces mucus and bicarbonate secretion, increases acid secretion and reduces mucosal blood flow. Back-diffusion of H+ ions in the mucosa adds to the damage. Misoprostol, a stable PG analogue, counteracts NSAID gastric toxicity.

front: Which COX product loss causes NSAID gastric damage?
back: Inhibition of COX-1 derived PGE2 and PGI2, the gastroprotective prostaglandins. Without them mucus and bicarbonate fall, acid rises and mucosal blood flow drops, so erosion and ulcer follow.

front: What gastroprotection is used when an NSAID-dependent arthritis patient develops a peptic ulcer?
back: Concurrent proton pump inhibitor. Alternatives for gastric intolerance or predisposed patients: a selective COX-2 inhibitor or paracetamol.

front: Which analgesics have been adequately evaluated in children, and which to avoid?
back: Only paracetamol, aspirin, ibuprofen and naproxen are well studied in children. Avoid aspirin because of Reye's syndrome, so paracetamol is preferred for fever.

front: What is a DMARD, and how does it differ from an NSAID?
back: A disease-modifying antirheumatic drug suppresses the rheumatoid process and slows progression. Unlike NSAIDs it has no nonspecific anti-inflammatory or analgesic action. Benefit takes months to appear, and relapse occurs after stopping.

front: What is sulfasalazine made of, and what is its role in RA?
back: It is sulfapyridine linked to 5-aminosalicylic acid. In RA it is a second-line or add-on DMARD of modest efficacy. Neutropenia or thrombocytopenia occurs in about 5 to 10% of patients, so blood counts need monitoring.

text: Non-biological DMARDs include {{methotrexate}}, {{sulfasalazine}}, {{hydroxychloroquine}}, {{leflunomide}}, {{azathioprine}} and the JAK inhibitor {{tofacitinib}}.

front: Why is methotrexate the first-choice DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis, and how does it act?
back: It is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor that reduces proliferation of immune-inflammatory cells and cytokine production. Relief starts in 3 to 6 weeks, response is predictable and sustained, and the weekly oral low dose (7.5 to 15 mg) is well accepted. It is standard even in juvenile RA.

front: What are the serious toxicities of methotrexate, and when is it contraindicated?
back: Oral ulceration and GI upset are common. Prolonged use causes dose-related liver damage progressing to cirrhosis, and chest infections increase. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, breast-feeding, liver disease, active infection, leucopenia and peptic ulcer, and is avoided in renal disease because excretion is impaired.

front: Which drugs increase methotrexate levels or toxicity?
back: Aspirin and probenecid raise methotrexate levels by reducing its excretion. Trimethoprim adds to dihydrofolate reductase inhibition and can depress bone marrow.

front: Why is hydroxychloroquine preferred over chloroquine when used in RA?
back: Both take 3 to 6 months to act and do not prevent bony erosions. Retinal damage and corneal opacity are the main concern; these are less frequent and reversible with hydroxychloroquine. It is best reserved for mild, non-erosive disease.

front: How does leflunomide act, and why is a loading dose needed?
back: It is converted to an active metabolite that inhibits dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase, blocking pyrimidine synthesis in dividing cells. The metabolite has a half-life of 2 to 3 weeks, so a loading dose of 100 mg daily for 3 days precedes 20 mg daily. It must not be used in pregnancy or children.

front: What is the main use of azathioprine in RA, and what interaction limits its dose?
back: It is converted to 6-mercaptopurine and is used mainly for its steroid-sparing effect, especially in systemic disease. It is not combined with methotrexate. Allopurinol inhibits its breakdown, so the azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine dose is cut to about one-third.

front: JAK inhibitors in rheumatoid arthritis: mechanism, agents and key adverse effects.
back: Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2) are tyrosine kinases activated by cytokine receptors; they phosphorylate STAT transcription factors that switch on inflammatory genes. Oral JAK inhibitors block this signalling and cytokine production. Tofacitinib (JAK1/JAK3, 5 mg twice daily) is used in severe RA not responding to methotrexate, alone or with methotrexate, but not with azathioprine, cyclosporine or biological DMARDs. Other JAK inhibitors approved for RA include baricitinib (JAK1/JAK2) and upadacitinib (JAK1). Adverse effects: respiratory infections, reactivation of tuberculosis, headache, diarrhoea, hypertension, anaemia and liver damage. GG14: an updated boxed warning covers serious heart-related events, cancer, blood clots and death; since 2021 the US label limits tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib to patients who responded poorly to TNF antagonists.

front: How do TNF inhibitors work, and what is their main hazard?
back: They neutralise TNF, either as a soluble receptor or an antibody, reducing macrophage and T-cell activation. They act faster than conventional DMARDs and slow erosions. The main hazard is opportunistic infection, including tuberculosis and Pneumocystis pneumonia, because TNF is needed against granulomatous infection.

back: Etanercept (TNF-receptor/Fc fusion protein), infliximab (chimeric monoclonal antibody), adalimumab (human monoclonal antibody), plus certolizumab and golimumab. back: It is a CTLA-4 Fc fusion protein that binds CD80 and CD86, blocking the second costimulatory signal needed for T-cell activation. It is used in active RA not responding to methotrexate. It must not be combined with TNF antagonists because infection risk rises greatly.

Xanthine oxidase inhibitors: {{allopurinol}} and {{febuxostat}}; uricosurics: {{probenecid}}, {{lesinurad}} and the largely disused {{sulfinpyrazone}}; uricase enzyme: {{pegloticase}}.

front: How does probenecid lower blood uric acid, and what are its limits?
back: It blocks URAT-1 (an organic acid transporter) so tubular reabsorption of urate falls and excretion rises. Ineffective in renal insufficiency, avoid in stone formers (give fluids), and aspirin blocks its effect. Cover the first 1 to 2 months with NSAID or colchicine to avoid precipitating acute gout.

front: How does colchicine act in acute gout, and what limits its use?
back: It binds tubulin and so blocks granulocyte migration into the joint and the release of chemotactic factors and glycoprotein. It has no general analgesic or anti-inflammatory effect, and it does not change uric acid levels; its action is specific to gouty inflammation. Dose-related GI toxicity limits it, so it is second line to NSAIDs.

front: What is the role of allopurinol in chronic gout, and what is its mechanism?
back: Its metabolite alloxanthine is a long-acting, noncompetitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid synthesis. It is the first-choice drug for chronic gout, in both over-producers and under-excretors. It must not be started during an acute attack, and NSAID or colchicine cover is needed for 1 to 2 months.

Long-term steroid use causes serious harm, so the dose is kept low
Suppresses cell-mediated immunity, mainly T-cell and NK-cell function
Given with corticosteroids to spare steroid dose
Used mostly where systemic features are present
Not combined with methotrexate; 50-150 mg/day
Cyclosporine, chlorambucil and cyclophosphamide are rarely used in RA
Reserved for patients not responding to other DMARDs

High dose for short periods in organ-threatening disease

front: Why does diclofenac not block low-dose aspirin's cardioprotection, but ibuprofen does?
back: Diclofenac spares COX-1 and has no appreciable antiplatelet action. Ibuprofen occupies the active serine of COX-1 reversibly and so blocks aspirin's irreversible acetylation.

front: Why is naproxen suited to acute gout?
back: It is a potent anti-inflammatory that inhibits leucocyte migration into the joint. Its long half-life (12-16 h) allows twice-daily dosing. Dose: 750 mg stat, then 250 mg 8-hourly until the attack subsides. With regular use it suppresses platelet function.

front: Why have phenylbutazone and oxyphenbutazone gone out of use?
back: Both are potent anti-inflammatories with slow onset, but they carry high gastric toxicity, Na+ and water retention, CNS and hypersensitivity reactions, hypothyroidism, and residual risk of bone-marrow depression.

front: Piroxicam: why once-daily dosing, and why is it not a first-choice NSAID?
back: Its plasma half-life is about 2 days, so steady state takes about a week and once-daily dosing is enough. Its GI toxicity, oedema and skin reactions are relatively high, so it is not a first choice for any condition.

front: Parenteral ketorolac: where is it used, and what restricts it?
back: Used for post-operative, dental and acute musculoskeletal pain, renal colic, migraine and bone-metastasis pain. Not for preanaesthetic or obstetric analgesia, not for OA or RA, and not with anticoagulants. Oral use beyond 5 days is not advised.

front: How does nabumetone spare the gastric mucosa?
back: Nabumetone is a prodrug. Its active COX inhibitor (6-methoxy naphthyl acetic acid) forms in the tissues after absorption, not in the gastric mucosa.

front: Mephenamic acid: which pain is it used for, and what is its main adverse effect?
back: Muscle, joint and soft-tissue pain, and dysmenorrhoea, where strong anti-inflammatory action is not needed. The main adverse effect is dose-related diarrhoea; haemolytic anaemia is rare but serious.

front: Which injury and procedural uses are listed for ibuprofen and its congeners?
back: Soft-tissue injury, fractures, vasectomy, tooth extraction, and post-operative and post-partum swelling and pain. They suppress swelling and inflammation in these settings.

front: Ketoprofen and flurbiprofen compared with ibuprofen: what is the trade-off?
back: Ketoprofen has similar anti-inflammatory efficacy but more side effects. Flurbiprofen is more effective but causes more gastric side effects.

front: Why is meloxicam called a preferential COX-2 inhibitor, and is it gentler on the stomach?
back: Its COX-2/COX-1 selectivity is about 10:1, yet it still measurably reduces platelet TXA2 at therapeutic doses. GI side effects are milder than piroxicam's, but ulcer complications occur on long use, and there is no convincing evidence it is safer than other NSAIDs.

front: Etodolac: what sets it apart in clinical use?
back: A moderately COX-2-selective indole acetic acid with better GI tolerance at lower doses. Post-operative analgesia lasts 6-8 h. Approved for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and acute musculoskeletal pain.

front: Which diclofenac congener has a proposed cartilage-protective action, and by what mechanism?
back: Aceclofenac, which is a moderately COX-2-selective congener of diclofenac. It enhances glycosaminoglycan synthesis, which is the proposed chondroprotective action.

front: Acute rheumatic fever: which drug is given first, and when are others added?
back: Aspirin is the first drug in all cases. Other drugs are added or substituted only if aspirin fails or the disease is severe. Corticosteroids act faster.

front: Why does colchicine not lower blood urate, and what does it do?
back: It does not inhibit uric acid synthesis or increase its excretion, and it is neither analgesic nor anti-inflammatory in general. It binds tubulin and blocks granulocyte migration into the joint, cutting the release of chemotactic factors and the aggravating glycoprotein.

front: Why do acute attacks become more frequent in the first 1-2 months of urate-lowering therapy?
back: Fluctuating plasma urate makes crystals repeatedly dissolve and re-form in the joints. Cover with NSAID or colchicine for this period. Urate-lowering drugs are not started during an acute attack.

front: Acute gout when NSAIDs are unsuitable: which steroid options exist?
back: One or a few joints: intra-articular triamcinolone (10 mg in small joints, 30 mg in wrist). Systemic: prednisolone 40-60 mg for one day, then tapered over 1-2 weeks, for renal failure or previous peptic ulcer bleed. Colchicine is second-line.

front: Febuxostat: class, use and key cautions
back: A non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor, as effective as or better than allopurinol. Start 40 mg OD, up to 80 mg (max 120 mg/day). Not combined with allopurinol, though they can be given in sequence. Not for malignancy-associated hyperuricaemia. Liver damage is the key adverse effect; avoid with mercaptopurine, azathioprine or theophylline.

front: Pegloticase: what is it and when is it used?
back: A recombinant uricase, coupled to methoxy-PEG, that converts urate to soluble allantoin. Given IV every 2 weeks, only for rare refractory symptomatic gout. It is immunogenic, causes infusion reactions including anaphylaxis, and the response is lost in many patients.

front: Lesinurad: what kind of drug is it and how is it used?
back: A newer uricosuric with a mechanism similar to probenecid, so it lowers urate by increasing its excretion. Approved as a treatment option alone or with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.

front: How do inflammatory cells worsen an acute gout attack?
back: They engulf urate crystals and release chemotactic factors that recruit granulocytes. Lactic acid lowers local pH and promotes more crystal precipitation. Lysosomal enzymes damage joint tissue, and a glycoprotein aggravates inflammation.

front: Low-dose corticosteroid in RA: what is its main drawback?
back: Prednisolone 5-7.5 mg supplements NSAIDs and gives prompt relief, but it cannot arrest the disease. Withdrawal is hard: flares occur and the patient becomes steroid-dependent.

front: Which immunosuppressants are rarely used in RA?
back: Cyclosporine, chlorambucil and cyclophosphamide. They are reserved for RA that does not respond to the other DMARDs.

front: Aspirin and COX: fill the blanks
text: Aspirin inhibits COX by {{acetylating}} a {{serine}} residue; the platelet effect lasts about {{one week}}, which matches platelet turnover time.
Allopurinol inhibits {{xanthine oxidase}}; its long-acting metabolite {{alloxanthine}} is mainly responsible for inhibiting uric acid synthesis in vivo.
Colchicine binds {{tubulin}} and blocks granulocyte migration into the joint; prophylactic maintenance is {{0.5-1 mg/day}} for {{4-8 weeks}}.

front: Probenecid: which other drugs does it affect?
back: It blocks tubular secretion of penicillins and ampicillin, prolonging their levels (used in gonorrhoea and SABE). It also reduces excretion of cephalosporins, sulfonamides, methotrexate and indomethacin, and it is given with cidofovir to protect the kidney. Aspirin blocks its uricosuric action.

front: Indomethacin in patent ductus arteriosus: fill the blanks
text: Indomethacin closes the ductus in most cases with {{three}} IV injections, given {{12-hourly}}, each of {{0.1-0.2 mg/kg}}.

front: What is thromboxane A2, and where is it made?
back: A platelet-derived eicosanoid made by COX-1 that promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction. Aspirin blocks its synthesis, which is why it prevents platelet clumping.

front: What is prostacyclin (PGI2), where is it made, and what does it do to platelets?
back: Made by the vascular endothelium; it inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates vessels, opposing TXA2.

front: Why does aspirin’s antiplatelet effect outlast the drug itself?
back: Aspirin acetylates platelet COX irreversibly, so TXA2 synthesis stays blocked until new platelets are made. The antithrombotic effect lasts more than 3 days.

front: Classify: selective COX-2 inhibitors available in India
text: Celecoxib, {{etoricoxib}} and {{parecoxib}} are the selective COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs) available in India; {{rofecoxib}} and {{valdecoxib}} are no longer available.

front: Why does a selective COX-2 inhibitor not protect the heart the way aspirin does?
back: It does not suppress platelet COX-1 TXA2, so it has no antiplatelet action or cardioprotection.

front: How do selective COX-2 inhibitors promote thrombosis?
back: They cut endothelial PGI2 formation while platelet COX-1 TXA2 is untouched, so the prothrombotic TXA2 effect goes unopposed.

front: Short note: Thromboxane-prostacyclin balance and coxib-related thrombosis

points: Platelet TXA2 promotes aggregation; endothelial PGI2 inhibits it
The two together control intravascular thrombus formation
Reduce endothelial PGI2 formation
Spare COX-1 TXA2, so the balance tips to thrombosis
Myocardial infarction and stroke
Hypertension and heart failure
Diclofenac carries a cardiovascular risk similar to the coxibs
Aspirin is cardioprotective because it blocks platelet TXA2

front: Why is low-dose aspirin cardioprotective, and why might high doses blunt that benefit?
back: 75 to 150 mg/day cuts platelet TXA2 and reduces MI. High doses also suppress vessel-wall PGI2, which can reverse the benefit.

front: What did the APC and APPROVE trials show about rofecoxib and celecoxib?
back: APPROVE (rofecoxib) was stopped early and withdrawn for more cardiovascular events; APC (celecoxib) was terminated after about a 2.5-fold rise in major fatal and nonfatal CV events.

front: How does diclofenac's cardiovascular risk compare with the coxibs?
back: Its rate of cardiovascular toxicity is similar to that of the COX-2 inhibitors, including MI and hypertension.

front: Which factors set the cardiovascular risk of an NSAID?
back: Dose and the patient's underlying cardiovascular risk: celecoxib's MI and stroke risk relates to dose and underlying cardiovascular disease. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest feasible time.

Their cardiovascular safety problem emerged in long-term trials
Platelet TXA2 (COX-1) promotes aggregation and vasoconstriction
Endothelial PGI2 inhibits aggregation and dilates vessels
The balance controls intravascular thrombosis
Coxibs suppress COX-2-dependent PGI2
Platelet COX-1 TXA2 is not blocked
Net shift towards thrombosis and vasoconstriction

Hazards include MI, stroke, hypertension and heart failure

Diclofenac carries a similar CV risk profile
Low-dose aspirin keeps the antiplatelet role; coxibs do not replace it
Reserve COX-2 selective drugs for patients at high GI risk
Lowest dose for the shortest period; paracetamol first where suitable

front: Case: an RA patient with ischaemic heart disease needs analgesia. Which drug choice is safest?
back: Avoid coxibs, because ischaemic heart disease predisposes to CV events. Paracetamol is the safer analgesic with no platelet or CV effect. If an NSAID is essential, use the lowest dose for the shortest time.

front: Into which three phases are anti-inflammatory screening models grouped?
back: Acute (transient: vasodilatation and raised capillary permeability), subacute (leucocyte and phagocyte infiltration) and chronic (granuloma formation).

front: What three measurable features of inflammation are used in anti-inflammatory assays?
back: Erythema (local vasodilatation), oedema (raised capillary permeability) and granulation tissue. Each one can be measured, so each has an assay.

front: What is the inflamed paw technique?
back: Oedema is raised in a rat hind paw by intra-plantar carrageenan or similar irritant and paw volume is measured. Together with adjuvant arthritis it best predicts anti-inflammatory activity in man.

front: What is the cotton wool granuloma assay?
back: Weighed cotton pellets are implanted under the skin of rats; the dried granulomatous tissue is weighed after about 8 days and compared with controls.

front: What is the granuloma pouch assay?
back: A subcutaneous air pouch is made on the rat's back, an irritant is injected into it, and the drug is given daily for about a week. Exudate volume, leucocyte count and granuloma weight are measured on day 8.

front: What does the Evans blue leakage assay measure?
back: Vascular permeability: a protein-bound dye leaks from the blood into tissue. Less dye in the peritoneal exudate after acetic acid means lower permeability.

front: What is the ulcer index in NSAID safety testing?
back: A score from the number of gastric ulcers per animal plus their severity, read microscopically. It measures GI damage, which is tested alongside anti-inflammatory activity.

front: Why does an NSAID mainly block the second phase of carrageenan paw oedema?
back: The first phase is due to histamine and serotonin. The second phase is due to prostaglandins, proteases and lysosomal enzymes, which COX inhibitors block, so NSAIDs act mainly on it.

front: Why is the xylene ear oedema test called neurogenic?
back: Xylene releases substance P from sensory nerves, which causes vasodilatation and plasma extravasation in the ear, so the test reflects neurogenic inflammation.

front: What do the arachidonic acid and croton oil ear tests measure?
back: Both test drugs that act on the arachidonic acid cascade. Croton oil activates phospholipase A2 to release arachidonic acid, so COX and 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors reduce the oedema.

front: Which phase do the granuloma pouch and cotton wool granuloma belong to, and why is carrageenan added to the pellet?
back: Granuloma pouch is subacute; cotton wool granuloma is chronic. Impregnating the pellet with carrageenan gives more intense granuloma formation.

front: How is the UV erythema assay in guinea pigs run and scored?
back: Shaved guinea pig skin is exposed to UV through a cuff; the drug is given before exposure. Erythema is scored on a graded scale (0 none, 1 weak, 2 strong, 4 very strong); scores of 0 or 1 count as protected.

Carrageenan granuloma pouch: exudate, leucocytes and granuloma weight after about a week of dosing
Formalin-induced paw oedema
Cotton wool granuloma: dried pellet weight after about 8 days
Glass rod and sponge implantation granulomas
Adjuvant arthritis in rat
Inflamed paw technique: the most useful predictors of human activity along with adjuvant arthritis
Ulcerogenicity: aspirin-induced ulcer model in rat
Ulcer index from lesion count and severity

front: How can the contact time of an eye medication on the ocular surface be prolonged?
back: Gels (e.g. pilocarpine 4% gel releasing drug as the polymer erodes), ointments (mineral oil/petrolatum base, used for antibiotics, cycloplegics, miotics), soft contact lenses, collagen shields and nanoparticle carriers. Blocking tear outflow with silicone punctal plugs also extends dwell time.

front: Classify: ocular routes of drug administration
text: Besides {{topical}} drops, drugs can be given by {{subconjunctival}}, {{sub-Tenon's}}, {{peribulbar}} or {{retrobulbar}} injection, or into the eye by {{intracameral}} (anterior chamber) and {{intravitreal}} injection or device; intravitreal delivery bypasses absorption and suits {{endophthalmitis}}, retinitis and age-related macular degeneration.

front: Why can eye-drop preservatives damage the cornea? Name them.
back: Drops and contact lens solutions often contain benzalkonium chloride, chlorobutanol, chelating agents and rarely thimerosal. Benzalkonium chloride can produce a punctate or even toxic ulcerative keratopathy. Most local toxicity of eye drops is hypersensitivity or direct toxicity to cornea, conjunctiva, periocular skin and nasal mucosa.

front: Short note: Pharmacokinetics of topically applied ocular drugs

points: Depends on dwell time in the cul-de-sac and tear film, nasolacrimal drainage, binding to tear proteins, local metabolism and diffusion across cornea and conjunctiva
Cornea acts as a fat-water-fat barrier (epithelium, stroma, endothelium): drugs with both lipophilic and hydrophilic character cross best
Penetration rises roughly in proportion to tear-film concentration and increases when the epithelium is breached (ulcer, defect)
Drug collects in aqueous humour, then reaches intraocular tissues and may drain via the trabecular route into the circulation
Melanin binding: alpha-agonist mydriasis is slower in dark irides; melanin acts as a slow-release reservoir
Ocular esterases, oxidoreductases, COMT, MAO and conjugating enzymes are present
Esterases allow ester prodrugs with better corneal entry (latanoprost); loteprednol is inactivated within the eye, limiting systemic effects
Tears dilute the drug; nasolacrimal drainage carries it to the nasal mucosa
Nasal absorption bypasses hepatic first pass, so eye drops can cause significant systemic effects

front: What are the risks of periocular (sub-Tenon's, peribulbar, retrobulbar) injections?
back: Local tissue injury, globe perforation (with direct retinal toxicity), optic nerve trauma, central retinal artery or vein occlusion, extraocular muscle trauma and a prolonged drug effect. They are used for anterior segment infections, posterior uveitis and cystoid macular oedema.

front: Essay: Why eye drops can cause systemic toxicity, and how ocular drug delivery is optimised

points: Drug drained into the nasolacrimal duct is absorbed from there (KDT8 PDF p183)
Dipivefrine is an ester prodrug of adrenaline, better tolerated and longer acting than adrenaline (KDT8 PDF p184)
Timolol has no local anaesthetic or intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (KDT8 PDF p183)

front: What is dipivefrine and how does it lower IOP?
back: A prodrug of adrenaline that crosses the cornea well and is hydrolysed there by esterases. The released adrenaline increases uveoscleral outflow, raises trabecular conductivity (beta-2) and reduces aqueous formation (alpha). It still causes ocular burning and is kept for add-on use.

front: What are Rho kinase inhibitors in glaucoma?
back: Netarsudil and ripasudil, the newest antiglaucoma class. Blocking Rho kinase in the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal reduces actin stress fibres and is thought to increase trabecular outflow. They often cause gold-brown corneal deposits (cornea verticillata) and conjunctival hyperaemia. They also promote corneal endothelial cell proliferation after Descemet stripping surgery.

front: Classify: antiglaucoma drugs by mode of action
text: Reduce aqueous secretion: {{beta-blockers}} (timolol), {{alpha-2 agonists}} (brimonidine, apraclonidine) and {{carbonic anhydrase inhibitors}} (dorzolamide, acetazolamide). Increase uveoscleral outflow: {{prostaglandin analogues}} (latanoprost). Increase trabecular outflow: {{miotics}} (pilocarpine) and {{Rho kinase inhibitors}} (netarsudil). Adrenaline/dipivefrine act on all three.

front: Which ocular structure makes aqueous humour, and which drug classes lower IOP by cutting its production?
back: The ciliary epithelium secretes aqueous humour. Topical timolol (a beta blocker) cuts aqueous secretion, with a 20–35% fall in IOP (KDT8 PDF p183). Alpha-2 agonists reduce secretion and raise uveoscleral outflow (KDT8 PDF p184).

front: How do topical beta-blockers lower intraocular pressure, and what properties suit an ocular beta-blocker?
back: They reduce aqueous formation: beta-2 blockade in the ciliary epithelium down-regulates adenylyl cyclase, with a secondary fall in ocular blood flow. Pupil size, ciliary tone and outflow are unchanged. A good ocular beta-blocker is lipophilic with high ocular capture and has little or no local anaesthetic action (to avoid corneal hypoaesthesia).

front: Why do timolol eye drops cause systemic adverse effects, and how can they be reduced?
back: Drug drains through the nasolacrimal duct and is absorbed from the nasal mucosa, avoiding first-pass metabolism. Results: bronchospasm (even life-threatening in asthma/COPD), bradycardia, worsening heart block and heart failure, especially in the elderly; all systemic beta-blocker contraindications apply. Pressing on the inner canthus for about 5 minutes after instillation limits entry into the duct.

IOP falls 20-35% within 1 h, effect lasts about 12 h; some effect persists 1-2 weeks after stopping, so a missed dose is safe
About 30% of open angle cases need another drug
Beta-1 selective: fewer bronchopulmonary effects
May protect retinal neurones by reducing Ca2+ influx
Less efficacious than timolol because ocular receptors are mainly beta-2; more stinging
Levobunolol: once-daily alternative to timolol
Carteolol and metipranolol

front: Why are topical beta-blockers preferred over miotics in open angle glaucoma?
back: No change in pupil size (no dim vision in dim light or with cataract), no induced myopia, no brow pain from ciliary/iris spasm, no swings in IOP as with pilocarpine, and once or twice daily dosing is enough.

front: Prostaglandin analogues in glaucoma: mechanism, why first choice, and adverse effects?
back: Latanoprost (a PGF2-alpha ester prodrug), travoprost (FP agonist) and bimatoprost (prostamide) mainly increase uveoscleral outflow, with a smaller trabecular effect; efficacy equals timolol and they work in normal-tension glaucoma. Once-daily use and no systemic effects make them first-line. Local effects: irritation, blurring, increased iris pigmentation, longer darker eyelashes, and macular oedema (watch aphakic eyes). Cost is a drawback.

Both are alpha-2 agonists that cut aqueous production (Gi, lower cAMP). Apraclonidine is polar, does not enter the brain, causes frequent allergy, mydriasis and lid retraction, and is used only short-term to blunt IOP spikes after laser procedures. Brimonidine is more alpha-2 selective and lipophilic, also increases uveoscleral outflow, causes less allergy, but can cause dry mouth, sedation and mild BP fall; it is used short- or long-term, usually as add-on. Both may cause rebound red eye.

front: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors in glaucoma: topical versus oral.
back: They inhibit carbonic anhydrase II in the ciliary epithelium, reducing bicarbonate and fluid secretion. Dorzolamide and brinzolamide drops lower IOP about 20% (less than timolol), cause stinging, bitter taste and corneal oedema, and are add-on drugs. Oral acetazolamide is used short-term (angle closure, peri-operative); paresthesia, hypokalaemia, acidosis, malaise, depression and kidney stones limit chronic use.

front: Why are miotics now a last resort in open angle glaucoma?
back: Pilocarpine contracts the ciliary muscle, pulling the scleral spur and opening the trabeculae. But it lasts only 4-6 h (6-8 hourly drops with fluctuating IOP), dims vision in poor light, causes accommodative spasm, induced myopia and brow ache, and stronger drops can give sweating, diarrhoea and bronchospasm. It still works in aphakic glaucoma.

front: Why are mitomycin and 5-fluorouracil used in glaucoma surgery?
back: Applied at the trabeculectomy site, they limit post-operative wound healing and scarring so the filtration bleb stays open. The trade-off is thin avascular tissue that can leak, causing hypotony and a higher infection risk.

A 50% glycerine retention enema may be used (KDT8 PDF p186)

front: Short note: recent advances in glaucoma management

points: Prostaglandin analogues have displaced topical beta blockers as first line in open angle glaucoma (KDT8 PDF p186)
Topical beta blockers remain useful as add-on or in fixed combinations (KDT8 PDF p185)
Dorzolamide 2% twice to thrice daily, as add-on (KDT8 PDF p185)
Brimonidine as an alpha-2 add-on (KDT8 PDF p167)
Pilocarpine is third-line in open angle glaucoma (KDT8 PDF p131)
Pilocarpine causes an initial stinging sensation and painful spasm of accommodation (KDT8 PDF p131)

text: Atropine: dilates in 30-40 min, cycloplegia in 1-3 h, effects last {{7-10 days}}. Homatropine: {{10 times}} less potent, mydriasis 1-3 days. Cyclopentolate: onset 30-60 min, lasts about {{a day}}; preferred for cycloplegic refraction. {{Tropicamide}}: quickest (20-40 min) and briefest (3-6 h) but an unreliable cycloplegic.

front: What is the main ocular contraindication to atropinic drugs?
back: A narrow iridocorneal angle: mydriasis can precipitate acute congestive (angle closure) glaucoma. A marked IOP rise is rare in wide angle glaucoma. Conventional systemic doses of atropine have only minor ocular effects.

front: Uses of miotics in ophthalmology apart from glaucoma.
back: Reversing mydriasis after refraction testing; alternating with mydriatics to prevent or break iris adhesions; intra-operative miosis with intracameral acetylcholine or carbachol; and echothiophate for accommodative esotropia.

front: Which drug is used for refraction testing in a child under 5 years, and why?
back: Atropine 1% ointment applied 24 h and again 2 h before testing (cyclopentolate drops are a faster alternative). Children have high ciliary muscle tone, so homatropine and tropicamide give inadequate cycloplegia. Cyclopentolate absorbed via the nasolacrimal duct can cause transient behavioural changes in children.

front: Which mydriatic is preferred for fundoscopy in an elderly patient, and why?
back: Only mydriasis is needed, so phenylephrine (an alpha agonist with no cycloplegia) is preferred, to avoid precipitating or worsening glaucoma; a short-acting antimuscarinic like tropicamide is the alternative, and phenylephrine is often combined with tropicamide for a faster, stronger mydriasis.

front: Why is atropine used in iritis, iridocyclitis and corneal ulcer?
back: Its long mydriatic-cycloplegic action rests the intraocular muscles and relieves their painful spasm, and it has a local anodyne effect on the cornea. Alternating a mydriatic with a miotic prevents adhesions between iris and lens or cornea and can break those already formed; an alpha agonist can also help break posterior synechiae.

front: How does echothiophate help accommodative esotropia?
back: In hyperopic children constant accommodation drives excess convergence. Echothiophate, an irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor, produces miosis and an accommodative lens change, so less accommodative effort and less convergence are needed. A mydriatic is often added to reduce the iris cysts it causes. Being quaternary, it is poorly absorbed.

front: What is the role of low-dose atropine in myopia?
back: Atropine drops at 0.01-0.5% can slow, even reverse, myopia progression in children; the mechanism is unclear. Dose-dependent effects include allergy, dilated pupils needing sunglasses, and loss of accommodation.

front: Which miotic is linked to cataract, and what other ocular side effects do miotics cause?
back: Echothiophate is linked to cataract, along with retinal detachment, iris cysts, pupillary block and punctal stenosis. Miotics in general cause miosis, induced myopia, decreased vision, brow ache and ciliary body spasm.

front: Essay: Choice of mydriatic and cycloplegic for different clinical situations

points: Cycloplegia is often unsatisfactory when ciliary muscle tone is high, as in young children (KDT8 PDF p146)
Refraction: cyclopentolate is the preferred cycloplegic for refraction (KDT8 PDF p146)
Tropicamide is quick and brief and an unreliable cycloplegic, but satisfactory for adult refraction and fundoscopy (KDT8 PDF p146)
Iritis and uveitis: cyclopentolate or other antimuscarinics prevent posterior synechiae and relieve ciliary spasm pain; an alpha agonist breaks existing synechiae (GG14 PDF p1482)
Cyclopentolate absorbed through the nasolacrimal duct can cause transient behavioural abnormalities in children (KDT8 PDF p146)

front: Name the topical ocular NSAIDs and their uses.
back: Flurbiprofen (prevents intra-operative miosis in cataract surgery), ketorolac (seasonal allergic conjunctivitis; with phenylephrine in irrigation fluid against miosis), diclofenac (post-operative pain and inflammation), ketorolac and diclofenac (post-cataract cystoid macular oedema, pain after refractive surgery), bromfenac and nepafenac (post-cataract pain and inflammation). Rarely they cause sterile corneal melts, mainly in older eyes with surface disease.

Mast cell stabilisers: cromolyn (vernal conjunctivitis), lodoxamide, nedocromil. H1 antagonists with mast-cell stabilising action: olopatadine, ketotifen, bepotastine, azelastine, alcaftadine. Epinastine blocks H1 and H2 and stabilises mast cells. Topical steroids for significant allergy; ketorolac for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis.

front: How is dry eye treated pharmacologically?
back: Artificial tears (electrolytes plus viscosity agents such as cellulose polymers, polyvinyl alcohol, PEG, glycerin, dextran), with or without preservative; bland ointments at bedtime; punctal plugs; topical cyclosporine or lifitegrast (blocks LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1) to raise tear production in inflammatory dry eye; doxycycline for blepharitis; autologous serum tears in severe cases.

front: What is cenegermin, and what is it used for in the eye?
back: Recombinant human nerve growth factor given as an ophthalmic solution. It supports corneal innervation and integrity through TrkA and p75 receptors, and is indicated for neurotrophic keratitis, applied 6 times daily for 8 weeks.

front: Short note: Corticosteroids in the eye

points: Topical: dexamethasone, prednisolone, fluorometholone, loteprednol, difluprednate
Implants: fluocinolone and dexamethasone for chronic non-infectious uveitis; intravitreal triamcinolone
Ocular allergy, dry eye, anterior uveitis, post-operative inflammation
Sub-Tenon's or systemic for posterior uveitis; intravitreal for diabetic and cystoid macular oedema
Parenteral then oral taper for optic neuritis
Posterior subcapsular cataract
Secondary open angle glaucoma: marked IOP rise in about 5% without, but up to 90% with, a family history of glaucoma
Worsen herpes simplex, fungal and acanthamoeba keratitis
Loteprednol reduces but does not abolish the IOP risk

front: Why is a topical corticosteroid harmful in herpetic epithelial keratitis but helpful in disciform (endothelial) keratitis?
back: In herpetic epithelial keratitis the virus is actively replicating, so steroids are harmful. In herpetic disciform keratitis, a presumed cell-mediated immune reaction, steroids accelerate recovery (GG12 PDF p1807). Steroids can raise IOP and cause glaucoma (GG14 PDF p1487).

front: Short note: Choosing between steroid, NSAID, mast-cell stabiliser and antihistamine in the eye

points: Strongest anti-inflammatory; risk of IOP rise, cataract and infection; loteprednol is inactivated in the eye
Avoid in active herpetic epithelial keratitis
Counter intra-operative miosis (flurbiprofen) and cystoid macular oedema, without steroid IOP effects
Cromolyn, lodoxamide, nedocromil prevent mast-cell release (vernal disease)
Olopatadine, ketotifen, azelastine and similar combine H1 block with stabilising action
Artificial tears first; cyclosporine and lifitegrast treat the inflammatory component

front: Which topical antiviral is a fluorinated nucleoside, and why is it not virus-selective?
back: Trifluridine inhibits HSV-1, HSV-2 and CMV, but its virus selectivity is low. Cellular kinases are also blocked, so host DNA synthesis is affected (KDT8 PDF p861).

front: Which topical sulfonamide is used in the eye, and how irritating is it?
back: Sulfacetamide sodium: a highly soluble solution that is only mildly irritating to the eye, even at concentrations up to 30%. It treats ocular infections and chlamydia, including ophthalmia neonatorum (KDT8 ch51).

front: What is the only commercially available topical ophthalmic antifungal, and what predisposes to fungal keratitis?
back: Natamycin, a polyene; other antifungals are compounded for topical, intracorneal, intracameral or intravitreal use. Risk factors: trauma, chronic ocular surface disease, contact lens wear and immunosuppression including topical steroids.

front: How is CMV retinitis treated locally, and what is special about the ganciclovir implant?
back: Intravitreal ganciclovir, injected or as an implant, is an alternative to long-term parenteral antivirals. The implant releases drug at a nearly constant (zero-order) rate over a long period rather than as a bolus. No antiviral is indicated for adenoviral conjunctivitis, which is self-limiting.

front: How is bacterial conjunctivitis and keratitis treated?
back: Bacterial conjunctivitis is usually treated empirically with a broad-spectrum topical antibiotic without culture. Small peripheral keratitis gets frequent broad-spectrum drops; severe central keratitis needs corneal scrapings for culture, then hourly round-the-clock topical antibiotics, often specially made fortified drops.

front: Short note: Management of endophthalmitis and infectious keratitis

points: Antibiotics given intravitreally, subconjunctivally or intracamerally, by route and dose (GG14 PDF p1480)
Fungal keratitis: natamycin is the only commercial topical antifungal (GG14 PDF p1479)
Other antifungals may be compounded for topical, subconjunctival, intracorneal, intracameral or intravitreal use (GG14 PDF p1479)
Viral eye infections are treated with combinations of oral, IV and intravitreal antivirals (GG14 PDF p1479)

front: Besides neovascular AMD, which retinal conditions does bevacizumab treat?
back: Macular oedema arising from diabetic retinopathy and from central retinal vein occlusion.

front: Which agents are anti-VEGF drugs for the eye?
back: Pegaptanib (selective VEGF165 antagonist), aflibercept (receptor fusion protein acting as a VEGF-A decoy), bevacizumab (VEGF-A antibody, widely used off-label), ranibizumab (affinity-matured antibody Fab) and brolucizumab (single-chain fragment). VEGF drives new vessel growth, leakiness and inflammation in wet AMD.

front: What is verteporfin and how does it work in wet AMD?
back: A photosensitiser given IV and activated by a non-thermal laser in the choroidal circulation. Free radicals damage vessel walls, causing platelet activation, thrombosis and occlusion of abnormal vessels. Patients must avoid bright light for about 5 days.

front: Short note: Drugs for neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration

points: Pegaptanib: blocks VEGF-165 binding
Aflibercept: VEGFR1/2 fusion protein acting as a decoy receptor for VEGF-A
Bevacizumab: anti-VEGF-A antibody, used off-label first line; ranibizumab: affinity-matured Fab variant
Brolucizumab: single-chain fragment, longer interval but more uveitis
Raised IOP and endophthalmitis after injection
Possible stroke risk with bevacizumab/ranibizumab
IV verteporfin activated by non-thermal laser in choroidal vessels: free radicals occlude new vessels
Photosensitivity: avoid sunlight and bright light for 5 days
Huge price gap between bevacizumab and ranibizumab with similar outcomes fuels cost-effectiveness debate

front: Compare bevacizumab, ranibizumab and brolucizumab as intravitreal anti-VEGF agents.
back: Bevacizumab is the original full antibody. Ranibizumab is derived from it by removing the Fc domain and changing six amino acids to raise VEGF affinity (GG14 PDF p1439). Brolucizumab is a single-chain fragment with a higher incidence of uveitis and less frequent dosing (GG14 PDF p1488). The cost-effectiveness of these treatments is debated (GG14 PDF p1488).

front: Essay: Pharmacotherapy of wet age-related macular degeneration and retinal vascular disease

points: Wet AMD is a leading cause of blindness; VEGF165 promotes angiogenesis, permeability and inflammation
Pegaptanib, aflibercept, bevacizumab, ranibizumab and brolucizumab given intravitreally
Verteporfin photodynamic therapy for classic CNV
Ocriplasmin for vitreomacular traction (lens subluxation risk)
Cost-effectiveness is debated; brolucizumab has a higher uveitis incidence (GG14 PDF p1488)

front: Complete: ocular toxicity of systemic drugs
text: Topiramate: choroidal effusion with {{angle-closure glaucoma}}. Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine: {{bull's-eye maculopathy}}. Vigabatrin: permanent {{concentric visual field}} loss. Sildenafil: bluish vision via {{PDE6}} inhibition. Ethambutol: {{optic neuropathy}}. Amiodarone: corneal whorls ({{cornea verticillata}}). Minocycline: blue-grey {{sclera}}. Tamoxifen: crystalline maculopathy and {{cataract}}. Rifabutin with clarithromycin/fluconazole: {{uveitis}}.

front: What ocular changes do steroids, phenothiazines and isotretinoin cause?
back: Steroids (inhaled, systemic or ocular): raised IOP, glaucoma and cataract. Chlorpromazine and thioridazine: brown deposits in cornea, conjunctiva and lids that persist after stopping. Isotretinoin: dry eye and severe meibomian gland dysfunction.

front: Which dyes are used in eye examination and for what?
back: Fluorescein (strip or solution) shows corneal and conjunctival epithelial defects and wound leaks, tests nasolacrimal patency, and is used in applanation tonometry and rigid contact lens fitting; fluorexon is used when soft lenses are worn. Rose bengal and lissamine green stain devitalised cells. IV fluorescein or indocyanine green angiography assesses retinal barriers and can cause nausea, pruritus and allergic reactions.

front: How does chloroquine damage the retina?
back: It accumulates in the retinal pigment epithelium, producing a bull's-eye maculopathy with decreased visual acuity. Chronic users need periodic eye exams.

front: Which anaesthetics are used in eye procedures, and which anaesthetic concerns are eye-specific?
back: Topical proparacaine or tetracaine drops and lidocaine gel; intracameral preservative-free lidocaine for cataract surgery; lidocaine and bupivacaine for infiltration and retrobulbar block. Most inhalational agents and CNS depressants lower IOP, but ketamine raises it. In a ruptured globe, avoid drugs that depolarise extraocular muscles, which could expel ocular contents.

points: Chloroquine has high affinity for melanin and binds tightly to ocular pigment tissue
Retinal damage may cause loss of vision
Corneal deposits may affect vision but are reversible on stopping the drug

front: Essay: Ocular adverse effects of systemic drugs

points: Many systemic drugs reach the lens, cornea, retina or optic nerve
Inhaled, systemic or ocular steroids: raised IOP and glaucoma (GG14 PDF p1487)
Topiramate: choroidal effusion leading to angle-closure glaucoma (GG14 PDF p1487)
Amiodarone: cornea verticillata, usually with little effect on vision (GG14 PDF p1487)
Isotretinoin: dry eye and severe meibomian gland dysfunction (GG14 PDF p1487)
Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine: bull's-eye maculopathy; periodic eye exams for chronic use (GG14 PDF p1477)
Vigabatrin: permanent bilateral vision loss (GG14 PDF p423)
Sildenafil-type drugs: mild PDE6 inhibition, causing bluish haze or light sensitivity (GG14 PDF p1487)
Ethambutol: stop at the first sign of optic neuritis (KDT8 PDF p838)

front: What is the Draize eye irritation test?
back: A rabbit test in which a test substance is placed in the eye and reactions (redness, swelling, ulceration) are scored for irritation. OECD guidelines use it to classify slightly and moderately irritating chemicals (Sarkar PDF p286-290).

front: Draize test: dose, restraint and observation period
back: 0.5 mL of test substance into the eye; animal restrained for 4 h; redness, swelling, discharge, ulceration, haemorrhage and blindness are monitored for 14 days.

front: Which in vitro methods replace the Draize eye test?
back: Reconstructed human corneal epithelium models (EpiOcular), the isolated chicken eye (ICE) test and the 3T3 neutral red uptake assay.

front: Short note: Assessment of ocular toxicity potential of a new chemical entity

points: New molecules must be screened for toxicity potential in animals before human use (Sarkar p251-255)
Ocular irritancy is a regulatory requirement for topical and ophthalmic products
0.5 mL instilled into the eye; restrained 4 h
Score redness, swelling, discharge, ulceration, haemorrhage, blindness
Observe for 14 days; sacrifice and examine pathology at the end
Corneal epithelium models (EpiOcular), isolated chicken eye (ICE) test and 3T3 NRU assay (Sarkar p286-290; Ghosh PDF p182)
Known ocular ADRs of drug classes guide the study: corneal deposits, retinal toxicity (chloroquine), cataract and glaucoma with steroids (see p2-ocular-037, p2-ocular-042, p2-ocular-044)

front: What is the water drinking test in glaucoma?
back: A provocative test: a water load lowers blood osmotic tension and raises intraocular pressure. A rise above 6 mm Hg suggests glaucoma.

front: What is the venous congestion test in glaucoma?
back: A provocative test in which venous congestion raises intraocular pressure. A rise above 10 mm Hg suggests glaucoma.

front: Normal intraocular pressure and how it is measured
back: Normal range is 16 to 23 mm Hg. It is measured by tonometry, such as applanation or digital tonometry.

front: Short note: Experimental (provocative) methods to produce raised IOP in glaucoma

points: Provoke a rise in IOP and watch how the eye copes under stress
Measure IOP with tonometry; normal 16 to 23 mm Hg
Water load lowers blood osmotic tension, so IOP rises
Rise above 6 mm Hg indicates glaucoma
Venous obstruction raises IOP
Rise above 10 mm Hg indicates glaucoma
Provocative tests above are used for chronic simple (wide angle) glaucoma

front: Which enzymes oxidise ethanol, and what are the products?
back: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethanol to acetaldehyde; aldehyde dehydrogenase converts acetaldehyde to acetate, which is broken down to carbon dioxide and water. A small share is oxidised by hepatic microsomal CYP2E1, and this minor route is induced by chronic drinking.

front: What effects go with rising blood alcohol levels in mg/dL?
back: About 30 to 60: loss of inhibition, apparent excitation, mood change. About 100 to 150: mental clouding, impaired attention and gait, drowsiness. About 150 to 200: ataxia and blackouts. About 200 to 300: stupor. Higher levels: unconsciousness, and death from paralysis of medullary centres. Even small amounts slow reflexes, so driving is unsafe.

front: What is acute tolerance to alcohol?
back: At the same blood alcohol level, central effects are stronger while the level is rising than while it is falling. This is taken as evidence of acute tolerance.

text: Absolute alcohol is {{99% w/w}} ethanol; rectified spirit is {{90% w/w}} ethanol; methylated spirit contains {{5 parts}} of wood naphtha per {{95 parts}} of rectified spirit and is tinted blue with {{methylene blue}}.

front: Classify: alcoholic beverages by typical alcohol content
text: Malted liquors such as beer contain about {{3 to 6%}}; light wines such as claret about {{9 to 12%}}; champagne about {{12 to 16%}}; fortified wines such as port about {{16 to 22%}}.

front: Short note: Alcohol content of beverages and the standard drink
back: Spirits contain 40 to 55% alcohol, standardised in India to 42.8% v/v; proof spirit is 57.1% v/v. One standard drink (about 16 g alcohol) gives about 30 mg/dL peak in an average adult male on an empty stomach.

front: Why does ethanol follow zero-order kinetics, and what is the practical consequence?
back: Alcohol dehydrogenase is saturated at ordinary blood levels (the supply of NAD+ is the limiting factor), so a roughly fixed amount, about 8 to 12 mL of absolute alcohol per hour, is removed whatever the level. Drinking faster than this keeps raising the blood level, and the level then falls only at this fixed rate.

front: Short note: Alcohol as a CNS depressant: how blood level sets the effect

points: 30 to 60 mg/dL: apparent excitation and euphoria; caution and restraint lost first
100 to 150 mg/dL: mental clouding, impaired attention and gait
200 to 300 mg/dL: stupor; above this unconsciousness and possible death from medullary paralysis
Effects are greater when blood level is rising than when it is falling
Anticonvulsant while acting, but seizures may follow; cortex and reticular formation most sensitive

front: Short note: Ethanol: mechanism of CNS action and why it differs from barbiturates and benzodiazepines

points: Enhances GABA release at GABA-A sites; inhibits NMDA receptors (memory impairment); augments 5-HT3 action; may affect nicotinic receptors
Inhibits voltage-sensitive Ca2+ channels; activates some K+ channels; alters Na+ K+ ATPase and adenylyl cyclase
Enhances dopamine release in nucleus accumbens via endorphin release (opioid-dependent), linked to reinforcement and dependence

front: Short note: Pharmacokinetics of ethanol: zero-order metabolism and the breath test

points: Limited by gastric emptying; peak in about 30 min when fasting; first-pass in stomach and liver is limited
Volume of distribution about 0.7 L/kg; crosses BBB and placenta freely
Alcohol dehydrogenase then aldehyde dehydrogenase; about 98% oxidised; CYP2E1 minor
Zero-order kinetics: 8 to 12 mL absolute alcohol per hour regardless of level
Exhaled air holds about 0.05% of blood alcohol concentration; used medicolegally

front: Short note: Alcohol and the liver: fatty liver, acetaldehyde and cirrhosis

Acetaldehyde damage, glutathione depletion and lipid peroxidation lead to necrosis and fibrosis (cirrhosis), worsened by malnutrition
Regular intake induces microsomal enzymes including CYP2E1, raising NABQI formation from paracetamol

front: Short note: Acute alcoholic intoxication: management and why analeptics are avoided

points: Patent airway, prevent aspiration of vomit, intubation and positive-pressure breathing if depressed
Fluids and electrolytes; glucose infusion for hypoglycaemia; thiamine 100 mg in glucose IV
Haemodialysis accelerates removal; insulin with fructose has minor effect
Analeptics (may precipitate convulsions); gastric lavage helps only very early

front: Short note: Alcohol and the foetus: foetal alcohol syndrome and safe drinking

points: Moderate drinking in pregnancy can cause growth retardation, low IQ, microcephaly, flat face, immune impairment
Heavy drinking adds miscarriage, stillbirth and low birth weight
About 1 to 2 drinks per day; not more than 3 on one occasion; more than 3 a day associated with harm

front: Why does alcohol cause hypoglycaemia and why does glucagon fail to correct it?
back: Acute intoxication inhibits gluconeogenesis and depletes hepatic glycogen, so the liver cannot release glucose. Glucagon therefore fails to reverse the hypoglycaemia; glucose must be given.

front: Short note: Disulfiram-like reactions with sulfonylureas, cefoperazone and metronidazole

points: Rare bizarre reactions in a few individuals taking these drugs with alcohol; mechanism unclear
Pass off as alcohol is metabolised; reassurance and supportive care

100 per cent ethanol is more dehydrating but a poorer antiseptic than 90%
Rubefacient and counterirritant; astringent; neurolysis in intractable pain
Appetite stimulant and carminative (7 to 10% in small volumes); antidote for methanol poisoning

front: Ethylene glycol poisoning: what is the antidote, and what causes the toxicity?
back: Fomepizole is the drug of choice, with ethanol as the alternative. Ethylene glycol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase through glycolaldehyde, glycolic acid and glyoxylic acid to oxalic acid. These products cause acidosis, cardiopulmonary complications and renal tubular necrosis.

text: {{Sodium bicarbonate}} infusion corrects the acidosis; {{fomepizole}} is the drug of choice; {{haemodialysis}} clears methanol and formate; {{calcium leucovorin}} hastens formate oxidation.

Peak blood alcohol after one standard drink is about {{30 mg/dL}}; alcohol is metabolised at {{8 to 12 mL}} of absolute alcohol per hour; methanol fatal dose is {{75 to 100 mL}}; 15 mL of methanol can cause {{blindness}}.

front: Ethylene glycol: uses and the order of its metabolites.
back: An industrial solvent, coolant and antifreeze. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts it to glycolaldehyde, then glycolic acid, glyoxylic acid and oxalic acid; these cause acidosis and renal tubular necrosis.

front: Why is methanol toxic, and which metabolite causes the acidosis and the eye damage?
back: Methanol is oxidised to formaldehyde and then to formic acid. Formic acid is cleared slowly through a folate-dependent step, and it causes the metabolic acidosis and the specific retinal toxicity. Optic disc congestion leads to blindness, and death is from respiratory failure.

front: Methanol poisoning: how does fomepizole work, and why is it preferred to ethanol?
back: Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) specifically inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, so methanol is not converted to formaldehyde and formic acid. It is the drug of choice because it has a longer half-life than ethanol, has no inebriating action, and its IV form allows regulated dosing. KDT 8e notes that it is not commercially available in India; ethanol, which saturates alcohol dehydrogenase at a blood level of about 100 mg/dL, is the alternative.

Symptoms appear only after a delay of a few hours
Vomiting, headache, epigastric pain, drunkenness, tachypnoea, dyspnoea, bradycardia, hypotension

front: Short note: Methanol poisoning: why toxicity comes from formic acid and how it is managed

Ethanol is used to treat methanol poisoning (KDT8 ch28)

front: Why do fomepizole and ethanol both treat methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning, and why is fomepizole preferred?
back: Both toxic alcohols are harmless until alcohol dehydrogenase makes toxic acids (formic acid; glycolic and oxalic acids). Fomepizole specifically inhibits that enzyme; ethanol is its preferred substrate and competes. Fomepizole has a longer half-life, gives no intoxication, and is given IV with regulated dosing, whereas ethanol has no IV form, is hard to titrate and causes intoxication and hypoglycaemia. Bicarbonate for acidosis and dialysis are added in methanol poisoning.

text: Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits {{aldehyde dehydrogenase}}, so {{acetaldehyde}} accumulates after alcohol; a milder disulfiram-like reaction can occur with {{metronidazole}}, {{cefoperazone}} and {{sulfonylureas}}.

front: Disulfiram: which enzyme does it block, and what builds up?
back: It irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase (probably through an active metabolite). Alcohol is then oxidised only as far as acetaldehyde, which accumulates and causes the unpleasant reaction that discourages drinking.

front: Disulfiram: regimen and how long the sensitisation lasts?
back: 500 mg daily for a week, then 250 mg daily, started only after at least 12 hours without alcohol. Sensitisation begins 2-3 hours after the first dose, peaks near 12 hours and persists 7-14 days after stopping, so a slip in the following fortnight still triggers the reaction.

front: Acamprosate and naltrexone: what does each do in alcohol dependence?
back: Both are anti-craving drugs started after withdrawal in a motivated patient. Naltrexone blocks opioid-mediated reward of alcohol, reducing craving and relapse. Acamprosate is a weak NMDA antagonist with modest GABA-A agonism; its efficacy is comparable to naltrexone and loose motions are its common side effect.

front: Which opioid receptor types exist, and what does each mainly mediate?
back: Mu receptors mediate most morphine actions: supraspinal and spinal analgesia, respiratory depression, euphoria, miosis, sedation and constipation; the endogenous ligands are endomorphins, and beta-endorphin acts mainly here too. Kappa receptors give spinal analgesia with a lower ceiling, dysphoria, psychotomimetic effects and sedation; the endogenous ligand is dynorphin. Delta receptors are linked to the affective component of analgesia, reinforcement, dependence and proconvulsant action; enkephalins bind here.

front: Morphine pharmacokinetics: oral bioavailability, metabolites and half-life.
back: Oral bioavailability is about one-quarter of the parenteral dose because of high first-pass metabolism. It is conjugated mainly to morphine-6-glucuronide, which is more potent than morphine at mu receptors and accumulates on chronic dosing, and to morphine-3-glucuronide, which is neuroexcitatory. Plasma half-life is 2 to 3 hours; effect lasts 4 to 6 hours; enterohepatic recirculation prolongs the stay; it crosses the placenta.

points: Endorphins: beta-endorphin (31 amino acids) from POMC, which also gives ACTH and MSH; mainly mu agonist

front: How does morphine produce spinal analgesia?
back: It acts on mu receptors in the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn and reduces release of excitatory transmitters, such as glutamate and substance P, from primary pain afferents. It also reduces postsynaptic excitation of dorsal horn neurones. Supraspinal action on the periaqueductal grey and descending pathways adds to this, and together they greatly amplify analgesia.

front: Why does morphine cause constipation, and does tolerance develop to it?
back: Mu receptors on the enteric plexus raise segmental tone and reduce propulsive movement, with spasm of the pyloric, ileocaecal and anal sphincters. Intestinal secretion falls and fluid is absorbed from stasis; a central effect also blunts the defecation reflex. No tolerance develops, so chronic users stay constipated. Miosis and the proconvulsant effect also do not show tolerance.

front: Morphine respiratory depression: which drives are lost first, and which centre is most sensitive?
back: The neurogenic drive is depressed first, then the hypercapnic drive, and later the hypoxic drive. Rate and tidal volume fall in a dose-dependent way, and a patient can lose the urge to breathe. The cough centre is more sensitive than the respiratory centre. Death from overdose is from respiratory failure.

front: Name the main precautions and contraindications for morphine.
back: Respiratory insufficiency (emphysema, cor pulmonale, pulmonary fibrosis): risk of sudden death. Bronchial asthma: histamine release can trigger an attack. Head injury: CO2 retention raises intracranial pressure and the drug masks neurological assessment. Hypotension or hypovolaemia: exaggerated fall in BP. Undiagnosed acute abdominal pain: can aggravate biliary colic, pancreatitis or diverticulitis. Elderly men: urinary retention. Infants and the elderly: more respiratory depression.
