points: Dopamine and dobutamine give prompt, short-lived support, especially when BP is low
Tolerance and arrhythmias limit prolonged use; no long-term role
Inamrinone is an inodilator; its dose-related problem is thrombocytopenia
Oral inamrinone and oral milrinone increased mortality, so they are restricted to short-term IV use
Milrinone is about 10 times more potent than inamrinone and causes little thrombocytopenia
Sensitises troponin C to Ca2+ without raising cytosolic Ca2+; also opens ATP-sensitive K+ channels
Relieves symptoms in acute decompensation but does not improve survival
Hypotension may last days because of its long-acting active metabolite
Diuretics and vasodilators are the main treatment of acute decompensation; inotropes are reserved for selected patients with low output
No drug given during acute decompensation has improved long-term prognosis

front: Short note: Vasodilators in heart failure

points: Venodilatation reduces preload and filling pressure
Useful in acute left failure with ischaemia; tolerance limits routine use
Arteriolar dilator that reduces afterload; useful with low cardiac index and modest CVP
Reflex tachycardia, ischaemia and fluid retention limit monotherapy
Dilates arterioles and veins; short-acting IV drug for crises, used with a loop diuretic and an inotrope
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate improves survival in severe heart failure in African-American patients on standard therapy
Also an option when an ACE inhibitor or ARB cannot be used, for example in renal insufficiency

front: Short note: Beta-blockers and aldosterone antagonists in heart failure

points: Metoprolol succinate (SR), bisoprolol, carvedilol and nebivolol reduce mortality in systolic dysfunction
Start only in clinically stable patients at very low doses and titrate slowly; EF may fall before improving
Do not start in new-onset or acutely decompensated failure; if decompensation occurs on therapy, reduce or stop and restart after stabilisation

Spironolactone (RALES, in severe failure) and eplerenone (EPHESUS; also effective in milder failure) reduce mortality; given in low doses to all patients with symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA II to IV), added to an ACE inhibitor or ARB
Use low doses (spironolactone 12.5 to 25 mg daily) and monitor potassium; eplerenone avoids gynaecomastia
Finerenone, a non-steroidal MRA, is more selective and may cause less hyperkalaemia
Aldosterone drives sodium retention, hypokalaemia, fibrosis and arrhythmias
Roles in heart failure with preserved EF are uncertain
Beta-blockers are also indicated in asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction
Rapid up-titration causes hypotension, fluid retention and dizziness

front: Why is hydralazine given with isosorbide dinitrate in heart failure?
back: The combination is the only long-term oral vasodilator regimen with survival benefit, though ACE inhibitors and ARBs are superior. It suits patients with renal insufficiency or renal artery stenosis who cannot take ACE inhibitors or ARBs; it added survival benefit in severe African-American patients already on ACE inhibitor, digoxin and diuretic.

front: Hydralazine in heart failure: which patients benefit and what limits it
back: Afterload reduction in forward failure when cardiac index is below 2.5 L/min/m2 without a marked rise in CVP (below 18 mm Hg); limited by tachycardia, worsened ischaemia and fluid retention.

Oral prodrug activated by esterases to sacubitrilat (neprilysin inhibitor); absolute bioavailability 60%; half-life about 12 hours. Combined with valsartan it gave a 20% greater reduction in death or heart-failure hospitalisation than enalapril in 8442 patients; common adverse effects were hypotension, hyperkalaemia and renal impairment.

front: Why is sacubitril-valsartan preferred to an ACE inhibitor in HFrEF, and what must be watched?
back: In PARADIGM-HF sacubitril-valsartan gave about 20% greater reduction in death or HF hospitalisation than enalapril, so it is an effective, well-tolerated alternative to ACE inhibitors. Neprilysin inhibition raises natriuretic peptides while valsartan blocks angiotensin II. Hypotension, hyperkalaemia and renal impairment need watching. It was tested on top of diuretics, beta-blockers and aldosterone antagonists.

front: What is PDE3, and where does it act in the cardiovascular system?
back: Phosphodiesterase 3 is the isoenzyme that breaks down cAMP in heart, blood vessels and bronchial smooth muscle; inhibiting it raises intracellular cAMP.

Vasodilatation lowers preload and afterload: an inodilator

Added to digoxin, diuretics and vasodilators

front: Cardiogenic shock: what does medical treatment aim to optimise?
back: Peripheral blood flow, by tuning preload, myocardial contractility and afterload. Prognosis is poor when shock follows myocardial infarction.

front: Short note: Drug management of cardiogenic shock

points: Restore peripheral perfusion by tuning preload, contractility and afterload
Prognosis is poor after an MI-related shock
Fluids may help, but rapid volume can worsen shock and cause pulmonary oedema
Diuretics and nitrates reduce preload
Dobutamine: beta-1 agonist, the usual choice
Dopamine: intravenous only, not for long-term use
Milrinone: PDE-3 inhibitor that raises cAMP

Nitroprusside reduces afterload when BP can be maintained

front: In cardiogenic shock, why can alpha-agonist pressors do harm?
back: Reflex vasoconstriction is already intense, so further alpha stimulation cuts flow to kidneys and gut and raises the heart's workload.
Beta-1 agonist giving a positive inotropic effect; given intravenously in cardiogenic shock and acute heart failure, with dose titrated to response.

front: Milrinone: how does it increase contractility?
back: It blocks PDE-3, so cAMP is not broken down; contractility rises and vessels dilate. It has been largely replaced by dobutamine in shock.

front: Which nephron segment does each major diuretic class act on?
back: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act mainly on the proximal tubule. Loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb of Henle. Thiazides act on the early distal convoluted tubule. Potassium-sparing agents act on the late distal tubule and collecting duct. Mannitol acts mainly in the proximal tubule and descending limb, by osmosis.

front: What is a diuretic, and why does the body settle at a Na+ deficit rather than keep losing fluid?
back: A diuretic causes net loss of Na+ and water in urine. Homeostatic mechanisms restore Na+ balance during regular use, leaving a Na+ deficit and a smaller extracellular volume.

front: What do 'high ceiling' and 'medium efficacy' mean for loop versus thiazide diuretics?
back: Loop (high-ceiling) diuretics give a far larger maximal natriuresis than thiazides, which are medium-efficacy drugs. Efficacy tracks how much Na+ the nephron segment normally reabsorbs.

Weakness and cramps; cardiac arrhythmias are the serious risk
Aim to keep serum K+ at or above 3.5 mEq/L; serum level is only a rough guide to body stores
Prevent with diet, KCl or a K+-sparing diuretic; supplements are reserved for documented or high-risk cases
Combined diuretic and KCl tablets are not advised because of gut ulceration
More common with thiazides than loop diuretics: ADH rises with hypovolaemia, the diluting capacity of the kidney is impaired, and thirst increases
Elderly women are most prone; recurs on rechallenge; prevent by lower dose or water restriction
Loop diuretics in heart failure can also cause dilutional hyponatraemia: withhold the drug, restrict water and correct K+

Hypokalaemic alkalosis, as more H+ is exchanged for Na+ in the distal tubule
Acute saline depletion: postural hypotension, haemoconcentration and venous thrombosis risk; treat with saline

front: What causes resistance to diuretics, and how is it overcome?
back: Renal insufficiency (low GFR and less tubular secretion, so less drug reaches its site); heart failure (poor oral absorption from gut congestion, reduced renal blood flow); cirrhosis (high aldosterone); nephrotic syndrome (drug bound to urinary protein, high aldosterone). Long-term loop diuretic use also causes distal nephron hypertrophy. Adding a distally acting thiazide, especially metolazone, restores diuresis; the combination can be very powerful and needs close monitoring.

front: Furosemide: what does it inhibit, and how does that abolish the medullary gradient?
back: It blocks the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter on the luminal membrane of the thick ascending limb; the drug reaches this site after organic acid secretion in the proximal tubule. Without this transport the corticomedullary osmotic gradient collapses, so both positive and negative free water clearance are lost. Loss of the lumen-positive potential also increases Ca2+ and Mg2+ excretion, and K+ loss rises because more Na+ reaches the distal tubule.

Oral bioavailability is about 60%, but it can fall in severe heart failure with gut oedema, when parenteral use is needed. Onset is about 2 to 5 min IV and 20 to 40 min orally, with a duration of 3 to 6 h. Plasma half-life is 1 to 2 h, prolonged in pulmonary oedema and in renal or hepatic failure. Usual dose is 20 to 80 mg once daily in the morning; 40 to 80 mg IV is used in pulmonary oedema.

text: Loop diuretics include {{furosemide}}, {{bumetanide}} and {{torasemide}}; they inhibit the {{Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter}} in the {{thick ascending limb of Henle}}.

front: Which loop diuretic was introduced in the mid-1960s alongside furosemide?
back: Ethacrynic acid (a high-ceiling diuretic; introduced in the 1960s and changed diuretic use)

front: Why does furosemide's natriuresis fade over time, and which system is responsible?
back: Blocking Na+ entry at the macula densa triggers renin release, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; reflex sympathetic activity adds to this. These changes restore sodium balance once the drug wears off. Because of this and its short half-life, once-daily dosing may give less overall sodium loss.

front: Furosemide: the early haemodynamic effect that gives quick relief in pulmonary oedema.
back: Intravenous furosemide increases systemic venous capacitance before any diuresis, lowering left ventricular filling pressure. This venodilatation is prostaglandin-mediated and gives rapid relief in left heart failure and pulmonary oedema. GFR is largely preserved.

front: What is the ototoxicity of loop diuretics, and what raises the risk?
back: Hearing loss is infrequent and occurs only with high-ceiling diuretics, not with thiazides. It is thought to reflect raised salt content of the endolymph and direct toxicity to inner ear hair cells. The risk rises with renal insufficiency and with concurrent aminoglycosides, which are also ototoxic and nephrotoxic.

front: Bumetanide compared with furosemide: potency, bioavailability and special uses.
back: Bumetanide is about 40 times more potent, with the same site, ceiling effect and duration. Its oral bioavailability is 80 to 100%, so it suits oral use in severe heart failure with gut oedema. It may act in some furosemide-unresponsive patients and can be used in furosemide-allergic patients. Hyperuricaemia, potassium loss, glucose intolerance and ototoxicity are reported to be less marked, but myopathy can rarely occur.

front: Short note: Uses of high-ceiling (loop) diuretics

points: Cardiac, hepatic and renal oedema; drugs of choice for nephrotic and other resistant oedema
Effective even in chronic renal failure, where large doses may be needed; thiazides fail there
Preferred over thiazides in heart failure for rapid mobilisation of fluid
Acute renal failure: help short-term fluid management, but have not changed long-term outcome
IV furosemide gives prompt relief through early venodilatation, followed by a fall in blood volume
Also useful in acute left ventricular failure after myocardial infarction
Only with renal insufficiency, heart failure, resistant cases or hypertensive emergencies
Otherwise thiazides are the first choice
Added to blood transfusion in severe anaemia to prevent volume overload
With hypertonic saline in hyponatraemia
Hypercalcaemia: after IV saline volume repletion, furosemide (KDT: 10 to 20 mg/h in the drip) increases Ca2+ excretion and prevents overload
Adjunct to osmotic agents in cerebral oedema
Forced diuresis with saline and furosemide to treat poisoning is no longer recommended

front: Why are high-ceiling diuretics given with i.v. saline in hypercalcaemia of malignancy?
back: Saline volume replacement comes first; then furosemide 10-20 mg/hour augments Ca2+ excretion and prevents volume overload.

front: Why is furosemide added to osmotic diuretics in cerebral oedema?
back: Furosemide is combined with an osmotic agent to improve the reduction of brain water and intracranial pressure.

front: When are high-ceiling diuretics preferred over thiazides for hypertension?
back: Only with renal insufficiency, heart failure, resistant cases or hypertensive emergencies; otherwise thiazides are preferred.

front: Why do NSAIDs blunt the action of furosemide?
back: NSAIDs such as indomethacin block renal prostaglandin synthesis, which furosemide's intrarenal haemodynamic effects depend on. The effect is stronger in cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome.

front: Why should diuretics be avoided in toxaemia of pregnancy?
back: Blood volume is low despite oedema; diuretics can further compromise placental circulation and raise the risk of miscarriage or foetal death.

front: Thiazides: site and mechanism of action.
back: After organic acid secretion in the proximal tubule, thiazides reach the early distal convoluted tubule and bind the luminal Na+-Cl- symporter, blocking NaCl reabsorption. The medullary gradient is not affected, so their site lies between the thick ascending limb and the late distal tubule. Extra Na+ delivered there is exchanged for K+, so kaliuresis runs in parallel with natriuresis.

front: Thiazides: effects on calcium, magnesium and urate.
back: Calcium: thiazides cut urinary Ca2+ excretion by a direct distal tubular action, so serum calcium tends to rise (loop diuretics do the opposite). Magnesium: excretion increases. Urate: they raise blood urate by competing with urate for proximal tubular secretion and by increasing proximal reabsorption after volume contraction; the effect is greater than with furosemide. A weak carbonic anhydrase action adds some bicarbonate and phosphate loss.

text: In the book's order, thiazide and related diuretics are {{hydrochlorothiazide}}, {{chlorthalidone}}, {{metolazone}}, {{xipamide}}, {{indapamide}} and {{clopamide}}; chlorthalidone is the longest acting, with a half-life of about {{40 to 50 hours}}.

front: Thiazides: metabolic adverse effects with long-term antihypertensive use.
back: Hyperglycaemia, which probably follows hypokalaemia-linked reduction in insulin release; dyslipidaemia; and hyperuricaemia. These effects are minimal with the low doses now used. Unlike loop diuretics, thiazides tend to raise serum calcium.

front: Why are thiazides weak in renal failure, and which thiazide-like drug is the exception?
back: Thiazides depend on delivery of drug to the tubule by filtration and secretion, and their volume contraction and intrarenal haemodynamic effects lower GFR further, so they fail at low GFR. Metolazone, which has an extra proximal action and is excreted unchanged, still gives a useful response at a GFR near 15 mL/min and has a marked additive effect with furosemide.

front: Why do thiazides fail in severe renal failure, yet metolazone still works?
back: Thiazides reduce GFR and rely on a filtered load; metolazone is still clinically useful at a GFR near 15 ml/min, and it acts additively with furosemide.

front: Which proximal tubular action does metolazone add?
back: It inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule. Metolazone is excreted unchanged in urine.

front: Why do some thiazides increase HCO3- and phosphate excretion?
back: They have weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitory action in the proximal tubule; chlorthalidone has the strongest.

front: Why is hyperuricaemia from thiazides less of a problem now than before?
back: Higher doses caused it in the past; current lower doses rarely raise urate, and allopurinol can counter the effect.

front: What is the main diuretic use of thiazides in renal stone patients?
back: Recurrent calcium stones with hypercalciuria: thiazides reduce renal Ca2+ excretion.

Acting from the interstitial side, it blocks aldosterone-induced protein synthesis, reducing Na+ reabsorption and K+ and H+ secretion. It has no effect when aldosterone is absent, and its potassium-retaining effect takes 3 to 4 days to develop.

Oral bioavailability is about 75% for microfine tablets. It is highly protein bound and is metabolised in the liver to active metabolites, chiefly canrenone, which contributes much of the in vivo effect. front: Amiloride and triamterene: mechanism of action.
back: Both are nonsteroidal organic bases that directly block the amiloride-sensitive epithelial Na+ channel on the luminal membrane of late distal tubule and collecting duct cells. Less Na+ entry reduces the lumen-negative potential, so K+ and H+ secretion fall while a small amount of Na+ is lost. The effect does not depend on aldosterone and does not change renal haemodynamics. Ca2+ and Mg2+ excretion also falls.

text: Aldosterone antagonists are {{spironolactone}} and {{eplerenone}}, acting on the {{mineralocorticoid receptor}}; epithelial Na+ channel blockers are {{amiloride}} and {{triamterene}}, acting on the {{luminal membrane}} of late distal tubule and collecting duct cells.

front: Triamterene pharmacokinetics: how is it absorbed and cleared?
back: Incompletely absorbed orally, partly protein bound, metabolised in the liver to an active metabolite and excreted in urine; half-life 4 hours.

front: Finerenone: how does it differ from spironolactone, and where is it used?
back: A nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor blocker with very low affinity for androgen and progesterone receptors, so hormonal side effects are minimal. Oral availability is about 44% because of first-pass metabolism by CYP3A4; half-life about 2 h. It reduces decline in renal function, cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalisation in CKD associated with type 2 diabetes. Hyperkalaemia is the main risk; avoid strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.

front: Why is hyperkalaemia from spironolactone a particular risk in renal impairment?
back: K+ retention is worse when renal function is inadequate, and it is increased further by ACE inhibitors and ARBs.

front: Why does spironolactone cause hormonal adverse effects?
back: It is a steroid that binds progestin and androgen receptors; it may also speed testosterone clearance or conversion to oestradiol.

front: Why is eplerenone less likely than spironolactone to cause gynaecomastia?
back: It is a more selective aldosterone antagonist with much lower affinity for androgen and progesterone receptors.

front: Why does clarithromycin matter for eplerenone?
back: CYP3A4 inactivates eplerenone in the liver, so inhibitors such as clarithromycin and itraconazole raise its blood level; inducers such as carbamazepine may reduce its effect.

front: Why is amiloride given as an aerosol in cystic fibrosis?
back: It increases the fluidity of respiratory secretions and gives symptomatic improvement.

front: Mannitol: how does an inert osmotic agent increase urine flow?
back: Mannitol is a low molecular weight non-electrolyte that is freely filtered and barely reabsorbed, so it stays in the tubular fluid. It holds water isosmotically in the proximal tubule and descending limb, dilutes the fluid and washes out medullary hypertonicity. By expanding extracellular volume it raises GFR and inhibits renin release, and it increases renal blood flow, especially to the medulla.

text: Systemic agents include {{acetazolamide}}, {{methazolamide}} and {{dichlorphenamide}}, while topical agents used in glaucoma are {{dorzolamide}} and {{brinzolamide}}.

Acetazolamide is used as an adjunct in {{glaucoma}}, to {{alkalinise urine}}, as an adjunct in {{absence seizures}}, and for prophylaxis of {{acute mountain sickness}}; it is not used as a diuretic because of {{acidosis}} and its self-limiting action.

front: Which carbonic anhydrase isoform does acetazolamide inhibit in proximal tubule cells, and which on the brush border?
back: Type II in the proximal tubule cell; type IV on the brush border of the tubular lumen.

front: Why does acetazolamide cause the most kaliuresis of all diuretics?
back: Acetazolamide blocks carbonic anhydrase in the distal tubule and collecting duct, so H+ secretion falls. Na+ exchange there then occurs mainly with K+, and for the same natriuresis more K+ is lost.

front: How does acetazolamide help in acute mountain sickness?
back: It alters CO2 transport in lungs, tissues and brain, and lowers CSF formation and CSF pH. Start it 1-2 days before travel.

front: Which mannitol use is contraindicated once acute renal failure has set in?
back: Giving it to maintain urine flow once the kidney cannot make urine: it expands plasma volume and risks pulmonary oedema and heart failure.

front: Why is mannitol used to counter dialysis disequilibrium?
back: It raises plasma and extracellular osmolality, which haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis may lower too quickly.

front: What is ADH (vasopressin), where is it made, and what controls its release?
back: Arginine vasopressin is a nonapeptide made in the supraoptic and paraventricular hypothalamic nuclei with neurophysin, and released from the posterior pituitary. Its main controls are plasma osmolarity, sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, and effective circulating volume, sensed by stretch receptors in the atria, ventricles and pulmonary veins. Angiotensin II, prostaglandins, histamine and acetylcholine increase release; atrial natriuretic peptide, GABA, alcohol and glucocorticoids decrease it.

front: How does vasopressin increase water permeability through V2 receptors?
back: V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of collecting duct principal cells raise cAMP through adenylyl cyclase. Protein kinase A then drives aquaporin-2 water-channel vesicles into the apical membrane and slows their retrieval. Sustained stimulation also increases aquaporin-2 synthesis. Water then follows the hypertonic medullary gradient. V2 stimulation also increases urea permeability of the inner medullary collecting duct.

front: V1 receptors: subtypes, signalling and main actions.
back: V1 receptors act through phospholipase C, IP3 and DAG to release intracellular calcium. V1a sits on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction, and also on visceral muscle, platelets and liver. V1b is on the anterior pituitary, where it promotes ACTH release. V1 receptors also constrict the vasa recta, which helps keep the medulla hypertonic.

front: Classify: vasopressin receptor agonists and antagonists
text: Selective V2 agonist: {{desmopressin}}; agonists acting on both V1 and V2: {{vasopressin}} and {{lypressin}}; prodrug used in variceal bleeding: {{terlipressin}}; selective V2 antagonists: {{tolvaptan}} and {{mozavaptan}}; V1a plus V2 antagonist: {{conivaptan}}.

front: Classify: vasopressin receptor subtypes and their signalling
text: V1 receptors signal through {{phospholipase C}}, {{IP3}} and {{DAG}} to release calcium, whereas V2 receptors signal through {{cAMP}} to insert {{aquaporin-2}} channels into the apical membrane of collecting duct cells.

front: Why is aqueous vasopressin not given orally?
back: It is destroyed by trypsin, and its peptide chain is rapidly cleaved in liver and kidney (plasma half-life about 25 minutes).

front: Name the nonpeptide vasopressin antagonists in clinical use and their receptor selectivity.
back: Tolvaptan and mozavaptan (V2 selective); conivaptan (V1a and V2).

front: Where does vasopressin act on the thick ascending limb, and what does this do?
back: V2 receptors in the TAL activate and translocate the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter, and in the long term increase its synthesis, reinforcing medullary hypertonicity.

front: Why does high-dose vasopressin not give pure antidiuresis?
back: V1 receptor activation constricts vasa recta, and V1 stimulation of medullary interstitial cells raises PG synthesis; at high levels V1 also activates PKC and reduces V2 responsiveness in the collecting duct.

front: Which drugs potentiate vasopressin's antidiuretic action in the kidney?
back: NSAIDs (especially indomethacin, which blocks renal prostaglandin synthesis), carbamazepine and chlorpropamide.

front: Which drugs partly antagonise the renal action of vasopressin?
back: Lithium and demeclocycline, which reduce concentrating ability and cause polyuria; demeclocycline has been used in inappropriate ADH secretion.

front: Why is vasopressin an effective pressor in shock, and what limits its use?
back: It constricts peripheral vessels, so it raises BP in shock. It can also cause bradycardia, raised afterload and angina by constricting coronary vessels.

front: What is diabetes insipidus, and how do neurogenic and nephrogenic forms differ in response to vasopressin?
back: DI is passage of large volumes of dilute urine. Neurogenic DI is ADH deficiency, so vasopressin or desmopressin cuts urine volume and raises osmolarity. In nephrogenic DI the kidney is unresponsive, so it does not.

front: Which drugs actually work in nephrogenic DI?
back: Thiazides are the only diuretics effective; they lower free-water clearance. Indomethacin can add some benefit, combined with a thiazide plus amiloride. Desmopressin is useless as the kidney cannot respond.
Intranasal route preferred (bioavailability 10-20%); oral tablets work but with only 1-2% bioavailability, so doses are 10-15 times higher. Slow enzymatic degradation gives action lasting 8-12 hours.

front: Desmopressin: why is it the drug of choice for V2 indications?
back: It is a synthetic V2-selective agonist, about 12 times more antidiuretic than vasopressin, with negligible vasoconstrictor action and slow enzymatic breakdown. Its half-life is 1 to 2 h and its duration of action 8 to 12 h. Intranasal bioavailability is 10 to 20%; oral tablets have only 1 to 2% bioavailability and need a dose 10 to 15 times higher, but they avoid nasal side effects.

front: Why do thiazides reduce urine volume in diabetes insipidus?
back: Sustained electrolyte depletion makes the proximal tubule reabsorb more of the filtrate iso-osmotically. Less salt is reabsorbed in the cortical diluting segment, so a smaller volume of less dilute urine reaches the collecting ducts. Thiazides also lower GFR. They work in both pituitary and nephrogenic DI, but they cannot make urine hypertonic, so they are less effective than vasopressin. Potassium supplements are usually needed. The mechanism is not fully understood.

front: Lithium-induced nephrogenic DI: which drug is preferred and why?
back: Amiloride, because it blocks sodium entry through the epithelial Na+ channel of collecting duct principal cells, which lithium also enters through. Indomethacin can also reduce polyuria by lowering renal prostaglandin synthesis, and it can be combined with a thiazide and amiloride. Other NSAIDs are less active.

front: Tolvaptan: class, indications and key cautions.
back: An oral nonpeptide selective V2 antagonist that increases free water clearance (aquaretic). Uses: hyponatraemia due to heart failure, cirrhosis or SIADH; in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease it slows kidney enlargement and loss of function. Too rapid correction of hyponatraemia must be avoided. Thirst and dry mouth are the most frequent side effects; others are fever, GI upset and hyperglycaemia. Liver test abnormalities occurred in 9% at the high doses used for polycystic kidney disease. It is a CYP3A4 substrate, so avoid CYP3A4 inhibitors; given once daily.

back: Chlorpropamide lowers urine volume only in pituitary DI (it sensitises the kidney to ADH); carbamazepine needs high doses with marked adverse effects.

front: How does indomethacin help in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

front: What is the main risk of desmopressin, and how is it limited?
back: Hyponatraemia from water retention and fluid overload; use the minimum effective dose guided by 24-hour urine volume.

back: It is 12 times more potent as an antidiuretic, has negligible vasoconstrictor activity and acts for 8-12 hours.

Thiazides reduce urine volume in nephrogenic and pituitary diabetes insipidus; they are the only drugs effective in nephrogenic DI

sections.h: Calcium and brain or eye pressure

front: Which antitussive is the standard reference drug, and how does it act?
back: Codeine (methylmorphine) is the reference antitussive: more selective for the cough centre than morphine, it suppresses cough for about 6 hours, and naloxone blocks this, showing an opioid-receptor action in the brain. The antitussive dose is lower than the analgesic dose. Constipation is the main drawback; abuse liability is low but real. It depresses breathing at higher doses, so avoid it in asthma, poor respiratory reserve and children. About 10% is O-demethylated to morphine by CYP2D6; ultra-rapid metabolisers get unexpectedly high morphine levels (dangerous via breast milk), while poor metabolisers get little analgesia. Morphine itself is unsuitable because of addiction and respiratory depression.

front: Noscapine: what kind of antitussive is it, and what is the caution in asthma?
back: A non-narcotic opium alkaloid of the benzoisoquinoline series. Its antitussive potency is close to codeine, but it has no narcotic, analgesic or dependence-producing action; it is especially useful in spasmodic cough. It can release histamine, so it may provoke bronchoconstriction in asthmatics. Headache and nausea occur occasionally.

front: How does bromhexine act as a mucolytic, and what is its active metabolite?
back: It depolymerises mucopolysaccharide chains directly and also by releasing lysosomal enzymes, which breaks up the fibre network of tenacious sputum. It is derived from vasicine, an alkaloid of Adhatoda vasica. Its metabolite ambroxol has a similar action.

text: Opioid antitussives: {{codeine}} is the standard; {{morphine}} is most effective but unsuitable. Nonopioid central agents: {{noscapine}}, {{dextromethorphan}} and {{chlophedianol}}. Peripheral agent: {{prenoxdiazine}}, which desensitises pulmonary stretch receptors.

front: Dextromethorphan: mechanism, advantages over codeine and important interaction
back: A synthetic central antitussive that blocks NMDA receptors and does not act on mu-opioid receptors; the d-isomer is antitussive (the l-isomer is analgesic). It is about as potent as codeine against cough but has no analgesic action, does not impair mucociliary function and hardly constipates, with fewer GI and subjective side effects. Though regarded as non-addicting, it is abused by some. Side effects: dizziness, nausea, drowsiness. It inhibits neuronal serotonin uptake, so it must be avoided with MAO inhibitors (serotonin syndrome). Not advised below 6 years.

front: When is an antitussive justified, and why should a productive cough not be suppressed?
back: Justified for dry, non-productive cough, or when cough disturbs sleep or is hazardous (hernia, piles, cardiac disease, after eye surgery). A productive cough clears airway secretions, so suppressing it can retain secretions and is harmful.

front: Short note: Management of cough by its cause

points: Upper or lower respiratory tract infection: appropriate antibiotics
Pulmonary tuberculosis: antitubercular drugs
Smoking, chronic bronchitis or bronchiectasis: stop smoking, avoid pollutants, steam inhalation and postural drainage

Eosinophilic lung disease: diethylcarbamazine with inhaled corticosteroid
Postnasal drip from allergic rhinitis or sinusitis: antihistamine, nasal steroid, decongestant or antibiotic as indicated
Avoid the precipitating allergen
Gastro-oesophageal reflux: head-of-bed elevation, light dinner, H2 blocker or proton pump inhibitor
ACE inhibitor cough: switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker
Post-viral cough needs no specific treatment and subsides by itself

Non-productive or troublesome cough is the target for suppression

front: Compare salmeterol and formoterol as long-acting beta-2 agonists.
back: Both last about 12 hours and are given twice daily for maintenance. Salmeterol is a partial agonist with a slower onset, so it is not used for relief; its long aliphatic side chain is thought to anchor it near the receptor. Formoterol is an almost full agonist with a rapid onset, so combined with an inhaled corticosteroid it can also be used as the reliever. In asthma a LABA must never be used alone, because it does not treat inflammation and may increase the risk of life-threatening and fatal attacks; it is given with an ICS, preferably in one combination inhaler.

points: Stimulate beta-2 receptors, raising cAMP in bronchial smooth muscle and relaxing it; also inhibit mediator release
Selective beta-2 agents cause fewer cardiac effects than isoprenaline or adrenaline
Salbutamol and terbutaline: onset within minutes, action 2 to 4 hours
Relievers, used as required; not for regular use
Salmeterol: slower onset, partial agonist, about 12 hours, twice daily
Formoterol: rapid onset, near-full agonist, about 12 hours; can be used as reliever with an ICS

front: Why should inhaled salbutamol not be used on a regular schedule?
back: Inhaled salbutamol acts within minutes and lasts only 2 to 4 hours, so it is a reliever, to be used as required by symptoms rather than on a regular schedule. Regular use can lead to receptor down-regulation and tolerance and may worsen bronchial hyperreactivity; rising use signals that more anti-inflammatory therapy is needed. GG14 notes that ICS-formoterol is now recommended as the rescue bronchodilator of choice because it avoids the dangers of SABA overuse.

front: What are the main mechanisms by which theophylline helps asthma and COPD?
back: Non-selective, weak inhibition of phosphodiesterases (PDE3 and PDE4 matter most), which raises cAMP and relaxes bronchial muscle and damps inflammatory cells. It also blocks adenosine receptors, and adenosine A1 blockade is implicated in toxic arrhythmias and seizures. At low concentrations it may enhance histone deacetylation, which suppresses inflammatory gene transcription.

front: What is aminophylline, and what are the rules for giving it parenterally?
back: Water-soluble theophylline-ethylenediamine salt (about 85% theophylline). Give slowly IV only, never IM or SC because it is highly irritating. Do not mix it in the same infusion with several drugs, e.g. ascorbic acid, chlorpromazine, phenytoin, penicillin G.

front: Besides asthma and COPD, what is theophylline used for, and what is the alternative?
back: Apnoea of prematurity: it reduces the frequency and duration of apnoeic episodes in preterm infants, with closely monitored oral or IV use for 1-3 weeks. Caffeine is equally effective.

front: Why does theophylline have a narrow safety margin and non-linear kinetics?
back: The safety margin is narrow: dose-related toxicity begins in the upper part of the therapeutic range (KDT: 5 to 20 µg/mL; GG14 now regards 5 to 15 mg/L as therapeutic, since anti-inflammatory benefit occurs below 10 mg/L). Metabolism, mainly by CYP1A2, is saturable, so at higher doses kinetics change from first to zero order, the half-life lengthens (up to about 60 hours) and plasma levels rise out of proportion to dose. Clearance varies widely between patients (age, smoking, heart failure, liver disease, interacting drugs), so only sustained-release preparations are used, to avoid high peaks.

front: Name drugs that lower and drugs that raise theophylline levels, and the dose response for each.
back: Lower (CYP1A2 inducers): smoking, phenytoin, rifampicin, phenobarbitone; the dose must be increased. Raise (CYP inhibitors): erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives, allopurinol; the dose is reduced to about two-thirds. Theophylline itself potentiates furosemide, sympathomimetics, digitalis, oral anticoagulants and hypoglycaemics, and reduces the effects of phenytoin and lithium.

text: CYP1A2 inducers such as {{smoking}}, {{phenytoin}} and {{rifampicin}} lower theophylline levels, so the dose must rise. Inhibitors such as {{erythromycin}}, {{ciprofloxacin}} and {{cimetidine}} raise levels, so the dose is cut to about {{two-thirds}}.

front: What is the role of inhaled corticosteroids in asthma, and when do they act?
back: Inhaled corticosteroids suppress bronchial inflammation and hyperreactivity, improve peak flow, reduce the need for rescue beta-2 agonist and prevent acute episodes. They have no role during an acute attack or status asthmaticus. Peak effect is seen after 4 to 7 days (KDT), though maximal effect on airway hyperresponsiveness may take several weeks or months (GG14); benefit persists for a few weeks after stopping. GINA recommends ICS for all asthmatics, however mild, at least on an as-needed basis with each bronchodilator dose. Systemic effects are clinically relevant only above about 600 µg/day (KDT).

front: Montelukast and zafirlukast: mechanism, role and limitations.
back: Competitive antagonists at the cysLT1 receptor, reducing bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular leakage and eosinophil recruitment. Taken orally. Used as alternative or add-on controllers in mild-to-moderate asthma, particularly aspirin-induced and exercise-induced asthma; they are less effective than even low-dose ICS and are not for acute attacks or COPD. Generally well tolerated, but headache and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis are reported, and montelukast now carries an FDA black-box warning for serious neuropsychiatric events, including suicidal thoughts.

front: Sodium cromoglycate: mechanism, uses and why it fails in an acute attack.
back: A chromone that stops mast cells degranulating, limiting release of histamine, leukotrienes and PAF. It is not a bronchodilator and does not block constrictor agonists, so it is useless during an attack. Oral absorption is negligible, so it is inhaled, and benefit takes 2 to 4 weeks. Used prophylactically in extrinsic and exercise-induced asthma, and in allergic rhinitis and conjunctivitis.

front: Classify: leukotriene and mast cell pharmacology
text: Cysteinyl leukotrienes act on the {{cysLT1}} receptor; {{zileuton}} blocks {{5-lipoxygenase}} but is limited by {{hepatotoxicity}}; cromoglycate {{stabilises}} mast cells and is {{not}} a bronchodilator.

front: Omalizumab: what is it, how does it work, and in which patients is it used?
back: A humanised monoclonal antibody against IgE, given subcutaneously every 2 to 4 weeks; the dose is set by the circulating total IgE level. It neutralises free IgE, so little is left to bind the high-affinity receptor (FcεRI) on mast cells, and mediator release on allergen challenge falls; it also lowers FcεRI expression and circulating IgE. Used in severe allergic (extrinsic) asthma, where it reduces exacerbations, including virus-induced ones, and steroid needs. No benefit in non-allergic asthma; very expensive.

front: Roflumilast: mechanism, use and adverse effects
back: An oral PDE4 inhibitor given once daily, converted by CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 to the more active N-oxide metabolite; it exerts an anti-inflammatory action mainly in the lungs rather than direct bronchodilation. Used as add-on therapy in severe COPD (FEV1 below 50%) with chronic bronchitis and frequent exacerbations, reducing exacerbations by about 20% with little effect on symptoms; not approved for asthma. Adverse effects: diarrhoea (commonest), nausea, headache, weight loss and psychiatric disturbances. CYP inhibitors raise and rifampicin lowers its levels; contraindicated in severe liver impairment (Child-Pugh B or C).

front: Classify: aerosol particle size and deposition
text: Particles of {{1 to 5 micrometres}} reach the bronchioles; larger particles settle in the {{oropharynx}}; very fine particles are {{exhaled}}. Only about {{10 percent}} of an inhaled dose reaches the site of action. A {{spacer}} lets larger particles settle out, reducing swallowed dose and {{candidiasis}}.

front: Why is a large-volume spacer used with a metered dose inhaler, especially for inhaled steroids?
back: It removes the need to coordinate actuation with inspiration. Large particles settle on the spacer walls instead of the throat, so less drug is swallowed, and oropharyngeal candidiasis and systemic exposure fall.

back: Recent evidence shows aminophylline adds no extra benefit and may cause more adverse effects, so it is kept for resistant cases. Inhaled drug may not reach narrowed, mucus-plugged small bronchi, so SC/IM salbutamol or terbutaline can be added.

front: Is bronchial asthma mainly bronchospasm or inflammation, and how do extrinsic and intrinsic types differ?
back: Asthma is now seen as chiefly an inflammatory disease with airway hyperreactivity, which is why anti-inflammatory preventers are central. Extrinsic (allergic) asthma is episodic and rarely goes into status asthmaticus; intrinsic asthma is perennial and status asthmaticus is more frequent.

front: Name the three waves of mediator release in asthma and what they do together.
back: Granule release (immediate): histamine, proteases, TNF. Membrane phospholipid products (minutes): prostaglandins, leukotrienes, PAF. Gene activation (hours): interleukins, TNF. Together they constrict bronchial muscle, cause mucosal oedema and viscid secretions, giving reversible airway obstruction.

front: Short note: Stepwise pharmacological management of asthma

points: Treatment is matched to severity and level of control; step up for poor control

Step 2, mild persistent: regular low-dose ICS (leukotriene antagonist or theophylline less satisfactory)
Step 3, moderate: low-dose ICS plus LABA, or medium-dose ICS alone
Step 4, severe: high-dose ICS plus LABA, with leukotriene antagonist or SR theophylline added
Step 5: oral corticosteroid, at the lowest dose, with attempts to withdraw

front: Why is ICS-formoterol now preferred over a SABA alone as the reliever in asthma?
back: Formoterol has a rapid onset, so unlike salmeterol it can relieve symptoms, and each reliever dose of the combination also delivers inhaled corticosteroid when symptoms flare. GG14 states that ICS-formoterol is now recommended as the rescue bronchodilator of choice, being more effective and avoiding the dangers of SABA overuse.

front: Ketotifen: is it a bronchodilator, and what kind of antiallergic is it?
back: It is an H1 antihistamine with some cromoglycate-like action: it reduces activation of mast cells, eosinophils and other inflammatory cells and the release of their mediators. It is not a bronchodilator and is infrequently used now, though it may be tried in patients with multiple allergic disorders. Sedation and dry mouth are common.

front: Why have many new anti-inflammatory COPD drugs given disappointing trial results?
back: Several candidates lowered sputum or lung inflammatory markers without a clear clinical gain, so a biomarker effect does not guarantee benefit to patients.

front: How does a sedative differ from a hypnotic, and where does general anaesthesia fit?
back: A sedative calms and reduces excitement, often with drowsiness but without true sleep, and has a flatter dose-response curve. A hypnotic induces and maintains sleep that resembles normal arousable sleep, with quicker onset, shorter action and a steeper dose-response curve. Sedation, hypnosis and general anaesthesia are increasing grades of CNS depression, and the drugs overlap; a hypnotic given at high dose can produce anaesthesia.

front: Describe the normal sleep cycle: its stages and approximate length.
back: Non-REM stages 1 to 4 are followed by REM sleep, and the cycle repeats every 80 to 100 minutes. Stage 2 is the largest share of sleep (about 40 to 50%). Stages 3 and 4 together form slow-wave sleep. REM sleep is about 20 to 30% of sleep, with irregular breathing, fluctuating heart rate, dreaming and full muscle relaxation.

text: Stage {{2}} forms the largest share of sleep (about {{40 to 50%}}), stages {{3 and 4}} together are called {{slow-wave sleep}}, and {{REM}} sleep takes about {{20 to 30%}} of the night.

front: How do barbiturates act on the GABA-A receptor, and how does this differ from benzodiazepines?
back: Barbiturates bind a site on the GABA-A chloride channel complex that is separate from the benzodiazepine site. They prolong the time the channel stays open, whereas benzodiazepines increase how often it opens. At high concentrations barbiturates can open the chloride channel directly, which benzodiazepines cannot do. This direct effect helps explain the higher depressant ceiling of barbiturates.

front: What happens to sleep on repeated barbiturate use, and what follows withdrawal?
back: Barbiturates shorten sleep onset and reduce night waking, but they suppress REM and deep (stage 3 and 4) sleep and disrupt the REM-NREM cycle. These sleep effects weaken with nightly use. When the drug is stopped after a few nights, REM sleep rebounds with vivid dreams or nightmares, and normal sleep may take several nights to return. Morning hangover is common.

front: Why do thiopentone and phenobarbitone differ so much in duration of action?
back: Duration depends on lipid solubility, redistribution, metabolism and excretion. Thiopentone enters the brain within seconds and redistributes to fat and muscle, so consciousness returns in minutes, although its eventual half-life is about 9 hours. Phenobarbitone enters the CNS slowly, is partly excreted unchanged in urine, and has a half-life of about 80 to 120 hours. Alkalinising the urine increases its excretion.

front: How is acute barbiturate poisoning managed?
back: Supportive care comes first: a patent airway, assisted ventilation, oxygen, fluids and vasopressors if needed, with dopamine preferred for renal perfusion. Gastric lavage with a charcoal suspension left in the stomach limits absorption. Alkaline diuresis helps mainly for long-acting, renally excreted barbiturates. Haemodialysis or haemoperfusion over activated charcoal removes both long- and short-acting drugs. There is no specific antidote.

front: Why are benzodiazepines safer than barbiturates?
back: Benzodiazepines are selective modulators rather than global CNS depressants, so their depression has a lower ceiling. Even large overdoses usually leave consciousness and breathing largely intact, whereas barbiturate overdose causes coma and respiratory failure. They also distort sleep architecture less, cause less rebound and dependence, and do not induce hepatic enzymes the way barbiturates do.

front: Classify the drugs acting at the benzodiazepine site: agonist, inverse agonist and antagonist.
back: Agonists such as diazepam increase GABA-induced chloride influx and produce sedation and anxiolysis. Inverse agonists such as DMCM reduce GABA action and are convulsant. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist that blocks both, so it reverses both sedative and convulsant effects at this site. Picrotoxin blocks the chloride channel directly rather than acting at the benzodiazepine site.

front: Flumazenil: what is its profile and main uses?
back: It is a benzodiazepine analogue with little intrinsic activity of its own. It acts within seconds after IV injection and lasts 1 to 2 hours, with an elimination half-life of about 1 hour, so resedation can occur. It is not given orally. Uses are reversal of benzodiazepine sedation after anaesthesia or procedures, and as an adjunct in benzodiazepine overdose alongside supportive care. It also reverses the hypnotic effect of zolpidem-type drugs.

front: Why are zolpidem, zaleplon and eszopiclone called non-benzodiazepine hypnotics?
back: They are chemically unrelated to benzodiazepines but act at benzodiazepine receptors that contain the alpha-1 subunit, which mediates hypnosis and amnesia. Because they lack meaningful anxiolytic, muscle relaxant and anticonvulsant action, their hypnotic effect is more selective. They have lower abuse potential, and their hypnotic action is reversed by flumazenil.

front: What are the roles of melatonin and ramelteon in sleep disorders?
back: Melatonin acts on MT1 and MT2 receptors to set the timing of the sleep-wake cycle. Low doses (2 to 10 mg) mainly shift the propensity to sleep, which helps jet lag, shift work and delayed sleep phase syndrome, but it is not a dependable hypnotic. Ramelteon is a selective MT1/MT2 agonist taken about 30 minutes before bed for sleep-onset insomnia. It has no GABA action and no benzodiazepine-type effects, and CYP inhibitors such as fluvoxamine raise its levels.

Long-acting drugs and those with active metabolites accumulate on nightly use and cause next-morning impairment. Choose by pharmacokinetic profile, use the lowest effective dose and keep the course short.

front: What is the typical presentation and EEG pattern of absence seizures?
back: Brief episodes, usually in children, lasting about half a minute. The child stares and freezes with no or only momentary loss of consciousness and no fall. The EEG shows a generalised 3 per second spike-and-wave pattern. Several episodes may occur daily, and seizures often remit in adolescence.

front: What are the key rules for starting and stopping antiseizure therapy?
back: Start early with a single drug at low dose, raise gradually, and switch gradually, lowering the old drug as the new one is raised. front: How does phenytoin block seizures at the cellular level?
back: It prolongs the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels, which limits high-frequency repetitive firing while leaving normal low-frequency activity largely unchanged. At therapeutic levels it does not alter resting membrane potential or normal synaptic transmission. Its effects on glutamate release and calcium entry need higher concentrations, so their contribution is uncertain.

front: List the chronic adverse effects of phenytoin.
back: Gum hypertrophy is the commonest, more common in younger patients, and oral hygiene reduces it. Others are hirsutism, coarsening of facial features, acne, rashes or lupus-like reactions, and rarely neutropenia. Long-term use can cause megaloblastic anaemia through folate malabsorption and osteomalacia through impaired vitamin D activation. Exposure in pregnancy can cause foetal hydantoin syndrome.

text: Phenytoin is hydroxylated by {{CYP2C9 and 2C19}} with {{capacity-limited}} kinetics; its therapeutic range is about {{10 to 20 mcg/ml}}, and its half-life can rise to about {{60 hours}} at higher levels.

front: Why does phenytoin plasma level rise disproportionately with small dose increments?
back: Its hepatic hydroxylation (mainly CYP2C9 and 2C19) is capacity limited, so clearance shifts from first-order to zero-order over the therapeutic range. Once levels exceed about 10 mcg/ml, the half-life lengthens from 12 to 24 hours towards about 60 hours. Small dose increases then produce large rises in concentration, so plasma level monitoring guides dosing.

back: Overdose gives cerebellar and vestibular signs (ataxia, vertigo, diplopia, nystagmus), then drowsiness, confusion, hallucinations and rigidity, plus epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting. i.v. phenytoin sodium injures the vein (intimal damage, thrombosis, limb oedema, necrosis if it leaks) and can cause hypotension and arrhythmias, so ECG monitoring is needed.

front: Which drug is the first choice for trigeminal neuralgia, and why does it work?
back: Carbamazepine. It selectively reduces high-frequency nerve firing that drives the temporal summation of pain impulses, so it has an almost diagnostic effect in these neuralgias, unlike a general analgesic. About 60% of patients respond well. Phenytoin, lamotrigine and baclofen are less effective alternatives, and gabapentin may be tried in non-responders. It is not useful for diabetic or other neuropathic pain.

front: What are the mechanisms and spectrum of valproate?
back: Valproate is broad spectrum. It prolongs sodium channel inactivation in a frequency-dependent way, weakly reduces the T-type calcium current, raises brain GABA by inhibiting its breakdown and possibly by increasing synthesis, and blocks NMDA-type glutamate receptors. It is the drug of choice for absence, myoclonic and atonic seizures, and a first-line drug for generalised tonic-clonic and partial seizures.

front: What are the key features of lamotrigine?
back: It is a broad-spectrum drug with a carbamazepine-like profile: it prolongs sodium channel inactivation and may reduce the release of glutamate and aspartate. It is used for partial and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, and also for absence and myoclonic seizures. Valproate doubles its level by inhibiting glucuronidation, so the dose should be halved when valproate is added; lamotrigine in turn lowers valproate levels. A severe rash, especially in children, requires withdrawal.

text: {{Phenytoin}}, {{carbamazepine}}, {{oxcarbazepine}}, {{lamotrigine}} and {{lacosamide}} act mainly by prolonging sodium channel inactivation, whereas {{ethosuximide}} acts on T-type calcium current.

front: Which seizure types can carbamazepine worsen, and why does that limit its use?
back: It can exacerbate myoclonic, absence and atonic seizures. It is the most effective drug for complex partial seizures and widely used for tonic-clonic and simple partial ones, so the seizure type must be identified before choosing it.

front: What happens to carbamazepine's half-life with chronic use, and which drugs does it affect?
back: Its half-life falls from 20 to 40 hours at first to about 10 to 20 hours on chronic use, because it induces its own metabolism. It is oxidised to an active 10,11-epoxide and is an inducer of CYP3A4 and 2C9. It lowers levels of valproate, lamotrigine, oral contraceptives and haloperidol, and phenytoin and phenobarbitone induce it in turn. Erythromycin, fluoxetine and isoniazid raise its levels.

front: What are the serious risks of valproate?
back: Fulminant hepatitis is rare but serious and occurs mainly in children below 3 years, especially those with liver disease, on other antiseizure drugs or on other hepatotoxic drugs; liver function should be monitored. Given in pregnancy it has caused spina bifida and other neural tube defects, so it should be avoided. Concurrent carbamazepine raises the risk of foetal abnormalities. Concurrent clonazepam is contraindicated because absence status may be precipitated.

front: What are the mechanism and main uses of gabapentin and pregabalin?
back: They are GABA derivatives that do not act at GABA-A receptors. They modulate calcium channels containing the alpha-2-delta subunit, which may reduce glutamate release, and gabapentin may also enhance GABA release. They are add-on drugs for partial seizures. Gabapentin is first-line for neuralgic pain, such as diabetic neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia. Gabapentin has no drug interactions and is excreted unchanged in urine, with a half-life of about 6 hours.

front: How do tiagabine and vigabatrin each raise GABA activity?
back: Tiagabine blocks the GAT-1 transporter that clears released GABA into neurones and glia, so GABA lingers in the synapse. Vigabatrin inhibits GABA-transaminase, the enzyme that degrades GABA, so GABA levels rise. Both are add-on drugs for partial seizures; vigabatrin is also used in infantile spasms.

front: Why is topiramate called a broad-spectrum antiseizure drug, and what are its notable adverse effects?
back: It acts by several mechanisms: prolongs Na+ channel inactivation, potentiates GABA postsynaptically, blocks certain glutamate receptors and hyperpolarises via K+ channels, so it works in partial, generalised tonic-clonic and some myoclonic or absence seizures. It is also a weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. Adverse effects: poor attention and memory, word-finding difficulty, sedation, ataxia, weight loss, paraesthesias, renal stones. It is also approved for migraine prophylaxis.

front: Explain the mechanism and interaction profile of levetiracetam.
back: It binds the synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, which may alter release of glutamate and GABA, and it inhibits N-type calcium channels. It is not oxidised by CYP enzymes and does not induce or inhibit them, so it has no pharmacokinetic interactions. It is mainly excreted unchanged in urine with a half-life of 6 to 8 hours. Side effects are sleepiness, dizziness, weakness and occasional behavioural change. It is not approved below 4 years.

front: What is the first-choice drug for status epilepticus, and what is the dose?
back: IV lorazepam, 0.1 mg/kg (about 4 mg in adults), injected at no more than 2 mg/min. It can be repeated once after 10 minutes if needed. It controls seizures in 75 to 90% of cases with a sustained effect of 6 to 12 hours, because it is less lipid soluble and redistributes more slowly than diazepam. Thrombophlebitis is also less likely. The airway, glucose and oxygenation should be secured at the same time.

front: How is status epilepticus defined, and why is it an emergency?
back: Seizure activity lasting over 30 min, or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness in between. Repeated tonic-clonic convulsions can cause death and permanent brain damage, so fits must be stopped as fast as possible after airway and general support.

front: Why is fosphenytoin preferred over phenytoin for intravenous use?
back: Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug converted to phenytoin in the body. It causes less intimal injury, can be infused faster (150 mg/min), and can be given in saline or glucose, unlike phenytoin, which precipitates in glucose. Doses are in phenytoin equivalents and ECG monitoring is still needed.

front: Why is diazepam used for emergency seizures but not for long-term epilepsy?
back: Diazepam is strongly anticonvulsant and acts fast, so it is first line for emergency convulsions (status epilepticus, tetanus, eclampsia, convulsant poisoning). Long-term use is limited by sedation and rapid tolerance to the antiepileptic effect; slow IV injection can cause thrombophlebitis.

front: Why is lorazepam better suited than diazepam for status epilepticus?
back: Diazepam is rapidly redistributed, so its effect is less sustained; it also causes more local thrombophlebitis. Lorazepam is less lipid soluble and redistributes slowly, giving more sustained action (about 6 to 12 h) and less thrombophlebitis, so it is the first-choice benzodiazepine in status epilepticus. Diazepam remains a first-line drug for emergency convulsions generally (tetanus, eclampsia, convulsant poisoning).

front: How is melatonin made in the pineal gland?
back: From serotonin, by N-acetylation followed by O-methylation. It is secreted mainly at night and entrains the sleep-wake cycle to the circadian rhythm.
A newer antiseizure drug for partial-onset seizures in adults, as monotherapy or add-on. It acts mainly through sodium channel effects and reduces focal seizures in a dose-dependent way.

front: Which amino acids are the inhibitory neurotransmitters of the CNS?
back: GABA is the main one. Glycine is the other fast inhibitory amino acid; taurine and beta-alanine also act as inhibitory amino acids. GABA and glycine both open chloride channels.

front: Where does glycine act as an inhibitory transmitter?
back: Mainly in the spinal cord and medulla, where it opens chloride channels. One site is the Renshaw cell to motoneurone junction, which inhibits antagonist muscles.

front: Which general anaesthetics and sedatives enhance glycine-mediated inhibition?
back: Barbiturates, propofol and many inhalational anaesthetics. They augment glycine-mediated inhibition; ketamine and N2O do not act on glycine or GABA-A channels.

front: How does GABA-B activation differ from GABA-A activation?
back: GABA-A is a fast chloride channel. GABA-B is a metabotropic G-protein receptor: it opens K+ channels and closes presynaptic Ca2+ channels, so it slows the neurone and cuts transmitter release. Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist.

front: What is the difference between toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics?
back: Toxicokinetics is the absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion of toxins or toxic doses of drugs and their metabolites; toxicodynamics is their injurious effect on body functions. Both resemble, but can differ importantly from, ordinary pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.

front: What are the common ways poisoned patients die?
back: CNS depression with loss of airway reflexes and respiratory drive (airway obstruction, aspiration, apnoea: opioids, sedatives); cardiovascular toxicity (hypotension, arrhythmias); cellular hypoxia despite oxygen (cyanide, hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide); seizures, rigidity and hyperthermia with rhabdomyolysis; delayed organ damage (paraquat lung fibrosis, acetaminophen or mushroom liver necrosis); and trauma from behavioural effects.

front: Define hazard and risk in toxicology.
back: Hazard is the capacity of a chemical to cause injury in a given setting, judged from its inherent toxicity and the likely exposure; it is often a subjective estimate. Risk is the expected frequency of an undesirable effect from exposure, estimated by extrapolating dose-response data to real exposure levels.

front: What is the therapeutic index and margin of safety in toxicology terms?
back: Therapeutic index = LD50/ED50 in animals, or TD50/ED50 in humans (TD50 = dose toxic to 50%). Margin of safety = LD1/ED99. Low-TI drugs such as digoxin and anticancer agents need caution and drug monitoring; high-TI drugs such as penicillin are relatively safe.

front: Why does volume of distribution matter in a poisoned patient? Give examples.
back: A large Vd means the toxin sits in tissues and cannot be removed by blood-cleansing methods like haemodialysis. Large Vd (>5 L/kg): antidepressants, antipsychotics, antimalarials, opioids, propranolol, verapamil. Small Vd (<1 L/kg), more accessible: salicylate, acetaminophen, ethanol, phenobarbital, lithium, valproate, phenytoin.

front: How does overdose alter a drug's pharmacokinetics?
back: Slow tablet dissolution or gastric emptying can delay peak toxicity; a corrosive poison may increase absorption by injuring the gut wall; saturated hepatic metabolism reduces first-pass effect; saturated protein binding raises the free fraction; and saturated elimination shifts first-order to zero-order kinetics, prolonging apparent half-life.

front: Case: a tablet overdose patient looks well at 1 h but deteriorates later. Using kinetics, why, and how does Vd guide whether dialysis will help?
back: Overdose can slow absorption, so peak toxicity may come late. Haemodialysis helps only some poisons: Katzung lists lithium, salicylate, phenobarbital, valproate and theophylline as dialysable, and antidepressants, propranolol and opioids as not useful. Large volume of distribution (tricyclics) means little drug is in plasma to clear.

front: Which poisons cause a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis?
back: Anion gap = (Na + K) - (HCO3 + Cl), normally 12-16 mEq/L (8-12 without K). Organic acid metabolites: methanol, ethylene glycol, diethylene glycol. Lactic acidosis: cyanide, carbon monoxide, ibuprofen, isoniazid, metformin, salicylates, valproate, and any seizures, hypoxia or hypotension. Iron also causes it.

front: What is the osmol gap and which poisons raise it?
back: Measured minus calculated serum osmolality (calculated from Na, glucose and BUN; normal 280-290 mOsm/L). Unmeasured osmoles raise the gap: ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol, isopropyl alcohol, acetone, propylene glycol.

front: What are the limits of toxicology screening?
back: Rapid urine drugs-of-abuse screens cover few drug classes and give false positives and negatives; comprehensive screens are slow and costly; many dangerous drugs (calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, isoniazid) are not detected; and a positive screen shows exposure but not time or amount. Clinical examination with routine labs usually suffices; quantitative levels (acetaminophen, salicylate, lithium, theophylline, methanol) guide antidotes or dialysis.

front: What is the current status of induced emesis and gastric lavage?
back: Syrup of ipecac (emetine, cephaeline) is ineffective, no longer recommended and no longer made in the USA. Gastric emptying removes only about a third of a dose even under ideal conditions; lavage risks oesophageal or gastric trauma, aspiration and vagal stimulation, so it is reserved for unusual cases on toxicologist advice and only with a protected airway.

text: Dialysis may help in poisoning with {{lithium}}, {{salicylate}}, {{methanol}} and ethylene glycol, theophylline, metformin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and valproate. It is not useful for {{tricyclic antidepressants}}, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, calcium channel blockers, {{digoxin}}, opioids and propranolol, mainly because of large Vd.

front: Which bedside clues suggest a corrosive or hydrocarbon poisoning?
back: Burns around the mouth suggest a corrosive substance; a hydrocarbon odour on the breath suggests a hydrocarbon solvent. A chest radiograph may show hydrocarbon pneumonia.
Kerosene or petroleum, corrosive acids or alkalis, and CNS stimulants. Emesis is also avoided in comatose or haemodynamically unstable patients, or those with an inadequate gag reflex.

front: Does activated charcoal adsorb hydrocarbons and organic solvents?
back: No. Strong acids and alkalis, metallic salts, iodine, cyanide, caustics, alcohol, hydrocarbons and other organic solvents are not adsorbed by charcoal. Charcoal is also withheld in paralytic ileus or intestinal obstruction.

front: Which supportive measures are used in phosphide poisoning?
back: Mechanical ventilation, organ support, vasoactive drugs, and correction of electrolyte and glucose abnormalities.

front: Where should phosphide-poisoned patients be managed, and why?
back: In an ICU, because of the high risk of multi-organ failure and death.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

front: What is the first step after inhaling phosphine?
back: Move the person away from the source and give supplemental oxygen if needed.

back: Amphetamines, antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, metoprolol, propranolol, opioids.

front: Activated charcoal: how does it work and what does it not bind?
back: Its huge porous surface adsorbs many poisons; aim for at least 10:1 charcoal to toxin by weight. It does not bind iron, lithium or potassium, binds alcohols and cyanide poorly, and is not useful for corrosive acids or alkalis. Repeated doses can enhance elimination of carbamazepine, dapsone and phenobarbital (gut dialysis) by interrupting enterohepatic cycling and drawing drug back into the gut.

front: Whole bowel irrigation: what is it and when is it used?
back: Oral or nasogastric iso-osmotic polyethylene glycol-electrolyte solution given until the rectal effluent is clear. Used for iron, sustained-release or enteric-coated tablets, drug packets in body packers and drug patches. Contraindicated with bowel perforation or obstruction, ileus, uncontrolled vomiting, an unprotected airway or GI bleeding.

front: When is urinary pH manipulated in poisoning?
back: Alkalinisation with IV sodium bicarbonate ion-traps weak acids: salicylate (first-line only for moderate poisoning not needing dialysis), phenobarbital, chlorpropamide. Acidifying urine for amphetamines or phencyclidine is not advised as it worsens renal injury from rhabdomyolysis. Forced diuresis is unproven and risks fluid overload.

front: Why is gastric lavage controversial in phosphide poisoning?
back: It may increase phosphine release and toxicity. Staff are also at risk, because phosphine can escape from vomit and faeces.

front: What role does activated charcoal play in metal phosphide ingestion?
back: It is described as beneficial for reducing toxicity. Evidence for coconut oil and potassium permanganate lavage is lacking.

front: Is there a specific antidote for phosphide poisoning?
back: No. None is known, so treatment is mainly supportive, usually in an ICU.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

front: What is the evidence for N-acetylcysteine in phosphide poisoning?
back: Used in some regimens for phosphide-related acute liver failure. A mortality benefit has not been proven.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

front: What is the evidence for pralidoxime in phosphide poisoning?
back: Animal data only so far: rat survival rose at 10 mg/kg of aluminium phosphide. Benefit in humans has not been studied.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

front: When is physostigmine used as an antidote, and when must it not be used?
back: For central and peripheral anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) delirium, given slowly IV with monitoring; effects last only 30-60 min. It can cause bradycardia, bronchial secretions and seizures (keep atropine ready) and must not be used in tricyclic overdose, where it can cause heart block or asystole.

front: Scorpion sting: why is prazosin the drug of choice, and what warning applies to its first dose?
back: Scorpion venom is neurotoxic and cardiotoxic. It can cause hypertension, which prazosin treats; severe cases also get pulmonary oedema. Early in prazosin treatment, marked postural hypotension can occur.

front: Scorpion sting: which drugs control seizures, muscle spasm and hypotension from anaphylaxis?
back: Diazepam for seizures; lignocaine for muscle spasm and pain; intramuscular adrenaline when anaphylaxis causes hypotension.

front: Cobra and krait bite: why does paralysis occur, and what is added for cobra paralysis?
back: Cobra venom is a curare-like neurotoxin that blocks nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing paralysis and respiratory paralysis. Specific antivenom serum is the primary treatment. For cobra paralysis, neostigmine with atropine is added: neostigmine raises acetylcholine to overcome the block, and atropine blocks its muscarinic effects. Krait paralysis is presynaptic and is not expected to respond to edrophonium, so the regimen is for cobra.

front: US rattlesnake envenomation: why should field remedies be avoided, and what is definitive treatment?
back: Incision and suction, tourniquets and ice packs do more harm than good, while avoiding unnecessary movement helps limit the spread of venom. Definitive treatment is early intravenous antivenom.

front: Pralidoxime: benefit in carbamate and organophosphate poisoning?
back: No proven benefit in carbamate poisoning; uncertain benefit in established organophosphate poisoning. Given early, it may restore cholinesterase activity, but studies conflict on clinical outcome.

front: Case: a confused patient has dilated pupils, dry skin and wide QRS after an overdose. Is physostigmine appropriate, and which antidote class fits instead?
back: Anticholinergic delirium alone would justify slow IV physostigmine, but a wide QRS suggests tricyclic overdose, where physostigmine can cause heart block or asystole and must be avoided. Tricyclic cardiotoxicity is treated with sodium bicarbonate.

Red as a beet (flushed), hot as a hare (hyperthermia), dry as a bone (no sweating), blind as a bat (mydriasis, cycloplegia), mad as a hatter (delirium), with sinus tachycardia, ileus and urinary retention. Seizures suggest an antihistamine or tricyclic. Treatment is supportive (benzodiazepine for agitation, bladder catheter), with physostigmine for marked agitation if no tricyclic is involved.

front: Which common plants contain cardiac glycosides with properties similar to digoxin?
back: Oleander, lily of the valley and milkweed, among others. Digoxin itself is obtained from the white foxglove (Digitalis lanata).

front: How soon do features of aluminium or zinc phosphide ingestion usually start?
back: Usually within about 30 minutes. Early features are nausea, vomiting and epigastric pain; garlic-like breath may occur.

front: Antidote preferred to ethanol in methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning?
back: Fomepizole: easier to use; ethanol gives blood levels that are difficult to keep safe.

front: Is haemodialysis useful for opioid overdose?
back: No: opioids are listed as not removed effectively by haemodialysis. Naloxone is the antidote.

front: Why is propranolol the most dangerous beta-blocker in overdose, and what is the antidote?
back: In overdose all beta-blockers lose selectivity; propranolol also blocks Na+ channels (like tricyclics, giving wide QRS and seizures) and is lipophilic, entering the CNS, so even 2-3 times the therapeutic dose can be serious. Fluids, beta agonists and atropine often fail; glucagon raises cardiac cAMP independent of beta-receptors.

front: How is calcium channel blocker overdose managed?
back: Supportive care plus early whole bowel irrigation and charcoal (most are sustained-release) before ileus sets in; IV calcium for depressed contractility; high-dose insulin with glucose, glucagon, methylene blue, veno-arterial ECMO, and lipid emulsion in case reports for severe verapamil toxicity. Verapamil and diltiazem cause bradycardia and shock; dihydropyridines cause vasodilation with reflex tachycardia, but selectivity is lost in massive overdose.

front: Methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning: why toxic and how treated?
back: Both cause drunkenness and an osmol gap, then a delayed severe anion gap acidosis as alcohol dehydrogenase makes toxic acids: formic acid from methanol (blindness) and oxalic and glycolic acids from ethylene glycol (renal failure; oxalate crystals in urine). Treatment: block alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole (or ethanol), and haemodialysis for acidosis or end-organ damage.

Vomiting; hyperkalaemia in acute overdose (hypokalaemia from diuretics worsens chronic toxicity); bradycardia, AV block, atrial tachycardia with block, junctional rhythm, ventricular ectopics and bidirectional VT. Atropine for bradycardia; IV digoxin-specific antibody fragments usually help within 30-60 min and may work for other cardiac glycosides such as oleander.

Tachycardia, tremor, vomiting, hypotension, hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia (beta-2 overactivity), atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, and refractory seizures in severe cases; sustained-release forms delay toxicity. Treat with repeated charcoal, whole bowel irrigation, a beta-blocker such as esmolol for hypotension and tachycardia, and haemodialysis at very high levels or with intractable seizures.

back: Datura (dhatura) poisoning is a form of belladonna poisoning. The plant is a source of atropine, which is D,L-hyoscyamine. Its toxicity is anticholinergic, and physostigmine is the specific antidote.

front: Why are iron-containing multivitamins a poisoning risk in young children?
back: Iron is widely present in over-the-counter vitamins, and as few as 10 to 12 prenatal multivitamin tablets with iron can cause serious illness in a small child.

front: Inhalant abuse: which substances are involved, and how is overdose managed?
back: Recreational inhalation of nitrites, ketones, and aliphatic or aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzene and toluene. Chronic aromatic hydrocarbon exposure causes toxicity in many organs, including white-matter lesions in the CNS. Overdose management is supportive.

front: Organochlorine pesticides: groups, mechanism and toxicity.
back: Groups: DDT and analogues, benzene hexachlorides, cyclodienes, toxaphenes. front: How do carbamate pesticides differ from organophosphates?

front: What does a bacteriostatic drug do when its level falls below the MIC?
back: Bacteria restart multiplying quickly, so infection can relapse. A cidal drug actually cuts the bacterial count and often has a prolonged postantibiotic effect, so levels need not stay above the MIC all the time.

front: What is the postantibiotic effect and how is it measured?
back: After brief exposure, bacteria moved to drug-free medium resume growth only after a lag. That lag is the PAE, taken as the time for a 10-fold rise in count in exposed minus unexposed cultures. It is long and dose dependent with fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides and rifampin.

front: Which bactericidal antibiotics show concentration-dependent killing and which show time-dependent killing?
back: Concentration-dependent: aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones. The rate and extent of killing rise with drug concentration, which (with their long postantibiotic effect) supports once-daily aminoglycoside dosing. Time-dependent: beta-lactams and vancomycin. Killing continues only while the serum level stays above the MBC, so the time above that level is what matters and divided doses are used.

front: Case: neutropenic patient with Pseudomonas infection is given ticarcillin plus gentamicin. Justify the choice.
back: Defences are impaired, so a cidal regimen is needed. Gentamicin kills by concentration, so one daily dose works better than split doses, whereas the beta-lactam depends on time above MIC, so splitting its dose helps.

front: How do natural resistance and acquired resistance differ?
back: Natural resistance is a trait of a whole species or group, for example gram-negative bacilli and penicillin G, or anaerobes and aminoglycosides; it rarely matters clinically. Acquired resistance develops in a previously sensitive strain after drug exposure and is a major clinical problem.

front: Contrast vertical and horizontal transfer of resistance.
back: Vertical transfer is selection of pre-existing mutants when the drug kills sensitive cells; it is slow and usually low grade, as with a single anti-TB drug. Horizontal transfer moves resistance genes between bacteria by conjugation (plasmids and R factors), transduction by phage, or transformation. It is fast and can spread multidrug resistance at once.

front: Name the three mechanistic types of drug-resistant bacteria.
back: Drug tolerant: the target changes so the drug binds poorly (for example altered RNA polymerase or penicillin-binding proteins). Drug destroying: an enzyme inactivates the drug (beta-lactamases, aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes). Drug impermeable: less drug gets in, through lost porins or active efflux pumps.
