Effective even in lamivudine-resistant disease; resistance rare
Watch renal function: creatinine rise is common
Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) 25 mg daily: as effective as TDF with less loss of bone density and kidney function (GG14)
Current first-line option; faster viral fall than lamivudine
Resistance rare, mainly in lamivudine-resistant patients
Least active of the nucleotide analogues; not first-line
Resistance in about 30% of patients
Nephrotoxic at higher doses
Telbivudine: not first-line; resistance frequent, especially after lamivudine resistance
Lamivudine: no longer first-line for HBV because resistance reaches up to 70% in 1 to 5 years
Do not stop abruptly: flare of hepatitis can follow
Continue nucleos(t)ide therapy until about 6 months after seroconversion
Combinations are not superior; drugs are used sequentially

back: A uridine nucleotide analogue prodrug converted in hepatocytes to its triphosphate, which inhibits the HCV NS5B RNA polymerase and terminates the viral RNA chain. Because NS5B is well conserved, it is active against all genotypes; it is always used in combination, e.g. with daclatasvir, ledipasvir or velpatasvir. It is a P-glycoprotein substrate, so avoid P-gp inducers such as rifampin. Severe bradycardia has been reported with amiodarone. GG14 states that there are now no renal restrictions on sofosbuvir-based therapy, as emerging data show it is safe and effective in renal impairment.

front: Why is entecavir taken on an empty stomach?
back: Food decreases its bioavailability; the dose is 0.5 mg OD, or 1.0 mg OD in lamivudine-resistant cases.

front: Essay: Treatment of chronic hepatitis C

points: Sustained viral response (SVR): KDT defines it as undetectable HCV-RNA 6 months after therapy; newer trials report SVR 12 weeks after therapy (SVR12)
Relapse only about 5% once achieved
Peginterferon alpha plus oral ribavirin
Response about 50 to 80%; long course and poor tolerability
NS5B, NS3/4A and NS5A inhibitors
Used in combination; monotherapy causes resistance
Most patients now have at least a 90% chance of SVR; decompensated cirrhosis responds less well
Pangenotypic: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks; glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks in treatment-naive patients
Sofosbuvir with daclatasvir or ledipasvir
Ribavirin added in decompensated cirrhosis and some genotype 3 or cirrhotic patients
Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir is a treatment of choice in renal impairment
Many interactions via P-gp and CYP3A4; potent inducers such as rifampin are avoided
Acid suppressants reduce ledipasvir and velpatasvir absorption

front: Which two viral enzymes are the established drug targets in HIV, and what does each do?
back: Reverse transcriptase, which copies viral RNA into proviral DNA, and protease, which cuts the large viral polyprotein into functional proteins. Newer targets include viral fusion with the CD4 cell, the CCR5 co-receptor and integrase, which inserts proviral DNA into the host genome.

front: Abacavir: main safety issue and what must happen when it occurs
back: A hypersensitivity reaction, potentially fatal, in about 2 to 9% of patients (KDT: 2 to 5%), usually within the first 6 weeks: fever, rash, abdominal pain, GI upset and sometimes respiratory symptoms. Stop immediately and never rechallenge. It is genetically linked to HLA-B*5701, so Katzung advises testing for this allele before starting, and GG14 says abacavir must not be used in carriers. Avoid in patients with cardiovascular risk factors.

front: Emtricitabine: what distinguishes it from lamivudine?
back: A cytidine analogue with a long intracellular half-life of the triphosphate (about 40 hours), so it is dosed once daily. Renally excreted and needs dose adjustment in renal impairment. It is one of the least toxic ARVs and is supplied only as fixed-dose combinations. It must not be combined with lamivudine, and stopping it in HIV-HBV coinfection can cause rebound hepatitis.

front: NNRTIs: mechanism and rules of use
text: NNRTIs bind HIV reverse transcriptase {{non-competitively}} and do not need {{intracellular phosphorylation}}. They act on HIV-1 but not {{HIV-2}}. Resistance appears {{rapidly}} if used alone, so they are always given with two other drugs. Nevirapine and efavirenz show {{cross-resistance}} with each other, but not with NRTIs or PIs.

front: Classify the adverse effects of protease inhibitors
text: PIs cause {{lipodystrophy}} (abdominal fat gain, buffalo hump, limb wasting), {{dyslipidaemia}} and {{insulin resistance}}, plus GI intolerance. Indinavir can crystallise in {{urine}} and cause {{nephrolithiasis}}. Atazanavir can cause {{jaundice}} without liver damage by inhibiting glucuronyl transferase.

front: Zidovudine: mechanism, main toxicity and key interaction
back: A thymidine analogue; after phosphorylation it inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase and terminates the DNA chain. Dose-related anaemia and neutropenia are the main toxicities; myopathy and lactic acidosis are less common. Paracetamol increases its toxicity by competing for glucuronidation. Never used alone.

front: Classify the toxicities of stavudine and didanosine
text: Stavudine causes {{lipodystrophy}}, {{lactic acidosis}} and {{peripheral neuropathy}}, so it is largely avoided. Didanosine's main dose-related toxicity is {{peripheral neuropathy}}, and it does not cause {{myelosuppression}}. Stavudine and zidovudine should not be combined because they compete for the same activation step.

front: Lamivudine: why is it used for both HIV and hepatitis B, and why is it no longer first-line for HBV?
back: It inhibits both HIV reverse transcriptase and HBV DNA polymerase. It is well absorbed, has low systemic toxicity, is mostly excreted unchanged (so usable in hepatic insufficiency) and is an essential part of most first-line HIV triple regimens. For HBV, resistance by point mutation reaches up to about 70% within 1 to 5 years, so it is no longer a first-line HBV drug.

front: Tenofovir disoproxil: why is it widely used, and what should be monitored?
back: It is the only nucleotide (not nucleoside) reverse transcriptase inhibitor in common use and is also active against HBV. It is well tolerated, with few GI side effects, and is in preferred first-line WHO regimens. Monitor renal function: creatinine rise is common and acute or chronic kidney injury is possible. Dose 300 mg daily.

points: Both are enzyme inducers that autoinduce their own metabolism
Nevirapine: 200 mg daily for 2 weeks, then 200 mg twice daily
Efavirenz: no lead-in; long half-life so occasional missed doses are less harmful
Nevirapine: rash (can be severe), fever, transaminase rise; potentially hepatotoxic; avoid in hepatic dysfunction
Efavirenz: headache, dizziness, insomnia, neuropsychiatric effects; gynaecomastia; teratogenicity not confirmed in humans
Rifampin lowers nevirapine levels: switch to efavirenz if TB needs treatment
Efavirenz is metabolised mainly by CYP2B6 and also inhibits CYP3A4
KDT (WHO 2016): efavirenz preferred first-line, including in pregnancy and breastfeeding
Newer texts: dolutegravir is increasingly the preferred starting agent (GG14); efavirenz is an alternative in pregnancy (Katzung16)
Nevirapine is an alternative but avoided with liver disease or rifampin

front: Protease inhibitors: mechanism, and why they act on both new and old infected cells
back: They block the aspartic protease that cleaves the viral polyprotein at the maturation step, so new virions are immature and non-infectious. They do not need intracellular activation, so they work in newly and chronically infected cells. They are not used alone because resistance develops within months.

front: What is ritonavir boosting, and which protease inhibitor is not boosted?
back: Low-dose ritonavir (100 mg) strongly inhibits CYP3A4, raising the partner PI's levels and allowing fewer tablets a day. Nelfinavir is not boosted because it is metabolised mainly by CYP2C19, which ritonavir does not inhibit. Full-dose ritonavir is rarely used as an antiretroviral because of its side effects.

front: Integrase inhibitors (raltegravir, dolutegravir): action and key interactions
back: They block strand transfer, so proviral DNA is not inserted into the host chromosome. Both act on HIV-1 and HIV-2 with no cross-resistance to other classes; dolutegravir also works against some raltegravir-resistant virus and resistance to it is rare. Dolutegravir (50 mg once daily) is increasingly used as a starting agent, often as a generic once-daily tablet with tenofovir and lamivudine. Adverse points (GG14): weight gain; a small, uncertain neural tube defect signal with use at conception; it inhibits renal OCT2, causing a small reversible creatinine rise and doubling metformin levels. Calcium, magnesium and iron products chelate them and should be staggered. With rifampin, give dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily and raltegravir 800 mg twice daily.

front: Enfuvirtide and maraviroc: where each blocks HIV entry and when each is used
back: Enfuvirtide is a synthetic peptide that binds gp41 and blocks fusion of viral and cell membranes; given s.c. twice daily to multidrug-resistant patients with no other option, and causes painful injection-site nodules. Maraviroc blocks the host CCR5 co-receptor, so it works only on CCR5-tropic virus and tropism must be shown first.

front: Short note: Protease inhibitors in HIV therapy

points: Bind the active site of HIV protease and stop it cleaving viral precursor proteins
Act late in the viral cycle, so infected cells release immature, non-infectious virus
Work in newly and chronically infected cells; no intracellular activation needed
Eight in use: atazanavir, indinavir, nelfinavir, saquinavir, ritonavir, lopinavir (only with ritonavir), fosamprenavir and darunavir
Mainly metabolised by CYP3A4; nelfinavir mainly by CYP2C19
Low-dose ritonavir (100 mg) boosts most PIs by blocking their metabolism, which cuts the tablet load; nelfinavir is not boosted
Never given alone: resistance develops within months
Combined with two NRTIs, or one NRTI plus one NNRTI
Kept out of first-line regimens because they limit later options; most guidelines reserve them for failure
GI upset, asthenia, headache, paraesthesia and rash
Lipodystrophy, dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance
Indinavir can crystallise in urine and cause stones

front: PrEP: which drugs are used and who should be offered it?
back: Tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg with emtricitabine 200 mg once daily; KDT cites a meta-analysis showing about a 51% reduction in HIV risk against placebo, and WHO advises offering it to people at high risk (men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, transgender people, and uninfected partners in serodiscordant couples). GG14 adds that tenofovir alafenamide with emtricitabine is also approved, and that long-acting injectable cabotegravir every 8 weeks was more effective than daily oral tenofovir-emtricitabine in prevention trials.

front: PEP: how soon must it start, and what is the regimen after sexual exposure?
back: Start as soon as possible, ideally within 1 to 2 hours. Benefit falls with delay, and it is generally not started beyond 72 hours. After sexual exposure the same regimen as for needle-stick is used; a popular US option is tenofovir plus emtricitabine daily with raltegravir 400 mg twice daily.

front: When should antiretroviral therapy start according to WHO 2016?
back: In all adults, including pregnant and breast-feeding women, adolescents and children, rather than delaying treatment.

front: After failure of first-line ART, what should change and what are the WHO 2016 second-line options?
back: Change the entire failed regimen, not a single drug, and avoid cross-resistant drugs (for example nevirapine for efavirenz, emtricitabine for lamivudine). Use two NRTIs plus one ritonavir-boosted PI. After failure on tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine, use zidovudine plus lamivudine; after failure on zidovudine or stavudine plus lamivudine, use tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine. Preferred boosted PIs are atazanavir or lopinavir.

front: Short note: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV

points: High: source symptomatic with high viral load or low CD4 and not on ART; deep or large-bore needle; visible blood on needle; sexual exposure
Low: source on ART or asymptomatic with low viral load and high CD4; superficial or small exposure
None: source HIV-negative; intact skin; urine, sweat, non-bloody saliva
KDT (WHO 2016) preferred: tenofovir + lamivudine (or emtricitabine), plus lopinavir/r
Alternative third drug: atazanavir/r, darunavir/r, efavirenz or raltegravir
Katzung16: dolutegravir is now used for non-occupational PEP; zidovudine is an NRTI option
Nevirapine is not recommended for PEP in adults or in children over 2 years, because of hepatotoxicity
Course is 4 weeks
Minimum two NRTIs, ideally with a third drug of another class

front: Classify the ARV combinations to avoid

front: What is immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) after starting ART?
back: As ART restores immunity, the recovering immune system can react strongly against residual organisms (e.g. latent TB or other opportunistic infections), causing inflammation and constitutional symptoms.

Two NRTIs plus one NNRTI
Tenofovir + lamivudine (or emtricitabine) + efavirenz
Efavirenz preferred over nevirapine; etravirine reserved for NNRTI failure
Zidovudine-based regimens with efavirenz or nevirapine
Tenofovir or abacavir with lamivudine plus dolutegravir
Dolutegravir-based regimens favoured where cost allows
Treatment is offered to all infected people regardless of CD4 count

Expected outcome: HIV-RNA below 50 copies/mL within 24 weeks
Monotherapy and three-NRTI regimens
Nevirapine with hepatic dysfunction or rifampin
PI-sparing regimens preferred for treatment-naive patients

Watch for IRIS when treating latent opportunistic infection

points: Transmission in utero, during delivery, or by breastfeeding
Highest risk is during the birth process
All HIV-positive women not on ART start standard triple ART
Continue through delivery and into the postnatal period
Benefits the mother's own health too
Tenofovir 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + efavirenz 600 mg as one daily tablet
WHO 2016 keeps efavirenz in the preferred first-line regimen for pregnant and breastfeeding women
Dolutegravir, raltegravir and boosted atazanavir or darunavir are among the agents recommended in pregnancy; efavirenz is an alternative
Nevirapine syrup for 6 weeks
Caesarean section advised if HIV-RNA is above 1000 copies/mL near delivery

front: Maribavir: what is it used for, and what does it spare?
back: Treatment of refractory CMV infection after transplantation. Unlike older anti-CMV agents, it does not cause myelotoxicity or nephrotoxicity, a point it shares with letermovir.

front: Antigenic drift: what it is and why vaccines change each year
back: Small point mutations in the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes that build up during each seasonal epidemic. Because these two proteins are the main targets of protective antibodies, vaccine antigens are updated every year.

front: Antigenic shift: how a new influenza strain arises
back: When two viruses infect one host (for example human and avian), the segmented genome is reassorted, producing a new virus that can cause a pandemic. It is a large change, unlike drift.

front: Neuraminidase: what it does for the virus
back: The viral enzyme that releases progeny virions from the infected cell. When it is blocked, new virions clump at the cell surface and spread in the respiratory tract is reduced.

front: Why have the adamantanes (amantadine, rimantadine) been dropped for influenza?
back: They act only on influenza A, and resistance now affects over 99% of recent circulating viruses (M2 mutation). Neuraminidase and endonuclease inhibitors cover influenza A and B, so they replaced the adamantanes.

front: Oseltamivir resistance: where does the mutation lie, and which drug is the fallback?
back: Mutation of the viral neuraminidase. It has appeared in seasonal influenza A and H5N1, while most 2009 H1N1 strains stay sensitive. Some oseltamivir-resistant strains remain sensitive to zanamivir.

front: Zanamivir resistance: which viral genes change, and what cross-resistance follows?
back: Resistance comes from mutations in the hemagglutinin or the neuraminidase. Hemagglutinin variants are cross-resistant to the other neuraminidase inhibitors. Zanamivir-resistant variants usually show reduced infectivity in animals.

front: Baloxavir: why it is useful when neuraminidase inhibitors fail, and who must not take it
back: It inhibits the viral cap-dependent endonuclease, binds a different site and acts early in replication, so it keeps activity against neuraminidase-inhibitor-resistant viruses. Avoid in immunocompromised patients (resistance risk) and in pregnancy (no data). Separate from antacids, calcium, laxatives and dairy.

front: Oseltamivir in infants: why it may fail
back: Infants may not generate enough of the active metabolite, oseltamivir carboxylate, so the drug can be ineffective in them.

Oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir and baloxavir work best within 48 hours of onset

Amantadine/rimantadine: M2 mutation; over 99% resistance in recent viruses
Oseltamivir: neuraminidase mutation seen in seasonal A and H5N1
Zanamivir: HA or NA mutation; HA variants cross-resistant to all neuraminidase inhibitors

Baloxavir: avoid in immunocompromised and in pregnancy; avoid with cation products
Annual vaccine update, since vaccine efficacy falls with antigenic mismatch
Early prophylaxis after exposure with oseltamivir
Baloxavir may act synergistically with other agents, mainly in uncomplicated infection (GG14)
Resistance, short treatment window and viral variability make influenza hard to control with drugs alone

front: NACO: which Indian body's ART guidelines does KDT8 cite for second-line regimens, and for which year?
back: NACO. KDT8 cites the NACO 2013 ART guidelines.

front: When should ART start, according to WHO 2016 as quoted in KDT8?
back: As soon as HIV is confirmed, whatever the CD4 count, in all adults, pregnant and breastfeeding women, adolescents and children. Earlier NACO and WHO advice delayed start until CD4 fell below 350 cells/mL.

front: What is the aim of ART, and what does a good response look like?
back: Maximal, durable suppression of HIV. Good response: plasma HIV-RNA below 50 copies/mL and CD4 near normal within 6 months. ART cannot eradicate HIV.

front: When is an ART regimen considered to have failed?
back: HIV-RNA not below 50 copies/mL within 6 months; repeated viraemia after suppression; or clinical decline, falling CD4 or serious opportunistic infection on therapy. Failure is due to resistance.

front: NACO 2013: which ritonavir-boosted PI is the first choice for second-line ART?
back: Atazanavir/ritonavir. Next choices: lopinavir/r, saquinavir/r, indinavir/r, then nelfinavir.

front: Fostemsavir: what is it and how does it stop HIV?
back: A prodrug converted to temsavir. Temsavir binds the HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein gp120 and blocks viral attachment and entry. Used in heavily treatment-experienced adults with multidrug-resistant HIV-1.

front: Which chronic hepatitis B drugs are prodrugs?
back: Adefovir dipivoxil (diester prodrug of adefovir), tenofovir disoproxil and tenofovir alafenamide.

front: Why is adefovir still useful despite being a weak HBV drug?
back: It has no cross-resistance with lamivudine or entecavir, so it helps in HBV resistant to those drugs. Slow viral suppression and renal toxicity limit it.

front: SARS-CoV-2 main protease (MPRO, 3CL): what does it do, and what inhibits it?
back: A viral protease that cleaves the viral polyproteins, which is essential for replication. Nirmatrelvir inhibits it.

front: Remdesivir: class and target in SARS-CoV-2
back: Adenosine nucleotide prodrug, phosphorylated to a triphosphate. The SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase incorporates it, causing chain termination.
Oral prodrug of beta-D-N4-hydroxycytidine (NHC). Its triphosphate is taken up by the viral RNA polymerase, causing lethal mutagenesis of SARS-CoV-2.

front: Spike protein as a COVID-19 target: which agents act here?
back: Neutralising monoclonal antibodies against the spike protein. They are parenteral, must be given early, and activity against Omicron subtypes varies; several have been discontinued.

front: Host-directed COVID-19 drugs: what do baricitinib, tocilizumab and anakinra block?
back: Baricitinib blocks Janus kinase (JAK). Tocilizumab blocks the interleukin-6 receptor. Anakinra blocks the interleukin-1 receptor.

front: Why is nirmatrelvir given with ritonavir?
back: Nirmatrelvir is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4. Low-dose ritonavir, a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, raises its concentration and prolongs its half-life to about 6 hours. Many CYP3A-dependent drugs are contraindicated.

front: Generic drug: what is it and why does it matter for prescribing?
back: A product with the same active molecule, dosage form, strength, route and intended use as the reference brand, usually off-patent. Prescribing by generic (non-proprietary) name lowers cost and avoids brand confusion.

front: Cloze: four aims of antimalarial therapy
text: Antimalarial therapy aims at {{prophylaxis}} against clinical attacks, {{clinical cure}} of an attack, {{radical cure}} to remove all parasites from the body, and {{gametocidal}} action to cut transmission to mosquitoes.

front: Why can a drug that kills only blood-stage parasites not fully cure vivax malaria?
back: Blood schizontocides end the clinical attack but do not touch the dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax and ovale, which later cause relapse. A tissue schizontocide such as primaquine is needed for radical cure.

front: Cloze: why a blood schizontocide alone can leave relapse in vivax malaria
text: P. vivax and P. ovale leave {{hypnozoites}} in the liver, so a blood schizontocide alone is followed by {{relapse}}. In falciparum malaria no such tissue stage persists, so clearing the blood adequately is a radical cure.

front: Why are proguanil and pyrimethamine called low-efficacy clinical curatives?
back: They are slow-acting blood schizontocides, too slow to be used alone in a non-immune patient, and parasites quickly develop resistance to them. They are therefore used only in combination, for example sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, for clinical cure.

front: How does chloroquine kill the malaria parasite inside the red cell?
back: As a weak base it concentrates in the parasite's acidic food vacuole and raises its pH, which interferes with haemoglobin digestion. It also blocks conversion of toxic haem into inert haemozoin, so free haem or the haem-drug complex damages the parasite membrane.

text: Chloroquine binds {{tightly}} to melanin and nuclear chromatin, so it concentrates in the {{liver, spleen, kidney and lungs}} and in the {{retina}}. Its terminal half-life can extend to {{1-2 months}}.

front: Name the drug groups in this subtopic and their key weakness or toxicity.
back: Chloroquine: blood schizontocide, long half-life, retinal damage with prolonged use and pfcrt-mediated resistance. Mefloquine: neuropsychiatric effects, QT prolongation, oral only. Quinine: cinchonism, hypoglycaemia, narrow therapeutic index.

front: What is the main mechanism of chloroquine resistance in P. falciparum?
back: A mutant transporter (encoded by the pfcrt gene) in the membrane of the acidic vacuole pumps chloroquine out, so less drug reaches haem. The P-glycoprotein encoded by pfmdr1 contributes and also reduces the activity of quinine and mefloquine.

front: Which drug gives radical cure of vivax malaria, what dose, and what must be checked first?
back: Primaquine, given with a full curative dose of chloroquine (or another blood schizontocide). KDT (Indian programme): 15 mg (0.25 mg/kg) daily for 14 days. GG14 (US CDC regimen): 30 mg base (0.5 mg/kg) daily for 14 days. Test for G6PD deficiency before starting, and give it with food to reduce GI upset.

front: What single primaquine dose is given after falciparum treatment to reduce transmission, and where do national and WHO guidance differ?
back: A single gametocidal dose given with the ACT for falciparum malaria. The Indian national programme in KDT uses 0.75 mg/kg (45 mg in adults) on day 2. WHO recommends a lower single dose of 0.25 mg/kg, and GG14 notes that at this dose G6PD testing is not required; it is given to non-pregnant patients older than 6 months in low-transmission areas. It is added even when an artemisinin is used, because artemisinins do not kill mature gametocytes.

text: Tafenoquine is a long-acting {{8-aminoquinoline}} derived from primaquine, with an elimination half-life of about {{14 days}} (primaquine: 6 to 8 hours). KDT describes it as awaiting approval; GG14 states it is now {{FDA-approved}} for malaria prophylaxis and for radical cure of P. vivax, where a {{single 300 mg dose}} is given with the blood-stage drug. It shares the risk of {{haemolysis in G6PD deficiency}}, so it is contraindicated when G6PD status is deficient or unknown and in pregnancy.

Methaemoglobinaemia, with tachypnoea and cyanosis

front: How do artemisinins act on the parasite?
back: Their endoperoxide bridge is cleaved by iron derived from haem, releasing free radicals that damage parasite membranes and proteins. A parasite calcium pump (PfATP6) is also reported to be inactivated. The result is rapid killing across ring to early schizont stages.

text: {{Artesunate}} is water soluble and can be given orally, i.m. or {{i.v.}}. {{Artemether}} is lipid soluble and given orally or i.m., not i.v. {{Arteether}} is an i.m. oil injection for adults only. {{Arterolane}} is an oral synthetic trioxolane, used only with a partner drug.

Malarone contains atovaquone {{250 mg}} and proguanil {{100 mg}}. Atovaquone disrupts {{mitochondrial electron transport}}. Absorption is {{increased by fatty food}}. For prophylaxis, the drug is stopped {{1 week}} after leaving the endemic area, against {{4 weeks}} for mefloquine or doxycycline.

front: Why must an artemisinin never be given alone for uncomplicated falciparum malaria?
back: It is short-acting, so recrudescence is common: about 50% after a 3-day course alone. A long-acting partner with a different mechanism clears the remaining parasites and prevents resistance. Monotherapy with oral artemisinins is prohibited in India.

front: Artemether-lumefantrine: why must it be taken with fatty food, and what are its key interactions?
back: Lumefantrine is highly lipophilic, and its absorption is poor without fat; inadequate absorption can lead to recrudescence. It inhibits CYP2D6, so drugs such as metoprolol, neuroleptics and tricyclics are affected, and it should not be given with other QT-prolonging drugs. Avoid it in the first trimester and during breastfeeding.

front: Essay: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for uncomplicated falciparum malaria

The partner drug's longer action clears the remaining parasites

Rapid clinical and parasitological cure

Good tolerability

Short-acting partners need about 7 days of therapy
Artemether-lumefantrine: used in north-east India under the national programme

Not for severe malaria, where parenteral artemisinins are used

front: What is the chapter's regimen for uncomplicated chloroquine-sensitive vivax malaria?
back: Chloroquine 600 mg base, then 300 mg after 8 hours, then 300 mg daily for 2 more days (about 25 mg/kg over 3 days), plus primaquine 15 mg daily for 14 days. For chloroquine-resistant vivax, use quinine with doxycycline or clindamycin for 7 days (or an ACT other than artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine), followed by primaquine.

front: Chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria in India: which regimens does the chapter list?
back: The national programme treats all P. falciparum cases with an ACT, plus a single primaquine dose of 0.75 mg/kg on day 2. Options: artesunate with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (first line, except north-east India); artemether-lumefantrine (north-east India); artesunate-mefloquine; artesunate-amodiaquine; dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine; arterolane-piperaquine. Non-ACT option: quinine with doxycycline or clindamycin for 7 days.

front: Severe falciparum malaria: first-choice regimen and when to switch to oral therapy
back: Artesunate i.v. or i.m. 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then once daily for 7 days, switching to a 3-day oral ACT as soon as the patient can take tablets. WHO (2015) uses 3 mg/kg for children under 20 kg (KDT). Alternatives are i.m. artemether or i.m. arteether (adults) and i.v. quinine; chloroquine i.v. is a last resort in adults. GG14 notes that parenteral artesunate has now replaced quinine and quinidine for severe malaria and was FDA-approved for this in 2020.

front: What is the role of doxycycline and clindamycin in malaria?
back: Both are slow-acting schizontocides with no useful effect on liver stages or gametocytes. They are never used alone for malaria; they are added to quinine or an artemisinin to potentiate it. Doxycycline is a second-line prophylactic for short trips to chloroquine-resistant areas, but is not used in children or pregnancy. Clindamycin can be used in children and pregnancy.

front: Why is quinine infused in 5% dextrose and given slowly?
back: Dextrose prevents hypoglycaemia caused by quinine-driven insulin release. Rapid IV injection drops blood pressure sharply and can cause cardiovascular collapse.

front: Why is sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine not used for severe malaria?
back: It acts more slowly than other antimalarials, so it is not suitable for severe disease.

text: Some patients taking metronidazole develop a {{disulfiram-like}} reaction when they drink {{alcohol}}, but most patients can drink without reaction. Because of this, alcohol is avoided during treatment and for a period afterwards.

front: What is the role of diloxanide furoate in amoebiasis?
back: It is a luminal amoebicide that kills intestinal trophozoites which would otherwise form cysts. The ester is hydrolysed in the gut and the released diloxanide is absorbed, but it has no useful systemic amoebicidal action. It is the preferred drug for mild intestinal disease and asymptomatic cyst passers, given with or after a tissue amoebicide, with 80-90% cure in mild disease.

text: Chloroquine kills {{trophozoites}} and is concentrated in the {{liver}}, so it is used only for {{hepatic amoebiasis}}. It does not clear the intestinal cyst reservoir, so a {{luminal amoebicide}} must always follow.

{{Metronidazole}} 400 mg TDS for 5-7 days, {{tinidazole}} as a 2 g single dose, or {{secnidazole}} as a 2 g single dose are first-choice options. {{Nitazoxanide}} 500 mg BD for 3 days is an alternative, and about {{10%}} of patients may need a second course.

front: Trichomoniasis: first-choice oral drugs and how to prevent reinfection
back: Metronidazole 2 g as a single dose (or 400 mg TDS for 7 days), tinidazole, or secnidazole 2 g single dose. Recurrence is common; repeat a course after 4-6 weeks if needed. Treat the male partner at the same time to prevent reinfection. Intravaginal agents are reserved for refractory cases.

front: How does metronidazole kill anaerobic protozoa and bacteria?
back: It diffuses into the organism, where anaerobic electron-transport proteins reduce its nitro group to a reactive nitro radical. The radical damages cell components and competes for electrons from the pyruvate-ferredoxin pathway, disrupting energy metabolism. Oxygen blocks this activation, which is why aerobic organisms are spared.

text: Tinidazole has a half-life of about {{12 hours}}, so it suits {{single-dose or once-daily}} regimens. It is {{equally efficacious}} but has {{fewer}} side effects than metronidazole.

front: Why are emetine and dehydroemetine now restricted in amoebiasis?
back: They are potent direct tissue amoebicides, but they must be given by injection because they cause vomiting. Cardiotoxicity (ECG changes, myocarditis, hypotension) and cumulative toxicity limit their use. They are reserved for patients who cannot take metronidazole, for no more than about 10 days, and a luminal amoebicide must always follow. Dehydroemetine is preferred because it is less cardiotoxic.

front: Why were 8-hydroxyquinolines withdrawn in some countries?
back: Prolonged, high-dose quiniodochlor caused an epidemic of subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON) in Japan in the 1970s, and other members caused neuropathy and visual impairment. They were banned in Japan and some other countries. In India their use is prohibited in children, because chronic use has caused blindness.

front: Which drug is first line for visceral leishmaniasis in India now, and why is sodium stibogluconate no longer used?
back: Oral miltefosine is the first-line drug under the national programme. Leishmania donovani in Bihar and nearby areas is resistant to sodium stibogluconate (SSG); over 60% of cases in Bihar did not respond, so SSG is no longer used in India.

front: Cloze: drug options for visceral leishmaniasis
text: {{Miltefosine}} is the first-line oral drug in India. {{Amphotericin B deoxycholate}} is the second-line drug under the national programme, while WHO prefers {{liposomal amphotericin B}}. {{Paromomycin}} given i.m. for 21 days is an alternative, and {{sodium stibogluconate}} is used only where the parasite is still sensitive.
Paromomycin 15 mg/kg/day ({{11 mg base}} per kg) IM for {{21 days}} gave a {{95%}} cure rate in Bihar, against {{99%}} for amphotericin B. Ototoxicity occurs in about {{2%}} of recipients.

front: Miltefosine: dosing, key adverse effects and pregnancy warning
back: Given orally with meals for 28 days. Under the national programme (KDT): 100 mg daily for adults over 25 kg, 50 mg daily for those under 25 kg, and 2.5 mg/kg daily for children aged 2-11. Common effects are anorexia, vomiting and diarrhoea; transaminase rise and renal dysfunction are usually reversible. It is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy. Contraception is needed during treatment and afterwards: KDT gives 3 months, while GG14 notes that US guidance requires 5 months, in keeping with its long half-life (1 to 4 weeks).

front: How does amphotericin B act on Leishmania, and why is it the drug of choice in pregnancy?
back: Leishmania, like fungi, has ergosterol in its membrane, and amphotericin B binds ergosterol to damage the membrane. It is the preferred drug in pregnant and breastfeeding women because miltefosine is teratogenic.

front: How does mebendazole kill intestinal worms?
back: It binds the parasite's beta-tubulin with high affinity and blocks microtubule formation, which also reduces glucose uptake and glycogen stores. Worms are immobilised and die slowly, over 2-3 days, and hatching of nematode eggs is inhibited. It is poorly absorbed, so it acts in the gut.

front: Pyrantel: mechanism, and why it should not be combined with piperazine
back: Pyrantel activates nicotinic receptors on worm muscle, causing persistent depolarisation that leads to slow spastic paralysis and expulsion. Piperazine has the opposite effect, hyperpolarising worm muscle, so it antagonises pyrantel and the two should not be used together.

It acts as a GABA agonist on Ascaris muscle, opening chloride channels. This hyperpolarises the muscle, producing flaccid paralysis, so worms are expelled alive. It is contraindicated in renal insufficiency and epilepsy, and is considered safe in pregnancy.

front: Diethylcarbamazine: how is the febrile reaction reduced?
back: Mass death of microfilariae and adult worms causes fever, rash, itching, lymphadenopathy, bronchospasm and fall in blood pressure. Start with a low dose and build up to the full dose over a few days; if a reaction occurs, hold DEC and give an antihistamine or corticosteroid (GG14: such pretreatment is often used). In loiasis and onchocerciasis reactions can be life-threatening: KDT advises a small test dose or initial ivermectin. GG14 states that DEC is contraindicated in onchocerciasis (it worsens eye lesions), ivermectin being preferred, and that ivermectin can itself cause encephalopathy in patients with very heavy Loa loa microfilaraemia.

It opens invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels, paralysing nematodes; it also kills scabies mites and lice. It poorly enters the mammalian CNS because of P-glycoprotein efflux. Key uses: onchocerciasis (repeated doses every 6-12 months), strongyloidiasis, scabies, pediculosis and cutaneous larva migrans. It is microfilaricidal but not macrofilaricidal.

It causes calcium leakage in susceptible worms, producing contracture and paralysis; at higher concentrations it vacuolates the tegument, so the host's immunity destroys the worm. It acts on schistosomes, most flukes and cestodes (adult and larval stages), but not on nematodes.

Mazzotti-type reactions (itching, rash, tachycardia, fall in blood pressure) are common after treatment. It has not been used in children under 12 years. front: What is teriparatide, and how does it differ from other osteoporosis drugs?
back: A recombinant fragment of PTH (residues 1 to 34) with the actions of full-length PTH. front: How does PTH raise plasma calcium through the intestine?
back: Indirectly: PTH activates renal 1-hydroxylase, so more calcitriol forms, and calcitriol promotes intestinal calcium absorption.

front: Where is calcipotriol used and why is it useful?

front: How does calcitonin lower plasma calcium, and what controls its release?
back: Thyroid parafollicular C cells release calcitonin in proportion to plasma Ca2+. It acts through a G-protein coupled receptor that raises cAMP and directly inhibits osteoclasts, reducing their ruffled border and bone resorption. Its role in day-to-day calcium control is minor. The hypocalcaemic effect lasts about 8 hours.

front: What are the main clinical uses of calcitonin?
back: Acute hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, hypervitaminosis D, malignancy): 4 to 8 IU/kg i.m. 6 to 12 hourly for only 2 days; it acts within about 4 hours, peaks at 48 hours, then refractoriness develops. It also relieves bone pain from osteolytic lesions. Paget's disease: bisphosphonates are preferred. Raised serum calcitonin is a marker of medullary thyroid carcinoma. Nasal calcitonin modestly increases bone density in osteoporosis but is less effective than bisphosphonates or HRT, and British guidelines no longer recommend it for postmenopausal osteoporosis because of the malignancy risk with long-term use.

front: How do bisphosphonates act on osteoclasts?
back: They bind strongly to bone mineral and concentrate at resorption sites. When the acidic resorption zone releases them, osteoclasts take them up, which triggers apoptosis and disrupts the ruffled border and cytoskeleton. They also inhibit osteoclast precursor differentiation. Second and third generation agents also block the mevalonate pathway, impairing prenylation of GTP-binding proteins needed for vesicle function.

front: Oral bisphosphonates: what limits them and how must they be taken?
back: Oral bioavailability is about 1%, and they irritate the oesophagus and stomach (oesophagitis, erosions, ulcers). Take them on an empty stomach each morning with a full glass of water, stay upright and eat for at least 30 minutes, and do not chew. Calcium, iron, antacids, mineral water, tea, coffee and juice reduce absorption. Avoid in gastro-oesophageal reflux, peptic ulcer and renal impairment. NSAIDs add to gastric irritation.

front: What is an atypical femoral fracture linked to long-term bisphosphonate use?
back: A low-trauma subtrochanteric (femoral shaft) fracture seen with long-term bisphosphonate treatment, thought to reflect over-suppression of bone turnover. It is rare, about as rare as osteonecrosis of the jaw, but it has led some authorities to recommend a drug holiday after about 5 years if the clinical situation allows. Denosumab suppresses turnover to a similar degree, so its risk is considered comparable.

front: What is denosumab, and when is it preferred over a bisphosphonate?
back: A fully human monoclonal antibody against RANKL. By blocking RANKL it prevents RANK activation, reducing osteoclast formation and function, and it lowers vertebral and hip fracture risk. Used for osteoporosis in women and men, bone loss from hormone-suppressing cancer therapy, and bone metastases. It can be used in severe renal disease, where bisphosphonates are contraindicated. Dose: 60 mg s.c. every 6 months. Adverse effects: flu-like symptoms, transient fall in Ca2+ (especially in CKD or vitamin D deficiency), dermatitis, infections, rarely osteonecrosis of the jaw. When it is stopped there is often a surge of bone resorption.

front: Why is strontium ranelate only a reserve drug for osteoporosis?
back: It reduces resorption by blocking osteoclast differentiation and promoting their apoptosis, and it also stimulates bone formation. It lowers vertebral and hip fracture risk. However, it raises the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke and thromboembolism. It is reserved for severe osteoporosis in elderly women or high-risk men when bisphosphonates and other drugs are contraindicated or not tolerated. Other effects: headache, GI upset, rashes and serious skin reactions.

front: Why is weekly alendronate often preferred?
back: Weekly 35-70 mg is equally effective, more convenient and better tolerated than daily dosing.

front: How do bisphosphonates affect osteoclast precursors?

front: Why do oral bisphosphonates cause oesophagitis?
back: They are poorly absorbed and irritate the gastric and oesophageal mucosa; NSAIDs add to the irritation.

front: What is Paget's disease of bone, and how is it treated?
back: Excess osteoclast activity causes disordered remodelling and a honeycomb-like bone architecture. Bisphosphonates are the standard therapy: they arrest lytic lesions, relieve bone pain and can give long remissions. Zoledronate as a single 5 mg IV infusion gives a high and long-lasting response; IV pamidronate can also induce long remission after one infusion. Calcitonin is second line, with short-lived benefit. KDT advises that an oral bisphosphonate course should not exceed 6 months, with repeat courses after a gap.

front: Besides bisphosphonates and calcitonin, which two other drugs lower plasma calcium in hypercalcaemia?
back: Gallium nitrate (blocks the osteoclast proton pump; reserve, nephrotoxic) and high-dose glucocorticoids (more urinary calcium loss, less absorption). Both act slowly, so they are adjuncts.

front: Why are glucocorticoids most useful in hypercalcaemia of hypervitaminosis D and sarcoidosis?
back: They cut gut calcium absorption and raise urinary excretion. Given over several days they normalise calcium in vitamin D excess and sarcoidosis; in cancer they are only adjuvant.

front: Gallium nitrate: mechanism and main limitation?
back: It inhibits bone resorption by depressing the ATP-dependent proton pump on the osteoclast ruffled membrane. It is given as a continuous IV infusion for about 5 days in malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia that does not respond to other drugs. It is nephrotoxic, so it is kept as a reserve drug.

front: Which drugs arrest osteolytic bone metastases and reduce bone pain?
back: Parenteral pamidronate or zoledronate; zoledronate also has an antitumour effect.

front: Why do thiazide diuretics matter in calcium disorders?
back: Thiazides help tubular reabsorption of calcium, so urinary calcium excretion falls. This is useful in calcium stone disease with high urinary calcium, but it means thiazides can raise plasma calcium and should be avoided in hypercalcaemia. Loop diuretics such as furosemide do the opposite: after volume repletion they raise calcium excretion in hypercalcaemia.

front: What is the first-line IV drug for seizures in pre-eclampsia and eclampsia?
back: Magnesium sulfate by slow i.v. infusion: documented efficacy in seizure prevention, with no adverse effect on mother or baby.

front: How does magnesium sulfate relax the uterus?
back: It competes with Ca2+ for entry into myometrial cells through voltage-sensitive and ligand-gated Ca2+ channels.

front: What role does magnesium sulfate play in acute asthma?
back: An added bronchodilator in acute severe asthma, i.v. or nebulised, alongside a nebulised beta2 agonist; it may reduce cytosolic Ca2+ in airway smooth muscle.

front: Which arrhythmias respond to IV magnesium sulfate?
back: Digitalis-induced arrhythmias when serum Mg2+ is low (low Mg2+ predisposes to them), and some patients with torsades de pointes.

front: Name two uses of magnesium hydroxide.
back: Antacid (neutralises gastric acid) and purgative (milk of magnesia); Mg2+ holds water osmotically in the gut.

front: Why are magnesium salts avoided in renal insufficiency?
back: With impaired renal function, hypermagnesaemia can develop and may lead to renal failure, so magnesium salts are contraindicated in renal insufficiency. Cardiac disease, existing electrolyte abnormality and diuretic use also call for caution.

front: Why does magnesium depletion matter in a digitalised or post-MI patient?
back: Prolonged thiazide or loop diuretic use depletes Mg2+, raising the risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Potassium-sparing diuretics reduce this loss.

front: What is peak bone mass, and when is it reached?
back: The maximum bone mineral content at skeletal maturity. About 60% of adult bone accrues in adolescence; mass peaks in the third decade, stays stable to about age 50, then declines. Inheritance, sex hormones, activity and dietary calcium all shape it.

front: Why does age-related bone loss occur even in healthy people?
back: Each bone remodelling cycle (about 6 months) removes bone by osteoclasts and rebuilds it by osteoblasts, but leaves a small deficit. These deficits accumulate over life, so bone loss starts soon after growth stops.

front: What are the primary and secondary types of osteoporosis?
back: Primary: type I (trabecular bone loss from estrogen lack at menopause) and type II (cortical and trabecular loss in men and women from remodelling inefficiency, diet and parathyroid activation with age). Secondary: caused by systemic illness or drugs such as glucocorticoids or phenytoin.

front: How does estrogen lack cause type I osteoporosis?
back: Estrogen normally restrains osteoclast formation (via OPG and RANKL), so its loss at menopause speeds bone resorption. The damage falls mainly on trabecular bone of the vertebrae, wrist and femoral neck, where fractures are most common.

front: Why is osteoporosis described as a coupling failure?
back: Resorption and formation are normally tightly coupled. In osteoporosis resorption outpaces formation, because remodelling deficits accumulate over each cycle.

front: Cell-cycle non-specific vs cell-cycle specific cytotoxic drugs: give one example of each and the key difference.
back: Non-specific drugs kill resting as well as dividing cells (e.g. alkylating agents, cisplatin, anthracyclines, actinomycin D). Specific drugs kill only cycling cells, usually in one phase (e.g. antimetabolites in S phase, vinca alkaloids and taxanes in M phase).

front: Which malignancies can chemotherapy cure or put into long remission, and which does it only palliate?
back: Cure or long remission: childhood acute leukaemias, Wilms tumour, Ewing sarcoma, retinoblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, choriocarcinoma, Hodgkin and Burkitt lymphoma, testicular teratoma and seminoma, mycosis fungoides. Palliation (shrinks tumour, prolongs life): breast, ovary, endometrium, prostate, myeloma, CLL, CML, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, small cell lung and head and neck cancers.

front: Complete: protective (rescue) agents paired with the drug whose toxicity they prevent.
text: Mesna protects the bladder from {{ifosfamide and cyclophosphamide}}; leucovorin rescues normal cells after high-dose {{methotrexate}}; dexrazoxane reduces cardiotoxicity of {{doxorubicin}}; amifostine protects against renal and neural toxicity of {{cisplatin}}; rasburicase treats acute hyperuricaemia from {{rapid tumour lysis}}; uridine triacetate rescues {{fluorouracil}} toxicity in DPD deficiency.

front: Why are cell-cycle specific drugs given in short pulses, and where do they sit in a regimen?
back: Resting cells are less drug-sensitive and re-enter the cycle between courses, so repeated pulses catch more of the tumour. Specific drugs are usually scheduled after a course of non-specific drugs to improve the kill.

front: Why do large solid tumours respond poorly to cytotoxic drugs compared with leukaemias and lymphomas?
back: Most large solid tumours have a low growth fraction, so few cells are dividing at any moment and cycle-dependent drugs have fewer targets. Leukaemias and lymphomas have a high growth fraction and respond better.

front: How do tumours become resistant to a drug used repeatedly, and what is the main multidrug resistance mechanism?
back: Repeated use of a single drug, especially at low dose, selects for less sensitive clones. Mutations in the target give drug-specific resistance. Overexpression of the MDR1 gene raises P-glycoprotein, an efflux pump that expels vinca alkaloids, anthracyclines and taxanes.

front: Why is cisplatin highly emetogenic, and what is the antiemetic approach?
back: Cisplatin stimulates the chemoreceptor trigger zone directly and also generates emetic signals from the upper GI tract, so antiemetics are given routinely before each infusion. Ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) has surpassed metoclopramide; adding dexamethasone and/or lorazepam or aprepitant (NK1 antagonist) gives further protection.

front: Which anticancer drugs have cumulative-dose limits, and what toxicity does each limit prevent?
back: Doxorubicin: cardiomyopathy, usual total limit about 550 mg/m2 (about 300 mg/m2 in children); epirubicin above 900 mg/m2. Bleomycin: pulmonary fibrosis; KDT keeps the total under 250 mg, and GG14 advises caution beyond that. Cisplatin: nephrotoxicity that depends on the total dose. Etoposide: weekly or twice-weekly dosing above a cumulative 2000 mg/m2 raises the risk of secondary leukaemia. Busulfan: pulmonary fibrosis with long-term use.

front: How do alkylating agents damage DNA, and what is their cell-cycle profile?
back: They form reactive carbonium ions that covalently alkylate macromolecules, most often at guanine N7. The result is cross-linking, abnormal base pairing or strand breaks. They are radiomimetic and mostly cell-cycle non-specific.

front: Complete: uses of selected alkylating agents.

front: Which alkylating agent spares myeloid tissue, and what is its dose?
back: Chlorambucil, which is slow acting and mainly affects lymphoid tissue; 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg daily for 3 to 6 weeks, then 2 mg daily maintenance.

front: Cyclophosphamide: why is it not directly toxic, and what are its characteristic toxicities?
back: It is a prodrug, activated by hepatic CYP enzymes to aldophosphamide, which splits into phosphoramide mustard (the antitumour alkylator) and acrolein. Acrolein causes haemorrhagic cystitis, so vigorous hydration is needed at high doses and mesna protects the bladder. Alopecia is prominent. It spares platelets better than many alkylators and is strongly immunosuppressive.

front: Ifosfamide versus cyclophosphamide, and why is mesna given with ifosfamide?
back: Ifosfamide has a longer, dose-dependent half-life and causes more neurotoxicity (confusion, hallucinations, seizures, coma) and haemorrhagic cystitis, but less alopecia and less emesis. Mesna is a sulfhydryl compound excreted in urine that binds the bladder-toxic metabolites and protects the bladder.

front: Carboplatin and oxaliplatin: how do their toxicity profiles differ from cisplatin?
back: Carboplatin has less nephro-, oto- and neurotoxicity and milder, delayed emesis; its dose-limiting toxicity is thrombocytopenia. Oxaliplatin's dose-limiting toxicity is peripheral neuropathy, with an acute form triggered by cold. It is not affected by cisplatin resistance and synergises with fluorouracil in colorectal cancer.

front: What is the dose-limiting toxicity of oxaliplatin, and how does it differ from cisplatin?
back: Peripheral neuropathy (sensory paraesthesia of arms, legs, mouth and throat); cisplatin's main problem is renal impairment, and oxaliplatin is active where cisplatin resistance has developed.

front: Why is cisplatin given with routine antiemetics?
back: It is highly emetic, so antiemetics are given before each infusion; its most important dose-limiting toxicity is renal impairment.

front: A young man with metastatic testicular cancer is to get platinum-based chemotherapy. Justify the drug combination and anticipate toxicities.
back: Cisplatin is a key drug in metastatic testicular cancer and is combined with bleomycin and vinblastine or etoposide: different mechanisms (DNA cross-linking, chain scission, tubulin or topoisomerase II), and bleomycin adds little marrow suppression. Anticipate cisplatin nephrotoxicity (total-dose dependent), ototoxicity (tinnitus, deafness), neuropathy and very severe emesis needing routine antiemetics, plus bleomycin pulmonary fibrosis. Cisplatin is cleared slowly in urine, so renal function and hydration matter.

front: L-asparaginase: mechanism, and why its toxicity profile differs from other cytotoxic drugs.
back: It hydrolyses circulating L-asparagine, starving asparagine-dependent leukaemic cells. It lacks marrow, alopecia and mucosal toxicity, but causes effects of defective protein synthesis: hyperglycaemia, raised triglycerides, pancreatitis, liver damage, clotting defects and CNS effects. Hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis occur, and neutralising antibodies limit repeat use; the PEG-conjugated form lasts longer and is less antigenic.

front: Classify the antimetabolites used in cancer, with the drugs in each group.
back: Folate antagonists: methotrexate, pemetrexed. Purine antagonists: mercaptopurine, thioguanine, azathioprine, fludarabine. Pyrimidine antagonists: fluorouracil, capecitabine, doxyfluridine, cytarabine, gemcitabine. They mimic normal metabolites, so DNA synthesis is blocked mainly in S phase.

front: How does methotrexate block DNA synthesis?
back: It enters through the folate carrier and is polyglutamated by FPGS. It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, so tetrahydrofolate cannot be regenerated, and also hits thymidylate synthase. Thymidylate and purine supply fall, so S-phase cells fail to make DNA.

front: Hydroxyurea: target, phase and main uses.
back: It blocks ribonucleotide reductase, cutting deoxynucleotide supply, so it is S-phase specific. Used in CML, polycythaemia vera and psoriasis, and as first-line for sickle cell disease in adults. Main toxicity is myelosuppression.

front: Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue: why does it work after high-dose methotrexate when folic acid does not, and how is it given?
back: Methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase, so folic acid cannot be converted to the active coenzyme. Folinic acid (N5-formyl tetrahydrofolate) is a fully reduced folate, so it bypasses the block and refills the tetrahydrofolate pool. High-dose methotrexate is given only if leucovorin rescue follows within 24 hours of the infusion; if the methotrexate level is still high at 48 hours, larger leucovorin doses are continued until it falls. Normal cells are said to be rescued more than tumour cells, which widens the therapeutic index. Leucovorin does not reverse methotrexate neurotoxicity.

front: Fluorouracil: how does it block DNA synthesis, what modulates it, and what determines its toxicity?
back: Its nucleotide FdUMP forms a covalent ternary complex with thymidylate synthase and methylene-tetrahydrofolate, irreversibly blocking thymidylate synthesis. Its triphosphate is also incorporated into RNA. Leucovorin enhances the effect, and cisplatin or oxaliplatin synergise (FOLFOX). It is inactivated by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD); DPD deficiency causes severe toxicity, which can be rescued with uridine triacetate. Capecitabine is an oral prodrug converted to fluorouracil by thymidine phosphorylase, an enzyme rich in many breast and colorectal tumours.

front: Cytarabine: which cancers respond, why is it given as repeated boluses or infusion, and what is its main toxicity?
back: Used for induction in acute myeloid and lymphoblastic leukaemia, blast crisis of CML and non-Hodgkin lymphoma; ineffective in solid tumours. It is S-phase specific and is rapidly deaminated, so it is given as repeated i.v. bolus or continuous infusion over days. Toxicity: marrow suppression, mucositis, diarrhoea and delayed pulmonary complications.

front: Complete: cytotoxic antibiotics and their key features.
text: Mitomycin C is now used mainly in {{anal cancer}} and intravesically for {{superficial bladder tumours}}; bleomycin causes {{pulmonary fibrosis}} with little {{myelosuppression}}; actinomycin D is used in {{Wilms' tumour}} and childhood {{rhabdomyosarcoma}}.

front: List the microtubule-damaging drugs and the camptothecin analogues.
back: Microtubule agents in book order: vincristine, vinblastine, vinorelbine, paclitaxel, docetaxel, estramustine. Camptothecin analogues: topotecan and irinotecan. Vincas stop microtubule assembly (metaphase arrest); taxanes do the opposite and stabilise microtubules.

front: How do etoposide and the camptothecins damage DNA, and in which phase?
back: Etoposide poisons topoisomerase II: cells arrest in G2 because DNA breaks cannot be resealed. Topotecan and irinotecan act on topoisomerase I: single-strand breaks are made but not resealed, which is lethal in S phase.

front: Bleomycin: mechanism, main uses and signature toxicity.
back: It chelates iron or copper and generates superoxide, causing DNA chain scission. Used in testicular tumours (with cisplatin and vinblastine or etoposide), squamous carcinomas and Hodgkin disease. Characteristic toxicity is mucocutaneous change and pulmonary fibrosis, with minimal marrow suppression, which is why it combines well with myelosuppressive drugs.

front: How do taxanes differ mechanistically from vinca alkaloids?
back: Taxanes bind beta-tubulin and promote excess polymerisation while stabilising microtubules against depolymerisation. Vinca alkaloids do the opposite. Both arrest mitosis, but taxanes produce abnormal microtubule bundles throughout the cell cycle.

front: Etoposide versus topotecan and irinotecan: which enzyme does each act on?
back: Etoposide inhibits topoisomerase II (G2 arrest) and prevents resealing of DNA breaks. Topotecan and irinotecan inhibit topoisomerase I, leaving single-strand breaks that become lethal during replication. Irinotecan is a prodrug activated to SN-38; its inactivation depends on UGT1A1, and the UGT1A1*28 allele raises the risk of diarrhoea and neutropenia. front: Imatinib: which kinases does it block, and which tumours respond?
back: It inhibits the Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase of CML and also PDGF receptor and c-KIT. It is the drug of choice for metastatic c-KIT-positive GIST, and produces remission in over 90% of chronic-phase CML. It is also used in dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. Resistance arises from point mutations in Bcr-Abl.

text: Dasatinib and nilotinib are second-generation {{Bcr-Abl}} inhibitors for CML resistant to or intolerant of imatinib, and nilotinib is now also used first-line; both can cause {{QT prolongation}}, and dasatinib can cause pleural effusion. Sunitinib and sorafenib are oral multi-kinase inhibitors that block the {{VEGF receptor}}, used in {{renal cell carcinoma}}; sorafenib is also approved for hepatocellular and thyroid cancer, and sunitinib for imatinib-resistant GIST.

front: Classify the targeted anticancer agents by target, listing the drugs.
back: Bcr-Abl kinase inhibitors: imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib. EGFR (HER1) inhibitors: gefitinib, erlotinib, cetuximab. EGFR/HER2: trastuzumab, lapatinib. Angiogenesis inhibitors: bevacizumab, sunitinib, sorafenib. Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells.

front: Gefitinib: which lung cancer patients respond, and what are its key adverse effects?
back: It is an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor effective mainly in non-small cell lung cancer with activating EGFR mutations (exon 19 deletions or the exon 21 L858R mutation), which are commoner in non-smokers and women. Common effects are skin rash and diarrhoea; interstitial lung disease is uncommon but serious. It is metabolised by CYP3A4. The third-generation inhibitor osimertinib is approved first-line for these mutations and for tumours that acquire the T790M resistance mutation.

front: Trastuzumab: target, main indications, and what must be monitored?
back: A humanised monoclonal antibody against the extracellular domain of HER2. Used in HER2-positive breast cancer and HER2-positive gastric cancer, usually with a taxane. Acute infusion reactions (fever, chills, dyspnoea) are common. Cardiotoxicity: LVEF falls in under 5% and symptomatic heart failure occurs in under 1%, but the risk rises to about 20% when combined with doxorubicin, so LVEF is monitored during and after treatment.

front: Rituximab: target antigen, how it kills cells, and key adverse effects.
back: A chimeric anti-CD20 antibody acting on B cells. It kills by inducing apoptosis, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and complement-dependent cytotoxicity. Used in B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, CLL and autoimmune diseases. Adverse effects: infusion reactions (reduce by slow escalation of rate and antihistamines), B-cell depletion, late neutropenia, tumour lysis when the tumour burden is high, reactivation of hepatitis B and JC polyomavirus, and rare severe mucocutaneous reactions.

front: Complete: hormonal drug classes for breast cancer.
text: The three main classes are {{selective oestrogen receptor modulators}} such as tamoxifen, {{selective oestrogen receptor down-regulators}} such as fulvestrant, and {{aromatase inhibitors}} such as letrozole; they form the backbone of adjuvant and palliative breast cancer hormone therapy.

front: Where do estrogens, antiandrogens, GnRH analogues and progestins fit in cancer therapy?
back: Estrogens give symptomatic relief in prostate cancer but have been superseded by GnRH agonists used with an antiandrogen. Antiandrogens (flutamide, bicalutamide) raise androgen secretion by blocking pituitary feedback, so they need orchiectomy or a GnRH analogue for full effect. Progestins give temporary remission in endometrial cancer at high doses and are used palliatively in breast cancer no longer responding to tamoxifen. Finasteride and dutasteride are occasionally used in advanced prostate cancer.

front: Why are glucocorticoids used in cancer therapy, and what limits their use?
back: Their lympholytic action makes them key in acute childhood leukaemia and lymphomas: remission is rapid but relapse eventually occurs. They also help in Hodgkin disease, manage complications such as hypercalcaemia, haemolysis, retinoic acid syndrome, raised intracranial pressure and mediastinal oedema, and potentiate antiemetics. Long-term corticosteroid toxicity limits use.

front: Compare how tamoxifen, fulvestrant and aromatase inhibitors differ from GnRH agonists with antiandrogens in hormone-dependent cancers.
back: Breast cancer: tamoxifen (SERM), fulvestrant (SERD) and aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole) act on the estrogen pathway. Prostate cancer: GnRH agonists suppress FSH and LH; antiandrogens (flutamide, bicalutamide) need orchiectomy or a GnRH analogue for full effect. None is cytotoxic; they only slow hormone-dependent growth and are palliative.

front: Outline the hormonal strategy in advanced prostate cancer and how it evolved.
back: Older: estrogens gave symptomatic relief but are superseded by GnRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin), which suppress FSH and LH, given with an antiandrogen. Antiandrogens (flutamide, bicalutamide, enzalutamide, nilutamide) work fully only with orchiectomy or a GnRH analogue. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) are occasionally used. Abiraterone, a steroid synthesis inhibitor, is given with prednisone in metastatic disease. Estramustine is used when hormones fail.

front: Cyclosporine: how does it suppress T-cell activation?
back: It binds cyclophilin, and the complex inhibits calcineurin. NFAT then cannot enter the nucleus, so IL-2 and other cytokine genes are not transcribed and the helper T-cell response fails. It spares marrow and humoral immunity, mainly suppressing cell-mediated immunity. It is most active when given before antigen exposure.

text: Temsirolimus is an intravenous {{ester}} of sirolimus that is converted in the body to {{sirolimus}}, an mTOR inhibitor; it is used in advanced {{renal cell carcinoma}} and refractory {{mantle cell lymphoma}}.

front: Why does cyclosporine need blood-level monitoring, and why is a microemulsion formulation preferred?
back: Oral absorption is variable and depends on bile, so the older soft-gelatin capsules were erratic. The microemulsion gives more consistent bioavailability. It is metabolised by CYP3A4 and excreted in bile, with a biphasic half-life. The intravenous form uses a polyoxyethylated castor oil vehicle that causes chills, fever and dyspnoea, so it is reserved for emergencies.

front: Tacrolimus versus cyclosporine: what is shared, what differs, and why is tacrolimus often preferred?
back: Both inhibit calcineurin through an immunophilin: cyclophilin for cyclosporine, FKBP for tacrolimus. Tacrolimus is a macrolide about 100 times more potent. It is preferred in transplantation for potency and easier monitoring, and its absorption does not depend on bile, which suits liver transplant. It causes more diabetes, neurotoxicity, alopecia and diarrhoea, and less hypertension, hirsutism and gum hyperplasia. Its dose-limiting toxicity is renal.

front: Azathioprine: how is it activated, and what are its main immunosuppressive uses?
back: It is a prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine and taken up preferentially by immune cells. It blocks purine synthesis and DNA function, mainly suppressing cell-mediated immunity. Uses: transplant rejection (less effective than cyclosporine, so usually combined with it or used when cyclosporine is toxic), low doses in rheumatoid arthritis, maintenance in inflammatory bowel disease, and vitiligo. Key interaction: allopurinol blocks its breakdown by xanthine oxidase, so the dose must be cut to about one-quarter to one-third.

front: Mycophenolate mofetil: which enzyme does it inhibit, and why do lymphocytes depend on it?
back: It is a prodrug of mycophenolic acid, which inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, the key enzyme of de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis. T and B cells lack a purine salvage pathway, so they are selectively affected. As an add-on to cyclosporine and steroid in kidney transplant it is as good as or better than azathioprine, and should not be combined with it. Adverse effects: vomiting, diarrhoea, leucopenia, CMV infection and GI bleeding. It is contraindicated in pregnancy.

front: Methotrexate in autoimmune disease: what does it do at low dose, and in which conditions is it first-line?
back: It markedly depresses cytokine production and cell-mediated immunity and has anti-inflammatory action. First-line in rapidly progressive rheumatoid arthritis, severe psoriasis, pemphigus, myasthenia gravis, uveitis and chronic active hepatitis. Low-dose maintenance is relatively well tolerated.

front: How do glucocorticoids act as immunosuppressants, and which arm of immunity do they mainly affect?
back: They reduce MHC class II expression, cytokine gene expression (IL-1, IL-2, IL-6) and adhesion molecule production, so helper T-cell activation falls. Their rapid lymphopenia reflects lymphocyte sequestration in tissue. They act mainly on cell-mediated immunity. They are the mainstay for graft-versus-host disease and acute rejection pulses, but long-term toxicity limits use.

text: Anakinra, a recombinant {{IL-1 receptor antagonist}}, is used in refractory rheumatoid arthritis; it is less effective as {{monotherapy}} and is usually given together with {{methotrexate}}.

front: Basiliximab and daclizumab: target, mechanism and use in transplantation.
back: Monoclonal antibodies against CD25, the alpha subunit of the IL-2 receptor on activated T cells; they block IL-2-driven activation and proliferation without lysing the cells. Used for induction in solid-organ transplantation, with steroid, a calcineurin inhibitor and/or azathioprine or mycophenolate. Basiliximab has the higher affinity and a half-life of about 1 week; daclizumab has a longer half-life (about 20 days in GG14, 3 weeks in KDT), but its cost reduced demand and it is now made only for multiple sclerosis. Risks include anaphylaxis, opportunistic infection, oedema and fever.

front: Anti-D immunoglobulin: what does it prevent, and when is it given?
back: A human IgG preparation with high titre against the Rh(D) antigen. It is given to Rh(D)-negative women within 72 hours of delivering or aborting an Rh(D)-positive baby, to stop them forming anti-D antibodies that would cause haemolytic disease in later pregnancies. It is also given around the 28th week of pregnancy. Higher doses are needed after accidental transfusion of Rh-positive blood. It is never given to Rh-positive people or to the infant.

front: What are the two general adverse effects of immunosuppressive therapy?
back: Increased risk of bacterial, fungal and viral (especially cytomegalovirus) and other opportunistic infections; and development of lymphoma and other malignancies after a long latency, because immune surveillance is weakened.

front: What is the role of TPMT in azathioprine and thiopurine therapy, and what happens in TPMT deficiency?
back: Thiopurine methyltransferase methylates the thiopurines as an alternative metabolic route. Genetic deficiency raises the risk of myelosuppression, mucositis and gut damage with mercaptopurine and increases azathioprine toxicity; with a TPMT polymorphism, myelosuppression can be severe and prolonged. Overexpression of TPMT is a cause of thiopurine resistance in leukaemic cells.

front: Etanercept, infliximab and adalimumab: what do they target, and how do they differ?
back: All block TNF. Etanercept is a fusion protein of the TNF receptor and an IgG1 Fc fragment that neutralises TNF. Infliximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody given i.v. every 4 to 8 weeks. Adalimumab is fully human and less antigenic. They are used in rheumatoid arthritis (often with methotrexate), Crohn disease with fistulae, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis and ankylosing spondylitis. Because TNF is needed against granulomatous infection, they raise the risk of tuberculosis and other opportunistic infections; infliximab can induce antinuclear antibodies and rarely a lupus-like syndrome.

front: IMiDs: name the class and its three members
back: Immunomodulatory imide drugs: thalidomide, lenalidomide and pomalidomide. All share a CO-NH-CO imide signature.

front: Lenalidomide: how does it kill myeloma cells?
back: A molecular glue. It binds cereblon in the CRL4 E3 ligase and recruits IKZF1 and IKZF3 for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
Multiple myeloma, and del(5q) myelodysplastic syndrome. It also shows activity in CLL.

front: Lenalidomide versus thalidomide: which adverse effects are milder?
back: Lenalidomide is far gentler on the nervous system and gut: sedation, constipation and neuropathy are minor. Its dose-limiting toxicity is marrow suppression, with leukopenia in about one patient in five.

front: Lenalidomide and thalidomide: thrombosis risk and management
back: They raise the risk of DVT, stroke and MI, more so with glucocorticoids or anthracyclines. Anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy is indicated in patients with clotting risk factors.

front: Lenalidomide in CLL: which reaction needs care?
back: Tumour flare with lymph node swelling and tumour lysis. It is more likely with renal dysfunction, so CLL patients start at 10 mg/day with hydration and allopurinol.

back: Given for morning sickness of pregnancy, then withdrawn for teratogenicity (dysmelia). It later returned for erythema nodosum leprosum and was studied for myeloma.

front: Thalidomide enantiomers: which one is teratogenic?
back: The S(-) enantiomer is teratogenic (phocomelia) and affects growth control. The R(+) enantiomer is sedative. The two interconvert in the body.

back: A third-generation thalidomide congener, approved for myeloma that is resistant to lenalidomide.

front: HDAC: what does the enzyme do, and what does inhibition do?
back: HDACs remove acetyl groups from histone lysines, condensing chromatin and silencing genes. Inhibition keeps histones acetylated, opening chromatin and reactivating silenced tumour genes. The result is differentiation or cell cycle arrest.

front: FDA-approved HDAC inhibitors: name the four
back: Panobinostat, romidepsin, vorinostat and belinostat.
Binds the active site of HDACs and chelates zinc. It inhibits HDAC1, 2, 3 and 6. Approved for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma after two systemic therapies.

A nonselective pan-HDAC inhibitor for myeloma after at least two prior treatments, including bortezomib and an immunomodulator. Serious cardiac risk: ischaemic events, arrhythmias and ECG change, so monitor electrolytes and avoid QT-prolonging drugs.
A natural depsipeptide prodrug. Inside cells its zinc-binding thiol is reduced and blocks HDAC. Used in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; the peripheral T-cell indication has been withdrawn.
Given intravenously for peripheral T-cell lymphoma. Warnings: haematological toxicity, infection, hepatotoxicity and fetal harm.

front: Proteasome inhibition: how does it kill myeloma cells?
back: It stops degradation of IκB, so NF-κB stays in the cytosol. Survival, adhesion and antiapoptotic genes such as cyclin D1, BCL-2 and cIAPs are then not switched on.

front: Bortezomib: class, target and approved use
back: A first-generation, reversible inhibitor of the chymotrypsin-like activity of the 20S proteasome (beta-5 subunit). Used in myeloma, both first line and at relapse, and in relapsed or refractory mantle cell lymphoma.

Thrombocytopenia (about 28%), fatigue (about 12%), peripheral neuropathy (about 12%), neutropenia, anaemia, vomiting, diarrhoea and nausea. Neuropathy is the most chronic toxicity. Injection can cause hypotension; rare cardiac effects include heart failure and QT prolongation.

front: Carfilzomib: how does it differ from bortezomib?
back: A second-generation, selective tetrapeptide epoxyketone. Used alone or with dexamethasone, or with lenalidomide and dexamethasone, after at least one prior therapy.

An oral second-generation peptide proteasome inhibitor acting on PSMB5. Elimination half-life about 9.5 days. Used with lenalidomide and dexamethasone. Causes diarrhoea, peripheral neuropathy and hepatotoxicity.

front: CDK4/6: which checkpoint do they control?
back: Cyclin D with CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb, releasing transcription of S-phase factors. CDK4/6 inhibition causes G1 arrest. Loss of Rb or p16INK4A, or cyclin D amplification, weakens the checkpoint.

back: Approved in 2017 for ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer. Most common reactions are diarrhoea and neutropenia, with nausea and fatigue. Metabolised by CYP3A.

front: VEGF: which receptors and what effect?
back: VEGF binds VEGFR1 (FLT1), VEGFR2 (KDR) and VEGFR3 (FLT4). Receptor kinase signalling drives endothelial proliferation, survival and vascular permeability.

front: Bevacizumab: adverse effects to counsel on
back: Hypertension, arterial thromboembolism, haemorrhage (nose and rectal), heart failure, proteinuria, GI perforation and defective wound healing.

front: Aflibercept: how does it differ from bevacizumab?
back: A recombinant VEGF trap. It uses the VEGFR1-binding domain to sequester VEGF as a soluble decoy receptor.
An oral multikinase inhibitor of KIT and VEGFR2. Approved in metastatic renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic NETs and imatinib-resistant GIST.
Sunitinib: hypertension, rash, diarrhoea, fatigue, bleeding, proteinuria, hypothyroidism and neutropenia. Sorafenib: hand-foot skin reaction, hypertension, haemorrhage and proteinuria.

front: Interleukin-2: what is its role in cancer therapy?
back: A cytokine that amplifies the killer T-cell response against tumour cells. It is used as an adjuvant alongside other treatment.

front: CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer: what are they combined with?
back: Palbociclib, ribociclib and abemaciclib are used for ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer. They are combined with an aromatase inhibitor as first endocrine-based therapy, or with fulvestrant after progression on endocrine therapy. Abemaciclib can also be used after endocrine therapy and chemotherapy.

front: Palbociclib: which co-administered drugs change its exposure?
back: Palbociclib is a CYP3A substrate and inhibitor. A strong CYP3A inhibitor such as itraconazole can raise exposure by about 87%, so the dose is reduced if the combination cannot be avoided. Strong inducers such as rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, enzalutamide and St John's wort lower exposure and should be avoided. Grapefruit should be avoided too.

front: What is the Drugs and Therapeutics Committee (DTC) of a hospital, and who is suited to convene it?
back: A hospital committee (called the Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee in US usage) that lays down policies and procedures for pharmacy services and medicine use, including the required content of chart orders. A clinical pharmacologist is expected to act as its convener.

front: How does a pharmacopoeia differ from a formulary? Give the Indian examples.
back: A pharmacopoeia (e.g. Indian Pharmacopoeia, IP; also BP, USP) is an official code that sets standards for drug preparations: physical properties and tests for identity, purity and potency. It has legal standing. A formulary (e.g. National Formulary of India) is not a regulatory document; it gives information on available drugs and guides prescribers.

front: Which criteria does the National Formulary of India 2011 use to include a drug?
back: Drugs in the National List of Essential Medicines 2011; drugs used in National Health Programmes; drugs in the Indian Pharmacopoeia; drugs an expert panel recommends though not otherwise covered; any drug the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission finds appropriate.
refs: WEB NHSRC National Formulary of India (NFI) 2011 https://qps.nhsrcindia.org/sites/default/files/2022-01/National%20Formulary%20of%20India%20(NFI),%202011.pdf

front: What must be weighed when choosing a medicine for a formulary from its therapeutic group?
back: Benefit, risk and cost: efficacy for the indication, safety (fewest adverse effects), and cost judged over the whole treatment course, not only the unit price.
refs: WEB NHSRC National Formulary of India (NFI) 2011 https://qps.nhsrcindia.org/sites/default/files/2022-01/National%20Formulary%20of%20India%20(NFI),%202011.pdf

front: Is the National Formulary of India a regulatory document?
back: No. It is a guidance document; physicians are expected to use professional judgement, and its drugs were chosen for rational and economic prescribing.
refs: WEB NHSRC National Formulary of India (NFI) 2011 https://qps.nhsrcindia.org/sites/default/files/2022-01/National%20Formulary%20of%20India%20(NFI),%202011.pdf
