front: How does a restricted formulary help a hospital or health system?
back: Keeping a limited list of medicines on the formulary, in standard concentrations, is one of the selection and procurement steps recommended to reduce medication errors. In managed-care settings, formulary controls steer prescribing toward cheaper or preferred generic drugs: the prescriber often picks the drug group and the pharmacist dispenses the single formulary member of that group. The listed drugs may change as prices and rebates are renegotiated.

front: Distinguish generic substitution from therapeutic substitution.
back: Generic substitution: the pharmacist dispenses the cheapest generically equivalent product of the same drug, which many payers require unless the prescriber writes "dispense as written". Therapeutic substitution: dispensing a different drug of the same class; private pharmacists may not do this without the prescriber's permission, though managed-care organisations may follow other policies.

front: Complete: formulary committee measures against prescribing error
text: Pharmacy and Therapeutics committees have added safeguards such as a {{High-Alert Medication}} list (from ISMP) and the use of a {{comma}} when a dose exceeds 999; a hospital order that gives no duration runs until the prescriber stops it or a {{stop-order}} policy ends it.

front: How can a hospital use pharmacoeconomic analysis when it prepares its formulary?
back: It can apply pharmacoeconomic methods (cost-minimisation, cost-effectiveness, cost-benefit and cost-utility) to compare treatments when preparing its formulary of essential medicines. The same analysis helps decide and fix the prices of old and new drugs and supports reimbursement.

front: Define drug information and a drug information centre (DIC). How does a drug information service (DIS) differ?
back: Drug information is written or verbal information on the safe and effective use of therapeutic and diagnostic drugs, given in response to requests from health professionals, committees, patients or the public. PAHO describes a DIC as an operational unit giving objective, timely technical and scientific information on drugs. A DIS is part of a health institution's pharmaceutical services and answers only within that institution. WHO treats independent DICs as a core part of national programmes for rational drug use.

front: Short note: Objectives of a drug information centre

points: Keep an organised database on medicines and therapeutics for practitioners
Give accurate, unbiased medicines information to pharmacists, doctors and other professionals in hospital and community
Train pharmacy students as future medicines-information providers
Promote patient care through rational use of medicines

front: Classify: types of drug information centre
text: {{Hospital-based}} DICs answer in-house queries, help formulary decisions and the P&T committee, coordinate ADR reporting and monitor investigational drugs; {{industry-based}} DICs hold all data on their own products from early development, including unpublished documents; {{community-based}} DICs inform the public about drugs used in national programmes and build awareness.

front: Where and when did drug information centres begin globally and in India?
back: The first DIC opened in 1962 at the University of Kentucky Medical Centre. In India, the Karnataka State Pharmacy Council set up the first independent DIC in August 1997 (registered with IRDIS). WHO India, with the KSPC, then supported five more centres: Sirsa (Haryana), Raipur, Jaipur, Dibrugarh and Panaji.

Research, e.g. drug utilisation studies

front: What resources does a drug information centre need, and how is its independence protected?
back: Adequate staff for peak demand, a manager (recruitment, training, promotion, resources, data, quality, liaison), its own library plus electronic databases, basic facilities (phones, internet, computers with backup, photocopier), and specifically trained staff (communication, literature searching, critical analysis, writing, summarising conflicting data). Funding should be independent and stable; external money is accepted only if neutrality is guaranteed, and the service to enquirers should be free.

front: How is quality assured in a drug information centre?
back: By assessing staff, regularly reviewing calls and answers, periodically reviewing resources and procedures, peer review of a random sample of enquiries (ideally with an external drug-information pharmacist or clinical pharmacologist), and feedback from enquirers. Networking between centres allows shared resources, common SOPs, external quality review and inter-site training.

It may arise in prescribing, order communication, labelling, packaging, naming, compounding, dispensing, distribution, administration, education, monitoring or use. Most are latent errors, "accidents waiting to happen", whose causes can be found and fixed.

front: How common are medication errors compared with adverse drug events, and what approach reduces them?
back: They are estimated to be 50 to 100 times more common than adverse drug events. Reduction needs a system-based approach covering prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, administering and monitoring, with trained staff and mandatory, redundant checkpoints.

front: How is the medication error rate calculated, and what rate signals a systemic problem?
back: Number of errors observed divided by the opportunities for error (all doses observed being given plus doses ordered but not given), multiplied by 100. A rate of 5% or more indicates a systemic problem in the facility's drug distribution system.

Do not abbreviate drug names (e.g. AZT misread as azathioprine or aztreonam)

front: Define polypharmacy and distinguish appropriate from inappropriate polypharmacy.
back: Concurrent use of many medicines, commonly taken as five or more (some say six or more) a day. Appropriate: every drug serves an agreed therapeutic goal that is being or can be met, ADR risk is minimised and the patient is willing and able to take them. Inappropriate: one or more drugs are not or no longer needed because there is no evidence-based indication, the goal is not met, the drugs cause or risk ADRs, or the patient cannot or will not take them.

A cause of polypharmacy in which an adverse drug reaction is misread as a new illness and treated with another drug, exposing the patient to further adverse effects from an unnecessary medicine. Other causes include multiple diseases, multiple prescribers, transitions of care, poor diagnostic skill and self-medication with OTC products and supplements.

front: Define deprescribing and list its steps.
back: The systematic identification and withdrawal of drugs whose actual or potential harm outweighs benefit for that patient's goals, function, life expectancy, values and preferences. Steps: full medication reconciliation; estimate overall risk of drug harm; check each drug for eligibility to stop; prioritise; carry out the withdrawal plan and monitor for withdrawal effects. Tools include Medstopper and deprescribing.org guidelines.

text: Polypharmacy is commonly taken as {{five}} or more medicines a day; it is {{appropriate}} when every drug serves an agreed goal, and a {{prescribing cascade}} arises when an ADR is mistaken for a new illness and treated with another drug.

front: Classify: tools to detect inappropriate prescribing in older patients
text: {{Beers}} criteria list potentially inappropriate medicines in older persons by body system; {{STOPP}} screens older persons' prescriptions for inappropriate drugs; {{START}} alerts doctors to the right treatment that is missing; the {{Medication Appropriateness Index}} checks indication, effectiveness, dose, cost and duplication; {{anticholinergic burden}} scales add up anticholinergic load; {{ARMOR}} is a stepwise Assess-Review-Minimize-Optimize-Reassess approach.

front: Complete: SAIL and TIDE techniques to reduce polypharmacy
text: SAIL: keep the regimen {{Simple}}, know the {{Adverse effects}}, give every drug an {{Indication}}, and keep a shared {{List}}. TIDE: give enough {{Time}}, {{Individualise}} doses ("start low, go slow"), avoid {{Drug-drug and drug-disease interactions}}, and {{Educate}} patient and carer.

front: What is medication reconciliation, when is it done, and how?
back: Comparing the patient's new medication orders with everything the patient has been taking, to catch omissions, duplications, dosing errors and interactions. It is done at every transition of care (admission, transfer, discharge, change of prescriber) and at office visits. Steps: obtain the best possible medication history (e.g. "brown bag" review of all medicines brought in, confirmed with carers), list intended prescriptions, compare the two lists, decide on changes, and communicate the new regimen with counselling.

front: What are the goals of a hospital antimicrobial stewardship programme (ASP)?
back: ASPs are ongoing institutional efforts to optimise antimicrobial use in inpatients. Goals: achieve clinical cure while limiting toxicity and resistance by avoiding misuse and overuse; choose the right drug, dose, duration and route, and de-escalate in time; and cut costs without lowering quality of care. Appropriate prescribing and education of patients and doctors achieve these goals.

front: What is the pharmacologist's role in antibiotic policy?
back: The pharmacologist is a core member in formulating national drug policy and the hospital antibiotic policy; in hospitals the clinical pharmacologist drafts the antibiotic policy together with the clinical microbiologist and the head of critical care medicine.

front: What is an antibiotic "time out" and why is it done at 48 hours?
back: A planned reassessment of the need for and choice of an antibiotic about 48 hours after it was started. By then culture and clinical data are clearer, so therapy can be narrowed, switched to oral, or stopped, which limits toxicity and resistance.

back: The local antibiogram and the severity of illness.

front: What is a prescription (drug) audit and what does it aim to achieve?
back: A regular review of physicians' prescriptions, typically led by a pharmacologist, to check that therapy is safe, effective and affordable and that hospital practice is evidence-based. It aims to reduce polypharmacy, medication errors and cost to the patient. WHO includes supervision, audit and feedback among its key interventions for rational drug use.

front: Define compliance (adherence) and give the four types of noncompliance.
back: The extent to which patients follow treatment instructions. Noncompliance: (1) the prescription is never obtained (about one-third of patients in some studies); (2) the drug is taken wrongly (dose, frequency, timing, route, duplication, wrong purpose); (3) the drug is stopped early, e.g. when symptoms improve or the bottle is empty; (4) the drug is taken inappropriately, e.g. shared with others.

front: Which four WHO core prescribing indicators does a prescription audit measure?
back: Average number of drugs per encounter; percentage of drugs prescribed by generic name; percentage of encounters with antibiotic or injection use; percentage of drugs from the essential medicines list.

front: What is the audit cycle, and why must it be closed?
back: Set a standard, measure current prescribing against it, give feedback and make changes, then re-audit. The cycle is closed only when re-audit shows whether practice actually improved; an audit without feedback and re-audit changes nothing.

front: Short note: Method of a prescription audit

points: State the aim and the drugs or wards to be audited
Choose the standard: standard treatment guidelines, hospital formulary, WHO prescribing indicators, NMC prescription format

Obtain institutional ethics approval; keep patient and prescriber data confidential
Retrospective: prescriptions or case records from a past period
Prospective: prescriptions collected as they are written (OPD, pharmacy, ward)
Random or systematic sample over a defined period, large enough to be representative
Standard proforma for every prescription

front: Compare retrospective and prospective prescription audit.
back: Retrospective audit reviews prescriptions or case records already written in a past period; it is quick and cheap, and prescribers cannot change their behaviour, but records may be incomplete. Prospective audit collects prescriptions as they are written; data are more complete and errors can be corrected before harm, but prescribers who know they are watched may change their practice.

front: What are real-world data in drug-safety studies?
back: Routinely collected clinical or insurance records that hold drug exposures, medical encounters and patient comorbidities. Observational pharmacoepidemiology uses them; they are much less cumbersome than trials but still slow and costly to analyse.

front: What is the FDA Sentinel System?
back: A partnership between the FDA and more than 30 organisations, including academic sites and managed-care organisations, with curated electronic health data on over 100 million people. Each site analyses data behind its own firewall and returns results, using a common data model.

front: Which colour bag takes sharps such as needles, glass syringes and blades?

front: Which colour bag takes cytotoxic drug waste?
back: Violet bag: cytotoxic drugs and related waste, contaminated sharps, contaminated animal carcasses and cage linings.

front: Why is a chromate solution prohibited for cleaning lab glassware?
back: Chromates are extremely toxic, including carcinogenic, so their use for cleaning glassware is banned.

front: What is an R-factor, and how does it spread resistance?
back: A plasmid carrying resistance genes. It passes between bacteria mainly by conjugation through a sex pilus; transduction (via bacteriophage) also spreads it.

points: Antibiotics given when not needed kill sensitive bacteria and let resistant mutants multiply
Resistance spreads by R-factor plasmids, mainly by conjugation
Mechanisms: inactivating enzymes, altered target, reduced accumulation, altered metabolic pathway
Use antibiotics only when necessary; choose the right agent, dose and duration
Combine drugs where indicated, as in tuberculosis
Empiric therapy covers likely pathogens and is changed once culture results arrive

Aim: appropriate prescribing, less overuse, less spread of multidrug-resistant infection

front: Are compliance and adherence the same term?
back: The owner books use them as near-synonyms. GG12 lists compliance, adherence, therapeutic alliance and concordance together and says the collaborative doctor-patient relationship matters whichever word is used. Bennett keeps compliance because it also covers doctors who do not follow instructions, and notes that some prefer adherence or concordance, the latter reflecting prescribing by the doctor and taking by the patient.

front: What does GG12 mean by concordance or therapeutic alliance?
back: A collaborative relationship in which doctor and patient each bring expertise: the doctor is the medical expert and the patient is the expert on his own beliefs. The prescriber negotiates and asks whether the patient intends to follow the plan.

front: Which matters more for compliance: actual or perceived disease severity?
back: Perceived severity. Patients comply more when they feel susceptible to the disease, see it as serious, believe the therapy works, judge benefit to outweigh cost, and believe they can carry out the treatment. Actual severity does not predict compliance.

front: Why does the pharmacist matter for patient compliance?
back: Pharmacists often see the patient more often than the physician. Asking about therapy lets them spot noncompliance, educate the patient and inform the prescriber. GG12 cites the Asheville Project as showing better compliance, outcomes and cost with pharmacist-led medication management.

Bennett keeps compliance because the term also fits doctors who do not follow prescribing instructions
Bennett notes some prefer adherence or concordance; concordance reflects prescribing and taking as a therapeutic alliance
No owner book gives a strict definitional line between the terms
Intentional or accidental errors in dosage or schedule
Overuse or underuse
Early termination of therapy
Prescription never filled
Noncompliance is the most frequent cause of failure in antiseizure therapy (GG14)
Common cause of diuretic resistance in heart failure (GG12)
Clear, respectful communication; ask how the patient takes the drug
Simplify; match dosage form and schedule to daily routine
Compliance aids: sectioned boxes, compliance packaging, colour-coding

front: A patient misses the morning dose of a once-daily drug on workdays. What is the likely problem and fix?
back: Dosage or schedule error (timing). Fix: link the dose to a fixed daily cue, such as the coffee-cup cabinet or a meal, and tailor the schedule to the patient lifestyle. GG12 gives a morning-only drug for a night-shift worker as an example of a regimen that does not fit the patient.

front: Why are elderly patients at risk of noncompliance, and is age alone the cause?
back: Barriers include forgetfulness, altered drug handling, less social and financial support, poorer dexterity or senses, and more concurrent medicines. But GG12 states elderly patients are not generally less compliant than other age groups, so the barriers, not age itself, drive the risk.

front: Short note: Types of hospital formulary

points: A formulary is a list of medicine formulations, with varying amounts of added information.
It may list every nationally licensed medicine that health professionals can prescribe.
Or it may list only preferred drugs.
What a third-party payer will reimburse.
The range stocked in one hospital, chosen by its local drugs and therapeutics committee.
A range agreed by a partnership of general practitioners or a primary-care health centre.
Restricted lists aim to contain cost without impairing appropriate prescribing.

front: What is an 'escape clause' in a restricted formulary, and why is it needed?
back: A provision that lets a prescriber obtain a medicine outside the restricted list when a patient has a special need. Without it, a cost-driven list could deny appropriate treatment.

front: Which group chooses the medicines on a hospital formulary?
back: The local drugs and therapeutics committee. Every hospital or group of hospitals should have one, and its restricted list exists to keep costs down without impairing appropriate prescribing.

front: How does computerised prescribing help a prescriber stay within the formulary and prescribe safely?
back: It prompts regular review of the patient's medication list, converts a brand name to its generic name, and gives ready access to formularies and prescribing guidelines.

front: What proportion of family-practice prescriptions are repeats, and what safety concern follows?
back: About two-thirds. Half are issued by the doctor at a consultation and half by the practice nurse or receptionist without the patient seeing the doctor; 95% of requests are granted without further discussion, 25% of repeat patients have had 40 or more repeats, and 55% of patients older than 75 are on repeat medication. The concern is continuing a medicine without periodic review.

front: Why can under-prescribing be as harmful as over-prescribing?
back: Withholding effective treatment harms health. Reasons include lack of information or lack of will to use it, fear of blame for adverse reactions, and fear of sanctions against costly prescribing. Older doctors prescribe less often and at lower cost, but there is no evidence that their patients are worse off.

front: What is a drug compendium, and what are its three groups?
back: A book that is a source of drug information. The groups are official compendia (pharmacopoeia and drug formulary), non-official compendia (textbooks, journals and periodicals), and Medline, an electronic biomedical database. Official compendia are recognised by the government as legal standards.

front: What is the British Pharmaceutical Codex, and what gap does it fill?
back: Published by the Council of the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain. It describes drugs, other pharmaceutical substances and formulated products, and provides identity and purity standards for materials for which the British Pharmacopoeia has none.

front: What does Martindale The Complete Drug Reference cover?
back: A compendium published for over 120 years by the Royal Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain. It gives unbiased information on medicines used worldwide, including trade names and manufacturer contacts, and also covers plant drugs, diagnostic agents, radiopharmaceuticals, excipients, toxins and poisons. It summarises disease treatments and supports its information with references, systematic reviews, meta-analyses or evidence-based guidelines.

front: Which references give brand-level information on formulations, strengths, cost, dose, precautions, adverse effects and contraindications?
back: Physicians Desk Reference (PDR), Indian Drug Review (IDR), Monthly Index of Medical Specialities (MIMS) and the CIMS India website.

front: What is clinical pharmacy, and what does the clinical pharmacist do?
back: The science of drug formulations, their stability, shelf life and handling. It also covers educating the patient about adherence, counselling on how to take medicines, and monitoring drug therapy for errors. The clinical pharmacist works with the physician to optimise patient care.

front: In one survey of adverse drug events, how severe were they and how many were preventable?
back: 1% were fatal, 12% life-threatening, 30% serious and 57% significant. About half of the life-threatening and serious events were preventable. Among the life-threatening and serious events, prescribing accounted for one-half and administration for one-quarter.

front: What administration error rates are reported in hospital studies, and when do they rise?
back: 15-25%. Rates rise rapidly once four or more drugs are given together. Hospital inpatients receive about six drugs on average, and up to 20 during a stay is not rare.

front: Which simple intervention reduced inappropriate antimicrobial prescribing in hospital studies?
back: Merely supplying information did not change prescribing. Gently asking physicians to justify each prescription produced a marked fall in inappropriate prescribing.

front: Explain the 'Swiss cheese' model of medication error.
back: Each safeguard in the medication-use system is a slice with holes. A single error is usually caught by another check. An adverse event occurs only when holes in several safeguards line up and the error passes through all of them.

front: Distinguish passive from active prevention of medication error.
back: Passive prevention needs no change in the person's behaviour and is the most effective, for example child-resistant packaging, fewer tablets per bottle, or removing a harmful ingredient. Active prevention needs sustained behaviour change by the individual.

front: What is underdosing, and which drugs are most often underdosed?
back: Giving less than the optimal dose in serious illness to avoid adverse effects, which sacrifices efficacy. It is commonest with drugs of low therapeutic index, where effective and toxic dose ranges are close or overlap, such as heparin, anticancer drugs and aminoglycosides.

front: How is polypharmacy defined in Harrison, and how common is it in older Americans?
back: Prescription of multiple medicines, with thresholds generally from five to nine simultaneous drugs. About 40% of Americans aged 65 or older take five to nine medicines, and close to 20% take 10 or more.

front: Why is polypharmacy becoming more common?
back: Rising multimorbidity, a large number of condition-specific guidelines, more medicines that can treat common geriatric conditions, and growing patient and family demand partly driven by television advertising and internet information.

front: How many hospital admissions do adverse drug events cause each year, and which drugs are the main culprits?
back: More than 100,000 per year. The main culprits are warfarin and other antiplatelet agents, and insulin and other hypoglycaemic agents. Cardiovascular drugs (electrolyte and volume disturbance, hypotension, falls, syncope), central nervous system drugs (altered mental status, falls) and antimicrobials are also involved.

front: Short note: General recommendations for prescribing in older patients

points: Evaluate all conditions that could benefit from, be harmed by, or alter the response to drug treatment.
Manage without drugs as often as possible.
Know the pharmacology of the drug and how renal function and hydration affect it.
Avoid serious drug-drug interactions.
For renally cleared drugs, estimate creatinine clearance with Cockcroft-Gault and adjust the dose.
Start with smaller doses and increase gradually until effective or intolerable.
Use blood concentrations to monitor potentially toxic drugs.
Simplify the regimen and use the same dosing schedule for all drugs when feasible.
Time doses with the daily routine.
Account for cognitive impairment, poor hearing and poor vision.
Involve relatives, caregivers and pharmacists.
Check that the patient can reach a pharmacist, afford the medicines and open the container.
Use pillboxes and drug calendars.
Reconcile medicines and educate the patient and family at every hospital discharge.
Keep an updated medication record and review it at each visit.
Monitor adherence, effectiveness and adverse effects regularly.

front: What is the Cockcroft-Gault equation, and why is it used in older patients?
back: Estimated creatinine clearance = (140 - age) x body weight in kg / (72 x serum creatinine), multiplied by 0.85 for women. It tends to underestimate creatinine clearance, which probably makes it the safer formula for adjusting renally cleared drugs in older patients.

front: Short note: Commonly prescribed drugs to consider for deprescribing

points: Diuretics and hypotensive agents when systolic or postural hypotension causes near-syncope or falls.
Antianxiety and hypnotic drugs, especially benzodiazepines.
Psychotropic and other anticholinergic drugs, which cause dry mouth and constipation and raise long-term cognitive risk.
Proton pump inhibitors whose indication is unclear.
Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine after years of use in severe cognitive impairment.
Hypoglycaemic agents in multimorbidity where tight control risks hypoglycaemia.
Statins and prophylactic aspirin in severe chronic illness near the end of life.

front: What are the rates of non-redemption, partial adherence and over-compliance in Bennett?
back: In the UK about 5% of prescriptions are never redeemed, rising to 20% or more in the elderly. Once dispensed, 25-50% of patients take only 50-90% of the prescribed dose or none at all. Up to 20% over-comply, sometimes by 50%.

front: What is antimicrobial stewardship, and what four elements define appropriate therapy?
back: Promoting the choice of the appropriate antimicrobial drug, dosage, route and duration. Programmes use several strategies to improve care through appropriate use, preserve antimicrobials by curbing resistance, reduce adverse effects and control costs.

front: Short note: Three established strategies of an antimicrobial stewardship programme

points: Orders for broad-spectrum or high-cost agents are reviewed regularly by an infectious disease physician or pharmacist.
An alternative is recommended when use can be optimised.
Only a limited set of antimicrobials is included in the hospital formulary.
This limits indiscriminate use and unnecessary expenditure.
Clinicians must obtain approval before using selected antimicrobials.
Approval may be electronic through computerised order entry, after criteria are met, or after discussion with the programme's infectious disease specialist.

front: How does prospective audit and feedback work in an antimicrobial stewardship programme?
back: An infectious disease physician or pharmacist regularly reviews orders for broad-spectrum agents such as carbapenems, or drugs with cheaper alternatives such as daptomycin and ceftazidime-avibactam. When use can be improved, the team recommends an alternative. The approach has reduced broad-spectrum use and Clostridioides difficile infection.

front: Which additional strategies does a stewardship programme use beyond audit, restriction and preauthorization?
back: Guidelines and pathways, dose optimisation, parenteral-to-oral conversion, antibiotic time-out and de-escalation. Teams also encourage documentation of the indication for every antimicrobial and provide ongoing education.

front: What are the CDC's four core elements of outpatient antibiotic stewardship?
back: Ambulatory use accounts for about 85% of antibiotic use in most developed countries. The elements are: commit to improving prescribing; implement at least one policy or practice and assess its effectiveness; monitor prescribing and provide feedback; and provide educational resources to clinicians and patients.

Multifaceted interventions.
State a clear diagnosis.

Review the expected course of the illness.

front: What is an antibiogram, and which one should guide empirical antibiotic therapy?
back: A summary of local antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. The most recent local laboratory antibiogram, updated yearly or half-yearly, is the most useful guide; national resistance rates serve only as a reference. For hospital-acquired infection, the local ICU antibiogram is important.

front: Short note: Requirements of a prescription

points: What is to be given, to whom, and by whom prescribed.
How much, how often, by what route, and for how long or in what total quantity.
Date.

Patient's name and address; date of birth is desirable and is legally required for UK children under 12.
Name and dose of the medicine.

Prescriber's signature.
The format is regulated for precision, safety, efficacy and prevention of fraudulent misuse.
Use only official abbreviations; never invent an abbreviation.

front: What conventions does Bennett give for writing quantities on a prescription?
back: Write 1 g or more in grams; less than 1 g in milligrams (500 mg, not 0.5 g); less than 1 mg in micrograms (100 micrograms, not 0.1 mg). Put a zero before a decimal when no other figure precedes it. Do not abbreviate microgram, nanogram or unit; use millilitre, not cubic centimetre.

Directly observed therapy is the most accurate. Finding the drug or its metabolite in plasma is persuasive evidence of recent intake. Tablet counts are weak because a missing tablet need not have been swallowed. Diaries, compartmented boxes, electronic containers that record opening times and physiological markers such as heart rate with a beta-blocker can help.

front: How does growth hormone act, and why do its growth effects depend on IGF-1?
back: GH binds a JAK-STAT-linked cytokine-type receptor on most cells, which alters gene transcription. Its growth-promoting and nitrogen-retaining effects are mostly indirect, carried by IGF-1 (somatomedin), made mainly in the liver. GH itself promotes lipolysis and gluconeogenesis and reduces glucose uptake, so it raises blood glucose.

front: List the main therapeutic uses of somatropin (recombinant GH).
back: GH deficiency in children (pituitary dwarfism), Turner syndrome (with timed oestrogen and androgen), growth failure from chronic renal insufficiency in children, adult GH deficiency and AIDS-related wasting. Use in idiopathic short stature is debated, and its use by athletes is banned.

front: Why is native somatostatin unsuitable as a drug for acromegaly?
back: Its half-life is only 2 to 3 minutes. It is not selective: it also suppresses insulin, glucagon, TSH, gastrin and gut secretions. Stopping it causes GH rebound. Long-acting analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) are used instead.

front: What adverse effects limit somatropin therapy?
back: Injection-site pain and lipodystrophy, glucose intolerance, hypothyroidism (by unmasking central TSH deficiency), salt and water retention, myalgia, hand stiffness and headache. Intracranial pressure can rise in a few patients. Immunogenicity is low, so allergy and resistance are uncommon.

front: How does octreotide differ from somatostatin, and what are its uses?
back: A synthetic octapeptide about 40 times more potent than somatostatin at suppressing GH, with a half-life of about 90 minutes. It is only a weak inhibitor of insulin. Uses: acromegaly, secretory diarrhoea (carcinoid, AIDS, chemotherapy or diabetes related) and IV control of variceal bleeding. Adverse effects: gallstones, steatorrhoea and abdominal pain.

front: How does pegvisomant work, and when is it used?
back: It is a pegylated mutant GH. One of its two receptor-binding sites binds more tightly and the other more weakly than native GH, so it allows receptor dimerisation but blocks the conformational change needed for signalling: a GH receptor antagonist. Pegylation slows clearance. Daily s.c. treatment normalises IGF-1 in most patients with acromegaly. It does not reduce GH secretion (GH levels may rise), so response is followed by IGF-1. KDT lists it for acromegaly due to small adenomas; it is used when GH excess persists after surgery.

front: What controls prolactin secretion, and which drugs raise prolactin levels?
back: Dopamine (prolactin-inhibiting factor) keeps prolactin low by acting on D2 receptors of lactotrope cells. Dopamine blockers (chlorpromazine, haloperidol, metoclopramide) and the dopamine-depleting drug reserpine raise prolactin. Suckling keeps levels high after delivery, and prolactinomas are a common cause of hyperprolactinaemia.

text: Cabergoline is the {{first-choice}} agent, given {{twice weekly}}; {{bromocriptine}} is the older ergot-derived drug that has largely been replaced.

front: Why does a dopamine antagonist such as haloperidol or metoclopramide raise prolactin?
back: Prolactin is held in check mainly by hypothalamic dopamine acting on D2 receptors of pituitary lactotropes. Blocking those receptors removes the brake, so prolactin rises.

front: What clinical syndrome does excess prolactin cause in women and in men?
back: Women: galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and infertility. Men: loss of libido, impotence and sterility, with possible gynaecomastia. These are the features that a D2 agonist is used to reverse.

front: Which common adverse effect limits bromocriptine, and which newer D2 agonist causes less of it?
back: Nausea and vomiting. Cabergoline, a newer D2 agonist that is more potent and longer acting, causes less nausea and vomiting.

front: A woman with galactorrhoea-amenorrhoea and a microprolactinoma wants to conceive. Which drug would you choose and why, and how long does the response last?
back: Cabergoline: it is the first choice, being more potent and selective for lactotrope D2 receptors, longer acting (about twice weekly dosing) and causing less nausea than bromocriptine. Prolactin normalises in 2-4 weeks and many women conceive within a year; stop it once pregnancy occurs. Most micro- and some macroprolactinomas regress.

front: Why is pulsatile GnRH stimulating but sustained GnRH exposure suppressing?
back: Only intermittent pulses of GnRH drive FSH/LH release. Continuous exposure suppresses gonadotropin release, which is why long-acting GnRH analogues are used to suppress the axis.

front: What is the half-life of native GnRH and what is it used for diagnostically?
back: Very short (about 4-8 minutes) because of rapid enzymatic breakdown. Given i.v. it prompts LH/FSH release and is used to test the pituitary-gonadal axis in hypogonadism.

front: Outline the steps in thyroid hormone synthesis and where TSH acts.
back: Iodide is trapped by the Na+/iodide symporter, a step TSH increases. Thyroid peroxidase oxidises it (using H2O2) and attaches it to tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin as MIT and DIT. Coupling of two DIT gives T4; MIT plus DIT gives T3. Stored colloid is re-endocytosed and proteolysed, releasing T4 and T3; MIT and DIT are deiodinated and the iodide reused. TSH stimulates trapping, organification, coupling and release.

front: Why is T4 called a prohormone of T3?
back: T4 is secreted in larger amounts and is bound much more tightly to plasma proteins, so it acts as a circulating reserve. About a third of T4 is converted to T3 by deiodinases in the liver, kidney and target tissues. T3 is the active form: it binds the nuclear receptor more strongly, acts faster and is about five times more potent.

front: Classify: thyroid hormone transport in plasma
text: Thyroid hormones are bound to {{TBG}} (highest affinity), then {{transthyretin}}, then {{albumin}}; only about {{0.03 to 0.08 percent}} of T4 circulates free.

front: Which deiodinase is inhibited by propylthiouracil, and which antiarrhythmic inhibits both D1 and D2?
back: Propylthiouracil inhibits type 1 deiodinase (D1), found mainly in liver, kidney and thyroid, but not D2. Amiodarone inhibits both D1 and D2. Carbimazole does not. High-dose propranolol and glucocorticoids also reduce T4 to T3 conversion, except in brain and pituitary.

front: How do thyroid hormones increase heart rate and contractility?
back: They act directly on the heart by increasing the myosin isoform with higher Ca2+-ATPase activity. They also raise beta-adrenergic receptor numbers and coupling, so catecholamines have a greater effect. The result is tachycardia, a bounding pulse, higher systolic pressure and atrial fibrillation. Thyroid hormones can also precipitate heart failure or angina.

front: Why is levothyroxine preferred over liothyronine?
back: Liothyronine (T3) acts faster, but its action is short and it carries a higher risk of arrhythmia and angina. Levothyroxine gives a more sustained and uniform effect, and its oral bioavailability is about 75 percent. Liothyronine is not freely available in India and is used IV with T4 only in selected cases such as myxoedema coma.

A medical emergency, best managed in intensive care, as intubation and ventilation may be needed. Give everything IV because absorption by other routes is poor. Drug of choice is an IV loading dose of levothyroxine (Katzung: 300 to 400 µg; KDT: 200 to 500 µg), then 50 to 100 µg IV daily until oral therapy is possible. IV T3 can be added, but it is more cardiotoxic; use lower doses in older or cardiac patients. Give IV hydrocortisone if adrenal or pituitary insufficiency may coexist, give IV fluids cautiously (risk of water intoxication), and treat the precipitating infection or heart failure.

front: Which drugs reduce levothyroxine absorption, and which speed its clearance?
back: Absorption is reduced by sucralfate, iron, calcium and proton pump inhibitors, and by food, so levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach. Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) speed T4 metabolism and may need a higher dose. Severe hypothyroidism itself reduces absorption.

front: When is subclinical hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine?
back: Subclinical hypothyroidism means raised TSH with normal thyroid hormone levels. Treatment is individualised. Levothyroxine is generally advised when TSH is above 10 mU/L. For milder TSH elevations, close TSH monitoring is appropriate; KDT adds that treatment for TSH 6 to 10 mU/L is optional and preferable if cardiovascular risk factors are present.

front: What is the pathogenesis of Graves' disease, and why is TSH low in it?
back: An IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin binds the TSH receptor and drives long-lasting thyroid stimulation. The excess hormone suppresses TSH through negative feedback. Stimulation of TSH receptors in periorbital tissue appears to cause exophthalmos. Toxic nodular goitre is TSH-independent, is more common in older people and usually lacks eye signs.

front: Name drugs that cause hypothyroidism or goitre, and the mechanism of each.

front: How do type 1 and type 2 diabetes differ in cause and insulin levels?
back: Type 1 results from loss of beta cells, usually autoimmune, so circulating insulin is low or absent and ketosis is common. Type 2 involves insulin resistance with impaired beta-cell secretion; insulin levels are normal or high and genetic predisposition is strong. Type 2 accounts for over 90 percent of cases.

front: How does glucose trigger insulin release from beta cells?
back: Glucose is phosphorylated by glucokinase and metabolised, which raises ATP. ATP closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels, depolarising the cell. Calcium enters and insulin granules undergo exocytosis. Oral glucose gives a stronger response than IV glucose because gut incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify secretion.

front: Why must insulin be injected, and what is its plasma half-life?
back: Insulin is a peptide that is broken down in the gut, so it is ineffective orally. It is distributed only in extracellular fluid, and its plasma half-life is about 5 to 9 minutes. Nearly half of pancreatic insulin is cleared by the liver on first pass.

front: What are the onset, peak and duration of regular insulin, and how should it be timed?
back: Onset within 30 minutes; peak about 2 to 3 hours and duration 6 to 8 hours (KDT). Katzung gives peak about 2 h and 5 to 7 h duration. Because absorption from the s.c. site is slow, it is optimally injected about 1 hour before a meal (KDT); injected just before eating it gives early post-meal hyperglycaemia and late hypoglycaemia. It is unsuitable for basal cover. Given IV its action is prompt, and it is the insulin used for IV infusion in DKA.

front: Classify: insulins by duration of action
text: Rapid: {{lispro}}, {{aspart}}, {{glulisine}}. Short: {{regular}}. Intermediate: {{NPH (isophane)}} and {{lente}}. Long: {{glargine}}, {{detemir}}, {{degludec}}.

front: Name the rapid-acting insulin analogues and how they are timed.
back: Insulin lispro (B28 and B29 residues reversed), insulin aspart (B28 proline replaced by aspartate) and insulin glulisine. They act within about 15 minutes, peak at 1 to 2 hours and last 3 to 5 hours. Lispro is given 0 to 20 minutes before a meal, giving better meal-time control and fewer late hypoglycaemic episodes than regular insulin.

front: What is insulin glargine, and how is it given?
back: A long-acting analogue that forms a depot after injection and releases a steady, peakless level for up to 24 hours. It is given once daily, often at bedtime, for basal cover; it does not control meal-time glucose. It is acidic and cannot be mixed with other insulins. It causes fewer night-time hypoglycaemic episodes than NPH.

back: A humanised monoclonal antibody against CD3, the main signalling part of the T-cell receptor, which modulates the autoimmune attack on beta cells. front: Metformin: what is its main site of action and role of AMPK?
back: It acts mainly by suppressing hepatic glucose output, the major glucose-lowering effect, and improves glucose uptake in muscle and fat. AMPK activation, an indirect consequence of interference with cellular respiration, appears to mediate these actions. It needs insulin to be present, so it does not work in type 1 diabetes.

front: Why is metformin avoided in renal insufficiency, and what other adverse effect occurs with prolonged high doses?
back: It is excreted unchanged by the kidney, so it accumulates in renal failure and the risk of lactic acidosis rises (also avoided in heart failure, hypotension, severe hepatic or respiratory disease and alcoholics). High doses can impair vitamin B12 absorption. Hypoglycaemia is rare, so it is called euglycaemic.

front: What is the mechanism of metformin's glucose-lowering effect?
back: Metformin does not stimulate insulin release, but it needs insulin to act. Its main effect is suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and glucose output, through AMPK activation that follows changes in cellular energy status. It also improves insulin-mediated glucose uptake in muscle and fat, and slightly reduces intestinal glucose absorption.

front: How do sulfonylureas lower blood glucose, and why is hypoglycaemia their main risk?
back: They bind the SUR1 subunit of the beta-cell KATP channel and close it. Depolarisation and calcium influx increase insulin release, mainly the second phase, and this happens even at low glucose. Because insulin is released regardless of meals, they can cause severe, unpredictable hypoglycaemia. They need functioning beta cells, so they do not work in type 1 diabetes.

front: How do DPP-4 inhibitors lower blood glucose?
back: They block DPP-4, the enzyme that breaks down GLP-1 and GIP, so incretin levels rise. This increases glucose-dependent insulin release and reduces glucagon, so hypoglycaemia risk is low and the drugs are weight neutral. Vildagliptin and saxagliptin bind DPP-4 covalently; sitagliptin binds without a covalent bond. Adverse effects: nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory infection, hypersensitivity (angioedema, Stevens-Johnson syndrome), possible pancreatitis, joint pains; saxagliptin and alogliptin have been linked to heart failure.

front: How do GLP-1 receptor agonists lower glucose, and what are their main adverse effects?
back: Exenatide is based on exendin-4, a lizard peptide that DPP-4 does not degrade. Liraglutide is GLP-1 with a C16 fatty acid chain; albumin binding hinders DPP-4 access and slows absorption, giving a half-life of about 12 hours and once-daily dosing (GG14 calls it DPP-4 resistant). Semaglutide is resistant through a position-2 substitution and binds albumin tightly (half-life 7 days; weekly injection or daily oral form). All act on GLP-1 receptors: glucose-dependent insulin release, less glucagon, slower gastric emptying and less appetite, so weight falls. Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; pancreatitis risk; avoid with medullary thyroid carcinoma (GLP-1 receptors on C cells).

front: How do SGLT-2 inhibitors act, and what are their main safety concerns?
back: They block SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, lowering the renal threshold for glucose and causing glycosuria. This lowers HbA1c by about 0.5 to 1%, with weight loss and little hypoglycaemia. They reduce heart failure hospitalisation and slow diabetic kidney disease, so they are used early in patients with cardiovascular disease, heart failure or nephropathy. Risks: genital mycotic and urinary infections, volume depletion and hypotension, ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose. Glucose-lowering efficacy falls with renal impairment: not recommended for glycaemic control below eGFR 45 and contraindicated below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.

front: How does pioglitazone work, and what limits its use?
back: It is a PPAR-gamma agonist acting mainly in fat and muscle, where it enhances insulin-responsive gene expression and GLUT4 translocation. It improves insulin sensitivity without raising insulin levels, and it lowers triglycerides and raises HDL. Limitations: fluid retention, weight gain, heart failure, fractures and the need for liver monitoring. A possible bladder cancer link has been reported, though large studies disagree. It is contraindicated in heart failure and liver disease.

front: Tirzepatide: what is it, and how does it compare with GLP-1 agonists?
back: A dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist, built on the GIP sequence with a fatty diacid chain that binds albumin, allowing once-weekly s.c. injection. Starts at 2.5 mg weekly, goes to 5 mg after 4 weeks, then rises in 2.5 mg steps every 4 weeks up to 15 mg. It lowered HbA1c by about 1.9 to 2.6% with weight loss of about 6 to 13 kg, and improved lipids, blood pressure and fatty liver. Safety resembles GLP-1 agonists: dose-related nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, and a slightly higher pancreatitis rate.

front: How do you treat an episode of insulin-induced hypoglycaemia?
back: Give 15 to 20 g of oral glucose or sugar, and repeat after 15 to 20 minutes if there is no improvement. In severe cases give 30 to 50 mL of 50 percent glucose IV over about 10 minutes. If the patient cannot take sugar and IV glucose is not available, glucagon 0.5 to 1 mg can be given as a stopgap; a 3 mg nasal glucagon device is now available. KDT also lists adrenaline 0.2 mg s.c. as a less desirable option. Continue oral carbohydrate because hypoglycaemia may recur.

text: {{Insulin}} is the drug of choice for diabetes in pregnancy. {{Metformin}} has been shown to be safe and effective in gestational diabetes, though it is not FDA-approved for it. {{Pioglitazone}} should not be used in pregnancy, and the safety of {{sulfonylureas}} is not established, so patients are switched to insulin.

front: What are the two groups of symptoms of insulin-induced hypoglycaemia?
back: Counter-regulatory sympathetic symptoms (sweating, anxiety, palpitation, tremor) and neuroglucopenic symptoms (dizziness, headache, behaviour change, visual disturbance, hunger, weakness, incoordination). Below about 40 mg/dl confusion, seizures and coma occur. Beta-blockers mask the sympathetic warning signs.

front: Which precipitating factors cause hypoglycaemia in a patient on insulin?
back: Inadvertent large dose, a missed meal after injection, and vigorous exercise; also labile diabetes. Acute alcohol intake can precipitate it by depleting hepatic glycogen.

front: How is insulin given in diabetic ketoacidosis?
back: Regular insulin IV only, alongside aggressive IV hydration (normal saline first) and potassium replacement. The usual starting infusion is about 0.1 U/kg/h; KDT precedes it with an IV bolus of 0.1 to 0.2 U/kg and doubles the rate if glucose has not fallen significantly in 2 hours (a fall of about 10% per hour is adequate). When glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL (usually in 4 to 6 h), KDT reduces the infusion to 2 to 3 U/h and adds 5% glucose, continuing until the patient is fully conscious and can start s.c. insulin.

back: Large amounts of K+ are lost in urine, but serum K+ stays near normal as intracellular stores exchange. Once insulin starts, K+ is driven back into cells and dangerous hypokalaemia can occur, so KCl is added after 2-3 hours.

front: Why is propranolol given in thyrotoxic crisis?
back: Non-selective beta blocker: fast relief of sympathetic symptoms (palpitation, tremor, sweating, nervousness). High doses also reduce peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.

front: What does iodide do in thyrotoxic crisis?
back: Stops further release of preformed T3 and T4 from the gland and reduces T4 to T3 conversion. It is used alongside an antithyroid drug and propranolol, not alone.

front: Why do alloxan and streptozotocin rodent models not suit NIDDM screening?
back: Alloxan and streptozotocin models mainly reproduce type 1-like diabetes. NIDDM screening uses models such as neonatal STZ or NAD-STZ, which resemble type 2 insulin secretion.

front: How does alloxan cause experimental diabetes?
back: It is a redox cycle with dialuric acid that generates superoxide radicals, which dismute to hydrogen peroxide and destroy the beta cells.

front: What does streptozotocin do to beta cells in experimental animals?
back: It destroys pancreatic beta cells by necrosis, so it induces type 1-like diabetes in animals.

front: What does nicotinamide do in the NAD-STZ model?

front: What did the Nuremberg Code establish?
back: Drawn up in 1947 after unethical experiments on prisoners in Nazi camps during World War II, it established that research subjects must give informed consent and must be free to withdraw from an experiment at any time.

front: What is the Declaration of Helsinki and why does it matter for trials?
back: A statement of ethical principles for medical research on human subjects, issued by the World Medical Association in 1964 and regularly updated. It sets the widely accepted ground rules for human research and forms the ethical base of ICH-GCP: trials must be conducted according to its principles.

front: What do the CIOMS guidelines add to the Declaration of Helsinki?
back: The Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (guidelines first published 1993) gives detailed guidance on applying Helsinki to present-day research: HIV/AIDS research, post-study availability of treatment, women as subjects, confidentiality, compensation for adverse events and consent, while avoiding unnecessary suffering and weighing risk against benefit.

front: How do the Nuremberg Code and the Declaration of Helsinki differ in origin and standing?
back: Nuremberg Code (1947) arose from the Nazi-camp experiments and laid down informed consent and the right to withdraw. Helsinki (1964, World Medical Association) is a regularly updated statement for research on human subjects and is the ethical base of ICH-GCP, so trials must follow it.

front: How does GG14 use the Belmont Report's justice principle in the debate on foreign drug trials?
back: The Belmont Report says research should not unduly involve groups unlikely to benefit from its later applications. Some ethicists argue that testing drugs abroad in populations who cannot afford the approved product breaches this principle. Defenders reply that such trials also bring medical care to underserved people.

front: Complete: the four principles of medical ethics (Beauchamp and Childress)
text: {{Autonomy}}: the person's right to make choices and hold views; {{beneficence}}: do good and contribute to welfare; {{non-maleficence}}: do no intentional harm; {{justice}}: treat everyone equally and share benefits fairly.

front: What are the cardinal principle and the principle of precaution in research on human participants?
back: The cardinal principle is respect for the dignity of persons. Precaution and risk minimisation require care at every stage so that participants and affected communities face minimum risk and no known irreversible harm. All guidelines demand both ethical and scientific review and informed consent.

front: How do ICH-GCP and WHO-GCP differ?
back: ICH-GCP was designed to harmonise technical requirements for drug registration across the US, Japan and EU and has 13 principles. WHO-GCP was written as a teaching tool for countries without their own guideline and has 14 principles (its principles 5 and 6 are combined in ICH-GCP). Both aim to promote good clinical practice.

front: What are the Indian GCP guidelines and what is the principle of essentiality?
back: CDSCO set up an expert committee that produced India's first GCP document in 2001, modelled on WHO, US FDA, ICH and EU guidelines. It lists 10 ethical principles in line with Helsinki, including informed consent, community agreement, non-exploitation, privacy and confidentiality, risk minimisation, and accountability and transparency of investigators and sponsors. Essentiality means human subjects should be used only when absolutely necessary and no alternative exists. The NDCT Rules 2019 define "GCP guidelines" as the CDSCO guidelines adopted by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board.

front: What role do the ICMR ethical guidelines play in Indian research?
back: ICMR issued Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human Subjects in 2000, with planned periodic revision to keep researchers updated on bioethics. Ethics committees for biomedical and health research (as opposed to drug trials) are constituted under ICMR's National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants. Standard guidelines also make studies comparable across centres and help prevent duplicated research.

front: What kinds of ongoing review does an ethics committee carry out after approval?
back: Periodic review of ongoing research at intervals of 6 months to 1 year; continuing review of any new information and adverse events; and interim review in special circumstances by a sub-committee, re-examined by the full committee as needed (e.g. quarterly).

front: What decisions can an ethics committee reach, and how are records kept?
back: Approval (only minor changes), approval with modifications, resubmission with more information, or outright disapproval. Decisions are preferably by consensus; invited subject experts give opinions but do not decide. Minutes are approved and signed by the chair, documents are confidential, and records are kept for 5 years after the trial ends.

front: What is clinical equipoise and why does it matter ethically?
back: Genuine uncertainty among experts about which treatment is better. It justifies randomising patients, because the trial is done precisely because doubt exists. Placebo-controlled trials are argued to violate equipoise and the principle of beneficence when a proven effective therapy is already available.

front: What does the Declaration of Helsinki say about placebo controls?
back: It discourages placebo controls when an alternative treatment is available, since patients randomised to placebo would in effect be denied treatment; every patient, including controls, should get the best proven methods and not suffer unnecessary pain. Where an available treatment prevents death or irreversible harm, a placebo control is generally inappropriate.

front: What must the consent form of a placebo-controlled trial tell participants?
back: What "placebo" means, in lay language; that they may receive it; why a placebo is used and what alternatives exist; how long they may be on placebo and the likely discomfort; the harm of not receiving or delaying effective treatment and that the condition may worsen; and that they may withdraw at any time.

front: Short note: When is a placebo-controlled trial ethically justified?

points: No proven or approved therapy exists

Existing therapy prevents death or irreversible morbidity
Add-on design so all receive standard care
Minimal placebo exposure; early-escape and withdrawal rules
Smaller placebo arm; DSMB interim review

front: When is it ethical to use a placebo in clinical practice?
back: Only with the patient's welfare as the sole motive, to relieve suffering, when the condition has an unpredictable course, standard treatment fails or is not tolerated, or no effective therapy exists. It must never replace effective treatment, must be stopped if ineffective, and the doctor should answer honestly if asked about it; if it helps and nothing better exists, stopping it is unethical.

front: What is a conflict of interest in research, and how should a reader handle it?
back: A situation where personal factors (e.g. funding or financial gain) could influence professional judgement or responsibilities. Such conflicts are common; what matters is whether they were recognised and managed. When appraising a paper, check the declared funding source and any statement on how a conflict was handled. Ethics committee members must also declare conflicts.

front: How does ICD-11 define burnout, and what are its three dimensions?
back: A syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, marked by (1) exhaustion or energy depletion, (2) mental distance from the job, negativism or cynicism, and (3) reduced professional efficacy.

front: Who described the standard features of burnout, and what is the traffic-light model for?
back: Christina Maslach and colleagues described the standard features in the 1970s. The traffic-light model gives a stepwise, colour-coded way to recognise and assess medical burnout: stop and recognise, pause and find causes, then start coping and treatment.

front: Why must burnout prevention in doctors include system-level changes and not only individual help?
back: Main causes are workplace factors (long hours, night duty, administrative load, poor teamwork, lack of reward, autonomy, resources). Individual measures such as mindfulness help, but cannot remove these causes, so system changes (e.g. flexible schedules) are needed as well. Untreated burnout raises medical errors and makes doctors leave practice.

front: A resident on repeated night duty shows exhaustion, cynicism and a medication error. Analyse using burnout concepts.
back: These are the ICD-11 dimensions of burnout (exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism, reduced efficacy), and the error is the consequence the text links to burnout. Use the traffic-light steps: recognise, find causes (night duty, workload, poor support), then start coping measures. Prevention needs system change such as flexible schedules, with mindfulness as a supplement.

front: What is the pharmacologist's role in medical education?

front: What is a drug and therapeutics committee (DTC)?
back: A body set up in districts and hospitals to promote rational drug use, one of the WHO key interventions. A hospital pharmacologist may act as its convener.

front: What does a DTC formulate for a hospital?
back: Policies for prescribing, storing and safely dispensing drugs, a hospital formulary, and hospital antibiotic policy (with the clinical microbiologist and the head of critical care). Purpose: rational and safe use of medicines.

The science and activities of detecting, assessing, understanding and preventing adverse drug effects or other drug-related problems (WHO definition). Its aim is to make drugs safer by monitoring adverse reactions.

front: What is a signal in pharmacovigilance?
back: Reported information on a possible causal link between a drug and an adverse event whose link was unknown or incompletely documented before. Early detection lets regulators act on it.

front: How is causality of an adverse drug event judged?
back: By temporal relation to the drug, previous knowledge of the reaction, dechallenge (it settles when the drug stops) and rechallenge (it returns on re-exposure, often unethical to test). Graded definite, probable, possible or doubtful. It separates drug-caused events from events caused by the disease.

front: Which scales do pharmacovigilance centres use to score ADR causality and severity?
back: The Naranjo algorithm for causality and the modified Hartwig scale for severity grading.

front: Why can spontaneous reporting not give the true incidence of an ADR?
back: The numerator (affected patients) and denominator (patients exposed) are unknown, and underreporting is substantial, so reports only flag possible signals.

front: What is the FDA Sentinel System?
back: A partnership of the FDA with many organisations that uses curated electronic health data for observational pharmacoepidemiologic studies of possible safety signals.

front: Short note: Methods of signal detection in pharmacovigilance

points: Spontaneous (voluntary) reports, e.g. UK Yellow Card and Indian ADR forms
Prescription-event monitoring and case reports in the literature
Relevance: new drug (4 years from approval), unknown reaction, serious reaction
Identify duplicate reports using sex, age or date of birth, and exposure dates
Causality assessment must validate the link before a case counts
Controlled observational studies, e.g. pharmacoepidemiology and the Sentinel System
Post-marketing trials, used sparingly because of ethical limits
Case reports suffice for rare events close in time to exposure, with a large excess risk
Signals go to the regulator (CDSCO and the national PvPI in India)
Action: label change, restriction or withdrawal

front: Elixir sulfanilamide disaster: which solvent caused the deaths, and what did US law change?
back: Diethylene glycol, an antifreeze, was used as the solvent, and more than 100 children died. The 1938 amendment to the US Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act then required toxicity studies and approval of a New Drug Application before marketing, but still did not require proof of efficacy.

front: What did the Harris-Kefauver amendments of 1962 require?
back: Passed after the thalidomide disaster. Proof of efficacy as well as documentation of relative safety by risk-to-benefit assessment before approval. They also introduced informed consent of trial participants, gave the FDA authority over prescription-drug advertising, and introduced good manufacturing practice standards.

front: Thalidomide: original use, trade name and the defect it caused
back: A hypnotic marketed in West Germany in 1957 as Contergan and used for morning sickness in pregnancy. Early intrauterine exposure caused phocomelia, with malformed or absent limbs.

front: What did the US FDA Amendments Act of 2007 add for drug safety?
back: It let the FDA require risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS) and postapproval studies, and set up a population-based surveillance system. REMS is one of three regulatory tools for changing prescribing behaviour, with communication and withdrawal.

front: Tuskegee syphilis study: who was studied, for how long, and why does it matter?
back: The US Public Health Service ran the Tuskegee syphilis study in Black men from 1932 to 1972. It is described as the most infamous example of medical experimentation in Black communities and left a lasting legacy of mistrust of health care and research.

An international ethical and scientific quality standard for designing, conducting, monitoring, auditing, recording, analysing and reporting clinical trials in human participants, ensuring their rights, safety and confidentiality and the credibility of trial data.

front: Which five parties does Katzung list as the stakeholders in GCP?
back: The sponsor, investigator, study participant, regulatory authority and ethics committee.

front: Short note: Katzung list of seven principles of good clinical practice

points: Conduct must follow the Declaration of Helsinki and be consistent with GCP

front: What does an IRB or IEC decide about a research proposal, and on what grounds?
back: It may approve, require modification of, or disapprove the research after judging that risks are minimised, risks are reasonable against benefit and scientific gain, subject selection is equitable, consent is effective, and vulnerable groups are safeguarded.

front: What membership does an IRB or IEC require?
back: At least five members of varied background, including at least one with primary expertise in a scientific area, one in a non-scientific area, and one not affiliated with the institution. Many also include clergy, social workers and attorneys. This lets the board judge protocols against law, professional standards and community attitudes.

front: How is an informed consent form signed and witnessed?
back: It records the study title, the subject initials and identifiers, consent statements initialled by the volunteer, the subject signature or thumb impression, the legally acceptable representative, the investigator signature and name, and the witness signature and name.

front: What does an investigator undertake in the investigator undertaking?
back: A legal commitment to conduct the trial under GCP and the approval conditions. Not to begin before ethics committee and DCGI approval, to adhere to the protocol under personal supervision, to ensure ethics review, to report unexpected serious adverse events to the sponsor within 24 hours and to the ethics committee within 7 days, and to maintain records for audit.

front: What is an academic clinical trial under the NDCT Rules 2019?
back: A trial of a drug already approved for a claim, started by an investigator or academic or research institution for a new indication, route, dose or dosage form, whose results are intended only for academic or research use and not for marketing approval.

front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define a serious adverse event?
back: An untoward medical occurrence during a trial causing death, permanent disability, hospitalisation or prolongation of hospitalisation, persistent or significant disability, congenital anomaly or birth defect, or a life-threatening event.

front: Under the NDCT Rules 2019, what affiliations must the chairperson and member secretary of a trial ethics committee have?
back: The chairperson must be a member not affiliated with the institute, while the member secretary must be a member affiliated with the institute.

front: What qualifications and training does the NDCT Rules 2019 require of ethics committee members?
back: Medical scientist and clinician members must have a postgraduate qualification, adequate experience and clarity of role. Every member must complete training specified by the Central Licensing Authority, and an untrained member ceases to hold office.

front: How does a trial ethics committee handle a member's conflict of interest under the NDCT Rules 2019?
back: No member with a conflict may take part in oversight of that protocol. All members sign a declaration, a conflicted member may withdraw in writing, and the conflict is recorded in the minutes.

front: Short note: Functions of a trial ethics committee under the NDCT Rules 2019

points: Review and approve the protocol and related documents
Oversee conduct to protect the rights, safety and well-being of trial subjects
Review at appropriate intervals using progress reports, monitoring or audit reports, or site visits
Record in writing the reasons for rejection or for requiring a protocol change, with a copy to the Central Licensing Authority
Keep records for five years after completion
Analyse serious adverse event documents and forward its report to the Central Licensing Authority
Order discontinuation or suspension if rights, safety or well-being are compromised
Allow authorised officers to inspect premises, records and documents

front: What happens if the Central Licensing Authority does not respond to an ethics committee registration application within 45 working days?
back: The registration is deemed granted and legally valid, and the applicant must inform the Authority in Form CT-02A before starting the committee functions. A rejection can be appealed within 60 working days.

front: How long is registration of an ethics committee for biomedical and health research valid?
back: Provisional registration is valid for two years. Final registration in Form CT-03 is valid for five years, and renewal is applied for at least 90 days before expiry.

front: How did the old Schedule Y ethics committee composition differ from ICH-GCP?
back: Schedule Y required at least seven members, while ICH-GCP required at least five including one non-scientific member. Indian GCP recommended a fairly small committee of 5 to 7 members, with 12 to 15 as the maximum.

points: An inert substance given as if it were a medicine

It therefore has a very limited role in practical therapeutics

front: Why is uncertainty about comparative safety not the same as clinical equipoise?
back: In a postmarketing comparison of two marketed drugs, entering the trial when one may carry a serious adverse effect means accepting increased risk with no expectation of added benefit. True equipoise requires genuine uncertainty about which treatment is better.

front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define post-trial access?
back: Making a new or investigational drug available to a trial subject after the trial, when the drug was found beneficial to that subject, for the period considered necessary by the investigator and ethics committee.

front: What three principles does the Charter on Medical Professionalism set out?
back: The primacy of patient welfare, patient autonomy, and social justice.

front: Short note: Qualities of a humane physician

points: Being available and expressing sincere concern
Taking time to explain all aspects of the illness
Dealing without judgement when culture, lifestyle, attitudes or values differ
Monitoring one own strong positive or negative reactions
Keeping the patient best interest as the motive
Appreciating what each patient values most
Learnt through deliberate, unhurried and repeated conversation

front: What must a physician discuss for informed consent in clinical care?
back: The alternatives for care, and the risks, benefits and likely consequences of each. The physician must ensure the patient understands, encourage questions, and have no real or apparent conflict of interest.

front: What are the steps of shared decision-making?
back: Inform and educate the patient, discuss the nature, risks, benefits and alternatives of care and their consequences, answer questions, check understanding, make a recommendation, and help the patient deliberate.

front: Define moral distress and name its consequences.
back: Distress when ethically appropriate action is hindered by institutional policy or culture, hierarchy, limited resources or other constraints. It can cause anger, anxiety, depression, frustration, fatigue, work dissatisfaction and burnout.

front: What is a just culture in response to medical errors?
back: A system that encourages open, honest reporting of errors as essential to learning and shifts focus from individual blame to system design. Professional discipline is still used for gross incompetence, recklessness, impairment or boundary violations.

front: How should conflicts of interest be managed?
back: Recognise them, disclose them, discuss with the chief of service, and manage or recuse as appropriate. Not all conflicts are financial, since conflicts of commitment can also arise.

front: What rules now apply to gifts from pharmaceutical companies to physicians?
back: Accepting gifts from drug companies is forbidden at many academic medical centres and by law in several US states. The federal Open Payments website lists payments and amounts given to named physicians.

front: What are the five goals of MD Pharmacology training?
back: Acquisition of knowledge, acquisition of skills, teaching and training, research, and professionalism, ethics and communication skills.

front: How is the MD Pharmacology practical examination organised?
back: It is spread over two days and focuses mainly on the psychomotor domain, with long exercises, short exercises, 10 to 15 OSPE stations, and assessment of teaching or presentation skills.

front: What are the prerequisites for appearing in the MD Pharmacology summative examination?
back: Submission of a log book of training, rotation postings, departmental presentations and internal assessment reports; at least two presentations at a national conference; and one research paper published or accepted in an indexed journal.

front: What is the recommended quarterly assessment schedule during MD Pharmacology training?
back: Case presentation once a week; laboratory performance twice a week; journal club once a week; seminar once a fortnight; case discussions once a fortnight or month; and an interdepartmental case or seminar once a month.

front: Which receptor does histamine use to switch on acid secretion by the parietal cell, and what does it do?
back: H2 receptors on the basolateral membrane. Activation raises cAMP, which switches on the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump, the final step of acid secretion. Histamine is the dominant physiological stimulus; gastrin and acetylcholine act partly by releasing histamine from ECL cells.

front: What imbalance is thought to cause peptic ulcer, and how does acid fit in gastric versus duodenal ulcer?
back: Ulcer arises when aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, bile, H. pylori) outweigh defensive ones (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, NO, mucosal blood flow). Gastric ulcer: acid is normal or low and weak defence matters more. Duodenal ulcer: acid is high in about half. Acid is still an aggressive factor either way, so lowering it is the main treatment.

front: Which stimuli and receptors drive the parietal cell, and which second messengers do they use?
back: Histamine (H2, via cAMP), acetylcholine (M3) and gastrin (CCK2) act on the basolateral membrane to switch on the apical H+/K+ ATPase. Muscarinic and gastrin receptors work through PLC-IP3-DAG and raised Ca2+. Gastrin comes from antral G cells; vagal ACh and GRP drive its release, with M1 receptors on enteric ganglion cells.

front: How do prostaglandins protect the gastric mucosa?
back: Prostaglandins from the mucosa lower acid output and raise mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow. The mucus-bicarbonate gel keeps H+ and pepsin off the epithelium.

front: Why do H2 blockers also reduce acid responses to gastrin and acetylcholine?
back: Histamine plays a permissive role. The cAMP made by H2 activation is needed for a full secretory response to gastrin and cholinergic agonists, so H2 blockade weakens the response to almost every secretagogue.

front: Compare cimetidine, ranitidine and famotidine on potency and antiandrogen effects.
back: Ranitidine is about 5 times as potent as cimetidine, and famotidine about 5 to 8 times as potent as ranitidine. Only cimetidine has antiandrogenic effects (gynaecomastia, loss of libido), raises prolactin and slows hepatic breakdown of estradiol. GG14 notes that some ranitidine and nizatidine preparations have been withdrawn because of contamination.

front: Why can cimetidine cause so many drug interactions and endocrine effects, and how do ranitidine and famotidine differ?
back: Cimetidine inhibits several CYP450 isoenzymes and cuts hepatic blood flow, so drugs such as theophylline, phenytoin, warfarin and lidocaine accumulate. It also blocks androgen receptors and raises prolactin (gynaecomastia, impotence). Ranitidine and famotidine lack these actions. Antacids reduce H2 blocker absorption, so separate by 2 h.

front: Why have PPIs replaced H2 blockers for ulcer healing, and where do H2 blockers still have a role?
back: PPIs heal ulcers faster with better pain relief and a higher healing rate, even in NSAID ulcers and H. pylori ulcers. H2 blockers still have a role in stress-ulcer bleeding prophylaxis (i.v.). For ulcer healing a single bedtime dose works as well as split doses because nocturnal acid is the target.
