front: TB in pregnancy under NTEP: which drugs are used, and what supplement is needed?
back: The standard 2HRZE/4HRE course is given in full; treatment is never withheld or delayed because of pregnancy. Isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide are considered safe to the fetus, and RNTCP 2016 treats the four oral first-line drugs as safe. Streptomycin is contraindicated because it is ototoxic to the fetus. Pyridoxine 10-25 mg/day is given to every pregnant woman on isoniazid.

front: Breastfeeding and the infant of a mother on anti-TB treatment
back: All first-line anti-TB drugs are compatible with breastfeeding, so the mother gets the full course and breastfeeding continues. After active TB is ruled out, the infant receives isoniazid preventive treatment for 6 months, followed by BCG. Breast-fed infants whose mothers take isoniazid, and infants on isoniazid preventive therapy, need pyridoxine 5 mg/day.

front: Short note: Principles of MDR-TB regimen design (RNTCP 2016)

points: Use at least 4 drugs certain to be effective; often 6 are included because some may fail
Base efficacy on drug-susceptibility testing and on drugs already used in that patient
Do not combine two fluoroquinolones
Do not combine kanamycin with amikacin
Do not combine ethionamide with prothionamide
Do not combine cycloserine with terizidone
Use group I drugs (pyrazinamide, ethambutol), one injectable, one fluoroquinolone and two group IV drugs
Group V drugs are reserved for XDR-TB
Intensive phase: 6 drugs for 6-9 months
Continuation phase: 4 drugs for 18 months
Pyridoxine 100 mg/day throughout
Extend intensive phase by 1 month, to a maximum of 9, if cultures remain positive at months 4-6

front: How are RR-TB, mono-resistant and poly-resistant TB treated under RNTCP 2016?
back: RR-TB is treated as MDR-TB but isoniazid is added: intensive phase has 7 drugs (kanamycin, levofloxacin, ethionamide, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, isoniazid) for 6 months, and continuation has 5 drugs for 18 months. Mono-resistant TB gets rifampin + two susceptible first-line drugs + one injectable + one fluoroquinolone (5 drugs) for 3-6 months, then 4 oral drugs for 6 months; total 9-12 months. Poly-resistant TB gets rifampin + an injectable + a fluoroquinolone + one susceptible first-line drug + one oral second-line drug, with the same total duration.

front: What is the RNTCP 2016 XDR-TB regimen?
back: Seven drugs are given in the intensive phase for 6-12 months: capreomycin 1000 mg, moxifloxacin 400 mg, high-dose isoniazid 900 mg, PAS 12 g, clofazimine 200 mg, linezolid 600 mg, and amoxicillin-clavulanate (875+125 mg) two tablets in the morning plus one in the evening (doses for 46-70 kg). Capreomycin is stopped in the continuation phase, and the remaining six drugs continue for 18 months.

front: How is TB managed in HIV coinfection under the programme?
back: The regimen is the same as in non-HIV patients: daily HRZE for 2 months, then HRE for 4-7 months (total 6-9 months). Thrice-weekly dosing is avoided because relapse and failure are 2-3 times higher. Pyridoxine 25-50 mg/day is routine, and cotrimoxazole preventive therapy is given throughout the anti-TB regimen. Rifampin is replaced by rifabutin for 9-12 months when protease inhibitors are used; efavirenz is the preferred NNRTI because rifampin induces it less.

front: When are corticosteroids used in TB, and when are they contraindicated?
back: They are used only under adequate anti-TB cover: in seriously ill patients with miliary or severe pulmonary TB, for hypersensitivity reactions to anti-TB drugs, in meningeal, renal, pericardial or pleural TB to reduce exudation and stricture formation, and in severe AIDS-related TB. They are contraindicated in intestinal TB because silent perforation can occur. When used, they are tapered gradually as the patient improves.

Mono/poly-resistant: 5 drugs, total 9-12 months

front: Lepra reaction versus reversal reaction: how do they differ and how are they treated?
back: Lepra reaction occurs in lepromatous leprosy, often when chemotherapy starts or with intercurrent infection; it is a Jarisch-Herxheimer (Arthus) reaction to antigens released from killed bacilli and may progress to erythema nodosum leprosum. Clofazimine 200 mg daily controls milder reactions; severe reactions need prednisolone 40-60 mg/day, tapered over 2-3 months; thalidomide is an alternative in ENL. Reversal reaction occurs in tuberculoid and borderline lepromatous leprosy as delayed hypersensitivity, with skin ulceration and painful swollen nerves even after treatment; it is treated like ENL with clofazimine or corticosteroids, but thalidomide is ineffective.

front: What alternative MDT regimens are used when rifampin cannot be given?
back: Used when rifampin cannot be given. Options include intermittent ROM (rifampin 600 mg + ofloxacin 400 mg + minocycline 100 mg once monthly for 3-6 months in PBL or 12-24 months in MBL); RMMx (moxifloxacin 400 mg + minocycline 200 mg + rifampin 600 mg once monthly, 6 doses for PBL and 12 for MBL); clofazimine 50 mg plus any two of ofloxacin, minocycline or clarithromycin daily for 6 months, then clofazimine plus one of them for 18 months; and a four-drug regimen of rifampin, sparfloxacin, clarithromycin and minocycline daily for 12 weeks. If clofazimine is refused, ofloxacin or minocycline can replace it; ethionamide is not recommended as a substitute.

front: Dapsone in the leprosy programme: contraindications and sulfone syndrome
back: Dapsone is avoided in severe anaemia (haemoglobin below 7 g/dL), G-6-PD deficiency and previous hypersensitivity. Sulfone syndrome appears 4-6 weeks after starting dapsone, especially in malnourished patients, with fever, malaise, lymph-node enlargement, skin desquamation, jaundice and anaemia. Management is to stop dapsone and give corticosteroids with supportive care.

front: Clofazimine in MDT: adverse effects and contraindications
back: The main disadvantage is reddish-black discolouration of skin, especially exposed parts, with harmless discolouration of hair and secretions. Dryness, itching, scaling, acneiform eruptions, phototoxicity and conjunctival pigmentation can occur. Higher doses cause nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, weight loss and loose stools. It is avoided in early pregnancy and in patients with liver or kidney damage.

front: Short note: Chemoprophylaxis of malaria in India

points: Causal prophylaxis: kill pre-erythrocytic liver stages
Suppressive prophylaxis: suppress the erythrocytic stage so fever does not appear
Primaquine is a causal prophylactic for all species but is not used in mass programmes because of toxicity
Proguanil is a causal prophylactic for P. falciparum but is not used in India
Mefloquine 250 mg weekly, starting 1-2 weeks before and continuing 4 weeks after exposure
Doxycycline 100 mg daily, started the day before travel and continued 4 weeks after
Chloroquine is no longer used as a prophylactic in India because chloroquine-resistant falciparum is widespread
Mefloquine prophylaxis is not allowed for residents but may be used by travellers for 6 weeks to 1 year
Doxycycline is for short-term use (maximum 6 weeks) and is contraindicated in pregnancy and children under 8 years
IPTp: sulfadoxine 1500 mg + pyrimethamine 75 mg once in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, at least 1 month apart
Used where falciparum endemicity is above 30%

front: How is radical cure of vivax malaria achieved?
back: A blood schizontocide is combined with primaquine 15 mg daily for 14 days to kill the hypnozoites and prevent relapse. Primaquine is given only after testing negative for G-6-PD deficiency. In G-6-PD-deficient patients, primaquine 0.75 mg/kg once weekly for 8 weeks may be used cautiously. Tafenoquine, a long-acting 8-aminoquinoline, is a single-dose antirelapse drug awaiting approval.

front: What is the programme dose of primaquine for gametocyte clearance?
back: After treating falciparum malaria, a single dose of primaquine is given on day 2 to kill gametocytes and reduce transmission. NVBDCP recommends 45 mg (0.75 mg/kg), while WHO recommends 15 mg (0.25 mg/kg), which is considered safer for mass use. It is given even when an artemisinin was used, because artemisinins do not kill all gametocytes.

front: Why does India use ACT rather than artemisinin monotherapy?
back: Artemisinins act fastest and kill over 95% of parasites, but their short half-life leaves a small residual biomass and allows recrudescence. Combining them with a long-acting partner drug clears the residual parasites and protects both components from resistance. Oral artemisinin monotherapy is therefore prohibited in India, and fixed-dose ACT combinations are encouraged.

front: What is India's first-line ACT for falciparum malaria, and why does the north-east differ?
back: The first-line ACT under NVBDCP is artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (AS-S/P). In the north-eastern states, artemether-lumefantrine is used instead because sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine resistance is high there, with 35-44% treatment failures reported near the Myanmar border. Elsewhere in India, S/P resistance is only sporadic.

front: How does chloroquine resistance arise, and what is its status in India?
back: Resistance is mainly due to an efflux transporter encoded by pfcrt, which pumps chloroquine out of the parasite's acidic vacuole; the pfmdr1 P-glycoprotein can also contribute. Chloroquine-resistant falciparum is now widespread in India, with the highest rates in the north-east (24-83%). Chloroquine-resistant vivax was first reported from Papua New Guinea in 1989 and is now focal and sporadic in India (Chennai, Mathura, tribal Madhya Pradesh, Mumbai and Bihar), so chloroquine remains the standard treatment for vivax.

front: What combination regimens are used for kala-azar, and why?
back: Three combinations are used: liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg single dose + miltefosine for 7 days; liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg single dose + paromomycin for 10 days; and miltefosine + paromomycin for 10 days. Each achieves 98-99% cure. Combining shortens treatment, lowers the total dose, reduces toxicity and cost, and improves compliance. Failures are treated with higher-dose amphotericin B.

front: How is kala-azar managed in pregnancy and HIV coinfection?
back: Amphotericin B is the drug of choice in pregnancy and breastfeeding because miltefosine is teratogenic. HIV and Leishmania infection worsen each other: HIV-positive people are more likely to develop visceral leishmaniasis, carry a higher parasite load and have a poorer prognosis. Visceral leishmaniasis in an HIV-positive person is regarded as a sign of AIDS and warrants intensive therapy, but response to both antileishmanial and anti-HIV drugs is poorer and mortality is high.

front: How is lymphatic filariasis treated in an individual patient?
back: DEC 2 mg/kg three times daily is the first-line drug. It clears microfilariae from peripheral blood in 7 days and makes the patient non-infective to mosquitoes, but adult worms survive in lymphatics, so microfilaraemia and symptoms can recur. A total dose of 72-126 mg/kg over 12 days to 3 weeks achieves cure in most patients, and more than one course may be needed after a 3-4 week gap. Elephantiasis from chronic lymphatic obstruction is not reversed because fibrosis is irreversible.

front: What is the role of doxycycline and ivermectin in filariasis?
back: Doxycycline 100-200 mg/day for 4-6 weeks kills Wolbachia, the obligate symbiotic bacteria needed by adult Wuchereria bancrofti and Onchocerca volvulus, and is an innovative indirect treatment. Ivermectin 0.2 mg/kg is microfilaricidal but not macrofilaricidal; a single annual dose with albendazole 400 mg for 5-6 years is used for filariasis. Ivermectin is preferred for onchocerciasis and causes less severe reactions than DEC.

front: How does the national programme prevent parent-to-child transmission of HIV?
back: All HIV-positive pregnant women not already on ART start the standard 3-drug regimen, continued through delivery and the postpartum period. The NACO 2013 first-line regimen is tenofovir 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + efavirenz 600 mg as a fixed-dose tablet once daily. The neonate receives nevirapine syrup for 6 weeks. Caesarean section is advised if HIV-RNA is above 1000 copies/mL near delivery; most transmission occurs during the birth process.

front: What is the WHO 2016 preferred first-line ART regimen, and what are the alternatives?
back: The preferred regimens are tenofovir + lamivudine + efavirenz, or tenofovir + emtricitabine + efavirenz. Alternatives include zidovudine + lamivudine + efavirenz, zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine, tenofovir + lamivudine or emtricitabine + dolutegravir, and tenofovir + lamivudine or emtricitabine + nevirapine. First-line therapy uses two NRTIs plus one NNRTI or integrase inhibitor; three-NRTI regimens are less effective and no longer recommended.

front: How is a failing first-line ART regimen changed?
back: The whole regimen is changed to drugs the patient has not received before; a single drug is never changed or added, because that amounts to virtual monotherapy. Lamivudine may be continued because it can retain residual activity and reduce viral fitness. A boosted PI is nearly always included in second-line therapy. NACO 2013 second-line NRTI choices are tenofovir + abacavir, didanosine + abacavir and tenofovir + zidovudine; PI choices are atazanavir/r, lopinavir/r, saquinavir/r, indinavir/r and nelfinavir.

front: Which antiretroviral combinations must be avoided, and why?
back: Zidovudine + stavudine: pharmacodynamic antagonism. Stavudine + didanosine: increased neuropathy and lactic acidosis. Lamivudine + didanosine: not clinically additive. Tenofovir + didanosine: lower efficacy. Lamivudine + emtricitabine: similar drugs, so no benefit. Efavirenz should not be replaced by nevirapine after failure, and lamivudine should not be replaced by emtricitabine, because of overlapping resistance.

front: When is ART considered to have failed?
back: ART failure is diagnosed when plasma HIV-RNA is not reduced to undetectable levels (below 50 copies/mL) within 6 months of therapy; when virus is repeatedly detected after initial suppression despite continuing the regimen; or when there is clinical deterioration, a fall in CD4 count or a serious opportunistic infection while on therapy. Failure is due to resistance to one or more components, and the regimen should be changed entirely.

front: What is immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)?
back: When ART is started in a patient with a latent or partially treated opportunistic infection, restoration of immune function can produce a marked inflammatory reaction against residual organisms, with constitutional symptoms. This is IRIS. It reflects recovery of immunity rather than treatment failure, and it is managed by continuing ART and treating the underlying infection.

front: What is the scale of the Universal Immunization Programme, and how is the cold chain maintained?
back: The UIP covers about 2.9 crore pregnant women and 2.67 crore newborns, with more than 90 lakh immunization sessions planned each year. The cold chain is a series of storage and transport links that keeps vaccines at the recommended temperature from manufacture to the beneficiary, using close to 27,000 cold-chain points.

front: Short note: AEFI surveillance and vaccine vigilance in India

points: Vaccine vigilance is the science and activities of detecting, assessing, understanding and communicating adverse events following immunization (AEFI)
AEFI surveillance began with the UIP in 1985
National guidelines were revised in 2005, 2010 and 2015
Vaccine product-related reaction
Vaccine quality defect-related reaction
Immunization error-related reaction (programme error)
Immunization anxiety-related reaction
Coincidental event
Serious AEFI: death, hospitalization, persistent or significant disability, or a cluster of two or more cases
Severe AEFI: not minor but not death, hospitalization or disability
India reported its highest number of serious AEFIs in 2010 (395, versus 55 in 2006)
VAERS-type surveillance detected the intussusception signal with rotavirus vaccine

front: What does the pentavalent vaccine contain, and why is it used?
back: It contains tetanus and diphtheria toxoids, pertussis vaccine, hepatitis B vaccine and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine. It replaces triple antigen (DPT) for primary immunization of infants and adds protection against two more infections while reducing the total number of injections. It is included in India's Essential Medicines List (2015) and used in the UIP.

front: Which vaccines in the UIP are restricted by geography, and why?
back: Japanese encephalitis vaccine is given only in JE-endemic districts. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is not available in all states. These two vaccines therefore vary across India.

front: Define pharmacovigilance and state its purpose.
back: WHO (2002): the science and activities for detecting, assessing, understanding and preventing adverse effects or any other drug-related problem. The word joins Greek pharmakon (drug) and Latin vigilare (to keep watch). Its purpose is to reduce drug-related harm, inform doctors and regulators, support rational use, and guard against ineffective, substandard or counterfeit medicines.

front: Define a signal, an adverse drug reaction and an adverse event.
back: Signal: reported information on a possible causal link between an adverse event and a drug that was previously unknown or incompletely documented. ADR: a noxious, unintended effect at doses normally used in humans for prophylaxis, diagnosis or therapy. Adverse event: any untoward occurrence during treatment, not necessarily caused by the drug.

front: Which landmark US laws were triggered by drug disasters?
back: 1938 Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act after more than 100 deaths from sulfanilamide elixir made with diethylene glycol (pre-marketing safety testing). 1962 Kefauver-Harris amendment after thalidomide (proof of efficacy, reporting of serious adverse effects). 2007 FDA Amendments Act after rofecoxib (population surveillance, mandatory label changes, post-approval studies, REMS and public trial registration).

front: Complete: drugs withdrawn or restricted after postmarketing surveillance
text: Terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride and grepafloxacin: {{QT prolongation}} and torsades. Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine: {{cardiac valve}} abnormalities. Rofecoxib: {{myocardial infarction}} and stroke. Cerivastatin: fatal {{rhabdomyolysis}}. Lorcaserin: increased {{cancer}} risk. Thalidomide: {{phocomelia}}, though now used again under risk controls for multiple myeloma.

front: Short note: Why premarketing trials cannot establish drug safety

points: Pivotal trials often involve only hundreds to a few thousand patients (median about 467): rare reactions are missed, e.g. nefazodone liver failure
Few patients with uncommon genetic variants (TPMT, HLA-B*5701, CYP2D6)
Median duration about 24 weeks; late effects missed (bisphosphonate jaw necrosis, atypical femoral fractures)
Children, pregnant women, the very old and patients with comorbidity are excluded
Mostly placebo-controlled; few active comparators
Surrogate endpoints can mislead: flecainide and encainide (CAST), rosiglitazone
High-dose rofecoxib approved for 5 days of acute pain was used long-term, increasing MI risk

front: A patient develops jaundice in week 4 of a drug. Which four criteria decide if the drug is the cause?
back: Temporal relationship (does onset fit the drug timing), previous knowledge (is the event a known effect), dechallenge (does it subside on stopping) and rechallenge (does it return on re-exposure; often unethical, so not done). Needed because the event may be due to the disease or other causes.

Regional PvPI centres do the causality analysis; reports reach the NCC through VigiFlow

front: When are individual case reports most convincing for causality?
back: When the event is otherwise rare, has few other risk factors, follows exposure closely in time (anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and the drug carries a large excess risk (e.g. rhabdomyolysis with cerivastatin, far higher per million prescriptions than other statins).

front: How are signals detected in large spontaneous-report databases?
back: Quantitative disproportionality methods compare how often a particular event is reported for a drug with how often it would be expected from the whole database; they need no exposure denominator but rest on unverifiable assumptions, so signals always need further evaluation.

A UK postmarketing method that follows cohorts of usually at least 10,000 patients on a new drug: questionnaires are sent to the prescribing general practitioners to record all significant events over about 6-12 months after starting the drug.

text: Pharmacovigilance uses {{spontaneous reporting}} and published case reports, {{prescription-event monitoring}}, computerised {{record linkage}}, observational {{cohort}} and case-control studies, {{targeted clinical investigations}} (PK, PD, genetic and interaction studies) and postmarketing {{clinical trials}}.

front: What is the FDA Sentinel System?
back: A distributed network of the FDA and more than 30 data partners covering over 100 million people. Each site analyses its own data under a common data model and reusable tools (e.g. propensity score matching) and returns results centrally, protecting privacy. It has evaluated signals such as olmesartan-associated sprue-like enteropathy and rotavirus vaccine intussusception, sometimes avoiding costly trials.

front: Why can spontaneous reporting raise a signal but not give the incidence of a reaction?
back: Only a fraction of ADRs is reported (about 10% voluntarily) and the number of patients exposed is unknown, so there is no denominator. Dramatic, early reactions get reported, so rare events can be spotted but not counted.

front: What are the goal and objectives of the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India?
back: Goal: ensure that the benefits of medicines outweigh their risks for the Indian population. Objectives: a nationwide patient-safety reporting system; identify and analyse new signals; assess benefit-risk of marketed drugs; generate evidence on medicine safety; support regulatory decisions; communicate safety information; collaborate with and train other national centres; become a centre of excellence.

front: Under PvPI, what should be reported and who may report (as given in Sarkar)?
back: All suspected adverse events, including those from herbal, traditional or alternative remedies; especially all events with new drugs and drugs of current interest, all suspected interactions, and reactions causing death, life-threat, hospitalisation, disability, congenital anomaly or needing intervention. Health care professionals (doctors, dentists, nurses, pharmacists) report; the source states lay reports are not accepted.

front: Trace the flow of an ADR report in PvPI.
back: The ADR monitoring centre (AMC, mostly medical colleges) collects the report, follows up for completeness and enters it into VigiFlow with source documents; causality is assessed (e.g. Naranjo algorithm, Hartwig severity scale); the National Coordination Centre at IPC Ghaziabad analyses the data and forwards it to the WHO Uppsala Monitoring Centre; CDSCO takes regulatory decisions and reports to DTAB.

front: How is an individual case safety report (ICSR) assessed?
back: For quality of documentation; coding of drugs (WHO Drug Dictionary based on ATC) and reactions (WHO-ART, MedDRA); relevance (new drug, i.e. within 4 years of first approval, unknown reaction not in the product information, or serious reaction); duplicate reports; and causality.

front: Which drugs does Sarkar list as banned in India following PvPI data?
back: Rosiglitazone, sibutramine, rimonabant, nimesulide in children under 12, cisapride, lorcaserin, phenylpropanolamine, gatifloxacin and tegaserod.

front: How are drug names and adverse events coded when an ICSR is assessed?
back: Drug names are registered in the WHO Drug Dictionary, which is based on the ATC classification. Adverse events are coded with WHO-ART or MedDRA.

front: How often must a periodic safety update report (PSUR) be filed during post-marketing surveillance of a new drug?
back: Every 6 months for the first 2 years, then yearly for the next 2 years. Post-marketing surveillance itself is mandatory.

front: For a similar biologic, when can safety and efficacy trials be waived under the Indian guideline?
back: Only when all of these hold: quality is comparable (physicochemical and in vitro); preclinical evaluation is comparable; clinical PK-PD, including PD markers and immunogenicity, is comparable; and a post-marketing risk management plan is provided. The waiver is not allowed if any one criterion is missing.

front: What actions can a regulator take once pharmacovigilance data show a drug is unsafe?
back: Change the label to restrict use or add warnings and precautions, or withdraw the drug; also circulate drug alerts, medical letters and advisories to doctors. Pharmacovigilance data feed these decisions.

points: FDA-mandated measures, pre- or postmarketing, to manage serious drug risks

About 60 drugs have REMS; effectiveness little evaluated

front: How do regulators communicate new drug safety information, and how effective is it?
back: Quarterly postings of potential signals, label changes, boxed (black-box) warnings, drug safety communications and public health alerts; also drug alerts and advisories sent to doctors. Evidence suggests communications are often ineffective: monitoring advice changes little, warnings affect new more than existing patients, work best when specific, repeated and with alternatives, and may cut prescribing in untargeted groups.

front: What ethical problems arise in postmarketing safety trials?
back: Randomising patients to a drug with a suspected serious harm and no expected extra benefit is hard to justify (e.g. rosiglitazone versus pioglitazone). An IOM review advised mandating such trials only when observational studies cannot answer a critical public health question, after reviewing all existing data, with heightened informed consent. Comparative studies early in a drug's life avoid the problem.

Therapeutic index is only a rough measure of safety margin
A clinical trial may begin only with a favourable risk-benefit ratio

Risk-benefit is reassessed continuously as adverse effects emerge
Tools: ADR reporting, label warnings, REMS and post-approval studies

front: Define pharmacoeconomics and the ECHO model.
back: The branch of health economics that measures and compares the costs and consequences of drug therapy (cost-benefit, cost-effectiveness, cost-minimisation, cost-utility and cost-of-illness analyses) to find best value for money. Drug decisions should balance Economic, Clinical and Humanistic Outcomes (ECHO). Regulators increasingly require economic analysis for licensing decisions.

front: Classify: pharmacoeconomic analyses by how outcome is measured
text: Cost-minimisation: outcomes proven {{equivalent}}, only costs compared. Cost-effectiveness: outcome in {{natural units}} (life-years gained, mmHg, cases cured). Cost-utility: outcome in {{QALYs}}. Cost-benefit: both costs and outcomes in {{money}}.

back: Only when two or more options are already proven equivalent in efficacy and safety (e.g. two equally effective antiulcer drugs, generics, me-too drugs or alternative regimens of one drug). Costs then compared should include acquisition, preparation, administration and storage. If equivalence is unproven, use cost-effectiveness analysis.

Framing medication policy and formularies, selecting essential medicines and devices, allocating limited resources, guiding individual prescribing, reimbursement decisions by insurers and government, and prescription audit to cut cost burden and polypharmacy. front: What is cost-utility analysis and what is a QALY?
back: CUA compares cost per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY), weighting survival by health-related quality of life on a utility scale from 1 (perfect health) to 0 (death); QALYs = time in a health state x its utility. It suits life-extending treatments with serious toxicity (cancer chemotherapy) and morbidity-reducing therapies (arthritis). Limits: no consensus on measuring utilities and difficulty comparing across populations.

front: What does a drug utilisation study investigate?
back: Why and how drugs are prescribed, delivered, consumed and self-medicated, together with the non-clinical factors that drive drug use. Social pharmacology studies these reasons; clinical pharmacologists also run drug utilisation studies at tertiary care centres.

front: Which study designs does Sarkar list for observing drug safety after marketing?
back: Non-interventional (observational) studies, post-marketing surveillance, adverse drug monitoring, case-control studies of ADRs, drug utilisation studies and observational registries.

front: What is Mendelian randomisation and how did it predict a statin adverse effect?
back: Grouping people by genetic variants that mimic a drug's action; since genes are fixed at conception, the comparison avoids biases of drug choice. Variants lowering HMG-CoA reductase activity mimic statins and predicted the higher diabetes risk with statins that clinical use took decades to reveal.

front: What are pragmatic trials and their drawbacks?
back: Large, simple, often open-label trials with remote enrolment and outcomes from health records, close to usual care. They suit relatively safe interventions. Poor adherence and uncontrolled co-therapy blur results: in ADAPTABLE (aspirin 81 vs 325 mg) many switched to the lower dose, so intention-to-treat showed no difference.

front: What is AEFI and how does Sarkar group AEFIs?
back: Adverse event following immunisation. Sarkar groups them into five categories: vaccine product-related reaction, vaccine quality defect-related reaction, immunisation error-related reaction, immunisation anxiety-related reaction and coincidental event. The grouping matters because immunisation-error reactions are preventable.

front: Give one example of an immunisation error-related AEFI.
back: Transmission of infection from a contaminated multidose vial. It is preventable, because the cause is poor handling, prescribing or administration.

front: When is an AEFI classed as serious?
back: When it causes death, needs hospitalisation, leaves persistent or significant disability or incapacity, or occurs as a cluster of two or more cases in one area. Serious cases get intensive investigation because risk acceptance for vaccines is low.

back: BCR = present value of benefits divided by present value of costs. A ratio above 1 means the programme's benefits outweigh its costs. Decision-makers prefer the alternative with the greatest benefit-cost ratio or net benefit.

front: Classify: the four scales of measurement
text: {{Nominal}} data are labels without order (e.g. sex, hair colour; a two-category nominal variable is dichotomous); {{ordinal}} data are ranked but the gaps are unknown (e.g. satisfaction scores, visual analogue scale); {{interval}} data have equal known gaps but no true zero (e.g. temperature in Celsius); {{ratio}} data have equal gaps and a true zero (e.g. weight, height).

front: Which summary measures can be used on each scale of data?
back: Nominal: mode only. Ordinal: mode or median, not the mean, because ranks cannot be added. Interval: mode, median, mean and SD (addition and subtraction allowed, ratios not, since there is no true zero). Ratio: all of these plus ratios and the coefficient of variation. Interval and ratio data suit parametric tests; nominal and ordinal data need non-parametric tests.

front: Distinguish discrete from continuous, and qualitative from quantitative data.
back: Continuous variables can take any value on a scale and be subdivided indefinitely (e.g. temperature, litres of fuel); discrete variables take fixed countable values (e.g. number of heads in 100 tosses). Quantitative data are measured numerically and can be computed; qualitative data describe attributes (e.g. honesty, creativity) that are observed but not calculated.

front: Define mean, median and mode. When is the median the better summary?
back: Mean: sum of values divided by their number. Median: middle value of ordered data (average of the two middle values when n is even). Mode: most frequent value. The median is better when outliers are present, e.g. for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 10,000 the mean is 2002 but the median is 3. In a normal distribution mean, median and mode are equal and half the values lie on each side of the mean.

front: What is standard deviation and how is it calculated?
back: A measure of how widely values are spread around the mean; a small SD means values cluster near the mean. Steps: find the mean; find each deviation from it; square and sum the deviations; divide by n - 1 to get the variance; take the square root. In a normal distribution, mean plus or minus 1 SD covers about 68% and plus or minus 2 SD about 95% of values. SD is also used to derive the standard error and to plan sample size.

front: Why is the sample variance divided by n - 1 rather than n?
back: Dividing by n - 1 makes the sample variance an unbiased estimate of the population variance: averaged over all possible samples it equals the population value, whereas dividing by n underestimates it.

front: Distinguish standard deviation from standard error of the mean.
back: SD describes the spread of individual observations in one sample. The standard error of the mean (SEM) is the SD of the sampling distribution of means, i.e. how much sample means scatter around the population mean. SEM = SD divided by the square root of n, so it shrinks as sample size grows.

front: Which pairs of central value and spread does a results section use?
back: Mean with standard deviation or standard error, or median with interquartile range.

front: Short note: Standard error and confidence limits

points: Used to determine confidence limits, in Student's t test and in analysis of variance
Increasing the number of observations reduces the margin of error

front: Define prevalence. How do point and period prevalence differ?
back: Prevalence is the proportion of a population with a condition at a given time: all existing cases (old and new) divided by the population. It is cross-sectional. Point prevalence uses the population at one moment; period prevalence uses the average or mid-period population over a defined interval and is mainly used for chronic disease, insurance and hospital statistics.

front: Distinguish incidence proportion (cumulative incidence) from incidence rate (incidence density).
back: Both count only new cases. Incidence proportion = new cases during a stated period divided by the number initially at risk; it is a risk (0 to 1), needs a closed cohort and a stated follow-up time. Incidence rate = new cases divided by person-time at risk (e.g. per 1000 person-years); it is a rate (0 to infinity) and can be measured in an open population.

front: What is an odds ratio, how is it calculated and interpreted?
back: The odds of exposure among cases divided by the odds of exposure among controls; from a 2x2 table (a, b = exposed cases, controls; c, d = unexposed cases, controls), OR = (a/c)/(b/d) = ad/bc. It is the measure of association in case-control studies. OR = 1: no association; above 1: exposure linked to the outcome; below 1: possibly protective. It needs no population denominator, but association does not prove causation.

front: What is relative risk and from which study design is it obtained?
back: Risk of the outcome in the exposed divided by risk in the unexposed: [a/(a+b)] / [c/(c+d)]. It needs incidence, so it comes from cohort studies, not case-control studies. RR = 1: no effect; above 1: exposure raises risk; below 1: exposure lowers risk. It is a descriptive measure and does not by itself test significance.

front: Complete: when the odds ratio approximates relative risk
text: In case-control and cohort studies the odds ratio approximates the relative risk when the outcome occurs in less than {{10%}} of the unexposed (i.e. a {{rare}} outcome); when the outcome is commoner, the OR {{overestimates}} the RR.

front: What is the number needed to treat (NNT), and why is it more informative than relative risk reduction?
back: The number of patients who must be treated for one more patient to benefit (or be harmed) in a defined way. It is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction, so it depends on baseline risk and is more informative than a relative risk alone.

front: What is a P value, and how are P values conventionally interpreted?
back: The probability, calculated from the test statistic, of getting the observed result if the null hypothesis were true. It is compared with a significance level (alpha) chosen in advance, usually 5% (also 1% or 0.1%); P below alpha leads to rejecting the null hypothesis. Rough guide: P > 0.10 no evidence against the null; 0.05-0.10 weak; 0.01-0.05 moderate; 0.001-0.01 strong; < 0.001 very strong.

front: Distinguish the null hypothesis, alternative hypothesis and research hypothesis.
back: Null hypothesis (H0): no difference between a sample and the population, or between samples; it can be rejected but never proved. Alternative hypothesis (H1): there is a difference (greater, smaller or simply different). Research hypothesis: a specific, clear, predictive and testable statement about the expected outcome based on background knowledge.

front: What does a 95% confidence interval mean, and why is it reported alongside the P value?
back: For a large sample, mean plus or minus 1.96 SE gives a range expected to contain the population mean in 95% of samples; values outside it would occur by chance only 5% of the time. Unlike a P value alone, a CI shows the direction and size of the effect and its precision. In a forest plot a study whose CI crosses the line of no effect is not statistically significant.

front: How does sample size affect the standard error of the mean?
back: The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n, so it falls as the sample grows. The variance of the sampling distribution of the mean is the population variance divided by n, so larger samples give means that cluster more tightly around the population mean.

front: What power is usually accepted for a clinical trial, and why?
back: Power of 0.8 to 0.9, an 80-90% chance of detecting a real effect, is often acceptable. Type II errors are regarded more leniently than type I errors, and a larger sample size gives greater power.

front: In the Rang and Dale example, how many subjects are needed to detect a fall in mortality from 50% to 40%?

front: How does trial size change the smallest relative risk a trial can detect?
back: For the same control event rate, a larger trial can detect a smaller relative risk. Rarer outcomes need a larger relative risk to be detected at the same trial size.

front: When is the t test used instead of the Z test, and what are its requirements?
back: Both test whether two means differ more than chance allows. For small samples (n < 30) Z values do not follow the normal distribution, so Student's t test (W.S. Gosset, pen-name "Student") is used, with probability read from the t table at the right degrees of freedom. Requirements: random sample, quantitative data, normally distributed variable.

text: The {{unpaired}} (independent) t test compares means of two separate groups, df = {{n1 + n2 - 2}}; the {{paired}} t test compares before-and-after values in the same subjects, df = {{n - 1}}; the {{one-sample}} t test compares a sample mean with a known or hypothesised population mean.

{{One-way}} ANOVA tests one factor with three or more levels; {{two-way}} ANOVA tests two factors and their interaction (equal numbers per cell needed); {{factorial}} ANOVA (e.g. 2x2 design) studies several factors and their interactions in one experiment; {{repeated measures}} ANOVA compares related means, e.g. the same patients at three time points, extending the paired t test.

front: Classify: non-parametric counterparts of parametric tests
text: Two independent groups: {{Mann-Whitney}} test (for the independent-measures t test); more than two independent groups: {{Kruskal-Wallis}} test (for one-way ANOVA); two repeated conditions: {{Wilcoxon}} test (for the matched-pair t test); more than two repeated conditions: {{Friedman's}} test (for repeated-measures ANOVA).
Correlation: parametric {{Pearson}} test; non-parametric {{Spearman}} test.

front: When is ANOVA used, what are its assumptions, and what statistic does it give?
back: To compare means of more than two groups, where repeated t tests become unreliable (for two groups it gives the same result as the t test). Assumptions: each group from a normal population, equal variances, independent samples, random independent observations. It splits total sum of squares into between- and within-group parts and gives the F ratio (between-group mean square divided by within-group mean square), read from the F table.

front: Define meta-analysis and outline how one is done.
back: Statistical analysis of results from many studies to integrate their findings (Glass, 1976); a quantitative alternative to a narrative review. Steps: frame the question as PICO(T); search databases and grey literature (e.g. MEDLINE, EMBASE, theses, congress abstracts); screen abstracts and full papers against inclusion criteria; extract data and assess study quality; compute effect sizes; examine their spread and moderators; interpret and report.

front: What is evidence-based medicine (EBM), and how is the evidence obtained?
back: Using the best available research evidence, after critical appraisal, together with the doctor's clinical skill and the patient's preferences to make care decisions. It aims to improve outcomes, reduce harm, improve cost-effectiveness and support shared decisions. Evidence is found by literature search (e.g. the TRIP database) and synthesised by systematic reviews and meta-analysis.

front: Classify: reporting guidelines by study type
text: {{CONSORT}} for randomised trials (25-item checklist plus flow diagram); {{PRISMA}} for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (27 items); {{STROBE}} for observational cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies (22 items); {{MOOSE}} for meta-analyses of observational studies; {{STARD}} for diagnostic accuracy studies; {{SPIRIT}} for trial protocols.

front: What are the strengths and weaknesses of meta-analysis?
back: Strengths: greater power and precision from pooled data, resolves conflicting trials, quantifies inconsistency, allows subgroup analysis, and pooled RCTs give the highest level of evidence. Weaknesses: selective reporting and publication bias (negative studies are less often published), double counting of the same data, heterogeneity of populations, time-consuming search and complex statistics.

front: Why are rare drug toxicities usually missed before marketing?
back: Some toxicities occur in about 1 in 10,000 patients or fewer, and several hundred thousand patients may need exposure before the first case appears. Trials are too small to detect them, so such effects usually surface only in phase 4, after marketing.

front: What does randomisation achieve, and what are the criteria of a good method?
back: It removes selection bias (with allocation concealment), balances known and unknown covariates between arms, and provides the basis for statistical tests. A good method is unpredictable (each participant has the same chance of any arm), produces balanced groups, and is simple to use.

front: What inputs set the sample size of a study?

front: How do block randomisation and minimisation keep groups balanced?
back: Block randomisation assigns equal numbers to each arm within small blocks (e.g. AABB, ABAB in blocks of 4), so groups stay equal in size even if the trial stops early; with fixed blocks, staff may predict the next allocation. Minimisation assigns each new patient to the arm that best reduces imbalance in key factors (e.g. sex, age, disease stage) and suits very small trials (about 50 patients).

Cluster sampling is cheaper and quicker but has higher sampling error and may miss diversity.

σ = standard deviation of the outcome; d = smallest clinically important difference in means

front: How does each input change the required sample size?
back: Larger SD raises n (n rises with σ²). Smaller difference to detect raises n (n rises with 1/d², so halving d quadruples n). Stricter significance level (smaller α) raises n. Higher power raises n. A one-sided test needs fewer subjects than a two-sided test. Expected dropouts require a larger starting sample.

front: Give the sample-size formula for estimating a single proportion (prevalence).
back: n = Z² p (1 − p) / L², where Z = 1.96 for 95% confidence, p = expected prevalence and L = allowable absolute error (precision).

front: Why is a post hoc power calculation uninformative?

front: Define the coefficient of variation and say when it is used.
back: Relative spread: the standard deviation divided by the mean, as a percentage (CV = SD / mean x 100). It lets you compare variability between data sets with different units or scales.

front: How is the coefficient of variation used in planning a study?
back: Preliminary results give the mean and SD, so the CV can estimate sample size with n = t^2 x CV^2 (t for the chosen probability, CV as a fraction). It also compares the variability of two measurement methods.

front: What is a Type I error?
back: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive). Its probability is the significance level alpha, usually 0.05; p < 0.05 means a false positive is less than 1 in 20.

front: What is a Type II error, and what is the power of a trial?
back: Type II error: failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative), with probability beta. Power = 1 - beta, the chance of detecting a real difference; trials are often designed for power of 0.8 to 0.9.
