Significance level (type I error), usually 0.05
Power, usually 0.8 to 0.9 (type II error = 1 - power)
Magnitude of the clinically important difference
Variability (SD or CV) from preliminary data
n = t^2 x CV^2 for the chosen probability, using preliminary mean and SD
Power and difference change the required n: smaller differences need more subjects
State the reasons for the sample size, the power, the significance level and the analysis plan
Adjust for expected drop-outs
An inadequate sample risks a missed effect or a false claim

front: Give the formula for the impact factor of a journal.
back: IF = citations received in one year / papers published in the previous two years, counting original papers, reviews and similar articles.

front: Essay: Impact factor, its calculation, use and misuse

points: Eugene Garfield introduced it in the 1950s
Measures the average citations per article of a journal over a time window
Citations in the year to articles published in the two previous years, divided by the number of those articles
Helps authors choose a journal with high citation frequency
High-IF journals such as the NEJM, Lancet and JAMA are read by both physicians and researchers
Average citation says little about one article
Garfield intended it to manage library journal collections
Misuse: judging scientists or grant decisions, which the inventor never intended
Use impact factor to compare journals, not to rank individual researchers

front: What does the biostatistics team do in a clinical trial?
back: It analyses the data as set out in the protocol and decides whether the study was positive or negative. It also prepares statistical tables, figures and graphs with their interpretation for the medical writers.

front: Essay: Role of the biostatistician in clinical research

points: Member of the trial team, working from the protocol
Helps plan the design, sample size and analysis plan
Specifies the outcomes and the handling of missing data
Analyses the data as per protocol
Tests the hypotheses and reports whether the result is positive or negative
Prepares tables, figures, graphs and their interpretation for the medical writers
The biostatistician makes the trial's conclusions defensible

front: Essay: Sampling and its various types

points: Sampling selects a subset of a population so that results can be generalised
The method depends on population size, homogeneity and the sampling frame
Simple random: every unit equally likely; chosen unit by unit
Systematic: sampling interval K = population / desired sample; random start, then every Kth unit
Stratified: population split into strata; sample drawn in proportion to each stratum
Cluster: natural groups (village, ward, school) chosen at random; cheaper, but higher sampling error
Multistage: random selection at successive levels (district, taluka, village)
Multiphase: all screened, subsample tested further
Systematic needs a complete list of the population
Cluster suits large, scattered populations such as immunisation surveys
A representative sample improves external validity

front: What is cluster sampling, and what is its main disadvantage?
back: Whole natural groups such as villages, wards or schools are chosen at random and surveyed in full. It is cheaper than sampling individuals, but it commonly has higher sampling error.

front: Short note: Volume of distribution and its clinical significance

points: Apparent volume into which a drug seems to distribute: amount in body / plasma concentration
Example from the book: 1000 mg giving 50 mg/L gives 20 L
Lipid to water partition coefficient, pKa, and plasma protein binding
Small V (e.g. warfarin) means the drug stays in plasma
Large V (e.g. digoxin) means most drug is in tissues, so haemodialysis removes little
Pathological states such as heart failure, uraemia and cirrhosis change V
Loading dose depends on V and F, not on clearance

back: The volume a drug would have to fill to produce its observed plasma concentration, V = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration. It is a proportionality constant, not a real fluid volume.

front: Essay: Imperfect data analysis and its remedies

points: Missing data from drop-outs or lost follow-up
Outliers and animal deaths
Inclusion and exclusion criteria that change results
Multiplicity in statistical testing
Missing follow-up can hide serious adverse events
Negative trials left unpublished exaggerate the benefit of new drugs
Plan prospectively how missing data and outliers will be handled
Report and discuss missing data, outliers and animal deaths with the results
Pre-specify the analysis and avoid changing it after data are seen
Honest reporting of imperfect data is part of valid appraisal

front: Short note: Preclinical drug disposition studies

points: Preclinical development includes pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and toxicology
Done in vitro and in animals before first human dosing
No-observed-adverse-effect level from overt toxicity, surrogate markers and exaggerated pharmacodynamic effects
Human equivalent dose obtained from animal dose on a body-surface-area basis
Data variability and bias in interpretation
Multiplicity in statistical testing, inadequately addressed
Shows whether an intervention works in routine practice, including its good and bad consequences
Lax inclusion criteria and a heterogeneous population, as seen in daily practice
Active or usual-care control and flexible dosing
Analysis restricted to those who actually received the intervention
Explanatory trials use strict criteria, placebo and fixed dose to show how an intervention works
Pragmatic trials with usual care as comparator are increasing in number

back: An explanatory trial uses a strict, homogeneous population, placebo and fixed doses to test whether and how an intervention works. A pragmatic trial uses real-world criteria and flexible practice to test how it works in routine care.

front: What is the principle of essentiality in medical research?
back: Research should use human subjects only when this is absolutely essential and no other alternative is available. It is one of the ten core principles of the Indian GCP guidelines.

front: Why does missing data matter in a clinical trial?
back: Participants who drop out, often because the drug did not help, leave gaps in the outcomes. Important events such as serious adverse effects may then go undetected, so the handling of missing data must be planned in advance.

front: Adverse drug reaction vs adverse event: how do they differ?
back: Adverse drug reaction (ADR): a noxious, unintended and undesired drug effect at doses used in humans; it requires treatment, a dose change or caution with future use, and trivial effects are excluded. Adverse event: any untoward medical occurrence during treatment that need not be caused by the drug. Causality is assessed afterwards.

Subjects are first grouped into strata by a key factor such as age, sex or disease severity, and then randomly allocated within each stratum. This keeps that factor balanced between arms, which matters most when the groups are small.

front: Distinguish randomisation from stratification in a trial.
back: Randomisation allocates every subject to a study arm by chance. Stratification first sorts subjects into strata by a known factor, and allocation within each stratum is still random.

front: Distinguish random error from systematic error in measurement.
back: Random error comes from imprecision: repeated readings scatter on either side of the true value, close to one another, and are amenable to statistical treatment. Systematic error comes from inaccurate or uncalibrated instruments and recurs in the same direction, so it is not corrected by statistics; recalibrating the instruments removes it.
Primary data are collected first-hand from the research experiment. Secondary data come from other sources such as published data, data collected by another individual, or other indirect sources.

front: Short note: Types of data distribution

points: Continuous, symmetric bell-shaped distribution
Mean, median and mode coincide; described by the mean and SD
Only two possible outcomes, a fixed number of observations and a constant probability for each event
The curve has two peaks
Counts of a random event in a fixed interval of time or space
Events occur randomly and independently; used when the event is rare over a long observation period
Logarithm, square root or reciprocal can bring skewed data nearer normal and make the variance more uniform

front: What is skewness in a distribution?
back: Skewness is departure from symmetry: it is zero in a normal distribution, positive when the tail runs to the right (positive skew) and negative when the tail runs to the left.

front: How can skewed data be made suitable for parametric tests?
back: Apply a mathematical transformation: logarithm, square root, reciprocal or another suitable function. A transformation that brings the data nearer a normal distribution often also makes the variance more uniform. After a log transformation, the antilog of the estimated mean is the geometric mean.
The difference between a value measured in the sample and the corresponding value in the population. It arises because a sample is only a subset of the population, not a replication of it.

front: Distinguish statistical significance from practical importance.
back: A statistically significant result is one unlikely to be due to chance alone. It need not be large enough to matter in practice: a finding can be statistically significant yet of no practical importance. Confidence intervals are preferred when the size of the effect, not only its statistical significance, is the question.

front: Short note: P value versus confidence interval

points: Probability that the observed result arose by chance when the null hypothesis is true
Compared with the pre-chosen significance level (alpha)
Range within which the true value is expected to lie in a stated proportion of samples
Has a lower and an upper confidence limit; 95% and 99% intervals are commonly used
P value indicates statistical significance
Confidence interval indicates clinical significance and shows the magnitude and direction of the effect
Confidence intervals are preferred in many clinical studies

front: What is the F test for homogeneity of variance, and what follows if it fails?
back: F is the ratio of the larger sample variance to the smaller. The calculated F is compared with the table value at the 5% level. If it exceeds the table value, variances are not homogeneous; the usual responses are logarithmic transformation before a t test, or a non-parametric test such as the Wilcoxon rank sum test.

front: What is an interim analysis, and when may a trial be stopped early?
back: An analysis done before the planned number of patients has been enrolled, usually by an independent data monitoring team so that the trial team remains unaware of the results. The trial may stop if the result is already conclusive, or if continuing is unlikely to give a conclusive answer (futility).

front: What is a quality-adjusted life year (QALY)?
back: A single measure of therapeutic benefit that combines length of survival with relief from suffering: health-related quality-of-life scores are combined with life expectancy. It is used when treatments are judged by both quantity and quality of life.

front: Fisher's exact test versus chi-square: what limitation do both share?
back: Both are used for nominal (categorical) data such as smoker or non-smoker. Neither indicates the strength of an association.

Multiple analysis of variance: an extension of ANOVA used when there are two or more dependent variables that are related to one another. It analyses them together and is more efficient and informative than running a separate ANOVA for each outcome.

Correlation measures the degree of association (covariation) between two variables and does not imply cause and effect. Regression estimates or predicts the value of a dependent variable from one or more independent variables; its main purpose is prediction.

points: Predicts the dependent variable from a single independent variable
Uses any number of independent variables together
Predicts a dichotomous outcome such as presence or absence of an event
Its coefficients can estimate the odds ratio for each independent variable
Regression describes the strength and direction of an association and predicts an outcome
Correlation alone does not imply causation

front: How is the Pearson correlation coefficient interpreted?
back: r lies between +1 and -1. +1 is a perfect positive straight-line relationship, -1 a perfect negative one, and 0 no correlation. Scatter around an ellipse rather than a straight line gives a value below 1. Correlation indicates association, not causation.

points: Paired before-and-after data; the non-parametric counterpart of the paired t test
Differences are ranked by absolute size, the smallest being rank 1
Tied values receive average ranks
Zero differences are excluded and the sample size reduced
The sign of each difference is attached to its rank
Positive and negative rank sums are added separately; the smaller sum is compared with the Wilcoxon table for the number of pairs

front: Short note: Wilcoxon two-sample rank test

points: Unpaired data from two groups; the groups need not be of equal size
Both samples are combined and ranked together, with average ranks for ties
Ranks of one sample are added
If this exceeds half the total rank sum, the other sum is obtained from n(n + 1)/2 minus it
The smaller rank total is compared with the table using the two sample sizes
A value equal to or below the table value rejects the null hypothesis

front: What is Dunnett's test used for?
back: A post hoc test used after a significant one-way ANOVA to identify which experimental groups differ from the control. It uses a modified t test based on the mean square error and the harmonic mean of the sample sizes; degrees of freedom are N minus the number of groups.

front: Short note: Measures of diagnostic test accuracy

points: True positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives, defined against a gold standard
TP/(TP + FN), the true-positive rate
False-negative rate = 1 - sensitivity
TN/(TN + FP), the true-negative rate
False-positive rate = 1 - specificity
Positive predictive value = a/(a + b)
Negative predictive value = d/(c + d)
Predictive values depend on prevalence, whereas sensitivity and specificity are usually regarded as independent of it

text: A highly {{sensitive}} test, when negative, helps {{rule out}} disease (SnNout). A highly {{specific}} test, when positive, helps {{rule in}} disease (SpPin).

front: What does a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve show?
back: It plots sensitivity on the y axis against 1 - specificity on the x axis for every possible cut point. Each point is a threshold with its own sensitivity and specificity. The area under the curve measures diagnostic information: 0.5 means no information (like a coin flip) and 1.0 a perfect test.

LR for a positive test = sensitivity/(1 - specificity). LR for a negative test = (1 - sensitivity)/specificity. A positive LR above 10 usually indicates high specificity and helps rule in disease; a negative LR below 0.10 usually indicates high sensitivity and helps rule out disease.

front: What inputs does Bayes' rule use to estimate post-test probability?
back: The pre-test probability of disease, the test sensitivity and the test specificity. For a positive test, post-test probability = (pre-test probability x sensitivity) / [(pre-test probability x sensitivity) + (1 - pre-test probability) x (1 - specificity)].

front: Short note: Biases of screening tests

points: Earlier diagnosis lengthens apparent survival without postponing death
Screening detects slow-growing, less aggressive cancers more readily than fast-growing ones
An extreme form of length bias: detection of tumours that would never become clinically significant
People who volunteer for screening are healthier and have a better prognosis (healthy volunteer effect)

front: What is lead-time bias in screening?
back: The patient is diagnosed earlier but death is not postponed. Survival measured from diagnosis appears longer even though life is not prolonged; the extra time is only the period of awareness of disease. It occurs whether or not screening changes the natural history.

front: What is length-biased sampling in screening, and what is overdiagnosis?
back: Screening more easily detects slow-growing, less aggressive cancers than fast-growing ones, so screen-detected cancers have a better average prognosis. Overdiagnosis is the extreme form: detection of a 'pseudo-disease' that meets histological criteria for cancer but would never become clinically significant or cause death in the patient's remaining life.

A small study in animals or humans done before the main protocol to check the hypothesis, the procedure and the technique, with relevant background information. If the data are supportive, the protocol, actual experiment and thesis follow.

front: Short note: Classification of bias in clinical trials

points: Any factor or process, intentional or unintentional, that systematically deviates the results or conclusions of a trial away from the truth
Choice-of-question bias
Hidden-agenda, cost-and-convenience and funding-availability bias
Selection bias, including subversion and technical bias
Ascertainment, contamination, compliance and attrition bias
Withdrawal bias and selective reporting bias
Publication bias

back: Allocation concealment protects the randomisation sequence so that the next assignment is unknown before a patient enters the trial; it prevents selection bias. Blinding keeps participants, investigators, assessors or analysts unaware of the assigned treatment after allocation; it prevents ascertainment and other post-allocation biases.

A multiple crossover trial, usually randomised and sometimes blinded, conducted in a single patient. Treatment is switched periodically between active drug and placebo, or between active treatments, in balanced sequences with repetition. It gives the strongest evidence of efficacy for that individual, and suits chronic stable disease with rapid drug onset and a short washout.

front: State the addition and multiplication rules of probability.
back: Addition: for mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B); if they are not mutually exclusive, subtract P(A and B). Multiplication: for independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Conditional probability is P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B).

front: What is absolute risk reduction, and how does it relate to NNT?
back: Absolute risk reduction is the arithmetic difference in event risk between the control and treated groups. Number needed to treat is its reciprocal: NNT = 1/ARR, the number of patients who must be treated for one additional patient to benefit.

front: What is a Latin square design used for?
back: It arranges treatments so that the number of replicates (rows) equals the number of treatments (columns), and each treatment appears once in each row and once in each column. In bioassay it balances the order of administration and removes the effect of a trend, such as a progressive change in response with repeated doses.
Stage after lead optimisation: the compound is profiled for pharmacology, PK/PD, genotoxicity and stability, then taken to a regulatory submission so human dosing can begin.
refs: WEB PMC Hughes Principles of early drug discovery 2011 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3058157/

front: Short note: Pharmaceutical background of a drug in development, and in vitro toxicity testing

points: Discovery: target identified and validated, then hits screened and refined to leads
Hit-to-lead and lead optimisation improve potency, selectivity and PK
Candidate selection weighs ADME: solubility, permeability, metabolic stability, CYP450 inhibition
Preclinical characterisation then leads to a regulatory submission before human use
Cytotoxicity: standard for regulators (FDA, EMA, OECD) before preclinical or clinical stages
Common endpoints: MTT (metabolic), LDH release (membrane integrity), neutral red uptake (lysosomal)
Use at least two independent endpoints, as no single assay is fully reliable
Hepatotoxicity screen in HepG2 cells; target no effect at 50 x IC50 or EC50
CYP450 inhibition: predicts drug-drug interactions; aim above 10 uM
hERG: aim above 30 uM or at least 1000-fold selectivity, to limit cardiac liability

refs: WEB PMC Hughes Principles of early drug discovery 2011 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3058157/
WEB PMC Ziemba Advances in Cytotoxicity Testing 2025 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12653452/

front: Indian Patents Amendment Act 2005: what changed for drugs?
back: Pharmaceutical product patents became available in India (the transition period ended), so new drug molecules, not only processes, could be patented. Why: TRIPS obligations under the WTO.
refs: WEB PMC Management of intellectual property rights in India: an updated review 2011 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3312695/

front: Short note: Indian Patents Act 2005 and drug patents

points: Patents Act 1970 revised to align with TRIPS
Earlier law: drug processes patentable, drug products not
Amendments in 2000, 2003 and 2005
Product patents for pharmaceuticals from 2005 (transition ended)
Mailbox applications for product patents examined after amendment
Exclusive marketing rights provision no longer needed
Patent term 20 years from filing date for all inventions
Section 3(d) restricts secondary patents on new forms of known molecules unless therapeutic efficacy is enhanced
Patent status shapes drug development and generic entry
Patent validity can be challenged by opposition

refs: WEB PMC Management of intellectual property rights in India: an updated review 2011 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3312695/
WEB PMC Indian pharmaceutical patent prosecution: the changing role of Section 3(d) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5880378

front: Define the h-index of a researcher.
back: A scientist has index h if h of their N papers each have at least h citations. The remaining papers each have fewer than h citations.
refs: WEB PMC Shah & Jawaid, The h-Index: An Indicator of Research and Publication Output, Pak J Med Sci 2023 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10025721/

points: Individual-level metric of research output and its impact, proposed by Hirsch
Counts papers by citations, not the journal they appear in
Rank papers by citations, highest first
h is the last rank where the paper's citations are at least its rank
Example: citations 25, 10, 8, 4, 3, 1 give h = 4
Does not account for position in the author list
Self-citation can inflate it
Depends on scientific age, career breaks, topic and article type (reviews are cited more)
Cannot judge the content or worth of research
Impact factor describes a journal; h-index describes a person
Both are citation-based and both can be misused

refs: WEB PMC Shah & Jawaid, The h-Index: An Indicator of Research and Publication Output, Pak J Med Sci 2023 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10025721/

front: How do glucocorticoids produce their slow, gene-mediated effects?
back: The steroid enters the cell and binds a high-affinity cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor. The activated complex moves into the nucleus, binds glucocorticoid response elements and alters transcription, so protein synthesis changes. This takes roughly 30 to 60 minutes, and the effects last longer than the drug because the proteins it switches on persist. A few fast actions, such as suppression of ACTH release, may work through membrane receptors instead.

front: Which oral doses are roughly equal in anti-inflammatory effect to 20 mg of hydrocortisone?
back: Prednisolone 5 mg, methylprednisolone 4 mg, triamcinolone 4 mg, deflazacort 6 mg, and dexamethasone or betamethasone 0.75 mg. Relative to hydrocortisone, dexamethasone and betamethasone are about 25 times as potent as anti-inflammatory agents and have practically no salt-retaining action.

front: Why is DOCA not given by mouth, and what is it used for?
back: DOCA is almost purely mineralocorticoid, but it is not effective when swallowed, so it is given sublingually or by intramuscular injection. It is used occasionally for replacement in Addison's disease.

front: Classify the systemic glucocorticoids by biological duration.
text: Short-acting: {{hydrocortisone}}. Intermediate-acting: {{prednisolone}}, {{methylprednisolone}}, {{triamcinolone}} and {{deflazacort}}. Long-acting: {{dexamethasone}} and {{betamethasone}}.

{{Fludrocortisone}} is orally active and has some glucocorticoid action; {{DOCA}} is an almost pure mineralocorticoid given parenterally or sublingually; {{aldosterone}} is the most potent natural one but is not used clinically because of poor oral bioavailability.

front: Compare hydrocortisone with prednisolone for duration and glucocorticoid potency.
back: Hydrocortisone is short acting and has glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity of roughly equal strength, so it is also the replacement drug in adrenal insufficiency. Prednisolone is about four times as potent as a glucocorticoid and has an intermediate duration, which makes it suitable for alternate-day or single-morning dosing.

Deflazacort is a slightly less potent glucocorticoid than prednisolone (6 mg is roughly 5 mg prednisolone) and lacks mineralocorticoid activity. It is claimed to cause fewer adverse effects, but this may simply reflect its lower potency. Some trials found less growth retardation in children, so it has been recommended for paediatric patients. It is used mainly for inflammatory and immunological disorders.

front: Short note: Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressant actions of glucocorticoids

points: Suppress inflammation whatever the cause
Palliative: the underlying disease keeps progressing
Induce annexins, which block phospholipase A2 and so reduce prostaglandins, leukotrienes and PAF
Suppress COX-2 and genes for cytokines such as IL-1, IL-2 and TNF
Reduce adhesion molecules, leukocyte recruitment and capillary leak
Cell-mediated immunity (T cells) is suppressed more than antibody production
Basis for use in autoimmune disease and transplantation
Impair defence against infection
Delay wound healing and can mask a perforating peptic ulcer

front: Short note: Choosing a glucocorticoid by potency, duration and mineralocorticoid activity

points: Pick the agent by the job: replacement, anti-inflammatory, or special site of action
Hydrocortisone: short acting, glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effects about equal, so it covers both needs
Prednisolone: about four times as potent as hydrocortisone, intermediate duration, suits single-morning or alternate-day dosing
Alternate-day dosing limits HPA suppression
Dexamethasone or betamethasone: long acting, little salt retention, preferred in cerebral oedema; given in late pregnancy for fetal lung maturation
DOCA: mineralocorticoid activity only; fludrocortisone: potent mineralocorticoid with some glucocorticoid activity

back: It is an orally active, potent mineralocorticoid with some glucocorticoid action. Uses: replacement in Addison's disease when sodium is still being lost, salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and idiopathic postural hypotension.

front: What is the first-line emergency treatment for acute adrenal insufficiency?
back: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV as a bolus, then given by continuous infusion (KDT: about 100 mg every 8 hours; GG14: 50 to 100 mg every 8 hours). IV isotonic saline with glucose is given, with the volume guided by central venous pressure because these patients handle a water load poorly; a short vasopressor infusion may be needed. Dexamethasone is an alternative (KDT gives 8 to 16 mg IV; GG14 suggests 4 mg when the diagnosis is not yet confirmed, because it does not interfere with the cortisol assay). The precipitating cause (infection, trauma, haemorrhage) must be treated.

front: Complete the list of adverse effects of prolonged glucocorticoid use.
text: Glucocorticoids cause {{hyperglycaemia}}, {{osteoporosis of the vertebrae}}, {{avascular necrosis of the femoral head}}, {{posterior subcapsular cataract}} and {{delayed wound healing}}.

front: Complete the list of relative contraindications to systemic corticosteroids.
text: Relative contraindications include {{peptic ulcer}}, {{diabetes mellitus}}, {{hypertension}}, {{viral and fungal infections}}, {{osteoporosis}}, {{herpes simplex keratitis}}, {{psychosis}}, {{epilepsy}}, {{heart failure}} and {{renal failure}}.

front: Why are dexamethasone or betamethasone preferred over prednisolone in cerebral oedema?
back: They have little sodium-retaining activity, so they do not worsen fluid retention when brain swelling must be controlled. Corticosteroids are also useful in oedema from tumours and in tubercular meningitis.

front: What antenatal steroid regimen is used when preterm delivery is expected, and why?
back: Betamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 18 to 24 hours apart (KDT: betamethasone or dexamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart), when delivery is expected before 34 weeks. Glucocorticoids speed fetal lung maturation and surfactant production, so respiratory distress syndrome and neonatal death fall. These two steroids are chosen because they cross the placenta well (less maternal protein binding and placental metabolism than cortisol).

front: What is the current role of corticosteroids in septic shock?
back: High-dose corticosteroid therapy for septic shock has been abandoned because it worsens outcome. Low-dose hydrocortisone (100 mg every 8 hours as an IV infusion for 5 to 7 days) is used in patients with relative adrenal insufficiency who respond poorly to fluids and vasopressors. GG14 describes this state as critical illness-related cortisol insufficiency, treated with hydrocortisone 50 to 100 mg every 6 hours or a 10 mg/hour infusion.

front: How does metyrapone work, and how is it used diagnostically?
back: Metyrapone blocks 11-beta-hydroxylase in the adrenal cortex, so cortisol synthesis falls. Pituitary ACTH output rises, and 11-deoxycortisol accumulates and is excreted in urine. The response is used to test whether the pituitary can mount an ACTH response. Related enzyme inhibitors such as ketoconazole are also tried in Cushing's disease when surgery is not an option.

front: Short note: Adverse effects of prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy

points: Rounded face, dorsocervical fat pad, central obesity with thin limbs
Thin skin, purple striae, easy bruising, hirsutism
Hyperglycaemia; can unmask or worsen diabetes
Protein catabolism; high-protein, high-potassium diet advised beyond 2 weeks
Osteoporosis of vertebrae; avascular necrosis of femoral head
Proximal myopathy; growth retardation in children
Posterior subcapsular cataract and glaucoma
Peptic ulcer, infections, latent TB flaring, mood change or psychosis

front: Short note: HPA axis suppression and steroid withdrawal

points: Exogenous steroid suppresses the hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal axis
Adrenal cortex atrophies with time; depends on dose and duration
More than about 20 to 25 mg/day hydrocortisone, or 5 mg/day prednisolone, for over 2 to 3 weeks
Malaise, fever, anorexia, nausea, postural hypotension, electrolyte upset, myalgia
Original disease may flare; stress can precipitate adrenal crisis and collapse
Taper gradually in weekly steps, with smaller steps near physiological dose
Cover stressful events for up to a year after stopping
ACTH does not hasten recovery

front: Short note: Relative contraindications and precautions with corticosteroids

points: Peptic ulcer, diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, renal failure
Viral and fungal infections, tuberculosis, herpes simplex keratitis
Osteoporosis, psychosis, epilepsy
Use only when the benefit justifies the risk, as they may be life-saving
Do not stop abruptly after 2 to 3 weeks
Increase the dose during infection, trauma or surgery
Use local routes (topical, inhaled, intranasal, intra-articular) where possible
Enzyme inducers such as phenytoin and phenobarbitone increase steroid clearance

front: Short note: Replacement therapy in chronic adrenal insufficiency and congenital adrenal hyperplasia

points: Oral hydrocortisone is the mainstay, typically about 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the afternoon
Add fludrocortisone if the patient still loses sodium
Adequate salt and water intake
Intravenous hydrocortisone with saline and glucose
Vasopressor if needed
Most often a 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Hydrocortisone suppresses ACTH drive and the excess androgens
Fludrocortisone added for salt wasting
Systemic and topical corticosteroids have one of the widest ranges of medicinal use, for anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive action

front: Essay: Systemic corticosteroids in non-endocrine disease

points: Empirical and largely palliative, but can be life-saving
Aim for the lowest effective dose and shortest course
A single high dose is usually harmless
Start high in severe disease, then taper once symptoms settle
Give extra cover during stress
Rheumatoid arthritis: only severe cases, as an adjuvant to NSAIDs, for exacerbations or systemic features
SLE, polyarteritis nodosa, dermatomyositis, nephrotic syndrome and glomerulonephritis often need steroids
Short courses in urticaria and serum sickness; adrenaline remains the first drug in anaphylaxis
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura respond
Asthma: inhaled steroids first; systemic courses for status asthmaticus or exacerbations
Under antimicrobial cover: severe TB (miliary, meningeal), severe lepra reaction, some bacterial meningitis, Pneumocystis pneumonia with hypoxia in AIDS
Cerebral oedema, Bell's palsy, MS relapse, neurocysticercosis
Lymphoid leukaemias and lymphomas; transplant rejection with other immunosuppressants

front: Essay: Adverse effects of long-term glucocorticoid therapy and how to limit them

points: Adverse effects are exaggerations of the pharmacological actions
Limit them mainly through duration and dose
Sodium and water retention, oedema, hypokalaemic alkalosis, rising BP
Less common with the more selective agents
Hyperglycaemia, central obesity, skin fragility, proximal myopathy
Osteoporosis, vertebral fracture, avascular necrosis
Cataract, glaucoma, growth retardation in children
Infections and TB flare; delayed healing
Peptic ulcer risk roughly doubles; bleeding or silent perforation
Euphoria, insomnia, mood change; rarely psychosis or depression
Lowest dose, shortest course, single morning dose
Alternate-day therapy with a short-acting agent when possible
Topical routes; calcium, vitamin D or bisphosphonates for bone
Monitor the HPA axis and withdraw gradually

front: Which enzyme converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, and why does DHT matter?
back: 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to DHT, which binds the androgen receptor more tightly. DHT mediates androgen action on the external genitalia, prostate, genital skin and hair follicles, while testosterone itself mediates feedback inhibition of LH, effects on muscle, erythropoiesis and spermatogenesis. Type 2 5-alpha reductase predominates in the urogenital tract and genital skin, which is why finasteride (mainly type 2) shrinks the prostate.

front: Why is free testosterone not given orally or as a simple injection?
back: Oral testosterone is inactivated by first-pass hepatic metabolism, and a plain intramuscular dose lasts only minutes to hours. Slowly released esters given intramuscularly last weeks, and oral testosterone undecanoate is absorbed through lymphatics, bypassing the liver.

front: What does finasteride do, and how is it used?
back: It is a competitive inhibitor of 5-alpha reductase, mainly type 2, which lowers DHT in the prostate. It shrinks the prostate and improves urinary flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia, but benefit takes about 6 months. It works best in large glands, and 1 mg daily can help male-pattern baldness. Typical side effects are reduced libido, impotence and lower ejaculate volume.

front: Complete the note on anabolic steroids.
text: Anabolic steroids include {{nandrolone}}, {{oxymetholone}}, {{stanozolol}} and {{methandienone}}. Their anabolic selectivity is only modest, and the 17-alkyl ones, such as oxymetholone and stanozolol, can cause {{cholestatic jaundice}} and adverse lipid changes.

front: Classify the antiandrogens and related agents.
text: {{Cyproterone acetate}} is a progesterone-related steroid antagonist; {{flutamide}} and {{bicalutamide}} are nonsteroidal androgen receptor blockers; {{finasteride}} inhibits 5-alpha reductase type 2; {{GnRH agonists}} suppress gonadal androgen output.

front: Which androgens cause cholestatic jaundice, and why are injectable esters preferred?
back: The 17-alkyl derivatives such as methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone, oxymetholone and stanozolol cause dose-related cholestatic jaundice, which reverses when the drug is stopped. Parenteral testosterone esters do not cause this, so they are preferred for long-term replacement.

front: How does cyproterone acetate reduce androgen action, and what is it used for?
back: It is a weak androgen receptor blocker related to progesterone. Its progestational action suppresses LH, which lowers testosterone and adds to the direct antiandrogen effect. Uses include precocious puberty, inappropriate sexual behaviour in men, and acne or hirsutism in women, given with an estrogen. Hepatotoxicity limits its use.

front: Why is flutamide given together with a GnRH agonist in metastatic prostate cancer?
back: Flutamide is a nonsteroidal androgen receptor blocker, but blocking feedback raises LH and testosterone, which partly offsets it, so monotherapy is poor. It is therefore used with a GnRH agonist or after orchidectomy (combined androgen blockade). KDT advises starting it about 3 days before the agonist to block the initial testosterone flare. Its main toxicity is hepatic; gynaecomastia and breast tenderness are common, while libido and potency are largely preserved. Bicalutamide is now preferred: once daily and less hepatotoxic.

front: Which newer drugs block androgen action in advanced prostate cancer, and how?
back: GnRH antagonists (degarelix by injection; relugolix orally) cut LH, FSH and testosterone quickly without the initial testosterone surge seen with GnRH agonists. Abiraterone acetate inhibits CYP17A1, blocking the synthesis of androgen precursors, and is given with prednisone. Enzalutamide, apalutamide and darolutamide are second-generation nonsteroidal androgen receptor antagonists; enzalutamide binds the receptor 5 to 8 times more tightly than older antiandrogens, and the bound receptor interacts poorly with coactivators and androgen response elements on DNA. These are used with androgen deprivation in metastatic and castration-resistant prostate cancer.

front: Complete the note on PDE-5 inhibitors.
text: The PDE-5 inhibitors used for erectile dysfunction are {{sildenafil}}, {{tadalafil}} and {{vardenafil}}. Of these, {{tadalafil}} has the longest action (half-life about 18 hours), so nitrates are contraindicated for up to {{3 days}} after it, and {{vardenafil}} can prolong the QT interval.

front: What is the physiological mediator of penile erection, and how does it act?
back: Nitric oxide released from nonadrenergic noncholinergic nerves and endothelium raises cGMP in cavernosal smooth muscle, which relaxes it and lets blood fill the sinusoids. Acetylcholine and prostaglandins help. PDE-5 destroys cGMP, which is why blocking it improves erection. This is the base for understanding every ED drug.

front: Name the PDE-5 inhibitors used in erectile dysfunction and state when they work.
back: Sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil are first-line drugs. They only enhance the response to sexual stimulation and do nothing without it, because they amplify the nitric oxide signal rather than start it.

front: Why must nitrates never be combined with sildenafil?
back: Both raise cGMP in vascular smooth muscle, so the combination can cause a precipitous fall in blood pressure and myocardial infarction. A gap of 24 hours is needed after sildenafil, and up to 3 days after tadalafil.

front: How does tadalafil differ from sildenafil?

Because of its long action, nitrates are contraindicated for up to 3 days after it (GG14: more than 24 hours, especially with tadalafil). It has lower PDE-6 affinity, so visual disturbance is less frequent, but it can cause back pain. Dose: 10 mg at least 30 minutes before intercourse (maximum 20 mg). It is also approved for pulmonary arterial hypertension.

front: How do estrogens act at the cell level?
back: Estradiol binds nuclear estrogen receptors, ERalpha and ERbeta. The receptor dimerises, binds estrogen response elements and changes gene transcription with the help of coactivators or corepressors. ERalpha predominates in uterus, breast, bone and blood vessels, while ERbeta predominates in the prostate and ovary. Some rapid membrane-initiated effects also exist.

front: What is the usual cyclical oral HRT regimen for a woman with an intact uterus?
back: Conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg daily for 3 weeks, then 1 week off. A progestin is added for the last 10 to 12 days of each cycle to protect the endometrium from hyperplasia and carcinoma. Lower estrogen doses of about 0.3 to 0.45 mg are also used now. In women without a uterus, estrogen is given alone.

text: Progesterone derivatives: {{medroxyprogesterone acetate}}, {{megestrol acetate}}, {{dydrogesterone}} and {{hydroxyprogesterone caproate}}; newer: {{nomegestrol acetate}}. 19-nortestosterone derivatives, estranes: {{norethindrone (norethisterone)}}, {{lynestrenol}} and {{allylestrenol}}. Gonanes: {{levonorgestrel}}, {{desogestrel}}, {{norgestimate}} and {{gestodene}}.

front: Why is ethinylestradiol used by mouth when natural estradiol is not?
back: Natural estrogens are inactivated by rapid first-pass metabolism in the liver, so oral estradiol is weak and short acting. Ethinylestradiol is metabolised slowly, so it is orally active and more potent, which is why it is used in oral contraceptives and oral hormone therapy.

front: What effects do estrogens have on clotting and lipids?
back: They increase synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower PAI-1, which raises the thrombotic tendency despite increased fibrinolysis. They lower LDL and raise HDL and triglycerides. They also raise SHBG, TBG and CBG levels in the liver.

front: Why is tamoxifen called a SERM, and where does it act as an agonist?
back: It is an estrogen antagonist in breast tissue and blood vessels, but a partial agonist in uterus, bone, liver and pituitary. Its antiestrogenic action inhibits breast cancer cells and causes hot flushes; its agonist action stimulates the endometrium (hyperplasia, carcinoma risk), improves bone density, lowers LDL and raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis 2 to 3 fold.

front: What is the mechanism of danazol?
back: Danazol is an orally active ethisterone derivative with weak androgenic, anabolic, progestational and glucocorticoid activity. Its main action is suppression of the mid-cycle gonadotropin surge, so ovarian or testicular function falls; it also directly inhibits steroidogenic enzymes (not aromatase). As a 17-alkylated steroid it raises C1 esterase inhibitor levels, so it prevents hereditary angioedema attacks. Other uses: endometriosis (now second line because of androgenic and hepatic adverse effects), menorrhagia and fibrocystic breast disease.

front: Classify the selective estrogen receptor agents.
text: Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) include {{tamoxifen}}, {{raloxifene}} and {{toremifene}}. {{Fulvestrant}} is a pure antagonist that down-regulates the estrogen receptor, so it is called a selective estrogen receptor down-regulator (SERD).
Nonsteroidal, reversible: {{letrozole}} and {{anastrozole}}. Steroidal, irreversible (suicide substrate): {{exemestane}}.

front: How does clomiphene induce ovulation, and what are its main adverse effects?
back: It blocks estrogen negative feedback on the pituitary, so more LH and FSH is released with each pulse; the ovaries enlarge and ovulate if they can respond. Course: 50 mg daily for 5 days from cycle day 5, monthly; if no conception after 1 to 2 cycles the dose may be doubled, and no more than 6 cycles are tried. Adverse effects: polycystic ovaries, multiple pregnancy, hot flushes, gastric upset and vertigo. GG14: letrozole gives a higher pregnancy and live-birth rate than clomiphene in PCOS; KDT notes India banned letrozole for ovulation induction in 2011.

front: What is the tissue profile of raloxifene, and what is it used for?
back: It is an estrogen agonist in bone and lipid metabolism, but an antagonist in breast and endometrium. It prevents postmenopausal bone loss and vertebral fracture and reduces the risk of ER-positive breast cancer. It does not relieve hot flushes, and it raises the risk of venous thrombosis.

front: Why are aromatase inhibitors not used in premenopausal women with functioning ovaries?
back: They block estrogen synthesis from androgens, but functioning ovaries keep making estrogen, so the block is incomplete. They are used in premenopausal women only after ovarian removal or with GnRH suppression. In postmenopausal women, extraglandular aromatisation is the main estrogen source, so they nearly abolish estrogen.

front: What is the textbook mifepristone and misoprostol regimen for medical termination of early pregnancy?
back: Mifepristone 600 mg as a single oral dose, followed 48 hours later by misoprostol 400 microgram orally, up to 7 weeks (49 days from the last menstrual period). This gives over 90 percent complete abortion; mifepristone alone gives 60 to 85 percent. Indian kits give mifepristone as three 200 mg tablets on day 1 and misoprostol as two 200 microgram tablets on day 3. Problems: prolonged bleeding and failed abortion; also cramps, nausea and loose stools.

front: What is the dose and time window for ulipristal as emergency contraception?
back: Ulipristal 30 mg as a single oral dose, taken within 120 hours of unprotected intercourse. It is as effective as levonorgestrel when taken within 72 hours and more effective than levonorgestrel from 72 to 120 hours. It is a selective progesterone receptor modulator.

front: Complete the note on long-acting progestin injectables.
text: Depot {{medroxyprogesterone acetate}} 150 mg is given intramuscularly every {{3 months}}; {{norethisterone enanthate}} 200 mg is given every {{2 months}}. The main drawback is disruption of menstrual bleeding or total {{amenorrhoea}}, and return of fertility after stopping is {{delayed by several months}}.

front: Why are desogestrel and gestodene preferred in some combined pills?
back: They are potent gonane progestins with strong antiovulatory action and little or no androgenic activity. Because they are potent, the ethinylestradiol dose in the pill can be reduced. Because they are weakly androgenic, they do not oppose estrogen's favourable effect on the lipid profile, so they are preferred in women with hyperandrogenism. Desogestrel and norgestimate are prodrugs.

front: How do oxytocin and vasopressin differ?
back: Both are nine-amino-acid peptides made in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary, and they differ at positions 3 and 8. Oxytocin acts mainly on the uterus and breast, while vasopressin mainly controls water excretion. Very high doses of oxytocin can show some antidiuretic effect.

front: How does oxytocin stimulate the uterus, and what changes its sensitivity?
back: It acts on G-protein-coupled receptors on the myometrium, raising intracellular calcium through depolarisation and IP3-mediated release. It also stimulates prostaglandin release from the endometrium. Estrogens increase receptor numbers, so sensitivity rises toward term and falls after delivery. Progestins reduce it.

front: How are ergometrine and methylergometrine used to control postpartum haemorrhage?
back: Give 0.2 to 0.3 mg IM at delivery of the anterior shoulder to prevent PPH in women prone to bleed (for example grand multipara, uterine inertia), or 0.5 mg IV if PPH is occurring; in severe bleeding 0.5 mg can be combined with oxytocin 5 IU. Routine use in all deliveries is not justified, and multiple pregnancy must be excluded first. GG14 describes oxytocin 10 units IM immediately after delivery as the standard measure to keep the uterus contracted.

front: What are the obstetric uses of prostaglandins?
back: PGE2, PGF2alpha and 15-methyl PGF2alpha are potent uterine stimulants, especially late in pregnancy, and they also soften the cervix. Misoprostol, a PG analogue with fewer side effects, is increasingly used for obstetric indications such as cervical ripening and induction.

front: Complete the note on ergot alkaloids in obstetrics.
text: Ergometrine and methylergometrine raise the force, rate and duration of uterine contraction, and high doses can cause {{contracture}}. Ergometrine given for many days after delivery can reduce milk through {{dopaminergic inhibition of prolactin release}}.

front: Complete the note on oxytocin pharmacokinetics.
text: Oxytocin is inactive by mouth and is given IM or IV. It is broken down by {{oxytocinase}} from the placenta, with a plasma half-life of about {{6 to 12 minutes}}. {{Carbetocin}} is a long-acting analogue used to prevent uterine atony after caesarean section.

Beta-2 agonists: {{ritodrine}}, {{salbutamol}}, {{terbutaline}}. Calcium channel blocker: {{nifedipine}}. Oxytocin receptor antagonist: {{atosiban}}. {{Magnesium sulfate}} also relaxes the uterus but is no longer recommended for this purpose. COX inhibitors such as {{indomethacin}} are used off-label (GG14), while KDT lists them among unreliable uterine depressants.

front: Which conditions must be checked before starting an oxytocin infusion for induction of labour?
back: Correct presentation, mature fetal lungs, no cephalopelvic disproportion, no placenta praevia, no fetal distress, and no previous uterine scar. The infusion is started slowly and titrated to the response, with contractions monitored closely, and it is stopped once contractions are strong enough.

front: What serious adverse effect of oxytocin is linked to its antidiuretic action?
back: Water intoxication, which can be fatal. It occurs when large doses are given with intravenous fluids, especially in toxaemia of pregnancy and renal insufficiency. Over-strong uterine contractions from injudicious use can also cause uterine rupture and fetal asphyxia.

front: In which conditions should ergometrine be avoided?
back: Hypertension, toxaemia, vascular or cardiovascular disease, sepsis (risk of gangrene), liver or kidney disease, and in pregnancy before the third stage of labour. In hypertensive women, oxytocin is the preferred uterotonic.

back: Isolated non-pregnant rat uterus. Rats are primed with diethylstilboestrol first so the strip responds reliably to oxytocin; this also keeps the uterus quiet but sensitive for routine assays.

back: Anterior-segment inflammation such as allergic conjunctivitis responds to eye drops or ointment. Posterior-segment disease (retinitis, optic neuritis, uveitis) needs systemic steroids, or a retrobulbar injection to limit systemic effects. Steroids are contraindicated in herpes simplex keratitis and in ocular injury.

front: Which animals are used to screen antifertility agents?
back: Rats most commonly; mice, rabbits and monkeys can also be used. Rats are routine because a test running 12 weeks covers every stage of spermatogenesis, which takes about 9 weeks.

front: How do superactive GnRH agonists act, and what does continuous dosing do?
back: They first trigger a brief rise in FSH and LH. After 1 to 2 weeks they desensitise and down-regulate pituitary GnRH receptors, so gonadotropins fall and gonadal steroids drop to castration levels. Recovery takes up to about 2 months after stopping.

front: Why do GnRH antagonists avoid the initial flare seen with agonists?
back: Antagonists block the GnRH receptor directly, so they inhibit FSH and LH secretion without a first stimulatory phase. Ganirelix and cetrorelix are short acting and block LH surges during controlled ovarian stimulation for IVF.

front: How does isoniazid act, and why is it selective for mycobacteria?
back: It is a prodrug activated inside the bacillus by the catalase-peroxidase KatG. The activated form binds NAD and blocks InhA and KasA, stopping mycolic acid synthesis in the cell wall. Human cells lack this activation step, so the drug is selective. A second adduct inhibits mycobacterial DHFR and disrupts DNA synthesis.

front: How does rifampicin kill mycobacteria, and why is it selective?
back: It binds the beta subunit of the bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (the rpoB gene product) and blocks chain elongation. Mammalian RNA polymerase binds it poorly, which gives selectivity. Resistance is almost always an rpoB mutation.

front: Why is pyrazinamide useful despite being a weak drug, and how does it act?
back: Bacterial pyrazinamidase (pncA) converts it to pyrazinoic acid, which accumulates in an acidic environment. Its activity at acidic pH suits intracellular bacilli and inflamed sites, so it gives sterilising activity and allows the course to be shortened. It is most useful in the first 2 months.

front: What does ethambutol inhibit, which gene mutation causes resistance, and why is it given?
back: It inhibits arabinosyl transferases (embAB) that make arabinogalactan, so mycolic acids cannot be incorporated into the cell wall. Resistance develops slowly, mostly through embB mutation. It is bacteriostatic; its main role is to prevent resistance when added to RHZ.

front: Classify: the five first-line anti-TB drugs and their activity.
text: The first-line drugs are {{isoniazid}}, {{rifampicin}}, {{pyrazinamide}}, {{ethambutol}} and {{streptomycin}}. Isoniazid and rifampicin are the most potent {{bactericidal}} drugs, {{ethambutol}} is {{bacteriostatic}}, and streptomycin acts only on {{extracellular}} bacilli.

front: Why does isoniazid acetylator status matter?
back: INH is acetylated by NAT2. Fast acetylators (about 30 to 40 percent of Indians) clear it in about 1 hour; slow acetylators (60 to 70 percent) take about 3 hours. Daily dosing works in both groups, but twice-weekly regimens are less effective in fast acetylators. Slow acetylators get peripheral neuritis more often.

front: Isoniazid neurotoxicity: cause, prophylaxis and treatment?
back: It interferes with formation of active pyridoxal phosphate and increases urinary loss of pyridoxine. Prophylaxis is pyridoxine 10 mg/day, and it is essential in diabetics, alcoholics, malnourished, pregnant, lactating and HIV-infected patients and with high-dose INH. Treatment is pyridoxine 100 mg/day.

front: Rifampicin: main adverse effects and the harmless finding patients notice first
back: Orange-red urine, sweat, tears and secretions, which is harmless. Flushing, pruritus, rash, flu-like symptoms and GI upset, commoner with intermittent dosing. Hepatitis is dose-related, rare below 600 mg/day, and worse in pre-existing liver disease. Rarely purpura, haemolysis, shock or renal failure.

front: Why does rifampicin lower the levels of other drugs?
back: It induces microsomal CYP450 enzymes (CYP3A4, CYP2C, CYP2D6, CYP1A2), speeding up its own metabolism (AUC down about 35 percent) and that of warfarin, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, sulfonylureas, HIV protease inhibitors, NNRTIs, theophylline, metoprolol, azoles, clarithromycin and phenytoin. Contraceptive failure has occurred; use a pill with 50 mcg estrogen or another method.

front: Which drugs' levels rise with isoniazid, and what lowers isoniazid levels?
back: INH inhibits CYP2C19 and CYP3A4, raising phenytoin, carbamazepine, diazepam, theophylline and warfarin. Aluminium hydroxide reduces its absorption. PAS competes for acetylation and prolongs its half-life. Rifampicin counteracts INH's inhibition, but the net effect on many drugs is unpredictable.

front: Ethambutol: main toxicity, monitoring and what to do
back: Retrobulbar neuritis: loss of visual acuity and colour vision, and central field defects. It is dose- and duration-dependent and largely reversible if stopped early. Patients must report any visual change at once; young children may not report it, so monitor them carefully. Stop at the first sign of optic neuritis, and use with caution in renal disease.

front: Pyrazinamide: main toxicities, contraindication and dose limit
back: Dose-related hepatotoxicity, so the daily dose is limited to 25 to 30 mg/kg (less common in Indians than in Western patients). Contraindicated in liver disease. Hyperuricaemia from reduced renal urate secretion can cause gout. Also abdominal upset, arthralgia, and it can disturb glucose control in diabetics. It is now considered safe in pregnancy.

Effective in HIV-positive contacts

Ethambutol: retrobulbar neuritis with loss of visual acuity and colour vision; stop at first visual change
Acts only on extracellular bacilli; given i.m. and used only alongside other first-line drugs
Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; contraindicated in pregnancy because it is ototoxic to the fetus

front: Which fluoroquinolone is most active against M. tuberculosis, and why is its use restricted?
back: Moxifloxacin is most active, followed by levofloxacin, ofloxacin and ciprofloxacin. They are oral bactericidal drugs that also kill bacilli inside macrophages. Use is restricted to drug-resistant TB to preserve them. Used alone they select resistance quickly by gyrase mutation, although resistance to moxifloxacin develops more slowly.

front: Classify: WHO grouping of drugs for MDR/RR-TB regimens (GG14), and the older grouping
text: Group A (include all three): {{levofloxacin or moxifloxacin}}, {{bedaquiline}} and {{linezolid}}. Group B (add both): {{clofazimine}} and {{cycloserine or terizidone}}. Group C (to complete the regimen when A and B drugs cannot be used): {{ethambutol}}, {{delamanid}}, {{pyrazinamide}}, meropenem with amoxicillin-clavulanate, {{amikacin}}, ethionamide or prothionamide, and PAS. The older RNTCP grouping in KDT put first-line oral drugs in group I, {{injectables}} in group II, fluoroquinolones in group III and bacteriostatic oral drugs in group IV.

front: Bedaquiline: mechanism and why it is selective
back: A diarylquinoline that inhibits subunit c of mycobacterial ATP synthase, cutting the bacillus's energy supply. Human ATP synthase is far less sensitive, which gives selectivity. It kills both multiplying and dormant bacilli. Resistance arises from ATP synthase mutation or from efflux pump mutations; GG14 notes that efflux-based resistance gives cross-resistance with clofazimine. WHO now classes it as a Group A drug for MDR-TB.

front: Bedaquiline dosing in pulmonary MDR-TB (as licensed)
text: 400 mg daily for {{2 weeks}}, then 200 mg {{three times a week}} for {{22 weeks}}. Maximum course {{24 weeks}}, with each tablet swallowed whole with meals. Use only in adults over 18 who are not pregnant, with at least 3 active background drugs.

back: A D-alanine analogue. It blocks the enzymes that make D-alanine and join two D-alanine residues, so cell wall peptide cross-linking fails. Toxicity is mainly neuropsychiatric (sleepiness, headache, tremor, psychosis, with seizures less often). Give pyridoxine 100 mg/day. Contraindicated in mental illness or seizure disorders.

front: Bedaquiline: adverse effects and why background drugs must continue after it stops
back: Nausea, headache, arthralgia, QTc prolongation (caution with other QT-prolonging drugs) and potential hepatotoxicity. It accumulates in tissues and has a terminal half-life of about 5.5 months, so it persists for months after stopping. KDT therefore stresses continuing the background drugs to the end of the course, so that surviving bacilli are not left exposed to bedaquiline alone.

front: Linezolid in drug-resistant TB: role, dose in the book regimen and key toxicities
back: The RNTCP XDR-TB regimen in KDT lists linezolid 600 mg daily for adults of 46 to 70 kg. GG14 states that WHO now classes linezolid as a Group A drug for MDR-TB and that it is part of the 6-month bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid regimen approved for XDR-TB, although adverse effects are frequent. It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis at the 50S ribosome. Main toxicities are bone marrow suppression, peripheral and optic neuropathy and lactic acidosis, so blood counts and vision are monitored.

front: Regimen for new drug-sensitive pulmonary TB (RNTCP 2016 in KDT, and GG14)
text: Intensive phase: {{2 months}} of daily HRZE. Continuation phase: {{4 months}} of daily HRE under RNTCP 2016 (GG14 gives daily HR). Total duration: {{6 months}}. GG14 notes that {{daily}} dosing is preferred over intermittent dosing because it gives the best chance of cure without relapse.

front: Regimen for previously treated pulmonary TB, presumed drug-sensitive (RNTCP 2016).
text: Intensive phase: {{2 months}} of daily HRZES, then streptomycin is stopped and HRZE is given for {{1 more month}}. Continuation phase: {{5 months}} of daily HRE. Total duration: {{8 months}}.

GG14: injectable agents (kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin) have now largely been {{phased out}}, and WHO builds MDR-TB regimens from Group A, B and C drugs given for 18 to 20 months.

front: Rifampicin-resistant TB with isoniazid sensitivity: how is it treated?
back: It is managed as MDR-TB, with isoniazid added to both phases without changing the duration or the other drugs. The intensive phase (6 months) has seven drugs: kanamycin, levofloxacin, ethionamide, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and isoniazid. The continuation phase (18 months) has five: levofloxacin, ethionamide, cycloserine, ethambutol and isoniazid.

front: Low-level versus high-level isoniazid resistance: when is high-dose INH used?
back: Low-level resistance (on LC-DST) or inhA mutation can be overcome with high-dose INH: 900 mg/day for 46 to 70 kg body weight, with pyridoxine. High-level resistance, or resistance from a katG mutation, makes INH ineffective, so it must not be given.

front: Initial regimens for mono-drug and poly-drug resistant TB (RNTCP 2016)
back: Mono-resistant (not rifampicin): rifampicin, two susceptible first-line drugs, one injectable second-line drug and one fluoroquinolone, daily for 3 to 6 months. Poly-resistant: rifampicin, an injectable, a fluoroquinolone, a susceptible first-line drug and one oral second-line drug (ethionamide, cycloserine or PAS). Both: stop the injectable after the intensive phase and give four oral drugs for 6 more months, for a total of 9 to 12 months.

front: How is rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) treated under RNTCP 2016?
back: As MDR-TB, but isoniazid is added in both phases without changing duration or other drugs. Intensive phase (6 months): kanamycin, levofloxacin, ethionamide, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and isoniazid. Continuation (18 months): levofloxacin, ethionamide, cycloserine, ethambutol and isoniazid. Isoniazid is kept because the bacilli stay sensitive to it.

front: TB in pregnancy: which drugs are safe and what supplement is needed?

Pregnant women on INH take {{pyridoxine 10 to 25 mg/day}}.

front: When are corticosteroids used in TB, and when are they contraindicated?
back: Not routinely. Used only under effective chemotherapy cover: in severe or miliary TB (to buy time), for drug hypersensitivity, and in meningeal, renal or pericardial TB or pleural effusion (to reduce exudation and adhesions). GG14 calls steroids standard care in TB meningitis; in TB pericarditis a large trial showed no overall benefit on the main outcome, though constrictive pericarditis was reduced. Contraindicated in intestinal TB because of the risk of silent perforation. Taper once the patient improves.

front: Case: HIV patient with TB on a protease inhibitor or nevirapine. What goes wrong with rifampicin and how is it fixed?
back: Rifampicin is a strong CYP inducer and markedly speeds metabolism of protease inhibitors and nevirapine, making them ineffective. Fix: substitute rifabutin (a much weaker inducer) for 9 to 12 months, with its dose reduced when used with a protease inhibitor. NRTIs are not induced, so need no adjustment, and an alternative 3-NRTI regimen is possible. If a 2 NRTI plus NNRTI regimen is used, choose efavirenz as it is induced least.

front: Anti-TB drug hepatitis: what is the first step?
back: Stop all anti-TB drugs and let the reaction subside. Isoniazid, rifampicin or pyrazinamide (one or more) are the usual culprits, and combination therapy raises the risk. If TB is severe, start streptomycin, ethambutol and one fluoroquinolone (all non-hepatotoxic) while the liver recovers.

front: Which anti-TB drugs cause hepatitis, and who is at higher risk?
back: Isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide (any one or more) are the usual culprits, and giving them together makes it commoner. INH hepatitis is rare in children but commoner in older people and alcoholics, because chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1, which makes a toxic minor metabolite from acetylhydrazine. The damage is dose-related and reversible on stopping the drug.

front: Streptomycin in TB: main toxicities and the limits placed on its use?
back: Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, worse in the elderly and in renal impairment. Because of this small safety margin and the need for i.m. injection, it is used only as an add-on to other first-line drugs or as a reserve, for at most 2 months (hence a 'supplemental' first-line drug). Above 50 years the maximum dose is 0.75 g/day. If the strain is streptomycin-resistant it must be stopped early, as dependence can develop.

Stop the last-added drug permanently and rebuild the regimen
Never re-introduce rifampicin after haemolysis, thrombocytopenia or renal failure
For rashes or itching: stop all drugs, then challenge one drug at a time with small doses, increasing every 3 days

front: How are minor adverse effects of first-line anti-TB drugs handled without changing the regimen?
back: Treat symptomatically and keep the drugs going. Nausea or anorexia: give with small meals. Drowsiness: give at bedtime. Pyrazinamide arthralgia: analgesic-NSAID. INH neuritis: pyridoxine. Stopping a drug from a combination risks resistance, so manage minor effects in place. Severe reactions such as rash with itching, or hepatitis, need all drugs stopped.

front: Case: a patient on HRZE for 3 weeks develops severe itching and rash. What is the plan, and when is rifampicin never re-given?
back: Stop all anti-TB drugs promptly. After the reaction settles, re-introduce drugs one at a time, challenging with a small dose and increasing every 3 days. When the culprit is found, stop it and rebuild the regimen. Rifampicin must never be re-introduced if the reaction was severe, such as haemolysis, thrombocytopenia or renal failure. Contrast with hepatitis, where the order is rifampicin first, then isoniazid 7 days later.

front: Dapsone: mechanism and why it is selective for M. leprae
back: It is a sulfone that blocks folate synthase, so PABA cannot be used to make folic acid; PABA reverses its action. The folate synthase of M. leprae binds dapsone with much higher affinity than that of most other bacteria, so it works at very low leprostatic levels. Doses needed for pyogenic infections are too toxic to use.

front: Dapsone: contraindications and uses beyond leprosy
back: Avoid in severe anaemia (Hb below 7 g/dL), G6PD deficiency and hypersensitivity. KDT lists its combination with pyrimethamine for chloroquine-resistant malaria, toxoplasmosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii infection; GG14 states that dapsone is no longer used for malaria, but it is used for Pneumocystis treatment and prophylaxis, Toxoplasma prophylaxis, and for its anti-inflammatory action in conditions such as pemphigoid.

front: Dapsone pharmacokinetics: why does it accumulate?
back: Absorbed completely orally and widely distributed, with poor CSF entry; about 70% protein bound but concentrated in skin (especially lepromatous skin), muscle, liver and kidney. It is acetylated and conjugated in the liver, and metabolites are excreted in bile and reabsorbed (enterohepatic cycling), so elimination is slow. Plasma half-life is often over 24 hours and the drug is cumulative, taking 1 to 2 weeks or longer to clear.

front: Dapsone resistance: primary versus secondary, and why dapsone still works
back: Primary resistance is found in a patient never treated with dapsone, meaning the infection came from a resistant source. Secondary resistance develops during monotherapy, in up to about 20 percent of patients. Mutated folate synthase has lower affinity. Peak serum levels still exceed the MIC by about 500 times, so relapse from resistance is only about 2 to 3 percent. Dormant persisters are a separate problem.

front: Dapsone adverse effects: which are dose-related and which depend on G6PD status?
back: Mild haemolytic anaemia is common and dose-related, from its oxidising action. G6PD-deficient patients haemolyse at doses above 50 mg/day. Also methaemoglobinaemia, early nausea and anorexia, headache, paraesthesia, drug fever, rashes, fixed drug eruption, hypermelanosis and phototoxicity. Hepatitis and agranulocytosis are rare.

front: Sulfone syndrome: timing, features and treatment
back: It starts 4 to 6 weeks after dapsone is begun: fever, malaise, lymph node enlargement, skin desquamation, jaundice and anaemia. It is commoner in malnourished patients and has become more frequent since MDT was introduced. Treatment: stop dapsone, give corticosteroids and supportive care.

front: Clofazimine: proposed mechanisms, absorption and why it can be given intermittently
back: A dye with leprostatic and anti-inflammatory action. Proposed actions: interference with DNA template function, disruption of membrane structure and transport, and disruption of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. About 40 to 70 percent is absorbed orally. It accumulates in macrophages as crystals in fat and other tissues, with a half-life of about 70 days, which allows intermittent dosing.

Moxifloxacin is the most potent; ciprofloxacin is weak
Used mainly as alternatives when rifampicin cannot be given

Vertigo is the main serious problem with long-term use

front: Clofazimine pharmacokinetics and what they mean for dosing
back: Orally active with 40 to 70% absorption. It accumulates in macrophages and is deposited as needle-shaped crystals in many tissues including subcutaneous fat, but enters CSF poorly. Its half-life is about 70 days, so intermittent (monthly supervised) dosing is possible in MDT. Used alone it acts more slowly than dapsone and resistance appears in 1 to 3 years.

The main problem is reddish-black skin discolouration, especially on exposed areas. Hair, body secretions and the conjunctiva may also be pigmented. Dryness, itching, acneiform eruptions and phototoxicity occur. GI upset, weight loss and enteritis are seen mainly at higher doses. Avoid in early pregnancy and in liver or kidney damage.

front: Rifampicin in leprosy: why a monthly dose is used and when it must be withheld
back: A 600 mg dose kills up to 99.99 percent of M. leprae within 3 to 7 days, so patients become non-infectious quickly. The monthly MDT dose is nearly non-toxic and causes no significant enzyme induction. Withhold it in hepatic or renal dysfunction, and during erythema nodosum leprosum or reversal reactions, because rapid killing releases large amounts of antigen.

front: Leprosy: what are the alternatives when rifampicin is resistant or a standard MDT drug cannot be used?
back: Alternatives are reserved for rifampicin resistance or when standard MDT is impossible or inadvisable. If clofazimine is refused: substitute ofloxacin 400 mg or minocycline 100 mg daily (ethionamide is not recommended). Intermittent monthly ROM (rifampicin 600, ofloxacin 400, minocycline 100) or RMMx (moxifloxacin 400, minocycline 200, rifampicin 600) regimens exist, as do daily clofazimine-plus-two-drug regimens and a 12-week four-drug regimen with sparfloxacin and clarithromycin. These work because fluoroquinolones, minocycline and clarithromycin have antileprotic activity.

front: NLEP 2009 classification of leprosy for treatment.
text: Paucibacillary (PB): {{1 to 5}} skin lesions, with no nerve or only {{one}} nerve involved, and skin smear {{negative}} at all sites. Multibacillary (MB): {{6 or more}} skin lesions, more than one nerve involved, or skin smear {{positive}} at any site.

Paucibacillary: rifampicin {{600 mg}} monthly plus dapsone {{100 mg}} daily, for {{6 months}}.

front: What is a lepra reaction and when does it occur?
back: An abrupt inflammatory episode in lepromatous leprosy, usually starting when chemotherapy begins or with an intercurrent infection; lesions enlarge and redden and constitutional symptoms appear. It resembles a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.

front: Why was multibacillary leprosy treatment shortened to 12 months?
back: Dapsone monotherapy had caused resistance and relapse in up to 20 percent of patients. Fixed-duration therapy of 24 months gave relapse rates similar to standard MDT, and a WHO committee (1997) found 12 months gave similar relapse rates over 3 to 5 years. So mass programmes use 12 months for MB and 6 months for PB. Private or institutional care may treat longer, up to 4 years in highly bacillated patients.

front: Leprosy relapse and leprosy-TB coinfection: what is the management?
back: Relapse: restart the same MDT (12 months for MB, 6 months for PB), because dormant bacilli remain sensitive to these drugs. Coinfection with TB: continue the leprosy MDT but give rifampicin daily, as for TB. HIV: there is no association with leprosy, and MDT can be given safely to HIV-positive patients and those on antiretroviral therapy.

back: A bicyclic nitroimidazole prodrug. The mycobacterial enzyme encoded by Rv3547 activates it to a reactive intermediate that inhibits mycolic acid production. MIC against M. tuberculosis is about 0.006 to 0.012 mg/L.

front: Delamanid and pretomanid: resistance, interactions and cautions
back: Resistance involves fgd (FGD1) point mutations for both; delamanid resistance is also linked to fbiA mutations, and some pretomanid-resistant isolates lack fgd mutations. Pretomanid is partly metabolised by CYP3A, so strong or moderate inducers are avoided, and rifampicin lowers its exposure. Delamanid has modest QT prolongation and is taken with food because absorption is low otherwise. Pretomanid was registered on only about 100 patients, so its safety is less established.

front: Six-month all-oral regimen for XDR-TB: which three drugs, and why is linezolid the limit?
back: Bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid (BPaL), given together for 6 months. GG14 cites a phase III trial (Conradie 2020) and says the regimen is FDA-approved for XDR-TB. Linezolid's use is limited by mitochondrial toxicity with prolonged dosing: marrow suppression and peripheral and optic neuropathy.

front: Second-line anti-TB drugs: when are they used?
back: Used when the bacilli are resistant to one or more first-line drugs, or when first-line drugs cannot be tolerated or are contraindicated. They are less effective, less well tolerated, or both, so they are reserved for these cases.

front: Ethionamide: what is it, and what limits its use?
back: A drug chemically like isoniazid but containing sulfur, active against extracellular and intracellular bacilli, with moderate efficacy. It is used for drug-resistant TB; in leprosy it is only a last-resort alternative. It is poorly tolerated and causes hepatotoxicity in about 10 percent of patients.

front: Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS): mechanism, role and adverse effects?
back: Related to sulfonamides and probably inhibits folate synthase, so it is weakly tuberculostatic. It adds little to stronger drugs but delays resistance. It competes with isoniazid for acetylation and prolongs its half-life. Poorly accepted: anorexia, nausea and epigastric pain; also rashes, fever, hypokalaemia, goitre, liver dysfunction, and rarely blood dyscrasias. Used only when tuberculocidal drugs cannot be given.

back: A large-molecule therapeutic, usually a protein (hormone, cytokine, monoclonal antibody, fusion protein), often made by recombinant DNA technology in living cells rather than by chemical synthesis. Oligonucleotide drugs are also grouped with biopharmaceuticals, although some (e.g. antisense oligonucleotides) are made synthetically, so the biological/small-molecule boundary is not sharp.

front: How are monoclonal antibodies named, and what change did WHO make in 2021?
back: Names end in -mab. The syllable before it shows origin: -omab mouse (murine), -ximab chimeric (human constant Fc fused to mouse variable Fv domains), -zumab humanised (only the antigen-binding CDRs are non-human, inserted into a human IgG scaffold), -umab fully human (from transgenic mice carrying human Ig genes, or phage display). Another syllable can show function, e.g. -li- immunomodulatory (nivolumab, cemiplimab). Examples: cetuximab, trastuzumab, bevacizumab. In October 2021 WHO changed the scheme for newly named antibodies: the single -mab stem is being replaced by four distinct stems that describe the antibody's composition; names assigned up to 2021 keep the old pattern.

front: Why do monoclonal antibody names end in -mab, and what does the syllable just before it tell you?
back: The stem -mab marks a monoclonal antibody. The infix before it shows origin: -momab mouse, -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab human.

back: Half-life about 22 days, so it is given weekly for 4 weeks, then as maintenance every 3 to 6 months (GG14 ch72).

front: Why does a chimeric antibody such as cetuximab still cause anti-drug antibodies, and how does humanisation help?
back: Chimeric antibodies keep mouse variable regions, which the immune system can recognise as foreign. Humanised antibodies keep only the mouse CDRs, so immunogenicity falls; fully human antibodies reduce it further.
