front: Ligand blockade versus receptor blockade: how do they differ, with one example each?
back: Ligand blockade: the antibody binds the soluble ligand so it cannot reach its receptor (bevacizumab binds VEGF-A; anti-TNF antibodies neutralise TNF-alpha). Receptor blockade: the antibody binds the receptor's extracellular domain and prevents ligand binding (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR).

front: What is antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), and which cells mediate it?
back: The antibody's Fc region engages Fc receptors on NK cells or phagocytes, which then kill the antibody-coated target cell. IgG1 interacts with Fc receptors more strongly than IgG2 or IgG4, and Fc engineering can enhance or suppress ADCC. Examples: elotuzumab (SLAMF7 on myeloma cells); rituximab, ofatumumab and obinutuzumab (CD20, together with complement-dependent lysis).

front: What is complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), and which antibody shows it?
back: Antibody bound to the target cell activates complement; the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9) then lyses the cell. IgG1 activates complement better than IgG2 or IgG4. Rituximab (anti-CD20) kills B cells mostly by CDC and ADCC; daratumumab (anti-CD38) may kill myeloma cells by CDC, ADCC or apoptosis.

text: Ipilimumab blocks {{CTLA-4}}, nivolumab and pembrolizumab block {{PD-1}}, and atezolizumab blocks {{PD-L1}}. Blocking these brakes releases antitumour T cells.

front: Name the antibody targets: rituximab, trastuzumab, bevacizumab, cetuximab.
back: Rituximab: CD20 on B cells. Trastuzumab: HER2 receptor. Bevacizumab: VEGF-A ligand. Cetuximab: EGF receptor. Bevacizumab is ligand blockade; the others hit a cell-surface antigen or receptor.

front: What is a bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE)? Give one example and its main toxicities.
back: A bispecific antibody with one arm binding a tumour antigen and the other binding CD3 on T cells, bringing T cells close to tumour cells so they kill them. Blinatumomab (CD19 x CD3) is used in relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor ALL and in ALL with minimal residual disease; teclistamab (BCMA x CD3) in multiple myeloma. Monitor for cytokine release syndrome, neurological toxicity and infections.

front: What is an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC), and how is its payload released?
back: A monoclonal antibody chemically linked to a cytotoxic payload (toxin or drug; radionuclides are used similarly). The antibody binds its tumour antigen, the complex is internalised, and the payload is released inside the cell by proteolytic cleavage. Payloads include microtubule disruptors (emtansine, MMAE) and topoisomerase inhibitors (deruxtecan).

front: What is the advantage of linking a toxin to an antibody rather than giving the toxin alone?
back: The antibody delivers the payload to cells carrying the tumour antigen; after internalisation the payload is released inside the cell, aiming the cytotoxic drug at the target.

front: Brentuximab vedotin: target, payload and main indications

Monitor mainly for neutropenia and peripheral sensory neuropathy.

front: What is cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which biologics cause it, and how is it treated?
back: A systemic reaction to a large release of cytokines (TNF, interleukins including IL-6, interferons). Features: fever, chills, rigors, nausea, headache, tachycardia, hypotension, dyspnoea and wheezing; can be life-threatening. front: What are the aims, subjects and dose strategy of a phase I trial?
back: First-in-human study of safety, tolerability and human PK. Subjects are mostly healthy volunteers; when the drug is expected to be toxic (e.g. cancer or AIDS therapy) volunteer patients are used instead. Size: about 20 to 80 subjects (KDT); 10 to 100 (GG14); 20 to 100 (Katzung). Done by trained clinical pharmacologists with vital functions monitored and resuscitation at hand. Subjects receive the drug one by one, starting at about 1/100 to 1/10 of the highest dose that was non-toxic in animals, escalated stepwise to find the dose range for later study. Open label (no blinding).

front: What does a phase II trial aim to establish?
back: Therapeutic exploration and dose ranging: the first study in patients with the target disease ('proof of concept'). Size: about 100 to 500 patients (KDT); 50 to 500 (GG14); 100 to 200 (Katzung). Patients are selected by inclusion and exclusion criteria. Aims: therapeutic efficacy, dose range and ceiling effect; tolerability and PK are extended from phase I. Mostly controlled and randomised, blinded or open, generally at 2 to 4 centres. A candidate drug may be dropped here if efficacy is inadequate.

front: What is a phase III trial, and what does its completion lead to?
back: Therapeutic confirmation: randomised, usually double-blind comparison with existing therapy, done at many centres by specialists in the disease. Size: about 500 to 3000 patients (KDT); a few hundred to a few thousand (GG14); usually thousands (Katzung). It confirms efficacy, assesses safety on a wider scale, finalises indications and may add PK data. Some immunologically mediated toxicities first appear here. Completion leads to the marketing application: NDA, or BLA for biologics. Toxic but valuable drugs may receive restricted marketing permission (e.g. hospital use only).

front: Classify: phases of a drug trial
text: Phase {{I}} is the first-in-human study in about {{20 to 80}} subjects, usually {{healthy volunteers}}, and open label; phase {{II}} explores dose and efficacy in about 100 to 500 patients; phase {{III}} is a {{randomised, double-blind}} multicentre comparison in about 500 to 3000 patients that supports the marketing application; phase {{IV}} is {{postmarketing}} surveillance.

front: What preclinical tests precede human trials?
back: Animal work checks the whole pharmacological profile: screening, isolated organ and culture tests, disease models, systemic pharmacology, dose-response, pharmacokinetics, and toxicity in at least two species (one rodent, one non-rodent). Toxicity tests are acute (LD50, 1 to 3 days), subacute (2 to 12 weeks), chronic (6 to 12 months), reproduction and teratogenicity, mutagenicity (Ames test), and carcinogenicity. Toxicity work follows Good Laboratory Practices (GLP).

front: What do phase IV studies detect that earlier phases cannot?
back: Postmarketing studies in the general treated population, with far larger numbers and everyday prescribing. They pick up uncommon or idiosyncratic adverse effects, effects of long-term use and unsuspected drug interactions, and show real patterns of use. They also study groups excluded from earlier trials (children, elderly, pregnant or lactating women, renal or hepatic disease), and new formulations, routes or fixed-dose combinations.

front: Why is randomisation used, and when is stratified randomisation chosen?
back: Subjects are allocated by a preselected random number table or computer programme, so each has an equal chance of entering the test or control group. Neither investigator nor patient can influence allocation, so that source of bias is removed. When groups may end up ill-matched (especially small groups), stratified randomisation is used: subjects are first divided by age, sex, disease severity or other variables, and randomised within each stratum. Too many strata defeat the purpose.

front: What is blinding in a clinical trial, and what is an open trial?
back: Blinding hides which treatment (test or control) a person is getting. Single blind hides it from the subject; double blind hides it from both subject and investigator. The two medicines must look, weigh and taste alike and come in unlabelled packs numbered per patient. The allocation code is held by a third party (data management) not involved in treatment or recording, and is broken only after the trial ends. Why: it removes conscious and unconscious expectation bias. A trial where the treatment is not hidden is called open (not every trial needs blinding).

front: What is a controlled trial, and what can the control group receive?
back: A controlled trial has a comparator group as similar as possible to the test group, so any difference can be credited to the test drug. The control gets either a placebo (only if ethically permissible) or the existing standard treatment (active control). The regimen (dose, frequency, duration) is fixed in advance, so results apply only to that regimen; separate dose-ranging trials are needed to judge other doses.

front: What are the advantages of a multicentric trial?
back: Many large trials run at more than one centre, sometimes in several countries. Advantages: more patients recruited in less time; results apply to a wider population; regulatory requirements of several countries can be met; credibility of the trial rises. Phase III trials are usually multicentric.

front: Compare parallel-group and crossover trial designs.
back: Parallel: test and control groups run at the same time, each with different patients. Crossover: the same patients receive both treatments in a random order, so each serves as its own control. Crossover reduces between-patient variation and the sample size needed, but carry-over and order effects can occur, and it suits only chronic diseases that stay stable over time.

front: What is an adaptive trial design?
back: Conventional statistical methods may fail to give a clear answer when trials meet unexpected confounders, loss of subjects or marked subgroup differences. Adaptive statistical methods allow the study design to be changed when interim data show the need. They may permit decisions on superiority as well as non-inferiority, shorten the trial, reveal new benefits and give more reliable conclusions.

front: Why does the Declaration of Helsinki discourage placebo controls when an effective treatment exists?
back: If a proven alternative exists, subjects randomised to placebo would in effect be denied treatment during the trial, which is an ethical problem (beneficence, non-maleficence). So the comparator then should be the existing standard treatment (active control). This is also why a placebo is used only where ethically permissible.

front: What is a sequential trial design, and when is it applicable?
back: Matched pairs of subjects are compared one pair at a time and scored as A better than B, B better than A, or no difference. The score is plotted continuously until a preset boundary for superiority, inferiority or no difference is crossed, and then the trial stops. It uses the fewest subjects, but suits only drugs and diseases where clinical end points come quickly and matched pairs can be recruited.

front: Classify: errors and power in a trial
text: A type {{I}} error is a {{false positive}} result, declaring a difference that does not exist; a type {{II}} error is a {{false negative}}; the {{power}} of a trial is 1 minus the type II error rate.

front: Why must sample size be calculated before a trial begins?
back: Money and ethics both require the smallest number of subjects that can still give a valid answer: too few cannot settle the question, too many expose people needlessly. The trial uses only a sample of all patients, which may not represent the population, so results are never absolutely conclusive. Hence the number needed to show test better, control better, or no difference is calculated statistically in advance.

front: What is the difference between a clinical end point and a surrogate end point?
back: A clinical end point is an outcome that matters to the patient, such as myocardial infarction, fracture or death. A surrogate end point is an easily measured marker that is expected to predict it: LDL cholesterol for myocardial infarction, bone mineral density for fracture, HbA1c for diabetic complications. Surrogates cut trial cost and time, but the marker may not truly reflect the disease outcome.

front: What factors determine the sample size of a clinical trial?
back: Four inputs: the significance level (type I error, usually 0.05); the power (1 minus type II error); the smallest clinically meaningful difference expected between groups; and the variability of the primary endpoint. A smaller expected difference, greater variability, higher power or a stricter significance level all increase the number needed. Sample size is calculated in advance because it must be minimal for both ethical and financial reasons.

front: Case: a drug approved on LDL lowering later shows no effect on carotid thickness. What does this teach about surrogate end points?
back: Ezetimibe lowers LDL further than a statin alone, and was approved assuming LDL is a good surrogate for myocardial infarction and stroke. A 7-year trial of over 18,000 patients (IMPROVE-IT) later showed fewer myocardial infarctions and strokes, vindicating approval. Lesson: surrogates save time and money but their link to hard outcomes must be shown, sometimes only by a later clinical-end-point trial.

front: What is the Declaration of Helsinki and how does it relate to GCP?
back: It is the World Medical Association statement of ethical principles for research on human subjects. Good Clinical Practice, laid down by the ICH, gives standards for design, ethics, conduct, monitoring, auditing, recording, analysis and reporting of trials; following it assures credible, accurate data and protects the rights, integrity and confidentiality of subjects as set out in Helsinki. In India, ICMR (2006) also framed ethical guidelines for biomedical research on human participants.

front: What are the roles of the sponsor, the investigators and the institutional review board in a drug trial?

Investigators: run the trial; in phase III they are usually specialists in the disease. Institutional review board (ethics committee) at each facility: an interdisciplinary body that must review and approve the scientific and ethical plan before testing in humans.

front: How does an ethics committee categorise proposals for review?
back: By risk. Expedited review is for research with minimal average risk, for example studies of drugs or devices that are already approved. Full review is for research with more than minimal risk. The member secretary screens each proposal for completeness and assigns the category.

front: Case: a company runs a multicentre phase III trial in India. What must happen before the first patient is enrolled?
back: The sponsor applies for permission to start the trial (the IND); the DCGI decides within 90 working days. The investigator signs an undertaking, a legal document filed with CDSCO, to follow the protocol and GCP. The ethics committee at each site must approve the protocol, and the trial must not begin until both EC and DCGI approve. Investigators then take written informed consent.

front: Classify: components of valid informed consent
text: Consent must be {{voluntary}}, informed and {{written}}; the subject keeps the right to decide whether to {{continue}} in the trial (autonomy).

front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define a serious adverse event (SAE) in a clinical trial?
back: An untoward medical occurrence during a clinical trial that results in death; in-patient hospitalisation (if the study was on out-patients) or prolonged hospitalisation (if on in-patients); persistent or significant disability or incapacity; a congenital anomaly or birth defect; or is otherwise life-threatening. The NDCT Rules amended the earlier Schedule Y rule (Rule 122DAB).

front: Name the four ethical principles an ethics committee must ensure a trial does not breach.
back: Autonomy (freedom, dignity, confidentiality; right to join or withdraw), beneficence (aim to do good to subject and society), non-maleficence (no harm or undue risk), justice (fairness, honesty and impartiality in obtaining, analysing and communicating data).

front: What is informed consent and why is it required?
back: Written, voluntary agreement of a subject after being told that the drug is investigational and of its possible risks, and that they may decline or withdraw from the trial. It puts autonomy into practice and is needed before enrolment.

front: What must trial subjects be told, and what are the limits of informed consent?
back: Subjects must be told that the drug is investigational, the nature and risks of the trial, and that they may be randomly and unknowingly assigned to test or control. They must be free to decline, or to stop participating (autonomy), and confidentiality is protected. Consent is proper and written. Limits: unconscious, demented or mentally ill patients cannot consent, and trials in children and the elderly raise similar concerns, yet such groups still need trials.

front: Recall: SAE reporting timelines under the NDCT Rules 2019

A drug or biological product for diagnosis, treatment or prevention of a rare disease, or of a commoner disease endemic only in resource-poor areas, for which there is no reasonable expectation that development and marketing costs will be recovered from sales. Under the US Orphan Drug Amendment (1983), a rare disease affects fewer than 200,000 people in the USA. Governments offer tax benefits and other incentives. Examples given orphan status: clofazimine, paromomycin, sodium stibogluconate, rituximab, bortezomib.

front: What is an academic clinical trial under the NDCT Rules 2019?
back: A trial intended solely for academic research. It needs only Ethics Committee approval; no permission from the DCGI is required. Its results must not be used for promotional purposes or to seek regulatory approval.

front: Under the NDCT Rules 2019, which products count as new drugs?
back: A modified or sustained-release form, or a novel delivery system, of an approved drug; and a vaccine, recombinant DNA product, living modified organism, monoclonal antibody, stem-cell or gene-therapy product, or xenograft intended as a drug. Phytopharmaceuticals were added to the definition too. Why: the 2019 Rules replaced Part XA and Schedule Y of the D&C Rules 1945.

text: The DCGI decides within {{90 days}} for drugs developed outside India and {{30 days}} for drugs developed in India; no reply means {{automatic approval}}. Permission is valid {{2 years}}, and a rejected applicant may seek reconsideration within {{60 days}}.

front: Why do orphan drugs need special incentives?
back: Proving safety and efficacy in small populations is complex; little basic research is done on rare diseases, so rational targets are few; and development cost weighs heavily when the target population is small. Excessive product-liability costs (e.g. failure-to-warn claims for rare harms not detected in small trials) are a further disincentive. Hence tax benefits and other incentives, and support from not-for-profit foundations.

front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define an orphan drug, and what concessions do they give?
back: An orphan drug is one intended to treat a condition affecting not more than five lakh (500,000) persons in India. Concessions: fast-track approval and special status, including a complete fee waiver for clinical trial filing; expedited review where safety and efficacy evidence is established even before all trial phases are complete (post-marketing trials may then be required); and waiver of the local clinical study and phase IV if the CLA is satisfied. Marketing still needs CDSCO authorisation to import or manufacture.

front: Why can orphan drugs be approved before all trial phases finish, and what safeguards remain?
back: Small patient numbers make large trials hard and returns low, so rules give incentives (India: fee waiver, fast-track; see also tax benefits in the US). In India, where safety and efficacy evidence is already established, expedited review is allowed even if not all phases are done, but post-marketing trials may then be required to confirm the benefit. Local clinical study and phase IV may be waived only if the CLA is satisfied, and marketing still needs CDSCO authorisation.

front: How is pharmacovigilance organised in India and internationally (as given in KDT)?
back: Pharmacovigilance centres exist in most countries, with the Uppsala Monitoring Centre (Sweden) as the international collaborating centre. In India, CDSCO coordinates the pharmacovigilance programme, with peripheral, regional and zonal monitoring centres and a National Pharmacovigilance Advisory Committee. Centres collect, communicate and disseminate ADR data by linking with hospitals and practitioners, and assess causality (Naranjo algorithm) and severity (modified Hartwig scale).

text: A {{cohort}} study follows users and non-users of a drug to find uncommon adverse effects; a {{case-control}} study compares the frequency of drug use in cases with an adverse response against controls.

front: Define adverse effect, adverse drug reaction (ADR) and adverse drug event (ADE).
back: Adverse effect: any undesirable or unintended consequence of drug use, trivial or serious. ADR: a noxious change suspected to be due to a drug, at normal doses, needing treatment, dose reduction or caution in future use; it excludes trivial or expected effects and poisoning. ADE: any untoward medical occurrence during treatment, not necessarily caused by the drug; all events are recorded first and causality is judged later on pooled data.

front: How is causality of an adverse event assessed?
back: Four criteria: temporal relationship (does timing fit drug exposure), previous knowledge (known to cause it before), dechallenge (event subsides on stopping) and rechallenge (event recurs on re-giving; often unethical so not done). Why: a clear yes/no link is seldom provable, so causality is graded. Grades: definite, probable, possible, doubtful. Centres use the Naranjo algorithm for causality and the modified Hartwig scale for severity.

front: Why can spontaneous adverse-event reports not give the true incidence of a drug reaction?
back: The denominator is unknown, because the number of patients exposed to the drug is not recorded. The numerator is also incomplete: most reactions go unreported, reporting patterns change over the life of the product, and reports often lack dose, concomitant drugs or outcome. Media attention and litigation further distort reporting, so reports cannot be used to compare rates between drugs.

front: What is a safety signal and how is it detected?
back: A signal is a possible link between a drug and an adverse event that needs evaluation. Signals are found by disproportionality analysis, which compares how often an event is reported with the drug against its frequency across the whole database. These methods need no drug-use denominator but rely on assumptions that are hard to verify, so a signal almost always needs confirmation from controlled studies.

front: When is a single case report strong evidence that a drug caused an event?
back: When the event is rare or unlikely from other causes, appears close in time after exposure, has few other risk factors, and the drug carries a large excess risk. Examples are anaphylaxis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and rhabdomyolysis with cerivastatin. Otherwise a case report only raises suspicion.

front: Is a phase IV trial the same as post-marketing surveillance?
back: No. Phase IV trials test the drug in real-life use: factors that change its effect, long-term and rare effects, special populations, and interactions. The CLA may require them or the sponsor may start them. Post-marketing surveillance (PMS), also called a non-interventional or observational study, is active surveillance run under the conditions of the approved package insert. Its protocol needs CLA approval, and PMS is mandatory for a new drug.

front: Which studies, besides phase IV, can be run in the post-marketing period?

front: What is a humanized animal in drug testing?
back: An animal, usually a mouse, given human genes, cells or tissue so it responds more like a human to a drug. Why: it tests human-specific metabolism or immune effects better than a normal animal, but it is still not a human.

front: Short note: Nanoscreen and humanized animals in preclinical drug testing

points: Screens a library of nanoparticles that differ in size, charge, pKa or hydrophobicity
Cell-based assays measure toxicity, uptake and efficacy; some libraries go straight to animals
Barcoded particles can be pooled and tracked in vivo by deep sequencing
Advantages: no prior hypothesis needed, fast and cost-efficient; results guide the next library
Limits: in vitro results correlate poorly with in vivo; most use 2D cell monocultures; scale-up and reproducibility are hard
Animal carrying human genes, cells or tissue, e.g. human drug-metabolising enzymes or human immune cells
Uses: predicting human pharmacokinetics and drug interactions; testing antibody drugs and immunotherapy
Limits: still an animal; weak human cell engraftment, short lifespan, immature immune environment
Both are preclinical tools, used before first-in-human (phase 1) trials
Both aim to predict human response more reliably than a normal animal model

front: Define bioassay and explain why a standard is run alongside the unknown.
back: Bioassay measures the potency of a drug or unknown mediator from the size of the biological effect it produces. The unknown (U) is compared with a standard (S) on the same test system, because absolute 'units' (e.g. pigeon or mouse units) differ between laboratories, whereas the relative potency of U and S can be agreed. The assay estimates the dose of U that gives the same effect as a known dose of S.

front: What is a 2 + 2 (parallel-line) bioassay, and why is it used?
back: The minimal parallel-line design: two doses of standard (S1, S2) and two of unknown (U1, U2), chosen to fall on the linear part of the log dose-response curve. Doses are given repeatedly in random order, which measures the variability of the test system and lets the confidence limits of the potency ratio be calculated. Example: a modified 2 + 2 assay in patients showed morphine to be about 13 times as potent an analgesic as codeine.

front: Parallel-line assay: how is potency read?
text: In a parallel-line assay the potency ratio is read from the {{horizontal distance}} between the standard and unknown log dose-response lines. A simple ratio is invalid if the lines are not {{parallel}} or the maximal responses differ.

front: Short note: Requirements of a valid bioassay

points: Compare unknown with a standard on the same preparation
Compare equi-effective doses from dose-response curves, not responses to equal doses
Log dose-response lines of standard and unknown must be parallel
Maximal responses must be similar; differing mechanisms or a partial agonist invalidate a simple potency ratio
Biological variation is the main problem
Minimise variation, avoid systematic error, and estimate limits of error
Randomised order of doses; observer (and subject) unaware of the dose
Graded or quantal responses need different statistics

front: In a bioassay, what goes wrong if the log dose-response lines of standard and unknown are not parallel?
back: Equi-effective doses and a single potency ratio are valid only if the log dose-response lines are parallel: the horizontal distance between parallel lines gives the log of the potency ratio. Non-parallel lines mean one ratio is not valid.

front: Case: you must estimate histamine in an unknown extract using an isolated tissue. Outline a valid design.
back: Use a histamine-sensitive preparation such as guinea pig ileum. Run standard and unknown on the same tissue, find equi-effective doses from dose-response curves, check the log dose-response lines are parallel, and express the unknown potency as a ratio to the standard.

front: Graded vs quantal dose-response: how do they differ?
back: Graded responses are continuous (e.g. fall in BP, strength of contraction) and are measured in each individual, giving a sigmoidal curve of response against log dose. Quantal responses are all-or-none (e.g. death, convulsion). The proportion of a population responding is plotted against dose, giving a cumulative curve from which median doses (ED50, LD50) are read.
ED50: the dose producing the specified therapeutic effect in 50% of subjects. TD50: the dose producing a defined toxic effect in 50% of subjects. LD50: the dose that kills 50% of the test animals.

front: Potency vs efficacy: define each and give one example.
back: Potency is the dose or concentration needed for a given effect (its position on the dose axis). Efficacy is the maximal effect a drug can produce (the height of the plateau). Morphine is more efficacious than aspirin as an analgesic; pethidine is less potent than morphine but equally efficacious.

text: Therapeutic index in animals = {{LD50}} / {{ED50}}. In humans the index uses {{TD50}} in place of LD50, because TD50 is the dose producing a defined toxic effect in 50% of people.

front: What is the dose ratio, and how does a Schild plot measure competitive antagonist affinity?
back: Dose ratio (r): the factor by which agonist concentration must be raised in the presence of an antagonist to restore a given response. With a reversible competitive antagonist the log concentration-effect curve shifts right without change in slope or maximum, and r increases linearly with antagonist concentration. A Schild plot of log(r - 1) against log antagonist concentration gives the antagonist's equilibrium dissociation constant (KB) from the abscissal intercept, e.g. propranolol on isolated guinea-pig atria. Antagonist affinity measured this way is used to classify receptors.

front: Short note: Therapeutic index and margin of safety

points: Gap between therapeutic and adverse-effect dose-response curves = safety margin or therapeutic index
Animals: TI = LD50 / ED50
Humans: TI = TD50 / ED50
Measurable only in animals (LD50 form)
LD50 does not reflect adverse effects at therapeutic doses
ED50 depends on the effect chosen (aspirin for headache vs as antirheumatic)
Individual variation in efficacy and toxicity is not captured
Clinically the therapeutic window (minimal therapeutic dose to maximal acceptable dose) is more relevant
Narrow-margin drugs need individualised dosing and monitoring

front: Why is the LD50/ED50 therapeutic index a poor guide to safety, and what is used clinically instead?
back: LD50 is measured only in animals and does not reflect the incidence of toxic effects, so it is not a useful guide to clinical safety. ED50 depends on the effect chosen. The therapeutic window, the range of doses between effective and toxic, is the clinical concept.

front: Frog rectus abdominis: what phenomenon does it demonstrate?
back: Repeated or high doses of acetylcholine produce progressively smaller contractions; shortly after a high (100-fold) dose the response is markedly reduced and returns only after time is allowed. This illustrates receptor desensitisation at the nicotinic end plate. The preparation is also a classical system for studying acetylcholine responses at nicotinic receptors.

front: Classify: isolated tissues and what each tests
text: Guinea pig ileum is used to show {{muscarinic}} actions of acetylcholine blocked by atropine, and its contraction is a standard bioassay for {{histamine}} (H1). Frog rectus abdominis shows {{nicotinic}} end-plate desensitisation. Isolated guinea pig {{atria}} are used to measure competitive antagonism of isoprenaline by propranolol.

front: Which isolated tissue shows muscarinic ACh contraction blocked by atropine and also serves as a histamine bioassay?
back: Guinea pig ileum. ACh contraction is blocked by atropine (muscarinic), while histamine contraction is not affected; the same tissue is the standard histamine bioassay.

front: Which isolated tissue is used to measure the positive chronotropic effect of isoprenaline?
back: Guinea pig atria. Isoprenaline increases the rate of isolated guinea pig atria (positive chronotropic effect), so this tissue is used to assay it.

front: Short note: Isolated organ bath preparations

points: A strip of smooth muscle or other tissue is held in an organ bath, and contraction or relaxation is recorded
Response is plotted against concentration as a concentration-effect curve
Estimate maximal response and potency of agonists
Detect specific activity early in screening (e.g. antihistaminic, vasodilator)
Measure antagonist affinity by dose ratio and Schild analysis
The classical technique of pharmacology, still widely used alongside molecular and cellular assays

front: Short note: Isometric force recording in isolated tissues

points: Tissue is held at a fixed length, so contraction appears as force
Force is recorded by a transducer and drawn on a polygraph
Strip or ring mounted in a small organ bath of physiological salt solution (e.g. Krebs bicarbonate)
One end fixed to the bath, the other to a strain gauge or force-displacement transducer
Resting tension applied, e.g. 2 g for spiral strips of bovine coronary artery in a 4 mL bath
Test relaxant or contractile drugs against standard agonists
Rabbit aorta rings contracted by KCl or noradrenaline show calcium-channel antagonism as relaxation
Isolated heart: contractile force measured isometrically by a force transducer

front: Short note: Human tissue assays in clinical development

points: Early human study with limited exposure and no therapeutic intent, to decide go or no-go
Aims: refine and validate a biomarker assay and test drug effect on its target in human tissue
Gives human PK-PD data and checks that the mechanism seen in animals occurs in humans
In vitro pyrogen test using donated human blood
Human skin from surgery or donated cadavers used for penetration studies
US National Disease Research Interchange supplies human tissue to researchers
Human blood monocytes incubated with a glucocorticoid; receptor expression measured by FACS
Pre-clinical safety data required for phase 0 are small, so fewer animal studies are needed

front: Case: design an organ-bath experiment to prove propranolol is a competitive antagonist of isoprenaline and estimate its affinity.
back: Record isoprenaline curves on guinea pig atria alone and with increasing propranolol. Competitive antagonism gives parallel rightward shifts with an unchanged maximum. Calculate the dose ratio r at each antagonist concentration and plot log(r - 1) against negative log antagonist concentration (Schild plot). The x-intercept is pA2, which equals -log KB.

front: Rat paw oedema: what does it screen, and what are its limits?
back: Irritant chemicals injected into a rat's paw make it swollen and tender. Drugs that reduce this swelling predict well the symptomatic relief of inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, so it is used to screen anti-inflammatory drugs. Limit: such simple models predict efficacy only with fair accuracy and are far from perfect.

front: MES vs PTZ anticonvulsant screens: what does each predict?
back: MES: a brief high-intensity shock to the rodent head gives tonic flexion, tonic extension and clonic convulsions. Drugs that abolish the tonic (extensor) phase (e.g. phenytoin, carbamazepine) are effective in GTCS and complex partial seizures; activity reflects action on seizure spread. PTZ: injection produces clonic seizures, prevented by drugs effective in absence and myoclonic seizures (e.g. ethosuximide, valproate, clonazepam); activity reflects action on the seizure focus. Other models: chronic focal seizures (alumina cream on monkey cortex) and kindling.

front: What makes a good animal model of human disease?
back: It should resemble the human disease in pathophysiological phenotype (face validity), causation (construct validity) and response to treatment (predictive validity). Difficulties: many psychiatric diseases cannot be observed in animals; causes of degenerative diseases are complex; selecting models by response to known drugs may miss new mechanisms; transgenic models can mislead (cystic fibrosis gene defect affects mainly the intestine in mice).

front: Classify: animal models of human disease used in drug screening
text: Examples include {{kindled}} seizures in rats, {{spontaneously hypertensive}} rats (genetic model), experimental tuberculosis in mice, and {{alloxan}}-induced diabetes in rats or dogs.

front: Animal models of depression: principle and limitations.
back: Mild stress procedures, such as the forced swim test or inescapable foot shock, produce behavioural states (social withdrawal, loss of appetite, reduced motor activity) that mimic aspects of human depression and are used to test antidepressants. Limitation: no known animal condition corresponds to inherited human depression, and no clear brain pathology is defined, so face and construct validity are poor; models selected on response to known drugs may miss new mechanisms.

front: Short note: Role of the mouse as an experimental animal

points: Rodents, including mice, are used first; larger animals follow
Unfavourable compounds are dropped at each stage, so few reach human trials
Transgenic mice carry an introduced gene (knock-in) or an inactivated gene (knockout)
Used to build disease models for drug testing
Rodents preferred for genetic toxicity tests, e.g. mouse-specific locus test and micronucleus test
Rodents preferred for embryotoxicity and reproductive toxicity studies
Mouse local lymph node assay: test substance applied to mouse ear for three days
Lymph node cell proliferation measured; accepted by EPA, OECD and FDA as preferred assay
Mice immunised to raise antibody-producing cells for monoclonal antibody production
Behaviour tests such as tail suspension and rota-rod

front: Short note: Animal models for testing learning and memory

points: Morris water maze: hidden platform in a circular pool; escape latency recorded over at least 5 days
Probe test 24 h after training, with platform removed, measures spatial memory
Y-maze, T-maze, radial arm maze and Barnes circular maze
Inhibitory (passive) avoidance uses negative reinforcement to test long-term memory
Step-through and step-down variants
Scopolamine (muscarinic antagonist) impairs learning and memory in rodents and humans
Dizocilpine (NMDA antagonist) produces memory impairment for testing memory enhancers

front: Short note: Guinea pig as an experimental animal

points: Ileum: acetylcholine contraction blocked by atropine, histamine response unaffected
Ileum contraction is a standard bioassay for histamine
Atria: competitive antagonism of isoprenaline by propranolol
Guinea pigs are the most sensitive common species to histamine
Histamine-induced bronchoconstriction is strong; anaphylactic bronchoconstriction is largely prevented by antihistamines
Draize eye and skin irritancy tests use rabbits and guinea pigs
Guinea pig maximisation test used for skin sensitisation
Armstrong/Harber test in guinea pig when a drug or metabolite may cause photosensitivity

front: Short note: Animal models in vaccine development and testing

points: Preclinical stage: in vitro work, then in vivo testing in animals, before any human dosing
Follows the exploratory stage, where candidate antigens are identified and may be modified by recombinant DNA technology
Immunogenicity: the immune response the vaccine provokes
Safety and toxicity
Approximate dose range and suitable formulation
Non-human primates (monkeys): the oral polio vaccine was first tested here for adverse effects and immunogenicity
Transgenic animals are now used in preclinical protocols for more accurate prediction of human reactions
Satisfactory preclinical data lead to phase I, the first human study in a small group (about 20) of healthy adults

front: Short note: Screening a new molecule for anti-anxiety activity

points: Rodents avoid brightly lit or open spaces, so anxiolytics change their exploration and avoidance
Test drug given about 30 min before testing (i.p. in the plus-maze protocol)
Elevated plus maze (Pellow, 1985): anxiolytic effect is more time and entries in the open arms
Light-dark (black and white) box: anxiolytics increase crossings between the chambers
Social interaction test: anxiolytics reverse the suppression of social contact in a bright, unfamiliar setting
Geller-Seifter operant conflict test: high predictive value for classical anxiolytics
Vogel lick-conflict test: anxiolytics increase the number of shocks accepted while drinking
Diazepam increases time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus maze
Animal carrying a foreign gene, or an altered gene, deliberately placed in its genome
The new gene is inherited by offspring in the same way as native genes
Mice are the usual species: over 80% of mouse genes work like human genes, and they breed quickly
DNA microinjection into the male pronucleus of a fertilised ovum: first effective method in mammals; insertion is random
Embryonic stem cell transfer: targeted by homologous recombination; the method of choice for knockout animals
Retrovirus-mediated transfer into an early embryo, which is then implanted
Disease models: mice carrying the human poliovirus receptor can be infected; APP transgenic mice model Alzheimer disease
Toxicology test animals, drug efficacy testing, production of pharmaceutical proteins, and veterinary uses such as higher milk yield
Insertional mutation can disrupt important biological processes
Unregulated gene expression and side effects such as arthritis, dermatitis or cancer
Animal welfare and ethical objections

front: Essay: Preclinical pharmacological screening of a new analgesic and anti-inflammatory drug

points: Animal tests expose the whole pharmacological profile before human use
Rodent first, then a larger animal; unfavourable compounds are rejected at each step
Simple rapid screening tests for the sought activity (e.g. analgesic activity)
Isolated organ tests for specific activities
Rat paw oedema from irritant chemicals predicts anti-inflammatory benefit
Models need face, construct and predictive validity
Detailed confirmatory tests; related activities such as antipyretic and anti-inflammatory action of an analgesic
Systemic pharmacology on major organ systems; mechanism of action
Dose-response relationship, maximal effect, potency and efficacy compared with existing drugs
Pharmacokinetics, then toxicity testing
Animal efficacy may not translate (e.g. substance P antagonists were analgesic in animals but inactive in humans)

front: Acute toxicity study: design and endpoint.
back: Single escalating doses are given to small groups of animals (usually two species, two routes) and observed for overt effects and mortality for 1 to 3 days. Goals: the no-effect dose, the maximum tolerated dose and, where needed, the LD50, now estimated with the smallest possible number of animals. Organ toxicity is examined by histopathology.

front: Subacute and chronic toxicity studies: duration and parameters.
back: Subacute (subchronic): repeated doses for about 2 to 12 weeks (Katzung: 2 weeks to 3 months), usually three doses in two species; the longer the intended human use, the longer the test. Doses are chosen from ED50 and LD50. Chronic: a rodent and at least one non-rodent for 6 to 12 months, required when the drug will be used long term, and usually run alongside early clinical trials. Both record overt effects, food intake, body weight, haematology, biochemistry and organ histopathology.

front: How is the LD50 estimated from acute toxicity data?
back: Two calculation methods. Graphical (Miller and Tainter): convert each group's percentage mortality to a probit, plot probit against log dose after correcting the 0% and 100% groups, and read the dose at 50% mortality. Arithmetical (Karber): no plotting; uses the mean number dead in each dose interval and the dose difference between groups.

Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p162

front: Classify: species and routes in toxicity testing
text: Toxicity testing uses at least {{two}} species, one {{rodent}} and one {{non-rodent}}, dosed by the {{oral}} and {{parenteral}} routes.

points: At least two species, one rodent and one non-rodent, by oral and parenteral routes
Acute, subacute and chronic studies
Effects on spermatogenesis, ovulation, fertility, mating, parturition and the developing foetus (teratogenicity)
Two species, usually one rodent and rabbits
Carcinogenicity: dosing for 2 years or the whole life of the animal, required for drugs used long term
Mutagenicity: bacteria (Ames test), mammalian cells and intact rodents
Conducted under Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)
Thalidomide disaster led to more extensive teratogenicity testing
Ames test: detects mutations in bacteria
Mutations and genetic stability in mammalian cells in culture
Intact rodents: dominant lethal test and clastogenicity (chromosome damage) in mice
Part of the preclinical safety package with carcinogenicity testing
Rare effects may still be missed for statistical reasons

front: Graphical versus Karber method for LD50: which to choose and why?
back: Graphical method is simple and accurate in most cases and should be tried first, but needs probit plotting. Karber's method needs no plot and is the simplest and quickest, though crude, so it suits small animal numbers. In the worked example the graphical value was 79.5 mg/kg and Karber's was 81 mg/kg.

Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p162

front: Essay: Preclinical safety evaluation of a new drug candidate

points: Aim: identify likely human toxicities and those to monitor in trials
Two species, two routes
No-effect dose, maximum tolerated dose, LD50 if needed
Subacute and chronic designs with haematology, biochemistry and histopathology
Reproduction and teratogenicity
Mutagenicity (Ames, mammalian cells, rodents)
Carcinogenicity where long-term use is planned
First human dose usually 1/100 to 1/10 of the no-effect (non-toxic) dose in animals
Time-consuming and expensive (2 to 6 years)
Large numbers of animals
Extrapolation to humans imperfect; rare effects missed
GLP-compliant data package before human trials

front: How is the use of animals in preclinical testing being reduced?
text: Progress has been made in {{reducing the number}} of animals needed while keeping data valid; {{cell and tissue culture}} in vitro methods and {{computer modelling}} are increasingly used, though their {{predictive value}} is still limited.

front: What is CPCSEA, and what are its functions?
back: The Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals: a statutory body under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, formed in 1964 and revived in 1998. Sarkar lists its member secretary under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying. Functions: register establishments that experiment on or breed animals; appoint nominees to Institutional Animal Ethics Committees (IAECs); approve animal house facilities after inspection; permit experiments on animals; recommend import of animals; act against violations; and train nominees.

front: Short note: The 3Rs and the 4th R in animal experimentation

points: Russell and Burch defined alternatives as the three Rs: Replacement, Reduction, Refinement
CPCSEA introduced the 3Rs in India in 1999 and adopted a 4th R, Rehabilitation, in 2006 (others use Responsibility)
Absolute: no animals (human cells, computer models, dummies); relative: animal cells or tissues
Using lower organisms (microorganisms, invertebrates, eggs) instead of higher animals
Fewer animals where use is essential: better skills, pilot studies, proper design and statistics
Modify methods to minimise pain and distress; define humane endpoints
After-care of experimental animals until natural death; aseptic procedures; one major procedure per animal; proper post-operative care

front: Short note: Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC)

points: Every animal study (including tissue or cell collection from animals) must be approved by the IAEC first
Constituted in every CPCSEA-registered laboratory; CPCSEA guidelines govern animal maintenance
Held at scheduled intervals, with expedited review if needed
Decisions by consensus; dissent minuted; unresolved cases referred to CPCSEA
Multiple surgical procedures on one animal only if specified in the protocol and approved by the IAEC
Knows CPCSEA guidelines and the 4Rs; reviews proposals for humane issues and animal numbers
Visits the animal house at least once a year and submits an inspection report
Informs CPCSEA if no meetings are held for 6 months

front: If alternatives to animals are improving, why does safety testing in two species remain required?
back: Species differ in responses to toxic agents, and many effects, especially rare ones, appear only in whole animals. In vitro and computer methods reduce animal numbers, but their predictive value is still limited, so two-species testing is still done before human trials.

front: Essay: Use of animals in pharmacological research: value, limits and alternatives

points: Animal studies expose the pharmacological and toxicological profile before human use
Simple models often predict human efficacy (ferret motion-sickness model, rat paw oedema)
Safety testing in two species is required before trials
Many human diseases have no animal counterpart
Validity (face, construct, predictive) often incomplete
Animal-to-human extrapolation imperfect; rare effects missed; large numbers of animals
Isolated organ, cell and tissue culture methods
Computer modelling
Human microdosing (phase 0) studies give early human PK
Reduce animal numbers while keeping data valid; Good Laboratory Practice standards

front: Which salt solutions contain no magnesium or phosphate ions?
back: De Jalon, Frog-Ringer and Ringer-Locke (Medhi). Ghosh names Ringer, Frog-Ringer and De Jalon.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p9

front: Which gas aerates each common PSS?
back: Air: Tyrode and Frog-Ringer. Oxygen alone: Ringer-Locke. 95% O2 + 5% CO2: Krebs, De Jalon and McEwen.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p11

front: Why is CaCl2 added last when making a PSS?
back: Calcium with bicarbonate precipitates and makes the solution turbid. Medhi says add CaCl2 last; Ghosh says add the bicarbonate only at set-up.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

front: How long may a prepared PSS be kept?
back: Prepare it fresh. Medhi allows up to 24 h in a fridge; longer storage invites microbial growth from glucose. Ghosh says prepare fresh on the day of the experiment.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

front: What is the maximum acceptable error when preparing a PSS?
back: 1%. Hygroscopic CaCl2 and MgCl2 are best added from stock solution.

front: How do you weigh a hydrated salt in place of an anhydrous one?
back: Scale the weight by the molar mass ratio: 0.2 g anhydrous CaCl2 needs 0.26 g CaCl2.2H2O (147/111).
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

front: Which non-hygroscopic magnesium salt replaces MgCl2 in a PSS?
back: MgSO4. MgCl2 is hygroscopic and hard to weigh; the sulphate ion has no harmful effect.

front: De Jalon solution: how does it differ from Ringer-Locke?
back: Same salts as Ringer-Locke, but one-quarter the CaCl2 and half the glucose. Medhi's table also gives bicarbonate 5 g vs 2 g per 10 L, which Ghosh does not mention.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p9

front: Which PSS suits non-innervated muscle, and which suits nerve-muscle preparations?
back: Tyrode for non-innervated muscle; Krebs for nerve-muscle preparations. Krebs may be used for any tissue.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p11

front: Why is carbogen, not pure oxygen, used with a bicarbonate PSS?
back: Pure O2 drives off CO2 from the bicarbonate buffer, so the PSS becomes alkaline. Adding 5% CO2 prevents this.

front: What pH range should a PSS be kept in, and what does a low pH do?
back: pH 7.3 to 7.4. At lower pH the tonus of the tissue tends to fall, altering drug effects.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

front: What happens to isolated intestine when the bath is cooled below 37 C?
back: Tonus rises, contractions become smaller, and contraction and relaxation times increase.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p8

front: Histamine stock 1 mg/mL: 0.2 mL added to a 10 mL bath gives what final concentration?
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology (2019) PDF p11

front: First human dose from acute animal toxicity data: what rule do rat and dog tests give?
back: Start from the minimum effective dose in the acute test. Rat test: one two-hundredth as the single starting dose; dog test: one-tenth. Same route.
