points: Biological standardisation is a specialised bioassay
Potency of material of unknown strength is compared with a standard of the same substance
Vaccines and sera are biologicals that are standardised by bioassay
Potency is therefore expressed in units, not by weight
Unfractionated heparin: 1 unit stops clotting of 1 mL citrated sheep plasma for 1 hour after 0.2 mL of 1% CaCl2
Heparin varies in molecular size, so only bioassay standardises it

back: Bioassay of a material of unknown potency against a standard preparation of the same substance, so potency is stated relative to that standard.

front: How is one unit of unfractionated heparin defined?
back: The amount that stops 1 mL of citrated sheep plasma from clotting for 1 hour after 0.2 mL of 1% CaCl2 is added. Because its molecular size varies, it is standardised only by bioassay.

front: Short note: Merits and demerits of screening methods for antidiabetic and antihypertensive activity

points: Alloxan or streptozotocin in rats: quick hyperglycaemia, but a type I model only
Neonatal STZ rat: hyperglycaemia resembling type II diabetes
Genetic obese models (ob/ob mouse, Zucker fatty rat) with obesity
In vitro enzyme and tissue assays (alpha-glucosidase, insulin secretion, glucose uptake): simple, but no whole-animal effect
SHR: hypertension with complications of hypertension, a disease-like model
Milan strain: hypertension driven mainly by renal sodium and water handling
Drug-induced models (cholinomimetic, angiotensin II) probe specific mechanisms
Tail-cuff method: non-invasive, sensitive and accurate in conscious rats
Direct arterial recording in anaesthetised animals: invasive and needs aseptic surgery

front: Why does stratifying animals reduce sampling error?
back: Animals are grouped into strata of similar individuals (same litter, sex or age), so compared groups are less variable. Selecting a less variable population, such as inbred animals, also reduces sampling error.

front: What do 95% fiducial limits of a mean tell you?
back: The range in which the population mean lies in 95% of cases. It is the sample mean plus or minus t(0.05) times the standard error, with N minus 1 degrees of freedom.

front: Short note: Fiducial limits in bioassay

points: Confidence (fiducial) limits: bounds for the population mean from a sample
Only 5% of samples would give a mean outside these limits by chance
m = x plus or minus t(0.05) x standard error
t is read from the t table at N minus 1 degrees of freedom
Potencies are compared on the log scale; geometric means and their limits are used
Index of precision (variance divided by regression coefficient): 0.05 or less is excellent, 0.1 to 0.2 acceptable

front: What does the between-group variation in an ANOVA represent?
back: The effect due to the treatment; this is the basis of the analysis of variance.

front: Why use the coefficient of variation instead of the standard deviation?
back: When two samples have widely different means, the standard deviation alone cannot say which is more variable. The coefficient of variation expresses variability relative to the mean, so the two can be compared.

front: Index of precision in a bioassay: what do the values mean?
back: Index of precision is the variance divided by the regression coefficient. Values of 0.05 or less are excellent, 0.1 to 0.2 are acceptable, and larger values are not acceptable.

front: Short note: Acetylcholine detection and estimation

points: Parallel assays on guinea pig ileum, rabbit tissues or blood pressure of anaesthetised cat or rat give muscarinic action blocked by atropine
Frog rectus abdominis and leech muscle give nicotinic action blocked by curare
Eserine potentiates the response in all these preparations
Activity is destroyed by boiling with NaOH, but not by weak acid
Blood cholinesterase destroys ACh quickly; eserine slows this
Bath fluid contains mepyramine, hexamethonium and morphine to block other receptors

front: Which tissue shows nicotinic acetylcholine action and what sensitises it to acetylcholine?
back: Frog rectus abdominis. Its acetylcholine action is nicotinic, and eserine (physostigmine) sensitises the muscle to acetylcholine.

front: Short note: In vitro evaluation of anticancer drugs

points: Cancer cell lines grown in microtitre plates; growth measured by colour proportional to cell number
Compare proliferation with and without the drug after a fixed time
Test normal cell lines alongside cancer lines
Clinical promise needs selectivity of at least two orders of magnitude
Two identical sets are exposed; one is assayed, the other is re-incubated in fresh medium
MTT and XTT tetrazolium reduction assays; cell lines from national repositories, e.g. NCCS Pune
National Cancer Institute runs screens on 60 cancer cell lines
Ehrlich ascites carcinoma in mice: median survival time and viable tumour cell count

front: What does an MTT assay measure?
back: Metabolic reduction of a tetrazolium dye by living cells gives a coloured formazan. Colour intensity is proportional to the number of growing cells, so it measures drug effect on proliferation.

front: What are the limits of in vitro studies, according to the owner's text?
back: No systemic effect can be studied, there is no in vivo dose-response, organ specificity is lacking, and chronic effects cannot be studied.

front: What is an in silico experiment?
back: An experiment performed on a computer or by computer simulation of a biological system, used to speed drug discovery and reduce lab work.

front: Short note: In vitro screening for drug interactions

points: Isolated human or animal liver microsomes are incubated with the drug of interest
Used to study metabolism and inhibition by other drugs
Intestinal permeability studies are also run in vitro
Competitive inhibition of a CYP isoenzyme raises levels of drugs it metabolises
Enzyme inducers speed up metabolism, lowering levels of co-administered drugs

front: Why is an enzyme-inhibiting drug a drug-interaction risk?
back: A drug that inhibits a CYP isoenzyme slows metabolism of co-administered drugs and raises their plasma levels, e.g. erythromycin and cimetidine raise theophylline levels.

front: Short note: Flame photometry in pharmacological assays

points: Flame photometry estimates potassium in the coronary outflow of the Langendorff heart
Potassium outflow correlates with the positive inotropic effect of cardiac glycosides

front: Essay: Screening of a potential anti-diabetic agent

points: Diabetes models are chosen by the type of diabetes they copy
Type I and type II models differ in how hyperglycaemia is produced
Alloxan and streptozotocin (STZ) destroy beta cells; alloxan acts through DNA lesions and free radicals, STZ through DNA alkylation
Neonatal STZ: 100 mg/kg to 1-day-old pups or 120 mg/kg to 2 to 5-day-old pups gives impaired glucose tolerance and hyperglycaemia
Nicotinamide plus STZ: nicotinamide partly protects beta cells against STZ
Obese strains: ob/ob mouse, Zucker fatty rat
Partial (70 to 90%) or total pancreatectomy produces hyperglycaemia
Alpha-glucosidase inhibition (carbohydrate digestion)
Insulin secretion and glucose uptake in cell or tissue systems

front: Why does streptozotocin destroy pancreatic beta cells?
back: STZ is taken up through the GLUT-2 transporter of beta cells. Its cytotoxicity is attributed to alkylation of DNA, which destroys the beta cells and produces hyperglycaemia.

front: How is the neonatal STZ model of type II diabetes made?
back: STZ 100 mg/kg i.p. to 1-day-old pups, or 120 mg/kg i.p. to 2-, 3- or 5-day-old pups. The beta cells then resemble those of type 2 patients.

front: Short note: Experimental evaluation of anticonvulsant drugs

points: Maximal electroshock (MES): tonic flexion, tonic extension and clonic convulsions; tests tonic-clonic protection
Corneal electroshock with a seizure severity score; minimal electroshock threshold and extensor seizure latency
Pentylenetetrazol (PTZ) clonic seizures
Kindling: repeated electrical stimulation of the amygdala produces secondarily generalised seizures
Ethosuximide suppresses PTZ clonic seizures at doses producing no other discernible effect
Carbamazepine modifies MES and raises the threshold to PTZ and electroshock

front: Short note: Methods to produce convulsions in rats and mice

points: Brief high-intensity shock to the head or corneal electroshock in rodents
PTZ, picrotoxin, bicuculline and isoniazid induced convulsions
Pilocarpine: status epilepticus at 380 to 400 mg/kg i.p. in rats; lithium pretreatment lowers the dose
Repeated amygdala stimulation gives partial seizures that generalise

front: What seizure does the maximal electroshock test produce, and what marks protection?
back: Tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizures. Protection is taken as abolition of hindlimb extensor tonic convulsions.

front: What does pentylenetetrazol produce in rodents?
back: Clonic seizures. Ethosuximide suppresses PTZ clonic seizures at doses that produce no other discernible effect.
Repeated electrical stimulation of a limbic site (e.g. amygdala) gradually produces seizures that become secondarily generalised, mimicking human focal epilepsy.

front: Short note: Experimental evaluation of an antihypertensive drug

points: Spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR) and related strains
Drug-induced: cholinomimetic (physostigmine, oxotremorine), angiotensin II infusion
Tail-cuff pressure and heart rate in conscious rats
Invasive arterial pressure in anaesthetised animals with autonomic drugs
Rabbit aorta rings: KCl contraction, relaxation by calcium antagonists
Langendorff heart: coronary flow and contractility

front: Essay: Methods for the evaluation of antihypertensive drugs

points: Antihypertensives are judged by lowering arterial pressure in animals with hypertension
SHR: hypertension with complications of hypertension
Wistar fatty rats: hypertension with hyperinsulinaemia
Induced: cholinomimetic (physostigmine, oxotremorine) and angiotensin II infusion
Non-invasive tail-cuff method in conscious rats
Direct arterial pressure under anaesthesia for accuracy
Rabbit aorta: calcium antagonism tested by relaxation after KCl
Langendorff heart: coronary flow and contractility
Models may not match essential hypertension (Milan strain: renal sodium and water handling)

front: What is the spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR)?
back: A rat strain that develops moderate to severe hypertension and complications of hypertension without any drug. It is the standard genetic model of hypertension.

front: What is the non-invasive tail-cuff method of blood pressure measurement?
back: A cuff on the tail measures arterial pressure and heart rate in a conscious, restrained rat. It is sensitive and avoids surgery.

front: Cholinomimetic-induced hypertension: how is it mediated?
back: Physostigmine and oxotremorine raise blood pressure through central cholinergic activation, with a peripheral sympathetic component.

front: Short note: Cardiovascular drug development: challenges and non-invasive evaluation

points: Arrhythmia models cover WPW, atrial flutter, atrial and ventricular fibrillation
Tail-cuff pressure and heart rate in conscious rats
Isolated (Langendorff) heart preparations record rate, force and coronary flow

front: What does a Langendorff heart preparation measure?
back: Heart rate by chronometer, contractile force by a force transducer, coronary flow, and left ventricular pressure with dp/dt max in the isolated perfused heart.

front: Which animal arrhythmia model is used for anti-arrhythmic screening?
back: Animal models include Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation and ventricular fibrillation, each used to test anti-arrhythmic drugs.

front: Short note: Screening for anti-ulcer activity

points: Rats fasted 48 hours, pylorus tied under light ether anaesthesia; drug given for two days before
Killed 19 hours after ligation; gastric pH, free and total acidity measured
Ulcers graded 0.5 to 3 by size and number
Rats fasted 36 to 40 hours, then restrained on a wire screen
Aspirin, phenylbutazone, indomethacin or ibuprofen by gavage
Histamine given to guinea pigs; stomach examined and ulcers graded
Continuous recording of gastric acid in anaesthetised rat by pH change with perfused NaOH; histamine used as secretagogue

front: Essay: Screening of a new compound for anti-ulcer activity

points: Ulcers are produced in animals by pylorus ligation, stress, drugs or histamine
Protection and secretion are tested separately
Shay rat pylorus ligation: fasted rats, ligation, sacrifice after 19 hours, ulcers graded 0.5 to 3
Restraint stress ulcer in fasted rats
Aspirin, phenylbutazone, indomethacin or ibuprofen as ulcerogenic agents; test drug given beforehand
Continuous gastric acid recording in anaesthetised rat with several doses
Guinea pig histamine-induced ulcer: drug tested against histamine
Isolated rat stomach fundus preparation for direct effects
Compare ulcer scores and gastric acidity with controls and a standard drug

front: What is the Shay rat model?
back: Pylorus ligation in fasted rats. Under light ether anaesthesia the pylorus is tied, the drug is given beforehand, and the rat is killed 19 hours later to measure gastric acidity and ulcers.

front: How are gastric ulcers graded in the pylorus ligation model?
back: Necro-haemorrhagic spots over 2 mm count as ulcers, graded 0.5 (minute, punctate lesions) to 3 (several large lesions) by size and number.

front: Name the agents used to produce ulcers in rats.
back: Aspirin (200 mg/kg), phenylbutazone (100 mg/kg), indomethacin and ibuprofen, given by gavage, produce gastric ulcers in rats.

front: What is the advantage of continuous gastric acid recording in one rat?
back: Several doses of drug can be given to the same animal, and each inhibition or potentiation of the secretagogue response is recorded as a change in pH.

front: Short note: Screening a new molecule for effect on intestinal motility

points: Charcoal meal in mice: drug given by gavage 45 minutes before; charcoal travel as percentage of small intestine length
Castor oil in mice: copious (++), mild (+) or none (0) scored two hours later
Castor oil in rats: intraluminal fluid volume between pylorus and caecum after drug
Mouse defaecation: faeces counted over 4 hours; percentage reduction against control

front: Charcoal meal test: what is the endpoint?
back: Distance travelled by the charcoal meal along the small intestine in mice, expressed against control, shows whether a drug inhibits or promotes motility.

front: Castor oil test: what is scored in mice and in rats?
back: In mice, diarrhoea is scored as copious (++), mild (+) or none (0) two hours after castor oil. In rats, the intraluminal fluid volume between the pylorus and caecum is measured.

front: Short note: Screening for an antipsychotic drug

points: Catalepsy in rodents: drug-induced posture maintained; typical antipsychotics produce it
Foot-shock induced aggression in mice; artificial hibernation in rats; influence on behaviour of cotton rats
Catalepsy is used to identify extrapyramidal side effects, which are linked to dopamine blockade
Typical neuroleptics block D2 receptors and, to some extent, D1 receptors

front: What is catalepsy in a rodent test, and what does it predict?
back: Catatonia in rats: failure to correct an externally imposed posture for a long time. Neuroleptics that block nigrostriatal dopamine produce it, so it flags extrapyramidal side effects.

front: Which receptor do typical antipsychotics block?
back: Typical antipsychotics mainly block dopamine D2 receptors. Phenothiazines such as prochlorperazine also have H1 antihistaminic action.

front: Short note: Experimental evaluation of an antidepressant

points: Forced swim test and tail suspension test in mice: immobility time reduced by antidepressants
Learned helplessness in rats (originally inescapable shock in dogs)
Chronic mild stress: uncontrollable mild stressors
Inhibition of tritiated noradrenaline, dopamine or serotonin uptake in rat brain synaptosomes
Effect judged by reduction in immobility time

front: What is the forced swim test and how is an antidepressant read from it?
back: Rodents placed in water become immobile. An antidepressant reduces the immobility time compared with control.

front: What is learned helplessness as a depression model?
back: Animals exposed to inescapable stress fail to escape later, a behavioural state used to simulate depression. It was first described in dogs and later used in rats and mice.

front: Why test a candidate antidepressant in an amine uptake assay?
back: It shows whether the drug blocks noradrenaline, dopamine or serotonin uptake into synaptosomes, linking the behavioural result to a mechanism.

front: Short note: Bioassay methods for analgesics

points: Hot plate at 55 C: reaction time for paw licking, with a 30 second cut-off
Tail-flick under radiant heat; tail immersion in hot water
Writhing test: phenylquinone or acetic acid i.p. in mice
Mechanical stimuli such as strain gauges and von Frey filaments in pain-state models
Discoordination test on a rotating wire-mesh drum excludes false positives from motor impairment
pA2 value from antagonist combination with different tests

front: Hot-plate test: what is the endpoint?
back: Reaction time for the mouse or rat to lick its fore or hind paws on a plate kept at 55 C. A cut-off of 30 seconds protects the paws.

front: Tail-flick test: what is the endpoint?
back: The time the animal takes to withdraw its tail from a radiant heat source.

front: Why run a discoordination test with analgesic screening?
back: Animals that fall off a slowly rotating wire-mesh drum are excluded. The test removes animals with motor impairment, because drugs that impair movement can give false positive analgesic results.

front: Short note: Instruments used to evaluate CNS depressants in animals

points: Rota-rod: fore and hind limb coordination on a rotating rod
Horizontal bar, static rods and parallel bars measure coordination on static apparatus
Horizontal bar also needs forelimb strength
Loss of righting reflex is a sign of acute CNS depression or toxicity

front: What does the rota-rod test measure?
back: Motor coordination of the fore and hind limbs. Drugs that impair coordination make the animal fall from the rotating rod; in mice a fall within 120 seconds counts as impaired.

front: Why is loss of the righting reflex used to judge CNS depressants?
back: Loss of the righting reflex is listed among the signs of acute toxicity and CNS depression, so it gives a simple measure of depression.

front: What is a key safety risk of potassium-sparing diuretics in renal failure?
back: They are contraindicated because they can cause hyperkalaemia, which leads to cardiac depression.

front: Why can a diuretic relieve congestion before its saluretic action?
back: Venodilator action increases venous capacitance and lowers ventricular filling pressure before the saluretic response appears.

front: Short note: Screening for anti-fertility activity

points: Screen for antifertility effects in laboratory animals (rats in the tests below)
Cohabitation test: vaginal smear for seven days; pairing; pregnancy and litter counts
Unilateral ovariectomy: ovarian weight of the other ovary compared with control
Uterine weight changes (oestrogenic); deciduoma (progestational)
Number of implants and resorptions of foetuses

front: Short note: Screening for an antimalarial agent

points: Delayed parasite clearance has been reported with artemisinins
Artemisinins are used only in combination (ACT) with a long-acting drug that acts by a different mechanism

front: Which regimen is used for uncomplicated falciparum malaria with artemisinins?
back: An artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT): an artemisinin given with a partner drug.

front: Short note: Zebrafish as an experimental model

points: Vertebrate model: Danio rerio, used for embryo development and genetics
Alimentary tract resembles human
Important model in cardiovascular research such as atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction

front: Why is zebrafish a useful model in drug testing?
back: Zebrafish (Danio rerio) is a recognised model for vertebrate development and genetics, and its early development can be studied.

front: Short note: The laboratory rat as an experimental animal

points: Derived from the Norway rat; Wistar and Sprague Dawley preferred for easy handling, sensitivity and low cost
SHR and the Milan strain are used in hypertension research

front: Which two outbred rat strains are preferred and why?
back: Wistar and Sprague Dawley: easy handling, sensitivity and low cost.
A hairless genetic mutant mouse that lacks a thymus gland.

front: Short note: Guinea pig (Cavia porcellus) as an experimental animal

points: Cannot make its own vitamin C, so ascorbic acid must be added to the chow
Isolated guinea pig ileum and trachea are standard bioassay tissues

front: Why must guinea pigs be given vitamin C?
back: Guinea pigs cannot synthesise vitamin C, so it must be added to their chow.

front: Short note: Inbred strains of animals in experimentation

points: Produced by mating brother and sister or parent and offspring for at least 20 generations
Homozygous, so responses are consistent and reproducible
Less variable population reduces sampling error in bioassays
Homogeneous strains are unwise for toxicity testing

back: A strain produced by sibling or parent-offspring mating for at least 20 generations, so its animals are homozygous and genetically uniform.

points: Gene construct introduced by DNA microinjection, embryonic stem cell mediated transfer or retrovirus
Germ-line chimeras are bred until homozygous transgenic animals are obtained
Mutant allele put into ES cells by homologous recombination; chimeras mated to get homozygous knockouts
Knock-in of human immunoglobulin genes gives humanised antibodies

front: What are the main methods of making a transgenic animal?
back: DNA microinjection, embryonic stem cell mediated gene transfer and retrovirus-mediated gene transfer.

front: Describe the steps to produce a gene-knockout mouse.
back: Mutant allele introduced into ES cells by homologous recombination; these cells go into early embryos to form chimeras; chimeras are mated to get germ-line heterozygotes; heterozygotes are mated to get homozygous knockouts.

front: Short note: Toxicity testing of a new drug in animals

points: Single dose; LD50 in a rodent and a non-rodent
Signs recorded: tremors, convulsions, sedation, respiratory depression
Daily doses for about two to three weeks in rats, with body weight and blood measurements
Effects on fertility and teratogenic potential, if the drug will be used in women of childbearing age

front: Why are two species used in toxicity studies?
back: Species differ in their responses to toxic agents, so at least two species (usually a rodent and a non-rodent) are used in toxicity testing.

front: What is the purpose of the LD50 in acute toxicity?
back: The single dose that kills 50% of animals. Acute toxicity studies use at least two species, a rodent and a non-rodent.

front: How is a first human dose estimated from animal toxicity?
back: Take the minimum effective dose from the animal data. If the rat was tested, use one two-hundredth of it; if the dog was tested, use one tenth. Surface-area conversion gives a wider margin.

front: Short note: Safety factor and first-in-human dose

points: NOAEL established by preclinical toxicology in a rodent 2-week study
Clinical starting dose is generally 1/50th of the rodent NOAEL dose (not a microdose)
Body surface area conversion of animal to human doses

front: What is the no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL)?
back: The highest dose in animal studies at which no adverse effect is seen. It is used to set the first human starting dose.

front: What starting dose is generally used for a first human study, relative to the rodent NOAEL?
back: About one-fiftieth (1/50th) of the rodent NOAEL dose.

points: Detect mutagenic and carcinogenic potential, since gene mutation can cause carcinogenesis
Bacterial reverse mutation (Ames) test using amino acid-dependent strains
Mammalian cells for gene mutation, clastogenicity and aneuploidy

front: What is the principle of the Ames test?
back: Histidine-dependent Salmonella typhimurium and E. coli strains can grow only if a mutation reverts. Mutagenic compounds increase revertant colonies above the spontaneous background.

front: Short note: Neurotoxicity screening of a new drug

points: Neurotoxicity studies in rodents assess effects of the test substance on the CNS
Histopathological and behavioural examination of the animals
Non-mammalian species with conserved neurodevelopmental process
In vitro cell culture models
In silico models
Cell proliferation, migration, differentiation, survival and apoptosis
Synaptogenesis, myelination, axonal and dendritic outgrowth
Chick embryo, wild-type and transgenic rodents, human neural progenitor cells
In vitro: small quantity, controlled and quick, but no systemic effect and no in vivo dose-response

front: Name three in vitro sources of tissue for developmental neurotoxicity models.
back: Chick embryos, rat and mouse (wild type or transgenic) tissue, and human neural progenitor cells from aborted foetuses or stem cell lines.

front: Short note: Regulatory toxicity studies required for a new drug

points: Genetic toxicity testing and carcinogenicity testing
Embryotoxicity and developmental toxicity; reproduction studies
Neurotoxicity studies in rodents; local toxicity
Preclinical animal safety studies precede human trials

front: What is the purpose of a subacute toxicity study?
back: Daily dosing for about two to three weeks in rats, to detect organ and other changes before longer studies.

front: Short note: Biomarkers in clinical and preclinical evaluation

points: Serum enzyme levels such as liver enzymes serve as surrogate markers of toxicity
Overt toxicity, surrogate markers and exaggerated pharmacodynamic effects are the three findings used to determine the NOAEL

front: Give an example of a surrogate marker of drug toxicity.
back: Serum liver enzyme levels, which signal hepatocellular damage.

front: Short note: Regulatory aspects of biopharmaceuticals

points: Generics: small, well-defined molecules; bioequivalence studies in healthy volunteers
Biosimilars: large, complex molecules; large clinical trials in patients

front: How do biosimilar approval requirements differ from generics?
back: Generics need bioequivalence studies in healthy volunteers. Biosimilars need large clinical trials in patients, because the molecules are large and complex.

front: Why is recreational use of some CNS-acting drugs a public-health concern?
back: It can lead to physical dependence, with enormous societal impact.

front: Why is post-marketing surveillance needed after accelerated approval?
back: Post-marketing trials are required to validate the anticipated clinical benefit that was accepted on accelerated approval.

front: Short note: Animal experimentation in new drug development: aim, utility and limits

points: Predict efficacy and toxicity before first human exposure
Screening, mechanism, pharmacokinetics and toxicity studies in two species
Species differ; an effect in one species does not guarantee the human effect
Inbred strains give less variation but may hide unexpected effects

front: Short note: Obesity models in experimental animals

points: Nicotinamide plus STZ model gives a type 2-like state
Ob/ob mouse and Zucker fatty rat models of obesity
Wistar fatty rat: hyperinsulinaemia and hypertension

front: What is pA2 for a competitive antagonist?
back: The negative log molar concentration of antagonist that doubles the agonist's EC50, i.e. the dose ratio is 2 (log(DR minus 1) = 0). It is read from a Schild plot.

front: Short note: Preclinical and clinical evaluation of a new anticonvulsant

points: Electroshock (MES) and chemical (PTZ) tests in rodents for activity
Genetic and kindling models to check efficacy against epilepsy types
Rota-rod to check motor impairment as a side effect
Acute, subacute and chronic toxicity studied in a rodent and a non-rodent
First human dose estimated from the NOAEL by conversion (about 1/50th of the rodent NOAEL)
Human studies proceed through clinical trial phases
Animal findings guide the human dose and monitoring

front: Short note: In silico models in drug design: types, advantages and disadvantages

points: Experiments performed on computer or by simulation of biological systems
Analysis of biological and medical data from many sources by software
Protein-ligand docking to screen candidate molecules
Speeds discovery and reduces the need for costly laboratory work and trials
Can be used before any animal or human exposure
Hits must be confirmed in the laboratory
Depends on the quality of the underlying model and data

front: Give one example of an in silico docking study mentioned in the owner's text.
back: Protein-ligand docking (EADock, 2010) identified potential inhibitors of a cancer-associated enzyme in silico; fifty percent of the molecules were later shown to be active in vitro.

front: What do changes in uterine weight and a deciduoma indicate?
back: Changes in uterine weight point to oestrogenic or anti-oestrogenic action; a deciduoma points to progestational action.

front: What is an anti-ovulatory test in female rats?
back: Checking whether a drug stops ovulation, e.g. by vaginal smear for normal oestrous cycle, and by ovarian weight and histology after unilateral ovariectomy.

front: Cell-line cytotoxicity test: what is measured?
back: Growth of actively dividing mammalian cells in microplate wells, with and without the test material; colour intensity tracks cell number.

front: Why run a normal cell line beside cancer cell lines?
back: To judge selectivity: whether the material hits cancer cells more than normal cells.

front: What is IC50 in cell-line toxicity?
back: The concentration of material that inhibits a biological or biochemical function by 50 per cent; found by cell counts or cytotoxicity readings.

front: How does trypan blue exclusion count living cells?
back: The dye enters only dead cells, so the unstained cells counted on a haemocytometer are viable.

front: Which tests tell apoptosis from necrosis in cell lines?
back: Fluorescence microscopy (acridine orange and ethidium bromide), confocal imaging with nuclear dyes, DNA fragmentation on agarose gel, and annexin V/propidium iodide flow cytometry.

front: Short note: In vitro cell-line toxicity testing

points: Cultured, actively dividing mammalian cells in microplates
Growth with versus without the test material
MTT or XTT reduction to formazan
Trypan blue exclusion counts; IC50 from cell counts or cytotoxicity
Selectivity from a normal cell line
Apoptosis vs necrosis: microscopy, DNA laddering, flow cytometry
Cell-cycle arrest by flow cytometry
Many materials screened fast, tiny quantities
Costly equipment, aseptic work, poor for insoluble materials

front: Name two drawbacks of cell-line toxicity assays.
back: Costly, sophisticated equipment under aseptic conditions; unreliable results for water-insoluble materials unless they dissolve in under 1 per cent DMSO.

front: 2 x 2 factorial design: which four groups?
back: A alone, B alone, A plus B, and neither (placebo), with subjects randomly allocated to one group.
It tests two treatments with the same subjects, examines their interaction, and maps the dose-response of the combination.

front: Short note: Factorial design in experiments

points: Factors each set at levels, e.g. 2 x 2 or 2 x 3
Subjects randomly allocated to each combination
Factorial ANOVA: effect of each factor
Whether the factors act independently or depend on each other
Efficient use of subjects
Detects interaction between treatments

front: Short note: Acute toxicity studies in animals

points: Effect of a single dose in a species
Standard testing: one rodent and one non-rodent species, at least two routes, one of them the proposed human route
Fixed dose procedure (non-lethal endpoint)
Acute toxic category method (sequential, three animals per step)
Up-and-down procedure (staircase, one animal at 48 h intervals)
LD50 introduced by Trevan (1920)
Draize method for eye and skin irritation in rabbits
Lethal endpoint and animal numbers in classical designs
Repeated-dose testing (minimum 28 days) is a separate study

front: Essay: Acute toxicity studies on animals: aims, methodology and limitations

points: Acute toxicity = effects of one dose in a species
LD50 history and its place in drug development
Identify target organs and dose range
Target organs and NOEL/NOAEL from low, medium and high doses
Two species (rodent and non-rodent), two routes
Fixed dose procedure at 5, 50, 500 and 2000 mg/kg
Acute toxic category method: three animals of one sex per step
Up-and-down procedure: one animal, 48 h intervals, female rodents
Classical LD50 is lethal and uses many animals
Repeated-dose (minimum 28 days) and 90-day studies are separate

front: What is the fixed dose procedure for?
back: Assessing non-lethal toxicity: fixed doses of 5, 50, 500 and 2000 mg/kg, with animals observed for a set period.

front: Up-and-down procedure: how is it run?
back: One animal at a time is dosed sequentially at 48 h intervals (staircase design); it is preferred because it cuts animal numbers.

front: Carcinogenicity study: when is it ended?
back: Run over most of the animal's lifespan; if no tumours appear it ends after about 18 months in mice and hamsters and 24 months in rats.

front: Embryotoxicity study: when is the drug given and when is the foetus examined?
back: Dosed from day 8 to 14 of pregnancy; caesarean section on day 21 to find embryolethal effects and malformations in the foetuses.

front: Short note: Genotoxicity studies on animals

points: Detect gene mutations, chromosome changes and DNA sequence alteration
Mutations can lead to carcinogenesis, so mutagenicity is checked in drug development
In vitro: two or three bacterial and mammalian cell tests
Rodent chromosome assay and dominant lethal assay in whole animals
Dominant lethal assay: the mutation kills the fertilised egg or embryo
Genotoxicity data for anticancer drugs not required until a phase 2 trial is passed
Rodents and non-rodents, over most of the lifespan
Ended after about 18 months (mice, hamsters) or 24 months (rats) if no tumours
One-generation study: dosing for a spermatogenic cycle (males) and two oestrous cycles (females)
Two-generation study: parental mating and offspring assessment
Dosing days 8 to 14 of pregnancy
Caesarean section on day 21
Behavioural and histopathological neurotoxicity in adult rodents (neurological dysfunction, memory and learning)

front: Apomorphine emesis model: which species and dose?
back: Dogs given apomorphine 0.15 mg/kg vomit; a test drug is judged by how much it reduces the emesis.

front: Why do dopamine blockers reduce apomorphine emesis?
back: Apomorphine acts on dopamine receptors; neuroleptics that block dopamine (e.g. metoclopramide) relieve the emetic response.

front: Short note: Screening for anti-emetic activity

points: Apomorphine stimulates dopamine receptors and causes emesis in dogs
Give apomorphine with the test drug or vehicle
Score the emetic response against control
Dopamine-blocking drugs (metoclopramide) reduce emesis
Anti-emetic activity is inferred from reduced emesis

front: Didactic lecture vs self-directed learning: key difference
back: Didactic: teacher-led, fixed content and pace delivered to learners. Self-directed: the learner sets own goals, pace and resources.

front: Short note: Animal experimentation in new drug development (aim, utility, limitations)

points: Test efficacy and likely side effects of a new drug before human trials
Regulatory and investigative studies in rats, mice, rabbits and dogs
Flags likely toxicity before human exposure
Supports drug projects through the preclinical stage
In vitro and in silico methods can decide which compounds need in vivo testing

Cutting animal numbers can reduce statistical power

Regulators (ICH S7A) expect a neurobehavioural screen before human trials
Modified Irwin test or functional observational battery (FOB)
Rodents, usually mice or rats, dosed and observed
Score about 18 endpoints with a semi-quantitative system
Observe at baseline (0 h) and at fixed times after dosing, e.g. 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 h
Survival and general condition
Neuromuscular and motor: locomotion, tremor, convulsion
Autonomic: body temperature, eyelid closure
Reflexes and sensory responses
Rotarod for motor coordination
Open-field test for locomotor and exploratory activity
Scoring is subjective and prone to observer bias
No neurotransmitter, receptor or electrophysiology data, so add objective measures

front: Earthworm acute toxicity test: what is it used for?
back: A rapid bioassay that measures acute toxicity of a substance directly in soil, using earthworms (Eisenia foetida) as test organisms. It is a modification of OECD 207 and can detect toxicity from contaminants bound to soil particles that filter-paper tests may miss.
refs: WEB PMC Soil contact bioassay for rapid determination of acute toxicity with Eisenia foetida 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6940645

front: Short note: Earthworm acute lethality test

points: Measures acute toxicity of a test substance to earthworms, used as an ecotoxicity screen for soil
Modification of OECD Test 207 (earthworm acute toxicity)
Test organism: Eisenia foetida
Soil contact bioassay: thin layer of moistened soil with the test substance in the test jar, worms added
Observation at 24 h and 48 h
Main endpoint: mortality, reported as percentage
Also recorded: biomass change, response to stimulus, sublethal signs (inflamed clitellus, expulsion of coelomic or bloody fluid)
Control mortality should be 10% or less (OECD acceptance threshold cited by the source)
Rapid and cheap, but standard acute assays give limited information on hazard to soil organisms overall

refs: WEB PMC Soil contact bioassay for rapid determination of acute toxicity with Eisenia foetida 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6940645

front: Charcoal meal test: what does it measure?
back: In vivo propulsive motility in mice: how far an orally given charcoal marker travels through the small intestine, expressed as a percentage of total small-intestine length.
refs: WEB PMC PMC7168896 Biopolymer Extracted from Anadenanthera colubrina (Red Angico Gum): Antidiarrheal Activity and Safety, mice charcoal meal https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7168896/

points: Measures transit of a non-absorbed marker along the gut
Slowing of transit suggests antimotility or antidiarrhoeal action; speeding suggests purgative action
Fast animals briefly, then give test drug or vehicle orally or s.c.
After the set interval, give activated charcoal suspension orally
Sacrifice after a fixed time, lay out the small intestine and measure the charcoal front
Transit (%) = distance travelled by charcoal front / total small-intestine length x 100
Compare with vehicle (maximal propulsion) and a reference drug
Vehicle group as negative control
Atropine as a reference that reduces transit
Loperamide as a reference antimotility agent
Whole-animal assay: absorption and central effects can change transit
Isolated gut preparations separate direct smooth-muscle action

front: Experimental glaucoma: how is raised IOP produced in animal models?
back: By blocking aqueous outflow (trabecular meshwork or episcleral/collector veins), or by abruptly narrowing the angle, so pressure rises and optic nerve and retinal ganglion cell damage can be studied.
refs: WEB PMC Evangelho, Mastronardi, de-la-Torre - Experimental Models of Glaucoma: A Review of the Literature 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630440

front: Short note: Experimental models of acute congestive and chronic simple glaucoma

points: Principle: abrupt IOP rise that mimics an angle-closure attack
Reperfusion ischaemia model: anterior chamber paracentesis with a saline reservoir raises IOP very high and blocks retinal and uveal blood flow; pressure is then released
Laser photocoagulation plus temporary angle narrowing by paracentesis: abrupt rise lasting weeks, with marked retinal ganglion cell loss
Limits: inflammation, ischaemia and corneal opacity; ganglion cell loss is not seen in human POAG
Angle-closure-like genetic and canine models: beagle dogs develop angle closure and cupping over months to years; PRSS56-mutant mice have short axial length and a narrow angle
Principle: slow, progressive rise in IOP by reducing outflow
Hypertonic saline into episcleral veins (rat): moderate IOP rise over about 7-10 days with high variability; progressive ganglion cell loss; used for neuroprotection studies
Laser photocoagulation of the trabecular meshwork: repeated applications to raise IOP; synechiae, hyphaema and corneal oedema are drawbacks
Microbead (latex microsphere) injection: blocks trabecular outflow; repeated injections sustain the rise
Episcleral vein cauterisation and nylon suture vein occlusion: moderate, sustained pressure rise
Intracameral hyaluronic acid (rat, rabbit): raises IOP for days, leaves outflow largely open
Steroid-induced ocular hypertension (rabbit) and genetic models (DBA/2J mice): progressive rise, often months to develop

refs: WEB PMC Evangelho, Mastronardi, de-la-Torre - Experimental Models of Glaucoma: A Review of the Literature 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630440

back: Pharmacogenetics studies the genetic basis of variable drug response and often involves a small number of DNA variants with large effects. Pharmacogenomics studies larger numbers of variants, in an individual or across a population, to explain genetic influence on drug response.

front: Short note: Star alleles and metaboliser phenotypes

points: Gene name, asterisk, then a number for the haplotype
*1 is the functional allele by convention
CYP2C19*2 and *3 have no function; CYP2C19*17 increases expression
Poor: no enzyme activity (two no-function alleles)
Intermediate: reduced activity (e.g. one functional and one no-function allele)
Normal: two functional alleles
Rapid and ultrarapid: greatly increased activity from increased-expression variants, e.g. CYP2C19*17 (ultrarapid = *1/*17 or *17/*17)
Phenotype reflects the combined effect of the maternal and paternal alleles
One gene can carry many variants (CYP2C19 has more than 35 alleles defined), plus deletions and duplications

text: A single-base substitution is a {{single-nucleotide variant (SNV)}}; deletion or duplication of a whole gene or a large DNA segment is a {{copy number variant (CNV)}}; variants that are inherited together on a chromosome are in {{linkage disequilibrium}}.

front: Name the three situations in which a single pharmacogene produces a large effect on drug response.
back: 1) The drug's key metabolic or transport step depends on one enzyme or transporter with variable function (e.g. codeine and CYP2D6). 2) The drug acts on a target, or an off-target protein, that varies (e.g. aminoglycosides and MT-RNR1). 3) The drug's effect depends on the wider biological setting (e.g. antimalarials and rasburicase in G6PD deficiency).

points: Study of the genetic basis for variability in drug response
Genetic influence on drug action (pharmacodynamics)
Genetic influence on drug handling by the body (pharmacokinetics)

front: Why can one variant cause toxicity with one drug and treatment failure with another?
back: The effect depends on the drug's pathway. Low enzyme function raises exposure to an active parent drug (omeprazole is inactivated by CYP2C19), but for a prodrug such as codeine or clopidogrel it prevents activation, so the drug fails. Increased enzyme function does the reverse: ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolisers make excess morphine from codeine, so toxicity follows.

front: Classify: CYP2C19 and proton pump inhibitors
text: Omeprazole and lansoprazole are inactivated by {{CYP2C19}}. CYP2C19 poor metabolisers have higher {{parent drug}} exposure, stronger acid suppression and a higher chance of {{ulcer cure}} than rapid or ultrarapid metabolisers.

front: Which transporter variant is linked to simvastatin myopathy, and how was it found?
back: SLCO1B1 encodes OATP1B1, an uptake transporter on the sinusoidal (blood-facing) side of hepatocytes that takes up statins. A common reduced-function variant lowers hepatic statin uptake, raising systemic exposure and myopathy risk. It was found by a GWAS of 85 simvastatin myotoxicity cases and 90 controls; the exact mechanism of muscle toxicity is undefined. Katzung's CPIC-based table advises a lower simvastatin dose or an alternative statin (e.g. pravastatin or rosuvastatin), with routine CK monitoring, for reduced-function genotypes.

front: List the CYP2C19 alleles and what each does.
back: *1 is the normal-function reference. *2 and *3 have no function, so carriers are poor or intermediate metabolisers. *17 has increased expression, giving faster metabolism. This is why a prodrug (clopidogrel) and an inactivated drug (omeprazole) respond in opposite directions.

front: CYP3A5 variants and tacrolimus: what is the link?
back: CYP3A5*3 is a splice variant giving no functional enzyme and is the predominant allele in European ancestry. The functional *1 allele is the most common allele in many African-ancestry populations. People with a functional CYP3A5 clear tacrolimus faster, so they need a higher dose to reach therapeutic levels.

front: What is the two-sided risk of codeine with CYP2D6 variation?
back: Codeine is a prodrug that CYP2D6 converts to morphine. Poor metabolisers make little morphine, so analgesia is absent. Ultrarapid metabolisers make excess morphine, which can cause respiratory depression and death.

front: Which enzyme's variants are linked to breast cancer recurrence on tamoxifen, and why?
back: CYP2D6. Tamoxifen relies on CYP2D6 for metabolic activation to endoxifen, a metabolite with high oestrogen-receptor affinity. The CYP2D6 poor metaboliser phenotype correlates with a higher risk of relapse in breast cancer treated with tamoxifen.

front: Clopidogrel: how does CYP2C19 status change the antiplatelet plan?
back: Clopidogrel is a prodrug: about 85% of a dose is hydrolysed by esterases to an inactive acid, and about 15% is converted (mainly by CYP2C19) to the active thiol metabolite. Carriers of the no-function CYP2C19*2 allele are at increased risk of serious adverse cardiovascular events, particularly in ACS treated with PCI; stent thrombosis is the event linked to failed clopidogrel activation. Poor metabolisers (about 2-3% of European and over 10% of East Asian ancestry) should get an alternative antiplatelet, because even large dose increases do not work. GG14: intermediate metabolisers may reach adequate effect with a higher dose. Katzung (CPIC, ACS with PCI): use prasugrel or ticagrelor in both poor and intermediate metabolisers;.

front: Essay: Loss-of-function and gain-of-function metabolic variants and their effect on drug action

points: Drugs with a narrow margin, cleared by a single enzyme, are the highest-risk group
Outcome depends on whether the parent drug or a metabolite is the active species
Parent drug and upstream metabolites rise, so toxicity or overdose-like effects follow
Downstream metabolites fall
If the active species is a metabolite formed by the enzyme, efficacy is lost
Parent drug falls, so efficacy can be lost
Downstream active metabolites rise, which can cause adverse effects
Loss of activation gives inefficacy (clopidogrel, codeine analgesia)
Gain of activation can give excess active drug (codeine and morphine)
Codeine and CYP2D6
Clopidogrel and CYP2C19
Tacrolimus and CYP3A5: functional alleles lower exposure, so higher doses are needed
Omeprazole and CYP2C19: poor metabolisers get a stronger acid-suppressing effect
Genotype the enzyme before using a narrow-margin drug that depends on it
Interpret results with ancestry in mind, since allele frequencies vary between populations

front: Classify: drug targets and variant-specific drug action
text: Warfarin's target is {{VKORC1}}; ivacaftor partly corrects the gating defect of the CFTR {{G551D}} variant; lumacaftor improves surface expression of the commonest CFTR variant, {{F508}}; vemurafenib inhibits {{BRAF V600E}} kinase.

front: What is the genetic basis of malignant hyperthermia, and which drugs trigger it?
back: Variants in RYR1 (the ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel of skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum) and CACNA1S. Triggers: volatile anaesthetics (halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, enflurane, methoxyflurane) and succinylcholine, which release massive intracellular calcium, causing persistent muscle contraction and heat production. Treatment: rapid external cooling, bicarbonate, 100% oxygen and IV dantrolene, which acts on RYR1 to block calcium-induced calcium release.

front: Which gene affects warfarin metabolism and which its target?
back: CYP2C9 metabolises the active S-warfarin; poor and intermediate metabolisers need lower steady-state doses and have higher bleeding risk. VKORC1 (vitamin K epoxide reductase) is the target; a low-expression promoter variant lowers dose need and is more common in Asian ancestry. CYP4F2 also influences vitamin K recycling.

points: CYP2C9 metabolises the more active S-enantiomer
CYP2C9 poor and intermediate metabolisers need lower steady-state doses and have more bleeding
Target VKORC1 is needed to recycle vitamin K to its active reduced form
Promoter variants that lower VKORC1 expression need lower doses (more common in Asian ancestry)
Rare coding variants cause partial or complete resistance and higher dose needs
CYP4F2 inactivates vitamin K by hydroxylation
CYP2C9, VKORC1 and CYP4F2 together explain over 50% of the dose variability

front: How do MT-RNR1 variants raise the risk of aminoglycoside hearing loss?
back: Aminoglycosides bind bacterial 16S rRNA, but in the inner ear they also bind human mitochondrial ribosomes (off-target). MT-RNR1 variants make human mitochondrial rRNA resemble bacterial rRNA, increasing binding affinity. Hearing loss can then occur even when serum levels are judged non-toxic.

front: Why must tumour genotype be checked before some targeted anticancer drugs?
back: Response depends on somatic (tumour) mutations as well as germline DNA. EGFR activating mutations predict response to gefitinib, and BRAF V600E predicts response to vemurafenib. Trastuzumab helps only HER2-expressing breast cancers, yet it can cause cardiomyopathy, and HER2-negative patients carry that risk without benefit.

front: Why does the optimal warfarin dose vary more than 10-fold, and why is genotype-guided dosing still debated?
back: Dose depends on several genes acting together: CYP2C9 (clearance), VKORC1 (target sensitivity, e.g. promoter variant lowers need, another variant raises it) and CYP4F2. Genotype explains much of the variation, yet trials using time in therapeutic range gave inconsistent results with few bleeding events, whereas one trial with bleeding as the primary endpoint showed significant benefit of genotype-guided dosing.

front: What does the UGT1A1*28 allele do, and which drugs does it affect?
back: UGT1A1*28 has seven TA repeats in the promoter instead of the common six, which lowers UGT1A1 expression. The allele frequency can reach about 30%, with up to 10% of people homozygous depending on ancestry. Reduced activity raises SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan, and so raises the risk of serious toxicity. It also causes Gilbert syndrome and atazanavir-related hyperbilirubinaemia.

text: TPMT and NUDT15: {{azathioprine}} and mercaptopurine cause marrow toxicity; DPYD (dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase): {{capecitabine}} and {{fluorouracil}} cause toxicity; UGT1A1: {{irinotecan}} causes toxicity; NAT2: {{isoniazid}} causes neurotoxicity; G6PD: {{rasburicase}} causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia.

front: Atypical plasma cholinesterase: what happens with succinylcholine, and how is it detected?
back: Plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase, BCHE) normally hydrolyses succinylcholine, so its action lasts only 5 to 8 minutes. Some people inherit an abnormal enzyme with low affinity for succinylcholine, or a deficiency of it. Homozygotes (about 1 in over 3000) develop prolonged block with muscle paralysis and apnoea lasting 4 to 6 hours; heterozygotes (about 1 in 50) show only a 2- to 3-fold prolongation. Succinylcholine also readily produces phase II block in these patients. The apnoea can only be managed by mechanical ventilation.

front: Why is NUDT15 testing relevant to thiopurine toxicity in East Asian patients?
back: TPMT and NUDT15 variants both alter the levels of active thiopurine metabolites and the risk of bone marrow toxicity. TPMT poor metabolisers are rare in East Asian populations, but NUDT15 poor and intermediate metabolisers are more frequent there. Thiopurine toxicity is more common in Asian patients, and NUDT15 was found by GWAS, so TPMT testing alone can miss risk.

front: Acetylator (NAT2) polymorphism: what are the consequences of slow and fast acetylation?
back: NAT2 variants give slow and fast acetylators; slow acetylation results from less NAT2 enzyme. About 60-70% of Indians are slow acetylators (isoniazid half-life about 3 h, versus 1 h in fast acetylators). Slow acetylators: isoniazid peripheral neuropathy; hydralazine- and procainamide-induced lupus; sulfonamide hypersensitivity; amonafide toxicity. The historical account in GG14 also links NAT deficiency with isoniazid hepatotoxicity (the hepatotoxic metabolite is formed from acetylhydrazine by CYP2E1). Fast acetylators: acetylator status does not matter with daily isoniazid, but biweekly regimens are less effective.

front: Short note: G6PD deficiency and drug response

points: Oxidant drugs lower the antioxidant glutathione in G6PD-deficient red cells, raising fragility and causing haemolysis
X-linked; commoner in Mediterranean, African and Southeast Asian people; severity varies with the variant and is largely dose related
Primaquine and other antimalarials; tafenoquine
Dapsone (haemolysis)
Rasburicase
Others: sulfonamides, cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, methylene blue, fluoroquinolones, chloramphenicol
Breaks uric acid down to allantoin and hydrogen peroxide
G6PD-deficient cells cannot handle the oxidative stress: haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia
Methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen; can cause arrhythmias, seizures and death
Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency
G6PD is neither the drug's metabolic enzyme nor its target; it changes the biological background (pharmacodynamic modifier)

front: DPYD testing before fluoropyrimidines: why, and how is the dose changed?
back: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD, gene DPYD) is the rate-limiting step of pyrimidine catabolism and eliminates about 80% of a fluorouracil dose; capecitabine and tegafur are oral prodrugs of 5-FU. Deficiency sharply lowers 5-FU clearance, causing severe toxicity. Clinically recognised variants: DPYD*2A and *13 (no function), rs67376798 and HapB3 (reduced function); all are rare. CPIC: intermediate metabolisers start at a reduced dose (50% reduction, then titrate by toxicity); complete deficiency calls for a non-fluoropyrimidine drug. Genotype-guided dose reduction lowered the risk of severe toxicity.

front: Essay: Pharmacogenetic approach to severe toxicity from antimetabolite and cytotoxic drugs

points: Many of these drugs have a narrow therapeutic margin, and toxicity can be life-threatening
Germline variants affect the host; somatic variants affect the tumour
TPMT and NUDT15 variants raise marrow toxicity risk
The same variants alter the risk of second cancers
NUDT15 matters more in Asian ancestry, where TPMT variants are less common
DPYD variants predict toxicity with fluorouracil and capecitabine
Reduced UGT1A1 activity raises SN-38 exposure
Higher SN-38 is linked to serious toxicity
TYMS enhancer repeat: two copies rather than three raises host toxicity and tumour susceptibility to TYMS inhibitors
Somatic markers such as EGFR and BRAF V600E select patients for targeted drugs
Genotype before prescribing where a validated test exists
Ancestry determines which variants are informative for a given patient

front: How does HLA-B*57:01 testing change abacavir treatment?
back: Carriers of HLA-B*57:01 are at risk of severe abacavir hypersensitivity, described as skin reactions particularly Stevens-Johnson syndrome. A randomised trial showed that genotyping before treatment eliminated this risk, and abacavir is contraindicated in HLA-B*57:01-positive patients. Proposed mechanism: non-covalent binding of the drug or a metabolite to HLA or the T-cell receptor, altering the peptides presented; the immune details are not fully characterised.

front: Which HLA allele predicts carbamazepine skin reactions in East Asian and in European-ancestry patients?
back: HLA-B*15:02 in East Asian individuals. In European-ancestry individuals, a GWAS of patients with Stevens-Johnson-type reactions (65 cases, 3987 controls) identified HLA-A*31:01.

front: Classify: HLA alleles and drug hypersensitivity
text: HLA-B*57:01 with {{abacavir}}; HLA-B*58:01 with {{allopurinol}}; HLA-B*15:02 with {{carbamazepine}} (East Asian), oxcarbazepine and {{phenytoin}}; HLA-A*31:01 with {{carbamazepine}} (European ancestry).

front: Why check both CYP2C9 and HLA-B genotype before starting phenytoin?
back: Phenytoin (and fosphenytoin) is metabolised by CYP2C9, so poor metabolisers have higher plasma levels and more toxicity. Phenytoin can also cause life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis; the risk appears especially high when a CYP2C9 variant occurs together with an HLA-B risk allele such as HLA-B*15:02. Knowing both genotypes helps predict response.

front: Short note: HLA testing for drug hypersensitivity and its limits

points: HLA-A, -B and -C encode MHC class I proteins that let the immune system tell self from foreign proteins
HLA-B is among the most polymorphic genes in the genome
HLA-B*15:02 is most prevalent in East Asian and Central/South Asian populations, carried by up to about 20% in some
It is absent or very rare in European and sub-Saharan African populations
Other regional phenytoin risk alleles include HLA-B*15:21, B*15:11, B*15:08 (Asian) and B*56:02 (Aboriginal Australian)
A negative result is reassuring only if the correct allele panel for the patient's population was tested
Incomplete panels give false reassurance
The immune mechanism is incompletely understood

front: Why must HLA screening be matched to ancestry and drug, and how can genotypes combine?
back: HLA-B*15:02 predicts carbamazepine skin reactions in East Asian people (allele frequency up to 20% in East and Central/South Asian groups, rare in European and sub-Saharan African), whereas in European ancestry a GWAS found HLA-A*31:01. Reactions can be drug-specific (abacavir with HLA-B*57:01) or shared across related drugs (oxcarbazepine, phenytoin). For phenytoin, severe SJS/TEN risk appears especially high when a CYP2C9 variant is carried together with an HLA-B allele such as HLA-B*15:02.

front: Why has the candidate-gene approach worked well in pharmacogenetics when it often fails elsewhere?
back: Pharmacogenetic candidate genes were chosen from known drug disposition or action pathways, and the variants found often have large effects that replicate. Elsewhere, candidate-gene findings frequently failed to replicate. GWAS is now used without a prior hypothesis and can give clear signals even with small samples when the effect is large (e.g. carbamazepine and HLA-A*31:01).

front: Classify: genomic evidence in drug development
text: Loss-of-function variants in {{PCSK9}} lower LDL cholesterol and point to it as a target; a GWAS found that an {{ADCY9}} variant predicts response to {{dalcetrapib}}; PheWAS can suggest {{repurposing}} of existing drugs; drugs with human genetic support are about {{three-fold}} more likely to be marketed.

points: Identify who is more or less likely to respond to a drug
Identify who needs an altered dose, and predict the best treatment option
Genetic basis of an individual's drug-response profile
Most drugs show continuous, bell-shaped variation in response; some specific defects give discontinuous responses
So far applied mainly to patients with known genetic abnormalities
Goal is personalised medicine on a wide scale; much genetic variability is still unexplained
Atypical pseudocholinesterase: prolonged succinylcholine apnoea
G6PD deficiency: haemolysis with primaquine and other oxidising drugs
CYP2D6 deficiency: more toxicity from antidepressants and antipsychotics
Optimal warfarin dose can vary more than 10-fold between patients

front: Why are the results of warfarin genotyping trials mixed?
back: Trials using time in therapeutic range over the first 30 to 90 days gave inconsistent results, none showing a large effect, and these studies had few bleeding events. An RCT with bleeding as the primary endpoint did show a significant benefit of genotype-guided dosing. EHR-based case-control studies link CYP2C9 and CYP4F2 variants to bleeding.

front: Short note: Clinical implementation of pharmacogenomic testing

points: Point-of-care: genotype when the drug is prescribed; each drug needs its own assay
Multi-gene panel stored in the EHR, with clinical decision support when a relevant drug is prescribed
Strongest: RCTs comparing a genotype-guided strategy with standard care
HLA-B*57:01 with abacavir: genotyping eliminated severe skin reactions
Clopidogrel: genotype-guided care gave fewer bleeding events without more stent thrombosis
Warfarin: mixed results overall
Non-randomised data are weaker, and RCTs for rare variants may be impractical
The variant must link to a clinically important outcome, and the test must lead to actionable advice (change drug or dose)
Evidence strength varies by drug-gene pair
CPIC publishes peer-reviewed, genotype-based prescribing guidance across drugs
Allele panels must suit the target population

front: Essay: Role of human genomics in new drug discovery and development

points: Genetic pathways in physiology and disease point to new drug targets
Drugs with human genetic support are about three times more likely to be marketed
Brown and Goldstein's FH studies identified a defect in regulation of HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme statins inhibit
PCSK9 gain-of-function variants raise LDL and cause FH; loss-of-function variants (African American subjects) lower LDL and coronary risk; PCSK9 antibodies (alirocumab, evolocumab) followed
Loss-of-function variants in APOC3, SLC30A8 and HSD17B13 reduce risk of common diseases
SCN9A loss of function causes insensitivity to pain, suggesting an analgesic target
After a negative phase III trial of dalcetrapib, a GWAS found an ADCY9 variant that predicted efficacy
Polygenic risk scores may pick patients most likely to benefit from costly LDL-lowering drugs
Phenome-wide association studies link variants to phenotypes, suggesting new indications
Such studies can also predict adverse effects of drugs
Variants are often population specific, so diverse cohorts are needed
Ancestry diversity drives discovery in all populations

front: Classify: CYP2D6 drugs whose efficacy, toxicity or dose depends on genotype: list all.
back: Amitriptyline, atomoxetine, codeine, nortriptyline, ondansetron, paroxetine, pitolisant, tamoxifen, tramadol, tropisetron. Why: CYP2D6 activity sets exposure to these drugs and their active metabolites; codeine gives no analgesia in poor metabolisers.

front: Classify: CYP2C9 drugs whose efficacy, toxicity or dose depends on genotype: list all.
back: Celecoxib, flurbiprofen, fosphenytoin, ibuprofen, lornoxicam, meloxicam, phenytoin, piroxicam, siponimod, tenoxicam, warfarin. Why: CYP2C9 clears these drugs (e.g. S-warfarin, phenytoin), so genotype changes toxicity or required dose.

front: Classify: CYP2C19 drugs whose efficacy depends on genotype: list all.
back: Amitriptyline, citalopram, clopidogrel, escitalopram, lansoprazole, omeprazole, pantoprazole, voriconazole. Why: CYP2C19 activates clopidogrel and inactivates omeprazole, so genotype changes drug efficacy.

front: What is a copy number variant (CNV) in a pharmacogene?
back: A change in the number of copies of a gene, such as whole-gene deletion or duplication. It changes how much enzyme is made, so it can shift drug handling.

front: What is a promoter variant, and what does it change?
back: A variant in the regulatory region before a gene that alters how much of the protein is made, while the protein itself is unchanged. Example: the UGT1A1*28 TA-repeat promoter allele lowers expression.

front: What is a missense variant, and give one pharmacogenetic example.
back: A single-nucleotide change that substitutes one amino acid in the protein. Example: the BCRP p.Gln141Lys substitution reduces intestinal efflux, which raises rosuvastatin response.

front: How do frameshift, premature stop and start-codon variants affect a protein?
back: A start-codon or stop-codon change, or a frameshift, alters the rest of the transcribed protein. A premature stop gives a truncated, inactive enzyme (the CYP3A5*3 splice defect is printed as an example).

front: Can a synonymous (silent) coding variant still change drug response?
back: Yes. A silent change in the coding region of ABCB1 (P-glycoprotein) is associated with variable drug concentrations, so an amino-acid change is not required for an effect.

front: Which two parameters of carrier-mediated transport can genetic polymorphism alter?
back: The density of the transporter in the membrane, which sets the maximal rate of transport, and its affinity for the substrate (Km). Either change alters drug pharmacokinetics.

front: Why are promoter variants tested in liver microsomes rather than by sequence alone?
back: Because a promoter variant changes expression, not the coding sequence, its effect must be measured functionally. Liver microsomes carrying wild-type or variant promoter sequences show the expression difference directly (VKORC1 is the printed example).

front: Essay: Molecular mechanisms of genetic polymorphism in drug metabolism

points: Polymorphism is inherited DNA variation that changes enzyme or transporter amount or function
Result: different drug handling and response between individuals
Single-nucleotide variants, small insertions and deletions, copy number variants
Regulatory variants in the promoter or splice sites
Coding variants: missense, frameshift, premature stop, start-codon change; synonymous variants can still matter
Amino-acid substitution can reduce catalytic or transport function (BCRP p.Gln141Lys)
Frameshift or early stop gives a truncated, inactive enzyme (CYP3A5*3 splice defect)
Copy number changes alter total enzyme amount (CYP2D6 whole-gene deletion or duplication)
Promoter variants change transcription, e.g. UGT1A1*28 with seven TA repeats lowers expression
VKORC1 promoter variants lower expression and lower warfarin dose needs

front: What does the WHO mean by rational use of medicines?
back: Patients receive medicines suited to their clinical needs, in doses that match their own requirements, for an adequate period, and at the lowest cost to them and their community. It covers the whole supply-use chain, though prescribing is the clinical core.

front: Which criteria show that a prescription is appropriate?
back: A sound indication; a drug that suits the patient for efficacy, tolerability, safety and cost; a dose, route and duration fitted to the patient; no contraindication, the drug acceptable to the patient, and expected benefit greater than likely harm; correct dispensing with instructions; and follow-up of adherence, benefit and adverse effects.

front: Why should a drug be prescribed by its generic (non-proprietary) name, and when is a brand name better?
back: A generic name is uniform, shorter and easier to remember than many brand names, and it lets the pharmacist supply any manufacturer's product, which is usually cheaper because no brand promotion is paid for. A brand name is safer when product consistency in quality and bioavailability matters and official quality control is weak.

front: Classify: the three names of a drug
text: A {{chemical}} name describes the molecule and is too cumbersome for prescribing; a {{non-proprietary}} name is the accepted generic name, and the WHO recommends {{rINN}} names for new drugs; a {{brand}} name is the manufacturer's trademark and can differ between countries.

front: Why does teaching the prescriber more pharmacology not by itself make prescribing rational?
back: Knowledge is the main determinant of prescribing, but it has been shown repeatedly that improving it alone fails to promote rational use. Other pressures act too: copying teachers and popular doctors, heavy patient load giving routine symptom-based prescribing, imprecise diagnosis, drug promotion and inducements, and patients who expect a pill for every ill.

front: What does the expiry date on a medicine mean, and how long may a manufacturer set it?
back: It is a legal requirement that every product carries its manufacture and expiry dates. The period between them is the life period; the manufacturer guarantees quality under stated storage only up to that date. Under Schedule P (Rule 96, Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940) life periods are mostly 1 to 5 years; other expiry dates may not exceed 5 years unless the licensing authority accepts stability proof.

front: Which antibiotic formulation past its expiry caused renal toxicity in man, and what did it cause?
back: Outdated tetracycline capsules. Their degradation product damaged renal tubules, producing a Fanconi-like picture in the early 1960s. The capsules have since been reformulated to limit degradation.

front: A mother insists on an antibiotic for her child's viral fever. Which irrationality is this, which pressures cause it, and what are the consequences?
back: It is use of a drug when none is needed. Patient demand ('pill for every ill'), the prescriber's wish to give prompt symptomatic relief and imprecise diagnosis all push towards it. Consequences of irrational prescribing include delayed or lost relief, more adverse effects, longer hospital stay, morbidity and mortality, and microbial resistance.

front: An expired tablet is still in the cabinet. Why is it not automatically dangerous, and what would speed the loss of potency?
back: Expiry means quality is no longer assured and the maker is not liable; it does not show the drug has become toxic or lost potency. Most solid oral forms kept unopened stay active for years. High humidity and temperature accelerate degradation, and liquids and injections are less stable (suspensions clump, injections precipitate or discolour). Use beyond the expiry date is still not legally allowed.

front: What are the steps of rational prescribing?
back: 1) Establish at least a provisional diagnosis. 2) Define the therapeutic problem and goals (symptom relief, cure, prevention of complications). 3) Select the drug class for each goal. 4) Choose the drug on efficacy, safety, suitability for this patient and cost. 5) Decide route, dose and duration for this patient. 6) Give information and instructions. 7) Monitor adherence, goal achievement and adverse effects, and change therapy as needed.

front: What information must a patient receive when a drug is prescribed?
back: What effect to expect and when; whether the disease is cured or only controlled; what happens if doses are missed; common side effects, told without alarming the patient; how and how long to take it, and which tests are needed; precautions such as not driving after sedating antihistamines or not drinking alcohol with metronidazole. The patient should repeat the instructions back to confirm understanding.

front: Why is rational prescribing more than choosing the correct drug for the diagnosis?
back: It also covers the whole therapeutic set-up: dose, route and duration fitted to the patient, correct dispensing and instructions, and follow-up of adherence, benefit and adverse effects. Therapy is reviewed and changed until the goals are reached, so the job continues after the prescription is handed over.

text: Write a {{zero}} before a decimal point (0.1, not .1); never add a {{trailing}} zero (1 mg, not 1.0 mg, which can be read as 10); write {{units}} in full instead of U; and write {{microgram}} in full because the shortened form can be misread as mg.

front: Why do patients become noncompliant, and how can compliance be improved?
back: Noncompliance is a main cause of treatment failure. It is encouraged by symptomless disease, painful chronic conditions, frequent dosing, living alone, hard-to-open packs, lack of transport and personal or cultural beliefs. Compliance improves with good communication with the patient, attention to social and economic conditions, linking doses to a daily routine such as meals, dose organisers, alarms, refill reminders and active patient participation.

front: Why should a prescription state the purpose of the drug and write directions out in full?
back: Simple, written-out directions with the purpose reduce misreading and omission errors. Abbreviations can be misread: QD is do-not-use, and OD means right eye. Write the drug name, purpose and duration on the label, and give specific directions with few doses and drugs per day. Telling the patient to take as directed leads to confusion, noncompliance and error.

front: How does the WHO define essential medicines?
back: Medicines that satisfy the priority health care needs of a population. They are chosen for public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness. They should be available at all times in working health systems, in adequate amounts and suitable dosage forms, with assured quality, adequate information and a price the individual and community can afford.

front: What is an orphan drug, and why do governments support it?
back: A drug or biological for a rare disease, or for a commoner disease endemic only in resource-poor areas, where the cost of developing and marketing it is not expected to be recovered from sales. Under the US Orphan Drug Amendment Act (1983), a rare disease affects fewer than 0.2 million people in the USA. Governments give tax benefits and other incentives to encourage development.

front: What are over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, and how is prescription status regulated in India?
back: OTC drugs can be bought without a prescription because they are relatively harmless, e.g. paracetamol, aspirin, antacids, senna, lactulose, vitamins and ferrous salts. Most drugs, including all antibiotics, are prescription-only; in India they are placed in Schedule H of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules.

front: Why do countries keep an essential medicines list, and what is it based on?
back: A small set of well-tested, cheaper drugs often meets most health needs as well as newer costly ones, so listing them improves availability, saves cost and promotes rational use. Selection rests on public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, comparative cost-effectiveness and assured quality.

back: Only when every ingredient is needed, its dose suits the population, and the combination offers a clear advantage over the single drugs. KDT notes that only a handful of FDCs are rational: the WHO 2017 list carries 25 FDCs and India's NLEM 2015 only 20.

front: When is a fixed-dose combination (FDC) rational? Give the main advantages.
back: When every component is needed at the stated doses. Advantages: better adherence and convenience; synergy (sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim, levodopa plus carbidopa); components with different mechanisms add their effect while side effects differ (amlodipine plus atenolol); one component offsets another's side effect (thiazide plus a potassium-sparing diuretic); a single drug cannot be given alone in TB, HIV or falciparum malaria; sometimes cheaper than separate tablets.

back: Corticosteroids. The reference states they should never be combined with any other drug meant for internal use, because the steroid dose can then not be adjusted on its own.

front: A patient on a fixed-dose combination develops an adverse reaction and later renal impairment. What problems arise with the FDC?
back: The offending drug cannot be identified easily, and an allergy or contraindication to one component bars the whole product. In renal or hepatic impairment the components' pharmacokinetics change unequally, yet the dose of one cannot be changed without altering the other. Components with different time courses are also given at one interval, which may suit neither.

front: Why are levodopa plus carbidopa and amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid sold in more than one ratio?
back: Dose individualisation is the main weakness of an FDC, so a few useful combinations are offered at different ratios, e.g. levodopa 100 mg with carbidopa 10 or 25 mg, and amoxicillin 250 or 500 mg with clavulanic acid. Most FDCs have a single ratio and cannot be adjusted.

text: Pharmacoeconomics is the branch of {{health economics}} that expresses the {{cost and benefit}} of therapeutic drugs in economic terms; regulators increasingly ask for an {{economic analysis}} alongside evidence of benefit.

front: What is a QALY and how is it used?
back: Quality-adjusted life years combine survival time with health-related quality of life into a single overall measure of therapeutic benefit, and are listed among clinical outcome measures in trials.

front: For which kinds of drugs is plasma level monitoring useful, and for which is it pointless?
back: Useful where the safety margin is low or individual variation is large: digoxin, anticonvulsants, antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycosides, lithium, and in renal failure, poisoning, unexplained failure or doubtful compliance. Pointless where the response is easily measured (antihypertensives, oral anticoagulants), for prodrugs such as levodopa, hit-and-run drugs and irreversible-action drugs, since plasma level does not track effect.

front: Why can a surrogate end-point mislead, and what do NNT and meta-analysis add to judging a drug?
back: In the CAST trial antiarrhythmics suppressed arrhythmias yet increased mortality compared with placebo, so the surrogate hid harm. NNT is the number of patients to be treated for one to show the effect, benefit or harm. Meta-analysis statistically pools several independent trials.
The process of systematically finding, critically evaluating and using current research findings as the basis of clinical decisions, instead of the impression of the individual physician.

front: What does a therapeutic evaluation of a drug cover?
back: Quantitation of the benefit it gives; the best way to use it (dose, duration and patient selection); how it compares with other available drugs; and surveillance of the adverse effects it produces.
