front: What does the NMC long exercise in the MD Pharmacology practical exam consist of?
back: Three kinds of task: designing a protocol for a given scenario, auditing a given case, and performing an experiment or a simulated experiment. The examiner watches the exercise, notes how the candidate responds and assesses it, and may ask questions on it. The practical exam runs over two days and mainly tests the psychomotor domain.

front: Guinea pig ileum: what is it used to show in the practical exam?
back: Acetylcholine contracts it through muscarinic receptors, and atropine blocks this response. Histamine contracts it through H1 receptors; the guinea pig ileum responds far more than human ileum and remains the standard tissue for histamine bioassay.

front: Frog rectus abdominis: which receptor does it test, and what phenomenon does it show?
back: Nicotinic receptors of skeletal muscle (the end plate). Repeated or large doses of acetylcholine give smaller and smaller contractions, and the response recovers only after a rest: this is receptor desensitisation.

front: Rat isolated gastric fundus: which 5-HT receptor mediates its contraction?
back: 5-HT2B receptor. The 5-HT2 receptor subtypes all couple to Gq, activate phospholipase C and generate IP3 and DAG; contraction of the rat gastric fundus is mediated by 5-HT2B.

front: Why is guinea-pig ileum used to assay histamine?
back: It is highly sensitive to histamine, which acts mainly on H1 receptors in the ileum. Atropine is added to the bath to improve specificity for histamine; mepyramine is added when assaying ACh.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p168 (printed p152)

front: How is the guinea-pig ileum prepared for the bath?
back: Fast the animal 24-48 hours and stun it. Open the abdomen and find the ileum about 10 cm before the caecum. Cut 2-3 cm, trim the mesentery, and tie it to the hook and lever in the direction it lies in the body. Relax it in Tyrode before use (Medhi gives 30-45 min for rat ileum, changing the solution 3-4 times).
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p168-169 (printed p152-153)
Medhi Practical Manual PDF p86 (printed p70)

front: Short note: Isolated organ bath set-up for a tissue experiment

points: A strip of tissue is suspended in an organ bath and its contraction or relaxation is recorded
Responses at increasing concentrations give a concentration-effect curve
Tissue bathed in a physiological salt solution chosen for the tissue
Solution aerated with gas and kept at a constant temperature
Fixed load applied and tissue allowed to relax before dosing
Tissue tied to a lever or force transducer
Response written on a kymograph or physiograph
Agonist potency and maximal response
Antagonist affinity by dose ratio and Schild analysis

front: Short note: Langendorff isolated perfused heart

points: Heart removed from an anaesthetised animal; aorta tied to a cannula
Oxygenated buffer (usually Krebs-Henseleit, 37 °C, pH 7.4) flows backwards into the aorta, shuts the aortic valve and enters the coronary arteries
The heart keeps beating without nerves or circulation
The rat heart is the best-characterised small-heart model; large hearts are costly and variable
Heart rate
Contractile force (isometric transducer)
Coronary flow
Left ventricular pressure (balloon in the ventricle)
Positive and negative inotropes (e.g. isoprenaline effect blocked by a beta-blocker)
Coronary dilators; calcium antagonism after barium chloride spasm
Antiarrhythmic and antifibrillatory testing
Ischaemia-reperfusion studies

front: Langendorff heart: constant-flow versus constant-pressure perfusion.
back: Constant flow: a pump fixes the flow, and changes in coronary perfusion pressure are measured; good for low-flow ischaemia and vasoactive drugs, but it overrides coronary autoregulation. Constant pressure: reservoir height (or feedback) fixes the pressure, so flow follows the heart's demand and autoregulation is kept; good for ischaemia-reperfusion work, but vascular reactivity is harder to measure.

front: How do you scale a drug concentration to the organ bath volume?
back: The tissue sees the stock concentration scaled down to the bath volume (10, 20, 50 or 100 ml). Example: 0.2 x 10^-7 M in a 10 ml bath reaches the tissue as 0.2 x 10^-8 M. Apply the same scaling to every concentration in the set.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p85 (printed p69)

front: Why avoid very high doses of a drug on one tissue preparation?
back: High drug concentrations can cause tachyphylaxis: the tissue loses sensitivity and may stay contracted, so later responses are unreliable.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p168 (printed p152)

front: Essay: Recording a dose-response curve of acetylcholine on an isolated tissue (step-wise)

points: State the aim (graded DRC of ACh; effect of an antagonist if asked)
Sacrifice the animal and dissect the tissue into aerated salt solution
Tie the tissue to the bath hook and the lever or transducer; set the load
Let it relax before dosing
Add increasing doses on a fixed dose cycle
Wash between doses and let the response return to baseline
Keep contact time constant; watch for tachyphylaxis
Measure the height of each contraction
Express as percent of maximum and plot against log dose: a sigmoid curve
Read EC50 from the curve
Keep temperature and aeration constant
Avoid exposing the tissue to air; a sudden kick appears as a vertical artefact

front: Why is a dose-response curve plotted on a log-dose scale?
back: On a linear dose scale the curve is a rectangular hyperbola, because drug-receptor binding follows the law of mass action. On a log-dose scale it becomes sigmoid, with a near-linear middle part (about 30 to 70% response). This spreads out the useful range and makes curves easy to compare.

EC50 is the concentration that gives half the maximal response. Relative potency compares two agonists by the doses that give the same response, usually their EC50s: a curve lying further right means a less potent drug.

pD2: the negative log of the molar concentration of an agonist that gives 50 per cent of its maximal response; a higher pD2 means a more potent agonist. pA2: the negative log of the molar antagonist concentration that gives a dose ratio of 2, i.e. a two-fold shift of the agonist curve. pA2 measures antagonist affinity.
The negative log10 of the molar antagonist concentration that gives a dose ratio of 2, i.e. a two-fold shift of the agonist dose-response curve. pA10 uses the same idea at a dose ratio of 10.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p80 (printed p64)
Medhi Practical Manual PDF p81 (printed p65)

front: How do competitive and noncompetitive antagonists change an agonist's log dose-response curve?
back: Competitive: parallel shift to the right with the same maximum, because enough agonist overcomes the block (surmountable). Noncompetitive: the antagonist acts at another site, so even high agonist concentrations cannot fully reverse it; the curve is flattened and the maximum falls.

front: Complete: Schild analysis of a competitive antagonist
text: The dose ratio (r) is the factor by which agonist concentration must be raised to restore a response in the presence of the antagonist. Plot {{log (r - 1)}} against {{log antagonist concentration}}; for a simple competitive antagonist this gives a straight line, and its intercept on the {{x-axis}} gives the antagonist dissociation constant {{KB}}.

front: How do pA2 and pA10 values show competitive antagonism?
back: For competitive antagonism, pA2 minus pA10 should be about 0.95 (Medhi accepts 0.8 to 1.20). In Ghosh's rat seminal vesicle example, values of 0.99 and 1.19 were judged in good agreement with 0.95.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p81 (printed p65)

front: What are the steps to build a Schild plot?
back: 1) Plot log dose-response curves without and with antagonist. 2) Get the dose ratio (DR) at each antagonist concentration. 3) Plot log(DR minus 1) against log molar antagonist concentration (or its negative). The x-intercept gives pA2; a slope near 1 fits competitive antagonism.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p81 (printed p65)

front: In a tracing exercise, how do you identify an unknown agonist on guinea pig ileum?
back: Compare it with known agonists and test which selective antagonist blocks it. If atropine blocks the response, the agonist acts on muscarinic receptors (ACh-like); if mepyramine, an H1 blocker, blocks it, the agonist is histamine-like. A parallel right shift of the curve points to competitive block.

front: What does a pA2 pattern across histamine and acetylcholine tell you?
back: Each antagonist is scored on guinea-pig ileum against both agonists. A high value means high specificity. A nearly flat line means the antagonist does not tell them apart (pethidine); a steep line means sharp discrimination (mepyramine, atropine).

front: Define bioassay. Why is a standard always run with the unknown?
back: Bioassay estimates the concentration or potency of a substance from the biological response it produces. Biological systems vary between laboratories and over time, so absolute units are unreliable; comparing the unknown with a standard on the same preparation gives a relative potency that different laboratories can agree on.

front: Classify: designs of bioassay on isolated tissue
text: In order of rising accuracy: {{matching (single-point)}} assay, {{bracketing}} assay, {{graphical interpolation}} assay, {{three-point (2 + 1)}} assay, {{four-point (2 + 2)}} assay and multiple-point assays.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual (Bikash Medhi), PDF p73 (printed p57): bracketing, matching, interpolation, multiple-point

front: Where is bioassay still important today?
back: Measuring activity of new or chemically undefined substances; studying endogenous mediators (e.g. cascade superfusion for short-lived mediators such as prostacyclin and nitric oxide); measuring toxicity; and standardising biopharmaceuticals (vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, recombinant proteins) that vary from batch to batch. Measuring drug levels in body fluids has largely moved to chemical analysis.

front: What are the three main classes of bioassay?
back: Direct end-point assay, quantal (all-or-none) assay and graded assay. Graded assays include bracketing, matching, interpolation and multiple-point designs.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p73 (printed p57)

front: What does an analytical dilution assay measure?
back: The potency of an unknown agonist as the factor by which it is diluted or concentrated relative to a standard of the same drug. Because both are the same drug, results are similar whatever tissue, species or method is used.

front: Matching (single-point) bioassay: principle, merit and drawback.
back: The standard and the test are matched by trial and error until they give equal responses; the matched doses are taken as equipotent. Merit: no assumption about the dose-response relationship and no statistics needed. Drawbacks: inefficient (earlier responses are not used), subjective matching, no error estimate from the assay itself, and no check that the dose-response curves are parallel.

The test response is placed between two standard responses, one just above and one just below it, and potency is found by interpolating between them. It copes with slow drift in tissue sensitivity better than matching, but still gives no measure of error.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual (Bikash Medhi), PDF p75 (printed p59): response bracketed between two standard responses
Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology PDF p92-93: matching or bracketing assay

front: Graphical interpolation bioassay: how is potency read?
back: A full log dose-response curve of the standard is drawn first. The test is then given and its response read off the linear part of the standard curve to find the equivalent standard dose. It needs a stable tissue, because the curve is built before the test is given.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual (Bikash Medhi), PDF p75-76 (printed p59-60): response read from standard dose-response plot

front: What are the main sources of error in bioassay, and how does the design control them?
back: The main problem is biological (tissue) variation. Controls: Latin square randomised dose order and repeated responses (these reduce tissue sensitivity error); a fixed dose cycle and contact time with washes; recognising tachyphylaxis (falling response with repeated doses). Accept only about plus or minus 10 per cent biological variability. Temperature and dilution errors also need control.

front: Morphine versus codeine: what does the human 2 + 2 analgesic assay show?
back: Four patients each received high and low doses of both drugs in random order, blinded, with pain relief scored by a trained observer. Morphine was about 13 times as potent as codeine. This shows only that less morphine is needed for the same effect, not that it is the better drug.

front: How is a 3-point bioassay set up?
back: Pick three graded responses: two of the standard (S1, S2) and one of the test (T), each between 25% and 75% of maximal. Arrange them in a Latin square. Relative potency comes from the sideways displacement of the parallel log dose-response lines.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p76-77 (printed p60-61)

front: How does a 4-point assay differ from a 3-point assay?
back: It uses two standard and two test responses, all taken from the dose-response curves and arranged in a Latin square. It is more sensitive than the 3-point design and reduces variability.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p78 (printed p62)

points: Two doses of standard (S1, S2) and one dose of test (T), all on the linear part of the log DRC
Test response should fall between the two standard responses
Doses given in randomised order (e.g. a Latin square) and repeated
Fixed contact time and time cycle with washes between doses
Potency read from where the test response lies on the line joining S1 and S2 on a log-dose scale
Only one test dose, so parallelism of standard and test cannot be checked

refs: Medhi Practical Manual (Bikash Medhi), PDF p76-77 (printed p60-61): three-point assay, s1 and s2 standard doses

points: Two doses each of standard and test (S1, S2, T1, T2), taken from the linear part of the dose-response curve (25 to 75 per cent of maximum)
Doses arranged in Latin square randomisation
Relative potency from the displacement of the parallel log-dose lines of standard and test
Same design as the 3-point assay but more sensitive
Reduces error and variability compared with the 3-point assay

front: When can a simple potency ratio NOT be given in a bioassay?
back: When the log dose-response lines of standard and unknown are not parallel, or their maximal responses differ. This happens when the two act by different mechanisms or one is a partial agonist. A single ratio then cannot describe their relative activity.

front: How should the objectives of a research protocol be written?
back: Simple rather than complex, specific rather than vague, and stated before the research starts. The primary objective comes first; secondary objectives follow. Goals describe what the proposal hopes to achieve; objectives state the research questions.

front: Which part of a protocol is the most important, and what must it contain?
back: The methodology. It gives the interventions, procedures, measurements, observations and lab tests; selection criteria and study population; the information sheet and consent process; and, for a randomised trial, randomisation, blinding and stopping rules.

front: Why are participants randomised in a clinical trial?
back: Random allocation gives every participant an equal chance of being put in each group, so the groups are similar at baseline. This removes selection bias and protects against accidental bias that could distort the result.

front: Why is a protocol primary objective fixed before the study starts?
back: Objectives must be simple, specific and stated in advance, not after the research is done. The primary objective comes first; secondary objectives follow it.

front: Protocol exercise: what must the informed-consent part contain?
back: A patient information sheet and a written informed-consent form, with the consent process described. Participation must be voluntary and informed.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology curriculum PDF p9

front: Essay: Designing a clinical trial protocol for a given scenario (exam approach)

points: Title, protocol number and date; sponsor; investigators and sites
Project summary of no more than about 300 words that stands alone
Why the study is needed (the problem and the gap)
Primary objective, then secondary objectives: simple, specific and fixed in advance
Type of study and phase; randomisation, blinding and control
Study population with inclusion, exclusion and withdrawal criteria; expected duration
Interventions, procedures, measurements and lab tests
Patient information sheet and written informed consent
Stopping rules and a flow chart
Adverse-event recording and reporting; follow-up
Sample size, data management and analysis plan; quality assurance
Ethics section and consent forms in English and local language
Budget, insurance, conflict of interest, publication policy

front: Scenario: you must test a new antihypertensive against standard therapy. Which protocol design choices do you state and why?
back: Randomised, controlled design (equal baseline groups, less selection bias); blinding where possible; clear inclusion, exclusion and withdrawal criteria; one primary objective; stopping rules; analysis plan written beforehand; ethics approval and informed consent.

front: How does KD Tripathi grade the causality of an adverse event?
back: Definite: causality proven. Probable: not proven, but the drug is the likely cause. Possible: the drug or other causes could be responsible. Doubtful: the drug is unlikely to be the cause but cannot be ruled out.
Certain; probable; possible; unlikely; unclassified; unclassifiable.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Agreement between Naranjo algorithm and WHO-UMC criteria for causality assessment 2014 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3912795/

front: What is the purpose of a causality assessment of an adverse event?
back: To decide how likely the suspected drug, rather than disease or another cause, produced the event. Graded as definite, probable, possible or doubtful using timing, previous knowledge, dechallenge and rechallenge.

front: Case audit exercise: what do you check in a given case and its treatment?
back: Whether each drug is indicated for the diagnosis; whether drug, dose, route, frequency and duration are right for this patient; contraindications, interactions and duplication; unnecessary or irrational combinations; generic versus brand and cost; and whether information and monitoring were planned. WHO criteria: right indication, medicine, dose and duration, patient, dispensing and adherence.

front: How well do the Naranjo and WHO-UMC causality scales agree?
back: Poorly overall, in one Indian comparison. Agreement was highest for the 'possible' category and absent for 'certain'. Both are widely used pharmacovigilance tools.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Agreement between Naranjo algorithm and WHO-UMC criteria for causality assessment 2014 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3912795/

front: Essay: ADR causality assessment exercise for a given case

points: Suspected drug, when it was started and stopped, and the time of onset of the event
Other drugs, the disease and other possible causes
Temporal relationship to drug administration
Previous knowledge: is the reaction known for this drug?
Dechallenge: did it subside on stopping?
Rechallenge: did it reappear on re-exposure (often unethical, so rarely done)?
Causality graded as definite, probable, possible or doubtful
Severity graded with the modified Hartwig scale
Naranjo algorithm is a standard causality scale (score cut-offs left for the owner to verify)
State the causality grade and severity
Report to the ADR monitoring centre for pharmacovigilance (PvPI)

front: ADR case exercise: the patient developed a rash 5 days after a new drug and improved on stopping it. How do you reason to a causality grade?
back: Check timing after the start, whether the event is known for the drug, dechallenge (did it settle on stopping), alternative causes and rechallenge if done. Settling on withdrawal with no other cause favours probable; definite needs proof; unresolved alternatives make it possible; drug unlikely makes it doubtful.

front: What are the five steps of critical appraisal in evidence-based medicine?
back: 1) Ask an answerable question (PICO: population, intervention, comparison, outcome). 2) Search for the evidence. 3) Appraise the methods and design. 4) Appraise the results. 5) Judge the significance of the results and their impact on practice.

front: Classify: reporting guidelines used to appraise papers
text: {{CONSORT}} for randomised trials (25-item checklist and flow diagram); {{PRISMA}} for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (27 items); {{STROBE}} for cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies (22 items); {{STARD}} for diagnostic accuracy studies; {{MOOSE}} for meta-analyses of observational studies; {{SPIRIT}} for trial protocols.

front: What does PICO stand for in framing a clinical question?
back: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome. It turns a vague doubt into an answerable question, which is step one of appraisal.

front: Why should a paper report confidence intervals and not only P values?
back: A P value only tells whether the null hypothesis is rejected. A confidence interval shows the direction and size of the effect and how precise the estimate is, so clinical importance can be judged.

front: Why does a CONSORT flow diagram help you appraise a trial?
back: It shows how many participants were enrolled, excluded, dropped out and analysed. Losses that are not analysed can under- or over-estimate the results, so you check them.

front: Essay: Critical appraisal of a published paper, section by section

points: Is the research question clear (population, intervention, outcome)?
Is the need explained, and is the hypothesis stated in advance?
Design suited to the question; inclusion and exclusion criteria; end points set beforehand
Randomisation, blinding and sources of bias
Sample size calculation and level of significance
Statistical tests suit the data (non-parametric for non-normal data)
All participants accounted for, including drop-outs and withdrawals (flow chart)
Appropriate summary measures; results match the abstract
Effect size with confidence intervals, not P values alone
Limitations and external validity discussed
Findings compared with earlier studies
Conclusions follow from the results
Funding source and conflict of interest declared and managed
Relevance to one's own patients

front: A trial reports P = 0.04 with a wide confidence interval reaching a clinically trivial effect. How do you judge it?
back: Statistically significant but imprecise: the confidence interval shows the true effect could be too small to matter. Judge effect size and precision, and check the methods for bias, before accepting it.

front: Rabbit eye practical: what does it demonstrate?
back: Effects of mydriatics and miotics on the pupil of the rabbit eye. Each drug is instilled in one eye and the other eye is kept as an untreated control.

front: Complete: Mechanism of drug-induced pupil size change
text: Atropine dilates the pupil by blocking {{M3}} receptors on the {{sphincter pupillae}}. Pilocarpine constricts it by stimulating M3 receptors on the same muscle. Phenylephrine dilates the pupil by stimulating {{alpha-1}} receptors on the {{dilator pupillae}}.

front: Measurement: how is intraocular pressure measured in the rabbit eye?
back: Schiotz tonometer: a weighted plunger rests on the cornea, and the scale reading is converted to IOP using a conversion table. A topical anaesthetic is needed first.

front: Which chart tests near vision, and which tests colour vision?
back: Jaeger chart tests near vision. Ishihara plates test colour vision (red-green deficiency). Neither replaces the Snellen chart for distance acuity.

front: Classify: drugs in the rabbit eye practical by effect on pupil
text: Mydriatics: {{atropine}}, {{phenylephrine}}, {{homatropine}}, {{tropicamide}}. Miotics: {{pilocarpine}}, {{physostigmine}}, {{eserine}}.

front: Which muscle of the iris does a mydriatic or miotic act on, and which receptor drives each?
back: Sphincter pupillae (M3, parasympathetic) constricts the pupil; dilator pupillae (alpha-1, sympathetic) dilates it. Drugs work by blocking or stimulating these receptors.

front: Why is atropine mydriasis called mydriatic-cycloplegic?
back: Atropine also paralyses the ciliary muscle (cycloplegia), so accommodation is lost. Near vision blurs for days, and it rests the eye in iritis or uveitis.

front: Why does phenylephrine dilate the pupil without cycloplegia?
back: It acts on alpha-1 receptors of the dilator pupillae only; the ciliary muscle is supplied by muscarinic receptors, which it does not block.

front: Why is pilocarpine used in glaucoma even though it causes miosis?
back: Ciliary muscle contraction opens the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal, so aqueous outflow rises and intraocular pressure falls. Miosis is a side effect of the same drug.

front: Which drug antagonises atropine-induced mydriasis in the practical, and how?
back: Pilocarpine. Its M3 agonism causes sphincter contraction, opposing the atropine block.

front: Short note: Snellen chart for visual acuity

points: Letters of decreasing size on a standard chart read at a fixed distance
Acuity is expressed as a fraction: test distance / distance at which the smallest line is read
Test at 6 m (20 ft); cover one eye and test the other
Record each eye separately; use glasses or pinhole if worn
6/6 = normal vision at 6 m
6/60 = letters seen at 6 m that a normal eye reads at 60 m
Counting fingers, hand movements and light perception are recorded when letters cannot be read
Cycloplegics blur near vision more than distance
Miotics can induce myopia-like blur, so test vision after drug instillation before judging the effect

front: Why test each eye separately on the Snellen chart?
back: One eye may see well and the other poorly; covering the other eye prevents the good eye from masking a deficit in the test eye.

front: Why is the untreated opposite eye kept as control in the rabbit eye practical?
back: The other eye of the same rabbit is the control. It gives a same-animal baseline to compare pupil size with, avoiding individual variation.

front: Essay: Rabbit eye experiment, mydriatic and miotic effects (step-wise)

points: Compare pupil size after a mydriatic (e.g. atropine) and a miotic (e.g. pilocarpine) in the rabbit eye
Hold the rabbit gently; keep the eye lids open without pressure on the eyeball
Use a millimetre scale or ruler held at the same distance each reading
Record baseline pupil diameter in both eyes under the same room light
Instil one drop of the test drug in one eye; leave the other eye as control
Note the time of instillation
Measure both pupils at fixed intervals (e.g. 5, 15, 30, 60 min)
Tabulate diameter against time for test and control eye
Atropine: dilation with slow recovery (long-acting antimuscarinic)
Pilocarpine: constriction (miosis), recovers in hours
Control eye stays constant, confirming the response is drug-induced

front: Rabbit eye: predict the pupil after atropine, then after pilocarpine.
back: Atropine blocks M3 so the pupil stays dilated; pilocarpine then reverses the mydriasis by acting on the same receptors.

front: Dog BP practical: what does it demonstrate?
back: Effects of autonomic drugs on mean arterial pressure (MAP) and heart rate (HR) in an anaesthetised dog. It is a standard in vivo practical for the autonomic nervous system.

front: Dog BP: why is the drug given i.v. and not orally?
back: Oral absorption is slow and variable; the i.v. route gives a rapid, measurable effect on the recorded pressure trace.

front: Complete: acetylcholine and atropine in the dog BP practical
text: Acetylcholine i.v. causes a brief fall in MAP through {{muscarinic}} vasodilation and a {{bradycardia}}. Atropine given first {{blocks}} these muscarinic effects, so acetylcholine then only {{raises}} the pressure.

front: Why is the dog anaesthetised in the blood pressure practical?
back: Autonomic drugs are tested on blood pressure in anaesthetised animals, so the dog is anaesthetised with a barbiturate and prepared for BP recording.

front: Adrenaline in the dog: what is the biphasic response?
back: Low doses cause a fall in MAP, from beta-2 vasodilation; higher doses cause a rise, from alpha-1 vasoconstriction. Heart rate rises through beta-1 stimulation. Atropine or a beta-blocker alters the HR change.

front: Why does adrenaline reverse its pressor effect after alpha blockade?
back: Phentolamine blocks alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors. Adrenaline then acts only on beta-2 receptors, so MAP falls. This is the adrenaline reversal (Dale) phenomenon.

front: Noradrenaline in the dog: why does HR fall?
back: Noradrenaline raises MAP through alpha-1 vasoconstriction. The rise in pressure triggers a baroreceptor reflex that slows the heart (reflex bradycardia). Atropine abolishes that slowing.

front: Isoprenaline in the dog: effect on MAP and HR?
back: Non-selective beta agonist. It causes vasodilation and fall in MAP (beta-2), and a marked tachycardia (beta-1). Not blocked by phentolamine.

front: Why does a beta-blocker change the adrenaline response in the dog?
back: Blocking beta-2 removes the vasodilator (depressor) phase and blocking beta-1 removes the tachycardia, leaving mainly the alpha-1 pressor effect.

front: Essay: Anaesthetised dog BP experiment, drug effects on MAP and HR (step-wise)

points: Compare MAP and HR responses to adrenaline, noradrenaline, isoprenaline, acetylcholine and atropine
Anaesthetise the dog (e.g. pentobarbitone i.v.) and keep it stable throughout
Cannulate a femoral vein for drug injection and a carotid or femoral artery for pressure recording
Connect the arterial cannula to a pressure transducer and kymograph or software
Record stable MAP and HR before any drug
Flush the cannula so it stays patent
Give each drug i.v. in increasing or fixed doses, one at a time
Allow MAP to return to baseline between doses
Read MAP and HR from the trace for each dose
Plot dose against response; note direction, size and onset of change

front: Dog BP: predict the effect on MAP and HR of noradrenaline, adrenaline and isoprenaline before and after phentolamine.
back: After phentolamine, noradrenaline pressor effect is reduced, adrenaline reverses to a fall in MAP, and isoprenaline is unchanged because it acts on beta receptors. Heart-rate changes depend on the reflex and beta-1 action.

front: Classify: example OSPE stations listed by the NMC
text: Drug {{delivery systems}}; calculating {{pharmacokinetic parameters}}; {{pharmaceutical calculations}}; a statistical exercise; {{pharmacoeconomics}}; critical appraisal and {{abstract writing}} of a published paper; evaluating {{drug promotional literature}}; {{ADR reporting and causality assessment}}; assessing {{preclinical toxicity data}}; rational and irrational formulations; choosing a {{P-drug}} and writing a rational prescription; {{analytical instruments}}; spotting ethics dilemmas or mistakes in clinical trial documents.

front: What does OSPE stand for, and how many stations does the NMC specify?
back: Objective Structured Practical Examination. The NMC specifies 10 to 15 stations, a mix of observed stations (observer present) and unobserved stations (without an observer).

front: Observed versus unobserved OSPE stations: what is assessed at each?
back: Observed: an examiner watches the candidate perform a task (e.g. taking consent, filling an ADR form, preparing a dilution) and scores the process on a fixed checklist. Unobserved: the candidate writes an answer or produces something (a calculation, a critique, an abstract) that is marked later against a key.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Standardization and validation of OSPE in pharmacology 2017 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754933/
WEB Indian J Pharmacol Introducing OSPE as a method of learning and evaluation for undergraduate pharmacology 2016 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5178055/

front: Why is OSPE preferred to a traditional practical exam?
back: Every candidate does the same tasks, each marked against a pre-set checklist, so marking is more objective. A single written exam does not assess knowledge, skill and attitude together; OSPE stations can.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Introducing OSPE as a method of learning and evaluation for undergraduate pharmacology 2016 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5178055/
WEB Indian J Pharmacol Standardization and validation of OSPE in pharmacology 2017 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754933/

front: How should a candidate work through an OSPE station?
back: Read the instruction card fully; note the time allowed; do exactly what is asked (e.g. "identify and give two uses" means two); show steps and units in calculations; for observed stations, say what you are doing (introduce yourself, explain, check understanding); leave the station tidy.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Standardization and validation of OSPE in pharmacology 2017 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754933/
NMC MD Pharmacology curriculum PDF p22

front: Why must OSPE stations and checklists be validated before use?
back: Validity (the station measures what it is meant to) and reliability (consistent results) must be shown. Many pharmacology OSPE stations were not standardised, so each station and checklist should be standardised, piloted and checked. Each station is typically about 5 minutes.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Standardization and validation of OSPE in pharmacology 2017 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754933/

front: Under PvPI, what should be reported and who may report?
back: All suspected adverse events with new drugs and "drugs of current interest", all suspected interactions, and reactions to any drug that affect patient management, especially serious ones. Any health care professional (doctor, dentist, nurse, pharmacist) may report; Sarkar notes the programme does not accept reports from lay people.

front: Complete: what makes an adverse reaction "serious"
text: It results in {{death}}, is {{life-threatening}}, causes or prolongs {{hospitalisation}}, causes significant or permanent {{disability}}, causes a {{congenital anomaly}}, or needs {{intervention to prevent permanent damage}}.

front: What must an informed consent form for a trial explain to the participant?
back: Purpose of the study; trial treatments and randomisation; procedures; risks; benefits; alternative treatments; compensation or treatment for trial-related injury; the participant's responsibilities; experimental aspects; and any payments.

front: Complete: essential elements of informed consent (Schedule Y)
text: {{Confidentiality}} of the participant; sharing of {{new information}} from the study; {{voluntary}} participation; {{persons to contact}} for study information; rights if {{study-related injury}} occurs; reasons the study may be {{terminated}}; total {{duration}} of the study; total {{number of subjects}}.

front: What appears in the signature part of the prescribed informed consent form?
back: Study title; subject's initials and identifiers (name, date of birth or age); consent statements initialled by the volunteer; signature or thumb impression of the subject or legally acceptable representative; investigator's name and signature; witness's name and signature.

front: Short note: Filling a suspected ADR reporting form (PvPI)

points: Initials (not full name), age or date of birth, sex, weight
Description of the event; date of onset and date it stopped
Relevant tests and history; seriousness; outcome
Name (brand and generic), manufacturer, batch number, dose, route, frequency
Dates started and stopped; indication
Dechallenge and rechallenge results
Concomitant drugs, including self-medication
Reporter name, profession, contact details and signature
Handled in confidence; causality assessed at the monitoring centre

front: Trace the path of an ADR report in PvPI.
back: The ADR monitoring centre collects the report, follows it up for completeness and enters it in VigiFlow, sending it to the PvPI National Coordination Centre at IPC Ghaziabad. Data go on to the WHO Uppsala Monitoring Centre database; CDSCO takes regulatory decisions on the NCC's advice.

front: Short note: Spotting mistakes in a consent form or trial document (OSPE)

points: Consent form must be in English and in the local language used with participants
No statement that participation is voluntary or can be withdrawn at any time
No contact person for study information; no statement of the participant's rights if injury occurs
Confidentiality of the participant not addressed
No provision for medical management and financial compensation for trial-related injury
No prior ethics committee review of the protocol
Vulnerable groups enrolled without a full review

front: Short note: Drug delivery systems that prolong or target action

points: Sustained-release tablets and spansules (coated particles)
Controlled-release tablets with a semipermeable membrane: part released at once, the rest slowly over hours
Insoluble depot injections (benzathine penicillin, lente insulin) and oily solutions (depot progestins)
Pellets and implants; vasoconstrictor added to a local anaesthetic
Drug-impregnated adhesive patches, e.g. glyceryl trinitrate
Liposomes taken up by reticuloendothelial and some tumour cells (liposomal amphotericin B)
Drug-releasing implants: progestin IUCD; drug-coated stents

front: Pharmaceutical calculation: how are percentage and ratio strengths read?
back: % w/v means grams of drug in 100 mL, so a 1% solution is 10 mg/mL. A ratio such as 1 in 1000 means 1 g in 1000 mL, i.e. 1 mg/mL (as for adrenaline 1:1000).

front: Dilution formula: what is C1 x V1 = C2 x V2 used for?
back: It finds how much stock to take. C1 and V1 are the stock strength and the volume taken; C2 and V2 are the final strength and the volume wanted.

front: Dosage-form or delivery-system identification station: what should your answer cover?
back: Name the dosage form or device, its route, the drug it usually carries and its class, why that form is used (advantage), how to use it correctly, and key precautions or adverse effects.

front: Which drugs are suited to controlled-release formulations?
back: Drugs with a half-life under about 4 hours benefit; those with a half-life over 12 hours do not need them. Drugs meant for a brief effect (hypnotics, headache remedies) or already long-acting (doxycycline, amlodipine, digoxin) should not be made long-acting.

front: How do you make a dilution of a stock solution?
back: Make the stock solution stronger, then dilute it stepwise to the final strength, using isotonic saline for the final dilution. Book example: 0.2 mL of a 1 mg/mL histamine stock in a 10 mL organ bath gives 20 µg/mL. The NMC expects candidates to prepare drug solutions of the right strength and volume.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology PDF p11: stock dilution example
NMC MD Pharmacology curriculum PDF p8

front: How is the final drug concentration in an organ bath calculated?
back: Final bath concentration = (concentration of the solution added x volume added) / volume of the bath. For example, 0.1 mL of a 10 microgram/mL solution in a 10 mL bath gives 0.1 microgram/mL.
refs: Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology PDF p11: 0.2 mg of 1 mg/mL stock in 10 mL bath = 20 ug/mL
Medhi Practical Manual PDF p87 (printed p71): dilution per organ-bath volume

front: Calculation: a 20 kg child needs a drug whose average adult dose is 500 mg. Dose by body weight?
back: Child dose by weight ratio = 20 / 70 x 500 mg = about 143 mg (arithmetic). Katzung says age- or weight-based estimates tend to underestimate the required dose; surface-area dosing is more likely to be adequate.

front: How is an i.v. drip rate calculated?
back: Drops per minute = volume to infuse (mL) x drop factor of the set (drops/mL) / time (minutes). Example: 500 mL over 4 hours with a 20 drops/mL set = 500 x 20 / 240 = about 42 drops per minute.
refs: Dosage Calculations (Pickar) PDF p2: IV flow rate V(mL)/T(min) x C(gtt/mL) = R(gtt/min); visually checked

front: Case: histamine stock is 1 mg/mL. You need 2 microgram/mL in a 10 mL organ bath. Why not add the stock directly, and what do you do?
back: The bath needs 20 microgram, which is 0.02 mL of stock: too small to measure accurately. So dilute the stock stepwise first (e.g. 1 in 100 gives 10 microgram/mL), then add 2 mL of that to the bath (2 x 10 / 10 = 2 microgram/mL). Check with the bath-concentration formula.
refs: Ghosh FEP PDF p11: histamine stock and stepwise dilution
Medhi PMECP PDF p87 (printed p71): dilution per organ-bath volume

front: What does a package insert contain?
back: Brand and generic names; active ingredients; name and address of the manufacturer; approved indications; dosage and method of use; contraindications, precautions and side effects. Renal dose adjustments are given here. The NMC expects candidates to prepare a package insert.
refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)
NMC MD Pharmacology curriculum PDF p9

front: What should the label of a dispensed medicine show?
back: Drug form, dosage strength and total container volume; administration route; directions for mixing, where needed; drug alerts. A manufacturer's label also shows the lot number, expiry date and NDC (National Drug Code).

front: What are primary, secondary and tertiary literature sources?
back: Primary: original research in journals and clinical trial data. Secondary: research data analysed, compiled and published, e.g. Medline, Index Medicus. Tertiary: drug compendia.

front: Answering a drug-information query at an OSPE station: what is the approach?
back: Answer the enquiry on therapeutic drug use. Use the primary medical and pharmaceutical literature and critically analyse it for clinical relevance before replying. Answers are reviewed regularly, and feedback is taken from the enquirer.

front: A promotional leaflet says "safest drug in its class" with no reference and lists no adverse effects. What is wrong?
back: The comparative safety claim is unsupported (such claims need current literature), no references are given, and the balance is missing: adverse effects, contraindications, precautions and warnings must also be shown. Check too that the generic name appears.

front: Short note: Evaluating drug promotional literature

points: Claims must be true, suggestive and backed by scientific references
Approved therapeutic use only; claims on relative safety, efficacy or population must be supported by current literature
Adverse effects, contraindications, precautions and warnings stated
Generic name shown, not only the brand
Active ingredients and doses, and the manufacturer's name and address
Scientific references given, and their quality assessed
Judge against the IFPMA Code and the OPPI code of marketing practice in India
Doctors must separate real information from promotional claims
The NMC lists evaluating promotional drug literature as a required skill

refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)
NMC MD Pharmacology curriculum PDF p9

front: Abstract-writing station: how do you write the abstract of a given paper?
back: Keep to the word limit: no more than 300 words and at most one page (font 12, single spacing), on its own page. Cover the central elements of the study, such as rationale, objectives, methods, population, time frame and expected outcomes. Sarkar gives this same rule for the abstract of a paper.

front: Name the main types of pharmacoeconomic analysis
back: Cost-minimisation, cost-effectiveness, cost-utility and cost-benefit. Sarkar also lists cost-of-illness. They differ mainly in how the outcome is measured (equal outcome, natural units, QALYs, money).

front: What is a QALY and which analysis uses it?
back: Quality-adjusted life year: years of life gained weighted by the quality of those years. It is the outcome unit of cost-utility analysis, letting treatments with different effects on survival and well-being be compared.

front: Pharmacoeconomics station: how do you name the analysis from a scenario?
back: Look at how outcomes are measured. Outcomes proven equal and only costs compared: cost-minimisation. Outcome in natural units (cases cured, mmHg, life-years): cost-effectiveness. Outcome in QALYs: cost-utility. Costs and outcomes both in money: cost-benefit.

front: Station: assess given preclinical toxicity data. What do you check?
back: Species (a rodent and a non-rodent) and routes; acute study (dose range, maximum tolerated dose); subacute and chronic studies of a length matching the intended human use, with haematology, biochemistry and histopathology; reproductive and teratogenicity data; mutagenicity (e.g. Ames test); carcinogenicity for long-term drugs; and GLP compliance.

front: Critical appraisal station: which core questions does Sarkar use for a first look at a paper?
back: Is the aim important and interesting? Will the outcome matter clinically? Is the method well designed? Is the primary outcome properly assessed? Is the sample large enough? Is there reason to doubt validity (poor method, small sample, confounding)?

front: Ethics-dilemma station: what faults are typically planted in a trial scenario?
back: No ethics committee review before the trial starts; consent not in the local language; vulnerable groups enrolled without a full review; placebo used when a proven effective treatment exists; no provision for compensation for trial-related injury; undeclared conflict of interest (for example, monetary gain); confidentiality not protected.

A solution in a cuvette absorbs light of a chosen wavelength, and a photometer measures the light that passes through. By the Beer-Lambert law, absorbance is proportional to the concentration of the substance and the path length, so concentration can be calculated.

front: HPLC: principle and the most common form.
back: An improved column chromatography in which solvent is pumped through a column of very fine particles at high pressure, separating compounds by their affinity for the stationary and mobile phases. Reversed-phase HPLC (non-polar modified silica, polar solvent) is most used. Each compound is identified by its retention time, and the peak gives its amount; HPLC can be coupled to mass spectrometry.

Compounds in a mixture move up a coated plate with the solvent by capillary action. Those with more affinity for the stationary phase move slowly, the others faster, so they separate into spots that are then identified by a detection method.

points: Antigen-antibody binding gives specificity
An enzyme label (alkaline phosphatase or horseradish peroxidase) turns a substrate into a coloured product, giving sensitivity
Coat wells with antigen
Block unbound sites
Add primary antibody
Add enzyme-linked secondary antibody
Add substrate and read the colour
Direct
Indirect
Sandwich (highly sensitive)
Competitive

front: In spectrophotometry, what happens to absorbance if the concentration doubles, and how is an unknown concentration found?
back: Absorbance doubles too, since by Beer-Lambert it is proportional to concentration (and path length). Read the sample's absorbance and compare with a standard curve made from solutions of known strength.

front: Instrument choice: match the task to HPLC, TLC, ELISA or spectrophotometry.
back: HPLC: compounds identified by retention time, amount read from the peak; can couple to mass spectrometry. TLC: components separated on a plate and seen as spots afterwards. ELISA: enzyme-labelled colour, proportional to the antibody bound. Spectrophotometry: absorbance proportional to concentration (Beer-Lambert).

Two or more drugs given in one preparation at a fixed dose ratio. It is justified only when every component is needed by the patient and the ratio suits them; otherwise the patient gets extra drugs and side effects with no benefit.

front: Name the six criteria for rational prescribing.
back: Appropriate indication; appropriate drug (efficacy, tolerability, safety, suitability); appropriate dose, route and duration; appropriate patient (no contraindication, acceptable, benefit above risk); correct dispensing with instructions; adequate monitoring of adherence and effects.

front: Why can a fixed-dose combination be rational?
back: Better compliance when all components are needed; synergy (e.g. sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim, isoniazid + rifampin); two components with different mechanisms add their effect while side effects differ (e.g. amlodipine + atenolol); a single drug cannot be given alone in TB, HIV-AIDS and falciparum malaria.

front: What are the built-in disadvantages of an FDC?
back: Patient may take drugs not needed, with extra side effects and cost; dose cannot be individualised; components may have different time courses or renal/hepatic handling; a contraindication to one part bars the whole product; adverse effects are hard to attribute.

front: Judge a fixed-dose combination on a prescription: what do you check?
back: Is each component needed for this patient? Is the fixed ratio right for dose individualisation? Do the components share a suitable time course and are renal or hepatic issues compatible? Is there a contraindication to one part? Is the product among the rational FDCs, since most are not justified and some are banned in India (KDT8 gives 344 irrational FDCs banned).

front: Short note: Parts of a prescription

points: Prescriber address (letter pad with name and address); signature with registration number
Date of writing
Patient name, age, sex and address
Superscription: Rx
Inscription: drug name and strength; no abbreviations
Subscription: instructions to the pharmacist (compounding, quantity to supply)
Directions to the patient: quantity, frequency, time, route and other relevant instructions
Common abbreviations include o.d., b.d., t.i.d., h.s., stat, s.o.s., p.o. and a.c.

text: {{Under-prescribing}} (needed drug not given, or dose/duration too small); {{over-prescribing}} (drug not indicated, or too long or too much); {{incorrect (inappropriate) prescribing}} (wrong diagnosis, ignores allergy or interactions); {{extravagant prescribing}} (costly drug when a cheaper equal one exists); {{multiple prescribing}} (two or more drugs for the same effect).

front: Give common irrationalities seen in prescriptions.
back: Antibiotics for viral fever or nonspecific diarrhoea; routine vitamins and tonics; drugs unrelated to the diagnosis (e.g. a PPI for any abdominal symptom); wrong drug (a beta-blocker for an asthmatic with hypertension); doubtful drugs (cough mixtures, memory enhancers); injections when oral will do; wrong dose or duration; needless combinations (ciprofloxacin + tinidazole for every diarrhoea); costly newer drugs; corticosteroids for fever; polypharmacy.

points: The personal drug a doctor has chosen to prescribe regularly for a given indication and knows well
Includes drug, dosage form, dosage schedule and duration
Differs between countries and doctors (cost, availability, formularies)
Define the diagnosis
Specify the therapeutic objective
List the effective drug groups
Choose a group by efficacy, safety, suitability and cost
Choose the P-drug (substance, dosage form, schedule, duration)
Newest and costliest is not always safest or best
Builds pharmacological knowledge and awareness of alternatives
Patient safety rests with the prescriber, not with seniors or sales representatives

front: What are the WHO steps for improving rational prescribing?
back: 1) Identify the patient's problem. 2) Make the diagnosis. 3) List possible drug and non-drug treatments and choose on efficacy, convenience and safety. 4) Start treatment with a complete, accurate prescription. 5) Give information and warnings. 6) Monitor the outcome (passively by the patient, or actively at a follow-up visit).

front: Prescription criticism: what is your checklist?
back: Legibility and completeness (prescriber, patient, date, signature); generic names; each drug justified by the diagnosis; correct dose, frequency, route and duration; no unnecessary drugs, tonics or irrational fixed-dose combinations; no interacting or contraindicated drugs; no unsafe abbreviations; injection only when oral is unsuitable; cost; and patient instructions.

front: P-drug versus P-treatment: what is the difference?
back: Not every problem needs a drug. P-treatment can be advice, non-drug treatment, a drug, referral, or a mix. In simple constipation the first P-treatment is advice (fluids, fibre, exercise); a laxative such as senna is kept for severe short-term cases, and persistent cases need investigation.

front: Essay: Choosing a P-drug for an acute attack of angina (WHO example)

points: Exertional chest pain relieved by rest: angina pectoris (classify stable/unstable, classic/variant)
Coronary stenosis cannot be dilated by drugs, so reduce myocardial oxygen demand quickly
Ways: lower preload, contractility, heart rate or afterload
Nitrates, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers
Efficacy and safety broadly similar
Suitability decides: the patient must treat the attack alone, and only nitrates come as sublingual tablets or oromucosal spray
Nitrates are cheap generics
Glyceryl trinitrate, isosorbide mononitrate and dinitrate do not differ in efficacy or safety, so cost decides
Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate tablet; a second tablet after 5-10 minutes if pain persists, then see a doctor
Prescribe a small supply because the drug is volatile

text: The patient may not need {{all the components}}; the dose of one cannot be {{adjusted}} without changing the other; components may have different {{durations of action}}; renal or hepatic disease may affect the components {{differently}}; an adverse effect cannot be {{attributed to one drug}}; a contraindication to one contraindicates {{the whole product}}.

front: How does Schedule Y group fixed-dose combinations for approval?
back: Group 1: one or more ingredients is a new drug (handled like any new drug). Group 2: approved drugs combined for the first time with likely PK or PD interaction (needs data and trials in India). Group 3: marketed FDC with a new ratio or new claim (needs rationale and trials). Group 4: ingredients long used together without expected interaction (no new animal or human data).

front: Which drug class should never be in a fixed-dose combination for internal use?
back: Corticosteroids.

front: When is a fixed-dose combination (FDC) rational? Give examples.
back: When the patient needs every component in the amounts present. Advantages: convenience, adherence and sometimes cost; synergy (sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim, levodopa + carbidopa); additive effect with different side effects (amlodipine + atenolol); one component offsetting another's side effect (thiazide + potassium-sparing diuretic); and preventing monotherapy in TB, HIV and falciparum malaria.

front: Why are fixed-dose combinations accepted in TB, HIV-AIDS and falciparum malaria but criticised in many other settings?
back: In TB, several drugs given together reduce resistance, and one combined tablet means no single drug is taken alone, which aids adherence. Elsewhere the patient may not need every component, and one dose cannot be changed without changing the other, so such a combination should not be prescribed.

front: Essay: Judging the rationality of a given fixed-dose combination (exam approach)

points: Is every component actually needed by the patient, in an appropriate amount?
Is any combination banned in India (listed in KDT8 Appendix-4)?
Do the components act by different mechanisms so that benefits add up while side effects do not?
Does one component counter a side effect of another?
Is the combination truly synergistic?
Antimicrobial combinations should be avoided
Corticosteroids should never be combined with any other drug meant for internal use
Rational or irrational, with reasons and a better alternative

text: Volume of distribution V = {{dose given i.v. / plasma concentration}}; clearance CL = {{rate of elimination / plasma concentration}}; elimination rate constant k = {{CL / V}}; half-life t½ = {{0.693 x V / CL}}.

front: How long does it take to reach steady state on repeated dosing?
back: About 4 to 5 half-lives (plateau principle). A new steady state after a change in dose rate also takes 4 to 5 half-lives. Smaller, more frequent doses reduce the swing between peak and trough.

front: First-order versus zero-order elimination: what is the difference?
back: First order: a constant fraction is removed per unit time and clearance is constant (most drugs). Zero order: a constant amount is removed per unit time because elimination is saturated, so clearance falls as concentration rises. Phenytoin is the book example that moves from first to zero order over the therapeutic range, so levels rise out of proportion to dose.

front: How is an individual or child dose calculated from the adult dose?
back: By body weight: dose = body weight (kg) / 70 x average adult dose. By body surface area: BSA is described as a more accurate basis for dose calculation, mainly for anticancer drugs. Body weight is used for children and for exceptionally obese or lean adults.

front: Worked example: 1000 mg given i.v. gives a plasma concentration of 50 mg/L. What is V?
back: V = dose / concentration = 1000 mg / 50 mg/L = 20 L. It is an apparent volume: the volume that would hold all the drug at the plasma concentration.

front: Formula method: what is the dose equation?
back: D/H x Q = X. D = dose desired, H = dose on hand, Q = quantity or form on hand, X = amount to give.

front: Ratio-proportion method: how do you set up the proportion?
back: Dosage on hand / amount on hand = dosage desired / X (amount to give). Cross-multiply to solve for X.

front: What are the three steps the book teaches for dosage calculation?
back: 1) Convert to the same system and same-size units. 2) Consider whether the dose is reasonable. 3) Calculate with the formula method.

front: IV drip rate in gtt/min: which formula?
back: V (mL) / T (min) x C (gtt/mL) = R (gtt/min). Total mL / total min x 60 min/h gives mL/h.

front: Shortcut from an infusion rate in mL/h to gtt/min?
back: Divide the mL/h rate by the drop factor constant. The result is R in gtt/min.

front: Loading dose: formula and what governs it.
back: Loading dose = target plasma concentration x V / F. It depends only on volume of distribution (and bioavailability), not on clearance or half-life. Used when a long-t½ drug must act quickly (digoxin, amiodarone, chloroquine).

front: Maintenance dose rate: formula and what governs it.
back: Maintenance dose rate = target steady-state concentration x CL / F. It depends on clearance (and so on t½). Doubling the dose rate doubles the average steady-state concentration in first-order kinetics.

front: How is a dose revised from a measured plasma level?
back: For a drug with first-order kinetics: new dose rate = previous dose rate x target Cpss / measured Cpss.

front: Acetaminophen for fever in a child: what does the book give as the dose and limit?
back: 10 to 15 mg/kg by mouth every 4 hours, and not more than 5 doses per day.

front: Amoxicillin for a child: what dose range is printed?
back: Label dose for amoxicillin in children: 20 to 40 mg/kg/day in divided doses every 8 hours. Convert the child weight to kg first, then multiply by the mg/kg/day range, then divide by the number of doses.

front: Worked problem: 60 kg patient; target Cpss 6 mg/L; F 0.7; V 1.4 L/kg; CL 80 mL/h/kg. Loading and daily maintenance dose?
back: V = 1.4 x 60 = 84 L; CL = 0.08 x 60 = 4.8 L/h. Loading dose = 6 x 84 / 0.7 = 720 mg. Maintenance = 6 x 4.8 / 0.7 = about 41 mg/h, or about 987 mg/day.

front: Statistics exercise: which test for which data?
back: Two independent group means: unpaired t test. Same subjects before and after: paired t test. More than two group means: ANOVA. Proportions or counts in categories: chi-square test. Data not normally distributed or ordinal: the non-parametric counterpart.

front: Degrees of freedom for unpaired and paired t tests.
back: Unpaired: n1 + n2 - 2. Paired: n - 1.

front: Standard deviation versus standard error of the mean: how are they related?
back: SD describes the spread of individual observations. SEM describes how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean: SEM = SD / square root of n, so it falls as sample size rises.

front: Worked example: case-control study of smoking and lung cancer. Cases 50 smokers, 10 non-smokers; controls 10 smokers, 50 non-smokers. Odds ratio?
back: Odds of exposure in cases = 50/10 = 5; in controls = 10/50 = 0.2. OR = 5/0.2 = 25 (equivalently ad/bc). OR above 1 means exposure is positively associated with disease; association does not prove causation.

front: Worked example: a drug cuts mortality of a disease from 50% to 25%. What is the NNT?
back: Absolute reduction = 0.50 - 0.25 = 0.25, so NNT = 1 / 0.25 = 4: four patients must be treated to save one life. The same halving of mortality in a rarely fatal disease gives a much larger NNT.

front: Case: a small trial reports drug A lowers blood pressure more than drug B with p = 0.03. How do you interpret this?
back: p = 0.03 is below 0.05, so the null hypothesis of no difference is rejected at the 5% level: the difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone. Two separate groups call for the unpaired t test, and a small trial should be confirmed with a larger sample.

front: Classify: drugs most likely to cause clinically important interactions
text: Drugs with a {{narrow safety margin}} (aminoglycosides, digoxin, lithium); drugs controlling {{closely regulated functions}} (antihypertensives, antidiabetics, anticoagulants); {{highly plasma protein bound}} drugs (NSAIDs, oral anticoagulants, sulfonylureas); drugs with {{saturation kinetics}} (phenytoin, theophylline).

back: Penicillin G or ampicillin mixed with gentamicin; thiopentone with succinylcholine or morphine; heparin with penicillin, gentamicin or hydrocortisone; noradrenaline in sodium bicarbonate solution. Avoid mixing parenteral drugs in one syringe or infusion.

front: Into which three broad mechanisms are drug interactions classified?
back: Pharmaceutical (chemical incompatibility in vitro, outside the body), pharmacokinetic (one drug changes absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion of another) and pharmacodynamic (drugs act on the same or related effect sites). Pharmaceutical ones occur when drugs are mixed in the same syringe, e.g. thiopental and suxamethonium.

front: Drug-interaction exercise: how do you work through a given pair?
back: Name the object and precipitant drug; classify the mechanism (pharmaceutical, pharmacokinetic: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion; or pharmacodynamic); state the clinical result; then manage it: avoid the pair, separate doses, adjust dose, or monitor. A possible interaction does not always forbid joint use.

front: Exercise: tetracycline taken with an antacid or iron. Mechanism and management?
back: Insoluble complexes form in the gut, so tetracycline absorption falls. Separate the two doses in time so they do not meet in the gut.

front: Case: a patient on warfarin is given an NSAID. Explain the interaction.

points: Object drug warfarin (oral anticoagulant, highly protein bound); precipitant an NSAID (aspirin and other NSAIDs are listed as precipitants)
Displacement: warfarin is highly protein bound and aspirin displaces it from plasma-protein binding sites
Pharmacodynamic: NSAID antiplatelet action and gastric mucosal damage add to warfarin-related bleeding
Book advice for this pair: caution in concurrent use
Bleeding risk rises as INR exceeds 4, so monitor INR

front: What do the NMC short exercises include?
back: Interpreting the results of a previous tracing (table exercise) and demonstrating or interpreting drug effects in humans; small-animal experiments are optional, as regulations allow. The exercises are observed and assessed.

front: Which human-volunteer test does the NMC list for drugs affecting psychomotor function?
back: The critical flicker fusion test, done under supervision, along with tests of memory, pain, cardiovascular and respiratory function.

front: What are the 3Rs in animal experimentation, and what fourth R is added?
back: Replacement, reduction and refinement of animal use. Rehabilitation is the added fourth R, a measure for the care of the animals.

front: Who approves experiments on animals in an Indian institution?
back: Experiments on animals are approved by the institutional animal ethics committee (IAEC). CPCSEA controls the IAEC under Government of India guidelines.

front: Tracing exercise: what do you look for in a given kymograph or physiograph record?
back: Baseline, dose cycle and responses; rising responses with dose (graded DRC); a parallel right shift with a competitive antagonist versus a fall in the maximum with a noncompetitive one; and falling responses with repeated doses (tachyphylaxis). Tabulate the responses and plot them against log dose.

front: Computer-assisted learning (CAL) and simulated experiments: why are they used?
back: CAL and simulated experiments can replace some live-animal practicals under the 3Rs (replacement, reduction, refinement). They cannot fully copy real biological variation. The NMC curriculum asks for dose-response and agonist-antagonist experiments on simulations, and says dog, cat and amphibian experiments should be done with computer-assisted simulation models.

sections.h: Right shift with fall in maximum

A flattened curve with suppressed maximum is noncompetitive (unsurmountable) antagonism
Falling response to repeated equal doses in quick succession is tachyphylaxis, not a curve shift

front: What does the NMC teaching-skills assessment in the MD Pharmacology practical exam include?
back: Assessment of teaching or presentation skills, for example presenting an undergraduate lecture, making a question paper, or writing learning objectives; and a discussion on the dissertation.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (practical exam, component d)

front: What does SMART stand for in a learning objective?
back: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. A SMART objective states exactly what the learner will be able to do, how it will be judged, and by when.

front: What are the ABCD parts of a well-written learning objective?
back: Audience (who will learn), Behaviour (the observable action, as an action verb), Condition (under what circumstances or with what resources) and Degree (the standard to be reached).

front: What are the three domains of learning that the NMC groups MD Pharmacology competencies under?
back: Cognitive (knowledge and thinking), affective (attitudes, professionalism, communication) and psychomotor (practical skills). Each competency is predominantly in one domain. The practical exam focuses mainly on psychomotor; the viva on psychomotor and affective.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (subject-specific competencies A, B, C; practical and viva)

front: Classify: levels of the cognitive domain in revised Bloom's taxonomy (lowest to highest)
text: {{Remember}}, {{understand}}, {{apply}}, {{analyse}}, {{evaluate}}, {{create}}.

front: Why should "know" and "understand" be avoided in objectives? Give better verbs.
back: They cannot be observed or measured. Use action verbs that match the level: list or define (recall), explain or classify (understanding), calculate or prescribe (application), compare or interpret (analysis), justify or appraise (evaluation), demonstrate or perform (skills).

front: Write a SMART objective for a class on loading dose.
back: Example: "At the end of this 45-minute session, each second-year MBBS student will be able to calculate the loading dose of a drug from its target plasma concentration, volume of distribution and bioavailability, correctly in at least four of five given problems."

points: Know who the learners are and what they already know (UG curriculum)
Choose a focused topic that fits the time

Method, aid and assessment must each match the objective
Check the objective was met with a short question or task at the end

front: What is set induction in a lesson?
back: The opening of a lesson that gains attention and rapport, using examples or devices and linking to what learners already know.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Microteaching: overview and examination evaluation 2023 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10657622/

front: What is micro-teaching and what is its cycle?
back: A scaled-down lesson: a short session for a small group that practises one teaching skill at a time. Cycle: plan, teach, observe with supervisor feedback, re-plan, re-teach, re-observe.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Microteaching: overview and examination evaluation 2023 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10657622/

front: Which teaching skills are practised in micro-teaching?
back: Lesson planning; set induction; presentation and explanation; stimulus variation; audiovisual aids; reinforcement; probing questions; classroom management; closure.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Microteaching: overview and examination evaluation 2023 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10657622/

front: Why use stimulus variation and reinforcement during a lecture?
back: Attention drifts if delivery stays monotonous, so changing speech pattern, interaction style or movement (stimulus variation) wins it back. Positive verbal and nonverbal cues (reinforcement) encourage learners to keep taking part. Both are micro-teaching skills.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Microteaching: overview and examination evaluation 2023 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10657622/

front: Which teaching-learning methods does the NMC PG guideline expect a pharmacology PG to apply?
back: Classroom lectures, self-directed learning, case-based learning, case discussions, integrated teaching, small group discussions, seminars, journal clubs and research presentations; also computer-assisted learning.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (competency A, Teaching and Assessment 3; teaching-learning methods)

back: Demonstrate, Observe, Assist, Perform: the NMC names it as a method for laboratory and bedside sessions, alongside skill-lab simulations and case-based discussions.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (teaching-learning methods E)

front: How often should journal clubs and seminars run in MD Pharmacology, and how are they assessed (NMC)?
back: Journal club and student seminar: at least once every 1-2 weeks; symposium at least once in 3 months. Journal club presents and critically appraises original research; the presenter is graded by faculty and the grade recorded in the logbook. Seminars are graded by faculty and peers.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (teaching-learning methods B, C, D)

front: Lecture versus small-group teaching: what does the NMC say?
back: Didactic lectures should be used sparingly; the NMC suggests a minimum of 10 lectures a year in a PG department. It recommends a judicious mix of methods, including small group discussions, seminars, journal clubs and case-based learning.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (teaching-learning methods, A. Lectures)

front: What is the place of computer-assisted learning (CAL) in teaching pharmacology?
back: The NMC expects PGs to know the utility of computer-assisted learning and use it to promote learning of pharmacology. Amphibian, dog and cat experiments should be done with computer-assisted simulation models or facilities. Alternatives to animal use follow the 3Rs (replacement, reduction, refinement).
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (competency A, Teaching and Assessment 5; animal experiments note)

front: How do you choose an audiovisual aid for a lesson?
back: Match it to the objective, group size, room and time: chalkboard or whiteboard for building a diagram step by step; flip chart for small groups; slides for images, graphs and large groups; video or simulation for processes and experiments; models and real dosage forms for identification. The aid should support, not replace, the teacher.

points: One idea per slide, a short headline
Few lines and few words per line; key words, not paragraphs
Large readable font, strong contrast, simple consistent background
Diagrams and graphs rather than tables of numbers
Do not read the slides aloud; face the audience
Allow time per slide; end with a summary slide

refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Microteaching: overview and examination evaluation 2023 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10657622/

front: Case: you must teach second-year students to calculate a loading dose. Which method and aid, and why not a plain lecture?
back: Calculation is a psychomotor-type skill that needs practice, so use a short demonstration followed by worked problems in small groups (DOAP-style: demonstrate, observe, assist, perform), with the board for stepwise working. A lecture alone is passive and the NMC asks for it to be used sparingly. Finish with a quick check problem to confirm the objective was met.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (teaching-learning methods A and E)

back: Formative: during training, to give feedback and improve learning (in MD Pharmacology, internal assessment covering all domains, with quarterly review). Summative: at the end, to certify competence (the final theory, practical and viva).
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (assessment: formative and summative)

front: Who conducts formative and summative assessment in PG medical exams, and what does each include?
back: The medical college conducts formative assessment and the university conducts summative assessment; both have theory, clinical or practical and viva voce components.

front: Which theory paper of the MD Pharmacology summative exam covers education?
back: Paper III: clinical pharmacology, experimentation, research, biostatistics and education.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (summative examination, theory papers)

front: What must MD Pharmacology internal assessment cover, and how often?
back: Theory and practical or clinical exams, held frequently, covering all domains of learning, professionalism and communication skills, with feedback to improve learning; quarterly assessment is included.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (formative assessment, quarterly)

front: Which domains should the viva voce test in the MD Pharmacology summative exam?
back: Psychomotor and affective domains, testing overall knowledge of the subject. Each examiner conducts the viva separately.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (summative examination, part 3)

front: How many examiners assess an MD Pharmacology thesis, and when must it be submitted?
back: At least three: one internal and two external, none of whom examine the theory or clinical exams. The thesis is submitted at least six months before the theory and clinical or practical examinations.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (summative examination, part 1: thesis)

front: How much of the MD practical and viva marks is given for the dissertation?
back: 5% of the practical or clinical and viva total (20 of 400 marks), counted within the practical marks. An external examiner from outside the state assesses the dissertation and its viva.

front: What forms may the PG theory examination take?
back: Descriptive (long or short answer) questions, multiple-choice questions, or a mix of both.

front: What does the NMC list among psychomotor skills for teaching and assessment material?
back: Demonstrating skills to prepare material for teaching-learning and assessment.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (psychomotor competencies, mandatory 9)

front: How many theory papers does the MD Pharmacology summative exam have, and what are Papers I and IV?
back: Four theory papers. Paper I is basic sciences as applied to pharmacology; Paper IV is recent advances. The theory exam is held well in advance of the clinical and practical exam.
refs: NMC MD Pharmacology 2022 curriculum (summative examination, theory papers)

front: What qualities make an assessment good?
back: Validity (measures what it is meant to measure), reliability (consistent results), objectivity (uniform marking) and practicability (feasible within time and resources).
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Standardization and validation of OSPE in pharmacology 2017 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5754933/

front: Short note: Setting a question paper

points: Table mapping topics against domains or levels, with marks for each, based on the objectives and their importance
Long essay, short notes and objective items in set proportions

Clear and unambiguous, with action verbs and marks shown
Avoid "write all you know"
Model answer and marking scheme prepared in advance
Review by a colleague before use

front: Parts of a single-best-answer MCQ, and common writing faults.
back: Stem (case or question), lead-in, the key (correct answer) and distractors (plausible wrong options). Faults: clues in grammar or length, "all of the above" or "none of the above", negative stems, implausible distractors, and testing trivia.

front: How can essay questions be made more objective?
back: Use structured or modified essay questions with defined parts and marks, a clear task, and a model answer with a key; use more short-answer questions to sample more content; mark question by question rather than paper by paper.
refs: WEB Cureus Structured and conventional viva voce in pharmacology teaching 2026 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13279708/ (predefined scoring and standard questions part only)

front: What is the main weakness of a traditional viva, and what does a structured viva add?
back: A traditional viva is criticised for subjectivity, low reliability, inter-examiner variability and bias. A structured viva uses standard questions, a predefined scoring scheme and uniform administration, improving objectivity and reliability.
refs: WEB Cureus Structured and conventional viva voce in pharmacology teaching 2026 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13279708/

Validity, reliability, objectivity, practicability
Blueprint links the paper to objectives, improving validity
Match tool to domain: knowledge by written tests, skills by practical stations, attitudes by observation and feedback

back: Timely and frequent (the NMC stresses this so students can improve); specific; based on observed behaviour, not personality; descriptive rather than judgemental; balanced between strengths and areas to improve; limited to a few points; and ending with an action plan.
